Chapter 0 · Start hereChapter 0 · Yahan se shuru karo

Backend from zeroBackend, bilkul zero se

Before any interview topic makes sense you need the map: what a backend is, how one request travels, where data lives, who does the work, and why speed and scale change everything. This chapter builds that map from nothing.

Koi bhi interview topic tab samajh aata hai jab tumhare paas poora map ho: backend kya hota hai, ek request kaise travel karti hai, data kahan rehta hai, kaam kaun karta hai, aur speed aur scale se sab kuch kyun badal jaata hai. Yeh chapter woh map bilkul zero se banata hai.

Level 0 The story: a restaurantKahani: ek restaurant

Imagine you walk into a restaurant. You sit down, read the menu and tell the waiter "one masala dosa, please". You never see the kitchen. Inside, a cook takes your order, walks to the store room for batter and potatoes, cooks, and hands the plate back to the waiter. A few minutes later the dosa is on your table. You only ever talked to the waiter, yet a whole hidden system worked for you.

Every software product works exactly like this.

  • The menu and the waiter are the frontend. This is the part you see and touch: the website in your browser or the app on your phone. Its job is to show things nicely and carry your wishes to the kitchen.
  • The kitchen is the backend. These are programs running on computers you never see. They receive your order, check the rules ("is this person logged in?", "is this item in stock?"), do the actual work, and send back a result.
  • The store room is the database. This is where everything that must be remembered is kept: users, orders, payments, or the vehicles in a car dealer's inventory. The cook does not carry ingredients around in their hands all day; they fetch them from the store room when needed.

When a company says "backend engineer", they mean the person who designs and runs the kitchen: the logic, the data, and, most importantly, making sure the kitchen keeps working when a thousand customers walk in at the same moment. Every one of the 13 interview topics in this guide is about some part of that kitchen.

Client and server. You will hear these two words in every chapter. A client is whoever asks for something. A server is whoever answers. The Swiggy app on your phone is a client; the computer at Swiggy that answers "here are the restaurants near you" is a server. The same machine can play both roles: when the backend program asks the database for data, the backend is the client and the database is the server. So "client" and "server" are roles in a conversation, not types of machines.

What a server physically is. A server is not magic. It is a computer, with a CPU (the brain that runs instructions), RAM (short-term memory), a disk (long-term storage) and a network card, much like your laptop. The differences are where it sits and what it does: it lives in a data center, a large building full of such computers with reliable power, cooling and very fast internet, and it runs one important program 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, waiting for requests. Today most companies do not buy these machines; they rent them from cloud providers such as AWS, Google Cloud or Azure. Often they rent a virtual machine (one physical computer sliced into several pretend computers) or run containers (you will meet those in Topic 11). When someone says "the server is down", they mean that program has stopped answering: the machine crashed, the program crashed, or the network path to it broke.

Remember: Frontend = what you see. Backend = the logic running on servers. Database = the memory that survives. A client asks, a server answers.

Socho tum ek restaurant mein jaate ho. Baith ke menu padhte ho aur waiter ko bolte ho "ek masala dosa, please". Kitchen tumhe kabhi dikhta hi nahi. Andar ek cook tumhara order leta hai, store room se batter aur aloo laata hai, dosa banata hai, aur plate waiter ko de deta hai. Kuch minute mein dosa tumhari table pe. Tumne sirf waiter se baat ki, lekin peeche ek poora chhupa hua system tumhare liye kaam kar raha tha.

Har software product bilkul aise hi kaam karta hai.

  • Menu aur waiter = frontend. Yeh woh hissa hai jo tum dekhte aur touch karte ho: browser mein website ya phone pe app. Iska kaam hai cheezein achhe se dikhana aur tumhari demand kitchen tak pahunchana.
  • Kitchen = backend. Yeh programs hain jo aise computers pe chalte hain jo tumhe kabhi dikhte nahi. Yeh tumhara order lete hain, rules check karte hain ("kya yeh banda logged in hai?", "kya yeh item stock mein hai?"), asli kaam karte hain, aur result wapas bhejte hain.
  • Store room = database. Yahan woh sab rakha jaata hai jo yaad rakhna zaroori hai: users, orders, payments, ya kisi car dealer ki inventory ki gaadiyan. Cook poore din ingredients haath mein lekar nahi ghoomta; jab zaroorat ho tab store room se laata hai.

Jab koi company "backend engineer" bolti hai, toh uska matlab hai woh insaan jo kitchen design karta hai aur chalata hai: logic, data, aur sabse important, yeh ensure karna ki jab ek hi pal mein hazaar customers aa jaayein tab bhi kitchen chalta rahe. Is guide ke saare 13 interview topics usi kitchen ke kisi na kisi hisse ke baare mein hain.

Client aur server. Yeh do words tum har chapter mein sunoge. Client woh hai jo kuch maangta hai. Server woh hai jo jawab deta hai. Tumhare phone ka Swiggy app client hai; Swiggy ka woh computer jo bolta hai "yeh rahe tumhare paas ke restaurants", woh server hai. Ek hi machine dono role nibha sakti hai: jab backend program database se data maangta hai, tab backend client hai aur database server. Matlab "client" aur "server" ek baatcheet ke roles hain, machine ke types nahi.

Server physically hota kya hai. Server koi jaadu nahi hai. Yeh ek computer hi hai, jismein CPU (dimaag jo instructions chalata hai), RAM (short-term memory), disk (long-term storage) aur network card hota hai, bilkul tumhare laptop jaisa. Farak bas itna hai ki yeh kahan rakha hai aur kya karta hai: yeh ek data center mein rehta hai, ek bada building jo aise computers se bhara hota hai, jahan reliable bijli, cooling aur bahut fast internet hota hai. Aur yeh ek important program 24 ghante, 7 din chalata rehta hai, requests ka wait karte hue. Aajkal zyada companies yeh machines khareedti nahi; cloud providers jaise AWS, Google Cloud ya Azure se kiraye pe leti hain. Aksar woh ek virtual machine leti hain (ek physical computer ko kaat ke kai nakli computers bana diye) ya containers chalati hain (inse Topic 11 mein miloge). Jab koi bole "server down hai", matlab woh program jawab dena band kar chuka hai: machine crash hui, program crash hua, ya uss tak ka network toot gaya.

Yaad rakho: Frontend = jo dikhta hai. Backend = servers pe chalne wala logic. Database = woh memory jo bachi rehti hai. Client maangta hai, server jawab deta hai.

Level 1 The journey of one requestEk request ka safar

Let us follow one order from your phone to the kitchen and back. You open a shopping app and tap "My order #42". Here is everything that happens, in order.

  1. The URL. The app wants https://api.shop.com/orders/42. A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is an address with parts: https:// is the protocol, meaning how to talk (the "s" means the conversation is encrypted); api.shop.com is the domain, meaning which building; /orders/42 is the path, meaning which room inside the building. Anything after a ?, like ?status=paid, is the query string: extra filters.
  2. DNS. Computers find each other by numbers called IP addresses, like 203.0.113.10, not by names. DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phone contacts list: you give it a name, it gives you the number. The answer is remembered (cached) for a while, so this lookup does not happen on every request.
  3. The connection. The phone opens a connection to that IP address. The underlying pipe is called TCP, which makes sure bytes arrive complete and in order. With HTTPS, a short TLS "handshake" adds encryption on top so nobody in between can read the conversation.
  4. The HTTP request. HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the language client and server speak. A request has four parts:
    • Method, the verb: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH change part of something, DELETE remove.
    • Path, the thing: /orders/42.
    • Headers, notes written on the envelope as key-value pairs: Host (which site), Authorization (who I am, usually a token), Content-Type (the format of the body).
    • Body, optional data sent along, usually JSON. A GET normally has no body; a POST usually does.
  5. The server does the work. A program on the server receives the request, checks the token, asks the database for order 42, and builds an answer.
  6. The HTTP response. It comes back with a status code (a three-digit number summarising the outcome), headers, and a body with the data.

Chalo ek order ko tumhare phone se kitchen tak aur wapas follow karte hain. Tum ek shopping app kholte ho aur "My order #42" pe tap karte ho. Yeh raha sab kuch jo hota hai, order mein.

  1. URL. App ko chahiye https://api.shop.com/orders/42. URL (Uniform Resource Locator) ek address hai jiske parts hote hain: https:// protocol hai, yaani baat kaise karni hai ("s" ka matlab baatcheet encrypted hai); api.shop.com domain hai, yaani kaunsi building; /orders/42 path hai, yaani building ke andar kaunsa kamra. ? ke baad jo bhi ho, jaise ?status=paid, woh query string hai: extra filters.
  2. DNS. Computers ek doosre ko naam se nahi, numbers se dhoondhte hain jinhe IP address kehte hain, jaise 203.0.113.10. DNS (Domain Name System) internet ki phone contacts list hai: tum naam do, woh number de deta hai. Jawab kuch der ke liye yaad (cache) rakha jaata hai, isliye yeh lookup har request pe nahi hota.
  3. Connection. Phone us IP address se connection kholta hai. Neeche wali pipe ko TCP kehte hain, jo ensure karti hai ki bytes poore aur sahi order mein pahunchein. HTTPS mein ek chhota TLS "handshake" upar se encryption laga deta hai taaki beech mein koi baatcheet padh na sake.
  4. HTTP request. HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) woh bhasha hai jo client aur server bolte hain. Request ke chaar parts hote hain:
    • Method, yaani verb: GET padhna, POST naya banana, PUT poora replace karna, PATCH kisi cheez ka ek hissa badalna, DELETE hatana.
    • Path, yaani kaunsi cheez: /orders/42.
    • Headers, envelope ke upar likhe notes, key-value pairs mein: Host (kaunsi site), Authorization (main kaun hoon, aksar ek token), Content-Type (body ka format).
    • Body, saath mein bheja gaya optional data, aksar JSON. GET mein normally body nahi hoti; POST mein aksar hoti hai.
  5. Server kaam karta hai. Server pe ek program request leta hai, token check karta hai, database se order 42 maangta hai, aur jawab banata hai.
  6. HTTP response. Jawab wapas aata hai ek status code ke saath (teen digit ka number jo result ka summary hai), headers, aur ek body jismein data hota hai.
# What the phone actually sends
GET /orders/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.shop.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9...
Accept: application/json

# What the server sends back
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "id": 42,
  "status": "paid",
  "items": [
    { "name": "Masala Dosa", "qty": 2, "price": 120 }
  ],
  "total": 240,
  "customer": { "id": 7, "name": "Asha" }
}
# Creating something new: POST with a JSON body
POST /orders HTTP/1.1
Host: api.shop.com
Content-Type: application/json

{ "itemId": 15, "qty": 2 }

# Answer: 201 Created, plus the new order in the body
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 43, "status": "pending" }

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a plain-text format for data. Curly braces { } hold an object, a set of "key": value pairs. Square brackets [ ] hold a list. A value can be text in double quotes, a number, true/false, null (nothing), or another object or list nested inside. Humans can read it and every programming language can parse it, which is why almost every API speaks JSON.

Status codes come in families. You only need the families now; Topic 08 goes deep.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) data likhne ka ek plain-text format hai. Curly braces { } ke andar ek object hota hai, yaani "key": value pairs ka set. Square brackets [ ] ke andar ek list hoti hai. Value ho sakti hai double quotes mein text, number, true/false, null (kuch nahi), ya andar nested ek aur object ya list. Insaan bhi padh sakta hai aur har programming language ise parse kar sakti hai, isliye lagbhag har API JSON bolti hai.

Status codes families mein aate hain. Abhi sirf families samajh lo; Topic 08 mein deep jaayenge.

FamilyFamilyMeaningMatlabCommon examplesCommon examples
2xxIt workedKaam ho gaya200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content200 OK, 201 Created (naya bana), 204 No Content (kaam hua, body khaali)
3xxLook somewhere elseKahin aur dekho301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified (tumhari copy abhi bhi sahi hai)
4xxThe client made a mistakeGalti client ki hai400 Bad Request, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests400 Bad Request, 401 login nahi kiya, 403 allowed nahi ho, 404 mila nahi, 429 bahut zyada requests
5xxThe server failedGalti server ki hai500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable (abhi available nahi)

API and endpoint. An API (Application Programming Interface) is a menu that one program offers to other programs: "here is what you can ask me, and in what format". An endpoint is one item on that menu: a method plus a path, like GET /orders/42 or POST /orders. A car-dealership example: an inventory API might offer GET /vehicles/{vin} to look up one car by its VIN (Vehicle Identification Number, the 17-character ID unique to every car). The frontend team reads the API "menu" and builds screens on top of it; the backend team promises the menu will keep working. That promise is called the API contract.

API aur endpoint. API (Application Programming Interface) ek menu hai jo ek program doosre programs ko deta hai: "yeh sab tum mujhse maang sakte ho, aur is format mein". Endpoint us menu ka ek item hai: ek method plus ek path, jaise GET /orders/42 ya POST /orders. Car dealership ka example: ek inventory API GET /vehicles/{vin} de sakti hai jisse ek gaadi uske VIN se dhoondhi jaaye (VIN = Vehicle Identification Number, 17 characters ki ID jo har gaadi ki alag hoti hai). Frontend team API ka "menu" padh ke uske upar screens banati hai; backend team promise karti hai ki menu chalta rahega. Isi promise ko API ka contract kehte hain.

The bigger picture. In a real company the path has more stops than the simple picture above. Requests first hit a load balancer that spreads them across several copies of the API server; the servers check a fast cache (Redis) before going to the database (Postgres); and slow jobs, like sending an email or resizing photos, are dropped into a message queue for a separate worker program to handle later. Do not worry about these words yet; each one is explained below and gets its own chapter. Keep this big diagram in mind as the "city map" of the whole guide.

Badi picture. Asli company mein raasta upar wali simple picture se lamba hota hai. Requests pehle ek load balancer pe aati hain jo unhe API server ki kai copies mein baant deta hai; servers database (Postgres) tak jaane se pehle ek fast cache (Redis) check karte hain; aur slow kaam, jaise email bhejna ya photos resize karna, ek message queue mein daal diye jaate hain taaki ek alag worker program baad mein unhe kare. Abhi in words ki tension mat lo; har ek neeche samjhaya gaya hai aur har ek ka apna chapter hai. Is bade diagram ko poori guide ka "city map" samjho.

Level 2 Where data lives: databases, and why RAM beats diskData kahan rehta hai: database, aur RAM disk se tez kyun hai

A database is a program whose whole job is to store data safely and find it quickly. The most common kind in interviews is the relational database, such as PostgreSQL ("Postgres") or MySQL. It stores data in tables.

Think of a table as an Excel sheet with strict rules:

  • A column is one property, with a fixed type: name is text, amount is a number.
  • A row is one record: one user, one order, one vehicle.
  • A primary key is a column whose value is unique for every row and never empty, usually id. It is like an Aadhaar number for the row: two rows can have the same name, never the same id.
  • A foreign key is a column in one table that points at the primary key of another table. orders.user_id points at users.id, which is how we know order 101 belongs to Asha. This is the "relational" in relational database.

Database ek program hai jiska poora kaam hai data ko safely store karna aur jaldi dhoondhna. Interviews mein sabse common type hai relational database, jaise PostgreSQL ("Postgres") ya MySQL. Yeh data ko tables mein rakhta hai.

Table ko ek Excel sheet samjho, bas strict rules ke saath:

  • Column ek property hai, fixed type ke saath: name text hai, amount number hai.
  • Row ek record hai: ek user, ek order, ek gaadi.
  • Primary key woh column hai jiski value har row ke liye unique hoti hai aur kabhi khaali nahi hoti, aksar id. Yeh row ka Aadhaar number jaisa hai: do rows ka naam same ho sakta hai, id kabhi same nahi.
  • Foreign key ek table ka woh column hai jo doosre table ki primary key ki taraf point karta hai. orders.user_id point karta hai users.id ki taraf, isi se pata chalta hai ki order 101 Asha ka hai. Relational database mein "relational" yahi hai.

SQL (Structured Query Language, said "sequel" or "S-Q-L") is how you talk to a relational database. Four verbs cover almost everything, often called CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete.

SQL (Structured Query Language, bolte hain "sequel" ya "S-Q-L") relational database se baat karne ki bhasha hai. Chaar verbs se lagbhag sab ho jaata hai, jise CRUD kehte hain: Create, Read, Update, Delete.

-- Define the tables once
CREATE TABLE users (
  id    SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,   -- auto-numbered 1, 2, 3...
  name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  city  TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id       SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id  INT REFERENCES users(id),   -- foreign key
  item     TEXT,
  amount   INT
);

-- Create: add a row
INSERT INTO users (name, city) VALUES ('Asha', 'Pune');

-- Read: fetch rows that match a condition
SELECT name, city FROM users WHERE id = 1;
SELECT item, amount FROM orders WHERE user_id = 1 AND amount > 20;

-- Update: change existing rows
UPDATE users SET city = 'Mumbai' WHERE id = 1;

-- Delete: remove rows
DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 103;

-- JOIN: combine two tables using the foreign key
SELECT u.name, o.item, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id;

Trap: an UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause changes every row in the table. Real outages have started this way.

Two more words you will need. A transaction is a group of SQL statements that succeed or fail together: move 500 rupees from Asha to Ravi means one UPDATE subtracting and one adding, and you never want just one of them to happen (Topic 02). An index is a sorted lookup structure, like the index at the back of a textbook, that lets the database jump to matching rows instead of reading the whole table (Topic 01). Not every database uses tables: NoSQL databases store data as documents (MongoDB), key-value pairs (Redis) or other shapes; Topic 09 compares them.

RAM versus disk: the fact behind half the guide. A computer has two kinds of storage.

  • RAM (memory) is extremely fast but temporary. When the power goes or the program restarts, it is wiped. It is also small and expensive per gigabyte.
  • Disk (SSD or the older spinning hard disk, HDD) is much slower but permanent, large and cheap.

A database keeps its data on disk so it survives crashes, and keeps the most-used parts copied in RAM for speed. The gap between the two is huge. The figures below are rough, widely quoted approximations that vary with hardware, but the ladder shape is what matters: each step down is many times slower.

Trap: bina WHERE ke UPDATE ya DELETE table ki har row badal deta hai. Asli outages aise shuru hue hain.

Do aur words chahiye honge. Transaction SQL statements ka ek group hai jo saath mein succeed ya fail hote hain: Asha se Ravi ko 500 rupaye bhejne ka matlab hai ek UPDATE jo minus kare aur ek jo plus kare, aur tum kabhi nahi chahoge ki sirf ek hi ho (Topic 02). Index ek sorted lookup structure hai, textbook ke peeche wale index jaisa, jisse database seedha matching rows pe jump kar sakta hai, poora table padhne ki bajaye (Topic 01). Har database tables use nahi karta: NoSQL databases data ko documents (MongoDB), key-value pairs (Redis) ya doosre shapes mein rakhte hain; Topic 09 mein compare karenge.

RAM vs disk: woh fact jispe aadhi guide tiki hai. Computer mein do tarah ki storage hoti hai.

  • RAM (memory) bahut hi fast hai lekin temporary. Bijli gayi ya program restart hua, sab saaf. Yeh chhoti bhi hai aur per gigabyte mehengi bhi.
  • Disk (SSD, ya purani ghoomne wali hard disk, HDD) kaafi slow hai lekin permanent, badi aur sasti.

Database apna data disk pe rakhta hai taaki crash ke baad bhi bacha rahe, aur sabse zyada use hone wale hisse ki copy RAM mein rakhta hai speed ke liye. Dono ke beech ka gap bahut bada hai. Neeche ke figures rough, bahut jagah quote kiye jaane wale approximations hain jo hardware ke hisaab se badalte hain, lekin ladder ka shape important hai: har neeche wala step kai guna slow hai.

Why this matters for everything later: caching (Topic 04) means keeping a copy of frequently read data in RAM, for example in Redis, so we skip slow trips to disk and to the database. Indexing (Topic 01) means reducing how many disk pages the database has to read. Durability (Topic 02) means a committed change has been safely written to disk, because anything only in RAM can vanish.

Remember: RAM is fast but forgets; disk is slow but remembers. Most backend performance work is about avoiding unnecessary trips to slow places.

Aage sab ke liye yeh kyun important hai: caching (Topic 04) ka matlab hai baar-baar padhe jaane wale data ki copy RAM mein rakhna, jaise Redis mein, taaki disk aur database tak ke slow chakkar bach jaayein. Indexing (Topic 01) ka matlab hai database ko kam disk pages padhne padein. Durability (Topic 02) ka matlab hai committed change safely disk pe likh diya gaya, kyunki jo sirf RAM mein hai woh gaayab ho sakta hai.

Yaad rakho: RAM fast hai par bhool jaati hai; disk slow hai par yaad rakhti hai. Backend performance ka zyada kaam slow jagahon ke faaltu chakkar bachane ke baare mein hai.

Level 3 Who does the work: processes, threads, Node.js and RedisKaam kaun karta hai: process, thread, Node.js aur Redis

Back to the kitchen. A recipe book on the shelf does nothing by itself; someone has to cook from it. Computers are the same.

  • A program is the recipe: code saved in a file on disk.
  • A process is the program actually running. The operating system (OS: Linux, Windows, macOS, the manager of the computer) gives each process its own private memory. It is like one kitchen with a cook actually cooking. Two processes do not share memory by default, so one crashing usually does not corrupt the other.
  • A thread is a worker inside a process. One process can have many threads, and they all share the same memory, like several cooks in one kitchen sharing the same counter. Sharing is fast, but dangerous: if two cooks grab the same bowl at the same moment, you get a mess. In software that mess is a race condition (Topic 03).
  • A CPU core is one real pair of hands that can execute instructions. An 8-core CPU can truly do 8 things at the very same instant. If there are more threads than cores, the OS switches between them thousands of times a second, so they look simultaneous. Handling many tasks by interleaving them is concurrency; truly running them at the same instant on different cores is parallelism.

Node.js is a program that runs JavaScript outside the browser, on servers. It is built on V8, the JavaScript engine from Google Chrome. Its special trick: your JavaScript runs on one main thread using an event loop. When your code asks the database for something, Node does not stand idle waiting. It hands the waiting to the operating system (and, for some tasks, a small pool of background threads), moves on to the next request, and comes back when the answer arrives. Picture one very efficient waiter who takes an order to the kitchen and serves other tables meanwhile, instead of standing at the kitchen door. This is excellent for I/O-heavy work (I/O = input/output: waiting on databases, networks, files). It is terrible if one request does heavy CPU calculation, because while that one thing runs, nobody else is served (Topic 03).

Wapas kitchen pe. Shelf pe rakhi recipe book khud kuch nahi karti; kisi ko usse khaana banana padta hai. Computers bhi aise hi hain.

  • Program recipe hai: disk pe ek file mein saved code.
  • Process woh program hai jo sach mein chal raha hai. Operating system (OS: Linux, Windows, macOS, yaani computer ka manager) har process ko apni private memory deta hai. Yeh ek kitchen jaisa hai jismein ek cook sach mein khaana bana raha hai. Do processes by default memory share nahi karte, isliye ek crash ho toh aam taur pe doosra kharab nahi hota.
  • Thread ek process ke andar ka worker hai. Ek process mein kai threads ho sakte hain, aur sab same memory share karte hain, jaise ek kitchen mein kai cooks ek hi counter share kar rahe hon. Sharing fast hai, lekin khatarnaak: agar do cooks ek hi pal mein same bowl uthayein, toh gadbad. Software mein is gadbad ko race condition kehte hain (Topic 03).
  • CPU core ek asli jodi haath hai jo instructions chala sakta hai. 8-core CPU sach mein ek hi pal mein 8 kaam kar sakta hai. Agar threads cores se zyada hain, toh OS unke beech ek second mein hazaaron baar switch karta hai, isliye woh ek saath chalte hue dikhte hain. Kai kaamon ko beech-beech mein switch karke sambhalna concurrency hai; sach mein ek hi pal mein alag cores pe chalana parallelism hai.

Node.js ek program hai jo JavaScript ko browser ke bahar, servers pe chalata hai. Yeh V8 pe bana hai, jo Google Chrome ka JavaScript engine hai. Iski khaas trick: tumhara JavaScript ek main thread pe chalta hai, ek event loop ke saath. Jab tumhara code database se kuch maangta hai, Node khaali khada wait nahi karta. Woh waiting ko operating system ko de deta hai (aur kuch kaamon ke liye background threads ke ek chhote pool ko), agli request pe chala jaata hai, aur jab jawab aata hai tab wapas aata hai. Socho ek bahut efficient waiter jo order kitchen mein de ke tab tak doosri tables serve karta hai, kitchen ke darwaze pe khada nahi rehta. Yeh I/O-heavy kaam ke liye zabardast hai (I/O = input/output: database, network, files ka wait). Lekin agar ek request bhaari CPU calculation kare toh bahut bura, kyunki jab tak woh ek kaam chal raha hai, kisi aur ko serve nahi kiya jaata (Topic 03).

// A tiny Node.js API server (using the popular Express library)
const express = require('express');
const app = express();

// Endpoint: GET /orders/:id   (":id" means "any value here")
app.get('/orders/:id', async (req, res) => {
  // "db" stands for a database client library, e.g. "pg" for Postgres.
  // $1 is a placeholder: the library safely inserts the value (prevents SQL injection).
  const result = await db.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]);

  if (result.rows.length === 0) {
    return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Order not found' });
  }
  res.status(200).json(result.rows[0]);
});

app.listen(3000); // wait for requests on port 3000, forever

Reading it line by line: app.get(...) registers an endpoint. await means "pause this request until the database answers, but let the event loop serve others meanwhile". res.status(404).json(...) sends a status code and a JSON body. A port is a door number on the machine: one server can run many programs, each listening at its own port (web traffic usually arrives at 80 for HTTP or 443 for HTTPS; apps often listen on 3000 or 8080 behind a proxy). The $1 placeholder matters: gluing user input directly into SQL text lets an attacker inject their own SQL.

Redis is an in-memory key-value store. Think of a giant dictionary living in RAM on its own server: you store a value under a key and read it back by that key. No tables, no SQL, no joins. Because the data sits in RAM and there is no query planning, a typical lookup takes well under a millisecond inside a data center.

Line by line padho: app.get(...) ek endpoint register karta hai. await ka matlab hai "is request ko tab tak roko jab tak database jawab na de, lekin tab tak event loop ko doosron ko serve karne do". res.status(404).json(...) ek status code aur JSON body bhejta hai. Port machine pe ek darwaze ka number hai: ek server pe kai programs chal sakte hain, har ek apne port pe sun raha hota hai (web traffic aam taur pe HTTP ke liye 80 ya HTTPS ke liye 443 pe aata hai; apps aksar kisi proxy ke peeche 3000 ya 8080 pe sunte hain). $1 placeholder important hai: user ka input seedha SQL text mein chipka diya toh attacker apna SQL inject kar sakta hai.

Redis ek in-memory key-value store hai. Socho ek bahut bada dictionary jo apne server pe RAM mein rehta hai: tum ek key ke neeche value rakhte ho aur usi key se wapas padhte ho. Na tables, na SQL, na joins. Kyunki data RAM mein hai aur query planning nahi hoti, data center ke andar ek normal lookup ek millisecond se bhi kaafi kam leta hai.

# Redis commands (typed in redis-cli). "→" shows the reply.
SET user:7:name "Asha"          → OK
GET user:7:name                 → "Asha"
SET otp:98765 "4821" EX 300     → OK        # auto-delete after 300 seconds (a TTL)
TTL otp:98765                   → 297       # seconds left before it expires
INCR page:views                 → 1
INCR page:views                 → 2         # atomic +1, safe even with many clients
SET lock:job:42 "worker-1" NX EX 30  → OK   # NX = only set if the key does not exist yet
DEL user:7:name                 → 1         # number of keys deleted

Two properties make Redis show up in almost every chapter. First, speed, because of RAM. Second, Redis executes commands one at a time, so a single command like INCR is atomic: it can never be interrupted halfway by another client. That is why it is used for caches (Topic 04), counters and rate limits (Topic 03), idempotency keys (Topic 05), sessions and token blocklists (Topic 10), and locks (Topics 03 and 07). The trade-off: RAM is limited and expensive, and Redis saving to disk is optional and weaker than a real database by default. So Redis usually holds copies or short-lived data, not the only copy of something important like a payment.

Remember: Process = running program with its own memory. Thread = worker inside it sharing memory. Node.js = one main thread plus an event loop, great at waiting, bad at heavy math. Redis = fast shared dictionary in RAM.

Do properties ki wajah se Redis lagbhag har chapter mein aata hai. Pehli, speed, RAM ki wajah se. Doosri, Redis commands ko ek-ek karke chalata hai, isliye INCR jaisa ek command atomic hota hai: koi doosra client usse beech mein kabhi interrupt nahi kar sakta. Isiliye yeh use hota hai caches (Topic 04), counters aur rate limits (Topic 03), idempotency keys (Topic 05), sessions aur token blocklists (Topic 10), aur locks (Topics 03 aur 07) ke liye. Trade-off: RAM limited aur mehengi hai, aur Redis ka disk pe save karna optional hai aur by default ek asli database se kamzor. Isliye Redis aam taur pe copies ya kam time ke liye data rakhta hai, kisi important cheez ki ekmaatra copy nahi, jaise payment.

Yaad rakho: Process = chalta hua program apni memory ke saath. Thread = uske andar ka worker jo memory share karta hai. Node.js = ek main thread plus event loop, wait karne mein zabardast, bhaari calculation mein bura. Redis = RAM mein ek fast shared dictionary.

Level 4 How fast is fast: latency and Big-OFast kitna fast: latency aur Big-O

Latency is the time one request takes from start to answer, usually measured in milliseconds (1 ms = one thousandth of a second). Throughput is how many requests per second the system handles. They are different things: a highway can carry thousands of cars an hour (high throughput) while each car still takes an hour to reach the city (latency). You can raise throughput by adding more lanes (more servers), but that does not make any single car faster.

Engineers rarely trust the average latency, because averages hide unhappy users. They use percentiles: p50 (the median, half of requests are faster than this), p95, and p99 (99% of requests are faster; the slowest 1% are worse). If p50 is 80 ms but p99 is 3 seconds, one in a hundred users is having a terrible time, and heavy users who make many requests will hit that slow tail often. Topic 13 returns to this.

Big-O is a way to describe how the amount of work grows as the data grows. It is not an exact time; it is the shape of the growth. The classic picture is a phone book with a million names, and you want one person's number.

  • O(1), constant. Someone tells you the exact page and line. The effort is the same whether the book has a thousand names or a billion. A hash map lookup, or Redis GET by key, works like this.
  • O(log n), logarithmic. Open the book in the middle; your name comes later alphabetically, so throw away the first half; open the middle of what is left; repeat. Each step discards half. A million names needs about 20 steps; a billion only about 30. This is how a B-tree index finds a row (Topic 01).
  • O(n), linear. Start at page one and read every name until you find it. A million names means up to a million checks. In a database this is the dreaded full table scan.
  • O(n²), quadratic. For every name, go through all the names again, for example comparing every pair. It explodes quickly and usually signals a nested loop that should not exist.

Latency woh time hai jo ek request start se jawab tak leti hai, aam taur pe milliseconds mein naapa jaata hai (1 ms = second ka hazaarwan hissa). Throughput matlab system ek second mein kitni requests sambhalta hai. Dono alag cheezein hain: ek highway ek ghante mein hazaaron gaadiyan le ja sakta hai (high throughput), phir bhi har gaadi ko shehar pahunchne mein ek ghanta lagta hai (latency). Zyada lanes (zyada servers) jodke throughput badha sakte ho, lekin isse koi ek gaadi fast nahi ho jaati.

Engineers average latency pe kam bharosa karte hain, kyunki average dukhi users ko chhupa deta hai. Woh percentiles use karte hain: p50 (median, aadhi requests isse fast hain), p95, aur p99 (99% requests isse fast hain; sabse slow 1% isse bhi buri hain). Agar p50 80 ms hai lekin p99 3 second, toh har sau mein se ek user ka bahut bura haal hai, aur jo heavy users bahut requests karte hain woh is slow tail ko baar-baar hit karenge. Topic 13 mein wapas aayenge.

Big-O yeh batane ka tareeka hai ki data badhne pe kaam kitna badhta hai. Yeh exact time nahi hai; yeh growth ka shape hai. Classic picture hai ek phone book jismein das lakh naam hain, aur tumhe ek insaan ka number chahiye.

  • O(1), constant. Koi tumhe exact page aur line bata deta hai. Book mein hazaar naam hon ya ek arab, mehnat utni hi. Hash map lookup, ya Redis ka key se GET, aise hi kaam karta hai.
  • O(log n), logarithmic. Book beech se kholo; tumhara naam alphabet mein aage aata hai, toh pehla aadha phenk do; bache hue ka beech kholo; repeat. Har step aadha hata deta hai. Das lakh naam ke liye lagbhag 20 steps; ek arab ke liye sirf lagbhag 30. B-tree index row aise hi dhoondhta hai (Topic 01).
  • O(n), linear. Page ek se shuru karke har naam padho jab tak mil na jaaye. Das lakh naam matlab das lakh tak checks. Database mein yeh dar wala full table scan hai.
  • O(n²), quadratic. Har naam ke liye saare naam dobara dekho, jaise har pair compare karna. Yeh bahut jaldi phat jaata hai aur aam taur pe ek aise nested loop ka sign hai jo hona hi nahi chahiye tha.
ShapeShapeSteps for 1,000 items1,000 items ke stepsSteps for 1,000,000 items10 lakh items ke stepsBackend exampleBackend example
O(1)11Redis GET by key, hash indexRedis GET by key, hash index
O(log n)~10~20B-tree index lookupB-tree index lookup
O(n)1,0001,000,000Full table scan, looping over a listFull table scan, list pe loop
O(n²)1,000,0001,000,000,000,000Nested loops over the same dataSame data pe nested loops

Remember: backend interviews rarely ask you to calculate Big-O, but they expect sentences like "without an index this query is a full scan, O(n); with a B-tree index it becomes O(log n), about 20 steps for a million rows."

Yaad rakho: backend interviews mein Big-O calculate karne ko kam hi bolte hain, lekin aise sentences expect karte hain: "bina index ke yeh query full scan hai, O(n); B-tree index ke saath yeh O(log n) ban jaati hai, das lakh rows ke liye lagbhag 20 steps."

Level 5 From your laptop to productionTumhare laptop se production tak

Local means your own laptop. You run the server, you are the only user, the database is on the same machine with a handful of test rows, and everything feels instant. Production ("prod") is the real system that real customers use: real data, thousands of people at the same moment, networks that sometimes fail, machines that restart without warning. Between the two, teams often keep a staging environment, a copy of production used for final testing.

"Works on my machine" is the famous excuse when code runs locally but breaks in production. The usual reasons: a different version of Node or the database, a missing configuration value or secret (like a database password), a different operating system, far more data than your test rows, or many requests arriving at once, which never happens when you are the only user. Docker (Topic 11) exists largely to shrink this gap by packaging the app together with its environment.

Why one server is not enough. One machine has limits: too much traffic and it slows to a crawl, and if it dies, everything dies with it. That is called a single point of failure. So we run many identical copies of the same program, called instances, on different machines. In front of them sits a load balancer: it receives every incoming request and spreads the requests across the instances (for example in turn, "round robin", or to whichever is least busy). It also sends each instance a regular health check ("are you alive?") and stops sending traffic to any instance that fails it. Adding more machines like this is horizontal scaling; buying a bigger machine is vertical scaling (Topic 11).

Local matlab tumhara apna laptop. Server tum chalate ho, akele user tum ho, database usi machine pe hai kuch test rows ke saath, aur sab kuch instant lagta hai. Production ("prod") woh asli system hai jo asli customers use karte hain: asli data, ek hi pal mein hazaaron log, network jo kabhi-kabhi fail hota hai, machines jo bina bataye restart ho jaati hain. Dono ke beech teams aksar ek staging environment rakhti hain, production ki ek copy jo final testing ke liye use hoti hai.

"Works on my machine" woh famous bahaana hai jab code local pe chalta hai lekin production mein toot jaata hai. Aam wajahein: Node ya database ka alag version, koi missing configuration value ya secret (jaise database password), alag operating system, tumhari test rows se kahin zyada data, ya ek saath bahut saari requests aana, jo tab kabhi nahi hota jab tum akele user ho. Docker (Topic 11) zyada tar isi gap ko chhota karne ke liye hai, app ko uske environment ke saath pack karke.

Ek server kaafi kyun nahi. Ek machine ki limits hoti hain: bahut zyada traffic aaya toh bahut slow ho jaati hai, aur agar woh mar gayi toh saath mein sab mar gaya. Ise single point of failure kehte hain. Isliye hum same program ki kai identical copies alag machines pe chalate hain, jinhe instances kehte hain. Unke aage baitha hota hai ek load balancer: yeh har aane wali request leta hai aur requests ko instances mein baant deta hai (jaise baari-baari, "round robin", ya jo sabse kam busy ho usko). Yeh har instance ko regular health check bhi bhejta hai ("zinda ho?") aur jo fail ho use traffic bhejna band kar deta hai. Aise zyada machines jodna horizontal scaling hai; badi machine khareedna vertical scaling hai (Topic 11).

Why "stateless" matters. Here is the catch. Asha's first request may land on instance 1 and her next one on instance 2. If instance 1 had kept "Asha is logged in" or "Asha's cart has two dosas" in its own memory, instance 2 knows nothing about it, and Asha is suddenly logged out with an empty cart. So instances must be stateless: they keep nothing about users between requests in their own RAM or local disk. Each request carries what is needed to identify the user (such as a token), and anything that must be remembered lives in shared storage, Redis or the database. Then any instance can serve any request, and instances can be added, killed or restarted at any time. Think of a bank with many counters: any cashier can serve you because your account lives in the central system, not in one cashier's notebook.

In real production: many instances also means many requests touching the same data at the same millisecond. Two instances may both try to sell the last seat, or both run the same nightly job. That is where concurrency (Topic 03), distributed locks and distributed systems (Topic 07) come in. And when something goes wrong at 2 a.m., logs, metrics and traces are how you find out why (Topics 12 and 13).

"Stateless" kyun important hai. Yahan hai asli pench. Asha ki pehli request instance 1 pe ja sakti hai aur agli instance 2 pe. Agar instance 1 ne apni memory mein rakha tha "Asha logged in hai" ya "Asha ke cart mein do dosa hain", toh instance 2 ko kuch pata nahi, aur Asha achaanak logged out ho jaati hai, cart khaali. Isliye instances ko stateless hona chahiye: woh do requests ke beech users ke baare mein apni RAM ya local disk mein kuch nahi rakhte. Har request apne saath woh laati hai jo user ko pehchanne ke liye chahiye (jaise ek token), aur jo bhi yaad rakhna hai woh shared storage mein rehta hai, Redis ya database mein. Tab koi bhi instance koi bhi request serve kar sakta hai, aur instances kabhi bhi jode, maare ya restart kiye ja sakte hain. Socho ek bank jismein kai counters hain: koi bhi cashier tumhe serve kar sakta hai kyunki tumhara account central system mein hai, kisi ek cashier ki notebook mein nahi.

Asli production mein: kai instances ka matlab yeh bhi hai ki ek hi millisecond mein kai requests same data ko touch karti hain. Do instances dono aakhri seat bechne ki koshish kar sakte hain, ya dono same raat wala job chala sakte hain. Yahin concurrency (Topic 03), distributed locks aur distributed systems (Topic 07) aate hain. Aur jab raat 2 baje kuch toot jaata hai, toh logs, metrics aur traces se hi pata chalta hai kyun (Topics 12 aur 13).

Now you have the whole journey: client, load balancer, stateless API instances, cache, database, queue, worker. Every later chapter zooms into one part of it.

Ab tumhare paas poora safar hai: client, load balancer, stateless API instances, cache, database, queue, worker. Aage ka har chapter iske ek hisse pe zoom karta hai.

How to answer any interview question. The source PDF's closing line is worth memorising: "Most candidates know the answers. Few know the reasoning." A definition is the floor; the reasoning is what gets you hired. So answer every concept question in four moves:

  1. What it is, in one plain sentence.
  2. Why it exists: the pain that came before it.
  3. What problem it solves, with a concrete example.
  4. What it trades off: the cost, and when you would not use it.

Example, caching: "A cache keeps a copy of frequently read data in fast memory like Redis. It exists because reading from the database on every request is slow and puts load on the database. For example, a product page read ten thousand times a minute can be served from Redis in under a millisecond. The trade-off is staleness: the copy can be out of date, so I have to decide how to invalidate it, and I would not cache something like an exact account balance."

For debugging and scenario questions, tell a structured story in five steps: observe (what exactly is wrong, since when, for whom; look at graphs and logs), hypothesise (list likely causes, most likely first), test (check the cheapest likely cause first), fix (the smallest safe change, which is sometimes simply rolling back), prevent (an alert, a test, a post-mortem so it does not happen again). Speak it as "I'd first check X because Y; if that's clear, I'd look at Z."

Study tips from the PDF: do not memorise; answer the interviewer's hint, not just the literal question; always give a situation and a trade-off; and prioritise the five most-asked topics: Indexing, Caching, API Design, Transactions and Production Debugging.

Kisi bhi interview sawaal ka jawab kaise dein. Source PDF ki aakhri line yaad kar lo: "Most candidates know the answers. Few know the reasoning." Matlab zyada log jawab jaante hain, reasoning bahut kam. Definition sirf floor hai; reasoning se job milti hai. Isliye har concept wale sawaal ka jawab chaar moves mein do:

  1. Yeh kya hai, ek simple sentence mein.
  2. Yeh kyun exist karta hai: isse pehle kya dard tha.
  3. Kaunsi problem solve karta hai, ek concrete example ke saath.
  4. Iska trade-off kya hai: keemat kya hai, aur kab use nahi karoge.

Example, caching: "Cache baar-baar padhe jaane wale data ki copy Redis jaisi fast memory mein rakhta hai. Yeh isliye exist karta hai kyunki har request pe database se padhna slow hai aur database pe load daalta hai. Jaise ek product page jo ek minute mein das hazaar baar padha jaata hai, Redis se ek millisecond se kam mein serve ho sakta hai. Trade-off hai staleness: copy purani ho sakti hai, isliye mujhe decide karna padega ki usse invalidate kaise karun, aur main exact account balance jaisi cheez cache nahi karunga." (Interview mein yeh English mein bologe.)

Debugging aur scenario wale sawaalon ke liye paanch steps mein ek structured kahani sunao: observe (exactly kya galat hai, kab se, kiske liye; graphs aur logs dekho), hypothesise (possible causes ki list, sabse likely pehle), test (sabse sasta likely cause pehle check karo), fix (sabse chhota safe change, kabhi-kabhi bas rollback), prevent (alert, test, post-mortem taaki dobara na ho). Aise bolo: "I'd first check X because Y; if that's clear, I'd look at Z."

PDF ki study tips: ratta mat maaro; interviewer ke hint ka jawab do, sirf literal sawaal ka nahi; hamesha ek situation aur ek trade-off do; aur paanch sabse zyada poochhe jaane wale topics ko priority do: Indexing, Caching, API Design, Transactions aur Production Debugging.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Frontend
The part users see and touch: website or mobile app.Woh hissa jo user dekhta aur touch karta hai: website ya mobile app.
Backend
Programs on servers that apply rules, do the work and talk to the database.Servers pe chalne wale programs jo rules lagate hain, kaam karte hain aur database se baat karte hain.
Client / Server
Roles in a conversation: the client asks, the server answers.Baatcheet ke roles: client maangta hai, server jawab deta hai.
Data center / Cloud
Buildings full of servers; the cloud is renting them (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure).Servers se bhari buildings; cloud matlab unhe kiraye pe lena (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure).
URL
An address: protocol + domain + path + optional query string.Ek address: protocol + domain + path + optional query string.
DNS / IP address
DNS turns a name (api.shop.com) into an IP address, the number machines use to find each other.DNS naam (api.shop.com) ko IP address mein badalta hai, woh number jisse machines ek doosre ko dhoondhti hain.
HTTP / HTTPS
The request-response language of the web; HTTPS is the encrypted version.Web ki request-response bhasha; HTTPS uska encrypted version hai.
Method
The verb of a request: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.Request ka verb: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.
Header / Body
Headers are key-value notes on the envelope; the body is the data inside.Headers envelope pe likhe key-value notes hain; body andar ka data hai.
Status code
Three-digit outcome: 2xx worked, 4xx client's fault, 5xx server's fault.Teen digit ka result: 2xx kaam hua, 4xx client ki galti, 5xx server ki galti.
JSON
Text format for data using { } objects and [ ] lists.Data ka text format jo { } objects aur [ ] lists use karta hai.
API / Endpoint
API = the menu a program offers; endpoint = one item, a method plus a path.API = woh menu jo program deta hai; endpoint = ek item, method plus path.
Database
A program that stores data safely on disk and finds it fast.Ek program jo data ko disk pe safely rakhta hai aur jaldi dhoondhta hai.
Table / Row / Column
Table = a sheet; row = one record; column = one property.Table = ek sheet; row = ek record; column = ek property.
Primary key / Foreign key
Primary key uniquely identifies a row; foreign key points at another table's primary key.Primary key row ko uniquely pehchanti hai; foreign key doosre table ki primary key ki taraf point karti hai.
SQL
The language of relational databases: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.Relational databases ki bhasha: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
RAM / Disk
RAM is fast but wiped on restart; disk is slower but permanent.RAM fast hai par restart pe saaf; disk slow hai par permanent.
Process / Thread
Process = a running program with its own memory; thread = a worker inside it sharing that memory.Process = apni memory wala chalta program; thread = uske andar ka worker jo woh memory share karta hai.
CPU core
One unit that executes instructions; N cores can truly do N things at once.Instructions chalane wali ek unit; N cores sach mein ek saath N kaam kar sakte hain.
Node.js / Event loop
JavaScript on servers; one main thread that switches between requests while they wait for I/O.Servers pe JavaScript; ek main thread jo requests ke beech switch karta hai jab woh I/O ka wait kar rahi hon.
Redis
An in-memory key-value store: SET, GET, INCR, EXPIRE; fast and atomic per command.In-memory key-value store: SET, GET, INCR, EXPIRE; fast aur har command atomic.
TTL
Time to live: how long a key survives before it is deleted automatically.Time to live: key kitni der zinda rahegi, phir apne aap delete.
Latency / Throughput
Latency = time for one request; throughput = requests handled per second.Latency = ek request ka time; throughput = ek second mein kitni requests.
p99
The latency that 99% of requests beat; shows how bad the slowest 1% is.Woh latency jisse 99% requests fast hain; dikhata hai sabse slow 1% kitna bura hai.
Big-O
How work grows with data: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n²).Data badhne pe kaam kaise badhta hai: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n²).
Production / Staging / Local
Prod = the real system for real users; staging = a test copy; local = your laptop.Prod = asli users ka asli system; staging = test copy; local = tumhara laptop.
Instance / Load balancer
Instance = one running copy of the app; load balancer = spreads requests across instances and skips unhealthy ones.Instance = app ki ek chalti copy; load balancer = requests ko instances mein baant-ta hai aur bimaar instances ko skip karta hai.
Stateless
An instance keeps nothing about users between requests; shared state lives in Redis or the database.Instance do requests ke beech users ke baare mein kuch nahi rakhta; shared state Redis ya database mein rehti hai.

Check yourselfKhud ko check karo

01 What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?Browser mein URL type karke Enter dabane pe kya-kya hota hai?
What they're really testing: whether you can hold the whole request journey in your head in the right order, not just say "it loads the page".
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum poora request ka safar sahi order mein dimaag mein rakh sakte ho, sirf "page load ho jaata hai" nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

First the browser splits the URL into protocol, domain and path. It needs an IP address for the domain, so it asks DNS, which is usually answered from a cache. Then it opens a TCP connection to that IP, and for HTTPS does a TLS handshake to encrypt the channel. It sends an HTTP request, say GET /orders/42 with headers like Host and Authorization. On the server side a load balancer forwards it to one of several API instances; the app checks the token, maybe checks a Redis cache, queries the database, and builds a JSON response with a status code like 200. The browser receives it and renders the page. So the trade-off in speed is mostly the network hops and the database trip, which is why caching and indexing matter.

Pehle browser URL ko protocol, domain aur path mein todta hai. Domain ke liye IP address chahiye, toh woh DNS se poochta hai, jiska jawab aksar cache se mil jaata hai. Phir woh us IP se TCP connection kholta hai, aur HTTPS ho toh channel encrypt karne ke liye TLS handshake karta hai. Phir ek HTTP request bhejta hai, jaise GET /orders/42, Host aur Authorization jaise headers ke saath. Server side pe ek load balancer use kai API instances mein se ek ko de deta hai; app token check karta hai, shayad Redis cache dekhta hai, database se query karta hai, aur 200 jaise status code ke saath JSON response banata hai. Browser use leke page render karta hai. Toh speed ka zyada kharcha network hops aur database trip mein hai, isiliye caching aur indexing important hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

DNS results carry a TTL, so they are cached at several levels: browser, operating system, and the resolver of your internet provider. The TLS handshake is why reusing connections (keep-alive) helps: opening a fresh secure connection costs extra round trips. Static files like images and JavaScript often come from a CDN, servers placed close to the user, rather than from the API servers at all. And the page may make many more API calls after it loads, each repeating the request journey.

DNS results ke saath TTL hota hai, isliye woh kai levels pe cache hote hain: browser, operating system, aur tumhare internet provider ka resolver. TLS handshake ki wajah se connections reuse karna (keep-alive) madad karta hai: naya secure connection kholne mein extra round trips lagte hain. Images aur JavaScript jaisi static files aksar CDN se aati hain, yaani user ke paas rakhe servers se, API servers se bilkul nahi. Aur page load hone ke baad kai aur API calls kar sakta hai, har ek phir se yahi request ka safar repeat karti hai.

Common mistake: skipping DNS and the connection step, or mixing up the order (for example, saying the server is called before the IP address is known).
Galti mat karna: DNS aur connection wala step chhod dena, ya order gadbad karna (jaise bolna ki IP pata chalne se pehle hi server ko call ho gaya).
02 What is an API endpoint, and what is inside an HTTP request and response?API endpoint kya hota hai, aur HTTP request aur response ke andar kya hota hai?
What they're really testing: whether you know the four parts of a request, the three parts of a response, and what the status code families mean.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum request ke chaar parts, response ke teen parts, aur status code families ka matlab jaante ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

An API is the set of operations a service exposes to other programs, and an endpoint is one of them: a method plus a path, like GET /vehicles/{vin} to fetch one car, or POST /orders to create an order. A request has a method, which is the verb; a path, which is the resource; headers, like Authorization and Content-Type; and an optional body, usually JSON. The response has a status code, headers and a body. The status code is the first thing a client checks: 2xx means success, 4xx means the client sent something wrong, like 404 not found or 401 not logged in, and 5xx means the server failed. Getting these right matters because clients and retry logic make decisions based on them.

API woh operations ka set hai jo ek service doosre programs ko deti hai, aur endpoint unmein se ek hai: method plus path, jaise ek gaadi laane ke liye GET /vehicles/{vin}, ya order banane ke liye POST /orders. Request mein ek method hota hai, yaani verb; ek path, yaani resource; headers, jaise Authorization aur Content-Type; aur ek optional body, aksar JSON. Response mein status code, headers aur body hoti hai. Client sabse pehle status code dekhta hai: 2xx matlab success, 4xx matlab client ne kuch galat bheja, jaise 404 not found ya 401 login nahi kiya, aur 5xx matlab server fail hua. Inhe sahi rakhna important hai kyunki clients aur retry logic inhi ke basis pe decisions lete hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Methods have meanings the whole web relies on. GET should only read and never change data, which lets browsers and CDNs cache it. PUT and DELETE are idempotent by spec: doing them twice leaves the same result as once. POST is not, so a retried POST can create a duplicate order, which is the whole reason Topic 05 exists. Also, returning 200 with an error message in the body is a classic mistake; monitoring and clients will think it succeeded.

Methods ke matlab hain jin pe poora web depend karta hai. GET sirf padhna chahiye, data kabhi nahi badalna chahiye, isiliye browsers aur CDNs use cache kar sakte hain. PUT aur DELETE spec ke hisaab se idempotent hain: do baar karo toh result ek baar jaisa hi. POST nahi hai, isliye retry hua POST duplicate order bana sakta hai, aur Topic 05 isi wajah se exist karta hai. Aur body mein error message ke saath 200 return karna classic galti hai; monitoring aur clients sochenge ki kaam ho gaya.

Common mistake: confusing 401 and 403. 401 means "we don't know who you are"; 403 means "we know who you are, and you are not allowed".
Galti mat karna: 401 aur 403 ko mix karna. 401 matlab "humein nahi pata tum kaun ho"; 403 matlab "humein pata hai tum kaun ho, aur tumhe allowed nahi hai".
03 What are a table, a primary key and a foreign key? Show the four basic SQL operations.Table, primary key aur foreign key kya hain? Chaar basic SQL operations dikhao.
What they're really testing: that you understand how relational data is shaped and linked, which every database topic (indexing, transactions, design) builds on.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum samajhte ho ki relational data ka shape kya hai aur woh kaise juda hota hai, jis pe har database topic (indexing, transactions, design) bana hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A table stores one kind of thing: each row is one record and each column is one typed property. The primary key, usually id, uniquely identifies every row and can never be null. A foreign key is a column that references another table's primary key, so orders.user_id references users.id, and the database can refuse an order for a user who doesn't exist. The four basic operations are CRUD: INSERT to create, SELECT to read, UPDATE to change and DELETE to remove, and JOIN combines tables through the foreign key, for example all orders with the customer's name. The trade-off with foreign keys is a small cost on every write, because the database has to check the referenced row exists.

Table ek tarah ki cheez store karta hai: har row ek record hai aur har column ek typed property. Primary key, aksar id, har row ko uniquely pehchanti hai aur kabhi null nahi ho sakti. Foreign key woh column hai jo doosre table ki primary key ko reference karta hai, jaise orders.user_id reference karta hai users.id ko, aur database aise user ka order mana kar sakta hai jo exist hi nahi karta. Chaar basic operations CRUD hain: INSERT banane ke liye, SELECT padhne ke liye, UPDATE badalne ke liye aur DELETE hatane ke liye, aur JOIN foreign key ke through tables ko jodta hai, jaise saare orders customer ke naam ke saath. Foreign keys ka trade-off hai har write pe thoda kharcha, kyunki database ko check karna padta hai ki referenced row exist karti hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Finding a row by primary key is fast because databases automatically build an index on it, a sorted B-tree, so the lookup is about O(log n) instead of scanning every row. Other columns you filter on, like user_id, are not indexed automatically in Postgres (MySQL InnoDB does create one for foreign keys), and a missing index there is one of the most common causes of slow queries. That is exactly where Topic 01 starts.

Primary key se row dhoondhna fast hai kyunki database us pe apne aap ek index banata hai, ek sorted B-tree, isliye lookup har row scan karne ki bajaye lagbhag O(log n) hota hai. Baaki columns jin pe tum filter karte ho, jaise user_id, Postgres mein apne aap index nahi hote (MySQL InnoDB foreign keys pe ek bana deta hai), aur wahan missing index slow queries ki sabse common wajahon mein se ek hai. Topic 01 bilkul yahin se shuru hota hai.

Common mistake: saying a primary key is "just the first column" or that it can repeat. It must be unique and not null, whatever column it is.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki primary key "bas pehla column" hai ya repeat ho sakti hai. Woh unique aur not null honi chahiye, chahe kaunsa bhi column ho.
04 Why is Redis so much faster than a database like Postgres, and why don't we store everything in Redis?Redis Postgres jaise database se itna fast kyun hai, aur hum sab kuch Redis mein kyun nahi rakhte?
What they're really testing: the RAM versus disk trade-off, speed against durability and cost, which is the foundation of caching.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: RAM vs disk ka trade-off, yaani speed vs durability aur cost, jo caching ki neenv hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Redis is an in-memory key-value store, so every read comes from RAM, which is orders of magnitude faster than disk. It also does very little per request: a GET by key is an O(1) hash lookup, with no SQL parsing, query planning or joins, so lookups typically take well under a millisecond. We don't put everything there because RAM is expensive and limited, and Redis is not as durable as a database by default; its disk persistence is optional, so a crash can lose recent writes. It also can't do rich queries or relational integrity. So I treat Postgres as the source of truth and Redis as a fast copy for hot data, like a cached product page, or for short-lived data like OTPs and rate-limit counters.

Redis ek in-memory key-value store hai, isliye har read RAM se aata hai, jo disk se kai guna (orders of magnitude) fast hai. Yeh har request pe bahut kam kaam bhi karta hai: key se GET ek O(1) hash lookup hai, na SQL parsing, na query planning, na joins, isliye lookups aam taur pe ek millisecond se kaafi kam lete hain. Hum sab kuch wahan nahi rakhte kyunki RAM mehengi aur limited hai, aur Redis by default database jitna durable nahi; uski disk persistence optional hai, isliye crash mein recent writes kho sakti hain. Yeh rich queries ya relational integrity bhi nahi kar sakta. Isliye main Postgres ko source of truth maanta hoon aur Redis ko garam data ki fast copy, jaise cached product page, ya kam time ke data ke liye, jaise OTPs aur rate-limit counters.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Redis executes commands one at a time on a single thread, which makes each command atomic: two clients calling INCR on the same key at the same moment always get 1 and 2, never both 1. That is why it is the standard tool for counters, rate limits and simple locks with SET key value NX EX 30. Persistence comes in two flavours, periodic snapshots (RDB) and an append-only log (AOF), and you choose based on how much data loss you can tolerate.

Redis commands ko ek single thread pe ek-ek karke chalata hai, isliye har command atomic hota hai: do clients ek hi pal mein same key pe INCR karein toh hamesha 1 aur 2 milega, kabhi dono ko 1 nahi. Isiliye counters, rate limits aur SET key value NX EX 30 wale simple locks ke liye yeh standard tool hai. Persistence do tarah ki hoti hai, periodic snapshots (RDB) aur append-only log (AOF), aur tum choose karte ho is basis pe ki kitna data loss bardasht kar sakte ho.

Common mistake: saying "Redis is faster because it is NoSQL". The real reason is that the data lives in RAM and each operation is tiny.
Galti mat karna: bolna "Redis fast hai kyunki woh NoSQL hai". Asli wajah hai ki data RAM mein rehta hai aur har operation bahut chhota hai.
05 What is the difference between a process and a thread? How does Node.js handle many requests?Process aur thread mein kya farak hai? Node.js bahut saari requests kaise sambhalta hai?
What they're really testing: memory isolation versus shared memory, and whether you understand that Node.js is concurrent through an event loop rather than multi-threaded for your code.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: alag memory vs shared memory, aur kya tum samajhte ho ki Node.js tumhare code ke liye multi-threaded nahi, balki event loop ke through concurrent hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A process is a running program with its own private memory given by the operating system, so processes are isolated from each other. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process; all threads in a process share its memory, which makes communication cheap but opens the door to race conditions. Node.js runs my JavaScript on a single main thread with an event loop. When a request waits on I/O, like a database query, Node hands that wait to the operating system or its background pool and serves other requests; when the result arrives, the callback continues. So one Node process can juggle thousands of I/O-bound requests. The trade-off is that CPU-heavy work, like resizing an image in JavaScript, blocks the loop and every other request waits.

Process ek chalta hua program hai jise operating system apni private memory deta hai, isliye processes ek doosre se alag rehte hain. Thread ek process ke andar execution ki unit hai; ek process ke saare threads uski memory share karte hain, jisse baatcheet sasti ho jaati hai lekin race conditions ka darwaza khul jaata hai. Node.js mera JavaScript ek single main thread pe event loop ke saath chalata hai. Jab request I/O ka wait karti hai, jaise database query, Node woh wait operating system ya apne background pool ko de deta hai aur doosri requests serve karta hai; jab result aata hai, callback aage chalta hai. Isliye ek Node process hazaaron I/O-bound requests sambhal sakta hai. Trade-off yeh hai ki CPU-heavy kaam, jaise JavaScript mein image resize karna, loop ko block kar deta hai aur baaki har request wait karti hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

This is concurrency, not parallelism: tasks are interleaved on one thread rather than run at the same instant on several cores. To use all CPU cores, you run several Node processes, with the cluster module, a process manager like PM2, or simply more containers behind a load balancer. For genuine CPU work you can use worker threads or push the job to a queue for a separate worker (Topic 06). Note that even single-threaded code can have race conditions, because two requests can interleave across an await.

Yeh concurrency hai, parallelism nahi: kaam ek thread pe beech-beech mein switch hote hain, kai cores pe ek hi pal mein nahi chalte. Saare CPU cores use karne ke liye tum kai Node processes chalate ho, cluster module se, PM2 jaise process manager se, ya bas load balancer ke peeche zyada containers se. Asli CPU kaam ke liye worker threads use kar sakte ho ya job ko queue mein daal ke alag worker ko de sakte ho (Topic 06). Dhyaan rahe, single-threaded code mein bhi race conditions ho sakti hain, kyunki do requests ek await ke aar-paar interleave ho sakti hain.

Common mistake: saying "Node.js is single-threaded so it can only handle one request at a time". It handles many at once; it just runs your JavaScript for one of them at any given instant.
Galti mat karna: bolna "Node.js single-threaded hai isliye ek time pe ek hi request sambhal sakta hai". Yeh ek saath kai sambhalta hai; bas kisi ek pal mein tumhara JavaScript unmein se ek ke liye chalata hai.
06 Why should API servers be stateless when you run many instances behind a load balancer?Jab load balancer ke peeche kai instances chalte hain, tab API servers stateless kyun hone chahiye?
What they're really testing: whether you understand horizontal scaling and where state must live so any instance can serve any request and instances can die safely.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum horizontal scaling samajhte ho aur yeh ki state kahan rehni chahiye taaki koi bhi instance koi bhi request serve kar sake aur instances safely mar sakein.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Stateless means an instance keeps nothing about a user between requests in its own memory or local disk. It matters because the load balancer can send a user's consecutive requests to different instances. If instance one stored the login session or the cart in memory, the next request landing on instance two would find nothing, and the user would appear logged out. Worse, if that instance restarts during a deploy, the data is simply gone. So each request carries its identity, for example a signed token, and shared state goes into Redis or the database. Then I can add instances when traffic grows, remove them, or let the load balancer skip one that fails its health check, with no user impact. The trade-off is an extra network call to fetch shared state.

Stateless matlab instance do requests ke beech user ke baare mein apni memory ya local disk mein kuch nahi rakhta. Yeh isliye important hai kyunki load balancer ek hi user ki lagaataar requests alag instances pe bhej sakta hai. Agar instance ek ne login session ya cart memory mein rakha, toh instance do pe aane wali agli request ko kuch nahi milega, aur user logged out dikhega. Aur bura, agar woh instance deploy ke dauraan restart ho gaya, toh data seedha gaayab. Isliye har request apni identity saath laati hai, jaise ek signed token, aur shared state Redis ya database mein jaati hai. Tab main traffic badhne pe instances jod sakta hoon, hata sakta hoon, ya load balancer ko health check fail karne wala instance skip karne de sakta hoon, bina user pe asar ke. Trade-off hai shared state laane ke liye ek extra network call.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The workaround people sometimes use is "sticky sessions", where the load balancer always sends a user to the same instance. It works until that instance dies, and it spreads load unevenly, so it hides the problem rather than solving it. Statelessness is also what lets containers be replaced freely (Topic 11) and is one of the REST constraints (Topic 08). Stateless does not mean the system has no state; it means the state lives in dedicated stores built to keep it safe.

Kabhi-kabhi log "sticky sessions" ka jugaad karte hain, jismein load balancer ek user ko hamesha same instance pe bhejta hai. Yeh tab tak chalta hai jab tak woh instance mar na jaaye, aur load bhi barabar nahi bant-ta, isliye yeh problem solve nahi karta, bas chhupata hai. Statelessness hi containers ko aaram se replace karne deta hai (Topic 11) aur REST ke constraints mein se ek hai (Topic 08). Stateless ka matlab yeh nahi ki system mein koi state nahi; matlab hai state un dedicated stores mein rehti hai jo use safe rakhne ke liye bane hain.

Common mistake: storing uploaded files, sessions or in-memory counters on one instance and assuming they will be there on the next request.
Galti mat karna: uploaded files, sessions ya in-memory counters ek instance pe rakhna aur maan lena ki agli request pe woh wahin milenge.

Topic 01 · ASKED EVERYWHERETopic 01 · Har jagah poocha jaata hai

Database IndexingDatabase Indexing

Why one missing index can turn a 1-millisecond lookup into a 2-second one, what an index physically is on disk, and how to prove a fix with EXPLAIN instead of guessing.

Ek missing index kaise 1 millisecond ki lookup ko 2 second ka bana deta hai, index disk par asal mein hota kya hai, aur guess karne ki jagah EXPLAIN se fix ko prove kaise karte hain.

Level 0 The storyKahani

Pick up any thick textbook and turn to the last few pages. You will find the index: every important word, listed in alphabetical order, with the page numbers where it appears. If you want to read about "photosynthesis", you do not read the book from page 1. You flip to the index, jump to "P", find the word in seconds, read "page 214", and go straight there.

Now imagine the same book with no index. To find every mention of "photosynthesis" you would have to read all 600 pages, top to bottom. That works, but it is slow, and it gets slower every time the book gets thicker.

A database has exactly the same problem. Picture a car dealership that keeps one record per vehicle: the VIN (the 17-character Vehicle Identification Number stamped on every car), make, model, year, price, status. The records are stored roughly in the order the cars were added. A service advisor types a VIN into a screen and asks, "show me this car". If the database has nothing but the raw records, it must check every single record, one by one, until it finds the matching VIN. This is called a full table scan (Postgres calls it a Seq Scan, short for sequential scan).

With a few hundred cars nobody notices. With millions of rows, or thousands of lookups per second from a website, the database spends all its time reading records it does not need, and every screen in the building gets slow. The fix is the same as the textbook: build a separate, sorted list of VINs where each VIN points to the exact place its record lives. That separate sorted list is a database index.

Analogy: the table is the book; the index is the alphabetical list at the back; the row pointer is the page number. The index does not contain the whole story, only enough to jump to the right page fast.

Interviewers ask about indexing everywhere because it is the number one real-world performance fix. They are not checking if you know the word. They want to hear that you have seen a slow query, run EXPLAIN, understood the plan, added the right index, and measured the result.

Koi bhi moti textbook uthao aur last ke kuch pages kholo. Wahan tumhe index milega: har important word, alphabetical order mein, saath mein woh page numbers jahan woh word aata hai. Agar tumhe "photosynthesis" ke baare mein padhna hai, toh tum page 1 se book nahi padhte. Tum index kholte ho, seedha "P" pe jaate ho, word kuch seconds mein mil jaata hai, "page 214" likha hai, aur tum seedha wahan pahunch jaate ho.

Ab socho wahi book bina index ke. "Photosynthesis" ka har mention dhoondhne ke liye tumhe poore 600 pages upar se neeche padhne padenge. Kaam ho jaayega, par slow hoga, aur jitni book moti hogi utna hi aur slow.

Database ki bhi bilkul yahi problem hai. Ek car dealership socho jo har gaadi ka ek record rakhti hai: VIN (17 character ka Vehicle Identification Number jo har gaadi pe stamped hota hai), make, model, year, price, status. Records roughly usi order mein stored hain jis order mein gaadiyan add hui thi. Ek service advisor screen pe VIN type karta hai aur bolta hai, "yeh gaadi dikhao". Agar database ke paas sirf raw records hain, toh use har ek record ek-ek karke check karna padega jab tak matching VIN na mil jaaye. Isko full table scan kehte hain (Postgres isko Seq Scan bolta hai, yaani sequential scan).

Kuch sau gaadiyon mein kisi ko farak nahi padta. Par jab millions rows hon, ya website se har second hazaaron lookups aa rahe hon, toh database apna saara time un records ko padhne mein laga deta hai jinki zaroorat hi nahi thi, aur building ki har screen slow ho jaati hai. Fix wahi hai jo textbook mein tha: VINs ki ek alag, sorted list banao jisme har VIN point kare ki uska record exactly kahan pada hai. Yahi alag sorted list database index hai.

Analogy: table = book; index = peeche wali alphabetical list; row pointer = page number. Index mein poori kahani nahi hoti, bas itna hota hai ki tum sahi page pe jaldi jump kar sako.

Interviewers indexing har jagah isliye poochte hain kyunki yeh real world ka number one performance fix hai. Woh yeh check nahi kar rahe ki tumhe word pata hai ya nahi. Woh sunna chahte hain ki tumne slow query dekhi hai, EXPLAIN chalaya hai, plan samjha hai, sahi index lagaya hai, aur result measure kiya hai.

Level 1 The basic idea and the wordsBasic idea aur zaroori words

Quick refresher from the foundations chapter: a table is a grid of rows (one per vehicle) and columns (vin, make, price...). The data lives on disk, which is big but slow compared with RAM (memory), which is fast but small. So the real cost of a query is mostly "how many chunks of disk did I have to read?"

The database does not read one row at a time from disk. It reads fixed-size chunks called pages (8 KB in Postgres, 16 KB in MySQL's InnoDB engine). Each page holds many rows. A full table scan means reading every page of the table.

An index is a separate data structure, stored in its own pages, that holds:

  • the key: the value of the column(s) you indexed, for example the VIN, kept in sorted order;
  • a row pointer: where the full row lives (in Postgres a physical address called the TID or ctid, meaning "page 5012, slot 3"; in MySQL InnoDB, the row's primary key).

Because the keys are sorted, the database does not need to look at all of them. Remember Big-O from the foundations chapter: a full scan is O(n), meaning the work grows in a straight line with the number of rows. Searching a sorted structure is O(log n): doubling the rows adds only one more step. For 1,000,000 sorted keys, a binary search needs about 20 comparisons, because 2 multiplied by itself 20 times is about a million. Twenty steps instead of a million is the whole magic.

-- A table of vehicles
CREATE TABLE vehicles (
  id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,   -- primary key gets an index automatically
  vin        TEXT NOT NULL,
  make       TEXT,
  model      TEXT,
  year       INT,
  price      NUMERIC(10,2),
  status     TEXT,                    -- 'in_stock', 'sold', 'in_service'
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Without this, WHERE vin = '...' reads the whole table
CREATE INDEX idx_vehicles_vin ON vehicles (vin);

-- Now this query can jump straight to the row
SELECT * FROM vehicles WHERE vin = '1HGCM82633A004352';

Two more words you will hear constantly:

  • Selectivity: what fraction of the rows a condition returns. vin = '...' returns 1 row out of a million, so it is highly selective. status = 'in_stock' might return half the table, so it is not selective.
  • Cardinality: how many distinct values a column has. VIN has very high cardinality (every value is different). A status column with three possible values has very low cardinality.

Primary keys and UNIQUE constraints get an index automatically, because the database needs a fast way to check "does this value already exist?" on every insert.

Remember: an index is a sorted copy of some columns plus a pointer to the full row. It makes reads that filter or sort on those columns fast, and it costs extra disk space plus extra work on every write, because the copy must be kept in sync.

Foundations chapter se quick yaad dila doon: table ek grid hai jisme rows hain (har gaadi ki ek row) aur columns hain (vin, make, price...). Data disk pe rehta hai, jo bada hai par slow hai, compared to RAM (memory), jo fast hai par chhoti. Toh kisi query ka asli cost zyaadatar yeh hota hai ki "mujhe disk ke kitne chunks padhne pade?"
