Database disk se ek-ek row nahi padhta. Woh fixed-size chunks padhta hai jinhe pages kehte hain (Postgres mein 8 KB, MySQL ke InnoDB engine mein 16 KB). Har page mein bahut saari rows hoti hain. Full table scan matlab table ka har page padhna.

Index ek alag data structure hai, apne alag pages mein stored, jisme hota hai:

  • key: us column (ya columns) ki value jispe tumne index banaya, jaise VIN, aur yeh sorted order mein rakhi jaati hai;
  • row pointer: poori row kahan padi hai (Postgres mein ek physical address jise TID ya ctid kehte hain, matlab "page 5012, slot 3"; MySQL InnoDB mein row ki primary key).

Kyunki keys sorted hain, database ko saari keys dekhni nahi padti. Foundations wala Big-O yaad karo: full scan O(n) hai, yaani kaam rows ke saath seedhi line mein badhta hai. Sorted structure mein search O(log n) hai: rows double karo toh bas ek step aur badhta hai. 10 lakh sorted keys mein binary search ko lagbhag 20 comparisons chahiye, kyunki 2 ko 20 baar khud se multiply karo toh lagbhag 10 lakh aata hai. 10 lakh ki jagah 20 steps, yahi poora jaadu hai.

-- A table of vehicles
CREATE TABLE vehicles (
  id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,   -- primary key gets an index automatically
  vin        TEXT NOT NULL,
  make       TEXT,
  model      TEXT,
  year       INT,
  price      NUMERIC(10,2),
  status     TEXT,                    -- 'in_stock', 'sold', 'in_service'
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Without this, WHERE vin = '...' reads the whole table
CREATE INDEX idx_vehicles_vin ON vehicles (vin);

-- Now this query can jump straight to the row
SELECT * FROM vehicles WHERE vin = '1HGCM82633A004352';

Do aur words jo tum baar-baar sunoge:

  • Selectivity: koi condition total rows ka kitna hissa return karti hai. vin = '...' 10 lakh mein se 1 row deta hai, toh yeh bahut selective hai. status = 'in_stock' shayad aadhi table de de, toh yeh selective nahi hai.
  • Cardinality: ek column mein kitni alag-alag (distinct) values hain. VIN ki cardinality bahut high hai (har value alag). status column jisme sirf teen possible values hain, uski cardinality bahut low hai.

Primary key aur UNIQUE constraint pe index automatically ban jaata hai, kyunki har insert pe database ko jaldi check karna padta hai ki "yeh value pehle se exist toh nahi karti?"

Yaad rakho: index kuch columns ki sorted copy hai plus poori row tak ka pointer. Jo reads un columns pe filter ya sort karti hain, woh fast ho jaati hain, aur badle mein extra disk space lagti hai plus har write pe extra kaam, kyunki copy ko sync mein rakhna padta hai.

Level 2 How it works inside: the B-treeAndar kaise kaam karta hai: B-tree

Why not just keep the keys in one long sorted list? Because inserting a new VIN in the middle would mean shifting everything after it, which is terribly slow on a big list. Why not a classic binary tree (each node has two children)? Because it gets very tall: a million keys need about 20 levels, and each level could be a separate disk read.

Databases solve this with the B-tree (almost all real ones use the B+tree variant, but everyone just says B-tree). It is a tree that is short and very wide:

  • Every node is one page. A page holds hundreds of keys, so each node can have hundreds of children. That number is called the fan-out.
  • The top node is the root. Middle nodes are internal (branch) nodes; they only hold "signpost" keys that say which child to go to.
  • The bottom nodes are leaves. They hold the actual keys in sorted order, each with its row pointer.
  • Leaves are linked to their neighbours, like train coaches, so the database can walk sideways through a range of keys.
  • The tree is always balanced: every leaf sits at the same depth, so every lookup costs the same number of steps.

With a fan-out of a few hundred, 3 levels can address tens of millions of keys and 4 levels can address billions. And the root and branch pages are used by every lookup, so they almost always stay cached in RAM. In practice a lookup is often one or two real disk reads.

Keys ko ek lambi sorted list mein kyun nahi rakh dete? Kyunki beech mein naya VIN daalna matlab uske baad ki har cheez ko shift karna, jo badi list pe bahut slow hai. Normal binary tree kyun nahi (har node ke do children)? Kyunki woh bahut lamba (tall) ho jaata hai: 10 lakh keys ke liye lagbhag 20 levels, aur har level ek alag disk read ho sakta hai.

Databases isko B-tree se solve karte hain (asal mein almost saare B+tree variant use karte hain, par sab isko B-tree hi bolte hain). Yeh ek aisa tree hai jo chhota aur bahut chauda hai:

  • Har node ek page hai. Ek page mein sau-sau keys aa jaati hain, toh har node ke sau-sau children ho sakte hain. Is number ko fan-out kehte hain.
  • Sabse upar wala node root hai. Beech ke nodes internal (branch) nodes hain; unme sirf "signboard" keys hoti hain jo batati hain ki kaunse child mein jaana hai.
  • Sabse neeche wale nodes leaves hain. Unme asli keys sorted order mein hoti hain, har ek ke saath uska row pointer.
  • Leaves apne padosiyon se linked hoti hain, train ke coaches ki tarah, taaki database keys ki ek range mein side-ways chal sake.
  • Tree hamesha balanced rehta hai: har leaf same depth pe hoti hai, toh har lookup ka cost same steps ka hota hai.

Kuch sau ke fan-out ke saath, 3 levels crores keys sambhaal lete hain aur 4 levels arabon. Aur root aur branch pages har lookup mein use hote hain, isliye woh almost hamesha RAM mein cached rehte hain. Practically ek lookup aksar sirf ek ya do asli disk reads hota hai.

How a lookup walks the tree (look at the picture, searching for 60):

  1. Read the root page. Keys are 42 and 81. 60 is between them, so follow the middle pointer.
  2. Read that branch page. Keys are 55 and 68. 60 is between them, so follow the middle pointer.
  3. Read the leaf page. It holds 55, 60, 63. Found 60, and next to it the row pointer.
  4. Follow the pointer to the table page and read the full row.

Range queries such as WHERE price BETWEEN 20000 AND 30000 (on an index on price) find the first matching leaf, then just follow the leaf links to the right until the value passes 30000. ORDER BY on an indexed column can come for free, because the leaves are already sorted. This is why a B-tree helps with =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY and prefix matches like LIKE 'Hon%'.

Inserting a key: walk down to the correct leaf and place the key in sorted position. If the leaf page is full, it splits into two half-full pages and one separator key is pushed up into the parent. If the parent is full it splits too. When the root itself splits, the tree grows one level taller from the top. That is how it stays balanced without ever rebuilding.

Where does the row itself live? Heap vs clustered

The index gives you a pointer. But what is the table itself, physically? Databases answer this in two different ways, and this is exactly the "clustered vs non-clustered" interview question.

  • Heap table (Postgres). Rows are stored in whatever free space is available, roughly in insertion order, in no particular sorted order. That pile is called the heap. Every index, including the primary key index, is a separate B-tree whose leaves hold a physical pointer (TID) into the heap. All Postgres indexes are "non-clustered" in this sense. Postgres does have a CLUSTER command, but it is a one-time reorder of the heap; new rows do not keep that order.
  • Clustered index (MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server). The table is a B-tree, sorted by the primary key, and the leaf pages hold the full rows. There is no separate heap. Because rows can only be physically sorted one way, a table has only one clustered index. In InnoDB it is the primary key (if there is no primary key, InnoDB uses the first UNIQUE NOT NULL index, or else a hidden row id). Every other index is a secondary (non-clustered) index whose leaves store the primary key value, not a physical address. So a lookup by a secondary index is two tree walks: secondary index to get the primary key, then the clustered index to get the row.

Lookup tree mein kaise chalta hai (picture dekho, 60 dhoondh rahe hain):

  1. Root page padho. Keys hain 42 aur 81. 60 inke beech mein hai, toh middle pointer follow karo.
  2. Woh branch page padho. Keys hain 55 aur 68. 60 inke beech mein hai, toh middle pointer follow karo.
  3. Leaf page padho. Usme 55, 60, 63 hain. 60 mil gaya, aur uske saath row pointer bhi.
  4. Pointer follow karke table ka page padho aur poori row le lo.

Range queries jaise WHERE price BETWEEN 20000 AND 30000 (price pe index ho toh) pehli matching leaf dhoondhti hain, phir bas leaf links ke saath right mein chalti hain jab tak value 30000 se aage na nikal jaaye. Indexed column pe ORDER BY free mein mil sakta hai, kyunki leaves already sorted hain. Isliye B-tree =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY aur LIKE 'Hon%' jaise prefix matches mein help karta hai.

Key insert karna: neeche sahi leaf tak jao aur key ko sorted position pe rakh do. Agar leaf page full hai, toh woh do aadhe-bhare pages mein split ho jaata hai aur ek separator key parent mein upar chali jaati hai. Parent bhi full ho toh woh bhi split hota hai. Jab root khud split hota hai, tab tree upar se ek level lamba ho jaata hai. Isi tarah woh bina kabhi rebuild kiye balanced rehta hai.

Row khud kahan rehti hai? Heap vs clustered

Index tumhe pointer deta hai. Par table khud physically kya hai? Databases iske do alag jawab dete hain, aur yahi "clustered vs non-clustered" wala interview sawaal hai.

  • Heap table (Postgres). Rows jahan free space mile wahan store hoti hain, roughly insertion order mein, koi sorted order nahi. Is dher ko heap kehte hain. Har index, primary key index bhi, ek alag B-tree hai jiske leaves mein heap ka physical pointer (TID) hota hai. Is sense mein Postgres ke saare indexes "non-clustered" hain. Postgres mein CLUSTER command hai, par woh heap ko ek baar reorder karta hai; nayi rows woh order follow nahi karti.
  • Clustered index (MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server). Table khud hi ek B-tree hai, primary key se sorted, aur leaf pages mein poori rows hoti hain. Alag heap hota hi nahi. Kyunki rows physically sirf ek hi tarike se sorted ho sakti hain, ek table ka sirf ek clustered index hota hai. InnoDB mein yeh primary key hai (primary key na ho toh InnoDB pehla UNIQUE NOT NULL index leta hai, warna ek hidden row id). Baaki har index ek secondary (non-clustered) index hai jiske leaves mein physical address nahi, balki primary key ki value hoti hai. Toh secondary index se lookup do tree walks hai: pehle secondary index se primary key lo, phir clustered index se row.

The other shape: hash index

A hash index runs each key through a hash function (a formula that turns any value into a bucket number) and stores the pointer in that bucket. Looking up an exact value is O(1) on average: compute the hash, go to the bucket, done. But a hash scrambles order. "Honda" and "Hyundai" end up in unrelated buckets, so a hash index can answer only =. It cannot do ranges, ORDER BY, or prefix LIKE. Postgres supports USING HASH (crash-safe since version 10). InnoDB does not let you create hash indexes on normal tables (it builds an internal "adaptive hash index" by itself); MySQL's MEMORY engine does support them. Redis and hash maps in code use the same idea.

Doosri shape: hash index

Hash index har key ko ek hash function se guzaarta hai (ek formula jo kisi bhi value ko ek bucket number mein badal deta hai) aur pointer us bucket mein rakh deta hai. Exact value dhoondhna average mein O(1) hai: hash calculate karo, bucket pe jao, ho gaya. Par hash order ko bigaad deta hai. "Honda" aur "Hyundai" bilkul alag buckets mein jaate hain, toh hash index sirf = ka jawab de sakta hai. Range, ORDER BY, ya prefix LIKE nahi kar sakta. Postgres USING HASH support karta hai (version 10 se crash-safe). InnoDB normal tables pe tumhe hash index banane nahi deta (woh khud andar ek "adaptive hash index" banata hai); MySQL ka MEMORY engine inhe support karta hai. Redis aur code ke hash maps bhi isi idea pe chalte hain.

Level 3 Using indexes in real productionReal production mein indexes

Composite indexes and the left-prefix rule

A composite (multi-column) index is one B-tree built on several columns, for example (make, model, year). The entries are sorted by make first; among equal makes, by model; among equal make and model, by year. Exactly like a phone directory sorted by surname, then first name.

That sort order decides which queries it can help. It can jump straight to rows when your WHERE uses a left prefix of the columns: make; or make + model; or make + model + year. It cannot jump to year = 2022 alone, because 2022 rows are scattered under every make and model, the same way a phone book cannot help you find everyone whose first name is "Rahul".

Composite index aur left-prefix rule

Composite (multi-column) index ek hi B-tree hai jo kai columns pe bana hai, jaise (make, model, year). Entries pehle make se sorted hain; same make ho toh model se; same make aur model ho toh year se. Bilkul telephone directory ki tarah jo pehle surname, phir first name se sorted hoti hai.

Yahi sort order decide karta hai ki kaunsi queries ko help milegi. Index seedha rows pe jump kar sakta hai jab tumhara WHERE columns ka left prefix use kare: make; ya make + model; ya make + model + year. Akele year = 2022 pe woh jump nahi kar sakta, kyunki 2022 wali rows har make aur model ke neeche bikhri padi hain, bilkul waise hi jaise phone book tumhe woh sab log nahi dhoondh ke de sakti jinka first name "Rahul" hai.

Two practical rules for column order: put columns used with equality (=) first and the column used for a range (>, BETWEEN) or ORDER BY last, because once the index hits a range, the columns after it can no longer be used to jump. And one index (A, B) already serves queries on A alone, so a separate index on just A is usually a waste.

Covering indexes: never touching the table

Normally an index lookup is two steps: find the key in the index, then fetch the row from the table to read the other columns. If the index already contains every column the query needs, the second step disappears. That is a covering index. Postgres shows it as Index Only Scan; MySQL shows Using index in the Extra column.

-- The inventory page lists price and status for one make/model
SELECT price, status FROM vehicles
WHERE make = 'Honda' AND model = 'Civic';

-- Postgres 11+: key columns to search on, INCLUDE extra columns just to carry along
CREATE INDEX idx_vehicles_make_model_cov
  ON vehicles (make, model) INCLUDE (price, status);

-- MySQL: just add them as trailing key columns
-- CREATE INDEX idx_vehicles_make_model_cov ON vehicles (make, model, price, status);

This is great for read-heavy API endpoints that run the same narrow query thousands of times. The cost is a fatter index (more disk, more RAM, more write work). In Postgres an index-only scan still has to peek at the table for pages not yet marked "all visible" by VACUUM; the plan shows this as Heap Fetches.

EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE: seeing what the database does

The query planner (also called the optimizer) is the part of the database that decides how to run your SQL: full scan or index, which index, which join order. EXPLAIN shows its plan and its estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows real times and row counts next to the estimates. Example output below uses a practice table of 2 million vehicles; the numbers are illustrative.

Column order ke do practical rules: jo columns equality (=) ke saath use hote hain unhe pehle rakho, aur jo column range (>, BETWEEN) ya ORDER BY ke liye use hota hai use last mein, kyunki jaise hi index range pe pahunchta hai, uske baad ke columns jump ke liye use nahi ho sakte. Aur ek index (A, B) already akele A wali queries bhi serve karta hai, toh sirf A pe alag index aam taur pe waste hai.

Covering index: table ko chhuna hi nahi

Normally index lookup do steps hai: index mein key dhoondho, phir baaki columns padhne ke liye table se row lao. Agar index mein pehle se woh saare columns hain jo query ko chahiye, toh doosra step gayab ho jaata hai. Yahi covering index hai. Postgres isko Index Only Scan dikhata hai; MySQL Extra column mein Using index dikhata hai.

-- The inventory page lists price and status for one make/model
SELECT price, status FROM vehicles
WHERE make = 'Honda' AND model = 'Civic';

-- Postgres 11+: key columns to search on, INCLUDE extra columns just to carry along
CREATE INDEX idx_vehicles_make_model_cov
  ON vehicles (make, model) INCLUDE (price, status);

-- MySQL: just add them as trailing key columns
-- CREATE INDEX idx_vehicles_make_model_cov ON vehicles (make, model, price, status);

Yeh un read-heavy API endpoints ke liye bahut badhiya hai jo wahi narrow query hazaaron baar chalate hain. Cost yeh hai ki index mota ho jaata hai (zyada disk, zyada RAM, zyada write ka kaam). Postgres mein index-only scan ko phir bhi un pages ke liye table mein jhaankna padta hai jinhe VACUUM ne abhi "all visible" mark nahi kiya; plan mein yeh Heap Fetches ke roop mein dikhta hai.

EXPLAIN aur EXPLAIN ANALYZE: database kya kar raha hai, dekhna

Query planner (optimizer bhi kehte hain) database ka woh hissa hai jo decide karta hai ki tumhari SQL kaise chalegi: full scan ya index, kaunsa index, joins kis order mein. EXPLAIN uska plan aur uske estimates dikhata hai. EXPLAIN ANALYZE query ko sach mein chalata hai aur estimates ke saath asli time aur row counts dikhata hai. Neeche wala example output 2 million vehicles ki practice table ka hai; numbers sirf samjhaane ke liye hain.

-- BEFORE: no index on vin
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM vehicles WHERE vin = '1HGCM82633A004352';

 Seq Scan on vehicles  (cost=0.00..45872.00 rows=1 width=96)
                       (actual time=0.031..212.884 rows=1 loops=1)
   Filter: (vin = '1HGCM82633A004352'::text)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 1999999
 Planning Time: 0.080 ms
 Execution Time: 212.910 ms

-- FIX (Postgres: CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking writes while it builds)
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_vehicles_vin ON vehicles (vin);

-- AFTER
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM vehicles WHERE vin = '1HGCM82633A004352';

 Index Scan using idx_vehicles_vin on vehicles  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1 width=96)
                                               (actual time=0.025..0.026 rows=1 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (vin = '1HGCM82633A004352'::text)
 Planning Time: 0.110 ms
 Execution Time: 0.041 ms

How to read a plan line:

  • Node type: Seq Scan (read the whole table), Index Scan (walk the index, fetch each row), Index Only Scan (answer from the index alone), Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan (collect many matching pointers first, then read table pages in physical order; used for medium-sized result sets or to combine two indexes).
  • cost=start..total: the planner's estimate in abstract units, not milliseconds.
  • rows=: in the first bracket it is the estimated rows; in the actual bracket it is the real count. A big gap between them means the planner's statistics are wrong, which leads to bad plans.
  • Rows Removed by Filter: rows read and thrown away. Two million read to return one is the classic "missing index" smell.
  • actual time: real milliseconds. This is how you verify the fix, not by feeling.

Useful extras: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows how many pages came from cache versus disk. MySQL has EXPLAIN (look at type: ALL means full scan, ref/range/const mean index use) and, from 8.0.18, EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

Careful: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the statement. On an UPDATE or DELETE, wrap it in BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK; or you will change real data.

Cardinality, statistics and the planner

The planner does not know your data; it keeps statistics about each column: roughly how many distinct values, the most common values and how often they appear, and a histogram of the value spread. Postgres stores these in pg_stats and refreshes them with ANALYZE (autovacuum does it automatically); MySQL shows index cardinality in SHOW INDEX and refreshes with ANALYZE TABLE.

From these it estimates how many rows a condition returns, and picks the cheapest plan. If status = 'sold' matches most of the table, jumping through the index for each row means lots of scattered, random page reads; reading the table straight through in order is cheaper. So the planner will correctly ignore that index. High-cardinality, selective columns (VIN, email, order id) make great indexes; low-cardinality columns on their own usually do not. Rules of thumb you may hear, like "an index stops helping past 5 to 20 percent of rows", are only rough; the real break-even depends on row width, caching and how physically ordered the table is.

The write cost

Every index is another structure that must be updated in the same transaction as the row.

Plan ki line kaise padhein:

  • Node type: Seq Scan (poori table padho), Index Scan (index mein chalo, har row fetch karo), Index Only Scan (sirf index se jawab do), Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan (pehle bahut saare matching pointers ikattha karo, phir table pages physical order mein padho; medium size results ke liye ya do indexes ko combine karne ke liye).
  • cost=start..total: planner ka estimate, abstract units mein, milliseconds nahi.
  • rows=: pehle bracket mein estimated rows; actual bracket mein asli count. Dono mein bada gap matlab planner ke statistics galat hain, aur usse bure plans bante hain.
  • Rows Removed by Filter: rows jo padhi gayi aur phenk di gayi. Ek row lautane ke liye 20 lakh padhna classic "missing index" ki nishaani hai.
  • actual time: asli milliseconds. Fix ko isi se verify karte hain, feeling se nahi.

Kaam ke extras: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) dikhata hai kitne pages cache se aaye aur kitne disk se. MySQL mein EXPLAIN hai (type dekho: ALL matlab full scan, ref/range/const matlab index use ho raha hai) aur 8.0.18 se EXPLAIN ANALYZE bhi.

Dhyaan se: EXPLAIN ANALYZE statement ko sach mein chalata hai. UPDATE ya DELETE pe ise BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK; mein wrap karo, warna asli data badal jaayega.

Cardinality, statistics aur planner

Planner tumhara data nahi jaanta; woh har column ke baare mein statistics rakhta hai: roughly kitni distinct values hain, sabse common values kaunsi hain aur kitni baar aati hain, aur values ke phailaav ka ek histogram. Postgres inhe pg_stats mein rakhta hai aur ANALYZE se refresh karta hai (autovacuum yeh automatically karta hai); MySQL index cardinality SHOW INDEX mein dikhata hai aur ANALYZE TABLE se refresh karta hai.

In stats se woh estimate karta hai ki ek condition kitni rows degi, aur sabse sasta plan chunta hai. Agar status = 'sold' table ki zyaadatar rows se match karta hai, toh har row ke liye index se jump karna matlab bahut saare bikhre hue, random page reads; table ko seedha order mein padh lena sasta padta hai. Toh planner us index ko sahi mein ignore karega. High-cardinality, selective columns (VIN, email, order id) badhiya indexes bante hain; low-cardinality columns akele aam taur pe nahi. "5 se 20 percent rows ke baad index kaam ka nahi" jaise rules of thumb sirf rough hain; asli break-even row ki width, caching aur table kitni physically ordered hai, is pe depend karta hai.

Write ka cost

Har index ek aur structure hai jise row ke saath same transaction mein update karna padta hai.

  • INSERT: one new entry in every index.
  • UPDATE: in principle only indexes on changed columns need work. In Postgres an update writes a new row version; if no indexed column changed and the page has room, a HOT (heap-only tuple) update skips the indexes, otherwise every index gets a new entry. In InnoDB, secondary indexes whose columns changed are updated; changing the primary key moves the whole row.
  • DELETE: index entries must be removed or marked dead, and cleaned up later (VACUUM in Postgres, purge in InnoDB).

So the write cost grows roughly with the number of indexes. It is not exactly "10 indexes = 10 times slower", but ten indexes really do mean around ten extra structures to modify, more log volume, more page splits and more RAM needed to keep them hot.

When NOT to add an index

  • Write-heavy tables (event logs, clickstreams, GPS pings) where rows are written far more than they are searched.
  • Low-cardinality columns on their own (boolean flags, a status with 3 values), unless combined with other columns or used as a partial index (Level 4).
  • Small tables (a few hundred or thousand rows, a lookup table of US states): a scan of a few pages is already instant.
  • Columns no query filters, joins or sorts on. "Maybe we will need it" is not a reason.
  • Duplicates: an index on (A) when (A, B) already exists.
  • INSERT: har index mein ek nayi entry.
  • UPDATE: theory mein sirf badle hue columns wale indexes ko kaam chahiye. Postgres mein update row ka naya version likhta hai; agar koi indexed column nahi badla aur page mein jagah hai, toh HOT (heap-only tuple) update indexes ko skip kar deta hai, warna har index mein nayi entry jaati hai. InnoDB mein jin secondary indexes ke columns badle woh update hote hain; primary key badalne se poori row move hoti hai.
  • DELETE: index entries hatani ya dead mark karni padti hain, aur baad mein saaf hoti hain (Postgres mein VACUUM, InnoDB mein purge).

Toh write ka cost roughly indexes ki sankhya ke saath badhta hai. Yeh exactly "10 indexes = 10 guna slow" nahi hai, par das indexes ka matlab sach mein lagbhag das extra structures modify karna, zyada log, zyada page splits aur unhe garam (RAM mein) rakhne ke liye zyada RAM.

Index kab NAHI lagana

  • Write-heavy tables (event logs, clickstreams, GPS pings) jahan rows search se kahin zyada likhi jaati hain.
  • Low-cardinality columns akele (boolean flags, 3 values wala status), jab tak doosre columns ke saath combine na ho ya partial index na ho (Level 4).
  • Chhoti tables (kuch sau ya hazaar rows, US states jaisi lookup table): kuch pages ka scan pehle se hi instant hai.
  • Woh columns jin pe koi query filter, join ya sort nahi karti. "Shayad kabhi zaroorat pade" koi reason nahi hai.
  • Duplicates: (A) pe index jab (A, B) pehle se hai.

Level 4 Senior-level nuancesSenior-level baarikiyan

Why the index "exists but is not used"

  • Function on the column. WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com' cannot use an index on email, because the tree is sorted by email, not lower(email). Fix: an expression index CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)); or store the value normalised. Same for WHERE date(created_at) = ...; rewrite as a range created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-09-02'.
  • Leading wildcard. LIKE '%civic' cannot seek; LIKE 'civic%' can. Full-text or trigram indexes (Postgres pg_trgm with GIN) handle "contains" searches.
  • Type mismatch. Comparing a text column to a number, or different collations, can force a conversion on every row and disable the index (especially in MySQL).
  • Wrong column order in a composite index (the left-prefix rule).
  • Stale statistics after a big bulk load: estimates are off, so run ANALYZE.
  • The planner is right. The query returns too many rows, so a scan is cheaper.

Specialised indexes worth knowing

  • Partial index (Postgres): index only the rows you query. CREATE INDEX ON vehicles (created_at) WHERE status = 'in_stock'; is small and fast if the app mostly lists in-stock cars. This is also the answer to "how do I index a low-cardinality column?"
  • Unique index: enforces a business rule (one row per VIN) as well as speeding lookups.
  • GIN for JSONB, arrays and full-text search; GiST for geometry and ranges; BRIN for huge, naturally ordered tables such as append-only time series (tiny index storing min/max per block range).

Operating indexes in production

  • Building without downtime. A plain CREATE INDEX in Postgres blocks writes to the table while it builds. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (slower, cannot run inside a transaction, and if it fails it leaves an INVALID index you must drop). MySQL InnoDB supports online index builds (ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE) for most cases.
  • Finding unused indexes. Postgres pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 over a long window (and check replicas, which have their own counters); MySQL sys.schema_unused_indexes. Drop them to speed up writes.
  • Bloat. Heavy updates and deletes leave half-empty pages; REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (Postgres 12+) rebuilds.
  • Primary key choice in InnoDB. Because the table is sorted by primary key, random UUIDv4 keys insert all over the tree, causing page splits and poor cache use. Sequential keys (auto-increment, or time-ordered UUIDv7/ULID) append at the right edge. Also, every secondary index copies the primary key, so a wide primary key makes every index bigger.
  • Skip scan. Newer versions (MySQL 8.0.13+, Postgres 18+) can sometimes use an (A, B) index for a query on B alone when A has very few distinct values, by jumping once per value of A. Useful to know, but do not design around it.

How to decide what to index in a large table

  1. Start from evidence: Postgres pg_stat_statements (queries ranked by total time) or the slow query log (log_min_duration_statement in Postgres, slow_query_log + long_query_time in MySQL).
  2. Pick the queries with the biggest total time (frequency multiplied by duration), not just the single slowest one.
  3. Look at their WHERE, JOIN ... ON and ORDER BY columns. Prefer high-selectivity columns; order composite columns equality-first, range last.
  4. Check what indexes already exist; extend one rather than adding a near-duplicate.
  5. Build concurrently, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after, and watch write latency.
  6. Revisit periodically and drop what is unused. Never index speculatively.

In real production: the most common slow-endpoint story is a list page, for example "open repair orders for this rooftop, newest first", filtering on dealer_id and status and sorting by created_at. A composite index (dealer_id, status, created_at) lets the database seek to the right group and read rows already in order, so it can stop after the first page of 50 instead of sorting thousands.

Index "hai par use nahi ho raha", kyun?

  • Column pe function. WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com' email wale index ko use nahi kar sakta, kyunki tree email se sorted hai, lower(email) se nahi. Fix: expression index CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)); ya value ko normalised form mein store karo. WHERE date(created_at) = ... ke saath bhi yahi; ise range mein likho created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-09-02'.
  • Shuru mein wildcard. LIKE '%civic' seek nahi kar sakta; LIKE 'civic%' kar sakta hai. "Contains" wali search ke liye full-text ya trigram indexes (Postgres pg_trgm with GIN).
  • Type mismatch. Text column ko number se compare karna, ya alag collations, har row pe conversion force kar sakte hain aur index band ho jaata hai (khaas kar MySQL mein).
  • Composite index mein galat column order (left-prefix rule).
  • Purane statistics bade bulk load ke baad: estimates galat, toh ANALYZE chalao.
  • Planner sahi hai. Query itni zyada rows lauta rahi hai ki scan hi sasta hai.

Specialised indexes jo pata hone chahiye

  • Partial index (Postgres): sirf un rows ka index jo tum query karte ho. CREATE INDEX ON vehicles (created_at) WHERE status = 'in_stock'; chhota aur fast hai agar app zyaadatar in-stock gaadiyan hi list karti hai. "Low-cardinality column ko index kaise karein?" ka jawab bhi yahi hai.
  • Unique index: lookup fast karne ke saath ek business rule bhi enforce karta hai (har VIN ki ek hi row).
  • GIN JSONB, arrays aur full-text search ke liye; GiST geometry aur ranges ke liye; BRIN bahut badi, naturally ordered tables ke liye jaise append-only time series (chhota sa index jo har block range ka min/max rakhta hai).

Production mein indexes chalana

  • Bina downtime build karna. Postgres mein simple CREATE INDEX build hote waqt table ke writes block kar deta hai. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY use karo (slow hai, transaction ke andar nahi chal sakta, aur fail ho jaaye toh ek INVALID index chhod deta hai jise drop karna padta hai). MySQL InnoDB zyaadatar cases mein online index build (ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE) support karta hai.
  • Unused indexes dhoondhna. Postgres mein lambe time window pe pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 (aur replicas bhi check karo, unke apne counters hote hain); MySQL mein sys.schema_unused_indexes. Inhe drop karo, writes fast honge.
  • Bloat. Bahut saare updates aur deletes aadhe-khaali pages chhod dete hain; REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (Postgres 12+) rebuild karta hai.
  • InnoDB mein primary key ka chunaav. Kyunki table primary key se sorted hai, random UUIDv4 keys tree mein har jagah insert hoti hain, page splits hote hain aur cache ka use kharab hota hai. Sequential keys (auto-increment, ya time-ordered UUIDv7/ULID) right edge pe append hoti hain. Aur har secondary index primary key copy karta hai, toh chaudi primary key har index ko bada bana deti hai.
  • Skip scan. Naye versions (MySQL 8.0.13+, Postgres 18+) kabhi-kabhi (A, B) index ko akele B wali query ke liye use kar lete hain jab A ki distinct values bahut kam hon, A ki har value pe ek jump karke. Jaan lena useful hai, par iske bharose design mat karo.

Badi table mein kya index karein, kaise decide karein

  1. Evidence se shuru karo: Postgres pg_stat_statements (total time se ranked queries) ya slow query log (Postgres mein log_min_duration_statement, MySQL mein slow_query_log + long_query_time).
  2. Woh queries chuno jinka total time sabse zyada hai (kitni baar chali guna kitna time), sirf ek sabse slow wali nahi.
  3. Unke WHERE, JOIN ... ON aur ORDER BY columns dekho. High-selectivity columns ko prefer karo; composite mein equality pehle, range last.
  4. Dekho kaunse indexes pehle se hain; near-duplicate banane ki jagah ek ko extend karo.
  5. Concurrently build karo, pehle aur baad mein EXPLAIN ANALYZE chalao, aur write latency pe nazar rakho.
  6. Time-time pe wapas dekho aur jo unused hai use drop karo. Kabhi "shayad kaam aaye" soch ke index mat banao.

Real production mein: sabse common slow-endpoint kahani ek list page hoti hai, jaise "is rooftop ke open repair orders, newest pehle", jo dealer_id aur status pe filter karta hai aur created_at se sort karta hai. Composite index (dealer_id, status, created_at) database ko sahi group pe seek karne deta hai aur rows pehle se order mein padhne deta hai, toh woh hazaaron rows sort karne ki jagah 50 ki pehli page ke baad ruk sakta hai.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Index
A separate, sorted structure holding copies of some columns plus a pointer to each full row, so lookups avoid reading the whole table.Ek alag, sorted structure jisme kuch columns ki copy aur har poori row ka pointer hota hai, taaki lookup ke liye poori table na padhni pade.
Page
The fixed-size chunk the database reads and writes (8 KB Postgres, 16 KB InnoDB). One B-tree node = one page.Fixed-size chunk jo database padhta aur likhta hai (Postgres 8 KB, InnoDB 16 KB). B-tree ka ek node = ek page.
Seq Scan / full table scan
Reading every page of a table to find matching rows. O(n).Matching rows dhoondhne ke liye table ka har page padhna. O(n).
B-tree
A short, wide, always-balanced tree of pages with sorted keys; leaves are linked for range scans. Supports =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, prefix LIKE. O(log n).Pages ka chhota, chauda, hamesha balanced tree jisme sorted keys hain; range scans ke liye leaves linked hain. =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, prefix LIKE support karta hai. O(log n).
Fan-out
How many children one B-tree node has (hundreds). High fan-out keeps the tree only 3 or 4 levels deep.Ek B-tree node ke kitne children hain (sau-sau). High fan-out tree ko sirf 3-4 levels gehra rakhta hai.
Heap
Postgres table storage: rows in no particular order; every index points into it by physical address (TID).Postgres ka table storage: rows kisi khaas order mein nahi; har index physical address (TID) se isme point karta hai.
Clustered index
The table itself stored as a B-tree sorted by a key (InnoDB: the primary key). Only one per table.Table khud ek key se sorted B-tree ke roop mein stored (InnoDB: primary key). Ek table mein sirf ek.
Secondary / non-clustered index
Any other index; its leaves point to the row (TID in Postgres, primary key value in InnoDB).Baaki koi bhi index; uski leaves row ki taraf point karti hain (Postgres mein TID, InnoDB mein primary key value).
Composite index
One index on several columns, sorted by the first, then the second, and so on.Kai columns pe ek index, pehle column se sorted, phir doosre se, aur aage.
Left-prefix rule
A composite (A,B,C) index can seek on A, A+B, A+B+C, but not on B or C alone.Composite (A,B,C) index A, A+B, A+B+C pe seek kar sakta hai, akele B ya C pe nahi.
Covering index
An index containing every column a query needs, so the table is never read (Index Only Scan).Aisa index jisme query ke saare zaroori columns hain, toh table padhni hi nahi padti (Index Only Scan).
Cardinality
Number of distinct values in a column. High = good index candidate.Column mein distinct values ki ginti. High = index ke liye achha candidate.
Selectivity
Fraction of rows a condition returns. Small fraction = highly selective = index helps.Condition total rows ka kitna hissa deti hai. Chhota hissa = highly selective = index kaam aata hai.
Query planner
The part of the database that chooses how to run a query, using table statistics.Database ka woh hissa jo table statistics use karke decide karta hai ki query kaise chalegi.
EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Show the planner's chosen plan (estimates only) / run it and show real times and row counts.Planner ka chuna hua plan dikhao (sirf estimates) / use chalao aur asli time aur row counts dikhao.
Hash index
Index that hashes keys into buckets: O(1) exact match, no ranges or sorting.Index jo keys ko hash karke buckets mein rakhta hai: O(1) exact match, range ya sorting nahi.
Partial index
An index over only the rows matching a WHERE condition (Postgres).Sirf un rows ka index jo ek WHERE condition match karti hain (Postgres).
Write amplification
One logical write causing many physical writes, here one per index.Ek logical write se kai physical writes hona, yahan har index ke liye ek.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What is a B-tree index and how does it work internally?B-tree index kya hai aur andar se kaise kaam karta hai?
What they're really testing: whether you know an index is a sorted, balanced tree of disk pages with O(log n) lookups, not just "something that makes queries faster".
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tumhe pata hai ki index disk pages ka ek sorted, balanced tree hai jisme O(log n) lookup hota hai, sirf "kuch jo queries fast karta hai" nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A B-tree index is a sorted, balanced tree stored in disk pages. The root and internal nodes hold separator keys that work like signposts, and the leaf nodes hold every key in sorted order, each with a pointer to its row. Because each node is a whole page holding hundreds of keys, the tree is very wide and shallow, typically three or four levels even for hundreds of millions of rows. So if I look up a vehicle by VIN, the database reads the root, follows the right pointer down a couple of levels and lands on the leaf: a handful of page reads instead of scanning millions of rows. The leaves are linked to each other, so range queries and ORDER BY are just a sideways walk. The trade-off is on writes: every insert has to put the key in its sorted place, sometimes splitting a page, and the index costs disk and memory.

B-tree index disk pages mein stored ek sorted, balanced tree hai. Root aur internal nodes mein separator keys hoti hain jo signboard ka kaam karti hain, aur leaf nodes mein saari keys sorted order mein hoti hain, har ek ke saath uski row ka pointer. Kyunki har node ek poora page hai jisme sau-sau keys aati hain, tree bahut chauda aur kam gehra hota hai, aam taur pe crores rows ke liye bhi teen-chaar levels. Toh agar main VIN se gaadi dhoondhta hoon, database root padhta hai, sahi pointer follow karke do-teen level neeche jaata hai aur leaf pe pahunch jaata hai: millions rows scan karne ki jagah bas kuch page reads. Leaves aapas mein linked hain, toh range queries aur ORDER BY bas side mein chalna hai. Trade-off writes pe hai: har insert ko key uski sorted jagah pe rakhni padti hai, kabhi-kabhi page split hota hai, aur index disk aur memory leta hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Most databases use the B+tree variant: internal nodes hold only separator keys, all data pointers live in the leaves, and leaves are chained. Lookup cost is O(log base fan-out of n), so with a fan-out of a few hundred the height barely grows. When a leaf is full it splits in two and pushes a separator into the parent; a root split adds a level at the top, which is why every leaf stays at the same depth. The top levels are hit by every query, so they stay in the buffer cache and a lookup often costs one or two real disk reads. The same structure serves =, <, >, BETWEEN, prefix LIKE, ORDER BY and MIN/MAX. Postgres uses a Lehman-Yao style B-tree with right-sibling links so readers and writers can work concurrently with short page locks.

Zyaadatar databases B+tree variant use karte hain: internal nodes mein sirf separator keys, saare data pointers leaves mein, aur leaves ek chain mein judi. Lookup cost O(log base fan-out of n) hai, toh kuch sau ke fan-out ke saath height mushkil se badhti hai. Leaf full ho toh do mein split hoti hai aur ek separator parent mein bhejti hai; root split upar ek level jodta hai, isliye har leaf same depth pe rehti hai. Upar ke levels har query mein touch hote hain, isliye woh buffer cache mein rehte hain aur lookup aksar ek-do asli disk reads ka hota hai. Yahi structure =, <, >, BETWEEN, prefix LIKE, ORDER BY aur MIN/MAX serve karta hai. Postgres Lehman-Yao style B-tree use karta hai jisme right-sibling links hote hain, taaki readers aur writers chhote page locks ke saath ek saath kaam kar sakein.

Common mistake: answering "it makes queries faster" with no mechanism, or describing a binary tree with two children per node (that would be about 20 levels deep for a million rows).
Galti mat karna: bina mechanism ke "yeh queries fast karta hai" bol dena, ya do children wala binary tree describe kar dena (10 lakh rows ke liye woh lagbhag 20 levels gehra hoga).
02 What is the difference between a clustered and non-clustered index?Clustered aur non-clustered index mein kya farak hai?
What they're really testing: that clustered means the rows themselves are stored in index order (so only one per table), while non-clustered means a separate structure holding a pointer to the row.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki clustered matlab rows khud index ke order mein stored hain (isliye ek table mein sirf ek), aur non-clustered matlab ek alag structure jisme row ka pointer hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

With a clustered index, the table rows themselves live in the leaf pages of the index, physically sorted by the key. You can only sort rows one way, so there is only one clustered index per table. In MySQL InnoDB that is always the primary key. A non-clustered index is a separate B-tree whose leaves hold the key plus a pointer to the row. For example, in an InnoDB users table clustered on id with a secondary index on email, a lookup by email first finds the id in the email index, then walks the primary key tree to get the row: two lookups. Postgres works differently: every table is an unordered heap, and every index, including the primary key, is non-clustered with a physical pointer. The trade-off: clustering makes primary-key lookups and range scans fast, but random-order inserts cause page splits and every secondary index has to carry the primary key.

Clustered index mein table ki rows khud index ke leaf pages mein rehti hain, key se physically sorted. Rows ko sirf ek hi tarike se sort kar sakte ho, isliye ek table ka sirf ek clustered index hota hai. MySQL InnoDB mein yeh hamesha primary key hai. Non-clustered index ek alag B-tree hai jiske leaves mein key aur row ka pointer hota hai. Example: InnoDB ki users table jo id pe clustered hai aur email pe secondary index hai, email se lookup pehle email index mein id dhoondhta hai, phir primary key tree mein chal ke row laata hai: do lookups. Postgres alag chalta hai: har table ek unordered heap hai, aur har index, primary key bhi, non-clustered hai jisme physical pointer hota hai. Trade-off: clustering se primary-key lookups aur range scans fast hote hain, par random order mein inserts page splits karte hain aur har secondary index ko primary key saath le ke chalni padti hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

If an InnoDB table has no primary key, InnoDB clusters on the first UNIQUE NOT NULL index, or else on a hidden 6-byte row id. That is why sequential primary keys (auto-increment, UUIDv7) are preferred over random UUIDv4: new rows append at the right edge instead of splitting pages everywhere. SQL Server lets you pick any column for the clustered index and treats a table without one as a heap. Postgres has a CLUSTER command, but it is a one-time physical reorder that is not maintained. A subtle difference: in Postgres, an update that moves a row changes its physical address, so every index may need a new entry (unless it is a HOT update); in InnoDB secondary indexes store the primary key, so they do not care where the row moves.

Agar InnoDB table mein primary key nahi hai, toh InnoDB pehle UNIQUE NOT NULL index pe cluster karta hai, warna ek hidden 6-byte row id pe. Isliye random UUIDv4 ki jagah sequential primary keys (auto-increment, UUIDv7) prefer ki jaati hain: nayi rows har jagah page split karne ki jagah right edge pe append hoti hain. SQL Server tumhe kisi bhi column ko clustered index ke liye chunne deta hai aur bina clustered index wali table ko heap maanta hai. Postgres mein CLUSTER command hai, par yeh ek baar ka physical reorder hai jo maintain nahi hota. Ek baareek farak: Postgres mein jo update row ko move karta hai uska physical address badal jaata hai, toh har index ko nayi entry chahiye ho sakti hai (jab tak HOT update na ho); InnoDB mein secondary indexes primary key store karte hain, toh unhe farak nahi padta ki row kahan gayi.

Common mistake: saying a table can have several clustered indexes, or assuming Postgres primary keys are clustered the way they are in MySQL.
Galti mat karna: yeh bolna ki ek table mein kai clustered indexes ho sakte hain, ya maan lena ki Postgres ki primary key MySQL ki tarah clustered hoti hai.
03 What is a composite index? Explain the left-prefix rule.Composite index kya hai? Left-prefix rule samjhao.
What they're really testing: that an index on (A,B,C) helps queries on A, A+B and A+B+C, but not on B alone, and that you can explain why from the sort order.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki (A,B,C) wala index A, A+B aur A+B+C wali queries mein help karta hai, par akele B mein nahi, aur tum sort order se iska reason samjha sako.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A composite index is a single B-tree on several columns, sorted by the first column, then by the second within that, then the third, exactly like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. Because of that order, it can seek on any left prefix: A, A plus B, or A plus B plus C. It cannot seek on B alone or C alone, because those values are scattered across every value of A, just as a phone book cannot find everyone named Rahul. For example, an index on (dealer_id, status, created_at) serves "all repair orders for dealer 42", "open ones for dealer 42", and "open ones for dealer 42, newest first" with no sort step. A query for "all open repair orders across every dealer" cannot use it to seek. So I order columns with equality filters first and the range or sort column last, and one good composite often replaces several single-column indexes.

Composite index kai columns pe bana ek hi B-tree hai, pehle column se sorted, uske andar doosre se, phir teesre se, bilkul phone book ki tarah jo pehle surname aur phir first name se sorted hoti hai. Isi order ki wajah se woh kisi bhi left prefix pe seek kar sakta hai: A, A plus B, ya A plus B plus C. Akele B ya akele C pe seek nahi kar sakta, kyunki woh values A ki har value ke neeche bikhri hain, jaise phone book Rahul naam ke sab logon ko nahi dhoondh sakti. Example: (dealer_id, status, created_at) pe index "dealer 42 ke saare repair orders", "dealer 42 ke open wale", aur "dealer 42 ke open wale, newest pehle" ko bina sort step ke serve karta hai. "Har dealer ke saare open repair orders" wali query isse seek nahi kar sakti. Isliye main equality filters wale columns pehle aur range ya sort wala column last rakhta hoon, aur ek achha composite aksar kai single-column indexes ki jagah le leta hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

With A = 1 AND C = 3 the index seeks on A and then checks C inside that slice of the index, which still beats a table scan. A range stops the prefix: for A = 1 AND B > 5 AND C = 3, C cannot narrow the seek, only filter. The order in which you write conditions in the WHERE clause does not matter; the order of columns in the index does. ORDER BY can use the index only if it matches the index order (or its exact reverse) after the equality columns. MySQL 8.0.13+ and Postgres 18+ can sometimes do a "skip scan" for B alone when A has very few distinct values, but I would not design around it. And an index on (A, B) makes a separate index on A redundant.

A = 1 AND C = 3 mein index A pe seek karta hai aur phir index ke usi hisse mein C check karta hai, jo phir bhi table scan se behtar hai. Range prefix ko rok deti hai: A = 1 AND B > 5 AND C = 3 mein C seek ko narrow nahi kar sakta, sirf filter karta hai. WHERE clause mein conditions kis order mein likhi hain, isse farak nahi padta; index mein columns ka order farak daalta hai. ORDER BY index ko tabhi use kar sakta hai jab woh equality columns ke baad index order (ya uska exact ulta) match kare. MySQL 8.0.13+ aur Postgres 18+ kabhi-kabhi akele B ke liye "skip scan" kar lete hain jab A ki distinct values bahut kam hon, par main iske bharose design nahi karunga. Aur (A, B) pe index hone se A pe alag index redundant ho jaata hai.

Common mistake: thinking the order of conditions in the WHERE clause matters, or that an (A,B,C) index helps a query that filters only on B.
Galti mat karna: sochna ki WHERE clause mein conditions ka order matter karta hai, ya ki (A,B,C) index sirf B pe filter karne wali query mein help karega.
04 When would you NOT add an index?Tum index kab NAHI lagaoge?
What they're really testing: that you see an index as a trade, and know the cases where the write cost outweighs the read gain: high write volume, low cardinality, small tables.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum index ko ek trade maante ho, aur jaante ho kin cases mein write ka cost read ke fayde se zyada hai: high write volume, low cardinality, chhoti tables.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Every index speeds some reads and taxes every write, so I skip it when the tax is not worth paying. First, write-heavy tables such as event logs or GPS pings, where rows are inserted constantly and rarely searched; each index adds work to every insert. Second, low-cardinality columns on their own, like an is_active flag or a status with three values. If most vehicles are "in_stock", a query on that value returns a big chunk of the table, and the planner will choose a sequential scan anyway, so the index is pure overhead. Third, small tables, where scanning a few pages is already instant. Fourth, columns no query actually filters, joins or sorts on, and duplicates of an existing composite. The costs I am avoiding are slower inserts and updates, more disk, more memory pressure on the cache, and slower bulk loads.

Har index kuch reads ko fast karta hai aur har write pe tax lagata hai, toh jab tax dene layak na ho main skip karta hoon. Pehla, write-heavy tables jaise event logs ya GPS pings, jahan rows lagataar insert hoti hain aur kabhi-kabhi hi search hoti hain; har index har insert mein kaam badhata hai. Doosra, low-cardinality columns akele, jaise is_active flag ya teen values wala status. Agar zyaadatar gaadiyan "in_stock" hain, toh us value pe query table ka bada hissa lauta degi, aur planner waise bhi sequential scan chunega, toh index sirf overhead hai. Teesra, chhoti tables, jahan kuch pages scan karna pehle se instant hai. Chautha, woh columns jin pe koi query asal mein filter, join ya sort nahi karti, aur existing composite ke duplicates. Main jo cost bacha raha hoon: slow inserts aur updates, zyada disk, cache pe zyada memory pressure, aur slow bulk loads.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Low cardinality is about the value you query, not only the column. If you often query the rare value (say "in_service" is a small slice), a Postgres partial index WHERE status = 'in_service' is tiny and very effective. A low-cardinality column can also be a fine leading column in a composite when combined with a selective one. For big bulk loads it can be faster to drop secondary indexes, load, and rebuild. Indexes also compete for the buffer cache with hot table data, and more indexes mean more options for the planner to evaluate. I confirm "not needed" with data: pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan or MySQL's sys.schema_unused_indexes.

Low cardinality us value ki baat hai jo tum query karte ho, sirf column ki nahi. Agar tum aksar rare value query karte ho (maano "in_service" ek chhota hissa hai), toh Postgres ka partial index WHERE status = 'in_service' chhota aur bahut effective hai. Low-cardinality column composite mein leading column bhi ban sakta hai jab kisi selective column ke saath ho. Bade bulk loads mein secondary indexes drop karke, load karke, phir rebuild karna fast ho sakta hai. Indexes buffer cache ke liye hot table data se competition bhi karte hain, aur zyada indexes matlab planner ko evaluate karne ke liye zyada options. "Zaroorat nahi" ko main data se confirm karta hoon: pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan ya MySQL ka sys.schema_unused_indexes.

Common mistake: "index every column that appears in a WHERE clause" or "extra indexes can't hurt". They hurt every write and crowd the cache.
Galti mat karna: "jo bhi column WHERE mein aaye us pe index" ya "extra indexes se nuksaan nahi". Woh har write ko nuksaan pahunchate hain aur cache bhar dete hain.
05 What is a covering index?Covering index kya hota hai?
What they're really testing: that a covering index holds every column the query needs, so the database never touches the table, and that this is a tool for hot, read-heavy APIs.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki covering index mein query ke saare zaroori columns hote hain, isliye database table ko chhuta hi nahi, aur yeh hot, read-heavy APIs ka tool hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A covering index is one that contains every column a query touches, in the WHERE, the SELECT list and the ORDER BY, so the database can answer from the index alone and never reads the table. Normally an index lookup is two steps: find the key, then jump to the table row for the other columns, and those jumps are random reads. Take a vehicle listing API that runs SELECT price, status FROM vehicles WHERE make = ? AND model = ? thousands of times a minute. In Postgres I would create (make, model) INCLUDE (price, status), and the plan changes to Index Only Scan; in MySQL, EXPLAIN shows "Using index". That removes the table hop for every row. The trade-off is a bigger index and more write work, so I only do it for hot, narrow queries. A SELECT * can never be covered.

Covering index woh hai jisme query ke har touch hone wale column ho, WHERE mein, SELECT list mein aur ORDER BY mein, taaki database sirf index se jawab de de aur table padhe hi nahi. Normally index lookup do steps hai: key dhoondho, phir baaki columns ke liye table row pe jump karo, aur yeh jumps random reads hote hain. Ek vehicle listing API socho jo SELECT price, status FROM vehicles WHERE make = ? AND model = ? ek minute mein hazaaron baar chalati hai. Postgres mein main (make, model) INCLUDE (price, status) banaunga, aur plan Index Only Scan ho jaayega; MySQL mein EXPLAIN "Using index" dikhayega. Isse har row ka table wala hop hat jaata hai. Trade-off: index bada aur write ka kaam zyada, isliye main yeh sirf hot, narrow queries ke liye karta hoon. SELECT * kabhi covered nahi ho sakta.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Postgres 11+ INCLUDE columns are stored only in the leaves, not used for ordering or searching, which keeps the upper tree small; it also lets you keep a UNIQUE constraint on the key columns while carrying extra payload. Postgres index-only scans still check the visibility map; pages not yet marked all-visible by VACUUM need a table visit, shown as Heap Fetches in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, so a table with heavy churn and lagging vacuum gets less benefit. In InnoDB every secondary index already contains the primary key, so an index on email covers SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = ? for free.

Postgres 11+ ke INCLUDE columns sirf leaves mein stored hote hain, ordering ya search ke liye use nahi hote, jisse upar ka tree chhota rehta hai; isse tum key columns pe UNIQUE constraint rakhte hue extra payload bhi le ja sakte ho. Postgres ke index-only scans phir bhi visibility map check karte hain; jo pages VACUUM ne abhi all-visible mark nahi kiye unke liye table visit chahiye, jo EXPLAIN ANALYZE mein Heap Fetches ke roop mein dikhta hai, toh jis table mein bahut churn hai aur vacuum peeche hai use kam fayda milta hai. InnoDB mein har secondary index mein primary key pehle se hoti hai, toh email pe index SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = ? ko free mein cover karta hai.

Common mistake: expecting an index-only scan while the query says SELECT *, or stuffing every column into indexes "to cover everything".
Galti mat karna: query mein SELECT * likh ke index-only scan expect karna, ya "sab cover karne ke liye" har column indexes mein thoos dena.
06 How do you diagnose a slow query in production?Production mein slow query ko diagnose kaise karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you have actually used EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE, know the smells (Seq Scan on a big table, bad row estimates, missing index) and verify a fix with actual time.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tumne sach mein EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE use kiya hai, nishaaniyan pehchaante ho (badi table pe Seq Scan, galat row estimates, missing index) aur fix ko actual time se verify karte ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I go step by step. First, find the actual query: pg_stat_statements or the slow query log, ranked by total time, or the slow span in our tracing tool. Second, run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with real parameters, ideally on a replica. I look for a Seq Scan on a large table with a huge "Rows Removed by Filter", estimated rows far from actual rows, which means stale statistics, and expensive sorts or nested loops over many rows. Third, form a hypothesis, usually a missing or wrongly ordered index on the WHERE or JOIN columns. Fourth, fix it safely with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Fifth, verify: rerun EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare actual time, then watch the endpoint's p95 latency. For example, a VIN lookup doing a Seq Scan over two million rows became an Index Scan in well under a millisecond. And I check the new index did not hurt write latency.

Main step by step chalta hoon. Pehla, asli query dhoondho: pg_stat_statements ya slow query log, total time se ranked, ya tracing tool mein slow span. Doosra, real parameters ke saath EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) chalao, ho sake toh replica pe. Main dekhta hoon: badi table pe Seq Scan jisme bahut bada "Rows Removed by Filter" ho, estimated rows jo actual se bahut door hon, matlab purane statistics, aur bahut saari rows pe mehnge sorts ya nested loops. Teesra, hypothesis banao, aam taur pe WHERE ya JOIN columns pe missing ya galat order wala index. Chautha, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY se safely fix karo. Paanchva, verify karo: EXPLAIN ANALYZE dobara chalao aur actual time compare karo, phir endpoint ki p95 latency dekho. Example: 20 lakh rows pe Seq Scan karne wali VIN lookup ek millisecond se bhi kam ka Index Scan ban gayi. Aur main check karta hoon ki naye index ne write latency kharab toh nahi ki.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Not every slow query is a missing index. I also check lock waits (pg_stat_activity wait events, pg_locks), a plan that changed after statistics shifted, a query that is fast alone but called hundreds of times per request (N+1 from the ORM), connection pool exhaustion, and cold cache, which BUFFERS shows as "read" versus "hit". auto_explain can log the plans of slow queries in production so you see the real plan, not the one you get on your laptop. Remember EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the statement: wrap writes in BEGIN/ROLLBACK and be careful running heavy queries on the primary.

Har slow query missing index nahi hoti. Main yeh bhi check karta hoon: lock waits (pg_stat_activity ke wait events, pg_locks), statistics badalne ke baad badla hua plan, aisi query jo akele fast hai par ek request mein sau baar call hoti hai (ORM ka N+1), connection pool ka khatam hona, aur cold cache, jo BUFFERS mein "read" vs "hit" ke roop mein dikhta hai. auto_explain production mein slow queries ke plans log kar sakta hai, taaki tum asli plan dekho, laptop wala nahi. Yaad rakho EXPLAIN ANALYZE statement ko sach mein chalata hai: writes ko BEGIN/ROLLBACK mein wrap karo aur primary pe heavy queries chalane mein savdhaan raho.

Common mistake: jumping straight to "add an index" without running EXPLAIN, or trusting EXPLAIN estimates without checking actual time and actual rows.
Galti mat karna: bina EXPLAIN chalaye seedha "index laga do" bolna, ya actual time aur actual rows check kiye bina EXPLAIN ke estimates pe bharosa karna.
07 What is index cardinality and why does it matter for query planning?Index cardinality kya hai aur query planning ke liye kyun matter karti hai?
What they're really testing: that high cardinality makes an index useful, low cardinality can make a full scan faster, and the planner decides using statistics.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki high cardinality index ko useful banati hai, low cardinality mein full scan fast ho sakta hai, aur planner statistics ke basis pe decide karta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Cardinality is the number of distinct values in a column. VIN or email is close to one value per row, so it is high; a status column with "in_stock", "sold" and "in_service" is low. It matters because the planner uses statistics, like the distinct count, the most common values and a histogram, to estimate how many rows a condition will return, and then prices each plan. If a condition matches a small slice, an index scan wins. If it matches a large share of the table, going through the index means a random page read per row, and reading the table sequentially is cheaper, so the planner correctly picks a Seq Scan even though an index exists. So WHERE vin = ? uses the index, while WHERE status = 'sold' on a table where most rows are sold probably will not. The risk is stale stats: wrong estimates lead to bad plans, so we keep ANALYZE running.

Cardinality ek column mein distinct values ki ginti hai. VIN ya email mein lagbhag har row ki alag value hai, toh high; "in_stock", "sold" aur "in_service" wala status column low. Yeh isliye matter karti hai kyunki planner statistics use karta hai, jaise distinct count, sabse common values aur histogram, yeh estimate karne ke liye ki condition kitni rows degi, aur phir har plan ki keemat lagata hai. Agar condition chhota hissa match karti hai, index scan jeetta hai. Agar table ka bada hissa match karti hai, toh index se jaana matlab har row ke liye ek random page read, aur table ko sequentially padhna sasta hai, toh planner index hone ke baawajood sahi mein Seq Scan chunta hai. Toh WHERE vin = ? index use karega, jabki us table pe WHERE status = 'sold' jahan zyaadatar rows sold hain, shayad nahi. Risk purane stats ka hai: galat estimates se bure plans bante hain, isliye ANALYZE chalte rehna chahiye.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Skew matters more than the average. A status column is low-cardinality overall, but if "in_service" is rare, the most-common-values list tells the planner that, and an index (or a partial index) is useful for that one value. The planner assumes columns are independent, so correlated columns such as make and model produce bad estimates; Postgres CREATE STATISTICS can teach it the dependency, and default_statistics_target controls sample size. MySQL's SHOW INDEX cardinality is a sampled estimate, refreshed by ANALYZE TABLE, and MySQL 8 adds column histograms.

Average se zyada skew matter karta hai. Status column overall low-cardinality hai, par agar "in_service" rare hai, toh most-common-values list planner ko yeh bata deti hai, aur us ek value ke liye index (ya partial index) useful hai. Planner maanta hai ki columns independent hain, toh make aur model jaise correlated columns galat estimates dete hain; Postgres ka CREATE STATISTICS use yeh dependency sikha sakta hai, aur default_statistics_target sample size control karta hai. MySQL ke SHOW INDEX ki cardinality ek sampled estimate hai, ANALYZE TABLE se refresh hoti hai, aur MySQL 8 column histograms bhi deta hai.

Common mistake: confusing this with relationship cardinality (one-to-many), or claiming a low-cardinality column can never benefit from any index.
Galti mat karna: ise relationship cardinality (one-to-many) se confuse karna, ya bolna ki low-cardinality column ko kabhi kisi index se fayda nahi ho sakta.
08 How does an index affect INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE performance?Index INSERT, UPDATE aur DELETE ki performance ko kaise affect karta hai?
What they're really testing: that every write must update every relevant index, so ten indexes means roughly ten extra structures touched per write.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki har write ko har relevant index update karna padta hai, toh das indexes matlab har write pe lagbhag das extra structures touch hona.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Each index is a separate B-tree that has to be updated in the same transaction as the row. On INSERT, every index gets a new entry in its sorted position, which may split a page and always writes to the transaction log. On UPDATE, any index containing a changed column needs its old entry removed and a new one added; in Postgres, an update that cannot be done as a HOT update adds an entry to every index. On DELETE, entries are marked dead and cleaned later by VACUUM in Postgres or purge in InnoDB. So write cost scales roughly with the number of indexes: if an events table has eight indexes, one insert is about nine structure updates, plus unique checks. That is why I keep write-heavy tables lean and drop indexes nobody reads. The trade-off is simply faster reads versus slower, heavier writes.

Har index ek alag B-tree hai jise row ke saath same transaction mein update karna padta hai. INSERT pe har index mein uski sorted jagah pe nayi entry jaati hai, jisse page split ho sakta hai aur transaction log mein hamesha likha jaata hai. UPDATE pe jis bhi index mein badla hua column hai, uski purani entry hatani aur nayi daalni padti hai; Postgres mein jo update HOT update nahi ban sakta, woh har index mein entry jodta hai. DELETE pe entries dead mark hoti hain aur baad mein Postgres mein VACUUM ya InnoDB mein purge saaf karta hai. Toh write ka cost roughly indexes ki ginti ke saath badhta hai: agar events table mein aath indexes hain, toh ek insert lagbhag nau structure updates hai, plus unique checks. Isliye main write-heavy tables ko halka rakhta hoon aur jo indexes koi nahi padhta unhe drop karta hoon. Trade-off seedha hai: fast reads vs slow, bhaari writes.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Postgres HOT updates skip index maintenance when no indexed column changes and the new row version fits on the same page; lowering fillfactor leaves room for that, and pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_hot_upd shows how often it happens. So indexing a frequently updated column like last_seen_at can kill HOT updates. InnoDB's change buffer can delay updates to non-unique secondary indexes, but unique indexes need an immediate lookup to check for duplicates. More indexes also mean more WAL or binlog volume, which can increase replication lag. For big imports, drop secondary indexes, load, and rebuild.

Postgres ke HOT updates index maintenance skip kar dete hain jab koi indexed column nahi badla aur naya row version usi page mein fit ho jaata hai; fillfactor kam karne se iske liye jagah bachti hai, aur pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_hot_upd dikhata hai yeh kitni baar hota hai. Toh last_seen_at jaise baar-baar update hone wale column pe index HOT updates ko khatam kar sakta hai. InnoDB ka change buffer non-unique secondary indexes ke updates ko delay kar sakta hai, par unique indexes ko duplicate check ke liye turant lookup chahiye. Zyada indexes matlab zyada WAL ya binlog volume bhi, jisse replication lag badh sakta hai. Bade imports ke liye secondary indexes drop karo, load karo, aur rebuild karo.

Common mistake: saying indexes only slow down INSERTs, or that UPDATE and DELETE never touch indexes.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki indexes sirf INSERT ko slow karte hain, ya UPDATE aur DELETE indexes ko kabhi touch nahi karte.
09 What is a hash index and when is it better than a B-tree?Hash index kya hai aur B-tree se kab behtar hai?
What they're really testing: that a hash index gives O(1) exact-match lookups but cannot do ranges or sorting.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki hash index O(1) exact-match lookup deta hai par range ya sorting nahi kar sakta.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A hash index runs each key through a hash function to get a bucket number and stores the row pointer in that bucket. An exact-match lookup is O(1) on average: hash the value, go to the bucket, done, versus O(log n) for a B-tree. But hashing destroys order, so it only supports equality. No ranges, no ORDER BY, no prefix LIKE, and no left-prefix use of multiple columns. It is a good fit for pure equality lookups on long, high-cardinality values, like looking up a session token or a hashed URL, where Postgres stores only a small hash code, so the index can be smaller than a B-tree on the full value. In practice a B-tree lookup is only a few page reads, mostly cached, so the gain is modest, and B-tree stays the default because it handles every query shape.

Hash index har key ko hash function se guzaar ke bucket number nikalta hai aur row pointer us bucket mein rakh deta hai. Exact-match lookup average mein O(1) hai: value hash karo, bucket pe jao, ho gaya, jabki B-tree mein O(log n). Par hashing order ko khatam kar deti hai, toh yeh sirf equality support karta hai. Range nahi, ORDER BY nahi, prefix LIKE nahi, aur multiple columns ka left-prefix use bhi nahi. Yeh lambi, high-cardinality values pe pure equality lookups ke liye achha hai, jaise session token ya hashed URL dhoondhna, jahan Postgres sirf chhota hash code store karta hai, toh index poori value wale B-tree se chhota ho sakta hai. Practically B-tree lookup bas kuch page reads hai, zyaadatar cached, toh fayda thoda hi hai, aur B-tree default rehta hai kyunki woh har query shape handle karta hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Postgres hash indexes (USING HASH) are WAL-logged and crash-safe since version 10; before that they were not recommended. They are single-column only, cannot enforce UNIQUE, and do not support index-only scans. MySQL InnoDB will not let you create a hash index on a normal table; it maintains an internal "adaptive hash index" over hot B-tree pages automatically, and the MEMORY engine supports explicit HASH indexes. Collisions (two keys in one bucket) are handled with overflow pages, so worst case degrades. The same idea powers Redis and in-memory hash maps.

Postgres ke hash indexes (USING HASH) version 10 se WAL-logged aur crash-safe hain; usse pehle recommend nahi kiye jaate the. Yeh sirf single-column hote hain, UNIQUE enforce nahi kar sakte, aur index-only scans support nahi karte. MySQL InnoDB normal table pe hash index banane nahi deta; woh hot B-tree pages ke upar khud ek internal "adaptive hash index" maintain karta hai, aur MEMORY engine explicit HASH indexes support karta hai. Collisions (ek bucket mein do keys) overflow pages se handle hote hain, toh worst case mein performance girti hai. Yahi idea Redis aur in-memory hash maps ke peeche hai.

Common mistake: claiming hash indexes are always faster, or suggesting one for a date-range or "sort by price" query.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki hash index hamesha fast hai, ya date-range ya "price se sort" wali query ke liye hash index suggest karna.
10 How do you decide which columns to index in a large table?Badi table mein kaunse columns index karne hain, yeh kaise decide karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you start from real query patterns (WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY) and the slow query log, prefer high-selectivity columns, and never index speculatively.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum asli query patterns (WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY) aur slow query log se shuru karte ho, high-selectivity columns prefer karte ho, aur kabhi "shayad kaam aaye" soch ke index nahi banate.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I let the workload decide, not the schema. First I pull the top queries by total time, meaning frequency times duration, from pg_stat_statements or the slow query log. For each, I look at the columns in WHERE, in JOIN conditions, and in ORDER BY. I favour high-selectivity columns, and when several queries share a leading column I design one composite, equality columns first and the range or sort column last, so it serves all of them. I check existing indexes and extend one rather than add a near-duplicate, and I make sure foreign key columns used in joins are indexed. For example, a repair-order list filtered by dealer and status and sorted by date gets (dealer_id, status, created_at). I build it concurrently, prove it with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after, watch write latency, and later drop anything unused. I never index speculatively, because every index is a permanent write tax.

Main workload ko decide karne deta hoon, schema ko nahi. Pehle main pg_stat_statements ya slow query log se total time ke hisaab se top queries nikaalta hoon, yaani kitni baar chali guna kitna time. Har ek ke liye WHERE, JOIN conditions aur ORDER BY ke columns dekhta hoon. High-selectivity columns ko prefer karta hoon, aur jab kai queries ka leading column same ho toh ek composite design karta hoon, equality columns pehle aur range ya sort column last, taaki woh sabko serve kare. Existing indexes check karta hoon aur near-duplicate jodne ki jagah ek ko extend karta hoon, aur ensure karta hoon ki joins mein use hone wale foreign key columns indexed hon. Example: dealer aur status se filter aur date se sort hone wali repair-order list ko (dealer_id, status, created_at) milta hai. Main use concurrently build karta hoon, pehle aur baad mein EXPLAIN ANALYZE se prove karta hoon, write latency dekhta hoon, aur baad mein jo unused ho use drop karta hoon. Main kabhi speculatively index nahi karta, kyunki har index ek permanent write tax hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Postgres does not automatically index the referencing side of a foreign key (MySQL InnoDB does), so unindexed FK columns are a classic cause of slow joins and slow parent deletes. For hot subsets use partial indexes; for the single hottest endpoint consider a covering index. Always test on production-sized data, because a planner looking at 100 dev rows will happily scan. The Postgres extension hypopg lets you test hypothetical indexes without building them. Keep an eye on total index size versus RAM, and review index usage on a schedule, including on read replicas, which keep their own usage counters.

Postgres foreign key ki referencing side pe automatically index nahi banata (MySQL InnoDB banata hai), toh bina index ke FK columns slow joins aur slow parent deletes ki classic wajah hain. Hot subsets ke liye partial indexes use karo; sabse hot ek endpoint ke liye covering index socho. Hamesha production jitne data pe test karo, kyunki 100 dev rows dekh ke planner khushi-khushi scan kar dega. Postgres extension hypopg bina banaye hypothetical indexes test karne deti hai. Total index size vs RAM pe nazar rakho, aur index usage schedule pe review karo, read replicas pe bhi, jinke apne usage counters hote hain.

Common mistake: indexing every column "just in case", or choosing columns by reading the schema instead of the queries that actually run.
Galti mat karna: "just in case" har column index kar dena, ya asli chalne wali queries ki jagah schema padh ke columns chun lena.

Topic 02 · ASKED EVERYWHERETopic 02 · Har jagah poocha jaata hai

Transactions & Isolation LevelsTransactions & Isolation Levels

Why a money transfer never loses half its rupees, what your database quietly lets two users see at the same moment, and how to name the isolation level your own app runs at and the bugs it allows.

Money transfer mein aadhe paise kabhi gaayab kyun nahi hote, ek hi moment pe do users ko database chupchaap kya dikhne deta hai, aur tumhari app kis isolation level pe chal rahi hai aur usmein kaunse bugs possible hain, yeh sab tum confidently bata paoge.

Level 0 The storyKahani

You open a UPI app and send ₹500 to your friend Priya. To you it is one tap. To the bank it is two separate steps: take ₹500 out of your account, and put ₹500 into Priya's account. In the database (remember: a database stores data in tables, and each account is one row in an accounts table), those are two separate UPDATE statements on two different rows.

Now imagine the bank's server crashes after the first step and before the second. Your balance went down by ₹500. Priya's did not go up. The money has vanished into thin air. If that happened even once in a million transfers, with crores of transfers a day, the bank would be losing money every hour.

There is a second, sneakier problem. Lakhs of people are paying at the same moment, and sometimes two of them touch the same account. Say you and your brother share an account with ₹1,000. At the same second you pay a ₹700 electricity bill from your phone and he pays ₹600 for groceries from his. Both payments ask "is there enough money?" and both see ₹1,000. Both say yes. Both deduct. Either the account goes to minus ₹300, or, worse, one deduction silently overwrites the other and the bank has handed out ₹600 it never collected.

So a bank needs two promises from its database:

  1. The crash promise: a group of steps either all happen or none happen. Never half.
  2. The rush promise: many people working at the same time must not trip over each other's half-finished work.

The tool a database gives you for both promises is called a transaction. The isolation level is a dial that controls how strictly the second promise is kept. Turning the dial up makes things safer and slower; turning it down makes things faster and lets certain bugs in. Most developers use transactions every day and have no idea where their dial is set. That is exactly what interviewers probe.
