Analogy: think of an old bank cashier with a passbook. While working on your transfer, he writes each step in pencil. Only when every step is done does he go over it in ink and stamp it. If the phone rings and he has to abandon the work, he erases the pencil and your passbook is exactly as it was. The pencil work is the transaction in progress; the ink and stamp is COMMIT; the eraser is ROLLBACK.

Tum UPI app kholte ho aur apni dost Priya ko ₹500 bhejte ho. Tumhare liye yeh ek tap hai. Bank ke liye yeh do alag steps hain: tumhare account se ₹500 nikaalo, aur Priya ke account mein ₹500 daalo. Database mein (yaad hai: database data ko tables mein rakhta hai, aur har account accounts table ki ek row hai) yeh do alag UPDATE statements hain, do alag rows pe.

Ab socho bank ka server pehle step ke baad aur doosre step se pehle crash ho gaya. Tumhara balance ₹500 kam ho gaya. Priya ka badha hi nahi. Paisa hawa mein gaayab. Agar aisa ek million transfers mein ek baar bhi ho, aur din mein crores transfers hote hain, toh bank har ghante paisa kho raha hoga.

Ek doosri, zyada chalaak problem bhi hai. Ek hi moment pe lakhs log payment kar rahe hain, aur kabhi kabhi do log same account ko touch karte hain. Maano tumhara aur tumhare bhai ka joint account hai jismein ₹1,000 hain. Same second pe tum apne phone se ₹700 ka bijli ka bill bharte ho aur woh apne phone se ₹600 ka grocery. Dono payments poochte hain "paise hain kya?" aur dono ko ₹1,000 dikhta hai. Dono haan bolte hain. Dono deduct karte hain. Ya toh account minus ₹300 ho jaata hai, ya usse bhi bura, ek deduction chupchaap doosre ko overwrite kar deta hai aur bank ne ₹600 de diye jo kabhi kaate hi nahi.

Toh bank ko apne database se do promises chahiye:

  1. Crash wala promise: steps ka ek group ya toh poora hoga ya bilkul nahi hoga. Kabhi aadha nahi.
  2. Rush wala promise: ek saath kaam kar rahe bahut saare log ek doosre ke aadhe-adhure kaam se takraayenge nahi.

Dono promises ke liye database jo tool deta hai usko transaction kehte hain. Isolation level ek dial (knob) hai jo control karta hai ki doosra promise kitni sakhti se nibhaaya jaaye. Dial upar karo toh safe aur slow; neeche karo toh fast, lekin kuch bugs andar aa jaate hain. Zyaadatar developers roz transactions use karte hain aur unhe pata hi nahi hota ki unka dial kahaan set hai. Interviewer exactly yahi check karta hai.

Analogy: ek purane bank cashier ko socho jiske paas tumhari passbook hai. Transfer karte waqt woh har step pencil se likhta hai. Jab saare steps ho jaate hain tabhi woh ink se likhta hai aur stamp lagata hai. Agar beech mein phone aa gaya aur kaam chhodna pada, toh woh pencil mita deta hai aur passbook bilkul pehle jaisi rehti hai. Pencil wala kaam = chalta hua transaction; ink aur stamp = COMMIT; rubber = ROLLBACK.

Level 1 The basic idea: a transaction and ACIDBasic idea: transaction aur ACID

A transaction is a bundle of SQL statements that the database treats as one single unit of work. You open the bundle with BEGIN (MySQL also accepts START TRANSACTION), run your statements, and then either COMMIT (make everything permanent and visible to others) or ROLLBACK (undo everything since BEGIN, as if it never happened).

Transaction SQL statements ka ek bundle hai jisko database ek single unit of work ki tarah treat karta hai. Bundle ko BEGIN se kholte ho (MySQL mein START TRANSACTION bhi chalta hai), apne statements chalaate ho, aur phir ya toh COMMIT karte ho (sab kuch permanent aur doosron ko visible) ya ROLLBACK (BEGIN ke baad ka sab kuch undo, jaise kabhi hua hi nahi).

BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 'rahul';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 'priya';
COMMIT;      -- both changes become permanent together

-- if anything failed in between, the app runs instead:
ROLLBACK;    -- both changes disappear together

If you do not write BEGIN, the database is in autocommit mode (the default in both Postgres and MySQL): every single statement is its own tiny transaction that commits immediately. That is fine for one statement, and dangerous for a transfer, because the two UPDATEs would commit separately and a crash between them loses money.

A transaction also has a life. It is active while statements are running. After the last statement it is partially committed: the work is done but the database has not yet made it crash-proof. Once it is safely on disk it is committed. If an error happens at any point it becomes failed, and the database undoes its work so it ends up aborted (rolled back).

Agar tum BEGIN nahi likhte, toh database autocommit mode mein hota hai (Postgres aur MySQL dono ka default): har ek statement apna chhota sa transaction hai jo turant commit ho jaata hai. Ek statement ke liye theek hai, lekin transfer ke liye khatarnaak, kyunki dono UPDATE alag alag commit honge aur beech mein crash hua toh paisa gaya.

Transaction ki ek life bhi hoti hai. Jab tak statements chal rahe hain woh active hai. Last statement ke baad woh partially committed hai: kaam ho gaya lekin database ne abhi usko crash-proof nahi banaya. Jab woh safely disk pe aa gaya tab committed. Agar kisi bhi point pe error aaya toh woh failed ho jaata hai, database uska kaam undo karta hai aur woh aborted (rolled back) state mein khatam hota hai.

The four guarantees a transaction gives are called ACID. Learn each one with the transfer example, because interviewers always ask for an example.

  • A — Atomicity (all or nothing). Either both the debit and the credit happen, or neither does. If the server dies after the debit, on restart the database sees that transaction never committed and throws its changes away. "Atomic" comes from the Greek for "cannot be split".
  • C — Consistency (valid state to valid state). The database has rules you declared: a balance can never be negative, every order must point to a real customer, an email must be unique. A transaction must leave all those rules true. If the debit would make Rahul's balance ₹-200 and there is a CHECK (balance >= 0) rule, the database rejects the statement and the whole transaction rolls back. Note: the database only enforces the rules you tell it about. Business rules that live only in your code are your job.
  • I — Isolation (others don't see your half-done work). While the transfer is halfway, a report running at the same time should not see ₹500 missing from both accounts. Ideally, concurrent (simultaneous) transactions behave as if they ran one after another. How close you get to that ideal is exactly what the isolation level controls.
  • D — Durability (committed means saved). Once the database says "COMMIT OK", the change survives a crash or power cut. It does this by first writing the change to a write-ahead log (WAL), an append-only file on disk, and forcing it onto the physical disk (an operation called fsync) before replying OK. After a crash, it replays the log.

Transaction jo chaar guarantees deta hai unko ACID kehte hain. Har ek ko transfer ke example se yaad karo, kyunki interviewer hamesha example maangta hai.

  • A — Atomicity (sab ya kuch nahi). Ya toh debit aur credit dono honge, ya dono nahi. Agar debit ke baad server mar gaya, toh restart pe database dekhta hai ki yeh transaction kabhi commit hi nahi hua aur uske changes phenk deta hai. "Atomic" Greek word se aaya hai jiska matlab hai "jisko toda na ja sake".
  • C — Consistency (valid state se valid state). Database mein tumhare declare kiye hue rules hain: balance kabhi negative nahi hoga, har order ek real customer ko point karega, email unique hoga. Transaction ke baad yeh saare rules sach hone chahiye. Agar debit se Rahul ka balance ₹-200 ho jaata aur CHECK (balance >= 0) rule laga hai, toh database statement reject karega aur poora transaction rollback. Dhyaan do: database sirf wahi rules enforce karta hai jo tumne usko bataye. Jo business rules sirf tumhare code mein hain, woh tumhari zimmedaari hain.
  • I — Isolation (doosre tumhara aadha kaam nahi dekhte). Jab transfer aadha hua hai, us waqt chal rahi koi report dono accounts se ₹500 gaayab nahi dekhni chahiye. Ideally, concurrent (ek saath chal rahe) transactions aise behave karein jaise ek ke baad ek chale. Is ideal ke kitne kareeb pahunchte ho, yahi isolation level control karta hai.
  • D — Durability (commit matlab save). Jab database ne bol diya "COMMIT OK", toh change crash ya light jaane ke baad bhi bachega. Iske liye database pehle change ko write-ahead log (WAL) mein likhta hai, jo disk pe ek append-only file hai, aur usko physical disk pe force karta hai (is operation ko fsync kehte hain), tab jaake OK bolta hai. Crash ke baad woh log replay kar deta hai.
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  balance NUMERIC NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)   -- a Consistency rule the DB enforces
);

Remember: ACID = all or nothing, rules still hold, others don't see your half-done work, committed means saved. And the "C" in ACID (rules hold) is a different idea from the "C" in the CAP theorem (every copy of the data agrees).

Yaad rakho: ACID = sab ya kuch nahi, rules bane rahein, doosre tumhara aadha kaam na dekhein, commit matlab save. Aur ACID wala "C" (rules sach rahein) CAP theorem wale "C" (data ki har copy same ho) se alag cheez hai.

Level 2 How it works inside: overlapping transactions and their bugsAndar kaise kaam karta hai: overlap hote transactions aur unke bugs

A database server handles hundreds of connections at once, and each one may have a transaction open. The perfectly safe approach would be to run transactions strictly one at a time, in a single queue. That would be painfully slow. So databases let transactions overlap, and they offer you a choice of how much overlap weirdness you will tolerate. The weirdness has names. These four are the ones you must know cold.

1. Dirty read. Your transaction reads a value that another transaction has written but not yet committed. If that other transaction then rolls back, you acted on data that never officially existed.

Ek database server ek saath sainkdon connections handle karta hai, aur har ek ka transaction khula ho sakta hai. Sabse safe tareeka yeh hota ki transactions ek ke baad ek, ek hi line mein chalein. Lekin woh bahut slow hoga. Isliye databases transactions ko overlap karne dete hain, aur tumhe choice dete hain ki overlap ki kitni ajeeb cheezein tum bardaasht karoge. In ajeeb cheezon ke naam hain. Yeh chaar tumhe ekdum pakke yaad hone chahiye.

1. Dirty read. Tumhara transaction ek aisi value padhta hai jo doosre transaction ne likhi hai lekin abhi commit nahi ki. Agar woh doosra transaction baad mein rollback ho gaya, toh tumne aise data pe action le liya jo officially kabhi tha hi nahi.

2. Non-repeatable read. Inside one transaction you read the same row twice and get two different values, because another transaction committed a change in between. Example: an end-of-day report reads Rahul's balance at the start (₹1,000) to compute interest and again at the end (₹500) to print it. The report now contradicts itself.

3. Phantom read. You run the same range query twice ("all transfers above ₹10,000 today") and the second time there is a new row, because another transaction inserted one and committed. The difference from a non-repeatable read: there, an existing row changed; here, the set of rows changed. A row appeared like a ghost, hence "phantom".

4. Lost update. Two transactions read the same row, each computes a new value in the application from what it read, and both write back. The second write overwrites the first, and the first change is silently lost. This one is the most dangerous in real apps, because the typical "load, modify in code, save" pattern produces it.

2. Non-repeatable read. Ek hi transaction ke andar tum same row do baar padhte ho aur do alag values milti hain, kyunki beech mein kisi aur transaction ne change commit kar diya. Example: din ke end ki report shuru mein Rahul ka balance padhti hai (₹1,000) interest nikaalne ke liye, aur end mein phir padhti hai (₹500) print karne ke liye. Report khud se hi contradict kar rahi hai.

3. Phantom read. Tum same range query do baar chalaate ho ("aaj ke ₹10,000 se upar ke saare transfers") aur doosri baar ek nayi row aa jaati hai, kyunki doosre transaction ne ek row insert karke commit kar di. Non-repeatable read se fark: wahaan ek existing row badli; yahaan rows ka set badal gaya. Ek row bhoot ki tarah aa gayi, isliye "phantom".

4. Lost update. Do transactions same row padhte hain, dono application mein padhi hui value se nayi value calculate karte hain, aur dono wapas likhte hain. Doosra write pehle wale ko overwrite kar deta hai, aur pehla change chupchaap kho jaata hai. Real apps mein yeh sabse khatarnaak hai, kyunki common "load karo, code mein modify karo, save karo" pattern exactly yahi bug banata hai.

The isolation level is your choice of which of these bugs the database must prevent. The SQL standard defines four levels, from loosest to strictest. Read the table row by row.

Isolation level tumhari choice hai ki in bugs mein se kaunse database ko rokne hain. SQL standard chaar levels define karta hai, sabse dheele se sabse sakht tak. Table ko row by row padho.

LevelLevel Dirty readDirty read Non-repeatable readNon-repeatable read Phantom readPhantom read Lost updateLost update Who uses it by defaultDefault kiska hai
READ UNCOMMITTED PossibleHo sakta hai PossibleHo sakta hai PossibleHo sakta hai PossibleHo sakta hai Almost nobody. Postgres silently treats it as READ COMMITTED.Lagbhag koi nahi. Postgres isko chupchaap READ COMMITTED maan leta hai.
READ COMMITTED PreventedRok diya PossibleHo sakta hai PossibleHo sakta hai PossibleHo sakta hai Default in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL ServerPostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server ka default
REPEATABLE READ PreventedRok diya PreventedRok diya Allowed by the standard. Postgres: prevented. MySQL: mostly prevented (snapshot + gap locks).Standard allow karta hai. Postgres: rok diya. MySQL: zyaadatar rok diya (snapshot + gap locks). Postgres: prevented (one txn gets an error). MySQL: still possible for read-then-write.Postgres: rok diya (ek txn ko error milta hai). MySQL: read-then-write mein ab bhi possible. Default in MySQL InnoDBMySQL InnoDB ka default
SERIALIZABLE PreventedRok diya PreventedRok diya PreventedRok diya PreventedRok diya Opt-in for critical paths. Slowest; needs retries.Sirf critical paths ke liye choose karte hain. Sabse slow; retries chahiye. 
-- Which level am I running at?
SHOW transaction_isolation;           -- PostgreSQL
SELECT @@transaction_isolation;       -- MySQL 8

-- Run one transaction at a stricter level
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;              -- PostgreSQL
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;       -- MySQL: applies to the next transaction
START TRANSACTION;

How does the database actually enforce this? With two tools.

Tool 1: locks. A lock is a "reserved" sign on a piece of data. A shared lock (read lock) lets many transactions read but blocks writers. An exclusive lock (write lock) lets only one transaction touch the row. When you UPDATE a row, the database puts an exclusive row lock on it, and keeps it until your transaction commits or rolls back. Another transaction that wants to update the same row simply waits.

Tool 2: MVCC (multi-version concurrency control). Locking readers too would make everything crawl, so modern databases (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle) keep several versions of a row. When you update a row, the old version is kept around for a while. Each transaction reads from a snapshot: a photograph of all committed data as of some moment. That is why, with MVCC, readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers.

  • At READ COMMITTED, every statement takes a fresh snapshot. So each query sees the latest committed data, which is why two reads in one transaction can differ.
  • At REPEATABLE READ, the transaction takes one snapshot at its first query and uses it until the end. Your view of the world is frozen, so repeated reads match.

Old row versions have to be cleaned up eventually. In Postgres a background process called VACUUM removes versions no snapshot can see any more; in MySQL a purge thread trims the undo log. Keep this in mind: it is why long transactions hurt, in Level 3.

Analogy for MVCC: a society notice board where nobody erases old notices. Each new notice is pinned on top with a timestamp. When you walk up, you take a photo and read only notices older than your photo. Someone pinning a new notice does not have to wait for you to finish reading, and you do not have to wait for them.

Database yeh sab actually enforce kaise karta hai? Do tools se.

Tool 1: locks. Lock data ke ek piece pe laga "reserved" board hai. Shared lock (read lock) bahut saare transactions ko padhne deta hai lekin likhne waalon ko rokta hai. Exclusive lock (write lock) sirf ek transaction ko row chhoone deta hai. Jab tum ek row UPDATE karte ho, database us pe exclusive row lock lagata hai, aur jab tak tumhara transaction commit ya rollback nahi hota tab tak rakhta hai. Koi doosra transaction jo same row update karna chahta hai, bas wait karta hai.

Tool 2: MVCC (multi-version concurrency control). Padhne waalon ko bhi lock karoge toh sab kuch reng ke chalega, isliye modern databases (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle) ek row ke kai versions rakhte hain. Jab tum row update karte ho, purana version kuch der ke liye rakha jaata hai. Har transaction ek snapshot se padhta hai: kisi moment tak ke saare committed data ki ek photo. Isiliye MVCC mein readers writers ko block nahi karte aur writers readers ko block nahi karte.

  • READ COMMITTED pe har statement nayi snapshot leta hai. Toh har query latest committed data dekhti hai, isiliye ek transaction ke andar do reads alag ho sakte hain.
  • REPEATABLE READ pe transaction apni pehli query pe ek snapshot leta hai aur end tak wahi use karta hai. Tumhari duniya ki photo freeze ho gayi, isliye repeated reads match karte hain.

Purane row versions ko kabhi na kabhi saaf karna padta hai. Postgres mein VACUUM naam ka background process woh versions hataata hai jo ab kisi snapshot ko nahi dikhne; MySQL mein ek purge thread undo log ko chhota karta hai. Yeh yaad rakhna: Level 3 mein isi wajah se long transactions nuksaan karte hain.

MVCC ki analogy: society ka notice board jahaan koi purane notice nahi mitaata. Har naya notice timestamp ke saath upar pin hota hai. Tum aate ho, ek photo lete ho aur sirf apni photo se purane notices padhte ho. Naya notice lagane waale ko tumhare padhne ka wait nahi karna padta, aur tumhe uska wait nahi karna padta.

Level 3 Real production: locking choices, deadlocks, savepoints, long transactionsReal production: locking choices, deadlocks, savepoints, long transactions

Most apps run at the default level (READ COMMITTED on Postgres), which, as the table shows, allows lost updates. So in production you protect the risky "read, decide, write" spots yourself. You have three tools, from simplest to most flexible.

Fix 1: let the database do the math (atomic update). Instead of reading the balance into your code and writing a new number back, send the change itself. The row lock and the calculation happen inside one statement, on the latest committed value, so nothing can sneak in between.

Zyaadatar apps default level pe chalti hain (Postgres pe READ COMMITTED), jo table ke hisaab se lost updates allow karta hai. Isliye production mein risky "padho, decide karo, likho" jagahon ko tum khud protect karte ho. Tumhare paas teen tools hain, simple se flexible tak.

Fix 1: hisaab database ko karne do (atomic update). Balance ko code mein padhke naya number wapas likhne ki jagah, change hi bhej do. Row lock aur calculation ek hi statement ke andar, latest committed value pe hote hain, toh beech mein kuch ghus nahi sakta.

-- Deduct only if there is enough money; check "rows affected" in the app
UPDATE accounts
SET    balance = balance - 500
WHERE  id = 'rahul' AND balance >= 500;
-- 1 row updated  -> success
-- 0 rows updated -> insufficient funds (or someone else spent it first)

Fix 2: pessimistic locking. "Pessimistic" means you assume a conflict will happen, so you lock the row the moment you read it. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads the row and takes the same exclusive lock an UPDATE would. Anyone else trying to lock or update that row waits until you commit. Use it when conflicts are frequent or when the logic between read and write is too complex for one statement.

Fix 2: pessimistic locking. "Pessimistic" matlab tum maan ke chalte ho ki conflict hoga hi, isliye padhte hi row lock kar lete ho. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE row padhta hai aur wahi exclusive lock leta hai jo UPDATE leta. Koi aur us row ko lock ya update karna chahe toh tumhare commit tak wait karega. Isko tab use karo jab conflicts zyada hote hain ya read aur write ke beech ka logic ek statement mein fit nahi hota.

BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 'rahul' FOR UPDATE;   -- row locked until COMMIT
-- app code: check balance >= 500, apply fraud rules, etc.
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 'rahul';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 'priya';
COMMIT;                                                        -- lock released

-- Variants
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;       -- fail immediately instead of waiting
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;  -- skip rows others hold (great for job queues)

Fix 3: optimistic locking. "Optimistic" means you assume conflicts are rare, so you take no lock at all. You add a version number column. You read the row with its version. When you write, you say "update only if the version is still what I read" and bump it. If zero rows changed, someone else got there first: re-read and retry, or tell the user. A dealership example: two salespeople editing the price on the same vehicle listing (the same VIN, the vehicle's unique 17-character ID). Conflicts are rare, and you would never want a database lock held while a human stares at a form.

Fix 3: optimistic locking. "Optimistic" matlab tum maante ho ki conflicts kam hote hain, isliye koi lock nahi lete. Ek version number column add karte ho. Row ko uske version ke saath padhte ho. Likhte waqt bolte ho "sirf tab update karo jab version abhi bhi wahi ho jo maine padha tha" aur version badha dete ho. Agar zero rows badli, matlab koi aur pehle pahunch gaya: dobara padho aur retry karo, ya user ko batao. Dealership ka example: do salespeople same vehicle listing (same VIN, gaadi ki unique 17-character ID) ka price edit kar rahe hain. Conflict kam hota hai, aur tum kabhi nahi chahoge ki jab tak insaan form ghoor raha hai tab tak database lock pakda rahe.

-- 1. Read (returns price 24500, version 7)
SELECT price, version FROM vehicle_listings WHERE vin = '1HGCM82633A004352';

-- 2. Write only if nobody changed it since
UPDATE vehicle_listings
SET    price = 23900, version = version + 1
WHERE  vin = '1HGCM82633A004352' AND version = 7;
-- 1 row  -> you won
-- 0 rows -> someone else updated first: re-read, retry or show "listing changed"

Rule of thumb: low contention (conflicts are rare) → optimistic, it scales because nobody waits. High contention (a hot row everyone hits) → atomic update or pessimistic lock, because optimistic would turn into a storm of retries.

Deadlocks. Locks bring a new danger. Two transfers run at the same time: T1 moves money Rahul → Priya and locks Rahul's row first; T2 moves money Priya → Rahul and locks Priya's row first. Now T1 needs Priya's row (held by T2) and T2 needs Rahul's row (held by T1). Each waits for the other. Forever. That is a deadlock.

Rule of thumb: low contention (conflicts kam) → optimistic, yeh scale karta hai kyunki koi wait nahi karta. High contention (ek hot row jisko sab hit karte hain) → atomic update ya pessimistic lock, kyunki optimistic retries ka toofan ban jaayega.

Deadlocks. Locks ke saath ek naya khatra aata hai. Do transfers ek saath chal rahe hain: T1 Rahul → Priya paisa bhej raha hai aur pehle Rahul ki row lock karta hai; T2 Priya → Rahul bhej raha hai aur pehle Priya ki row lock karta hai. Ab T1 ko Priya ki row chahiye (jo T2 ke paas hai) aur T2 ko Rahul ki row chahiye (jo T1 ke paas hai). Dono ek doosre ka wait kar rahe hain. Hamesha ke liye. Isko deadlock kehte hain.

Databases detect deadlocks by drawing exactly this wait-for graph and looking for a cycle. Postgres checks after a waiting transaction has been stuck for deadlock_timeout (1 second by default); MySQL InnoDB checks immediately. The database picks a victim, rolls it back with a deadlock error, and the other transaction continues. Your app must catch that error and retry. To make deadlocks rare: always lock rows in the same order (for example, lower account ID first, whichever direction the money flows), keep transactions short, lock as few rows as possible (a missing index can make an UPDATE lock far more rows than you meant), and set a lock_timeout so nothing waits forever.

Databases deadlock ko detect karne ke liye exactly yahi wait-for graph banaate hain aur usmein cycle dhoondhte hain. Postgres tab check karta hai jab koi transaction deadlock_timeout (default 1 second) se atka hai; MySQL InnoDB turant check karta hai. Database ek victim chunta hai, usko deadlock error ke saath rollback karta hai, aur doosra transaction aage badh jaata hai. Tumhari app ko woh error pakadke retry karna hoga. Deadlocks kam karne ke liye: rows hamesha same order mein lock karo (jaise chhoti account ID pehle, paisa kisi bhi direction mein jaaye), transactions chhote rakho, kam se kam rows lock karo (missing index ki wajah se ek UPDATE socha tha usse kahin zyada rows lock kar sakta hai), aur lock_timeout set karo taaki koi hamesha wait na kare.

-- Deadlock-safe transfer: lock both rows in a fixed order (by id), whichever way money moves
BEGIN;
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN ('priya', 'rahul') ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 'rahul';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 'priya';
COMMIT;

SERIALIZABLE and the retry loop. When a rule depends on several rows at once and you cannot afford any anomaly (money, stock, legal limits), you can run that transaction at SERIALIZABLE. The database then guarantees the result is as if transactions had run one by one. The price: some transactions get aborted with a serialization failure (Postgres error code 40001) and must be retried from the start. So SERIALIZABLE always comes with a retry loop in code.

SERIALIZABLE aur retry loop. Jab ek rule ek saath kai rows pe depend karta hai aur tum koi bhi anomaly afford nahi kar sakte (paisa, stock, legal limits), toh us transaction ko SERIALIZABLE pe chala sakte ho. Tab database guarantee deta hai ki result waisa hi hoga jaise transactions ek ek karke chale. Keemat: kuch transactions serialization failure ke saath abort honge (Postgres error code 40001) aur unhe shuru se retry karna padega. Isliye SERIALIZABLE hamesha code mein retry loop ke saath aata hai.

// Node.js + pg: run a unit of work at SERIALIZABLE, retry on serialization failure or deadlock
async function withSerializableRetry(pool, work, maxTries = 5) {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxTries; attempt++) {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    try {
      await client.query('BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE');
      const result = await work(client);
      await client.query('COMMIT');
      return result;
    } catch (err) {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      const retryable = err.code === '40001' || err.code === '40P01'; // serialization / deadlock
      if (retryable && attempt < maxTries) {
        await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 20 * 2 ** attempt + Math.random() * 20)); // backoff + jitter
        continue;
      }
      throw err;
    } finally {
      client.release();
    }
  }
}

Savepoints: undoing only part of a transaction. A savepoint is a bookmark inside a transaction. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work done after the bookmark, and the transaction carries on. Use it when one optional step may fail but the main work should still be saved. This matters extra in Postgres: after any error inside a transaction, Postgres refuses every further command ("current transaction is aborted") until you roll back. A savepoint is how you recover and continue.

Savepoints: transaction ka sirf ek hissa undo karna. Savepoint transaction ke andar ek bookmark hai. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sirf bookmark ke baad ka kaam undo karta hai, aur transaction chalta rehta hai. Isko tab use karo jab koi optional step fail ho sakta hai lekin main kaam save hona chahiye. Postgres mein yeh aur bhi zaroori hai: transaction ke andar koi bhi error aaya toh Postgres rollback hone tak har agla command mana kar deta hai ("current transaction is aborted"). Savepoint se tum recover karke aage badh sakte ho.

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total) VALUES (901, 42, 1500);
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, sku, qty) VALUES (901, 'CHAI-1KG', 2);
SAVEPOINT before_bonus;
INSERT INTO loyalty_bonus (customer_id, order_id, points) VALUES (42, 901, 50);
-- ERROR: duplicate key (bonus already given for this order)
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_bonus;   -- undo only the bonus insert
COMMIT;                               -- the order and its items are saved
-- RELEASE SAVEPOINT name;  forgets a bookmark you no longer need

Long-running transactions: the silent production killer. A transaction that stays open for minutes (or a connection that ran BEGIN and then went quiet, shown in Postgres as idle in transaction) causes a chain of problems:

  • It holds its locks until it ends. Every writer that needs those rows queues behind it; requests time out.
  • It blocks cleanup. Its old snapshot may still need old row versions, so VACUUM cannot remove them. Tables and indexes swell with dead rows (bloat) and every query gets slower. This is true even if the long transaction only reads.
  • It raises deadlock risk: the longer locks are held, the more chances to collide.
  • It blocks schema changes. An ALTER TABLE must wait for its lock, and every normal query then queues behind the waiting ALTER. A two-second migration can freeze the whole table.
  • It pins a pooled connection, so fewer connections are left for everyone else.

The usual cause is doing slow things inside a transaction: calling a payment gateway, sending an email, waiting for user input. The fix: keep transactions tiny, do slow work before or after, and set guard rails such as idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout and lock_timeout in Postgres.

In real production: a nightly script opens a transaction, then updates two million rows one by one while calling an external API for each. Hours later, the main tables are bloated, a deploy's migration hangs, and checkout requests start timing out. Nobody's query is "slow"; they are all waiting behind one forgotten transaction. You find it with pg_stat_activity sorted by xact_start.

Long-running transactions: production ka silent killer. Ek transaction jo minutes tak khula rehta hai (ya ek connection jisne BEGIN chalaaya aur phir chup ho gaya, jo Postgres mein idle in transaction dikhta hai) kai problems ki chain banata hai:

  • Woh apne locks pakde rehta hai jab tak khatam na ho. Un rows ko chahne waala har writer uske peeche line mein lagta hai; requests timeout hoti hain.
  • Woh cleanup rokta hai. Uski purani snapshot ko shayad purane row versions chahiye, isliye VACUUM unhe hata nahi sakta. Tables aur indexes dead rows se phool jaate hain (bloat) aur har query slow hoti hai. Yeh tab bhi sach hai jab long transaction sirf padh raha ho.
  • Deadlock ka risk badhta hai: locks jitni der pakde rahoge, takraane ke utne chances.
  • Schema changes block hote hain. ALTER TABLE ko apne lock ka wait karna padta hai, aur phir har normal query us waiting ALTER ke peeche line mein lag jaati hai. Do second ka migration poori table freeze kar sakta hai.
  • Pool ka ek connection atka rehta hai, toh baaki sab ke liye kam connections bachte hain.

Aam wajah hoti hai transaction ke andar slow kaam karna: payment gateway call, email bhejna, user input ka wait. Fix: transactions ekdum chhote rakho, slow kaam pehle ya baad mein karo, aur Postgres mein idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout aur lock_timeout jaise guard rails set karo.

Real production mein: ek nightly script transaction kholti hai, phir do million rows ek ek karke update karti hai aur har row ke liye external API call karti hai. Ghanton baad main tables bloated hain, ek deploy ka migration atak gaya, aur checkout requests timeout hone lagti hain. Kisi ki query "slow" nahi hai; sab ek bhoole hue transaction ke peeche wait kar rahe hain. Isko pg_stat_activity ko xact_start se sort karke pakadte ho.

-- Postgres: oldest open transactions first
SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS open_for, state, left(query, 60) AS query
FROM   pg_stat_activity
WHERE  xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER  BY xact_start
LIMIT  10;

Level 4 Senior nuances: real DB behaviour, write skew, two-phase commitSenior nuances: asli DB behaviour, write skew, two-phase commit

Real databases do not match the standard exactly. The SQL standard only says which anomalies each level must forbid; each database implements it differently.

  • Postgres REPEATABLE READ is really snapshot isolation. It also prevents phantoms. If your transaction tries to update a row that someone else changed after your snapshot was taken, Postgres throws could not serialize access due to concurrent update instead of overwriting. So the lost update is prevented, but you must retry.
  • MySQL REPEATABLE READ gives plain SELECTs a consistent snapshot, but an UPDATE always works on the latest committed row (a "current read"). So "SELECT balance, compute in app, UPDATE balance = computed" can still lose updates. You still need FOR UPDATE or an atomic update. For locking reads MySQL takes gap locks / next-key locks, locking the gaps between index entries so nobody can insert a phantom.
  • SERIALIZABLE in Postgres is Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): optimistic, it watches read/write dependencies and aborts one transaction on a dangerous pattern. In MySQL it turns plain SELECTs into shared-lock reads: pessimistic, more blocking and deadlocks.

Write skew: the bug only SERIALIZABLE catches. A hospital rule says at least one doctor must be on call. Two doctors are on call; both feel unwell and click "go off call" at the same time. Each transaction checks "are at least 2 on call?", sees 2, and updates its own row. No row was written by both, so row locks and snapshot isolation see no conflict, yet now zero doctors are on call. The same shape appears in "two service advisors book the last free service bay slot, each inserting their own booking row". Fixes: SERIALIZABLE, a unique constraint (for example on (bay_id, slot_time)), or "materializing the conflict" by locking a shared parent row with FOR UPDATE.

Two-phase commit (2PC): atomicity across databases. Everything so far lives inside one database. What if a transfer debits a payments database and credits a separate ledger database? No single BEGIN spans both. Two-phase commit adds a coordinator:

  1. Phase 1, prepare: the coordinator asks each participant "can you commit?". Each does all its work, writes it durably to disk, keeps its locks, and votes YES or NO. After voting YES a participant may no longer decide on its own.
  2. Phase 2, commit: if every vote was YES, the coordinator records its decision and tells everyone COMMIT. If any vote was NO or timed out, it tells everyone ROLLBACK.

Real databases standard ko exactly follow nahi karte. SQL standard sirf yeh bolta hai ki har level kaunsi anomalies mana kare; har database isko alag tareeke se implement karta hai.

  • Postgres REPEATABLE READ asal mein snapshot isolation hai. Yeh phantoms bhi rokta hai. Agar tumhara transaction aisi row update karna chahe jo tumhari snapshot ke baad kisi aur ne badli, toh Postgres overwrite karne ki jagah could not serialize access due to concurrent update error deta hai. Toh lost update ruk gaya, lekin tumhe retry karna padega.
  • MySQL REPEATABLE READ plain SELECTs ko consistent snapshot deta hai, lekin UPDATE hamesha latest committed row pe kaam karta hai ("current read"). Toh "SELECT balance, app mein calculate, UPDATE balance = calculated" mein ab bhi update kho sakta hai. Tumhe phir bhi FOR UPDATE ya atomic update chahiye. Locking reads ke liye MySQL gap locks / next-key locks leta hai, yaani index entries ke beech ke gaps lock karta hai taaki koi phantom insert na kar sake.
  • Postgres mein SERIALIZABLE Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) hai: optimistic, read/write dependencies pe nazar rakhta hai aur khatarnaak pattern dikhe toh ek transaction abort kar deta hai. MySQL mein yeh plain SELECTs ko shared-lock reads bana deta hai: pessimistic, zyada blocking aur deadlocks.

Write skew: woh bug jo sirf SERIALIZABLE pakadta hai. Hospital ka rule hai ki kam se kam ek doctor on call hona chahiye. Do doctors on call hain; dono ki tabiyat kharab hai aur dono same time pe "off call" click karte hain. Har transaction check karta hai "kam se kam 2 on call hain?", 2 dikhte hain, aur apni khud ki row update karta hai. Kisi row ko dono ne nahi likha, isliye row locks aur snapshot isolation ko koi conflict nahi dikhta, lekin ab zero doctors on call hain. Yahi shape "do service advisors aakhri free service bay slot book karte hain, dono apni booking row insert karte hain" mein bhi aata hai. Fixes: SERIALIZABLE, ek unique constraint (jaise (bay_id, slot_time) pe), ya "conflict ko materialize karna" yaani ek shared parent row ko FOR UPDATE se lock karna.

Two-phase commit (2PC): kai databases ke across atomicity. Ab tak sab kuch ek database ke andar tha. Agar transfer payments database se debit kare aur ek alag ledger database mein credit kare toh? Koi ek BEGIN dono ko cover nahi karta. Two-phase commit ek coordinator jodta hai:

  1. Phase 1, prepare: coordinator har participant se poochta hai "commit kar sakte ho?". Har ek apna poora kaam karta hai, usko durably disk pe likhta hai, apne locks rakhta hai, aur YES ya NO vote deta hai. YES vote dene ke baad participant khud se decide nahi kar sakta.
  2. Phase 2, commit: agar saare votes YES the, coordinator apna decision record karta hai aur sabko COMMIT bolta hai. Agar koi vote NO tha ya timeout hua, sabko ROLLBACK bolta hai.

2PC gives true atomicity across systems, at a price. It is slow: extra network round trips and extra disk flushes on every participant. And it blocks: if the coordinator crashes after participants voted YES, they sit in doubt, holding locks, until it recovers. Postgres supports the participant side with PREPARE TRANSACTION 'id' and COMMIT PREPARED 'id' (disabled until you raise max_prepared_transactions); MySQL supports it through XA transactions. In microservices, teams usually avoid 2PC and use a saga instead: a chain of local transactions where each step has a compensating action (debit, then credit; if the credit fails, refund the debit). A saga gives up instant all-or-nothing in exchange for never blocking, and pairs with the outbox pattern (write the event into a table in the same local transaction, publish it afterwards) so no step is silently skipped.

Senior summary: know your database's default level, know which anomaly your hot path is exposed to, prefer an atomic statement or a constraint over a clever lock, use SERIALIZABLE only with a retry loop, and never let a transaction wait on the network.

2PC systems ke across sachchi atomicity deta hai, lekin keemat pe. Yeh slow hai: har participant pe extra network round trips aur extra disk flushes. Aur yeh block karta hai: agar participants ke YES vote ke baad coordinator crash ho gaya, toh woh in doubt baithe rehte hain, locks pakde hue, jab tak coordinator wapas na aaye. Postgres participant side ko PREPARE TRANSACTION 'id' aur COMMIT PREPARED 'id' se support karta hai (jab tak max_prepared_transactions nahi badhaate tab tak band hai); MySQL isko XA transactions se support karta hai. Microservices mein teams aam taur pe 2PC se bachti hain aur saga use karti hain: local transactions ki ek chain jahaan har step ka ek compensating action hota hai (debit, phir credit; agar credit fail hua toh debit refund). Saga turant wala all-or-nothing chhod deta hai, badle mein kabhi block nahi karta, aur outbox pattern ke saath aata hai (event ko usi local transaction mein ek table mein likho, baad mein publish karo) taaki koi step chupchaap skip na ho.

Senior summary: apne database ka default level jaano, jaano ki tumhara hot path kis anomaly ke saamne khula hai, clever lock ki jagah atomic statement ya constraint prefer karo, SERIALIZABLE sirf retry loop ke saath use karo, aur kabhi bhi transaction ko network ka wait mat karne do.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Transaction
A group of SQL statements treated as one unit: all commit or all roll back.SQL statements ka group jo ek unit ki tarah treat hota hai: ya sab commit ya sab rollback.
BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK
Start a transaction / make it permanent / undo all of it.Transaction shuru karo / permanent karo / poora undo karo.
Autocommit
Default mode where every single statement commits on its own.Default mode jismein har statement apne aap commit hota hai.
ACID
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the four guarantees of a transaction.Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: transaction ki chaar guarantees.
WAL (write-ahead log)
Append-only log on disk written before COMMIT returns; replayed after a crash. Gives durability.Disk pe append-only log jo COMMIT se pehle likha jaata hai; crash ke baad replay hota hai. Durability isi se aati hai.
Isolation level
The setting that decides which concurrency anomalies the database prevents.Setting jo decide karti hai ki database kaunsi concurrency anomalies rokega.
Dirty read
Reading another transaction's uncommitted change.Doosre transaction ka uncommitted change padh lena.
Non-repeatable read
Same row read twice in one transaction gives different values.Ek transaction mein same row do baar padhne pe alag values.
Phantom read
Same range query run twice returns a different set of rows.Same range query do baar chalaane pe rows ka alag set.
Lost update
Two read-modify-write cycles on one row; the second overwrites the first.Ek row pe do read-modify-write; doosra pehle ko overwrite kar deta hai.
Write skew
Two transactions read the same condition and each updates a different row, together breaking a rule.Do transactions same condition padhte hain aur alag alag row update karte hain, milke rule tod dete hain.
MVCC / snapshot
Keeping multiple row versions so each transaction reads a consistent photo of committed data.Row ke kai versions rakhna taaki har transaction committed data ki ek consistent photo padhe.
Row lock (shared / exclusive)
A reservation on a row; shared allows other readers, exclusive allows only one holder.Row pe reservation; shared mein doosre padh sakte hain, exclusive mein sirf ek holder.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
Read a row and lock it until the transaction ends (pessimistic locking).Row padho aur transaction khatam hone tak lock rakho (pessimistic locking).
Optimistic locking
No lock; a version column is checked on write, retry if it changed.Koi lock nahi; write pe version column check hota hai, badla hai toh retry.
Deadlock / victim
Two transactions waiting on each other's locks; the database kills one (the victim).Do transactions ek doosre ke locks ka wait kar rahe hain; database ek ko maar deta hai (victim).
Serialization failure (40001)
Error a strict level raises to abort a conflicting transaction; the app must retry.Strict level conflict waale transaction ko abort karne ke liye yeh error deta hai; app ko retry karna hai.
Savepoint
A bookmark inside a transaction you can roll back to without losing earlier work.Transaction ke andar bookmark jahaan tak rollback kar sakte ho, pehle ka kaam khoye bina.
VACUUM / bloat
Postgres cleanup of dead row versions / tables swollen with dead rows it could not clean.Postgres ka dead row versions ka cleanup / dead rows se phooli hui tables jo saaf nahi ho paayi.
Two-phase commit (2PC)
Prepare-then-commit protocol run by a coordinator to commit atomically across several databases.Coordinator ka prepare-phir-commit protocol, kai databases mein ek saath atomic commit ke liye.
Saga
A chain of local transactions with compensating actions instead of one distributed transaction.Ek distributed transaction ki jagah compensating actions ke saath local transactions ki chain.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What are ACID properties? Explain each one with a real example.ACID properties kya hain? Har ek ko real example ke saath samjhao.
What they're really testing: that you can tie each letter to a concrete scenario (atomicity all-or-nothing, consistency valid to valid, isolation not seeing others' work, durability committed means persisted) and know roughly how the database delivers it.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum har letter ko ek concrete scenario se jod sakte ho (atomicity sab ya kuch nahi, consistency valid se valid, isolation doosron ka kaam na dikhe, durability commit matlab persist) aur roughly jaante ho ki database yeh kaise deta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"ACID is the set of guarantees a database transaction gives. I'll use a ₹500 transfer from Rahul to Priya, which is two UPDATEs. Atomicity is all or nothing: if the server crashes after the debit, the database discards the uncommitted debit, so money never vanishes. Consistency means the database moves from one valid state to another: every rule I've declared, like CHECK balance >= 0 or a foreign key, must hold at commit, or the whole transaction is rejected. Isolation means concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work, so a report running mid-transfer never sees ₹500 missing from both accounts; how strict that is depends on the isolation level. Durability means once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash, because it's been flushed to the write-ahead log on disk first. Each guarantee has a cost: durability costs a disk flush per commit, and isolation costs locking or retries."

"ACID woh guarantees hain jo database transaction deta hai. Main Rahul se Priya ko ₹500 transfer ka example lunga, jo do UPDATEs hain. Atomicity matlab sab ya kuch nahi: agar debit ke baad server crash hua, database uncommitted debit phenk deta hai, toh paisa kabhi gaayab nahi hota. Consistency matlab database ek valid state se doosri valid state mein jaata hai: jo bhi rule maine declare kiya, jaise CHECK balance >= 0 ya foreign key, commit pe sach hona chahiye, warna poora transaction reject. Isolation matlab ek saath chal rahe transactions ek doosre ka aadha kaam nahi dekhte, toh transfer ke beech chal rahi report ko dono accounts se ₹500 gaayab nahi dikhte; yeh kitna strict hai woh isolation level pe depend karta hai. Durability matlab COMMIT return hone ke baad change crash mein bhi bachega, kyunki pehle woh disk pe write-ahead log mein flush ho chuka hai. Har guarantee ki keemat hai: durability har commit pe ek disk flush, aur isolation locking ya retries."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Atomicity is implemented differently per engine: InnoDB keeps an undo log to reverse changes, while Postgres simply never makes an aborted transaction's row versions visible. Durability can be traded for speed: Postgres synchronous_commit = off or MySQL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 can lose the last fraction of a second of commits on a crash. With replicas, "durable" may also mean "confirmed by a synchronous replica". And the C in ACID is partly my job: the database enforces only declared constraints; a rule living only in application code is not protected. It's also different from CAP's consistency, which is about replicas agreeing.

Atomicity har engine mein alag implement hoti hai: InnoDB changes ulatne ke liye undo log rakhta hai, jabki Postgres aborted transaction ke row versions ko kabhi visible hi nahi hone deta. Durability ko speed ke liye trade kar sakte ho: Postgres synchronous_commit = off ya MySQL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 crash pe aakhri second ke kuch hisse ke commits kho sakte hain. Replicas ke saath "durable" ka matlab "synchronous replica ne confirm kiya" bhi ho sakta hai. Aur ACID ka C kuch had tak meri zimmedaari hai: database sirf declared constraints enforce karta hai; jo rule sirf application code mein hai woh protected nahi hai. Yeh CAP ki consistency se bhi alag hai, jo replicas ke agree karne ke baare mein hai.

Common mistake: reciting four definitions with no example, or saying consistency means "all replicas have the same data" (that is CAP, not ACID).
Galti mat karna: bina example ke chaar definitions ratna, ya bolna ki consistency matlab "saare replicas mein same data" (woh CAP hai, ACID nahi).
02 What are the 4 isolation levels? What problem does each one prevent?4 isolation levels kaunse hain? Har ek kaunsi problem rokta hai?
What they're really testing: that you can map each level to the anomaly it prevents and know what your database actually defaults to (most default to READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB to REPEATABLE READ).
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum har level ko us anomaly se map kar sakte ho jo woh rokta hai, aur jaante ho ki tumhara database actually kis default pe chalta hai (zyaadatar READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ).

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"The SQL standard defines four, weakest to strongest. READ UNCOMMITTED lets me see other transactions' uncommitted changes, so dirty reads are possible. READ COMMITTED only shows committed data, which prevents dirty reads, but if I read the same row twice I might get different values. REPEATABLE READ guarantees rows I've read don't change under me for the whole transaction, which prevents non-repeatable reads; by the standard, phantoms are still possible. SERIALIZABLE makes the result identical to running transactions one at a time, so it prevents everything, including write skew. Defaults matter: Postgres, Oracle and SQL Server default to READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ. So in a typical Postgres app, a read-modify-write can lose updates unless I use an atomic update or a lock. Going stronger costs throughput: more blocking, or more aborted transactions to retry."

"SQL standard chaar define karta hai, kamzor se strong tak. READ UNCOMMITTED mujhe doosre transactions ke uncommitted changes dikhne deta hai, toh dirty reads possible hain. READ COMMITTED sirf committed data dikhata hai, jo dirty reads rokta hai, lekin agar main same row do baar padhun toh alag values mil sakti hain. REPEATABLE READ guarantee karta hai ki jo rows maine padhi woh poore transaction mein mere neeche nahi badlengi, yeh non-repeatable reads rokta hai; standard ke hisaab se phantoms ab bhi possible hain. SERIALIZABLE result ko waisa hi banata hai jaise transactions ek ek karke chale, toh sab kuch rokta hai, write skew bhi. Defaults important hain: Postgres, Oracle aur SQL Server ka default READ COMMITTED hai; MySQL InnoDB ka REPEATABLE READ. Toh typical Postgres app mein read-modify-write se updates kho sakte hain jab tak main atomic update ya lock use na karun. Strong level ki keemat throughput hai: zyada blocking, ya zyada aborted transactions jinhe retry karna padta hai."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The standard defines levels only by forbidden anomalies; engines implement them with MVCC and differ. Postgres treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, so dirty reads never happen there. Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and also blocks phantoms. MySQL REPEATABLE READ uses a snapshot for plain SELECTs and next-key locks for locking reads. SERIALIZABLE in Postgres is SSI, which aborts with error 40001; in MySQL it turns SELECTs into shared-lock reads. I set it per transaction with BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE in Postgres or SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ... in MySQL, and check it with SHOW transaction_isolation.

Standard levels ko sirf mana ki gayi anomalies se define karta hai; engines inhe MVCC se implement karte hain aur alag hain. Postgres READ UNCOMMITTED ko READ COMMITTED maanta hai, toh wahaan dirty reads kabhi nahi hote. Postgres REPEATABLE READ snapshot isolation hai aur phantoms bhi rokta hai. MySQL REPEATABLE READ plain SELECTs ke liye snapshot aur locking reads ke liye next-key locks use karta hai. Postgres mein SERIALIZABLE SSI hai, jo error 40001 ke saath abort karta hai; MySQL mein yeh SELECTs ko shared-lock reads bana deta hai. Main isko har transaction ke liye set karta hoon, Postgres mein BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE se ya MySQL mein SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ... se, aur SHOW transaction_isolation se check karta hoon.

Common mistake: saying "every database defaults to READ COMMITTED" (MySQL InnoDB is REPEATABLE READ), or not knowing which level your own service runs at.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki "har database ka default READ COMMITTED hai" (MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ hai), ya apni hi service ka level na pata hona.
03 What is a dirty read, phantom read, and non-repeatable read?Dirty read, phantom read aur non-repeatable read kya hote hain?
What they're really testing: crisp definitions with examples: dirty = reading uncommitted data, non-repeatable = same query, different values in one transaction, phantom = new rows appear. And whether you can tell the last two apart.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: examples ke saath saaf definitions: dirty = uncommitted data padhna, non-repeatable = ek transaction mein same query, alag values, phantom = nayi rows aa jaana. Aur kya tum aakhri do ka fark bata sakte ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"They're three ways concurrent transactions can show me inconsistent data. A dirty read is reading data another transaction has written but not committed. If it rolls back, I acted on data that never existed: say I see a balance of zero mid-transfer and decline a payment, then the transfer rolls back. A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values because someone committed an update in between, for example a report that reads a balance at the start and end and the two numbers don't match. A phantom read is rerunning the same range query and getting a different set of rows: 'count transfers above ₹10,000' returns 5, then 6, because someone inserted one. The key difference: non-repeatable is an existing row changing; phantom is rows appearing or disappearing. READ COMMITTED stops dirty reads, REPEATABLE READ stops non-repeatable reads, SERIALIZABLE stops all three."

"Yeh teen tareeke hain jinse concurrent transactions mujhe inconsistent data dikha sakte hain. Dirty read matlab aisa data padhna jo doosre transaction ne likha hai lekin commit nahi kiya. Agar woh rollback ho gaya, toh maine aise data pe action liya jo kabhi tha hi nahi: jaise transfer ke beech mujhe balance zero dikha aur maine payment decline kar di, phir transfer rollback ho gaya. Non-repeatable read matlab ek transaction mein same row do baar padhna aur alag values milna kyunki beech mein kisi ne update commit kar diya, jaise ek report jo shuru aur end mein balance padhti hai aur dono numbers match nahi karte. Phantom read matlab same range query dobara chalaana aur rows ka alag set milna: 'count transfers above ₹10,000' pehle 5 deta hai, phir 6, kyunki kisi ne ek insert kar diya. Main fark: non-repeatable mein existing row badalti hai; phantom mein rows aati ya jaati hain. READ COMMITTED dirty reads rokta hai, REPEATABLE READ non-repeatable reads, SERIALIZABLE teeno."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Phantoms really bite in check-then-insert logic: "is this service bay slot free? If no booking row exists, insert one." Two transactions both see zero rows and both insert, a double booking. Row locks can't help, because there's no row to lock yet. Fixes are a unique constraint on (bay_id, slot_time), SERIALIZABLE, or locking a parent row. MySQL handles phantoms for locking reads with gap and next-key locks, which lock the gaps between index entries so no one can insert into the range. Postgres REPEATABLE READ avoids phantoms because the whole transaction reads one snapshot.

Phantoms asli mein check-then-insert logic mein kaat-te hain: "yeh service bay slot free hai? Agar koi booking row nahi hai, toh insert karo." Dono transactions ko zero rows dikhti hain aur dono insert kar dete hain, double booking. Row locks madad nahi kar sakte, kyunki lock karne ke liye abhi row hai hi nahi. Fixes hain (bay_id, slot_time) pe unique constraint, SERIALIZABLE, ya ek parent row lock karna. MySQL locking reads ke liye phantoms ko gap aur next-key locks se handle karta hai, jo index entries ke beech ke gaps lock karte hain taaki koi range mein insert na kar sake. Postgres REPEATABLE READ phantoms se bachta hai kyunki poora transaction ek hi snapshot padhta hai.

Common mistake: mixing up non-repeatable and phantom reads, or claiming Postgres can show dirty reads (it can't, even at READ UNCOMMITTED).
Galti mat karna: non-repeatable aur phantom reads ko mix karna, ya bolna ki Postgres dirty reads dikha sakta hai (nahi dikha sakta, READ UNCOMMITTED pe bhi nahi).
04 What is a deadlock? How do you detect and prevent one?Deadlock kya hota hai? Isko detect aur prevent kaise karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you know two transactions wait on each other's locks, that the database detects it and kills one, and that prevention means consistent lock ordering, timeouts and short transactions, plus retrying in the app.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum jaante ho ki do transactions ek doosre ke locks ka wait karte hain, database isko detect karke ek ko maar deta hai, aur prevention matlab consistent lock ordering, timeouts aur chhote transactions, saath mein app mein retry.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"A deadlock is when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed. Classic case: two opposite transfers at once. T1 moves money A to B and locks A first; T2 moves money B to A and locks B first. Now T1 waits for B and T2 waits for A, forever. Databases detect this by building a wait-for graph and looking for a cycle; Postgres checks after deadlock_timeout, one second by default, and InnoDB checks immediately. It picks a victim, rolls it back with a deadlock error, and the other one continues. To prevent it, I lock rows in a consistent order, for example lowest account ID first regardless of direction; keep transactions short; lock only what I need, with proper indexes so an UPDATE doesn't lock extra rows; and set lock timeouts. Since you can't eliminate deadlocks completely, the app catches the deadlock error and retries the whole transaction."

"Deadlock tab hota hai jab do transactions mein se har ek ke paas woh lock hai jo doosre ko chahiye, toh koi aage nahi badh sakta. Classic case: ek saath do ulte transfers. T1 A se B paisa bhejta hai aur pehle A lock karta hai; T2 B se A bhejta hai aur pehle B lock karta hai. Ab T1 B ka wait karta hai aur T2 A ka, hamesha ke liye. Databases isko wait-for graph banaake aur usmein cycle dhoondh ke detect karte hain; Postgres deadlock_timeout ke baad check karta hai, default ek second, aur InnoDB turant. Woh ek victim chunta hai, usko deadlock error ke saath rollback karta hai, aur doosra chalta rehta hai. Prevent karne ke liye main rows consistent order mein lock karta hoon, jaise direction kuch bhi ho, chhoti account ID pehle; transactions chhote rakhta hoon; sirf zaroori cheez lock karta hoon, sahi indexes ke saath taaki UPDATE extra rows lock na kare; aur lock timeouts set karta hoon. Deadlocks poori tarah khatam nahi ho sakte, isliye app deadlock error pakadke poora transaction retry karti hai."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Error codes: Postgres SQLSTATE 40P01, MySQL error 1213; InnoDB usually picks the transaction that changed fewer rows as the victim. To debug, Postgres writes both queries to the log, and MySQL's SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS shows the "LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK" section. Hidden causes: a missing index so an UPDATE scans and locks many rows, foreign-key checks taking locks on parent rows, or lock upgrades, where both hold a shared lock and both want exclusive. In code I enforce ordering with WHERE id IN (...) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE. Detection handles cycles; lock_timeout caps any wait, cycle or not.

Error codes: Postgres SQLSTATE 40P01, MySQL error 1213; InnoDB aam taur pe us transaction ko victim chunta hai jisne kam rows badli. Debug ke liye Postgres dono queries log mein likhta hai, aur MySQL ka SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS "LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK" section dikhata hai. Chhupi wajahein: missing index jisse UPDATE scan karke bahut rows lock karta hai, foreign-key checks jo parent rows pe lock lete hain, ya lock upgrades, jahaan dono ke paas shared lock hai aur dono exclusive chahte hain. Code mein ordering main WHERE id IN (...) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE se enforce karta hoon. Detection cycles handle karta hai; lock_timeout kisi bhi wait ko cap karta hai, cycle ho ya na ho.

Common mistake: saying the database just "hangs forever", or forgetting that the application must retry the transaction that was chosen as the victim.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki database bas "hamesha ke liye atak jaata hai", ya bhool jaana ki jo transaction victim bana use application ko retry karna hai.
05 Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?Optimistic vs pessimistic locking mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: pessimistic locks before reading, optimistic reads freely and checks a version on write then retries, and you know optimistic scales better when contention is low.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: pessimistic padhne se pehle lock karta hai, optimistic free padhta hai aur write pe version check karke retry karta hai, aur tum jaante ho ki low contention mein optimistic behtar scale karta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"Both stop two users from overwriting each other on the same row. Pessimistic locking assumes a conflict will happen, so I lock before reading: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction, and anyone else trying to lock that row waits until I commit. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: I read freely along with a version number, and on write I run UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? with the version I read. If zero rows changed, someone got there first, so I re-read and retry or show a conflict. Example: two salespeople editing the same vehicle listing. Optimistic fits perfectly, because conflicts are rare and no lock is held while a human thinks. For a hot row, like the stock count in a flash sale, optimistic would cause a storm of retries, so I'd use an atomic update or a pessimistic lock. Optimistic scales under low contention; pessimistic wins under high contention."

"Dono same row pe do users ko ek doosre ko overwrite karne se rokte hain. Pessimistic locking maanta hai ki conflict hoga, isliye main padhne se pehle lock karta hoon: transaction ke andar SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, aur jo bhi us row ko lock karna chahe woh mere commit tak wait karega. Optimistic locking maanta hai ki conflicts kam hote hain: main version number ke saath free padhta hoon, aur write pe padhe hue version ke saath UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ? chalaata hoon. Agar zero rows badli, matlab koi pehle pahunch gaya, toh main dobara padhke retry karta hoon ya conflict dikhata hoon. Example: do salespeople same vehicle listing edit kar rahe hain. Optimistic perfect hai, kyunki conflicts kam hain aur jab insaan soch raha hai tab koi lock nahi pakda jaata. Hot row ke liye, jaise flash sale mein stock count, optimistic retries ka toofan la dega, toh main atomic update ya pessimistic lock lunga. Low contention mein optimistic scale karta hai; high contention mein pessimistic jeet-ta hai."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Optimistic locking works across HTTP requests: the version travels to the client, often as an ETag, and comes back in an If-Match header, with 412 Precondition Failed on mismatch. Pessimistic locks can't span requests, because they die when the transaction ends. Pessimistic variants: NOWAIT fails instantly instead of waiting, and SKIP LOCKED lets many workers grab different rows from a job table. ORMs support optimistic locking out of the box (JPA @Version, TypeORM @VersionColumn, Sequelize version: true). Using updated_at as the version is risky because two writes can land in the same timestamp. Pessimistic locks also hold a connection and raise deadlock risk.

Optimistic locking HTTP requests ke across kaam karta hai: version client tak jaata hai, aksar ETag ke roop mein, aur If-Match header mein wapas aata hai, mismatch pe 412 Precondition Failed. Pessimistic locks requests ke across nahi chal sakte, kyunki transaction khatam hote hi mar jaate hain. Pessimistic variants: NOWAIT wait karne ki jagah turant fail karta hai, aur SKIP LOCKED bahut workers ko job table se alag alag rows uthaane deta hai. ORMs optimistic locking seedha support karte hain (JPA @Version, TypeORM @VersionColumn, Sequelize version: true). updated_at ko version banana risky hai kyunki do writes same timestamp pe aa sakte hain. Pessimistic locks connection bhi pakde rehte hain aur deadlock risk badhaate hain.

Common mistake: thinking optimistic locking takes a lock (it takes none), or forgetting to check the affected-row count, which makes the version column useless.
Galti mat karna: sochna ki optimistic locking lock leta hai (koi nahi leta), ya affected-row count check karna bhool jaana, jisse version column bekaar ho jaata hai.
06 When would you use SERIALIZABLE and what does it cost?SERIALIZABLE kab use karoge aur uski keemat kya hai?
What they're really testing: that you reserve it for logic that can't tolerate any anomaly (financial), and you know the cost: serialization failures, mandatory retries and lower throughput.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum isko sirf aise logic ke liye rakhte ho jo koi anomaly bardaasht nahi kar sakta (financial), aur keemat jaante ho: serialization failures, zaroori retries aur kam throughput.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"SERIALIZABLE guarantees the outcome is the same as if transactions ran one after another, so no anomalies at all, not even write skew. I use it where any anomaly means lost money or a broken invariant, and the rule spans several rows so one row lock can't protect it. For example, 'a wallet's total withdrawals today across many rows must stay under the limit', or 'at least one doctor must stay on call'. The cost: in Postgres it's Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which tracks read/write dependencies and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure, SQLSTATE 40001, so my code must retry the whole transaction. In MySQL, plain SELECTs become shared-lock reads, which means more blocking and deadlocks. Either way throughput drops as contention rises. So I scope it to the few critical transactions, keep them short, and wrap them in a retry loop with backoff."

"SERIALIZABLE guarantee karta hai ki result waisa hi hoga jaise transactions ek ke baad ek chale, toh koi anomaly nahi, write skew bhi nahi. Main isko wahaan use karta hoon jahaan koi bhi anomaly matlab paisa khona ya toota hua invariant, aur rule kai rows pe faila hai toh ek row lock usko protect nahi kar sakta. Jaise, 'wallet ke aaj ke total withdrawals, kai rows milake, limit se neeche rehne chahiye', ya 'kam se kam ek doctor on call rehna chahiye'. Keemat: Postgres mein yeh Serializable Snapshot Isolation hai, jo read/write dependencies track karta hai aur ek transaction ko serialization failure, SQLSTATE 40001, ke saath abort karta hai, toh mera code poora transaction retry karega. MySQL mein plain SELECTs shared-lock reads ban jaate hain, matlab zyada blocking aur deadlocks. Dono tarah contention badhne pe throughput girta hai. Isliye main isko sirf kuch critical transactions tak rakhta hoon, unhe chhota rakhta hoon, aur backoff wale retry loop mein wrap karta hoon."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Write skew is the anomaly that justifies it: two transactions read the same condition and each updates a different row, so no row-level conflict exists. Often there are cheaper fixes: an atomic update with a condition in the WHERE, a unique or exclusion constraint, or "materializing the conflict" by locking a shared parent row with FOR UPDATE. For long reports in Postgres, SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE waits for a safe snapshot and then never aborts. Because retries re-run the whole transaction, no side effects like emails or HTTP calls may live inside it. I'd also monitor the 40001 rate as a contention signal.

Write skew woh anomaly hai jiske liye yeh zaroori hai: do transactions same condition padhte hain aur har ek alag row update karta hai, toh row-level conflict hota hi nahi. Aksar sasti fixes hoti hain: WHERE mein condition ke saath atomic update, unique ya exclusion constraint, ya ek shared parent row ko FOR UPDATE se lock karke "conflict ko materialize karna". Postgres mein lambi reports ke liye SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE ek safe snapshot ka wait karta hai aur phir kabhi abort nahi hota. Kyunki retries poora transaction dobara chalaate hain, andar emails ya HTTP calls jaise side effects nahi hone chahiye. Main 40001 ki rate ko contention signal ki tarah monitor bhi karunga.

Common mistake: switching the whole app to SERIALIZABLE "to be safe" without adding retry logic, which just turns into random 40001 errors in production.
Galti mat karna: poori app ko "safe rehne ke liye" SERIALIZABLE pe daal dena bina retry logic ke, jo production mein bas random 40001 errors ban jaata hai.
07 What is a two-phase commit and what problem does it solve?Two-phase commit kya hai aur yeh kaunsi problem solve karta hai?
What they're really testing: prepare (everyone agrees) then commit (everyone executes), that it gives atomicity across distributed resources, and that it costs latency and can block.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: prepare (sab agree karein) phir commit (sab execute karein), yeh distributed resources ke across atomicity deta hai, aur iski keemat latency hai aur yeh block kar sakta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"Two-phase commit solves atomicity across more than one database or resource, because a normal transaction can't span two databases. Say a transfer debits a payments database and credits a separate ledger database. A coordinator runs two phases. In phase one, prepare, it asks every participant 'can you commit?'. Each does all its work, writes it durably, keeps its locks and votes yes or no. In phase two, if everyone voted yes, the coordinator logs the decision and tells all of them to commit; if anyone said no or timed out, it tells all to roll back. Postgres supports this with PREPARE TRANSACTION and COMMIT PREPARED; MySQL with XA. The trade-offs are latency, from extra round trips and disk flushes, and blocking: if the coordinator dies after the prepare phase, participants sit 'in doubt' holding locks until it recovers. That's why microservices usually prefer sagas with compensating actions."

"Two-phase commit ek se zyada database ya resource ke across atomicity solve karta hai, kyunki normal transaction do databases ko cover nahi kar sakta. Maano ek transfer payments database se debit karta hai aur ek alag ledger database mein credit. Ek coordinator do phases chalaata hai. Phase one, prepare, mein woh har participant se poochta hai 'commit kar sakte ho?'. Har ek apna poora kaam karta hai, durably likhta hai, locks rakhta hai aur yes ya no vote karta hai. Phase two mein, agar sabne yes bola, coordinator decision log karta hai aur sabko commit bolta hai; agar kisi ne no bola ya timeout hua, sabko rollback bolta hai. Postgres isko PREPARE TRANSACTION aur COMMIT PREPARED se support karta hai; MySQL XA se. Trade-offs hain latency, extra round trips aur disk flushes ki wajah se, aur blocking: agar prepare phase ke baad coordinator mar gaya, participants locks pakde 'in doubt' baithe rehte hain jab tak woh recover na ho. Isiliye microservices aam taur pe compensating actions wale sagas prefer karte hain."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The key rule: after voting yes, a participant gives up the right to decide alone, so the coordinator must durably log its decision before phase two. Three-phase commit tries to remove blocking but assumes bounded network delays, which real networks don't give. Systems like Google Spanner make it practical by running 2PC across participants that are each a consensus-replicated group, so no single machine failure blocks. In Postgres, max_prepared_transactions is 0 by default, and an orphaned prepared transaction holds locks and blocks VACUUM until someone resolves it. The saga alternative is a sequence of local transactions with compensations, such as a refund, plus an outbox table to publish events reliably, accepting eventual consistency.

Main rule: yes vote ke baad participant akele decide karne ka haq chhod deta hai, isliye coordinator ko phase two se pehle apna decision durably log karna padta hai. Three-phase commit blocking hataane ki koshish karta hai lekin maanta hai ki network delays bounded hain, jo real networks nahi dete. Google Spanner jaise systems isko practical banaate hain: 2PC aise participants pe chalta hai jinmein har ek consensus-replicated group hai, toh ek machine fail hone se block nahi hota. Postgres mein max_prepared_transactions default 0 hai, aur ek anaath (orphaned) prepared transaction locks pakde rehta hai aur VACUUM rokta hai jab tak koi usko resolve na kare. Saga alternative local transactions ka sequence hai compensations ke saath, jaise refund, plus events reliably publish karne ke liye outbox table, eventual consistency accept karte hue.

Common mistake: describing 2PC as "committing twice", confusing it with sagas, or presenting it as free and ignoring the blocking problem.
Galti mat karna: 2PC ko "do baar commit karna" batana, isko sagas se confuse karna, ya isko free bataana aur blocking problem ignore karna.
08 What is a savepoint? When would you use one?Savepoint kya hai? Isko kab use karoge?
What they're really testing: that a savepoint is a rollback point inside a transaction, used to handle a partial failure without throwing away all the work.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: savepoint transaction ke andar ek rollback point hai, jo poora kaam phenke bina partial failure handle karne ke liye use hota hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"A savepoint is a bookmark inside a transaction that I can roll back to without discarding the whole transaction. SAVEPOINT name marks the spot, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name undoes only the work after it, and RELEASE SAVEPOINT drops the bookmark. I use it for partial-failure handling. Example: when creating an order, I insert the order and its items, then try to add a loyalty-points bonus. If the bonus insert fails, say with a duplicate-key error because the bonus was already given, I roll back to the savepoint and still commit the order. It matters extra in Postgres, because after any error the whole transaction is marked aborted and rejects every further command; a savepoint is the only way to recover and carry on. ORMs also use savepoints to implement nested transactions. The trade-off is a bit of overhead per savepoint."

"Savepoint transaction ke andar ek bookmark hai jahaan tak main rollback kar sakta hoon bina poora transaction phenke. SAVEPOINT name jagah mark karta hai, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name sirf uske baad ka kaam undo karta hai, aur RELEASE SAVEPOINT bookmark hata deta hai. Main isko partial-failure handling ke liye use karta hoon. Example: order banaate waqt main order aur uske items insert karta hoon, phir loyalty-points bonus add karne ki koshish karta hoon. Agar bonus insert fail hua, jaise duplicate-key error kyunki bonus pehle hi mil chuka tha, toh main savepoint tak rollback karta hoon aur phir bhi order commit karta hoon. Postgres mein yeh aur zaroori hai, kyunki koi bhi error aane pe poora transaction aborted mark ho jaata hai aur har agla command reject karta hai; savepoint hi recover karke aage badhne ka tareeka hai. ORMs bhi nested transactions ke liye savepoints use karte hain. Trade-off yeh hai ki har savepoint ka thoda overhead hai."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

A savepoint never commits anything early: if the outer transaction rolls back, everything goes, including work under a released savepoint. For bulk imports you can put a savepoint around each row to skip bad rows, but in Postgres each savepoint is a subtransaction, and heavy use (many open subtransactions in one transaction) has known performance costs, so for large batches I'd rather validate first or commit in small chunks. psql's ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK setting works by silently adding a savepoint before every statement. Nested transaction() calls in Sequelize, TypeORM or Django usually become savepoints under the hood.

Savepoint kabhi kuch jaldi commit nahi karta: agar outer transaction rollback hua toh sab jaata hai, released savepoint ke neeche ka kaam bhi. Bulk imports mein har row ke around savepoint lagaake kharab rows skip kar sakte ho, lekin Postgres mein har savepoint ek subtransaction hai, aur heavy use (ek transaction mein bahut saare khule subtransactions) ki performance keemat jaani-maani hai, isliye bade batches ke liye main pehle validate karna ya chhote chunks mein commit karna prefer karunga. psql ki ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK setting har statement se pehle chupchaap savepoint lagaake kaam karti hai. Sequelize, TypeORM ya Django mein nested transaction() calls aam taur pe andar se savepoints hi bante hain.

Common mistake: thinking RELEASE SAVEPOINT makes that part permanent; nothing is permanent until the outer COMMIT.
Galti mat karna: sochna ki RELEASE SAVEPOINT us hisse ko permanent kar deta hai; outer COMMIT tak kuch bhi permanent nahi hai.
09 What is a lost update and which isolation level prevents it?Lost update kya hai aur kaunsa isolation level isko rokta hai?
What they're really testing: two transactions read the same row and both write back stale values; REPEATABLE READ or higher (engine-dependent) or optimistic locking prevents it.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: do transactions same row padhte hain aur dono purani values wapas likhte hain; REPEATABLE READ ya usse upar (engine pe depend) ya optimistic locking isko rokta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"A lost update is when two transactions read the same row, each computes a new value from what it read, and both write back, so the second write silently overwrites the first. Balance is 100; T1 reads 100, adds a 50 refund and writes 150; T2 also read 100, subtracts a 30 bill and writes 70. The final balance is 70, and the refund is gone. It happens at READ COMMITTED, which is Postgres's default. In Postgres, REPEATABLE READ prevents it: T2 gets 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' and must retry. SERIALIZABLE prevents it everywhere. But MySQL's REPEATABLE READ does not prevent it for a plain read-then-write, because the UPDATE acts on the latest row.
