The practical fixes at any level: do the math in the database with SET balance = balance + 50, which is atomic; or lock with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; or use optimistic locking with a version column."

"Lost update tab hota hai jab do transactions same row padhte hain, har ek padhi hui value se nayi value calculate karta hai, aur dono wapas likhte hain, toh doosra write chupchaap pehle ko overwrite kar deta hai. Balance 100 hai; T1 100 padhta hai, 50 ka refund jodta hai aur 150 likhta hai; T2 ne bhi 100 padha tha, 30 ka bill ghataata hai aur 70 likhta hai. Final balance 70, aur refund gaayab. Yeh READ COMMITTED pe hota hai, jo Postgres ka default hai. Postgres mein REPEATABLE READ isko rokta hai: T2 ko 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' milta hai aur usko retry karna hota hai. SERIALIZABLE isko har jagah rokta hai. Lekin MySQL ka REPEATABLE READ plain read-then-write mein isko nahi rokta, kyunki UPDATE latest row pe kaam karta hai. Kisi bhi level pe practical fixes: hisaab database mein karo SET balance = balance + 50 se, jo atomic hai; ya SELECT ... FOR UPDATE se lock karo; ya version column ke saath optimistic locking."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The atomic update works because the row lock is taken inside the statement and the new value is computed from the current committed row, not a stale copy in app memory. In Postgres READ COMMITTED, if the UPDATE had to wait for another writer, it re-checks its WHERE against the newest row version before applying. Some lost updates can't be fixed by any isolation level: two users open the same edit form over HTTP and both save. Those are separate transactions minutes apart, so you need a version column or ETag. ORMs that "load entity, change a field, save the whole entity" are a classic source of lost updates.

Atomic update isliye kaam karta hai kyunki row lock statement ke andar hi liya jaata hai aur nayi value current committed row se calculate hoti hai, app memory ki purani copy se nahi. Postgres READ COMMITTED mein, agar UPDATE ko doosre writer ka wait karna pada, toh apply karne se pehle woh apna WHERE newest row version pe dobara check karta hai. Kuch lost updates kisi isolation level se fix nahi hote: do users HTTP pe same edit form kholte hain aur dono save karte hain. Woh minutes ke gap wale alag transactions hain, toh version column ya ETag chahiye. Jo ORMs "entity load karo, ek field badlo, poori entity save karo" karte hain woh lost updates ka classic source hain.

Common mistake: answering "just wrap it in a transaction"; the lost update happens inside transactions at READ COMMITTED, so a transaction alone fixes nothing.
Galti mat karna: jawab dena "bas transaction mein daal do"; lost update READ COMMITTED pe transactions ke andar hi hota hai, toh akela transaction kuch fix nahi karta.
10 How do long-running transactions cause problems in production?Long-running transactions production mein problems kaise create karte hain?
What they're really testing: that you know long transactions hold locks, block cleanup (VACUUM), cause bloat, increase deadlock risk and block writers, and that you can find and prevent them.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum jaante ho ki long transactions locks pakde rehte hain, cleanup (VACUUM) rokte hain, bloat karte hain, deadlock risk badhaate hain aur writers ko block karte hain, aur tum inhe dhoondh aur rok sakte ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"A long transaction, or a connection left 'idle in transaction', hurts in several ways. First, it holds its row locks until it ends, so other writers queue behind it and requests time out. Second, in MVCC databases it blocks cleanup: Postgres VACUUM can't remove dead row versions that the old snapshot might still need, so tables and indexes bloat and every query slows down; in MySQL the undo history grows. Third, the longer locks are held, the higher the deadlock risk. Fourth, a migration like ALTER TABLE waits for its lock, and then every normal query queues behind the waiting ALTER, so a tiny migration can freeze a table. It also pins a pooled connection. The usual cause is doing slow work inside the transaction, like calling a payment API. So I keep transactions short, do slow work outside them, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout."

"Ek long transaction, ya 'idle in transaction' mein chhoda hua connection, kai tarah se nuksaan karta hai. Pehla, woh khatam hone tak apne row locks pakde rehta hai, toh doosre writers uske peeche line lagate hain aur requests timeout hoti hain. Doosra, MVCC databases mein woh cleanup rokta hai: Postgres VACUUM woh dead row versions nahi hata sakta jo purani snapshot ko shayad chahiye, toh tables aur indexes bloat hote hain aur har query slow hoti hai; MySQL mein undo history badhti hai. Teesra, locks jitni der pakde rahein, deadlock risk utna zyada. Chautha, ALTER TABLE jaisa migration apne lock ka wait karta hai, aur phir har normal query us waiting ALTER ke peeche line mein lagti hai, toh chhota sa migration table freeze kar sakta hai. Yeh pool ka ek connection bhi atkaata hai. Aam wajah hai transaction ke andar slow kaam, jaise payment API call. Isliye main transactions chhote rakhta hoon, slow kaam bahar karta hoon, aur idle_in_transaction_session_timeout aur statement_timeout set karta hoon."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

To find them in Postgres I query pg_stat_activity ordered by xact_start and look for 'idle in transaction'; in MySQL, information_schema.innodb_trx and the history list length in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS. Replicas matter too: long queries on a replica with hot_standby_feedback on hold back cleanup on the primary. For migrations I set a short lock_timeout so the ALTER gives up and retries instead of blocking everyone. Big backfills should run in chunks of a few thousand rows per transaction, not one giant transaction. Even a read-only transaction holds back VACUUM in Postgres, because its snapshot pins old versions.

Postgres mein inhe dhoondhne ke liye main pg_stat_activity ko xact_start se order karke query karta hoon aur 'idle in transaction' dekhta hoon; MySQL mein information_schema.innodb_trx aur SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS mein history list length. Replicas bhi matter karte hain: agar replica pe hot_standby_feedback on hai toh wahaan ki lambi queries primary pe cleanup rok deti hain. Migrations ke liye main chhota lock_timeout set karta hoon taaki ALTER sabko block karne ki jagah haar maan ke retry kare. Bade backfills ek giant transaction mein nahi, har transaction mein kuch hazaar rows ke chunks mein chalne chahiye. Postgres mein read-only transaction bhi VACUUM rokta hai, kyunki uski snapshot purane versions ko pakde rakhti hai.

Common mistake: assuming a long read-only transaction is harmless; in Postgres it still stops VACUUM and causes bloat.
Galti mat karna: maan lena ki lamba read-only transaction harmless hai; Postgres mein woh bhi VACUUM rokta hai aur bloat karta hai.

Topic 03 · VERY COMMONTopic 03 · Bahut common

ConcurrencyConcurrency

What really happens when two requests hit the same line of code in the same millisecond, why it sells one train seat twice, and the handful of tools (atomic operations, pools, locks, rate limiters) that make it safe.

Jab do requests same millisecond mein code ki same line pe pahunchti hain toh asal mein kya hota hai, ek train seat do baar kyun bik jaati hai, aur woh chand tools (atomic operations, pools, locks, rate limiters) jo isko safe banaate hain.

Level 0 The storyKahani

It is 9:59:58 AM. Tatkal booking for tomorrow's Rajdhani opens at 10:00. Lakhs of people across India have the IRCTC page open, fingers on the mouse. At 10:00:00 they all click at once.

Deep inside, the booking code is simple. For each request it does three things: read how many seats are left, check that the number is more than zero, and write back the number minus one, then issue the ticket. With one customer at a time this is perfect.

Now there is exactly one seat left, and Aman in Delhi and Bhavna in Pune click "Book" in the same millisecond. Aman's request reads "1 seat left". Before it can write, Bhavna's request also reads "1 seat left". Both check "1 is more than 0, fine". Both write "0". Both get a confirmed ticket. One seat, two passengers, one very unpleasant scene at the train door.

Nobody wrote a wrong line of code. Each request was correct on its own. The bug exists only in the timing between them, which is why it never appears when you test alone on your laptop and always appears at 10:00 AM in production. That is a race condition, and this whole topic is about taming it.

The same Tatkal rush raises four more questions this chapter answers. How does one server handle lakhs of requests at once? How do those requests share a limited number of database connections? When IRCTC runs on many servers, how do they agree that only one of them does a certain job? And how do you stop one bot from firing 10,000 requests a second?

Analogy: a single whiteboard in the society office says "Parking passes left: 1". Two residents walk in at the same moment, both read "1", both write "0", and both walk out with a pass. The whiteboard now says the right number, 0, and still two passes went out. The number looks fine; the damage is invisible.

Subah ke 9:59:58 hain. Kal ki Rajdhani ki Tatkal booking 10:00 baje khulegi. Poore India mein lakhs log IRCTC ka page khol ke, mouse pe ungli rakh ke baithe hain. 10:00:00 pe sab ek saath click karte hain.

Andar booking ka code simple hai. Har request ke liye teen kaam: padho kitni seats bachi hain, check karo ki number zero se zyada hai, aur likho number minus one, phir ticket issue karo. Ek time pe ek customer ho toh yeh perfect hai.

Ab bilkul ek seat bachi hai, aur Delhi mein Aman aur Pune mein Bhavna same millisecond mein "Book" click karte hain. Aman ki request padhti hai "1 seat bachi hai". Woh likh paaye usse pehle Bhavna ki request bhi padhti hai "1 seat bachi hai". Dono check karti hain "1, 0 se zyada hai, theek". Dono "0" likhti hain. Dono ko confirmed ticket mil jaata hai. Ek seat, do passengers, aur train ke darwaaze pe ek bahut bura scene.

Kisi ne code ki galat line nahi likhi. Har request akele sahi thi. Bug sirf dono ke beech ki timing mein hai, isiliye laptop pe akele test karne pe kabhi nahi dikhta aur production mein 10:00 baje hamesha dikhta hai. Isko race condition kehte hain, aur yeh poora topic isi ko kaabu karne ke baare mein hai.

Yahi Tatkal rush chaar aur sawaal khade karta hai jinke jawab is chapter mein hain. Ek server ek saath lakhs requests kaise handle karta hai? Woh requests limited database connections kaise share karti hain? Jab IRCTC bahut saare servers pe chalta hai, toh woh kaise agree karte hain ki ek kaam sirf unmein se ek hi kare? Aur ek bot ko ek second mein 10,000 requests bhejne se kaise roko?

Analogy: society office mein ek whiteboard pe likha hai "Parking passes bache: 1". Do residents same moment pe andar aate hain, dono "1" padhte hain, dono "0" likhte hain, aur dono pass le ke nikal jaate hain. Whiteboard pe ab sahi number hai, 0, phir bhi do passes chale gaye. Number theek dikhta hai; nuksaan dikhta hi nahi.

Level 1 The basic idea: shared state, races, concurrency vs parallelismBasic idea: shared state, races, concurrency vs parallelism

Quick recap of words from the foundations chapter. A process is a running program with its own memory. A thread is a worker inside a process; threads in one process share its memory. A request is one message from a user's browser or app asking the server to do something.

Shared state is any data that more than one request can touch: a row in the database, a key in Redis, a variable in your server's memory. Concurrency bugs only happen around shared state.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the exact timing or order in which concurrent operations run. The most common shape is read-modify-write: read a value, change it in your code, write it back. Its cousin is check-then-act: check a condition ("seat free?"), then act on it ("book it"), while the condition may have changed in between. The stretch of code that must not be run by two requests at once is called the critical section.

Foundations chapter ke words ka quick recap. Process ek chalta hua program hai jiski apni memory hai. Thread process ke andar ka ek worker hai; ek process ke threads uski memory share karte hain. Request user ke browser ya app se aaya ek message hai jo server se kuch karne ko kehta hai.

Shared state koi bhi data hai jisko ek se zyada requests touch kar sakti hain: database ki ek row, Redis ki ek key, tumhare server ki memory ka ek variable. Concurrency bugs sirf shared state ke aas paas hote hain.

Race condition ek bug hai jismein result is baat pe depend karta hai ki concurrent operations kis exact timing ya order mein chale. Sabse common shape hai read-modify-write: value padho, code mein badlo, wapas likho. Iska cousin hai check-then-act: condition check karo ("seat free hai?"), phir us pe action lo ("book karo"), jabki beech mein condition badal sakti hai. Code ka woh hissa jisko do requests ek saath nahi chala sakti, usko critical section kehte hain.

Concurrency vs parallelism. These two words sound alike and interviewers love to test them.

  • Concurrency means dealing with many tasks at once by interleaving them: start one, pause it while it waits, work on another, come back. One worker can be concurrent.
  • Parallelism means doing many tasks at literally the same instant, which needs several workers, for example several CPU cores.

Analogy: one chaiwala with four customers puts milk on the stove, and while it boils he crushes ginger for the second order, then takes payment from the third. He is concurrent: many orders in progress, one pair of hands. Hire a second chaiwala at another stove and now two cups are made at the same instant: that is parallel. A concurrent system can run on one core; a parallel one needs more than one.

Node.js, which you met in foundations, runs your JavaScript on one main thread. So Node is concurrent but not parallel for your JavaScript code. It can have ten thousand requests "in progress", but at any single instant only one line of your JavaScript runs. Hold on to that; Level 2 shows how it works and why it still has race conditions.

Concurrency vs parallelism. Yeh do words sunne mein same lagte hain aur interviewers inhe test karna pasand karte hain.

  • Concurrency matlab bahut saare tasks ko interleave karke ek saath sambhaalna: ek shuru karo, jab woh kisi cheez ka wait kare toh rok do, doosre pe kaam karo, wapas aao. Ek worker bhi concurrent ho sakta hai.
  • Parallelism matlab bahut saare tasks ko literally same instant pe karna, jiske liye kai workers chahiye, jaise kai CPU cores.

Analogy: ek chaiwala ke paas chaar customers hain. Woh stove pe doodh chadhaata hai, aur jab tak doodh ubal raha hai, doosre order ke liye adrak kootata hai, phir teesre se paise leta hai. Woh concurrent hai: kai orders chal rahe hain, haath ek hi jodi. Doosre stove pe ek aur chaiwala rakh lo, ab do cup same instant pe ban rahe hain: yeh parallel hai. Concurrent system ek core pe chal sakta hai; parallel ko ek se zyada chahiye.

Node.js, jo tumne foundations mein dekha, tumhari JavaScript ko ek main thread pe chalaata hai. Toh tumhare JavaScript code ke liye Node concurrent hai, parallel nahi. Uske paas das hazaar requests "chal rahi" ho sakti hain, lekin kisi bhi ek instant pe tumhari JavaScript ki sirf ek line chalti hai. Yeh yaad rakho; Level 2 dikhata hai ki yeh kaise kaam karta hai aur phir bhi race conditions kyun hoti hain.

Level 2 How it works inside: the event loop and atomic operationsAndar kaise kaam karta hai: event loop aur atomic operations

How can one thread serve thousands of requests? Because a backend request spends most of its life waiting: for the database to reply, for Redis, for a payment gateway over the network. Waiting needs no CPU. Node's trick is to never sit and wait. It is built from four pieces:

  • Call stack: the list of JavaScript functions currently running on the one main thread. Only one thing runs at a time.
  • OS / libuv: libuv is the C library under Node. When your code asks for I/O (input/output: network, disk, timers), Node hands the job to the operating system, which can watch thousands of network sockets at once. For work the OS can't do asynchronously (file system, DNS lookup, some crypto, compression) libuv has a small thread pool, 4 threads by default.
  • Callback queue: when an I/O job finishes, the function you said should run "when it's done" (the callback, or the rest of your async function after an await) is put in a queue.
  • Event loop: a loop that keeps asking "is the call stack empty? then take the next callback from the queue and run it".

This is called non-blocking I/O: starting an I/O operation returns immediately, and your code continues when the result arrives.

Ek thread hazaaron requests kaise serve kar sakta hai? Kyunki ek backend request apni zindagi ka zyaadatar hissa wait karne mein bitaati hai: database ke reply ka, Redis ka, network pe payment gateway ka. Wait karne mein CPU nahi lagta. Node ki trick yeh hai ki woh kabhi baith ke wait nahi karta. Yeh chaar pieces se bana hai:

  • Call stack: un JavaScript functions ki list jo abhi ek main thread pe chal rahe hain. Ek time pe sirf ek cheez chalti hai.
  • OS / libuv: libuv Node ke neeche ki C library hai. Jab tumhara code I/O maangta hai (input/output: network, disk, timers), Node woh kaam operating system ko de deta hai, jo ek saath hazaaron network sockets pe nazar rakh sakta hai. Jo kaam OS asynchronously nahi kar sakta (file system, DNS lookup, kuch crypto, compression) uske liye libuv ke paas ek chhota thread pool hai, default 4 threads.
  • Callback queue: jab I/O kaam khatam hota hai, toh jo function tumne kaha tha "ho jaaye tab chalana" (callback, ya await ke baad tumhare async function ka baaki hissa) woh ek queue mein daal diya jaata hai.
  • Event loop: ek loop jo baar baar poochta hai "call stack khaali hai? toh queue se agla callback uthao aur chalao".

Isko non-blocking I/O kehte hain: I/O operation shuru karna turant return karta hai, aur result aane pe tumhara code aage chalta hai.

The weak spot: if your JavaScript does heavy CPU-bound work (a long loop, resizing an image, hashing a password synchronously, parsing a 200 MB JSON), the call stack is busy and the event loop cannot run anything else. Every other user waits. The fixes are to move that work to worker_threads (real extra threads in Node), run several Node processes with cluster or PM2 (one per CPU core, which gives parallelism), or send it to a separate job worker.

Kamzor jagah: agar tumhari JavaScript bhaari CPU-bound kaam karti hai (lamba loop, image resize, password ko synchronously hash karna, 200 MB ka JSON parse), toh call stack busy hai aur event loop kuch aur nahi chala sakta. Baaki har user wait karta hai. Fix hai woh kaam worker_threads pe bhejna (Node mein asli extra threads), cluster ya PM2 se kai Node processes chalaana (har CPU core ke liye ek, jisse parallelism milta hai), ya usko alag job worker ko bhej dena.

// Non-blocking: while the DB works, the thread serves other requests
app.get('/pnr/:id', async (req, res) => {
  const result = await db.query('SELECT * FROM bookings WHERE pnr = $1', [req.params.id]);
  res.json(result.rows[0]);
});

// Blocking: pure CPU work. For these seconds, NOBODY else is served.
app.get('/report', (req, res) => {
  let total = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 5e9; i++) total += i;   // the event loop is stuck here
  res.json({ total });
});

Trap: "Node is single-threaded, so it can't have race conditions." Wrong. Every await is a pause point where the event loop may run another request's code. If you read the seat count, await something, then write, another request can slip in between. And in production you run several Node processes on several servers anyway, all touching the same database.

Trap: "Node single-threaded hai, isliye usmein race conditions nahi ho sakti." Galat. Har await ek pause point hai jahaan event loop kisi aur request ka code chala sakta hai. Agar tumne seat count padha, kuch await kiya, phir likha, toh beech mein doosri request ghus sakti hai. Aur production mein tum waise bhi kai servers pe kai Node processes chalaate ho, sab same database ko touch karte hue.

// BAD: read-modify-write across an await. Two requests interleave here.
app.post('/book', async (req, res) => {
  const { rows } = await db.query('SELECT seats_left FROM trains WHERE id = $1', [req.body.trainId]);
  const left = rows[0].seats_left;
  if (left > 0) {
    // another request can run its SELECT right here and also see left = 1
    await db.query('UPDATE trains SET seats_left = $1 WHERE id = $2', [left - 1, req.body.trainId]);
    return res.json({ booked: true });
  }
  res.status(409).json({ booked: false, reason: 'sold out' });
});

The cure: atomic operations. An operation is atomic if it happens as one indivisible step: nobody can observe or interfere with it halfway. The fix for the seat bug is to stop doing read, check and write as three separate steps in your code, and hand all three to the database as one statement. The database takes a row lock, checks the condition and decrements, all as one step. Two requests cannot both succeed on the last seat.

Ilaaj: atomic operations. Ek operation atomic hai agar woh ek hi, na tootne waale step mein hota hai: koi usko beech mein dekh ya chhed nahi sakta. Seat bug ka fix yeh hai ki padhna, check karna aur likhna apne code mein teen alag steps mein karna band karo, aur teeno database ko ek statement ke roop mein de do. Database row lock leta hai, condition check karta hai aur ghataata hai, sab ek step mein. Aakhri seat pe do requests dono succeed nahi kar sakti.

// GOOD: one atomic statement; the DB checks and decrements under a row lock
app.post('/book', async (req, res) => {
  const result = await db.query(
    'UPDATE trains SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND seats_left > 0',
    [req.body.trainId]
  );
  if (result.rowCount === 1) return res.json({ booked: true });
  res.status(409).json({ booked: false, reason: 'sold out' });
});

Redis (the fast in-memory key-value store from foundations) has atomic commands too. Redis executes commands one at a time on a single thread, so a single command like INCR (add 1 and return the new value) can never be interleaved with another command. But two separate commands (a GET then a SET from your code) are not atomic together; another client's command can run in between. To make a multi-step operation atomic in Redis you use a MULTI/EXEC block or a small Lua script, which Redis runs start-to-finish without interruption.

Redis (foundations wala fast in-memory key-value store) mein bhi atomic commands hain. Redis commands ek ek karke ek hi thread pe chalaata hai, isliye INCR jaisa single command (1 jodo aur nayi value return karo) kabhi kisi aur command ke saath interleave nahi ho sakta. Lekin do alag commands (tumhare code se pehle GET phir SET) saath mein atomic nahi hain; beech mein kisi aur client ka command chal sakta hai. Redis mein multi-step operation ko atomic banane ke liye MULTI/EXEC block ya chhota sa Lua script use karte ho, jisko Redis shuru se end tak bina rukawat chalaata hai.

INCR   views:train:12951           # atomic +1, returns the new count
INCRBY cashback:user:42 50         # atomic +50
DECR   stock:sku:CHAI-1KG          # atomic -1 (check the result is not below 0)

Remember: never read-increment-write in application code. Push the whole change into one atomic operation: UPDATE ... SET x = x + 1, WHERE ... AND x > 0, Redis INCR, or a Lua script.

Yaad rakho: application code mein kabhi read-increment-write mat karo. Poora change ek atomic operation mein daalo: UPDATE ... SET x = x + 1, WHERE ... AND x > 0, Redis INCR, ya ek Lua script.

Level 3 Real production: connection pools, mutexes, semaphores, distributed locks, rate limitsReal production: connection pools, mutexes, semaphores, distributed locks, rate limits

Connection pools. To talk to Postgres or MySQL, your server needs a connection: a live network channel with the database. Opening one is expensive: a TCP handshake, often a TLS (encryption) handshake, a login check, and in Postgres the database even starts a separate process for each connection. That can take several milliseconds or more, far longer than a simple query. And the database allows only a limited number at once (Postgres max_connections defaults to 100; MySQL's max_connections defaults to 151).

If every request opened its own connection, at 10:00 AM you would pay that setup cost on every request and then hit the limit: the database starts refusing with errors like "too many clients already", and it slows down from the memory each connection uses. A connection pool fixes this. At startup you open a small set of connections and keep them. Each request borrows one, runs its query and returns it. If all are busy, new requests wait in a short queue instead of opening more.

Connection pools. Postgres ya MySQL se baat karne ke liye tumhare server ko ek connection chahiye: database ke saath ek live network channel. Ek kholna mehenga hai: TCP handshake, aksar TLS (encryption) handshake, login check, aur Postgres mein toh database har connection ke liye ek alag process shuru karta hai. Isme kai milliseconds ya zyada lag sakte hain, ek simple query se kahin zyada. Aur database ek saath limited connections hi allow karta hai (Postgres ka max_connections default 100; MySQL ka max_connections default 151).

Agar har request apna connection kholti, toh 10:00 baje tum har request pe setup ki keemat chukaate aur phir limit se takraate: database "too many clients already" jaise errors ke saath mana karne lagta hai, aur har connection ki memory se slow ho jaata hai. Connection pool isko fix karta hai. Startup pe tum connections ka ek chhota set kholte ho aur rakh lete ho. Har request ek udhaar leti hai, query chalaati hai aur wapas kar deti hai. Agar saare busy hain, nayi requests zyada kholne ki jagah ek chhoti queue mein wait karti hain.

import pg from 'pg';

// Create the pool ONCE at startup and share it across all requests
const pool = new pg.Pool({
  max: 10,                        // at most 10 open connections from this instance
  idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,       // close connections idle for 30 s
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000,  // fail fast if no connection frees up within 2 s
});

app.get('/trains/:id', async (req, res) => {
  // pool.query borrows a connection and returns it automatically
  const { rows } = await pool.query('SELECT * FROM trains WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]);
  res.json(rows[0]);
});

Sizing rule: number of app instances × pool max must stay below the database's connection limit, with headroom for admin tools and migrations. Ten instances with max: 20 is 200 connections, already over Postgres's default of 100. Bigger is not faster: a database with a few CPU cores can only truly run a few queries at a time, and extra connections just fight each other.

Locks inside one process: mutex and semaphore. Sometimes you need to protect a critical section in your own code, not in the database.

  • A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) lets exactly one holder into the critical section. Whoever locked it must unlock it. Think of a single-key washroom at a petrol pump: one key, one person inside, everyone else waits, and only the person with the key brings it back.
  • A semaphore is a counter that lets up to N holders in at once. Think of a parking lot with 3 slots and a board showing free slots. Each car that enters decrements the count; each that leaves increments it; at 0, new cars wait.

Sizing rule: app instances ki ginti × pool max database ki connection limit se neeche rehna chahiye, admin tools aur migrations ke liye jagah chhod ke. Das instances max: 20 ke saath matlab 200 connections, jo Postgres ke default 100 se pehle hi zyada hai. Bada matlab fast nahi: kuch CPU cores wala database ek time pe sach mein kuch hi queries chala sakta hai, extra connections bas aapas mein ladte hain.

Ek process ke andar locks: mutex aur semaphore. Kabhi kabhi tumhe database nahi, apne khud ke code ka critical section protect karna hota hai.

  • Mutex (mutual exclusion lock) critical section mein exactly ek holder ko andar jaane deta hai. Jisne lock kiya wahi unlock karega. Petrol pump ka ek-chaabi wala washroom socho: ek chaabi, andar ek insaan, baaki sab wait karte hain, aur chaabi wahi wapas laata hai jiske paas hai.
  • Semaphore ek counter hai jo ek saath N holders tak ko andar aane deta hai. 3 slots wala parking lot socho jiske board pe free slots dikhte hain. Har andar aane waali car count ghataati hai; har jaane waali badhaati hai; 0 pe nayi cars wait karti hain.
import { Mutex } from 'async-mutex';
import pLimit from 'p-limit';

// Mutex: only one request at a time refreshes the shared partner API token
const tokenMutex = new Mutex();
async function getAccessToken() {
  return tokenMutex.runExclusive(async () => {
    if (!cached || cached.expiresAt < Date.now()) cached = await refreshTokenFromProvider();
    return cached.token;
  });
}

// Semaphore: at most 5 calls to a VIN-decoding partner API at once
const limit = pLimit(5);
const decoded = await Promise.all(vins.map(vin => limit(() => decodeVin(vin))));

Notice the connection pool itself is a semaphore: N connections, and requests wait when all are taken.

Distributed locks: one lock across many servers. A mutex lives in one process's memory. In production, IRCTC-style systems run the same code on many instances (copies of the server) behind a load balancer. A mutex on instance 1 means nothing to instance 2. When you need "only one instance in the whole fleet does this" (the nightly invoice job must run once, not six times; only one worker should rebuild a big cache entry), you need a distributed lock: a lock stored in a shared place every instance can see, usually Redis.

Dhyaan do, connection pool khud ek semaphore hai: N connections, aur sab le liye gaye toh requests wait karti hain.

Distributed locks: bahut saare servers ke across ek lock. Mutex ek process ki memory mein rehta hai. Production mein IRCTC jaise systems same code ko load balancer ke peeche kai instances (server ki copies) pe chalaate hain. Instance 1 ka mutex instance 2 ke liye kuch nahi hai. Jab tumhe chahiye "poore fleet mein sirf ek instance yeh kare" (nightly invoice job ek baar chale, chhe baar nahi; ek bada cache entry sirf ek worker rebuild kare), toh tumhe distributed lock chahiye: ek lock jo aisi shared jagah rakha hai jisko har instance dekh sake, aam taur pe Redis.

# Acquire: set only if nobody holds it (NX) and auto-expire after 30 s (PX)
SET lock:nightly-invoices 3f9c2e7a-instance-4 NX PX 30000
# OK    -> you hold the lock
# (nil) -> someone else holds it: skip, or retry later
-- Release safely: delete only if the lock is still MINE (atomic compare-and-delete)
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

const token = randomUUID();   // unique per holder, so we never delete someone else's lock
const ok = await redis.set('lock:nightly-invoices', token, 'PX', 30000, 'NX');
if (ok === 'OK') {
  try {
    await runNightlyInvoices();
  } finally {
    await redis.eval(RELEASE_LUA, 1, 'lock:nightly-invoices', token);
  }
}

Two details carry the whole design. The TTL (PX 30000, time to live) means that if the holder crashes, the lock expires by itself instead of blocking everyone forever. The random token means you only delete your own lock; a plain DEL could delete a lock that already expired and was taken by someone else. SETNX is the older command for "set if not exists"; SET ... NX PX does the same and sets the expiry in the same atomic step.

Rate limiting under concurrency. To stop a bot from firing thousands of Tatkal requests a second, you allow each user, say, 100 requests per minute. The counter must be shared and atomic: shared because requests are spread across many instances (a per-instance in-memory counter with 5 instances quietly allows 500, and resets on every restart), atomic because a "GET the count, compare, then INCR" sequence is itself a race. Redis INCR plus EXPIRE gives a fixed-window limiter in a few lines. When the user is over the limit, reply HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.

Do details poora design sambhaalti hain. TTL (PX 30000, time to live) ka matlab hai ki agar holder crash ho gaya, toh lock sabko hamesha ke liye rokne ki jagah khud expire ho jaata hai. Random token ka matlab hai ki tum sirf apna lock delete karte ho; plain DEL aisa lock bhi mita sakta hai jo pehle hi expire hoke kisi aur ne le liya. SETNX "set if not exists" ka purana command hai; SET ... NX PX wahi karta hai aur expiry bhi usi atomic step mein set karta hai.

Concurrency ke saath rate limiting. Ek bot ko ek second mein hazaaron Tatkal requests bhejne se rokne ke liye tum har user ko, maano, ek minute mein 100 requests allow karte ho. Counter shared aur atomic hona chahiye: shared kyunki requests kai instances pe bikhri hain (5 instances ke saath per-instance in-memory counter chupchaap 500 allow kar deta hai, aur har restart pe reset hota hai), atomic kyunki "count GET karo, compare karo, phir INCR" wala sequence khud ek race hai. Redis INCR plus EXPIRE kuch lines mein fixed-window limiter de deta hai. Jab user limit ke upar ho, HTTP 429 Too Many Requests ke saath Retry-After header bhejo.

// Fixed-window limiter: 100 requests per user per minute, shared by ALL instances
async function rateLimit(req, res, next) {
  const windowSec = 60, limit = 100;
  const nowSec = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  const key = `rl:${req.user.id}:${Math.floor(nowSec / windowSec)}`;

  const [[, count]] = await redis.multi()
    .incr(key)                          // atomic: returns the new count
    .expire(key, windowSec, 'NX')       // set the TTL only once (NX option needs Redis 7+)
    .exec();

  if (count > limit) {
    res.set('Retry-After', String(windowSec - (nowSec % windowSec)));
    return res.status(429).json({ error: 'rate_limited' });
  }
  next();
}

In real production: a service-appointment booking API (the kind a dealership's service drive uses) gets the same race as Tatkal: two customers, or a customer and a BDC agent on the phone, grab the same 9:00 AM slot. The durable fix is not a clever lock in Node but a database guarantee: a unique constraint on (service_bay_id, slot_start), so the second insert fails cleanly and the app offers the next slot.

Real production mein: service-appointment booking API (jaisi dealership ka service drive use karta hai) mein bhi Tatkal wali race hoti hai: do customers, ya ek customer aur phone pe ek BDC agent, same 9:00 AM slot pakad lete hain. Pakka fix Node mein koi clever lock nahi, balki database ki guarantee hai: (service_bay_id, slot_start) pe unique constraint, taaki doosra insert saaf fail ho aur app agla slot offer kare.

Level 4 Senior nuances: thundering herds, lock failure modes, counters at scaleSenior nuances: thundering herds, lock failure modes, bade scale pe counters

Thundering herd. Many waiters woken at the same moment, all rushing the same resource. Tatkal at 10:00 is a human thundering herd. In systems it shows up as:

  • Cache expiry: the cached train schedule expires at 10:00:05; the next 5,000 requests all miss the cache and all hit the database with the same query.
  • Lock release: 200 workers wait on a lock; it is released; all 200 wake and fight, one wins, 199 go back to sleep, wasting CPU.
  • Recovery: a service comes back after an outage and every client retries in the same second, knocking it down again.

The fixes: add jitter (a small random amount) to TTLs, retry delays and cron schedules so things do not line up; exponential backoff with jitter for retries; let only one request rebuild an expired cache entry (a lock around the refresh, often called single-flight or request coalescing) while others wait briefly or get the slightly stale value; and probabilistic early expiration, where each read has a small chance of refreshing the value before it expires, rising as expiry approaches, so one request refreshes early instead of everyone at once. Simply raising the TTL does not fix a herd, it just moves it.

Distributed lock failure modes. A Redis lock with a TTL has a hole. The holder takes a 30-second lock, then pauses for 40 seconds (a long garbage-collection pause, a slow network, a frozen VM). The lock expires, a second worker takes it, and now two workers believe they hold it. The fix is a fencing token: each time the lock is granted, hand out an increasing number, and have the storage being protected reject writes carrying an older number than it has already seen. Redlock is an algorithm that takes the lock on a majority of several independent Redis nodes to survive one node failing, but it relies on reasonably synchronized clocks and bounded pauses, and it is debated. Practical rule: a Redis lock is great for efficiency (avoid doing the same work twice). When correctness depends on it (money, stock), back it with a database guarantee: a unique constraint, a conditional update, or Postgres advisory locks, or use a consensus system such as etcd or ZooKeeper.

Counters at huge scale. INCR on one Redis key or UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1 on one row is safe, but a single hot key or row becomes a bottleneck because every increment queues on it. Options: sharded counters (split into N sub-counters like views:12951:0 to :15, increment a random one, sum on read); batching (count in memory for a second, then one INCRBY), accepting a small loss on crash; or a dedicated counter service. For "how many unique users", Redis HyperLogLog gives an approximate count in tiny memory.

Better rate limits. A fixed window lets a burst through at the boundary: 100 requests at 10:00:59 and 100 more at 10:01:00. A sliding window (store timestamps in a Redis sorted set, or weight the previous window's count) smooths that. A token bucket refills tokens at a steady rate and lets short bursts spend saved tokens; it is what most API gateways use. Both are written as Lua scripts so the check-and-update stays atomic. Decide ahead of time what happens if Redis is down: fail open (allow traffic) or fail closed (reject).

Senior summary: find the shared state, make every change to it one atomic operation, keep the pool smaller than you think, use in-process locks only for in-process state, treat Redis locks as an optimisation backed by a database guarantee, and add jitter anywhere many things could wake up together.

Thundering herd. Bahut saare waiting log ek hi moment pe jaag jaate hain aur sab same resource pe toot padte hain. 10:00 baje ka Tatkal insaanon ka thundering herd hai. Systems mein yeh aise dikhta hai:

  • Cache expiry: cached train schedule 10:00:05 pe expire hota hai; agli 5,000 requests sab cache miss karti hain aur sab same query ke saath database pe pahunchti hain.
  • Lock release: 200 workers ek lock ka wait kar rahe hain; lock release hota hai; saare 200 jaagte hain aur ladte hain, ek jeet-ta hai, 199 wapas so jaate hain, CPU barbaad.
  • Recovery: outage ke baad service wapas aati hai aur har client same second mein retry karta hai, aur usko phir gira deta hai.

Fixes: TTLs, retry delays aur cron schedules mein jitter (thoda random amount) jodo taaki cheezein ek line mein na aayein; retries ke liye jitter ke saath exponential backoff; expired cache entry ko sirf ek request rebuild kare (refresh ke around lock, jisko aksar single-flight ya request coalescing kehte hain) jabki baaki thoda wait karein ya thodi purani value le lein; aur probabilistic early expiration, jahaan har read ka value ko expire hone se pehle refresh karne ka chhota sa chance hota hai, jo expiry paas aane pe badhta hai, taaki sab ek saath ki jagah ek request jaldi refresh kar de. Sirf TTL badhaana herd ko fix nahi karta, bas usko aage khisaka deta hai.

Distributed lock ke failure modes. TTL wale Redis lock mein ek chhed hai. Holder 30 second ka lock leta hai, phir 40 second ke liye ruk jaata hai (lamba garbage-collection pause, slow network, freeze hua VM). Lock expire ho jaata hai, doosra worker le leta hai, aur ab do workers maante hain ki lock unke paas hai. Fix hai fencing token: har baar lock milne pe ek badhta hua number do, aur jis storage ko protect kar rahe ho woh aisa write reject kare jiska number usne pehle dekhe number se purana ho. Redlock ek algorithm hai jo ek node fail hone pe bhi bachne ke liye kai independent Redis nodes ke majority pe lock leta hai, lekin yeh kaafi synchronized clocks aur bounded pauses pe bharosa karta hai, aur ispe bahas hai. Practical rule: Redis lock efficiency ke liye badhiya hai (same kaam do baar karne se bachna). Jab correctness uspe depend karti hai (paisa, stock), toh usko database guarantee se back karo: unique constraint, conditional update, ya Postgres advisory locks, ya etcd ya ZooKeeper jaisa consensus system use karo.

Bahut bade scale pe counters. Ek Redis key pe INCR ya ek row pe UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1 safe hai, lekin ek single hot key ya row bottleneck ban jaati hai kyunki har increment uspe line lagata hai. Options: sharded counters (N sub-counters mein baanto jaise views:12951:0 se :15 tak, random ek ko increment karo, padhte waqt jodo); batching (ek second tak memory mein gino, phir ek INCRBY), crash pe thoda loss accept karke; ya ek dedicated counter service. "Kitne unique users" ke liye Redis HyperLogLog bahut kam memory mein approximate count deta hai.

Behtar rate limits. Fixed window boundary pe burst nikalne deta hai: 10:00:59 pe 100 requests aur 10:01:00 pe 100 aur. Sliding window (timestamps ko Redis sorted set mein rakho, ya pichhle window ke count ko weight do) isko smooth karta hai. Token bucket tokens ko steady rate pe refill karta hai aur bache hue tokens se chhote bursts allow karta hai; zyaadatar API gateways yahi use karte hain. Dono Lua scripts ke roop mein likhe jaate hain taaki check-and-update atomic rahe. Pehle se decide karo ki Redis down ho toh kya hoga: fail open (traffic allow) ya fail closed (reject).

Senior summary: shared state dhoondho, uske har change ko ek atomic operation banao, pool ko jitna socho usse chhota rakho, in-process locks sirf in-process state ke liye, Redis locks ko database guarantee se backed optimisation samjho, aur jahaan bhi bahut cheezein ek saath jaag sakti hain wahaan jitter daalo.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Shared state
Data more than one request can touch: a DB row, a Redis key, an in-memory variable.Aisa data jisko ek se zyada requests touch kar sakti hain: DB row, Redis key, in-memory variable.
Race condition
A bug whose outcome depends on the timing of concurrent operations.Aisa bug jiska result concurrent operations ki timing pe depend karta hai.
Read-modify-write / check-then-act
The two classic race shapes: read, change, write back; or check a condition, then act on it.Race ke do classic shapes: padho, badlo, wapas likho; ya condition check karo, phir us pe action lo.
Critical section
Code that must not be run by two workers at the same time.Code jisko do workers ek saath nahi chala sakte.
Concurrency / parallelism
Interleaving many tasks / literally running many at the same instant on several cores.Bahut saare tasks ko interleave karna / kai cores pe literally same instant pe chalaana.
Event loop
Node's loop that runs the next queued callback whenever the call stack is empty.Node ka loop jo call stack khaali hote hi queue ka agla callback chalaata hai.
Non-blocking I/O / libuv
Starting I/O without waiting for it / the C library under Node that does this with the OS and a thread pool.I/O shuru karna bina uska wait kiye / Node ke neeche ki C library jo OS aur thread pool se yeh karti hai.
CPU-bound vs I/O-bound
Work limited by computation (blocks Node's loop) vs work that mostly waits on network or disk.Calculation se limited kaam (Node ka loop block karta hai) vs kaam jo zyaadatar network ya disk ka wait karta hai.
Atomic operation
An operation that happens as one indivisible step; nobody sees it half done.Operation jo ek na tootne waale step mein hota hai; koi usko aadha nahi dekhta.
Connection pool
A reusable set of open DB connections that requests borrow and return.Khule DB connections ka reusable set jisse requests udhaar leti aur wapas karti hain.
Mutex
A lock with exactly one holder; the owner must release it.Lock jiska exactly ek holder hai; owner hi release karta hai.
Semaphore
A counter that allows up to N holders at once.Counter jo ek saath N holders tak allow karta hai.
Distributed lock
A lock stored in a shared system (e.g. Redis) so it works across many server instances.Shared system (jaise Redis) mein rakha lock taaki kai server instances ke across kaam kare.
TTL
Time to live: how long a key or lock exists before it expires by itself.Time to live: key ya lock kitni der rahega phir khud expire ho jaayega.
Fencing token
An increasing number issued with each lock grant; storage rejects writes with an older number.Har lock grant ke saath diya gaya badhta number; storage purane number wale writes reject karta hai.
Thundering herd
Many waiters waking at once and overwhelming the same resource.Bahut saare waiters ek saath jaag ke same resource ko overwhelm kar dete hain.
Jitter
A small random delay added so events don't line up at the same instant.Chhota random delay jo jodte hain taaki events same instant pe line mein na aayein.
Rate limiter / 429
Caps requests per client per time window / the HTTP status sent when the cap is hit.Har client ki time window mein requests cap karta hai / cap hit hone pe bheja jaane wala HTTP status.
Token bucket / sliding window
Rate-limit algorithms that allow controlled bursts / avoid the fixed-window boundary burst.Rate-limit algorithms jo controlled bursts allow karte hain / fixed-window boundary burst se bachte hain.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What is a race condition? Give a real backend example.Race condition kya hai? Ek real backend example do.
What they're really testing: a concrete lost-update story (both read balance 100, both deduct 50, both write 50) and that you know where it shows up: payments, inventory, counters.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ek concrete lost-update kahani (dono balance 100 padhte hain, dono 50 ghataate hain, dono 50 likhte hain) aur kya tum jaante ho yeh kahaan dikhta hai: payments, inventory, counters.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of concurrent operations on shared state. The classic backend example is a wallet. The balance is 100 and two ₹50 payments arrive at the same moment. Both requests read 100, both compute 100 minus 50, and both write 50. The user paid 100 in total but was charged 50, a lost update. The same shape double-sells the last train seat or the last unit of stock, lets a one-time coupon be used twice, and makes view counters undercount. It's usually read-modify-write or check-then-act done in application code. The fix is to make the change atomic: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 50 and check the affected row count, or use a row lock or a unique constraint. The trade-off with locks is contention; atomic statements are cheapest."

"Race condition ek bug hai jismein result shared state pe chal rahe concurrent operations ki timing pe depend karta hai. Classic backend example wallet hai. Balance 100 hai aur same moment pe do ₹50 ke payments aate hain. Dono requests 100 padhti hain, dono 100 minus 50 calculate karti hain, aur dono 50 likhti hain. User ne total 100 pay kiya lekin sirf 50 kata, yeh lost update hai. Yahi shape aakhri train seat ya stock ka aakhri unit do baar bech deti hai, ek-baar wala coupon do baar use karwa deti hai, aur view counters ko kam ginti karwaati hai. Aam taur pe yeh application code mein kiya gaya read-modify-write ya check-then-act hota hai. Fix hai change ko atomic banana: UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 50 aur affected row count check karo, ya row lock ya unique constraint use karo. Locks ke saath trade-off contention hai; atomic statements sabse saste hain."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Races are hard to reproduce because the window is milliseconds wide and only opens under real concurrency, so they show up at peak load, not in unit tests. To find one I'd log both write points with request IDs and precise timestamps and look for overlapping windows, then reproduce with a load test firing many identical requests in parallel. In Node, races happen across await points within one process and across instances. Prevention hierarchy: first a database guarantee (atomic update, unique constraint), then row locks or optimistic versioning, and only then application-level or distributed locks.

Races reproduce karna mushkil hai kyunki window milliseconds ki hoti hai aur sirf real concurrency mein khulti hai, isliye yeh peak load pe dikhti hain, unit tests mein nahi. Dhoondhne ke liye main dono write points ko request IDs aur precise timestamps ke saath log karunga aur overlapping windows dekhunga, phir ek load test se reproduce karunga jo parallel mein bahut saari same requests bheje. Node mein races ek process ke andar await points ke across aur instances ke across hoti hain. Prevention ka order: pehle database guarantee (atomic update, unique constraint), phir row locks ya optimistic versioning, aur uske baad hi application-level ya distributed locks.

Common mistake: saying "Node.js is single-threaded, so we can't have races"; every await and every extra instance opens the window.
Galti mat karna: bolna "Node.js single-threaded hai, toh races nahi ho sakti"; har await aur har extra instance window khol deta hai.
02 Concurrency vs parallelism?Concurrency aur parallelism mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: concurrency is many tasks interleaved (possible on one CPU), parallelism is many at literally the same time (needs many CPUs), and Node.js is concurrent, not parallel.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: concurrency matlab bahut tasks interleave (ek CPU pe bhi possible), parallelism matlab literally same time pe bahut saare (kai CPUs chahiye), aur Node.js concurrent hai, parallel nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"Concurrency is about structure: dealing with many tasks at once by interleaving them, so while one waits another makes progress. It works even on a single CPU core. Parallelism is about execution: literally running several tasks at the same instant, which needs multiple cores or machines. My analogy is a chaiwala who boils milk for one order while crushing ginger for another; that's concurrency. Two chaiwalas at two stoves is parallelism. Node.js is the classic example: it's concurrent but not parallel for JavaScript. One thread juggles thousands of in-flight requests, because most of their time is spent waiting on I/O. If I need parallelism for CPU-heavy work in Node, I use worker threads or run one process per core with cluster or PM2. The trade-off: parallelism adds throughput for CPU work but brings shared-memory complexity; concurrency alone is enough for I/O-bound services."

"Concurrency structure ke baare mein hai: bahut saare tasks ko interleave karke ek saath sambhaalna, taaki jab ek wait kare toh doosra aage badhe. Yeh ek CPU core pe bhi kaam karta hai. Parallelism execution ke baare mein hai: kai tasks ko literally same instant pe chalaana, jiske liye kai cores ya machines chahiye. Meri analogy ek chaiwala hai jo ek order ka doodh ubaalte hue doosre order ke liye adrak kootata hai; yeh concurrency hai. Do stoves pe do chaiwale parallelism hai. Node.js classic example hai: JavaScript ke liye yeh concurrent hai, parallel nahi. Ek thread hazaaron chalti requests sambhaalta hai, kyunki unka zyaadatar time I/O ke wait mein jaata hai. Agar Node mein CPU-heavy kaam ke liye parallelism chahiye, toh main worker threads use karta hoon ya cluster ya PM2 se har core pe ek process chalaata hoon. Trade-off: parallelism CPU kaam ka throughput badhata hai lekin shared-memory complexity laata hai; I/O-bound services ke liye akeli concurrency kaafi hai."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Even "not parallel" Node does parallel work under the hood: libuv's thread pool (4 threads by default, set by UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE) runs file, DNS and crypto work in parallel, and the OS handles many sockets at once. Other runtimes differ: Go multiplexes goroutines across all cores, so it's concurrent and parallel; Java has real threads; CPython has the GIL, which lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound Python uses multiple processes. Concurrency without parallelism still has race conditions, because interleaving alone is enough to break read-modify-write.

"Parallel nahi" wala Node bhi andar se parallel kaam karta hai: libuv ka thread pool (default 4 threads, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE se set) file, DNS aur crypto ka kaam parallel chalaata hai, aur OS ek saath bahut sockets sambhaalta hai. Doosre runtimes alag hain: Go goroutines ko saare cores pe multiplex karta hai, toh woh concurrent aur parallel dono hai; Java mein real threads hain; CPython mein GIL hai, jo ek time pe sirf ek thread ko Python bytecode chalaane deta hai, isliye CPU-bound Python multiple processes use karta hai. Bina parallelism ke concurrency mein bhi race conditions hoti hain, kyunki read-modify-write todne ke liye akela interleaving kaafi hai.

Common mistake: using the two words interchangeably, or claiming Node "can't use multiple cores" (it can, with cluster or worker threads).
Galti mat karna: dono words ko ek hi matlab mein use karna, ya bolna ki Node "multiple cores use nahi kar sakta" (cluster ya worker threads se kar sakta hai).
03 How does Node.js handle concurrent requests without multiple threads?Node.js bina multiple threads ke concurrent requests kaise handle karta hai?
What they're really testing: event loop plus non-blocking I/O, I/O handed to the OS with a callback fired on completion, and the caveat that CPU-bound work blocks the loop.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: event loop plus non-blocking I/O, I/O OS ko diya jaata hai aur complete hone pe callback chalta hai, aur yeh caveat ki CPU-bound kaam loop ko block karta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"Node runs JavaScript on one thread with an event loop and non-blocking I/O. When a request handler calls the database, Node doesn't wait. It hands the I/O to the operating system through libuv and immediately moves on to other requests. When the database replies, the callback, or the rest of the async function after the await, goes into a queue, and the event loop runs it as soon as the call stack is empty. Because a typical API request spends most of its time waiting on the network, one thread can keep thousands in flight. Work the OS can't do asynchronously, like file access, DNS lookups or some crypto, goes to libuv's small thread pool. The big caveat is CPU-bound work: a heavy loop, a synchronous hash or a huge JSON parse blocks the one thread, and every other user waits. For that I use worker threads, a cluster of processes, or a separate job queue."

"Node JavaScript ko ek thread pe event loop aur non-blocking I/O ke saath chalaata hai. Jab request handler database ko call karta hai, Node wait nahi karta. Woh I/O ko libuv ke through operating system ko de deta hai aur turant doosri requests pe chala jaata hai. Jab database reply karta hai, callback, ya await ke baad async function ka baaki hissa, ek queue mein jaata hai, aur call stack khaali hote hi event loop usko chala deta hai. Kyunki ek typical API request apna zyaadatar time network ke wait mein bitaati hai, ek thread hazaaron ko chalu rakh sakta hai. Jo kaam OS asynchronously nahi kar sakta, jaise file access, DNS lookups ya kuch crypto, woh libuv ke chhote thread pool mein jaata hai. Bada caveat CPU-bound kaam hai: bhaari loop, synchronous hash ya bahut bada JSON parse us ek thread ko block kar deta hai, aur baaki har user wait karta hai. Uske liye main worker threads, processes ka cluster, ya alag job queue use karta hoon."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The loop runs in phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll (where it waits for I/O events using epoll on Linux or kqueue on macOS), check (setImmediate), and close callbacks. Between each callback, Node drains the microtask queue: resolved promises and process.nextTick, which is why a recursive promise chain can starve I/O. I'd measure event-loop lag with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay, and a rising p99 lag means something is blocking. Wrapping CPU work in a Promise doesn't help; it still runs on the same thread. The thread pool size can be raised with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE if many bcrypt or file calls are queuing.

Loop phases mein chalta hai: timers, pending callbacks, poll (jahaan woh I/O events ka wait karta hai, Linux pe epoll ya macOS pe kqueue se), check (setImmediate), aur close callbacks. Har callback ke beech Node microtask queue khaali karta hai: resolved promises aur process.nextTick, isiliye ek recursive promise chain I/O ko bhookha maar sakti hai. Main event-loop lag ko perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay se measure karunga, aur badhta p99 lag matlab kuch block kar raha hai. CPU kaam ko Promise mein lapetne se kuch nahi hota; woh ab bhi same thread pe chalta hai. Agar bahut saare bcrypt ya file calls queue ho rahe hain toh thread pool size UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE se badha sakte ho.

Common mistake: believing async makes CPU-heavy code non-blocking; only I/O is offloaded, computation still blocks the loop.
Galti mat karna: maan lena ki async CPU-heavy code ko non-blocking bana deta hai; sirf I/O offload hota hai, calculation ab bhi loop block karti hai.
04 What is an atomic operation? Why does it matter for counters?Atomic operation kya hai? Counters ke liye yeh kyun zaroori hai?
What they're really testing: that Redis INCR and SQL UPDATE counter = counter + 1 are atomic, while read-then-write from app code is not.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: Redis INCR aur SQL UPDATE counter = counter + 1 atomic hain, jabki app code se read-then-write nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"An atomic operation happens as one indivisible step: no other operation can see it half done or slip in the middle. It matters for counters because the naive version, read the count, add one in code, write it back, is three steps, and two concurrent requests can both read 41 and both write 42, so one increment is lost. Under heavy traffic you lose many. The atomic versions push the whole change into one operation. In SQL, UPDATE posts SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = ? takes a row lock and computes from the current value inside the database. In Redis, INCR views:post:42 is atomic because Redis runs commands one at a time on a single thread. Both return or reflect the new value safely. The trade-off is that a single very hot counter becomes a contention point, which I'd solve by sharding the counter."

"Atomic operation ek na tootne waale step mein hota hai: koi aur operation usko aadha nahi dekh sakta ya beech mein ghus nahi sakta. Counters ke liye yeh isliye zaroori hai kyunki naive version, count padho, code mein ek jodo, wapas likho, teen steps hai, aur do concurrent requests dono 41 padh ke dono 42 likh sakti hain, toh ek increment kho gaya. Heavy traffic mein bahut saare kho jaate hain. Atomic versions poore change ko ek operation mein daalte hain. SQL mein UPDATE posts SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = ? row lock leta hai aur database ke andar current value se calculate karta hai. Redis mein INCR views:post:42 atomic hai kyunki Redis commands ek ek karke single thread pe chalaata hai. Dono nayi value safely return ya reflect karte hain. Trade-off yeh hai ki ek bahut hot counter contention point ban jaata hai, jisko main counter shard karke solve karunga."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Atomicity is about the unit, not the product: each Redis command is atomic, but a GET followed by a SET from my code is not. To group steps I use MULTI/EXEC, which runs queued commands back to back but has no rollback, or a Lua script, which runs as one uninterruptible unit and can branch on values. Underneath, CPUs provide atomic instructions like compare-and-swap, which is how mutexes are built; JavaScript exposes them as Atomics for SharedArrayBuffer between worker threads. The database equivalent of compare-and-swap is a conditional update, which is exactly optimistic locking.

Atomicity unit ke baare mein hai, product ke nahi: har Redis command atomic hai, lekin mere code se GET ke baad SET nahi. Steps ko group karne ke liye main MULTI/EXEC use karta hoon, jo queued commands ek ke baad ek chalaata hai lekin rollback nahi deta, ya Lua script, jo ek na rukne waale unit ki tarah chalta hai aur values pe branch kar sakta hai. Neeche, CPUs compare-and-swap jaise atomic instructions dete hain, jinse mutexes bante hain; JavaScript inhe worker threads ke beech SharedArrayBuffer ke liye Atomics ke roop mein deta hai. Compare-and-swap ka database equivalent conditional update hai, jo exactly optimistic locking hai.

Common mistake: assuming a Redis GET then SET is safe "because Redis is single-threaded"; only each individual command is atomic.
Galti mat karna: maan lena ki Redis GET phir SET safe hai "kyunki Redis single-threaded hai"; sirf har individual command atomic hai.
05 What is a connection pool and what happens if you don't use one?Connection pool kya hai aur use na karo toh kya hota hai?
What they're really testing: reuse of DB connections, and the two failure modes without it: per-request setup overhead and the database running out of connections.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: DB connections ka reuse, aur iske bina do failure modes: har request pe setup overhead aur database ke connections khatam ho jaana.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"A connection pool is a set of open database connections the app keeps and reuses. Each request borrows one, runs its query and returns it; if all are busy, the request waits briefly in a queue. It exists because opening a connection is expensive: a TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication, and in Postgres a new backend process per connection. That's milliseconds of overhead, often more than the query itself. Without a pool, two things go wrong under load. Every request pays that setup cost, so latency rises. And the database runs out of connections: Postgres defaults to 100, so a traffic spike gets 'too many clients' errors and the database wastes memory on connections. In Node I create one pg.Pool at startup with a max of, say, 10 per instance, and make sure instances times pool size stays under the database limit. The trade-off is that too small a pool queues requests and too large overloads the database."

"Connection pool khule database connections ka ek set hai jo app rakhti hai aur baar baar use karti hai. Har request ek udhaar leti hai, query chalaati hai aur wapas karti hai; agar sab busy hain, request thodi der queue mein wait karti hai. Yeh isliye hai kyunki connection kholna mehenga hai: TCP handshake, aksar TLS, authentication, aur Postgres mein har connection ke liye naya backend process. Yeh milliseconds ka overhead hai, aksar query se bhi zyada. Pool ke bina load pe do cheezein bigadti hain. Har request woh setup cost chukaati hai, toh latency badhti hai. Aur database ke connections khatam ho jaate hain: Postgres ka default 100 hai, toh traffic spike pe 'too many clients' errors aate hain aur database connections pe memory barbaad karta hai. Node mein main startup pe ek pg.Pool banata hoon, har instance ka max maano 10, aur ensure karta hoon ki instances guna pool size database limit se neeche rahe. Trade-off: bahut chhota pool requests ko queue karta hai aur bahut bada database ko overload."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Smaller pools are often faster: a database with a few cores can only execute a few queries truly at once, and hundreds of connections just add context switching and lock contention. Pool exhaustion usually comes from leaks, like a client checked out with pool.connect() and never released on an error path, or from long transactions holding connections; I'd watch the pool's waiting count and set a connection timeout so requests fail fast. With many small instances or serverless functions, I'd put PgBouncer or RDS Proxy in front; its transaction-pooling mode multiplexes many clients over few connections but breaks session features like session-level SET or advisory locks.

Chhote pools aksar fast hote hain: kuch cores wala database ek time pe sach mein kuch hi queries chala sakta hai, aur sainkdon connections bas context switching aur lock contention badhaate hain. Pool exhaustion aam taur pe leaks se hota hai, jaise pool.connect() se liya client jo error path pe kabhi release nahi hua, ya connections pakde long transactions se; main pool ka waiting count dekhunga aur connection timeout set karunga taaki requests jaldi fail hon. Bahut saare chhote instances ya serverless functions ke saath main aage PgBouncer ya RDS Proxy lagaunga; uska transaction-pooling mode bahut clients ko kam connections pe multiplex karta hai lekin session features jaise session-level SET ya advisory locks tod deta hai.

Common mistake: creating a new pool (or client) inside every request handler, or assuming a bigger pool always means more throughput.
Galti mat karna: har request handler ke andar naya pool (ya client) banana, ya maan lena ki bada pool hamesha zyada throughput deta hai.
06 What is a distributed lock and when do you need one?Distributed lock kya hai aur iski zaroorat kab padti hai?
What they're really testing: a lock that works across instances, for the same job or resource, typically Redis SETNX (SET NX PX) or Redlock.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ek lock jo instances ke across kaam kare, same job ya resource ke liye, aam taur pe Redis SETNX (SET NX PX) ya Redlock.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"A distributed lock is a lock held in a shared system, usually Redis, so that it works across all instances of a service, not just inside one process. I need one when several instances could pick up the same job or resource and it must be done by only one: a nightly invoicing cron running on six instances, rebuilding one expensive cache entry, or processing a given account's reconciliation. In Redis I acquire it with SET lock:invoices <random-token> NX PX 30000: NX means only if nobody holds it, PX gives a TTL so a crashed holder can't lock everyone out forever. I release it with a small Lua script that deletes the key only if the token is still mine. For higher availability there's Redlock across several independent Redis nodes. The trade-off: it adds a network hop and new failure modes, so I use it only when the database can't enforce the rule itself."

"Distributed lock ek shared system mein, aam taur pe Redis mein, rakha lock hai taaki woh service ke saare instances ke across kaam kare, sirf ek process ke andar nahi. Iski zaroorat tab hai jab kai instances same job ya resource utha sakte hain aur usko sirf ek ko karna hai: chhe instances pe chalne wala nightly invoicing cron, ek mehenga cache entry rebuild karna, ya ek account ka reconciliation process karna. Redis mein main isko SET lock:invoices <random-token> NX PX 30000 se leta hoon: NX matlab sirf tab jab kisi ke paas na ho, PX ek TTL deta hai taaki crash hua holder sabko hamesha ke liye bahar na rakhe. Release main ek chhote Lua script se karta hoon jo key sirf tab delete karta hai jab token abhi bhi mera ho. Zyada availability ke liye kai independent Redis nodes pe Redlock hai. Trade-off: ek network hop aur naye failure modes aate hain, isliye main isko tabhi use karta hoon jab database khud rule enforce nahi kar sakta."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The main failure mode: the holder pauses longer than the TTL (GC pause, network stall), the lock expires, another worker takes it, and two think they hold it. Mitigations are a watchdog that extends the lease while work is running (Redisson does this) and, for correctness, fencing tokens: an increasing number issued with each grant that the protected storage checks, rejecting stale writes. Redlock also depends on clocks and bounded pauses, and its safety is debated. So I treat Redis locks as an efficiency tool; where correctness matters I rely on a unique constraint, a conditional update, a Postgres advisory lock, or a consensus store like etcd or ZooKeeper.

Main failure mode: holder TTL se zyada der ruk jaata hai (GC pause, network atakna), lock expire hota hai, doosra worker le leta hai, aur do log maante hain lock unke paas hai. Bachaav hai ek watchdog jo kaam chalte waqt lease badhata rahe (Redisson yeh karta hai) aur, correctness ke liye, fencing tokens: har grant ke saath ek badhta number jo protected storage check karta hai aur purane writes reject karta hai. Redlock clocks aur bounded pauses pe bhi depend karta hai, aur uski safety pe bahas hai. Isliye main Redis locks ko efficiency tool maanta hoon; jahaan correctness matter karti hai wahaan unique constraint, conditional update, Postgres advisory lock, ya etcd ya ZooKeeper jaise consensus store pe bharosa karta hoon.

Common mistake: taking the lock without a TTL, or releasing it with a plain DEL that can delete another worker's lock.
Galti mat karna: bina TTL ke lock lena, ya plain DEL se release karna jo kisi aur worker ka lock mita sakta hai.
07 What is the thundering herd problem in the context of concurrency?Concurrency ke context mein thundering herd problem kya hai?
What they're really testing: many waiters woken at once (cache expiry, lock release) and the fixes: jitter, probabilistic early expiry, and a single lock for the refresh.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: bahut saare waiters ek saath jaagte hain (cache expiry, lock release) aur fixes: jitter, probabilistic early expiry, aur refresh ke liye ek single lock.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"Thundering herd is when many waiting clients or processes wake up at the same moment and all hit the same resource, overwhelming it. The common backend case is cache expiry: a hot key, say today's train schedule, expires, and the next few thousand requests all miss and fire the same heavy query at the database at once. Another case is lock release: hundreds of waiters wake, one wins, the rest burn CPU and go back to sleep. A third is recovery, when every client retries the second a service comes back. My fixes: first, only one request rebuilds, using a lock around the refresh while others briefly wait or get the slightly stale value. Second, add jitter to TTLs and retry delays so expiries and retries don't line up. Third, probabilistic early expiration, so one request refreshes the value a little before it expires. The trade-off is serving slightly stale data for a moment."

"Thundering herd tab hota hai jab bahut saare waiting clients ya processes ek hi moment pe jaagte hain aur sab same resource pe pahunch ke usko overwhelm kar dete hain. Common backend case cache expiry hai: ek hot key, maano aaj ka train schedule, expire hoti hai, aur agli kuch hazaar requests sab miss karti hain aur ek saath database pe same bhaari query bhejti hain. Doosra case lock release hai: sainkdon waiters jaagte hain, ek jeet-ta hai, baaki CPU jalaake wapas so jaate hain. Teesra recovery hai, jab service wapas aate hi har client usi second retry karta hai. Mere fixes: pehla, sirf ek request rebuild kare, refresh ke around lock lagaake, jabki baaki thoda wait karein ya thodi purani value lein. Doosra, TTLs aur retry delays mein jitter jodo taaki expiries aur retries ek line mein na aayein. Teesra, probabilistic early expiration, taaki ek request value ko expire hone se thoda pehle refresh kar de. Trade-off hai ek pal ke liye thoda purana data dena."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Layer the defences: in-process request coalescing (single-flight) so each instance sends at most one rebuild, plus a Redis lock so the whole fleet sends one. Stale-while-revalidate keeps serving the old value while one worker refreshes. Probabilistic early expiration (the XFetch idea) refreshes with a probability that rises as expiry nears and with how expensive the rebuild is. For retries, exponential backoff with full jitter. For scheduled jobs, don't fire every instance's cron at exactly :00. For lock waiters, a fair queue-based lock wakes only the next waiter. Raising the TTL alone just moves the herd to a later time.

Defences ko layer karo: in-process request coalescing (single-flight) taaki har instance zyada se zyada ek rebuild bheje, plus Redis lock taaki poora fleet ek bheje. Stale-while-revalidate purani value serve karta rehta hai jab tak ek worker refresh kare. Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch wala idea) ek probability ke saath refresh karta hai jo expiry paas aane pe aur rebuild kitna mehenga hai us hisaab se badhti hai. Retries ke liye full jitter ke saath exponential backoff. Scheduled jobs ke liye har instance ka cron exactly :00 pe mat chalao. Lock waiters ke liye fair queue-based lock sirf agle waiter ko jagaata hai. Sirf TTL badhaana herd ko baad ke time pe khisaka deta hai.

Common mistake: "just increase the TTL"; that delays the herd, it does not remove it.
Galti mat karna: "bas TTL badha do"; isse herd der se aata hai, khatam nahi hota.
08 How do you make a counter increment safe under high concurrency?High concurrency mein counter increment ko safe kaise banaoge?
What they're really testing: atomic DB update, Redis INCR, or a counter service, and never read-increment-write in the application.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: atomic DB update, Redis INCR, ya counter service, aur application mein kabhi read-increment-write nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"The rule is: never read, increment and write in application code, because concurrent requests will read the same value and overwrite each other. Instead I push the increment into one atomic operation. If the counter lives in the database, UPDATE listings SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = ?; the database locks the row and adds to the current value. If it has a limit, like remaining stock, I put the condition in the same statement, SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0, and check the affected row count. If it's high-traffic and can live in memory, Redis INCR or INCRBY, which is atomic and very fast. At very large scale I'd use a dedicated counter service or sharded counters. The trade-off: the database is durable but a hot row contends; Redis is fast but I need to think about persistence."

"Rule yeh hai: application code mein kabhi padho, badhao aur likho mat karo, kyunki concurrent requests same value padh ke ek doosre ko overwrite karengi. Uski jagah main increment ko ek atomic operation mein daalta hoon. Agar counter database mein hai, toh UPDATE listings SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = ?; database row lock karta hai aur current value mein jodta hai. Agar limit hai, jaise bacha hua stock, toh condition same statement mein daalta hoon, SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0, aur affected row count check karta hoon. Agar high-traffic hai aur memory mein reh sakta hai, toh Redis INCR ya INCRBY, jo atomic aur bahut fast hai. Bahut bade scale pe main dedicated counter service ya sharded counters use karunga. Trade-off: database durable hai lekin hot row pe contention hota hai; Redis fast hai lekin persistence ke baare mein sochna padta hai."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

A single hot row serializes all increments on its lock. Sharded counters split it into N rows or keys (views:42:0 to views:42:15), increment a random one, and sum on read. For analytics-grade counts I batch: count in memory for a second, then one INCRBY, or buffer in Redis and flush to the database periodically, accepting a small loss on a crash. For stock decrement in Redis I use a Lua script that checks and decrements together, or DECR and compensate with INCR if it goes negative. Redis durability depends on AOF or RDB settings, so money-grade counters stay in the database. HyperLogLog handles approximate unique counts.

Ek hot row apne lock pe saare increments ko line mein laga deti hai. Sharded counters usko N rows ya keys mein baant-te hain (views:42:0 se views:42:15), random ek ko increment karte hain, aur padhte waqt jodte hain. Analytics-level counts ke liye main batch karta hoon: ek second memory mein gino, phir ek INCRBY, ya Redis mein buffer karke periodically database mein flush karo, crash pe thoda loss accept karke. Redis mein stock ghataane ke liye main Lua script use karta hoon jo check aur decrement saath karta hai, ya DECR aur negative ho jaaye toh INCR se compensate. Redis durability AOF ya RDB settings pe depend karti hai, isliye paise waale counters database mein rehte hain. Approximate unique counts ke liye HyperLogLog hai.

Common mistake: an ORM listing.views += 1; await listing.save(), or a per-instance in-memory counter that undercounts across instances and resets on restart.
Galti mat karna: ORM wala listing.views += 1; await listing.save(), ya per-instance in-memory counter jo instances ke across kam ginta hai aur restart pe reset hota hai.
09 What is a mutex vs a semaphore?Mutex aur semaphore mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: a mutex is binary with one owner; a semaphore is a counter that allows N holders.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: mutex binary hai aur uska ek owner hai; semaphore ek counter hai jo N holders allow karta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"A mutex, short for mutual exclusion, lets exactly one holder into a critical section, and it has ownership: whoever locked it must unlock it. It's like a single-key washroom: one key, one person inside, the rest wait. I use it to protect shared state, for example making sure only one request at a time refreshes a shared partner API token in memory. A semaphore is a counter initialised to N: each acquire decrements it, each release increments it, and at zero new callers wait. It's like a parking lot with N slots. I use it to cap concurrency rather than to protect data, for example allowing at most five parallel calls to a rate-limited VIN-decoding partner API. A database connection pool is really a semaphore. The trade-off: a mutex serializes work completely, which is safe but slow if held long; a semaphore allows throughput up to N but doesn't protect shared data from those N holders."

"Mutex, yaani mutual exclusion, critical section mein exactly ek holder ko jaane deta hai, aur usmein ownership hai: jisne lock kiya wahi unlock karega. Yeh ek-chaabi wale washroom jaisa hai: ek chaabi, andar ek insaan, baaki wait. Main isko shared state protect karne ke liye use karta hoon, jaise ensure karna ki memory mein shared partner API token ko ek time pe sirf ek request refresh kare. Semaphore N se shuru hone wala counter hai: har acquire usko ghataata hai, har release badhata hai, aur zero pe naye callers wait karte hain. Yeh N slots wale parking lot jaisa hai.
