Main isko data protect karne ki jagah concurrency cap karne ke liye use karta hoon, jaise rate-limited VIN-decoding partner API pe zyada se zyada paanch parallel calls allow karna. Database connection pool asal mein ek semaphore hai. Trade-off: mutex kaam ko poori tarah line mein laga deta hai, jo safe hai lekin der tak pakda toh slow; semaphore N tak throughput deta hai lekin un N holders se shared data ko protect nahi karta."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

A binary semaphore (N = 1) looks like a mutex but differs on ownership: any thread can signal a semaphore, while only the owner may release a mutex. That ownership enables features like reentrant (recursive) mutexes and priority inheritance, which fixes priority inversion, where a low-priority holder blocks a high-priority waiter. A read-write lock is a middle ground: many readers or one writer. In Node, the async-mutex package provides both Mutex and Semaphore, and p-limit is a simple semaphore. Across instances, a distributed semaphore can be built in Redis, for example with a sorted set of holders with expiry.

Binary semaphore (N = 1) mutex jaisa dikhta hai lekin ownership pe alag hai: koi bhi thread semaphore ko signal kar sakta hai, jabki mutex sirf owner release kar sakta hai. Yahi ownership reentrant (recursive) mutexes aur priority inheritance jaise features possible banaati hai, jo priority inversion fix karta hai, jahaan low-priority holder high-priority waiter ko rok deta hai. Read-write lock beech ka raasta hai: bahut saare readers ya ek writer. Node mein async-mutex package Mutex aur Semaphore dono deta hai, aur p-limit ek simple semaphore hai. Instances ke across Redis mein distributed semaphore bana sakte ho, jaise expiry ke saath holders ka sorted set.

Common mistake: saying a semaphore with N = 1 is exactly a mutex; it ignores ownership, which is the real difference.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki N = 1 wala semaphore exactly mutex hai; isse ownership ignore ho jaati hai, jo asli fark hai.
10 How would you rate-limit an API safely under concurrent requests?Concurrent requests ke beech API ko safely rate-limit kaise karoge?
What they're really testing: an atomic, shared counter (Redis INCR + EXPIRE) or a token bucket, and that you never rely on an in-memory counter per instance.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ek atomic, shared counter (Redis INCR + EXPIRE) ya token bucket, aur yeh ki tum kabhi per-instance in-memory counter pe bharosa nahi karte.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

"The limiter needs a counter that is shared across all instances and updated atomically. I'd use Redis. For a fixed window, say 100 requests per user per minute, the key is user ID plus the current minute. On each request I run INCR on that key, which atomically returns the new count, and set EXPIRE for 60 seconds the first time, in a MULTI block or Lua script so the two can't be separated. If the count is over 100, I return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header. An in-memory counter per instance doesn't work: with five instances behind a load balancer the real limit becomes 500, and it resets on every deploy. And a 'GET, compare, then INCR' is itself a race. If I need to allow short bursts smoothly, I'd use a token bucket in a Lua script. The trade-off is one Redis round trip per request."

"Limiter ko aisa counter chahiye jo saare instances mein shared ho aur atomically update ho. Main Redis use karunga. Fixed window ke liye, maano har user ke liye ek minute mein 100 requests, key hai user ID plus current minute. Har request pe main us key pe INCR chalaata hoon, jo atomically naya count return karta hai, aur pehli baar 60 second ka EXPIRE set karta hoon, MULTI block ya Lua script mein taaki dono alag na ho sakein. Agar count 100 se upar hai, toh main Retry-After header ke saath 429 Too Many Requests return karta hoon. Per-instance in-memory counter kaam nahi karta: load balancer ke peeche paanch instances ho toh asli limit 500 ban jaati hai, aur har deploy pe reset hoti hai. Aur 'GET, compare, phir INCR' khud ek race hai. Agar chhote bursts smoothly allow karne hain, toh main Lua script mein token bucket use karunga. Trade-off hai har request pe ek Redis round trip."

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Fixed windows allow up to double the limit around a boundary (100 at 10:00:59, 100 at 10:01:00). A sliding-window log stores request timestamps in a sorted set (ZADD, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZCARD in one Lua script); a sliding-window counter weights the previous window's count, which is cheaper. A token bucket stores tokens and last-refill time per key. Since Redis 7, EXPIRE key ttl NX sets the TTL only if none exists. I'd decide fail-open vs fail-closed if Redis is down, return RateLimit-* headers so clients can pace themselves, and also enforce coarse limits at the gateway or load balancer.

Fixed windows boundary ke aas paas limit ka double tak allow kar dete hain (10:00:59 pe 100, 10:01:00 pe 100). Sliding-window log request timestamps ko sorted set mein rakhta hai (ek Lua script mein ZADD, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZCARD); sliding-window counter pichhle window ke count ko weight deta hai, jo sasta hai. Token bucket har key ke liye tokens aur last-refill time rakhta hai. Redis 7 se EXPIRE key ttl NX TTL sirf tab set karta hai jab pehle se na ho. Main decide karunga ki Redis down ho toh fail-open ya fail-closed, RateLimit-* headers bhejunga taaki clients apni speed adjust karein, aur gateway ya load balancer pe bhi mote limits lagaunga.

Common mistake: reading the count, comparing in code, then incrementing; two concurrent requests both pass the check, which is the very race you were trying to prevent.
Galti mat karna: count padhna, code mein compare karna, phir increment karna; do concurrent requests dono check paas kar leti hain, yahi woh race hai jisse tum bachna chahte the.

Topic 04 · ASKED EVERYWHERETopic 04 · Har jagah poocha jaata hai

CachingCaching

Why "just use Redis and add a TTL" is the wrong answer, and what the right one sounds like: strategy, invalidation, eviction and the ways a cache breaks in production.

"Bas Redis laga do aur TTL daal do" galat answer kyun hai, aur sahi answer kaisa sunai deta hai: strategy, invalidation, eviction, aur production mein cache kaise-kaise tootta hai.

Level 0 The storyKahani

Picture Raju's chai stall outside a busy railway station. Behind the stall, a two-minute walk away, is his store room: sacks of sugar, crates of biscuits, boxes of samosas from the kitchen. Everything he sells lives in that store room.

But when a customer asks for Parle-G, Raju does not walk to the store room. He reaches for the counter, because the counter already holds a few packets of the most popular things. Two seconds instead of two minutes.

Now someone asks for a rare cream biscuit that is not on the counter. Raju walks to the store room, gets it, and, being smart, brings back a few extra packets and keeps them on the counter in case the next person wants the same thing.

The counter is small. When it is full and he needs space for something new, he removes the item nobody has asked for in the longest time.

Some things go bad. Samosas made at 7 am are not served at 11 am. He throws them out after a fixed time and brings a fresh batch.

Prices change. If the owner updates the price in the store room register but the little price card on the counter still shows yesterday's price, customers see the wrong number. The counter is stale.

And the rush. The evening express arrives and fifty people ask for samosas at the exact moment the tray becomes empty. If every helper runs to the kitchen at once, the kitchen jams and nobody gets anything. A smart stall sends one helper and tells everybody else: "wait half a minute, the tray is coming."

That is the whole topic of caching. You have already seen every idea in this chapter at Raju's stall.

Chai stallBackend
Counter (small, instant)Cache, usually Redis in RAM
Store room (has everything, slow to reach)Database, the source of truth
Item found on the counterCache hit
Walk to the store roomCache miss
Throw out the item nobody asked forEviction (LRU)
Samosas thrown out after 2 hoursTTL (time to live)
Old price card on the counterStale data, needs invalidation
Everyone runs to the kitchen at onceCache stampede
Send one helper, others waitMutex on rebuild

Socho railway station ke bahar Raju ki chai ki stall hai. Stall ke peeche, do minute ki doori pe, uska store room hai: cheeni ki bori, biscuit ke crate, kitchen se aaye samose ke dabbe. Jo kuch bhi woh bechta hai, sab kuch us store room mein hai.

Lekin jab koi customer Parle-G maangta hai, Raju store room nahi jaata. Woh bas counter se utha deta hai, kyunki counter pe sabse zyada bikne waali cheezon ke kuch packet pehle se rakhe hain. Do minute ki jagah do second.

Ab koi ek rare cream biscuit maangta hai jo counter pe nahi hai. Raju store room jaata hai, le aata hai, aur smart hai toh saath mein do-teen extra packet bhi le aata hai aur counter pe rakh deta hai, taaki agla banda wahi maange toh turant mil jaaye.

Counter chhota hai. Jab bhar jaata hai aur kuch naya rakhna hai, toh woh cheez hata deta hai jo sabse lambe time se kisi ne nahi maangi.

Kuch cheezein kharab ho jaati hain. Subah 7 baje ke samose 11 baje nahi diye jaate. Ek fixed time ke baad phenk do, fresh batch le aao.

Daam badalte hain. Agar owner ne store room ke register mein price update kar diya, par counter pe rakha chhota price card abhi bhi kal ka daam dikha raha hai, toh customer ko galat number dikhega. Counter stale ho gaya.

Aur rush. Shaam ki express aati hai aur pachaas log ek saath samosa maangte hain, theek usi second jab tray khaali hui. Agar har helper ek saath kitchen bhaage, toh kitchen jam ho jaayega aur kisi ko kuch nahi milega. Smart stall ek helper bhejti hai aur baaki sabko bolti hai: "aadha minute ruko, tray aa rahi hai."

Bas yahi poora caching ka topic hai. Is chapter ka har idea tum Raju ki stall pe already dekh chuke ho.

Chai stallBackend
Counter (chhota, turant)Cache, aksar RAM mein Redis
Store room (sab kuch hai, door hai)Database, source of truth
Cheez counter pe mil gayiCache hit
Store room tak jaana padaCache miss
Jo kisi ne nahi maanga woh hataoEviction (LRU)
2 ghante baad samose phenkoTTL (time to live)
Counter pe purana price cardStale data, invalidation chahiye
Sab ek saath kitchen bhaageCache stampede
Ek helper jaaye, baaki rukeRebuild pe mutex

Level 1 The basic idea and the wordsBasic idea aur zaroori words

A cache is a small, fast store that keeps a copy of data you would otherwise fetch from somewhere slower. Recall from the foundations chapter: RAM is fast but small and costly; disk is big and cheap but slower. A database like Postgres keeps data on disk and does real work for every query: it parses the SQL, plans it, reads pages, joins tables, sorts. Redis keeps everything in RAM and answers a simple GET by key, usually in well under a millisecond inside the same data centre. So we keep a ready copy in Redis and skip the database work.

A quick Redis refresher (Redis stores key → value pairs in memory):

Cache ek chhota, fast storage hai jo us data ki copy rakhta hai jo warna tumhe kisi slow jagah se laana padta. Foundations chapter yaad karo: RAM fast hai par chhoti aur mehngi; disk badi aur sasti par slow. Postgres jaisa database data disk pe rakhta hai aur har query pe asli kaam karta hai: SQL parse karna, plan banana, pages padhna, tables join karna, sort karna. Redis sab kuch RAM mein rakhta hai aur key se simple GET ka jawab aam taur pe same data centre ke andar ek millisecond se bhi kam mein de deta hai. Isliye hum Redis mein ek ready copy rakh lete hain aur database ka kaam bacha lete hain.

Redis ka chhota sa refresher (Redis memory mein key → value pairs rakhta hai):

# store a value for 300 seconds (EX = expire after N seconds)
SET vehicle:1HGCM82633A004352 '{"make":"Honda","model":"Accord","price":18900}' EX 300
GET vehicle:1HGCM82633A004352     # returns the JSON string, or (nil) if missing/expired
TTL vehicle:1HGCM82633A004352     # seconds left before it expires
DEL vehicle:1HGCM82633A004352     # remove it now (this is "invalidation")

The words you will hear in every caching interview:

  • Hit: the data was in the cache. Fast. Miss: it was not, so we went to the database.
  • Hit ratio: hits ÷ (hits + misses). If 95 of 100 reads are hits, the hit ratio is 95%. This is the single most important cache health number.
  • TTL (time to live): how long an entry may stay before it expires by itself. The samosa rule.
  • Stale data: the cache still holds an old copy after the database changed. The old price card.
  • Invalidation: deliberately removing or updating a cache entry because the real data changed.
  • Eviction: the cache is full, so it throws something out to make room. Not because it is wrong, just because space ran out.
  • Working set: the portion of data that is actually being read right now. Raju's counter only needs today's popular items, not the whole store room.
  • Source of truth: the database. The cache is only a copy. If the whole cache is wiped, you must be able to rebuild it from the database without losing anything.

A dealership website example: every shopper opening a vehicle details page (VDP) for one car makes the server read the vehicle row, its photos and its price. That car's data changes rarely compared with how often it is viewed. That shape, many reads and few writes, is exactly what a cache is for. Even better: the make, model and year decoded from a VIN never change for that VIN, so a VIN-decode result is an almost perfect thing to cache.

Where caches live. A cache is not one thing; there are layers between the user and the database, and each one can answer a request before it goes further:

  • Browser cache: the user's own browser keeps images and files it downloaded before.
  • CDN (Content Delivery Network): a network of servers in many cities that keep copies of HTTP responses (images, JavaScript, CSS, public pages) close to the user. Controlled by the Cache-Control HTTP header, e.g. Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600.
  • Local (in-process) cache: a plain object or map inside your app server's own memory. Fastest possible, no network at all, but each server has its own separate copy.
  • Distributed cache: Redis or Memcached, a separate server that all your app servers share over the network.
  • Database: the source of truth. (It also has its own internal memory cache of disk pages, but that is the database's business.)

Yeh words har caching interview mein aayenge:

  • Hit: data cache mein mil gaya. Fast. Miss: nahi mila, toh database jaana pada.
  • Hit ratio: hits ÷ (hits + misses). Agar 100 mein se 95 reads hit hain, toh hit ratio 95% hai. Cache ki health ka yeh sabse important number hai.
  • TTL (time to live): ek entry kitni der reh sakti hai jab tak woh khud expire na ho jaaye. Samose waala rule.
  • Stale data: database badal gaya par cache mein abhi bhi purani copy padi hai. Purana price card.
  • Invalidation: jaan-boojh ke cache entry hatana ya update karna kyunki asli data badal gaya.
  • Eviction: cache full ho gaya, toh jagah banane ke liye kuch bahar phenkta hai. Isliye nahi ki woh galat hai, bas jagah khatam ho gayi.
  • Working set: data ka woh hissa jo abhi actually padha ja raha hai. Raju ke counter ko sirf aaj ki popular cheezein chahiye, poora store room nahi.
  • Source of truth: database. Cache sirf copy hai. Agar poora cache mit jaaye, toh tumhe database se bina kuch khoye use dobara bana paana chahiye.

Dealership website ka example: har shopper jo ek car ka vehicle details page (VDP) kholta hai, server ko vehicle ki row, uski photos aur price padhne padte hain. Us car ka data jitni baar dekha jaata hai uske comparison mein bahut kam badalta hai. Yeh shape, bahut saare reads aur kam writes, bilkul wahi hai jiske liye cache bana hai. Aur bhi achha: kisi VIN se decode hua make, model aur year us VIN ke liye kabhi nahi badalta, isliye VIN-decode ka result cache karne ke liye almost perfect cheez hai.

Cache kahan-kahan hota hai. Cache ek hi cheez nahi hai; user aur database ke beech kai layers hoti hain, aur har layer request ko aage jaane se pehle hi jawab de sakti hai:

  • Browser cache: user ka apna browser pehle download ki hui images aur files rakh leta hai.
  • CDN (Content Delivery Network): kai shehron mein servers ka network jo HTTP responses ki copies (images, JavaScript, CSS, public pages) user ke paas rakhta hai. Isko Cache-Control HTTP header control karta hai, jaise Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600.
  • Local (in-process) cache: tumhare app server ki apni memory ke andar ek simple object ya map. Sabse fast, network bilkul nahi, par har server ki apni alag copy hoti hai.
  • Distributed cache: Redis ya Memcached, ek alag server jise tumhare saare app servers network pe share karte hain.
  • Database: source of truth. (Iska bhi apna andar ka memory cache hota hai disk pages ke liye, par woh database ka apna maamla hai.)

The cache is a copy; the database is the truth. Every design choice in caching is a trade between how fresh the copy is and how much work you save.

Cache ek copy hai; database sach hai. Caching ka har design choice isi ka trade hai: copy kitni fresh hai vs kitna kaam bacha.

Level 2 How it works inside: the four strategies, invalidation, evictionAndar kaise kaam karta hai: chaar strategies, invalidation, eviction

A caching strategy answers two questions: who puts data into the cache, and what happens on a write. There are four classic strategies. Interviewers want all four, plus the way each one fails.

1. Cache-aside (lazy loading). The most common one, and the one you should describe first. The application is in charge. On a read, the app checks the cache; on a miss, the app reads the database, then puts the result into the cache with a TTL. On a write, the app updates the database and then deletes the cache entry so the next read reloads fresh data. The cache only ever holds things somebody actually asked for. Raju fetching the cream biscuit and keeping a few extra is exactly this.

Caching strategy do sawaalon ka jawab deti hai: cache mein data kaun daalta hai, aur write hone pe kya hota hai. Chaar classic strategies hain. Interviewer ko chaaron chahiye, aur saath mein yeh bhi ki har ek kaise fail hoti hai.

1. Cache-aside (lazy loading). Sabse common, aur interview mein sabse pehle yahi batao. Application in charge hai. Read pe app pehle cache check karti hai; miss hua toh app database se padhti hai, phir result ko TTL ke saath cache mein daal deti hai. Write pe app database update karti hai aur phir cache entry ko delete kar deti hai, taaki agla read fresh data laaye. Cache mein sirf wahi cheezein hoti hain jo kisi ne actually maangi. Raju ka cream biscuit laana aur do extra packet rakh lena, bilkul yahi hai.

// Cache-aside in Node.js (ioredis-style client). The APP does all the work.
async function getVehicle(vin) {
  const key = `vehicle:${vin}`;

  // 1. Look in the cache first
  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached !== null) {
    return JSON.parse(cached);                       // cache HIT: no DB work
  }

  // 2. Cache MISS: ask the database (source of truth)
  const rows = await db.query('SELECT * FROM vehicles WHERE vin = $1', [vin]);
  const vehicle = rows[0] || null;

  // 3. Save a copy for the next reader, with a TTL of 5 minutes
  if (vehicle) {
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(vehicle), 'EX', 300);
  }
  return vehicle;
}

async function updateVehiclePrice(vin, newPrice) {
  // Write to the source of truth FIRST...
  await db.query('UPDATE vehicles SET price = $1 WHERE vin = $2', [newPrice, vin]);
  // ...then DELETE the cached copy (do not try to patch it)
  await redis.del(`vehicle:${vin}`);
}

Why delete on write instead of updating the cache? Imagine two admins change the price at the same moment: A sets 18,900, B sets 19,200. Both update the database, then both write their value into the cache. If the database ends with B's value but the cache writes land in the opposite order, the cache holds A's 18,900 forever (until TTL). Deleting is order-independent: whoever deletes last, the cache is simply empty and the next read loads the true value.

Failure modes of cache-aside: the first read of anything is slow (a cold miss); data can be stale until the TTL or the delete; and if many readers miss at once they all hit the database (the stampede, Level 3).

Read-through is a close cousin: the application only ever talks to the cache, and the cache layer itself knows how to load missing data from the database (you give it a loader function, or a library/managed cache does it). Same idea as cache-aside, but the "go to the DB on a miss" logic moves out of your application code into the cache layer.

2. Write-through. Every write goes to the cache and to the database, synchronously, before the write is confirmed. The cache is always up to date for anything that was written, so reads right after a write are fresh. Cost: every write pays for two writes (slower writes), and you fill the cache with data that may never be read. Good for data that is read soon after it is written, like a user profile or cart.

3. Write-behind (write-back). The app writes only to the cache and gets an immediate "OK". The cache (or a background worker) writes to the database later, often in batches. Writes are extremely fast and the database sees fewer, bigger writes. The danger: if the cache node crashes before it flushes, those writes are lost, because the database never got them. Use it only for data where losing a few seconds of updates is acceptable, like view counters or analytics events, never for money.

4. Refresh-ahead. Instead of waiting for a key to expire and making some unlucky user pay for the miss, a background process reloads popular keys shortly before their TTL ends. Users almost always hit a warm cache. The cost: you need to predict which keys will be needed; refreshing keys nobody reads wastes database work.

Write pe cache ko update karne ki jagah delete kyun? Socho do admins ek hi second pe price badalte hain: A ne 18,900 set kiya, B ne 19,200. Dono database update karte hain, phir dono apni value cache mein likhte hain. Agar database mein last value B ki bachi, par cache writes ulte order mein pahunchi, toh cache mein A ka 18,900 TTL khatam hone tak pada rahega. Delete karna order pe depend nahi karta: jo bhi last mein delete kare, cache bas khaali ho jaata hai aur agla read sahi value le aata hai.

Cache-aside ke failure modes: kisi bhi cheez ka pehla read slow hota hai (cold miss); TTL ya delete tak data stale ho sakta hai; aur agar bahut saare readers ek saath miss karein toh sab database pe toot padte hain (stampede, Level 3 mein).

Read-through iska kareebi bhai hai: application sirf cache se baat karti hai, aur cache layer khud jaanti hai ki missing data database se kaise laana hai (tum use ek loader function dete ho, ya koi library/managed cache yeh karta hai). Idea cache-aside jaisa hi hai, bas "miss pe DB jao" waala logic tumhare app code se nikal ke cache layer mein chala jaata hai.

2. Write-through. Har write cache mein aur database mein, dono jagah, synchronously jaata hai, aur tabhi write confirm hota hai. Jo kuch likha gaya woh cache mein hamesha up to date hai, toh write ke turant baad ka read fresh milta hai. Keemat: har write do writes ki keemat deta hai (writes slow), aur cache aise data se bhar jaata hai jo shayad kabhi padha hi na jaaye. User profile ya cart jaise data ke liye achha hai jo likhne ke thodi der baad padha jaata hai.

3. Write-behind (write-back). App sirf cache mein likhti hai aur turant "OK" mil jaata hai. Cache (ya ek background worker) database mein baad mein likhta hai, aksar batches mein. Writes bahut fast hote hain aur database ko kam, bade writes milte hain. Khatra: agar flush karne se pehle cache node crash ho gaya, toh woh writes kho gaye, kyunki database tak pahunche hi nahi. Sirf aise data ke liye use karo jahan kuch second ke updates khona chalega, jaise view counters ya analytics events; paise ke liye kabhi nahi.

4. Refresh-ahead. Key expire hone ka intezaar karke kisi bechare user se miss ki keemat dilwaane ki jagah, ek background process popular keys ko TTL khatam hone se thoda pehle reload kar deta hai. Users ko almost hamesha warm cache milta hai. Keemat: tumhe andaaza lagana padta hai ki kaunsi keys chahiye hongi; jo keys koi padhta hi nahi unhe refresh karna database ka kaam barbaad karna hai.

StrategyStrategy Who loads the cacheCache kaun bharta hai Main failure modeMain failure mode Use whenKab use karo
Cache-asideApp, on a missApp, miss hone peStale until TTL/delete; stampede on hot missTTL/delete tak stale; hot miss pe stampedeDefault for read-heavy dataRead-heavy data ka default
Read-throughCache layer, on a missCache layer, miss hone peSame as cache-aside; tied to the cache libraryCache-aside jaisa; cache library pe dependYou want loading logic in one placeLoading logic ek jagah chahiye
Write-throughEvery writeHar writeSlower writes; cache full of unread dataSlow writes; cache mein bina padha dataRead-after-write must be freshWrite ke baad read fresh chahiye
Write-behindEvery write, DB laterHar write, DB baad meinData loss if cache dies before flushFlush se pehle cache mara toh data lossWrite-heavy, loss-tolerant (counters)Write-heavy, thoda loss chalega (counters)
Refresh-aheadBackground job, before expiryBackground job, expiry se pehleWasted refreshes; needs good predictionBekaar refresh; achha andaaza chahiyeFew very hot keys, misses hurtKam par bahut hot keys, miss dard deta hai

Invalidation: keeping the copy honest. When the database changes, the cache copy becomes a lie. You have four tools:

  1. TTL: let entries expire on their own. Simple and a safety net for everything, but data can be stale for up to the full TTL.
  2. Explicit delete on write: the code that updates the database also deletes the key (the cache-aside pattern above).
  3. Event-driven invalidation: when data changes, publish an event ("vehicle 123 changed") on a message queue or Redis pub/sub; every service that caches it deletes its copy. Needed when many services or many local caches hold copies.
  4. Versioned keys: put a version in the key, e.g. vehicle:123:v7. When data changes, bump the version to v8; readers now look up a key that does not exist yet and load fresh data. Old versions just expire. No delete race is possible because nobody ever overwrites a key.

Why is this "one of the hardest problems in computer science"? Because there is no perfect moment to invalidate. Too early or too often and your hit ratio collapses, and every invalidation sends a wave of misses to the database. Too late and users see wrong data. The right TTL is not a technical number; it is a business question: how stale may this data be before it hurts someone? A vehicle's description may be fine 10 minutes stale; its "sold" status may not; an account balance should not be cached at all. On top of that, in a distributed system the database update and the cache delete are two separate steps that can fail or interleave with other requests (Level 4 shows the exact race).

Eviction: what to throw out when the cache is full. RAM is limited. In Redis you set maxmemory and a maxmemory-policy. Note: the default policy is noeviction, which means once memory is full, new writes fail with an error. For a cache you almost always change it.

  • LRU (Least Recently Used): throw out the item that was used longest ago. Raju's rule. Great general default. Redis: allkeys-lru.
  • LFU (Least Frequently Used): throw out the item used the fewest times. Better when some items are steadily popular and you do not want one burst of one-time reads to push them out. Redis: allkeys-lfu.
  • TTL-based: prefer to evict keys that have an expiry, soonest-expiring first. Redis: volatile-ttl (the volatile-* policies only evict keys that have a TTL).

(Redis implements LRU and LFU as close approximations by sampling a few keys rather than tracking a perfect order, which keeps it cheap.) Here is LRU worked by hand with a tiny cache that holds only 3 items:

Invalidation: copy ko imaandaar rakhna. Jab database badalta hai, cache ki copy jhooth ban jaati hai. Tumhare paas chaar tools hain:

  1. TTL: entries ko apne aap expire hone do. Simple hai aur har cheez ke liye safety net hai, par data poore TTL tak stale reh sakta hai.
  2. Write pe explicit delete: jo code database update karta hai wahi key bhi delete karta hai (upar waala cache-aside pattern).
  3. Event-driven invalidation: data badle toh ek event publish karo ("vehicle 123 badal gaya") kisi message queue ya Redis pub/sub pe; jo bhi service use cache karti hai woh apni copy delete kar deti hai. Jab kai services ya kai local caches copies rakhte hon tab yeh zaroori hai.
  4. Versioned keys: key mein version daal do, jaise vehicle:123:v7. Data badle toh version v8 kar do; readers ab aisi key dhoondhte hain jo abhi exist hi nahi karti, toh fresh data load hota hai. Purane versions apne aap expire ho jaate hain. Delete ka race ho hi nahi sakta kyunki koi key kabhi overwrite hoti hi nahi.

Isse "computer science ke sabse mushkil problems" mein kyun ginte hain? Kyunki invalidate karne ka koi perfect moment nahi hai. Bahut jaldi ya bahut baar karo toh hit ratio gir jaata hai, aur har invalidation database pe misses ki ek lehar bhejta hai. Bahut der se karo toh users galat data dekhte hain. Sahi TTL koi technical number nahi hai; yeh business ka sawaal hai: yeh data kitna stale ho sakta hai jab tak kisi ko nuksaan na ho? Vehicle ka description 10 minute stale chal jaayega; uska "sold" status shayad nahi; account balance toh cache hi nahi karna chahiye. Upar se, distributed system mein database update aur cache delete do alag steps hain jo fail ho sakte hain ya doosri requests ke saath beech mein uljh sakte hain (Level 4 mein exact race dikhaya hai).

Eviction: cache full ho toh kya phenkein. RAM limited hai. Redis mein tum maxmemory aur ek maxmemory-policy set karte ho. Dhyaan do: default policy noeviction hai, matlab memory full hote hi naye writes error ke saath fail honge. Cache ke liye tum ise almost hamesha badalte ho.

  • LRU (Least Recently Used): woh item phenko jo sabse lambe time pehle use hua tha. Raju ka rule. Badhiya general default. Redis: allkeys-lru.
  • LFU (Least Frequently Used): woh item phenko jo sabse kam baar use hua. Tab better hai jab kuch items lagataar popular hon aur tum nahi chahte ki ek baar ke reads ki ek burst unhe bahar dhakel de. Redis: allkeys-lfu.
  • TTL-based: un keys ko pehle nikalo jinki expiry hai, jo sabse jaldi expire hone waali hain woh pehle. Redis: volatile-ttl (volatile-* policies sirf unhi keys ko evict karti hain jinpe TTL laga hai).

(Redis LRU aur LFU ko perfect order track karne ki jagah kuch keys sample karke approximately implement karta hai, isse sasta padta hai.) Yeh raha LRU haath se chala ke, ek chhote cache ke saath jisme sirf 3 items aate hain:

Notice step 5: when D arrives, the cache holds A, C, B. B was touched longest ago, so B goes. An LFU cache would reason differently: A has been used twice, B and C once each, so it would also keep A and evict one of the single-use items. LRU and LFU often agree; they disagree when an item was popular for a long time but not in the last few seconds (LFU keeps it) or when a burst of new items arrives (LRU lets them push old favourites out).

Sizing: you size a cache for the working set, not the whole database. If a dealer group has a large inventory history but shoppers mostly look at cars currently for sale, the cache only needs those. Estimate: number of hot keys × average value size × some headroom for Redis overhead. Then measure the hit ratio and the eviction count. If evictions are high and hit ratio is low, the cache is too small (or your TTL too short). If memory is mostly unread keys, it is too big or your TTLs are too long.

Step 5 dekho: jab D aata hai, cache mein A, C, B hain. B ko sabse lambe time pehle chhua gaya tha, toh B nikal gaya. LFU cache alag sochta: A do baar use hua, B aur C ek-ek baar, toh woh bhi A ko rakhta aur ek single-use item nikaalta. LRU aur LFU aksar ek hi jawab dete hain; fark tab aata hai jab koi item lambe time se popular tha par pichhle kuch second mein nahi chhua gaya (LFU use rakhega), ya jab naye items ki ek burst aati hai (LRU unhe purane favourites ko bahar dhakelne dega).

Sizing: cache ka size working set ke liye rakhte hain, poore database ke liye nahi. Agar ek dealer group ki inventory history badi hai par shoppers zyaadatar abhi bikne waali cars dekhte hain, toh cache ko sirf unki zaroorat hai. Andaaza: hot keys ki ginti × average value size × Redis overhead ke liye thodi extra jagah. Phir hit ratio aur eviction count measure karo. Agar evictions zyada aur hit ratio kam hai, toh cache chhota hai (ya TTL bahut chhota). Agar memory mein zyaadatar bina padhi keys hain, toh cache bahut bada hai ya TTL bahut lambe.

Level 3 Production: how caches break, and what to cache at allProduction: cache kaise tootta hai, aur cache karna bhi chahiye ya nahi

Failure 1: the cache stampede (thundering herd). A popular key, say the home page's "featured vehicles" list, expires at 10:00:00. In that same second, 2,000 requests arrive. All of them see a miss. All of them run the same heavy query on the database at once. The database slows down, the queries take longer, more requests pile up behind them, and it can fall over. This is the evening express and every helper running to the kitchen. The cache was protecting the database; the moment the key expired, the protection vanished for everyone at once.

Three fixes, often combined:

  1. Mutex (lock) on rebuild: only the first request to miss gets a short lock and rebuilds the value; everyone else waits a few milliseconds and reads the cache again (or is served the old value if you kept it). One helper goes to the kitchen.
  2. Staggered TTLs (jitter): instead of TTL = 300 for every key, use 300 plus a random 0–60 seconds, so keys written together do not all expire in the same second.
  3. Probabilistic early expiration: as a key gets close to expiry, each request has a small, growing chance of deciding to refresh it early. Usually one lucky request refreshes it before it actually expires, so nobody ever sees the cold miss. (Refresh-ahead is the scheduled version of the same idea.)

Failure 1: cache stampede (thundering herd). Ek popular key, maan lo home page ki "featured vehicles" list, 10:00:00 pe expire hoti hai. Usi second mein 2,000 requests aati hain. Sabko miss milta hai. Sab ek saath database pe wahi bhaari query chalate hain. Database slow hota hai, queries lambi chalti hain, peeche aur requests jama hoti hain, aur database gir bhi sakta hai. Yahi hai shaam ki express aur har helper ka kitchen bhaagna. Cache database ko bacha raha tha; jaise hi key expire hui, sabke liye protection ek saath gayab.

Teen fixes, aksar saath mein use hote hain:

  1. Rebuild pe mutex (lock): jo pehli request miss karti hai sirf wahi ek chhota lock leti hai aur value dobara banati hai; baaki sab kuch milliseconds rukte hain aur cache dobara padhte hain (ya agar purani value rakhi hai toh woh de di jaati hai). Ek helper kitchen jaata hai.
  2. Staggered TTLs (jitter): har key ke liye TTL = 300 ki jagah 300 plus random 0–60 second use karo, taaki ek saath likhi gayi keys ek hi second mein expire na hon.
  3. Probabilistic early expiration: jaise-jaise key expiry ke paas aati hai, har request ke paas ek chhota, badhta hua chance hota hai ki woh use jaldi refresh kar de. Aam taur pe koi ek lucky request asli expiry se pehle hi refresh kar deti hai, toh cold miss kisi ko dikhta hi nahi. (Refresh-ahead isi idea ka scheduled version hai.)
// Cache-aside + mutex on rebuild + jittered TTL
async function getWithLock(key, loadFromDb, ttlSec, triesLeft = 20) {
  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached !== null) return JSON.parse(cached);          // HIT

  // SET ... NX EX 10 = "create lock only if nobody has it; auto-expire in 10s"
  const gotLock = await redis.set(`lock:${key}`, '1', 'NX', 'EX', 10);

  if (gotLock) {
    try {
      const fresh = await loadFromDb();                     // only ONE request does this
      const jitter = Math.floor(Math.random() * 60);        // stagger expiry
      await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(fresh), 'EX', ttlSec + jitter);
      return fresh;
    } finally {
      await redis.del(`lock:${key}`);  // production: store a unique token, delete only if still yours
    }
  }

  if (triesLeft === 0) return loadFromDb();                 // give up waiting, fall back
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50));               // someone else is rebuilding
  return getWithLock(key, loadFromDb, ttlSec, triesLeft - 1);
}

Failure 2: the hot key. Redis in production is usually a cluster: data is split across several Redis servers (shards), and each key lives on exactly one of them (Redis Cluster hashes the key into one of 16,384 slots, and each shard owns some slots). That spreads load nicely, until one key gets most of the traffic: a flash-sale banner, a celebrity profile, or one vehicle listing that went viral. Now one shard is melting while the others are idle, and adding more shards does not help, because the key still lives on one of them. Fixes:

  • Local in-memory cache in front: each app server keeps the hot value in its own memory for a few seconds. Thousands of Redis calls become a handful.
  • Key sharding (replication of the key): store N copies, banner:1 … banner:10, which hash to different shards; each reader picks one at random. Writes must update all copies.
  • Read replicas: let replicas of that shard serve reads, spreading the load over more machines.

Failure 3: cache penetration. Requests for things that do not exist (a mistyped VIN, or an attacker requesting random IDs) always miss the cache and always hit the database, because there is nothing to cache. Fix: cache the "not found" result too, with a short TTL (negative caching), or put a Bloom filter (a compact structure that can say "definitely not present") in front.

Failure 4: the cache itself goes down. If Redis dies and every request falls through to the database at once, it is a stampede on everything. Your app must treat the cache as optional (short timeouts on Redis calls, fall back to the database), but also protect the database while the cache is cold: rate limit, a circuit breaker, or serving slightly stale data from a local cache.

Local cache vs distributed cache.

Failure 2: hot key. Production mein Redis aam taur pe ek cluster hota hai: data kai Redis servers (shards) mein baanta hota hai, aur har key theek ek shard pe rehti hai (Redis Cluster key ko hash karke 16,384 slots mein se ek mein daalta hai, aur har shard kuch slots ka maalik hai). Isse load achhe se bat jaata hai, jab tak ek key pe zyaadatar traffic na aa jaaye: flash-sale banner, kisi celebrity ka profile, ya ek vehicle listing jo viral ho gayi. Ab ek shard pighal raha hai aur baaki khaali baithe hain, aur zyada shards jodne se bhi fayda nahi, kyunki woh key toh ek hi shard pe hai. Fixes:

  • Aage ek local in-memory cache: har app server hot value ko kuch second ke liye apni memory mein rakhta hai. Hazaaron Redis calls kuch hi reh jaati hain.
  • Key sharding (key ki copies): N copies rakho, banner:1 … banner:10, jo alag-alag shards pe hash hoti hain; har reader random ek chun leta hai. Write pe saari copies update karni padti hain.
  • Read replicas: us shard ki replicas ko bhi reads serve karne do, load zyada machines pe bat jaata hai.

Failure 3: cache penetration. Aisi cheezon ki requests jo exist hi nahi karti (galat type kiya VIN, ya koi attacker random IDs maang raha hai) hamesha cache miss karti hain aur hamesha database tak jaati hain, kyunki cache karne ko kuch hai hi nahi. Fix: "not found" result ko bhi chhote TTL ke saath cache karo (negative caching), ya aage ek Bloom filter lagao (ek compact structure jo bol sakta hai "yeh pakka nahi hai").

Failure 4: cache khud down ho gaya. Agar Redis mar gaya aur har request ek saath database pe gir padi, toh yeh sab cheezon pe ek saath stampede hai. Tumhari app ko cache ko optional maanna chahiye (Redis calls pe chhote timeouts, database pe fallback), par cache cold hone tak database ko bachana bhi chahiye: rate limit, circuit breaker, ya local cache se thoda stale data dena.

Local cache vs distributed cache.

Local (in-process)Local (in-process)Distributed (Redis)Distributed (Redis)
SpeedSpeedFastest: plain memory, no networkSabse fast: seedhi memory, network nahiFast, but one network round tripFast, par ek network round trip
ConsistencyConsistencyEach server has its own copy; they drift apartHar server ki apni copy; aapas mein alag ho jaati hainOne shared copy for all serversSaare servers ke liye ek shared copy
SizeSizeLimited by app server RAM; duplicated per serverApp server ki RAM tak; har server pe duplicateLarge, scales with clusterBada, cluster ke saath badhta hai
Survives restart/deployRestart/deploy ke baad bachta hai?No, lost every deployNahi, har deploy pe gayaYesHaan
Good forKiske liye achhaTiny, very hot, rarely-changing data (config, feature flags, a hot key)Chhota, bahut hot, kam badalne waala data (config, feature flags, hot key)Shared data: sessions, query results, rate-limit countersShared data: sessions, query results, rate-limit counters

Many real systems use both: a small local cache (L1) with a TTL of a few seconds, in front of Redis (L2), in front of the database.

CDN vs application cache. A CDN caches whole HTTP responses at the edge, meaning servers physically close to the user, keyed by URL. It is ideal for static files and public pages that look the same for everyone; you control it with headers like Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 and you invalidate by "purging" a URL or by changing the file name (e.g. app.3f9a.js). Redis caches data (objects, query results) next to your application, and your code decides the key and the invalidation. The CDN reduces latency for the user and offloads your whole server; Redis reduces load on your database. A listing photo belongs on the CDN; the logged-in shopper's saved-vehicles list belongs, if anywhere, in Redis.

When NOT to cache.

  • Data that changes faster than your TTL: you would be serving stale data most of the time and paying for writes you never read.
  • Exact financial values used for decisions: account balances, available credit, the amount about to be charged. Read them from the source of truth.
  • Per-user, per-request data that is never read twice: you pay memory and a write for a hit ratio near zero.
  • Anything where staleness is a security problem: permissions, a revoked session, a banned user, a password change. A cached "is admin = true" after you removed admin rights is a real incident.
  • Anything cheap already: a primary-key lookup on a small table may be as fast as a Redis round trip; caching it adds complexity for nothing.

Kai real systems dono use karte hain: ek chhota local cache (L1) jiska TTL kuch second ka ho, Redis (L2) ke aage, jo database ke aage hai.

CDN vs application cache. CDN poore HTTP responses ko edge pe cache karta hai, matlab aise servers jo physically user ke paas hain, aur key URL hota hai. Static files aur public pages ke liye perfect hai jo sabke liye ek jaise dikhte hain; isko tum Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 jaise headers se control karte ho aur invalidate karte ho URL ko "purge" karke ya file ka naam badal ke (jaise app.3f9a.js). Redis data (objects, query results) ko tumhari application ke paas cache karta hai, aur key aur invalidation tumhara code decide karta hai. CDN user ke liye latency kam karta hai aur tumhare poore server ka bojh halka karta hai; Redis tumhare database ka load kam karta hai. Listing ki photo CDN pe jaani chahiye; logged-in shopper ki saved-vehicles list, agar kahin cache ho, toh Redis mein.

Kab cache NAHI karna.

  • Jo data tumhare TTL se tez badalta hai: zyaadatar time stale data doge aur un writes ki keemat doge jo kabhi padhe hi nahi gaye.
  • Decision ke liye use hone waali exact financial values: account balance, available credit, jo amount abhi charge hone waala hai. Inhe source of truth se padho.
  • Per-user, per-request data jo kabhi dobara nahi padha jaata: memory aur write ki keemat do aur hit ratio almost zero.
  • Kuch bhi jahan stale hona security problem hai: permissions, revoked session, banned user, password change. Admin rights hatane ke baad bhi cache mein "is admin = true" pada hai, yeh ek real incident hai.
  • Jo pehle se sasta hai: chhoti table pe primary-key lookup Redis round trip jitna hi fast ho sakta hai; use cache karna bina fayde ki complexity hai.

Level 4 Senior nuances: consistency races, sizing, what to measureSenior nuances: consistency races, sizing, kya measure karein

The classic cache-aside race. Even "update DB, then delete cache" is not perfectly safe. Watch this interleaving:

  1. Reader R misses the cache and reads the old price 18,900 from the database.
  2. Writer W updates the database to 19,200 and deletes the cache key.
  3. R, which was slow (a GC pause, a slow network), now writes its old 18,900 into the cache.

The cache now holds the wrong value until the TTL expires. It is rare, because R has to be slower than a whole write, but at scale rare things happen daily. Defences:

  • Always keep a TTL, even with explicit invalidation. It bounds how long any bug or race can last.
  • Delayed double delete: delete the key, then delete it again a short moment later (e.g. from a queue) to clean up any slow reader's stale write.
  • Versioned keys or version checks: store a version (or updated_at) with the value and never overwrite a newer version with an older one.
  • Change data capture (CDC): instead of trusting every code path to remember to invalidate, a tool such as Debezium reads the database's own change log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog) and emits an event for every committed change; a small consumer deletes the matching cache keys. Invalidation then follows the truth, including changes made by scripts or other services.
  • Write-through for data where read-after-write freshness matters, accepting slower writes.

And remember the two-step problem: if the database write succeeds but the cache delete fails (Redis timeout), you have stale data. Retry the delete, publish it to a queue, or rely on CDC and TTL as the backstop. Say this in an interview; it shows you know caching is a distributed-systems problem, not a Redis command.

Local caches need invalidation too. With an L1 cache on 20 app servers, deleting from Redis does not touch the 20 local copies. Either keep L1 TTLs very short (seconds), or broadcast invalidations over Redis pub/sub so every server drops its copy.

Stale-while-revalidate. A gentle middle ground: when a value expires, serve the old value one more time and trigger a background refresh. Users never wait; data is at most one refresh cycle stale. HTTP has this built in: Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30. You can do the same in app code by storing a "soft expiry" inside the value and a longer "hard" TTL on the key.

Probabilistic early expiration in one line. Each read computes now - rebuildTime * beta * ln(random()); if that passes the expiry time, this request refreshes early. Because ln(random()) is negative, the check fires with a probability that grows as expiry approaches and is higher for values that are slow to rebuild. No locks, no coordination.

Sizing and eviction, the senior way. Start from access patterns, not from the table size: which keys, how many are hot at once, how big each value is. Pick the policy from the pattern: LRU for general "recent things get re-read"; LFU when popularity is stable and you want to resist one-off scans; TTL-driven (volatile-ttl) when freshness is the main rule. Then verify with data. Watch these numbers:

  • Hit ratio (Redis INFO stats: keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses).
  • evicted_keys: rising fast means the cache is too small for the working set.
  • used_memory vs maxmemory, and p99 latency of Redis calls.
  • Database load when the cache is cold: the true test of whether you can survive a cache restart.

In real production, the number to watch after adding a cache is not "Redis is fast". It is: did database load go down, did p99 latency go down, and what happens to both when the cache is empty? A cache you cannot survive losing has quietly become your database, without a database's guarantees.

Classic cache-aside race. "Pehle DB update, phir cache delete" bhi poori tarah safe nahi hai. Yeh interleaving dekho:

  1. Reader R ko cache miss hota hai aur woh database se purana price 18,900 padhta hai.
  2. Writer W database ko 19,200 pe update karta hai aur cache key delete kar deta hai.
  3. R, jo slow tha (GC pause, slow network), ab apna purana 18,900 cache mein likh deta hai.

Ab cache mein TTL khatam hone tak galat value hai. Aisa kam hota hai, kyunki R ko poore write se bhi slow hona padta hai, par scale pe "kam hone waali" cheezein roz hoti hain. Bachaav:

  • Hamesha TTL rakho, explicit invalidation ke saath bhi. Isse koi bhi bug ya race kitni der chalega uski limit lag jaati hai.
  • Delayed double delete: key delete karo, phir thodi der baad dobara delete karo (jaise queue se), taaki kisi slow reader ka stale write saaf ho jaaye.
  • Versioned keys ya version check: value ke saath version (ya updated_at) rakho aur kabhi bhi naye version ko purane se overwrite mat karo.
  • Change data capture (CDC): har code path pe bharosa karne ki jagah ki woh invalidate karna yaad rakhega, Debezium jaisa tool database ka apna change log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog) padhta hai aur har committed change pe ek event nikaalta hai; ek chhota consumer matching cache keys delete kar deta hai. Ab invalidation sach ke peeche chalta hai, scripts ya doosri services ke kiye changes bhi pakde jaate hain.
  • Write-through us data ke liye jahan write ke baad ka read fresh hona zaroori hai, slow writes accept karke.

Aur do-step waali problem yaad rakho: agar database write ho gaya par cache delete fail ho gaya (Redis timeout), toh stale data hai. Delete ko retry karo, queue pe daalo, ya backstop ke liye CDC aur TTL pe bharosa karo. Interview mein yeh bolo; isse dikhta hai ki tum jaante ho caching ek distributed-systems problem hai, sirf ek Redis command nahi.

Local caches ko bhi invalidation chahiye. 20 app servers pe L1 cache hai, toh Redis se delete karne se woh 20 local copies nahi hatengi. Ya toh L1 TTL bahut chhote rakho (seconds), ya Redis pub/sub pe invalidation broadcast karo taaki har server apni copy gira de.

Stale-while-revalidate. Ek naram beech ka raasta: value expire ho toh purani value ek baar aur de do aur background mein refresh chala do. Users kabhi wait nahi karte; data zyada se zyada ek refresh cycle stale hota hai. HTTP mein yeh built-in hai: Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30. App code mein bhi yahi kar sakte ho: value ke andar ek "soft expiry" rakho aur key pe lamba "hard" TTL.

Probabilistic early expiration ek line mein. Har read now - rebuildTime * beta * ln(random()) calculate karta hai; agar yeh expiry time se aage nikal gaya, toh yeh request jaldi refresh karti hai. Kyunki ln(random()) negative hota hai, yeh check aisi probability se fire hota hai jo expiry paas aane pe badhti hai aur slow-to-rebuild values ke liye zyada hoti hai. Na lock, na coordination.

Sizing aur eviction, senior tareeke se. Table ke size se nahi, access patterns se shuru karo: kaunsi keys, ek saath kitni hot hain, har value kitni badi hai. Pattern dekh ke policy chuno: general "recent cheezein dobara padhi jaati hain" ke liye LRU; jab popularity stable ho aur ek baar ke scans se bachna ho tab LFU; jab freshness main rule ho tab TTL-driven (volatile-ttl). Phir data se verify karo. Yeh numbers dekho:

  • Hit ratio (Redis INFO stats: keyspace_hits aur keyspace_misses).
  • evicted_keys: tezi se badh raha hai matlab working set ke liye cache chhota hai.
  • used_memory vs maxmemory, aur Redis calls ki p99 latency.
  • Cache cold ho tab database ka load: asli test ki kya tum cache restart jhel paoge.

Real production mein, cache lagane ke baad dekhne waala number "Redis fast hai" nahi hai. Number yeh hai: kya database load kam hua, kya p99 latency kam hui, aur cache khaali hone pe in dono ka kya hota hai? Jis cache ko khona tum jhel nahi sakte, woh chupke se tumhara database ban gaya hai, database ki guarantees ke bina.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Cache
A small, fast store holding a copy of data that normally lives somewhere slower.Chhota, fast storage jo us data ki copy rakhta hai jo aam taur pe kisi slow jagah rehta hai.
Cache hit / miss
Hit: found in the cache. Miss: not found, so you go to the database.Hit: cache mein mil gaya. Miss: nahi mila, database jaana pada.
Hit ratio
Hits divided by all reads; the main health number of a cache.Hits ko total reads se divide karo; cache ki health ka main number.
TTL
Time to live: how long an entry stays before expiring on its own.Time to live: entry apne aap expire hone se pehle kitni der rehti hai.
Stale data
A cached copy that no longer matches the database.Cache ki copy jo ab database se match nahi karti.
Invalidation
Removing or replacing a cache entry because the real data changed.Asli data badla isliye cache entry hatana ya badalna.
Eviction
Removing entries because the cache is full (LRU, LFU, TTL policies).Cache full hai isliye entries nikaalna (LRU, LFU, TTL policies).
LRU / LFU
Evict the least recently used item / the least frequently used item.Jo sabse pehle use hua tha woh nikalo / jo sabse kam baar use hua woh nikalo.
Working set
The part of the data actively being read right now; what you size the cache for.Data ka woh hissa jo abhi actively padha ja raha hai; cache ka size isi ke hisaab se.
Cache-aside
App checks the cache, loads from DB on a miss, and fills the cache itself.App cache check karti hai, miss pe DB se laati hai, aur khud cache bharti hai.
Read-through
The cache layer loads from the DB on a miss; the app only talks to the cache.Miss pe cache layer khud DB se laati hai; app sirf cache se baat karti hai.
Write-through / write-behind
Write to cache and DB together / write to cache now and DB later.Cache aur DB mein saath likho / cache mein abhi, DB mein baad mein.
Refresh-ahead
Reload popular keys shortly before they expire.Popular keys ko expire hone se thoda pehle reload karna.
Cache stampede
Many requests miss the same expired key and all rebuild it from the DB at once.Bahut saari requests ek hi expired key miss karke sab ek saath DB se rebuild karti hain.
Jitter
A small random amount added to a TTL so keys do not expire together.TTL mein thoda random time jodna taaki keys ek saath expire na hon.
Hot key
One key receiving so much traffic that the single Redis node holding it overloads.Ek key pe itna traffic ki use rakhne waala akela Redis node overload ho jaaye.
Negative caching
Caching "not found" results so repeated lookups for missing data skip the DB."Not found" result ko cache karna taaki missing data ke baar-baar lookups DB tak na jaayein.
CDN / edge
A network of servers close to users that cache HTTP responses such as images and static files.Users ke paas servers ka network jo images aur static files jaise HTTP responses cache karta hai.
Cache-Control
The HTTP header that tells browsers and CDNs whether and how long to cache a response.HTTP header jo browsers aur CDNs ko batata hai ki response cache karna hai ya nahi aur kitni der.
CDC
Change data capture: reading the database's change log to react to every committed change.Change data capture: database ka change log padh ke har committed change pe react karna.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 Explain the four main caching strategies and when to use each.Chaar main caching strategies explain karo aur batao kab kaunsi use karni chahiye.
What they're really testing: that you know more than "use Redis", and that you can name the failure mode of each strategy, not just its happy path.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum "Redis use karo" se aage jaante ho, aur har strategy ka sirf happy path nahi, uska failure mode bhi bata sakte ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

The four are cache-aside, write-through, write-behind and refresh-ahead. Cache-aside is my default: the app checks Redis, on a miss reads the database and fills the cache with a TTL, and on writes it updates the database and deletes the key. Its failure mode is stale data until the TTL or delete, and stampedes on a hot miss. Write-through writes cache and database together, so reads after writes are fresh, but every write is slower. Write-behind writes the cache and flushes to the database later, which is very fast but loses data if the cache dies before the flush, so I only use it for things like view counters. Refresh-ahead reloads hot keys before they expire so users never see a cold miss, at the cost of refreshing keys nobody reads. For a vehicle listing page I would use cache-aside with jittered TTLs.

Chaar hain: cache-aside, write-through, write-behind aur refresh-ahead. Cache-aside mera default hai: app Redis check karti hai, miss pe database padhti hai aur TTL ke saath cache bharti hai, aur write pe database update karke key delete karti hai. Iska failure mode hai TTL ya delete tak stale data, aur hot miss pe stampede. Write-through cache aur database dono mein saath likhta hai, toh write ke baad read fresh milta hai, par har write slow hota hai. Write-behind cache mein likhta hai aur database mein baad mein flush karta hai, bahut fast hai par flush se pehle cache mara toh data gaya, isliye main ise sirf view counters jaisi cheezon ke liye use karta hoon. Refresh-ahead hot keys ko expire hone se pehle reload karta hai taaki users ko cold miss na dikhe, par jo keys koi nahi padhta unhe bhi refresh karne ki keemat hai. Vehicle listing page ke liye main jittered TTL ke saath cache-aside use karunga.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I would mention read-through as a variant of cache-aside where the cache layer owns the loading logic. On write-through, I would point out it does not remove the need for TTLs: data written by other paths (a batch job, a direct SQL fix) still bypasses the cache. On write-behind, durability depends on the cache: Redis with AOF persistence reduces the loss window but does not make it a database, so I would never put payments behind it. And I would explain why cache-aside deletes instead of updating on write: two concurrent writers can update the cache in the opposite order from the database, while a delete is order-independent.

Main read-through ko cache-aside ka variant bataunga jisme loading logic cache layer ke paas hota hai. Write-through pe main bataunga ki isse TTL ki zaroorat khatam nahi hoti: doosre raaston se likha gaya data (batch job, seedha SQL fix) phir bhi cache ko bypass karta hai. Write-behind mein durability cache pe depend karti hai: AOF persistence waala Redis loss ka window kam karta hai par use database nahi banata, isliye payments uske peeche kabhi nahi. Aur main samjhaunga ki cache-aside write pe update ki jagah delete kyun karta hai: do concurrent writers cache ko database se ulte order mein update kar sakte hain, jabki delete order pe depend nahi karta.

Common mistake: listing the four names with no failure modes, or claiming write-behind is "just faster" without mentioning data loss.
Galti mat karna: chaar naam gina dena bina failure modes ke, ya write-behind ko "bas fast hai" bolna bina data loss bataye.
02 What is cache invalidation and why is it one of the hardest problems in CS?Cache invalidation kya hai aur ise CS ke sabse mushkil problems mein kyun gina jaata hai?
What they're really testing: that you see the two-sided trade-off (too early means miss storms, too late means stale data) and that the right answer depends on how much staleness the business tolerates.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum dono taraf ka trade-off dekhte ho (bahut jaldi = miss storm, bahut der = stale data) aur ki sahi jawab is baat pe depend karta hai ki business kitna stale data jhel sakta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Invalidation means removing or replacing a cached copy when the real data changes, so users do not see a lie. It is hard because there is no perfect moment. Invalidate too early or too often and the hit ratio collapses, every invalidation sends a wave of misses to the database, and you have a miss storm. Invalidate too late and users see stale data. On top of that, the database write and the cache delete are two separate operations in a distributed system: one can fail, or a slow reader can write old data back after you deleted it. So I start from a business question: how stale can this be? A vehicle description can be minutes stale; a sold status should be invalidated on write; a balance should not be cached at all. Then I pick TTL, delete-on-write, events or versioned keys to match.

Invalidation matlab jab asli data badle toh cache ki copy hatana ya badalna, taaki users ko jhooth na dikhe. Mushkil isliye hai kyunki koi perfect moment nahi hai. Bahut jaldi ya bahut baar invalidate karo toh hit ratio gir jaata hai, har invalidation database pe misses ki lehar bhejta hai, aur miss storm ban jaata hai. Bahut der se karo toh users stale data dekhte hain. Upar se, distributed system mein database write aur cache delete do alag operations hain: ek fail ho sakta hai, ya ek slow reader tumhare delete ke baad purana data wapas likh sakta hai. Isliye main business ke sawaal se shuru karta hoon: yeh kitna stale ho sakta hai? Vehicle description kuch minute stale chalega; sold status write pe invalidate hona chahiye; balance cache hi nahi hona chahiye. Phir usi hisaab se TTL, delete-on-write, events ya versioned keys chunta hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I would walk through the race: reader misses and reads the old value, writer updates the database and deletes the key, then the slow reader writes the old value into the cache. Defences are keeping a TTL as a backstop on everything, a delayed second delete, storing a version with the value and refusing to overwrite newer with older, or driving invalidation from the database's change log with CDC so every committed change, from any service or script, triggers a delete. If the delete itself fails, I retry it through a queue rather than ignore it.

Main race samjhaunga: reader miss karke purani value padhta hai, writer database update karke key delete karta hai, phir slow reader purani value cache mein likh deta hai. Bachaav: har cheez pe backstop ke liye TTL rakhna, thodi der baad doosra delete, value ke saath version rakhna aur naye ko purane se overwrite na hone dena, ya CDC se database ke change log se invalidation chalana taaki kisi bhi service ya script ka har committed change delete trigger kare. Agar delete khud fail ho, toh use ignore nahi, queue ke through retry karta hoon.

Common mistake: saying "just set a short TTL". A short TTL trades staleness for miss storms; it does not remove the problem.
Galti mat karna: "bas chhota TTL laga do" bolna. Chhota TTL staleness ke badle miss storms deta hai; problem khatam nahi karta.
03 What is a cache stampede / thundering herd and how do you prevent it?Cache stampede / thundering herd kya hai aur ise kaise rokte ho?
What they're really testing: whether you know the three standard fixes: a mutex on rebuild, probabilistic early expiry, and staggered TTLs.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum teen standard fixes jaante ho: rebuild pe mutex, probabilistic early expiry, aur staggered TTLs.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A stampede happens when a popular key expires and many requests miss at the same moment, so they all run the same expensive query on the database together. The cache was shielding the database, and the shield disappears for everyone at once; the database can slow down or fall over. I prevent it three ways. First, a mutex on rebuild: the first request that misses takes a short Redis lock with SET lock:key 1 NX EX 10 and rebuilds; the others wait a few milliseconds and re-read the cache. Second, jitter on TTLs, like 300 seconds plus a random 0 to 60, so keys written together do not expire together. Third, probabilistic early expiration or refresh-ahead, so one request refreshes the key before it actually expires. For the home page's featured-vehicles list, I would combine the lock with serving the slightly stale value while it rebuilds.

Stampede tab hota hai jab ek popular key expire hoti hai aur bahut saari requests ek hi pal mein miss karti hain, toh sab database pe wahi mehngi query ek saath chalati hain. Cache database ki dhaal tha, aur woh dhaal sabke liye ek saath gayab ho jaati hai; database slow ho sakta hai ya gir sakta hai. Main ise teen tareekon se rokta hoon. Pehla, rebuild pe mutex: jo pehli request miss karti hai woh SET lock:key 1 NX EX 10 se chhota Redis lock leti hai aur rebuild karti hai; baaki kuch milliseconds ruk ke cache dobara padhti hain. Doosra, TTL pe jitter, jaise 300 second plus random 0 se 60, taaki saath likhi keys saath expire na hon. Teesra, probabilistic early expiration ya refresh-ahead, taaki koi ek request asli expiry se pehle key refresh kar de. Home page ki featured-vehicles list ke liye main lock ke saath-saath rebuild hone tak thodi stale value dena combine karunga.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The lock needs a TTL so a crashed rebuilder does not block everyone forever, and it should hold a unique token so a slow holder does not delete someone else's lock. Waiters need a limit, after which they fall back or serve stale data. Probabilistic early expiration works without any lock: each read checks now - rebuildTime * beta * ln(random()) against the expiry, so the chance of an early refresh grows near expiry and is higher for values that are slow to rebuild. The same herd appears when the whole cache restarts, so I also think about warming critical keys and rate limiting the database path.

Lock pe TTL hona chahiye taaki crash hua rebuilder sabko hamesha ke liye block na kare, aur usme ek unique token hona chahiye taaki slow holder kisi aur ka lock delete na kar de. Wait karne waalon ki ek limit honi chahiye, jiske baad woh fallback karein ya stale data dein. Probabilistic early expiration bina lock ke kaam karta hai: har read now - rebuildTime * beta * ln(random()) ko expiry se compare karta hai, toh early refresh ka chance expiry ke paas badhta hai aur slow-to-rebuild values ke liye zyada hota hai. Yahi herd tab bhi aata hai jab poora cache restart ho, isliye main critical keys ko warm karne aur database path pe rate limit ke baare mein bhi sochta hoon.

Common mistake: giving every key the same fixed TTL, which guarantees that keys cached together all expire in the same second.
Galti mat karna: har key ko ek hi fixed TTL dena, jisse pakka hai ki saath cache hui keys ek hi second mein expire hongi.
04 What is a hot key problem in Redis and how do you solve it?Redis mein hot key problem kya hai aur ise kaise solve karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you understand one key lives on one node, so a key with most of the traffic overloads that node, and that the fixes are a local cache, key sharding or read replicas.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum samajhte ho ek key ek hi node pe rehti hai, toh jis key pe zyaadatar traffic ho woh us node ko overload kar deti hai, aur fixes hain local cache, key sharding ya read replicas.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

In a Redis cluster each key hashes to one slot, and each slot lives on one shard. That spreads load well until a single key gets a huge share of traffic, say a flash-sale banner or one listing that goes viral. Then one shard is saturated on CPU or network while the rest are idle, and adding shards does not help because that key still lives in one place. I solve it in layers. First, a small local in-memory cache on each app server with a TTL of a few seconds, so thousands of Redis calls per server become a handful. Second, key sharding: store copies like banner:1 to banner:10 that land on different shards and have readers pick one at random. Third, let replicas of that shard serve reads. I find hot keys with monitoring, for example redis-cli --hotkeys when an LFU policy is enabled.

Redis cluster mein har key ek slot mein hash hoti hai, aur har slot ek shard pe rehta hai. Isse load achhe se bat-ta hai jab tak ek akeli key pe traffic ka bahut bada hissa na aa jaaye, jaise flash-sale banner ya ek listing jo viral ho gayi. Tab ek shard CPU ya network pe full ho jaata hai aur baaki khaali baithe hain, aur shards jodne se fayda nahi kyunki woh key toh ek hi jagah hai. Main ise layers mein solve karta hoon. Pehla, har app server pe ek chhota local in-memory cache jiska TTL kuch second ho, taaki har server ki hazaaron Redis calls kuch hi reh jaayein. Doosra, key sharding: banner:1 se banner:10 jaisi copies rakho jo alag shards pe jaayein aur readers random ek chunein. Teesra, us shard ki replicas ko reads serve karne do. Hot keys main monitoring se dhoondhta hoon, jaise LFU policy on ho toh redis-cli --hotkeys.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Each fix has a cost. The local cache adds staleness across servers, so it suits data that tolerates a few seconds of lag, and I would invalidate it via pub/sub if needed. Key sharding multiplies writes, since every update must touch all N copies, so it fits read-heavy keys. Replica reads can return slightly stale data because Redis replication is asynchronous. A related problem is a big key, like a huge hash or list, which hurts even at modest traffic because each read moves a lot of bytes; the fix there is splitting the value into smaller keys.

Har fix ki keemat hai. Local cache servers ke beech staleness laata hai, toh yeh us data ke liye hai jo kuch second ka lag jhel sake, aur zaroorat ho toh main use pub/sub se invalidate karunga. Key sharding writes ko multiply karta hai, kyunki har update ko saari N copies chhooni padti hain, toh yeh read-heavy keys ke liye hai. Replica reads thoda stale data de sakte hain kyunki Redis replication asynchronous hai. Isse juda problem hai big key, jaise bahut bada hash ya list, jo kam traffic pe bhi dard deta hai kyunki har read bahut saare bytes le jaata hai; wahan fix hai value ko chhoti keys mein todna.

Common mistake: saying "add more Redis nodes". A single key never spreads across nodes, so more shards do nothing for it.
Galti mat karna: "aur Redis nodes jod do" bolna. Ek key kabhi nodes pe nahi bat-ti, toh zyada shards usme kuch nahi karte.
05 When should you NOT cache something?Kab kisi cheez ko cache NAHI karna chahiye?
What they're really testing: judgment. Data that changes faster than the TTL, exact financial balances, per-request user data, and cases where staleness is a security issue.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: judgment. TTL se tez badalne waala data, exact financial balances, per-request user data, aur woh cases jahan staleness security issue hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A cache only pays off when data is read many times between changes and a little staleness is acceptable. So I do not cache when those conditions fail. One, data that changes faster than any sensible TTL: I would mostly serve stale values and pay for writes that are never read. Two, exact financial numbers used for decisions, like an account balance or the amount about to be charged; those come from the source of truth, ideally inside a transaction. Three, per-user, per-request data that is never read twice, where the hit ratio is near zero. Four, anything where staleness is a security problem: permissions, sessions, a banned user. If I revoke someone's admin rights and a cached "isAdmin: true" lives for ten more minutes, that is an incident. And five, things that are already cheap, like a primary-key lookup on a small table.

Cache tabhi fayda deta hai jab data do changes ke beech kai baar padha jaaye aur thoda stale chalega. Toh jab yeh shartein fail hon tab main cache nahi karta. Ek, jo data kisi bhi sensible TTL se tez badalta hai: main zyaadatar stale values dunga aur un writes ki keemat dunga jo kabhi padhe nahi gaye. Do, decision ke liye use hone waale exact financial numbers, jaise account balance ya jo amount abhi charge hone waala hai; yeh source of truth se aate hain, ideally transaction ke andar. Teen, per-user, per-request data jo kabhi dobara nahi padha jaata, jahan hit ratio almost zero hai. Chaar, kuch bhi jahan staleness security problem hai: permissions, sessions, banned user. Agar maine kisi ke admin rights hataaye aur cache mein "isAdmin: true" das minute aur zinda hai, toh yeh incident hai. Aur paanch, jo cheezein pehle se sasti hain, jaise chhoti table pe primary-key lookup.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

It is not always all-or-nothing. For a balance, I might cache a display value on a dashboard with a clear "as of" time, but always re-read from the database before a debit. For permissions, I can cache for seconds and invalidate on change via an event. Also, caching adds real costs: memory, an extra network hop on every miss, invalidation code, and a new failure mode when Redis is down. I would measure first; if the database handles the load with the right indexes, a cache may be unnecessary complexity.

Hamesha sab-ya-kuch-nahi nahi hota. Balance ke liye main dashboard pe ek display value clear "as of" time ke saath cache kar sakta hoon, par debit se pehle hamesha database se dobara padhunga. Permissions ke liye kuch second cache karke change pe event se invalidate kar sakta hoon. Aur caching ki asli keemat hai: memory, har miss pe ek extra network hop, invalidation code, aur Redis down hone pe ek naya failure mode. Main pehle measure karunga; agar sahi indexes ke saath database load jhel leta hai, toh cache bekaar complexity ho sakta hai.

Common mistake: caching auth or permission checks with a long TTL for speed, and forgetting that revocation then does not take effect.
Galti mat karna: speed ke liye auth ya permission checks ko lambe TTL ke saath cache karna, aur bhool jaana ki phir revocation kaam nahi karega.
06 Local cache vs distributed cache?Local cache vs distributed cache mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: that you know local is in-process, fastest but inconsistent across servers, while distributed (Redis) is shared and consistent at the cost of a network hop.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum jaante ho local in-process hai, sabse fast par servers ke beech inconsistent, jabki distributed (Redis) shared aur consistent hai, ek network hop ki keemat pe.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A local cache lives inside the application process, like a map in Node's memory. It is the fastest possible, no network at all, but each server has its own copy, so with ten servers you have ten copies that drift apart, it is limited by the server's RAM, and it disappears on every deploy or restart. A distributed cache like Redis is a separate server that all instances share, so there is one copy, it survives app deploys, and it can be much bigger, but each read costs a network round trip and Redis becomes another dependency. I use local caches for tiny, very hot, rarely changing data like feature flags, config or a hot key, with short TTLs. I use Redis for shared data like sessions, query results and rate-limit counters. Often both together: local as L1, Redis as L2.

Local cache application process ke andar rehta hai, jaise Node ki memory mein ek map. Sabse fast hai, network bilkul nahi, par har server ki apni copy hoti hai, toh das servers pe das copies jo aapas mein alag ho jaati hain, server ki RAM tak limited hai, aur har deploy ya restart pe gayab. Redis jaisa distributed cache ek alag server hai jise saare instances share karte hain, toh ek copy hai, app deploys ke baad bhi bachti hai, aur bahut badi ho sakti hai, par har read ek network round trip leta hai aur Redis ek aur dependency ban jaata hai. Local cache main chhote, bahut hot, kam badalne waale data ke liye use karta hoon jaise feature flags, config ya hot key, chhote TTL ke saath. Redis shared data ke liye: sessions, query results, rate-limit counters. Aksar dono saath: local L1, Redis L2.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The hard part of a local cache is invalidation: deleting from Redis does not clear twenty in-process copies. Options are very short TTLs, or broadcasting invalidation messages over Redis pub/sub so each instance drops its entry. Another concern is memory: an unbounded local map is a classic memory leak in Node, so it must have a size limit with LRU eviction. And correctness: a rate-limit counter kept locally is wrong the moment you have two instances, because each one counts separately; that one must be in Redis.

Local cache ka mushkil hissa invalidation hai: Redis se delete karne se bees in-process copies saaf nahi hoti. Options hain bahut chhote TTL, ya Redis pub/sub pe invalidation messages broadcast karna taaki har instance apni entry gira de. Doosri chinta memory hai: Node mein bina limit ka local map classic memory leak hai, toh uski size limit aur LRU eviction honi chahiye. Aur correctness: local rakha rate-limit counter do instances hote hi galat hai, kyunki har ek alag ginta hai; woh Redis mein hi hona chahiye.

Common mistake: using an in-process cache for data that must be the same on every server, such as rate limits or session state.
Galti mat karna: un cheezon ke liye in-process cache use karna jo har server pe same honi chahiye, jaise rate limits ya session state.
07 How do you handle cache consistency when data changes?Jab data change hota hai tab cache consistency kaise handle karte ho?
What they're really testing: concrete techniques: event-driven invalidation, write-through, and versioned keys, plus awareness of the race conditions.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: concrete techniques: event-driven invalidation, write-through, aur versioned keys, saath mein race conditions ki samajh.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

First I write to the database, then I delete the cache key, rather than updating it, because a delete does not depend on the order of concurrent writers. That covers one service. When several services or many local caches hold copies, I use event-driven invalidation: the writer publishes "vehicle 123 changed" on a queue or Redis pub/sub, and each cache holder deletes its copy. Even better is CDC, reading the database change log, so changes from any path trigger invalidation. For data where a read right after a write must be fresh, like a user's own profile, I use write-through. And versioned keys, such as vehicle:123:v8, avoid overwrite races entirely: a change bumps the version and old keys just expire. Under all of it, every key keeps a TTL as a safety net.

Pehle main database mein likhta hoon, phir cache key delete karta hoon, update nahi, kyunki delete concurrent writers ke order pe depend nahi karta. Yeh ek service ke liye hua. Jab kai services ya bahut saare local caches copies rakhte hain, main event-driven invalidation use karta hoon: writer queue ya Redis pub/sub pe "vehicle 123 badla" publish karta hai, aur har cache holder apni copy delete karta hai.
