Aur bhi achha hai CDC, database ka change log padhna, taaki kisi bhi raaste se hua change invalidation trigger kare. Jis data mein write ke turant baad ka read fresh hona chahiye, jaise user ka apna profile, wahan write-through. Aur versioned keys, jaise vehicle:123:v8, overwrite races ko poori tarah hata deti hain: change version badhata hai aur purani keys expire ho jaati hain. In sabke neeche, har key pe safety net ke liye TTL rehta hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Delete-after-write still has a window: a slow reader can read the old row, the writer updates and deletes, then the reader writes the old value back. Fixes are a delayed second delete, a version or updated_at check so older data never overwrites newer, and a TTL to bound the damage. If the delete call fails after the database commit, I retry through a queue or rely on CDC. I would also be honest that a cache gives eventual consistency at best; if a flow needs strict consistency, like checking stock before confirming a booking, that read goes to the database.

Delete-after-write mein bhi ek window hai: slow reader purani row padh sakta hai, writer update aur delete karta hai, phir reader purani value wapas likh deta hai. Fixes: thodi der baad doosra delete, version ya updated_at check taaki purana data naye ko overwrite na kare, aur nuksaan ki limit ke liye TTL. Agar database commit ke baad delete call fail ho, toh main queue se retry karta hoon ya CDC pe bharosa karta hoon. Main yeh bhi imaandaari se bolunga ki cache zyada se zyada eventual consistency deta hai; agar kisi flow ko strict consistency chahiye, jaise booking confirm karne se pehle stock check, toh woh read database se hoga.

Common mistake: deleting the cache before writing the database; a reader can refill the old value in between and it stays until the TTL.
Galti mat karna: database mein likhne se pehle cache delete karna; beech mein koi reader purani value dobara bhar sakta hai aur woh TTL tak rehti hai.
08 What is a CDN and how is it different from an application-level cache?CDN kya hai aur application-level cache se kaise alag hai?
What they're really testing: that a CDN caches static or cacheable HTTP responses at the edge to cut latency, while Redis caches data near the app to cut database load.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki CDN static ya cacheable HTTP responses ko edge pe cache karta hai latency kam karne ke liye, jabki Redis app ke paas data cache karta hai database load kam karne ke liye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A CDN is a network of servers spread across many cities that keep copies of HTTP responses close to users, at the edge. It caches whole responses by URL, which suits images, JavaScript, CSS, video and public pages that are the same for everyone, and it is controlled by headers like Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400. Its job is to reduce latency for the user and take traffic off my servers entirely. An application cache like Redis sits next to my backend and caches data, like query results or objects, with keys and invalidation my code controls. Its job is to reduce load on the database. On a dealership site, vehicle photos and the site's scripts go on the CDN; the result of an inventory search query might go in Redis; a logged-in user's personal data does not go on a shared CDN.

CDN kai shehron mein faile servers ka network hai jo HTTP responses ki copies users ke paas, edge pe, rakhta hai. Yeh URL se poore responses cache karta hai, jo images, JavaScript, CSS, video aur public pages ke liye sahi hai jo sabke liye ek jaise hain, aur ise Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 jaise headers control karte hain. Iska kaam user ke liye latency kam karna aur mere servers se traffic poori tarah hata dena hai. Redis jaisa application cache mere backend ke paas baithta hai aur data cache karta hai, jaise query results ya objects, jiski keys aur invalidation mera code control karta hai. Iska kaam database ka load kam karna hai. Dealership site pe, vehicle photos aur site ke scripts CDN pe; inventory search query ka result shayad Redis mein; logged-in user ka personal data shared CDN pe nahi.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Invalidation differs. On a CDN I either purge a URL through the provider's API, which takes time to spread across edges, or better, use versioned file names like app.3f9a.js so a new deploy simply references a new URL and I can cache the old ones for a year. For HTML I prefer short max-age with stale-while-revalidate. I must be careful with Cache-Control: private or no-store on personalised responses, and with the cache key including things like query strings or headers, or one user's page can be served to another.

Invalidation alag hai. CDN pe main ya toh provider ki API se URL purge karta hoon, jo saare edges tak phailne mein time leta hai, ya better, app.3f9a.js jaise versioned file names use karta hoon taaki naya deploy bas naya URL refer kare aur purane ko main saal bhar cache kar sakoon. HTML ke liye main chhota max-age aur stale-while-revalidate pasand karta hoon. Personalised responses pe Cache-Control: private ya no-store ka dhyaan rakhna padta hai, aur cache key mein query strings ya headers jaisi cheezein sahi se aani chahiye, warna ek user ka page doosre ko dikh sakta hai.

Common mistake: treating the CDN and Redis as interchangeable; they solve different problems (distance vs database work) and usually work together.
Galti mat karna: CDN aur Redis ko ek doosre ka substitute samajhna; dono alag problems solve karte hain (doori vs database ka kaam) aur aam taur pe saath kaam karte hain.
09 Cache-aside vs read-through?Cache-aside vs read-through mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: who owns the loading logic. In cache-aside the app checks and fills the cache; in read-through the cache layer loads from the database on a miss.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: loading logic kiske paas hai. Cache-aside mein app check karti hai aur cache bharti hai; read-through mein miss pe cache layer database se load karti hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Both load data lazily on a miss; the difference is who does it. In cache-aside the application talks to both: it calls redis.get, and on a miss it queries the database itself and calls redis.set. The cache is a dumb key-value store. In read-through the application only talks to the cache, and the cache layer is configured with a loader, so on a miss it fetches from the database, stores the value and returns it. Cache-aside gives me full control per call and works with plain Redis, which is why it is the most common. Read-through keeps loading logic in one place and makes app code cleaner, and a good read-through layer can collapse concurrent misses into one load, but it ties me to a library or managed cache that supports it.

Dono miss pe data lazily load karte hain; fark yeh hai ki kaun karta hai. Cache-aside mein application dono se baat karti hai: redis.get call karti hai, aur miss pe khud database query karke redis.set call karti hai. Cache ek simple key-value store hai. Read-through mein application sirf cache se baat karti hai, aur cache layer mein ek loader configure hota hai, toh miss pe woh database se laata hai, value store karta hai aur return karta hai. Cache-aside mujhe har call pe poora control deta hai aur plain Redis ke saath chalta hai, isliye yeh sabse common hai. Read-through loading logic ek jagah rakhta hai aur app code saaf karta hai, aur achhi read-through layer concurrent misses ko ek hi load mein jod sakti hai, par yeh mujhe kisi aisi library ya managed cache se baandh deta hai jo ise support kare.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Plain Redis has no built-in read-through; you get it from a library wrapper in your app, from caches such as those in Hazelcast or Ehcache, or from services that provide a loader. Read-through pairs naturally with write-through, since both put the cache layer in front of the database. Failure behaviour differs too: in cache-aside, if Redis is down, my code can skip it and go to the database; in read-through, the cache layer is in the request path, so its outage is my outage unless it has a fallback.

Plain Redis mein built-in read-through nahi hota; yeh tumhe app mein library wrapper se milta hai, Hazelcast ya Ehcache jaise caches se, ya aisi services se jo loader dete hain. Read-through aur write-through ki jodi natural hai, kyunki dono cache layer ko database ke aage rakhte hain. Failure behaviour bhi alag hai: cache-aside mein Redis down ho toh mera code use skip karke database jaa sakta hai; read-through mein cache layer request path mein hai, toh uska outage mera outage hai jab tak uska fallback na ho.

Common mistake: saying they are "the same thing". The data flow is similar, but ownership of the loading logic and the failure behaviour are different.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki dono "ek hi cheez" hain. Data flow milta-julta hai, par loading logic ka maalik aur failure behaviour alag hai.
10 How do you size a cache and decide eviction policy?Cache ka size kaise decide karte ho aur eviction policy kaise chunte ho?
What they're really testing: that you size for the working set, not total data, and match the policy to the access pattern: LRU general, LFU for stable popularity, TTL for time-sensitive data.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum working set ke liye size karte ho, total data ke liye nahi, aur policy ko access pattern se match karte ho: LRU general, LFU stable popularity ke liye, TTL time-sensitive data ke liye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I size for the working set, the data actually being read in a given window, not the whole database. For a vehicle inventory site, shoppers mostly look at cars currently for sale, not years of sold history, so I estimate hot keys times average value size plus overhead headroom. Then I choose eviction by access pattern. LRU, least recently used, is the general default: recently read things tend to be read again. LFU, least frequently used, is better when popularity is stable and I do not want a one-off scan to push out genuinely popular keys. TTL-based eviction fits time-sensitive data where freshness is the main rule. In Redis that means setting maxmemory and a policy like allkeys-lru, because the default noeviction makes writes fail when memory is full. Then I verify with hit ratio and eviction counts.

Main working set ke liye size karta hoon, yaani woh data jo ek time window mein actually padha ja raha hai, poora database nahi. Vehicle inventory site pe shoppers zyaadatar abhi bikne waali cars dekhte hain, saalon ki sold history nahi, toh main andaaza lagata hoon: hot keys × average value size, plus overhead ke liye extra jagah. Phir access pattern se eviction chunta hoon. LRU, least recently used, general default hai: jo haal mein padha gaya woh dobara padhe jaane ke chances zyada hain. LFU, least frequently used, tab better hai jab popularity stable ho aur main nahi chahta ki ek baar ka scan sach mein popular keys ko bahar dhakel de. TTL-based eviction time-sensitive data ke liye hai jahan freshness main rule hai. Redis mein iska matlab hai maxmemory aur allkeys-lru jaisi policy set karna, kyunki default noeviction memory full hone pe writes fail kar deta hai. Phir hit ratio aur eviction counts se verify karta hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I would explain LRU with an example: with room for three items holding C, B, A, reading A moves it to the front, and a new item D then evicts B, the one used longest ago. Redis approximates LRU and LFU by sampling keys rather than keeping a perfect list. I would watch keyspace_hits, keyspace_misses and evicted_keys from INFO stats: rising evictions with a falling hit ratio means the cache is too small; lots of memory held by keys that are never read means TTLs are too long. The volatile-* policies only evict keys with a TTL, useful when some keys must never be evicted.

Main LRU ek example se samjhaunga: teen items ki jagah mein C, B, A hain, A padhne se woh aage aa jaata hai, aur phir naya item D aane pe B nikalta hai, jo sabse lambe time pehle use hua tha. Redis LRU aur LFU ko perfect list ki jagah keys sample karke approximate karta hai. Main INFO stats se keyspace_hits, keyspace_misses aur evicted_keys dekhunga: evictions badh rahe hain aur hit ratio gir raha hai matlab cache chhota hai; bahut saari memory aisi keys ne pakdi hai jo kabhi padhi nahi jaati matlab TTL bahut lambe hain. volatile-* policies sirf TTL waali keys evict karti hain, jab kuch keys kabhi evict nahi honi chahiye tab kaam aata hai.

Common mistake: sizing the cache to hold the entire dataset, or leaving Redis on the default noeviction policy and getting write errors when it fills.
Galti mat karna: cache ko poore dataset ke size ka rakhna, ya Redis ko default noeviction policy pe chhod dena aur bharne pe write errors khaana.

Topic 05 · VERY COMMONTopic 05 · Bahut common

IdempotencyIdempotency

Why tapping "Pay" twice must not charge you twice, and exactly how a backend makes a retry safe: idempotency keys, stored results, crash windows, queues and batches.

"Pay" do baar dabane pe do baar paise kyun nahi katne chahiye, aur backend retry ko safe kaise banata hai: idempotency keys, stored results, crash windows, queues aur batches.

Level 0 The storyKahani

You are in a mall basement paying ₹500 at a shop with UPI. You tap Pay. The app shows a spinner: "Processing...". Ten seconds. Twenty. The network down here is weak. Finally: "Something went wrong. Please try again."

Your thumb hovers over Pay again. Here is the question this whole chapter answers: if you tap it again, should you be charged twice?

Think about what might have actually happened to the first tap. There are three possibilities, and from your phone they look exactly the same:

  1. The request never reached the bank. No money moved. Retrying is correct.
  2. The request reached the bank, ₹500 left your account, but the "success" reply got lost on the way back to your phone. Retrying naively would take another ₹500.
  3. The bank is still working on it. Retrying now creates a second, parallel payment.

Your phone cannot tell these apart. All it knows is "I did not hear back". So the only sane design is: the phone is allowed to retry, and the server must make sure that a retry of the same payment has no extra effect.

Now picture a sensible shopkeeper with a register. When you pay, he writes: "Order A17: ₹500, PAID". If you come back and say "I paid for order A17, did it go through?", he checks the register and says "yes, already paid, here is your receipt" instead of taking another ₹500. The order number is what makes this safe. Without it, he only knows "someone wants to pay ₹500", and every visit looks like a new payment.

That order number is an idempotency key. The register is the server's stored record. Giving you the old receipt is returning the stored result. That is the whole topic.

Two buttons to remember. A lift call button is idempotent: press it once or five times, one lift comes. A "add ₹500 to cart total" button is not: press it five times and you owe ₹2,500. Good backend design turns dangerous buttons into lift buttons.

Tum mall ke basement mein ek shop pe UPI se ₹500 de rahe ho. Pay dabaya. App spinner dikhata hai: "Processing...". Das second. Bees. Neeche network kamzor hai. Aakhir mein: "Something went wrong. Please try again."

Tumhara angootha phir se Pay pe hai. Yahi woh sawaal hai jiska jawab yeh poora chapter deta hai: agar dobara dabaya, toh kya do baar paise katne chahiye?

Socho pehle tap ke saath asal mein kya hua hoga. Teen possibilities hain, aur tumhare phone se teeno bilkul ek jaisi dikhti hain:

  1. Request bank tak pahunchi hi nahi. Paisa nahi hila. Retry karna sahi hai.
  2. Request bank tak pahunchi, ₹500 tumhare account se nikal gaye, par "success" ka reply tumhare phone tak aate-aate kho gaya. Seedha retry karoge toh ₹500 aur katenge.
  3. Bank abhi bhi us pe kaam kar raha hai. Abhi retry kiya toh ek doosri, parallel payment ban jaayegi.

Tumhara phone inme fark nahi kar sakta. Use bas itna pata hai ki "mujhe jawab nahi mila". Toh ek hi samajhdaar design bachta hai: phone ko retry karne ki permission hai, aur server ki zimmedari hai ki same payment ka retry koi extra asar na kare.

Ab ek samajhdaar dukaandaar socho jiske paas register hai. Jab tum pay karte ho, woh likhta hai: "Order A17: ₹500, PAID". Agar tum wapas aake bolo "maine order A17 ka payment kiya tha, hua kya?", toh woh register dekh ke bolta hai "haan, ho gaya, yeh lo receipt", aur ₹500 dobara nahi leta. Order number hi isse safe banata hai. Uske bina use sirf itna pata hai ki "koi ₹500 dena chahta hai", aur har visit ek nayi payment lagti hai.

Woh order number hi idempotency key hai. Register server ka stored record hai. Tumhe purani receipt dena hai stored result return karna. Bas yahi poora topic hai.

Do buttons yaad rakho. Lift ka call button idempotent hai: ek baar dabao ya paanch baar, ek hi lift aati hai. "Cart total mein ₹500 jodo" waala button idempotent nahi hai: paanch baar dabao toh ₹2,500 dene padenge. Achha backend design khatarnaak buttons ko lift waale buttons mein badal deta hai.

Level 1 The basic idea and the wordsBasic idea aur zaroori words

An operation is idempotent if doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once. The word comes from maths: applying the function again changes nothing.

  • SET status = 'PAID' is idempotent. Run it ten times, the status is still PAID.
  • balance = balance - 500 is not. Run it twice and you have taken ₹1,000.
  • "Delete vehicle 123" is idempotent. After the first time it is gone; later attempts change nothing.
  • "Create a new service appointment" is not. Two taps on Book, two slots on the service calendar.

Why it matters so much for APIs. Recall from the foundations chapter that a client sends an HTTP request over a network and waits for a response. Networks are unreliable: packets get dropped, Wi-Fi switches to 4G, a load balancer restarts, a server is slow and the client gives up after its timeout (the maximum time it is willing to wait). When the client does not hear back, it retries: sends the same request again. Retries come from everywhere: the user tapping again, the mobile app's automatic retry, an HTTP library, a proxy, a message queue redelivering. So in real systems you must assume every request may arrive more than once. If the operation is not idempotent, duplicates turn into double charges, double orders, double emails.

Important subtlety: effect, not response. Idempotency is about what happens to the server's state, not about getting an identical reply. DELETE /vehicles/123 may return 204 No Content the first time and 404 Not Found the second time. Different responses, same effect (the vehicle is gone once). That is still idempotent.

What the HTTP specification says (RFC 9110). "Safe" methods only read and change nothing: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE. "Idempotent" methods are the safe ones plus PUT and DELETE. POST is neither. PATCH is not idempotent by the spec: it applies a set of changes, and whether repeating it is harmless depends on what the changes are.

Koi operation idempotent hai agar use N baar karne ka asar utna hi ho jitna ek baar karne ka. Yeh word maths se aaya hai: function ko dobara lagao toh kuch nahi badalta.

  • SET status = 'PAID' idempotent hai. Das baar chalao, status phir bhi PAID hai.
  • balance = balance - 500 idempotent nahi hai. Do baar chalao aur ₹1,000 kat gaye.
  • "Vehicle 123 delete karo" idempotent hai. Pehli baar mein chala gaya; baad ki koshishein kuch nahi badalti.
  • "Nayi service appointment banao" idempotent nahi hai. Book pe do tap, service calendar pe do slots.

APIs ke liye yeh itna zaroori kyun hai. Foundations chapter yaad karo: client network pe HTTP request bhejta hai aur response ka wait karta hai. Networks bharosemand nahi hain: packets gir jaate hain, Wi-Fi se 4G pe switch hota hai, load balancer restart hota hai, server slow hai aur client apne timeout (jitni der woh maximum wait karega) ke baad haar maan leta hai. Jab client ko jawab nahi milta, woh retry karta hai: wahi request dobara bhejta hai. Retries har jagah se aate hain: user ka dobara tap, mobile app ka automatic retry, HTTP library, proxy, message queue ka redeliver. Toh real systems mein tumhe maan ke chalna padta hai ki har request ek se zyada baar aa sakti hai. Agar operation idempotent nahi hai, toh duplicates double charges, double orders, double emails ban jaate hain.

Ek zaroori baareeki: asar, response nahi. Idempotency server ki state pe hone waale asar ke baare mein hai, same reply milne ke baare mein nahi. DELETE /vehicles/123 pehli baar 204 No Content de sakta hai aur doosri baar 404 Not Found. Response alag, asar same (vehicle ek hi baar gaya). Yeh phir bhi idempotent hai.

HTTP specification kya kehti hai (RFC 9110). "Safe" methods sirf padhte hain aur kuch nahi badalte: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE. "Idempotent" methods hain safe waale plus PUT aur DELETE. POST dono mein se kuch nahi. PATCH spec ke hisaab se idempotent nahi hai: yeh changes ka ek set lagata hai, aur use repeat karna nuksaan-rahit hai ya nahi yeh un changes pe depend karta hai.

MethodSafe?Safe?Idempotent by spec?Spec se idempotent?ExampleExample
GET, HEAD, OPTIONSYesHaanYesHaanGET /vehicles/123
PUTNoNahiYes: "make it exactly this"Haan: "ise bilkul aisa bana do"PUT /vehicles/123 {price: 19200}
DELETENoNahiYes: gone is goneHaan: gaya toh gayaDELETE /vehicles/123
POSTNoNahiNo: "create a new one" each timeNahi: har baar "naya banao"POST /payments
PATCHNoNahiNot guaranteed; depends on the patchGuarantee nahi; patch pe depend{price: 19200} yes, {views: +1} no{price: 19200} haan, {views: +1} nahi

A spec label is a promise the developer must keep. If your PUT handler secretly increments a counter, it is not idempotent just because it is called PUT. And the most important operations in business, creating a payment or an order, are POSTs. So we need a way to make a POST safe to retry. That way is the idempotency key.

Clients will retry. The network guarantees it. Your job is to make sure a retry cannot cause a second effect.

Spec ka label ek waada hai jo developer ko nibhana padta hai. Agar tumhara PUT handler chupke se ek counter badhata hai, toh sirf PUT naam hone se woh idempotent nahi ho jaata. Aur business ke sabse zaroori operations, payment ya order banana, POST hote hain. Toh hume POST ko retry ke liye safe banane ka tareeka chahiye. Woh tareeka hai idempotency key.

Clients retry karenge hi. Network iski guarantee deta hai. Tumhara kaam yeh pakka karna hai ki retry se doosra asar na ho.

Level 2 How it works inside: the idempotency keyAndar kaise kaam karta hai: idempotency key

The idempotency key is a unique ID the client generates for one logical operation, usually a random UUID (a 128-bit random identifier such as 5f1c2a9e-7b3d-4c8e-9a61-2d4f0b8e7c13, so two clients never pick the same one). The client sends it in a header, and crucially sends the same key on every retry of that operation. A new payment gets a new key; a retry of the same payment reuses the old one. The key is the order number in the shopkeeper's register.

The pattern is used by major payment APIs (Stripe's API, for example, accepts an Idempotency-Key header), and there is an IETF draft standardising the header name.

Idempotency key ek unique ID hai jo client ek logical operation ke liye banata hai, aam taur pe ek random UUID (128-bit random identifier jaise 5f1c2a9e-7b3d-4c8e-9a61-2d4f0b8e7c13, taaki do clients kabhi same na chunein). Client ise ek header mein bhejta hai, aur sabse zaroori baat, us operation ke har retry pe wahi key bhejta hai. Nayi payment ko nayi key milti hai; same payment ka retry purani key hi use karta hai. Key dukaandaar ke register ka order number hai.

Yeh pattern bade payment APIs use karte hain (jaise Stripe ki API Idempotency-Key header accept karti hai), aur header ke naam ko standard banane ke liye ek IETF draft bhi hai.

POST /v1/payments HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: 5f1c2a9e-7b3d-4c8e-9a61-2d4f0b8e7c13

{"amount": 50000, "currency": "INR", "payee": "shop-117"}

--- first attempt: the work is done ---
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
{"id": "pay_8812", "status": "succeeded", "amount": 50000}

--- retry with the SAME key: nothing is charged, stored result is replayed ---
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Idempotent-Replayed: true
{"id": "pay_8812", "status": "succeeded", "amount": 50000}

(Amounts are in paise, the smallest unit, so 50000 means ₹500. Idempotent-Replayed is a convention some APIs use to tell the client "this is a replay"; it is optional.)

What the server does with the key, step by step:

  1. Read the key from the header. For endpoints that move money, reject the request with 400 if the key is missing.
  2. Claim it atomically. Try to create a record "key → IN_PROGRESS" only if it does not already exist. This must be one atomic step, so two copies of the same request arriving in the same millisecond cannot both win. In Redis that is SET key value NX EX ttl (NX = only if Not eXists, EX = expire after N seconds). In a SQL database it is an INSERT into a table with a unique constraint on the key.
  3. If we claimed it: this is the first time. Do the real work (charge the card), then save the result (HTTP status + response body) under the key, marked COMPLETED.
  4. If the key already exists and is COMPLETED: it is a retry. Do not charge again. Return the stored result exactly as it was the first time.
  5. If it exists and is IN_PROGRESS: the original is still running (a duplicate arrived in parallel). Return 409 Conflict and let the client retry shortly.
  6. If it exists but the request body is different: the client reused a key for a different operation, which is a bug. Return an error (the IETF draft suggests 422 Unprocessable Content). We detect this by storing a fingerprint of the body (a hash such as SHA-256) with the key.

(Amount paise mein hai, sabse chhoti unit, toh 50000 matlab ₹500. Idempotent-Replayed ek convention hai jo kuch APIs client ko batane ke liye use karti hain ki "yeh replay hai"; yeh optional hai.)

Server key ke saath kya karta hai, step by step:

  1. Header se key padho. Paisa hilaane waale endpoints pe, key missing ho toh request 400 ke saath reject karo.
  2. Use atomically claim karo. Ek record "key → IN_PROGRESS" banane ki koshish karo sirf tab jab woh pehle se exist na kare. Yeh ek atomic step hona chahiye, taaki same request ki do copies ek hi millisecond mein aayein toh dono na jeet paayein. Redis mein yeh hai SET key value NX EX ttl (NX = sirf agar exist Nahi karti, EX = N second baad expire). SQL database mein yeh hai aisi table mein INSERT jisme key pe unique constraint ho.
  3. Agar humne claim kar liya: pehli baar hai. Asli kaam karo (card charge karo), phir result (HTTP status + response body) key ke neeche COMPLETED mark karke save karo.
  4. Agar key pehle se hai aur COMPLETED hai: yeh retry hai. Dobara charge mat karo. Stored result bilkul waisa hi return karo jaisa pehli baar tha.
  5. Agar hai aur IN_PROGRESS hai: original abhi chal raha hai (duplicate parallel mein aaya). 409 Conflict return karo aur client ko thodi der baad retry karne do.
  6. Agar hai par request body alag hai: client ne ek key ko alag operation ke liye dobara use kiya, yeh bug hai. Error return karo (IETF draft 422 Unprocessable Content suggest karta hai). Yeh hum body ka fingerprint (SHA-256 jaisa hash) key ke saath store karke pakadte hain.

Here is a handler in Node.js using Redis. Read the comments: every line maps to a step above.

Yeh raha Node.js mein Redis use karta hua ek handler. Comments padho: har line upar ke kisi step se judi hai.

// POST /v1/payments   (Express-style handler, ioredis-style client)
const DAY = 24 * 60 * 60;   // seconds

async function createPayment(req, res) {
  const clientKey = req.get('Idempotency-Key');
  if (!clientKey) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key header is required' });
  }

  // Scope the key to the caller: one user can never collide with, or read, another's result
  const redisKey = `idem:${req.user.id}:${clientKey}`;
  const fingerprint = sha256(JSON.stringify(req.body));   // "is this really the same request?"

  // 1. Claim the key atomically. NX = set ONLY if it does not exist. EX = TTL in seconds.
  const claimed = await redis.set(
    redisKey,
    JSON.stringify({ state: 'IN_PROGRESS', fingerprint }),
    'EX', DAY,
    'NX'
  );

  if (!claimed) {
    // 2. Seen before: a retry, or a duplicate arriving in parallel
    const raw = await redis.get(redisKey);
    if (raw === null) return createPayment(req, res);     // expired in between: start over
    const saved = JSON.parse(raw);

    if (saved.fingerprint !== fingerprint) {
      return res.status(422).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key reused with a different body' });
    }
    if (saved.state === 'IN_PROGRESS') {
      return res.status(409).json({ error: 'Original request still processing, retry shortly' });
    }
    res.set('Idempotent-Replayed', 'true');
    return res.status(saved.status).json(saved.body);     // 3. replay. Do NOT charge again.
  }

  // 4. First time: do the real work
  try {
    // pass the same key downstream so the payment provider ALSO de-duplicates
    const payment = await paymentProvider.charge(req.body, { idempotencyKey: clientKey });
    const result = { state: 'COMPLETED', fingerprint, status: 201, body: payment };
    await redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify(result), 'EX', DAY);
    return res.status(201).json(payment);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.definitelyNotCharged) {
      await redis.del(redisKey);   // nothing happened: let the client retry cleanly
    }
    // otherwise leave IN_PROGRESS; a reconciliation job checks the provider's status
    throw err;
  }
}

What exactly do we store, and where? Per key: the state (IN_PROGRESS or COMPLETED), the request fingerprint, and the final HTTP status and body. Redis is a natural fit: lookups by key are fast, SET NX gives the atomic claim, and the TTL cleans old keys up automatically. The key is namespaced by user (idem:{userId}:{key}) so keys from different customers can never clash.

Which outcomes do we store? Final, deterministic ones: success, and business rejections like "card declined" or "insufficient funds". A retry of a declined payment should get the same "declined", not silently try again. What we must not do is store a result for a failure where we are sure nothing happened (say, our own validation rejected it before touching the bank); there we can delete the key and let the client retry fresh.

Exactly kya store karte hain, aur kahan? Har key ke liye: state (IN_PROGRESS ya COMPLETED), request ka fingerprint, aur final HTTP status aur body. Redis natural fit hai: key se lookup fast hai, SET NX atomic claim deta hai, aur TTL purani keys apne aap saaf kar deta hai. Key user ke naam se namespace hoti hai (idem:{userId}:{key}) taaki alag customers ki keys kabhi takraayein nahi.

Kaunse outcomes store karte hain? Final, deterministic waale: success, aur business rejections jaise "card declined" ya "insufficient funds". Declined payment ke retry ko wahi "declined" milna chahiye, chupke se dobara try nahi. Jo nahi karna chahiye woh hai aise failure ka result store karna jahan humein pakka pata hai ki kuch nahi hua (jaise humari apni validation ne bank chhoone se pehle hi reject kar diya); wahan hum key delete karke client ko fresh retry karne de sakte hain.

Level 3 Production: crashes, queues, batches, and turning unsafe operations safeProduction: crashes, queues, batches, aur unsafe operations ko safe banana

The crash before the response. The nastiest case: the server charges the card and then crashes (a deploy, an out-of-memory kill, a lost machine) before it sends the reply. The client times out and retries with the same key. Whether this double-charges depends entirely on when the server wrote down the key.

  • If the server writes the key only after finishing the work, a crash in the middle leaves no trace. The retry looks brand new, and the customer is charged again.
  • If the server writes the key before doing the work (the IN_PROGRESS claim), a retry always finds it: either COMPLETED (replay the result) or IN_PROGRESS (tell the client to wait, and let recovery figure out what happened).

Response se pehle crash. Sabse bura case: server card charge karta hai aur phir reply bhejne se pehle crash ho jaata hai (deploy, out-of-memory kill, machine chali gayi). Client timeout hota hai aur same key ke saath retry karta hai. Double charge hoga ya nahi, yeh poori tarah is pe depend karta hai ki server ne key kab likhi.

  • Agar server key sirf kaam khatam hone ke baad likhta hai, toh beech mein crash koi nishaan nahi chhodta. Retry bilkul naya lagta hai, aur customer se dobara paise kat jaate hain.
  • Agar server kaam karne se pehle key likhta hai (IN_PROGRESS claim), toh retry ko key hamesha milti hai: ya toh COMPLETED (result replay karo) ya IN_PROGRESS (client ko ruko bolo, aur recovery ko pata lagane do ki kya hua).

Look at the bottom timeline again: there is still one gap, between "charge card" and "save result COMPLETED". If the crash lands exactly there, the key says IN_PROGRESS but money did move. Three ways to close it:

  1. One database transaction. If the "work" is a write to your own database (create the payment row, reduce stock), put the idempotency record and the business write in the same transaction. Recall from the transactions chapter: a transaction is all-or-nothing. Either both are saved, or neither is. There is no gap.
  2. Pass the key downstream. If the work is a call to an external payment provider that supports idempotency keys, send the same key. If you retry after a crash, the provider itself recognises it and returns the original charge instead of creating a new one.
  3. Reconciliation. A background job looks for keys stuck in IN_PROGRESS for too long, asks the provider "what happened to k1?", and marks them COMPLETED with the real outcome.

Idempotent message queue consumers. Message queues (Topic 06) such as Kafka, RabbitMQ or SQS usually promise at-least-once delivery: the queue keeps giving you a message until you acknowledge (ack) it. If your consumer processes the message and crashes before the ack, the queue delivers it again. So duplicates are normal, not an error. The fix is the same idea with the message's own unique ID as the key: record "message X processed" in the same transaction as the work, skip if already recorded, and ack only after the commit.

Neeche waali timeline phir se dekho: ek gap abhi bhi hai, "charge card" aur "save result COMPLETED" ke beech. Agar crash theek wahin hua, toh key IN_PROGRESS bolti hai par paisa hil chuka hai. Isse band karne ke teen tareeke:

  1. Ek database transaction. Agar "kaam" tumhare apne database mein write hai (payment row banana, stock kam karna), toh idempotency record aur business write ko ek hi transaction mein daalo. Transactions chapter yaad karo: transaction all-or-nothing hota hai. Ya toh dono save honge, ya dono nahi. Koi gap nahi.
  2. Key aage bhejo. Agar kaam kisi external payment provider ko call hai jo idempotency keys support karta hai, toh wahi key bhejo. Crash ke baad retry karoge toh provider khud use pehchaan ke original charge return karega, naya nahi banayega.
  3. Reconciliation. Ek background job un keys ko dhoondhta hai jo bahut der se IN_PROGRESS mein atki hain, provider se poochta hai "k1 ka kya hua?", aur asli outcome ke saath unhe COMPLETED mark kar deta hai.

Idempotent message queue consumers. Kafka, RabbitMQ ya SQS jaisi message queues (Topic 06) aam taur pe at-least-once delivery ka waada karti hain: queue tumhe message deti rehti hai jab tak tum use acknowledge (ack) na karo. Agar tumhara consumer message process karke ack se pehle crash ho gaya, toh queue use dobara deliver karti hai. Toh duplicates normal hain, error nahi. Fix wahi idea hai, message ki apni unique ID ko key banake: "message X processed" ko kaam ke saath ek hi transaction mein record karo, pehle se record hai toh skip karo, aur commit ke baad hi ack karo.

-- one table remembers every message we have fully processed
CREATE TABLE processed_messages (
  message_id   TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  processed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
async function handleMessage(msg) {
  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    // returns 0 rows if this message_id was already processed
    const inserted = await tx.query(
      `INSERT INTO processed_messages (message_id) VALUES ($1)
       ON CONFLICT (message_id) DO NOTHING
       RETURNING message_id`, [msg.id]);

    if (inserted.rowCount === 0) return;         // duplicate delivery: skip the work

    await tx.query('UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2', ['PAID', msg.orderId]);
  });                                            // both writes commit together, or neither

  await msg.ack();                               // ack ONLY after the commit
}

If the consumer crashes after the commit but before the ack, the message comes back, the INSERT finds the ID, and we just ack and move on. Exactly the shopkeeper checking his register.

Batch endpoints. Suppose a dealer group's finance system sends one request with 100 payouts. Item 37 times out; the other 99 succeed. If the whole batch has one key and the client retries, what should happen? Replaying the whole old response leaves item 37 unpaid; reprocessing everything pays 99 people twice. The answer is per-item keys and per-item status: each item carries its own key, the server processes each item idempotently, and the response reports each item separately. The client retries the batch (or just the failed items) with the same keys; done items are replayed for free, only the failed one is actually processed.

Agar consumer commit ke baad par ack se pehle crash hua, toh message wapas aata hai, INSERT ko ID mil jaati hai, aur hum bas ack karke aage badh jaate hain. Bilkul dukaandaar ka register check karna.

Batch endpoints. Maan lo ek dealer group ka finance system ek request mein 100 payouts bhejta hai. Item 37 timeout ho jaata hai; baaki 99 succeed. Agar poore batch ki ek hi key hai aur client retry kare, toh kya hona chahiye? Poora purana response replay karo toh item 37 ka payment reh gaya; sab dobara process karo toh 99 logon ko do baar paisa. Jawab hai per-item keys aur per-item status: har item ki apni key, server har item ko idempotently process karta hai, aur response har item ka alag status batata hai. Client batch (ya sirf failed items) same keys ke saath retry karta hai; done items free mein replay hote hain, sirf failed waala asal mein process hota hai.

POST /v1/payouts/batch
{ "items": [
    { "itemKey": "a1", "payee": "shop-1", "amount": 50000 },
    { "itemKey": "a2", "payee": "shop-2", "amount": 20000 },
    { "itemKey": "a3", "payee": "shop-3", "amount": 75000 } ] }

HTTP/1.1 207 Multi-Status        (many APIs use 200 with a results array instead)
{ "results": [
    { "itemKey": "a1", "status": "succeeded", "payoutId": "po_101" },
    { "itemKey": "a2", "status": "failed", "retryable": true, "error": "upstream timeout" },
    { "itemKey": "a3", "status": "succeeded", "payoutId": "po_103" } ] }

Making a non-idempotent operation safe to retry. The idempotency key is the general tool: "check if this key was done; if not, do it and record the result", with the check and the claim done atomically (never a separate read and then write, or two parallel requests both pass the check). But there are also natural tricks:

  • Natural unique keys: "create shipment for order 42" becomes safe with a unique constraint on shipments.order_id. The second INSERT fails, and you return the existing shipment.
  • Conditional updates: UPDATE orders SET status = 'PAID' WHERE id = 42 AND status = 'PENDING'. The second run matches 0 rows and changes nothing.
  • Absolute instead of relative: "set price to 19,200" is idempotent; "increase price by 300" is not. Where you can, design the operation as "make it this state".

Non-idempotent operation ko retry ke liye safe banana. Idempotency key general tool hai: "check karo yeh key ho chuki hai kya; nahi toh karo aur result record karo", jahan check aur claim atomically hote hain (kabhi alag se pehle read phir write nahi, warna do parallel requests dono check paas kar lengi). Par kuch natural tricks bhi hain:

  • Natural unique keys: "order 42 ke liye shipment banao" shipments.order_id pe unique constraint se safe ho jaata hai. Doosra INSERT fail hota hai, aur tum existing shipment return kar dete ho.
  • Conditional updates: UPDATE orders SET status = 'PAID' WHERE id = 42 AND status = 'PENDING'. Doosri baar 0 rows match hoti hain aur kuch nahi badalta.
  • Relative ki jagah absolute: "price 19,200 set karo" idempotent hai; "price 300 badhao" nahi. Jahan ho sake, operation ko "ise is state mein laao" jaisa design karo.

Level 4 Senior nuances: exactly-once, key expiry, storage choicesSenior nuances: exactly-once, key expiry, storage choices

Idempotency vs exactly-once delivery. People often ask for "exactly-once delivery": every message delivered one time, never lost, never duplicated. Over an unreliable network this is impossible to guarantee in general. The sender can never be sure whether a lost acknowledgement means "not delivered" or "delivered, ack lost" (this is the two-generals problem you will meet in Topic 07). So a sender must choose: do not resend (at-most-once, may lose messages) or resend until acknowledged (at-least-once, may duplicate). Real systems choose at-least-once and make the processing idempotent. The combination behaves like "exactly-once effect", sometimes called effectively-once. So: exactly-once delivery is a guarantee a system would have to provide; idempotency is a property of an operation that you can build yourself, cheaply, in your own code.

Kafka does advertise "exactly-once semantics", but read the fine print: it covers reading from Kafka, processing, and writing back to Kafka, using idempotent producers and transactions. The moment your consumer does something outside Kafka, like charging a card or sending an email, you are back to needing an idempotent operation.

Key expiry: a cost and security decision. How long should a key live?

  • Never expire: storage grows without limit. Every payment ever made keeps a record with a full response body in memory. That is real money in Redis RAM, and a pile of sensitive responses sitting around forever.
  • Expire too fast: a slow retry arrives after the key is gone and is treated as new. Think of a phone that was offline for an hour and retries when it reconnects, or a queue redelivering after a long outage. That is the double charge we tried to prevent.
  • The rule: TTL must be longer than the longest realistic retry window of every client and queue that can resend. Stripe, for example, documents that keys can be pruned once they are at least 24 hours old. If your mobile app retries for up to a day, 24 hours is not enough.

Security points to mention: scope keys to the caller (idem:{userId}:{key}), or someone who learns another user's key could receive that user's stored payment response; require keys to be random UUIDs, not guessable counters; check the fingerprint so a key cannot be replayed with a different body; store only what you need in the saved response and remember it is sensitive data at rest; and rate limit, because an attacker sending millions of unique keys fills your storage.

Redis or the database? Redis is fast and has TTLs built in, but Redis replication is asynchronous: if the primary dies right after your SET NX, a promoted replica may not have it, and a retry could slip through. For payments many teams therefore keep the idempotency record in the main database, in the same transaction as the payment, with a unique constraint on (user_id, idempotency_key), and optionally use Redis as a fast front-line check. Durable truth in the database, speed in Redis: the same "copy vs source of truth" thinking as caching.

In real production, the question that exposes weak designs is: "the server charged the card and died before replying; what happens on the retry?" If your answer includes "the key was recorded before the work", "the business write and key are one transaction or the key is passed to the provider", and "stuck IN_PROGRESS records are reconciled", you are answering at senior level.

Idempotency vs exactly-once delivery. Log aksar "exactly-once delivery" maangte hain: har message ek baar deliver ho, na khoye, na duplicate ho. Unreliable network pe iski general guarantee dena namumkin hai. Bhejne waala kabhi pakka nahi jaan sakta ki khoya hua acknowledgement matlab "deliver nahi hua" hai ya "deliver hua, ack kho gaya" (yeh two-generals problem hai jo tum Topic 07 mein dekhoge). Toh sender ko chunna padta hai: dobara mat bhejo (at-most-once, message kho sakte hain) ya ack aane tak bhejte raho (at-least-once, duplicate ho sakte hain). Real systems at-least-once chunte hain aur processing ko idempotent banate hain. Yeh combination "exactly-once effect" jaisa behave karta hai, jise kabhi-kabhi effectively-once kehte hain. Toh: exactly-once delivery ek guarantee hai jo system ko deni padti; idempotency ek operation ki property hai jo tum apne code mein khud, sasti mein, bana sakte ho.

Kafka "exactly-once semantics" advertise karta hai, par fine print padho: yeh Kafka se padhna, process karna aur wapas Kafka mein likhna cover karta hai, idempotent producers aur transactions ke saath. Jaise hi tumhara consumer Kafka ke bahar kuch karta hai, jaise card charge karna ya email bhejna, tumhe phir se idempotent operation chahiye.

Key expiry: cost aur security ka decision. Key kitni der zinda rahe?

  • Kabhi expire na ho: storage bina limit ke badhta hai. Aaj tak ki har payment ka record poori response body ke saath memory mein. Yeh Redis RAM mein asli paisa hai, aur hamesha ke liye pade sensitive responses ka dher.
  • Bahut jaldi expire ho: ek slow retry key jaane ke baad aata hai aur naya maana jaata hai. Socho ek phone jo ghante bhar offline tha aur reconnect hote hi retry karta hai, ya lambe outage ke baad queue ka redeliver. Yahi woh double charge hai jise hum rokna chahte the.
  • Rule: TTL har us client aur queue ke sabse lambe realistic retry window se lamba hona chahiye jo dobara bhej sakta hai. Jaise Stripe document karta hai ki keys kam se kam 24 ghante purani hone ke baad hataayi ja sakti hain. Agar tumhara mobile app ek din tak retry karta hai, toh 24 ghante kaafi nahi.

Security ke points jo bolne chahiye: keys ko caller tak scope karo (idem:{userId}:{key}), warna jise kisi aur user ki key pata chal gayi use us user ka stored payment response mil sakta hai; keys random UUIDs honi chahiye, guess hone waale counters nahi; fingerprint check karo taaki key ko alag body ke saath replay na kiya ja sake; saved response mein sirf zaroori cheezein rakho aur yaad rakho yeh sensitive data at rest hai; aur rate limit lagao, kyunki lakhon unique keys bhejta attacker tumhara storage bhar dega.

Redis ya database? Redis fast hai aur TTL built-in hai, par Redis replication asynchronous hai: agar tumhare SET NX ke turant baad primary mar gaya, toh promote hui replica ke paas woh key shayad na ho, aur ek retry nikal sakta hai. Isliye payments ke liye kai teams idempotency record main database mein rakhti hain, payment ke saath ek hi transaction mein, (user_id, idempotency_key) pe unique constraint ke saath, aur optionally Redis ko fast front-line check ki tarah use karti hain. Durable sach database mein, speed Redis mein: caching jaisi hi "copy vs source of truth" waali soch.

Real production mein, jo sawaal kamzor designs ko pakad leta hai woh hai: "server ne card charge kiya aur reply se pehle mar gaya; retry pe kya hoga?" Agar tumhare jawab mein hai "key kaam se pehle record hui thi", "business write aur key ek transaction mein hain ya key provider ko bheji gayi", aur "atke hue IN_PROGRESS records reconcile hote hain", toh tum senior level pe jawab de rahe ho.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Idempotent
Doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once.N baar karne ka asar utna hi jitna ek baar karne ka.
Idempotency key
A unique ID the client sends with a request, reused on every retry of that same operation.Client request ke saath ek unique ID bhejta hai, aur usi operation ke har retry pe wahi ID.
UUID
A 128-bit random identifier; practically never collides, so clients can generate keys themselves.128-bit random identifier; practically kabhi takraata nahi, isliye clients khud keys bana sakte hain.
Retry / timeout
Timeout: how long a client waits for a reply. Retry: sending the same request again after no reply.Timeout: client reply ka kitni der wait karta hai. Retry: reply na aane pe wahi request dobara bhejna.
Safe method
An HTTP method that only reads and changes nothing (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE).HTTP method jo sirf padhta hai aur kuch nahi badalta (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE).
Stored result / replay
Saving the first response under the key, and returning it unchanged for any retry.Pehla response key ke neeche save karna, aur har retry pe wahi bina badle lautana.
Request fingerprint
A hash of the request body stored with the key, to detect a key reused for a different request.Request body ka hash jo key ke saath store hota hai, taaki alag request ke liye key reuse pakdi ja sake.
SET NX EX
Redis: set the key only if it does not exist, with an expiry; an atomic "claim".Redis: key sirf tab set karo jab exist na kare, expiry ke saath; ek atomic "claim".
At-most-once / at-least-once / exactly-once
May lose, never duplicate / never lose, may duplicate / neither (impossible to guarantee in general over a network).Kho sakta hai, duplicate nahi / khoyega nahi, duplicate ho sakta hai / dono nahi (network pe general guarantee namumkin).
Ack (acknowledge)
A consumer telling the queue "I have finished this message, you can drop it".Consumer ka queue ko batana "yeh message ho gaya, ab hata do".
Deduplication
Detecting and skipping a request or message that was already processed.Jo request ya message pehle process ho chuka hai use pehchaan ke skip karna.
Reconciliation
A background check that compares your records with the provider's and fixes stuck or unclear states.Background check jo tumhare records ko provider ke records se milata hai aur atki ya unclear states theek karta hai.
409 / 422
409 Conflict: original still in progress. 422 Unprocessable Content: key reused with a different body.409 Conflict: original abhi chal raha hai. 422 Unprocessable Content: key alag body ke saath reuse hui.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What is idempotency? Why does it matter for APIs?Idempotency kya hai? APIs ke liye yeh kyun zaroori hai?
What they're really testing: that you connect the definition (N calls = same effect as one) to the real cause: unreliable networks, client retries and the resulting duplicate charges.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum definition (N calls = ek call jaisa asar) ko asli wajah se jodte ho: unreliable networks, client retries aur usse hone waale duplicate charges.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

An operation is idempotent if calling it N times has the same effect on the server as calling it once. Setting an order's status to PAID is idempotent; subtracting 500 from a balance is not. It matters because networks are unreliable. A client sends a payment, the server processes it, but the response is lost or the client times out. The client cannot tell "never arrived" from "done but reply lost", so it retries, and so do mobile apps, HTTP libraries, proxies and message queues. If the endpoint is not idempotent, that retry becomes a second charge. So I design every write API assuming any request can arrive twice, and make sure the second arrival has no additional effect, for example with an idempotency key.

Koi operation idempotent hai agar use N baar call karne ka server pe asar utna hi ho jitna ek baar ka. Order ka status PAID set karna idempotent hai; balance se 500 ghataana nahi. Yeh zaroori isliye hai kyunki networks unreliable hain. Client payment bhejta hai, server process karta hai, par response kho jaata hai ya client timeout ho jaata hai. Client "pahunchi hi nahi" aur "ho gayi par reply kho gaya" mein fark nahi kar sakta, toh woh retry karta hai, aur mobile apps, HTTP libraries, proxies aur message queues bhi yahi karte hain. Agar endpoint idempotent nahi hai, toh woh retry doosra charge ban jaata hai. Isliye main har write API yeh maan ke design karta hoon ki koi bhi request do baar aa sakti hai, aur pakka karta hoon ki doosri baar aane ka koi extra asar na ho, jaise idempotency key se.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I would stress that idempotency is about effect, not response. A second DELETE may return 404 instead of 204, but the state is the same, so it is still idempotent. For POST-style operations I would want the retry to return the original response, so the client behaves the same either way. I would also note idempotency is what makes retries with backoff safe; without it, automatic retries are dangerous for anything that moves money or sends messages.

Main zor dunga ki idempotency asar ke baare mein hai, response ke baare mein nahi. Doosra DELETE 204 ki jagah 404 de sakta hai, par state same hai, toh phir bhi idempotent hai. POST jaise operations mein main chahunga ki retry original response hi lautaye, taaki client dono cases mein same behave kare. Aur main bataunga ki idempotency hi backoff ke saath retries ko safe banati hai; iske bina paisa hilaane ya messages bhejne waali kisi bhi cheez ke liye automatic retries khatarnaak hain.

Common mistake: defining it as "returns the same response every time"; the definition is about the effect on server state.
Galti mat karna: ise "har baar same response deta hai" define karna; definition server state pe asar ke baare mein hai.
02 Which HTTP methods are idempotent by spec? Which aren't?Spec ke hisaab se kaunse HTTP methods idempotent hain? Kaunse nahi?
What they're really testing: that you know GET, PUT, DELETE and HEAD are idempotent, POST is not, and PATCH is not guaranteed by the spec.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum jaante ho GET, PUT, DELETE aur HEAD idempotent hain, POST nahi, aur PATCH spec se guaranteed nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Per the HTTP spec, the safe methods, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE, are idempotent because they do not change state. PUT and DELETE are also idempotent: PUT means "make this resource exactly this", so sending it twice leaves the same result, and deleting something twice still leaves it deleted. POST is not idempotent; it usually means "create a new one", so two POSTs to /orders create two orders. PATCH is not idempotent by the spec, because it applies changes and the changes may be relative. Setting price to 19,200 in a PATCH is harmless to repeat; incrementing a view count is not. So for POST and PATCH on important resources, I add an idempotency key to make retries safe.

HTTP spec ke hisaab se safe methods, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS aur TRACE, idempotent hain kyunki yeh state nahi badalte. PUT aur DELETE bhi idempotent hain: PUT ka matlab hai "is resource ko bilkul aisa bana do", toh do baar bhejne pe result same rehta hai, aur kisi cheez ko do baar delete karo toh bhi woh deleted hi rehti hai. POST idempotent nahi hai; iska matlab aam taur pe "naya banao" hai, toh /orders pe do POST do orders banate hain. PATCH spec se idempotent nahi hai, kyunki yeh changes lagata hai aur changes relative ho sakte hain. PATCH mein price 19,200 set karna repeat karne mein koi nuksaan nahi; view count badhana hai. Isliye important resources pe POST aur PATCH ke liye main idempotency key jodta hoon taaki retries safe hon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The spec label is a contract the implementation has to honour. A PUT handler that also appends an audit row or sends an email on every call has side effects that repeat, so I keep those side effects idempotent too. Safe and idempotent are different: DELETE is idempotent but not safe. Another point: because GET is assumed safe, browsers, crawlers and prefetchers call it freely, so a GET that changes state, like GET /cancel?id=5, is a real bug.

Spec ka label ek contract hai jo implementation ko nibhana padta hai. Jo PUT handler har call pe audit row bhi jodta hai ya email bhejta hai, uske side effects repeat hote hain, toh main un side effects ko bhi idempotent rakhta hoon. Safe aur idempotent alag hain: DELETE idempotent hai par safe nahi. Ek aur point: kyunki GET ko safe maana jaata hai, browsers, crawlers aur prefetchers use bina soche call karte hain, toh state badalne waala GET, jaise GET /cancel?id=5, ek asli bug hai.

Common mistake: saying PATCH is idempotent like PUT, or treating "idempotent" and "safe" as the same thing.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki PATCH bhi PUT jaisa idempotent hai, ya "idempotent" aur "safe" ko ek hi cheez maanna.
03 How do you implement idempotency for a payment API endpoint?Payment API endpoint ke liye idempotency kaise implement karte ho?
What they're really testing: the standard pattern: the client sends a UUID idempotency key in a header, the server stores key plus result, and a duplicate gets the stored result back.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: standard pattern: client header mein UUID idempotency key bhejta hai, server key plus result store karta hai, aur duplicate ko stored result wapas milta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

The client generates a UUID for each payment and sends it as an Idempotency-Key header, reusing the same key on every retry of that payment. On the server, I first atomically claim the key, for example with Redis SET idem:user:key ... NX EX 86400, storing state IN_PROGRESS and a hash of the request body. If I win the claim, I charge the card, then save the status code and response body under the key as COMPLETED. If the key already exists and is COMPLETED, I return the stored response without charging again. If it is IN_PROGRESS, I return 409 so the client retries shortly. If the body hash differs, the key was reused for a different payment and I reject it with 422. So a customer who taps Pay twice in a weak-network basement is charged once and sees the same receipt both times.

Client har payment ke liye ek UUID banata hai aur use Idempotency-Key header mein bhejta hai, us payment ke har retry pe wahi key. Server pe main pehle key ko atomically claim karta hoon, jaise Redis SET idem:user:key ... NX EX 86400 se, state IN_PROGRESS aur request body ka hash store karke. Agar claim jeet gaya, toh card charge karta hoon, phir status code aur response body key ke neeche COMPLETED ki tarah save karta hoon. Agar key pehle se hai aur COMPLETED hai, toh dobara charge kiye bina stored response lautata hoon. Agar IN_PROGRESS hai, toh 409 deta hoon taaki client thodi der baad retry kare. Agar body hash alag hai, toh key alag payment ke liye reuse hui hai aur main 422 se reject karta hoon. Toh jo customer kamzor network waale basement mein do baar Pay dabata hai, uska ek hi baar charge hota hai aur dono baar same receipt dikhti hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I would scope the key to the user so keys never collide across customers or leak another user's response. I would pass the same key to the payment provider, since providers like Stripe support it, so even my own crash between charge and save cannot double charge. For the strongest guarantee I would store the idempotency record in the payments database in the same transaction as the payment row, with a unique constraint on user and key. And I would store final business outcomes like "card declined" too, so a retry gets the same answer instead of a second attempt.

Main key ko user tak scope karunga taaki keys customers ke beech kabhi na takraayein ya kisi aur user ka response leak na ho. Main wahi key payment provider ko bhi bhejunga, kyunki Stripe jaise providers ise support karte hain, taaki charge aur save ke beech mera apna crash bhi double charge na kar sake. Sabse mazboot guarantee ke liye main idempotency record ko payments database mein payment row ke saath ek hi transaction mein store karunga, user aur key pe unique constraint ke saath. Aur "card declined" jaise final business outcomes bhi store karunga, taaki retry ko doosri koshish ki jagah wahi jawab mile.

Common mistake: checking "does the key exist?" with a GET and then writing it separately; two parallel duplicates both pass the check. The claim must be atomic.
Galti mat karna: GET se "key hai kya?" check karna aur phir alag se likhna; do parallel duplicates dono check paas kar lenge. Claim atomic hona chahiye.
04 How do you store and look up idempotency keys efficiently?Idempotency keys ko efficiently kaise store aur look up karte ho?
What they're really testing: Redis with a TTL, a key mapping to the request hash and the stored response, and a lock while the request is processing.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: TTL ke saath Redis, key jo request hash aur stored response pe map ho, aur request process hote waqt ek lock.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I usually store them in Redis, because lookups by key are fast and TTLs clean up old keys automatically. The Redis key is namespaced, like idem:{userId}:{idempotencyKey}, and the value holds three things: the state, IN_PROGRESS or COMPLETED; a hash of the request body, so I can detect a key reused for a different request; and, once done, the HTTP status and response body to replay. The IN_PROGRESS record doubles as a lock: I create it with SET ... NX EX, which only succeeds if the key does not exist, so exactly one copy of a duplicated request gets to do the work while others get a 409. The TTL is set longer than any client's retry window, for example 24 hours or more depending on how long clients retry.

Main aam taur pe inhe Redis mein store karta hoon, kyunki key se lookup fast hai aur TTL purani keys apne aap saaf kar deta hai. Redis key namespaced hoti hai, jaise idem:{userId}:{idempotencyKey}, aur value mein teen cheezein hoti hain: state, IN_PROGRESS ya COMPLETED; request body ka hash, taaki alag request ke liye reuse hui key pakad sakoon; aur kaam ho jaane pe, replay karne ke liye HTTP status aur response body. IN_PROGRESS record lock ka kaam bhi karta hai: main use SET ... NX EX se banata hoon, jo sirf tab succeed hota hai jab key exist na kare, toh duplicate request ki theek ek copy kaam karti hai aur baaki ko 409 milta hai. TTL kisi bhi client ke retry window se lamba rakhta hoon, jaise 24 ghante ya zyada, is pe depend karke ki clients kitni der retry karte hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Redis replication is asynchronous, so after a failover a just-written key can vanish and a retry might slip through. For money, I would keep the durable record in the main database: a table with a unique constraint on (user_id, idempotency_key), written in the same transaction as the payment, and use Redis only as a fast first check. The IN_PROGRESS lock needs its own expiry shorter than the key TTL, or a reconciliation job, so a crashed worker does not block retries forever. I keep stored responses small and avoid storing sensitive fields I do not need to replay.

Redis replication asynchronous hai, toh failover ke baad abhi-abhi likhi key gayab ho sakti hai aur ek retry nikal sakta hai. Paise ke liye main durable record main database mein rakhunga: ek table jisme (user_id, idempotency_key) pe unique constraint ho, payment ke saath ek hi transaction mein likhi jaaye, aur Redis ko sirf fast pehle check ki tarah use karunga. IN_PROGRESS lock ki apni expiry key TTL se chhoti honi chahiye, ya ek reconciliation job, taaki crash hua worker retries ko hamesha ke liye block na kare. Stored responses chhote rakhta hoon aur aise sensitive fields store nahi karta jinhe replay karne ki zaroorat nahi.

Common mistake: storing only the key without the response; then a retry is recognised but the server has nothing correct to return to the client.
Galti mat karna: sirf key store karna, response nahi; phir retry pehchaan liya jaata hai par server ke paas client ko lautane ke liye kuch sahi nahi hota.
05 What happens if the server processes the request but crashes before responding?Agar server request process kar le par respond karne se pehle crash ho jaaye toh kya hota hai?
What they're really testing: that the client retries with the same key, and that the server must write the key before processing so the retry can be recognised.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki client same key ke saath retry karta hai, aur server ko processing se pehle key likhni chahiye taaki retry pehchaana ja sake.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

From the client's side it is just a timeout, so it retries with the same idempotency key. Whether that is safe depends on when the server recorded the key. If it only writes the key after finishing, a crash after charging leaves no trace, the retry looks new, and the customer is charged twice. So I write the key before doing the work, as IN_PROGRESS, then do the work, then store the result as COMPLETED. If the crash happens after COMPLETED, the retry simply replays the stored response. If it happens while IN_PROGRESS, the retry gets a 409, and recovery decides what really happened. The principle is: record intent first, then act, then record the outcome.

Client ki taraf se yeh bas ek timeout hai, toh woh same idempotency key ke saath retry karta hai. Yeh safe hai ya nahi, yeh is pe depend karta hai ki server ne key kab record ki. Agar woh kaam khatam hone ke baad hi key likhta hai, toh charge ke baad crash koi nishaan nahi chhodta, retry naya lagta hai, aur customer se do baar paise katte hain. Isliye main kaam karne se pehle key likhta hoon, IN_PROGRESS ki tarah, phir kaam karta hoon, phir result COMPLETED ki tarah store karta hoon. Agar crash COMPLETED ke baad hua, toh retry bas stored response replay karta hai. Agar IN_PROGRESS ke dauraan hua, toh retry ko 409 milta hai, aur recovery decide karti hai ki asal mein kya hua. Principle hai: pehle irada record karo, phir kaam karo, phir nateeja record karo.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The remaining gap is between doing the work and saving COMPLETED. I close it three ways. If the work is a database write, the idempotency record and the business row go in one transaction, so they commit together or not at all. If the work is an external charge, I pass the same key to the provider, so re-sending after a crash returns the original charge. And a reconciliation job finds keys stuck in IN_PROGRESS, queries the provider for the real outcome, and completes them. I would never just let an IN_PROGRESS lock expire and reprocess blindly.

Bacha hua gap kaam karne aur COMPLETED save karne ke beech hai. Main ise teen tareekon se band karta hoon. Agar kaam database write hai, toh idempotency record aur business row ek transaction mein jaate hain, toh saath commit hote hain ya bilkul nahi. Agar kaam external charge hai, toh wahi key provider ko bhejta hoon, taaki crash ke baad dobara bhejne pe original charge hi mile. Aur ek reconciliation job IN_PROGRESS mein atki keys dhoondhta hai, provider se asli outcome poochta hai, aur unhe complete karta hai. Main kabhi bhi IN_PROGRESS lock ko bas expire hone deke aankh band karke dobara process nahi karunga.

Common mistake: saving the idempotency key only after a successful response, which leaves exactly the crash window this question is about wide open.
Galti mat karna: idempotency key sirf successful response ke baad save karna, jisse wahi crash window poori khuli reh jaati hai jiske baare mein yeh sawaal hai.
06 How do you handle idempotency in a message queue consumer?Message queue consumer mein idempotency kaise handle karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you know queues deliver at least once, so the consumer checks whether the message ID was already processed, and acks and skips duplicates.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum jaante ho queues at least once deliver karti hain, toh consumer check karta hai ki message ID pehle process hui hai kya, aur duplicates ko ack karke skip karta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Most queues, Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, give at-least-once delivery: if my consumer processes a message and crashes before acknowledging it, or the ack is lost, the message is delivered again. So duplicates are normal. I give every message a unique ID from the producer, and the consumer keeps a processed_messages table with that ID as the primary key. In one database transaction, I insert the message ID with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and, only if the insert succeeded, do the actual work, say marking an order as paid. Then I commit, and only after the commit do I ack. If the same message comes again, the insert finds the ID, I skip the work and ack it. The side effect happens once no matter how many times the message arrives.

Zyaadatar queues, Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, at-least-once delivery deti hain: agar mera consumer message process karke acknowledge karne se pehle crash ho gaya, ya ack kho gaya, toh message dobara deliver hota hai. Toh duplicates normal hain. Main har message ko producer se ek unique ID deta hoon, aur consumer ek processed_messages table rakhta hai jisme woh ID primary key hai. Ek database transaction mein main message ID ko ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING ke saath insert karta hoon aur, sirf agar insert succeed hua, tabhi asli kaam karta hoon, jaise order ko paid mark karna. Phir commit karta hoon, aur commit ke baad hi ack karta hoon. Agar wahi message dobara aaya, toh insert ko ID mil jaati hai, main kaam skip karke ack kar deta hoon. Side effect ek hi baar hota hai chahe message kitni bhi baar aaye.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Order matters: ack before processing gives at-most-once and can lose messages; ack after commit gives at-least-once plus dedup, which is what I want. If the side effect is outside my database, like sending an email or calling a partner API, I cannot put it in the same transaction, so I pass the message ID as an idempotency key to that API, or record intent first and use an outbox. The processed table grows forever, so I prune entries older than the queue's maximum redelivery window. Using the business key, like order ID plus event type, can be better than a random message ID when producers might publish the same event twice.

Order zaroori hai: processing se pehle ack karo toh at-most-once milta hai aur messages kho sakte hain; commit ke baad ack karo toh at-least-once plus dedup milta hai, jo mujhe chahiye. Agar side effect mere database ke bahar hai, jaise email bhejna ya partner API call karna, toh use same transaction mein nahi daal sakta, toh message ID ko us API ko idempotency key ki tarah bhejta hoon, ya pehle irada record karke outbox use karta hoon. Processed table hamesha badhti rehti hai, toh main queue ke maximum redelivery window se purani entries prune karta hoon. Jab producers same event do baar publish kar sakte hon, tab random message ID ki jagah business key, jaise order ID plus event type, better ho sakti hai.

Common mistake: relying on the broker to never redeliver, or checking the processed table and doing the work in separate, non-transactional steps.
Galti mat karna: broker pe bharosa karna ki woh kabhi redeliver nahi karega, ya processed table check karna aur kaam karna alag, bina transaction ke steps mein.
07 Idempotency vs exactly-once delivery?Idempotency vs exactly-once delivery mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: that idempotency is a property of an operation while exactly-once is a guarantee of the system, and that idempotency is the cheaper, practical path.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki idempotency ek operation ki property hai jabki exactly-once system ki guarantee hai, aur idempotency sasta, practical raasta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Exactly-once delivery is a guarantee the messaging system would give: every message arrives one time, never lost, never duplicated. Idempotency is a property of the operation itself: processing the same message twice has the same effect as once. The problem is that exactly-once delivery cannot be guaranteed in general over an unreliable network, because a sender cannot distinguish "not delivered" from "delivered but the acknowledgement was lost". So a sender must either risk losing messages or resend and risk duplicates. The practical solution is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which gives an exactly-once effect. Idempotency is cheaper and under my control, because I implement it in my consumer with a message ID check, instead of depending on heavy coordination across systems.

Exactly-once delivery ek guarantee hai jo messaging system deta: har message ek baar aaye, na khoye, na duplicate ho. Idempotency operation ki apni property hai: same message do baar process karne ka asar ek baar jaisa. Problem yeh hai ki unreliable network pe exactly-once delivery ki general guarantee nahi di ja sakti, kyunki sender "deliver nahi hua" aur "deliver hua par acknowledgement kho gaya" mein fark nahi kar sakta. Toh sender ko ya toh messages khone ka risk lena padta hai ya dobara bhej ke duplicates ka. Practical solution hai at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, jo exactly-once jaisa asar deta hai. Idempotency sasti hai aur mere control mein hai, kyunki main ise apne consumer mein message ID check se implement karta hoon, systems ke beech bhaari coordination pe depend karne ki jagah.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

This is the two-generals problem: no finite number of messages over a lossy channel makes both sides certain. Kafka advertises exactly-once semantics, but it is scoped to read-process-write inside Kafka using idempotent producers and transactions. The moment my consumer charges a card or sends an email, that external effect is outside Kafka's transaction, so I still need idempotency there. I would say "effectively-once" is what systems actually deliver: at-least-once plus dedup.

Yeh two-generals problem hai: lossy channel pe koi bhi finite messages dono taraf pakki certainty nahi de sakte. Kafka exactly-once semantics advertise karta hai, par yeh Kafka ke andar read-process-write tak scoped hai, idempotent producers aur transactions ke saath. Jaise hi mera consumer card charge karta hai ya email bhejta hai, woh external asar Kafka ke transaction ke bahar hai, toh wahan mujhe abhi bhi idempotency chahiye. Main bolunga ki systems asal mein "effectively-once" dete hain: at-least-once plus dedup.

Common mistake: saying "we use Kafka exactly-once, so duplicates cannot happen", ignoring side effects outside Kafka.
Galti mat karna: bolna "hum Kafka exactly-once use karte hain, toh duplicates ho hi nahi sakte", Kafka ke bahar ke side effects ko ignore karke.
08 Can a non-idempotent operation be made safe to retry? How?Kya non-idempotent operation ko retry ke liye safe banaya ja sakta hai? Kaise?
What they're really testing: check-then-act using an idempotency key, with the result stored so a repeat returns it instead of acting again.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: idempotency key ke saath check-then-act, result store karke taaki repeat pe dobara kaam ki jagah wahi result lautaya jaaye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Yes. The general technique is check-then-act with an idempotency key: before doing the operation, I check whether this key has already been handled; if not, I do the operation and store its result under the key; if yes, I return the stored result without acting again. The check and the claim must be one atomic step, like Redis SET NX or an insert with a unique constraint, so two parallel duplicates cannot both pass. For example, "book a service appointment" is not idempotent, two taps create two bookings. With a client-generated key per booking attempt, the second tap finds the key and gets back the first booking's confirmation. There are natural options too: a unique constraint on a business key, a conditional update, or rewriting a relative change as an absolute one.

Haan. General technique hai idempotency key ke saath check-then-act: operation karne se pehle check karta hoon ki yeh key pehle handle ho chuki hai kya; nahi, toh operation karta hoon aur uska result key ke neeche store karta hoon; haan, toh dobara kaam kiye bina stored result lautata hoon. Check aur claim ek atomic step hona chahiye, jaise Redis SET NX ya unique constraint ke saath insert, taaki do parallel duplicates dono paas na ho sakein. Jaise, "service appointment book karo" idempotent nahi hai, do taps do bookings banate hain. Har booking attempt ke liye client ki banayi key ke saath, doosre tap ko key milti hai aur use pehli booking ka confirmation wapas milta hai. Natural options bhi hain: business key pe unique constraint, conditional update, ya relative change ko absolute bana dena.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Concrete examples: a unique constraint on shipments.order_id means "create shipment for order 42" can only succeed once; UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=42 AND status='PENDING' changes zero rows on a repeat; "set price to 19,200" is safe where "add 300 to price" is not; and for counters, dedup on an event ID before incrementing. Some things can never be undone, like an email already sent, so for those I record the intent with the key first and make the sender check it.

Concrete examples: shipments.order_id pe unique constraint ka matlab "order 42 ke liye shipment banao" sirf ek baar succeed ho sakta hai; UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=42 AND status='PENDING' repeat pe zero rows badalta hai; "price 19,200 set karo" safe hai jahan "price mein 300 jodo" nahi; aur counters ke liye, increment se pehle event ID pe dedup. Kuch cheezein kabhi undo nahi hoti, jaise bheja hua email, toh unke liye main pehle key ke saath irada record karta hoon aur sender se woh check karwata hoon.

Common mistake: doing the check with a plain read and then acting separately, which is itself a race condition under concurrent retries.
Galti mat karna: check ek simple read se karna aur phir alag se kaam karna, jo concurrent retries mein khud ek race condition hai.
09 How would you design idempotency for a bulk/batch endpoint?Bulk/batch endpoint ke liye idempotency kaise design karoge?
What they're really testing: per-item keys, per-item status, and safe retry of only the items that failed.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: per-item keys, per-item status, aur sirf failed items ka safe retry.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A single key for the whole batch breaks on partial failure. If 99 of 100 payouts succeed and one times out, replaying the old batch response leaves that one unpaid, while reprocessing everything pays 99 people twice. So I give every item its own idempotency key, supplied by the client, and process each item independently and idempotently, storing a result per item key. The response returns a status for every item, succeeded, failed with a reason, and whether it is retryable. The client then retries the batch, or just the failed items, with the same keys.
