Items already done are replayed from storage with no work, and only the failed item is actually processed. The retry is always safe, whatever state the previous attempt left behind.

Poore batch ke liye ek key partial failure pe toot jaati hai. Agar 100 mein se 99 payouts succeed hue aur ek timeout hua, toh purana batch response replay karne se woh ek bina paise reh jaata hai, jabki sab dobara process karne se 99 logon ko do baar paisa milta hai. Isliye main har item ko uski apni idempotency key deta hoon, jo client deta hai, aur har item ko alag se aur idempotently process karta hoon, har item key ke neeche result store karke. Response har item ka status lautata hai: succeeded, failed kaaran ke saath, aur retry ho sakta hai ya nahi. Phir client batch, ya sirf failed items, same keys ke saath retry karta hai. Jo items ho chuke hain woh bina kaam ke storage se replay hote hain, aur sirf failed item asal mein process hota hai. Retry hamesha safe hai, pichhli koshish ne chahe koi bhi state chhodi ho.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I can also add a batch-level key so a duplicate submission of the entire batch is recognised quickly. For the response, some APIs use 207 Multi-Status, many use 200 with a results array; the important part is never reporting a partially failed batch as a plain success. For very large batches I would accept with 202 and a job ID, let the client poll per-item progress, and process items in chunks. If the business truly needs all-or-nothing, that is a different design: one transaction or a saga, not per-item retries.

Main ek batch-level key bhi jod sakta hoon taaki poore batch ka duplicate submission jaldi pehchaana ja sake. Response ke liye kuch APIs 207 Multi-Status use karti hain, kai 200 ke saath results array; zaroori baat yeh hai ki partially failed batch ko kabhi simple success mat batao. Bahut bade batches ke liye main 202 aur job ID ke saath accept karunga, client ko per-item progress poll karne dunga, aur items ko chunks mein process karunga. Agar business ko sach mein all-or-nothing chahiye, toh woh alag design hai: ek transaction ya saga, per-item retries nahi.

Common mistake: using one idempotency key for the entire batch and returning a single success or failure for it.
Galti mat karna: poore batch ke liye ek idempotency key use karna aur uske liye ek hi success ya failure lautana.
10 Why is idempotency key expiry a security and cost consideration?Idempotency key ki expiry security aur cost ka mudda kyun hai?
What they're really testing: never expiring means unbounded storage, expiring too fast lets slow retries become duplicates, and the TTL must be set against the retry window.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kabhi expire na karna matlab bina limit ka storage, bahut jaldi expire karna matlab slow retries duplicates ban jaate hain, aur TTL retry window ke hisaab se set hona chahiye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

It is a trade-off with a failure on each side. If keys never expire, storage grows without bound: every request ever made keeps a record with its full response, which costs real memory in Redis and keeps sensitive data around forever. If keys expire too quickly, a slow retry, say a phone that was offline for an hour or a queue redelivering after an outage, arrives after the key is gone and is processed as new, which is exactly the duplicate charge we wanted to prevent. So I set the TTL longer than the longest realistic retry window of any client or queue that can resend. Stripe, for example, documents pruning keys after they are at least 24 hours old. If our mobile app retries for longer than that, the TTL must be longer too.

Yeh ek trade-off hai jisme dono taraf failure hai. Agar keys kabhi expire na hon, toh storage bina limit ke badhta hai: aaj tak ki har request ka record poore response ke saath rehta hai, jo Redis mein asli memory ka kharcha hai aur sensitive data hamesha ke liye pada rehta hai. Agar keys bahut jaldi expire hon, toh ek slow retry, jaise ghante bhar offline raha phone ya outage ke baad queue ka redeliver, key jaane ke baad aata hai aur naya maan ke process hota hai, jo bilkul wahi duplicate charge hai jise hum rokna chahte the. Isliye main TTL ko kisi bhi client ya queue ke sabse lambe realistic retry window se lamba rakhta hoon. Jaise Stripe document karta hai ki keys kam se kam 24 ghante purani hone pe prune hoti hain. Agar humara mobile app usse zyada der retry karta hai, toh TTL bhi lamba hona chahiye.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

On security: I scope keys to the authenticated caller, so a leaked or guessed key cannot fetch another user's stored payment response; I require random UUIDs, not sequential IDs; I compare a body fingerprint so a key cannot be replayed with different parameters; and I rate limit key creation, since an attacker flooding unique keys is a storage attack. On cost: I store a minimal response, and for long retention I move records from Redis to cheaper database storage. The client side matters too: it should stop retrying before the server's TTL ends.

Security pe: main keys ko authenticated caller tak scope karta hoon, taaki leak hui ya guess ki gayi key kisi aur user ka stored payment response na nikaal sake; random UUIDs zaroori karta hoon, sequential IDs nahi; body fingerprint compare karta hoon taaki key alag parameters ke saath replay na ho; aur key creation pe rate limit lagata hoon, kyunki unique keys ki baadh laata attacker ek storage attack hai. Cost pe: minimal response store karta hoon, aur lambi retention ke liye records ko Redis se saste database storage mein le jaata hoon. Client side bhi zaroori hai: use server ke TTL khatam hone se pehle retry band kar dena chahiye.

Common mistake: picking a TTL like 5 minutes "to save memory" without checking how long clients and queues actually keep retrying.
Galti mat karna: "memory bachane ke liye" 5 minute jaisa TTL chun lena, bina check kiye ki clients aur queues asal mein kitni der tak retry karte hain.

Topic 06 · VERY COMMONTopic 06 · Bahut common

Message QueuesMessage Queues

Why a backend stops calling everyone directly and starts leaving messages instead: queues, pub/sub, delivery guarantees, Kafka partitions and consumer groups, retries and dead letters, from absolute zero.

Backend sabko seedha call karna kyun band karta hai aur "message chhod ke aage badhna" kyun shuru karta hai: queue, pub/sub, delivery guarantees, Kafka partitions aur consumer groups, retries aur dead letters, bilkul zero se.

Level 0 The story: one Swiggy order, four teamsKahani: ek Swiggy order, chaar teams

You open Swiggy and order a biryani. The moment you tap Place order, four separate things have to happen:

  • the restaurant must see the order and start cooking,
  • a delivery partner must be found nearby,
  • you must get an SMS saying "order confirmed",
  • an invoice (the bill PDF) must be generated and emailed.

The naive way. The order server does all four itself, one after another, while you stare at a spinner. It calls the restaurant system and waits for a reply. Then it calls the delivery system, which has to search for riders, and waits. Then it calls the SMS provider and waits. Then the invoice service, and waits. Only when all four have answered does your screen turn green. This style is called a synchronous (sync) call chain: the caller waits for each answer before it moves on.

Now picture a bad evening. The SMS provider is slow, so your order screen hangs. The invoice service is down for a deploy, so your whole order fails because a PDF could not be made, which is absurd. It is a festival night and orders jump many times over, so every downstream system gets hammered in the same second, and the slowest one drags everyone else down with it.

The smarter way. The order server does only the one thing that truly must happen before it replies: it saves the order in its own database. Then it pins a note on a shared notice board: "Order #123 placed: biryani, customer Puneet, Koramangala". It immediately tells you "Order placed!". The restaurant team, the delivery team, the SMS team and the invoice team each watch that notice board and act on the note at their own speed. If SMS is slow, only the SMS is late. If the invoice service is down, the note simply waits on the board until the service comes back. Nobody else even notices.

That notice board is a message broker, and the note is a message. That is the whole topic in one picture. Everything else in this chapter (queues, topics, Kafka, acknowledgements, retries, dead letters) is about making that notice board reliable, fast and safe.

Analogy: the post office. When you post a letter you drop it in the post box and walk away. You do not stand outside the receiver's door until they open it. The post office holds the letter, delivers it when it can, tries again if nobody is home, and if the address is impossible it sends the letter to the dead letter office. Keep this picture: we will meet every one of these ideas (hand-off, retry, dead letter) in software.

Tum Swiggy kholte ho aur biryani order karte ho. Jaise hi tum Place order dabaate ho, chaar alag kaam hone chahiye:

  • restaurant ko order dikhna chahiye aur cooking shuru honi chahiye,
  • paas mein koi delivery partner dhoondhna hai,
  • tumhe SMS aana chahiye "order confirmed",
  • ek invoice (bill ka PDF) banna chahiye aur email hona chahiye.

Seedha-saadha (naive) tarika. Order server khud chaaron kaam ek ke baad ek karta hai, aur tum spinner ko ghoorte rehte ho. Pehle restaurant system ko call karta hai aur jawab ka wait karta hai. Phir delivery system ko call karta hai, jo riders dhoondhta hai, phir wait. Phir SMS provider, phir wait. Phir invoice service, phir wait. Jab chaaron jawab de dete hain tab jaake tumhari screen green hoti hai. Is style ko synchronous (sync) call chain kehte hain: call karne wala har jawab ka wait karta hai, tabhi aage badhta hai.

Ab ek kharab shaam socho. SMS provider slow hai, toh tumhari order screen atak jaati hai. Invoice service deploy ki wajah se down hai, toh tumhara poora order hi fail ho jaata hai kyunki ek PDF nahi ban paaya, jo bilkul bekaar baat hai. Festival ki raat hai aur orders kai guna badh gaye, toh har downstream system ek hi second mein pit jaata hai, aur sabse slow wala baaki sabko bhi neeche kheench leta hai.

Samajhdaar tarika. Order server sirf woh ek kaam karta hai jo reply dene se pehle sach mein zaroori hai: order ko apne database mein save karna. Phir woh ek shared notice board pe ek note chipka deta hai: "Order #123 placed: biryani, customer Puneet, Koramangala". Aur turant tumhe bol deta hai "Order placed!". Restaurant team, delivery team, SMS team aur invoice team, sab us notice board ko dekhte rehte hain aur apni-apni speed se note pe kaam karte hain. SMS slow hai toh sirf SMS late hoga. Invoice service down hai toh note board pe wait karega jab tak service wapas na aa jaaye. Baaki kisi ko pata bhi nahi chalega.

Woh notice board hai message broker, aur woh note hai message. Poora topic isi ek picture mein hai. Is chapter mein baaki sab kuch (queues, topics, Kafka, acknowledgements, retries, dead letters) bas is notice board ko reliable, fast aur safe banane ke baare mein hai.

Analogy: post office. Jab tum letter post karte ho, post box mein daal ke chale jaate ho. Receiver ke darwaaze ke bahar khade nahi rehte jab tak woh khol na le. Post office letter ko sambhaal ke rakhta hai, jab ho sake deliver karta hai, ghar pe koi na ho toh dobara try karta hai, aur agar address hi galat hai toh letter dead letter office bhej deta hai. Yeh picture yaad rakho: software mein yeh saare ideas (hand-off, retry, dead letter) hum aage milenge.

Level 1 The basic words, and the two shapes: queue and pub/subBasic words, aur do shapes: queue aur pub/sub

Let us name every piece of the story.

  • Message: a small packet of data describing something that happened, or a job to be done. Usually JSON, for example {"messageId":"m-9f2","type":"OrderPlaced","orderId":123,"amount":349}.
  • Producer (or publisher): the program that sends the message. Here, the order service.
  • Consumer (or subscriber, or worker): the program that receives the message and does something with it. Here, the SMS service, the invoice service and so on.
  • Broker: the separate server in the middle that stores messages and hands them out. Popular brokers are Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SQS and Redis Streams. A "message queue" in casual talk means this whole setup.
  • Synchronous vs asynchronous: sync means "I call you and wait for your answer". Async means "I hand this off and carry on; the work happens later".
  • Ack (acknowledgement): the consumer telling the broker "I have finished this message, you can forget it". If the broker never gets the ack (because the consumer crashed, say) it assumes the work failed and hands the message out again.

Brokers come in two basic shapes. Interviewers love asking about the difference.

1. Queue (point-to-point, also called a work queue). The producer puts messages into a queue. Several consumers may be connected, but each message goes to exactly one of them. When that consumer acks, the broker deletes the message. Think of the token counter at a bank: many clerks, many tokens, but each token is served by one clerk only. If you add more clerks, the line moves faster, because they share the work. This pattern is called competing consumers. Use it for jobs: "send this email", "resize this photo", "generate invoice #123".

2. Publish/subscribe (pub/sub). The producer publishes to a topic (a named channel), and every subscriber gets its own copy of every message. Think of your society WhatsApp group: the secretary posts "water supply off tomorrow" once, and every member sees it. Adding a new member does not take the message away from anyone else. Use it for events, facts that several teams care about: "order placed" is needed by restaurant, delivery, SMS and invoice.

A useful rule of thumb: an event says "this happened" (OrderPlaced) and anybody may care, so it fits pub/sub. A command says "please do this" (SendSms to one number) and exactly one worker should do it, so it fits a queue.

Where Kafka fits. Kafka blurs the two shapes. It does not delete a message when someone reads it. Instead it keeps every message in an append-only log for a configured retention period (7 days by default, configurable by time or size). Each reading application keeps its own bookmark, called an offset, telling it how far it has read. Applications that share one bookmark form a consumer group. Inside one group, each message is processed by one member, which looks like a queue. Across different groups, every group gets every message, which looks like pub/sub. And because messages are retained, a brand-new group can start from the beginning and replay history. We will open up Kafka properly in Level 2.

Queue: adding consumers splits the work. Pub/sub: adding subscribers copies the message. Kafka: queue-like inside a consumer group, pub/sub-like across groups, and replayable because it retains the log.

Kahani ke har hisse ko naam dete hain.

  • Message: data ka ek chhota packet jo batata hai ki kuch hua hai, ya koi kaam karna hai. Usually JSON hota hai, jaise {"messageId":"m-9f2","type":"OrderPlaced","orderId":123,"amount":349}.
  • Producer (ya publisher): woh program jo message bhejta hai. Yahan, order service.
  • Consumer (ya subscriber, ya worker): woh program jo message leta hai aur uspe kaam karta hai. Yahan SMS service, invoice service, waghera.
  • Broker: beech mein baitha ek alag server jo messages store karta hai aur baant-ta hai. Popular brokers: Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SQS, Redis Streams. Normal baat-cheet mein "message queue" matlab yeh poora setup.
  • Synchronous vs asynchronous: sync matlab "main tumhe call karunga aur jawab ka wait karunga". Async matlab "main yeh kaam aage pass karke apna kaam karta rahunga; kaam baad mein hoga".
  • Ack (acknowledgement): consumer broker ko bolta hai "yeh message ho gaya, ab bhool jao". Agar broker ko ack kabhi nahi milta (maan lo consumer crash ho gaya) toh broker maan leta hai ki kaam fail hua aur message dobara de deta hai.

Brokers do basic shapes mein aate hain. Interviewers ko inka difference poochna bahut pasand hai.

1. Queue (point-to-point, ya work queue). Producer messages queue mein daalta hai. Kai consumers connected ho sakte hain, lekin har message sirf ek consumer ko jaata hai. Woh consumer ack kar de toh broker message delete kar deta hai. Bank ka token counter socho: kai clerks, kai tokens, lekin har token ko sirf ek clerk handle karta hai. Aur clerks badhao toh line jaldi chalti hai, kyunki woh kaam baant lete hain. Is pattern ko competing consumers kehte hain. Isko jobs ke liye use karo: "yeh email bhejo", "yeh photo resize karo", "invoice #123 banao".

2. Publish/subscribe (pub/sub). Producer ek topic (ek naam wala channel) pe publish karta hai, aur har subscriber ko har message ki apni copy milti hai. Apni society ka WhatsApp group socho: secretary ek baar post karta hai "kal paani nahi aayega", aur har member ko dikhta hai. Naya member add karne se kisi aur ka message chhin nahi jaata. Isko events ke liye use karo, yaani facts jinki kai teams ko zaroorat hai: "order placed" restaurant, delivery, SMS aur invoice sabko chahiye.

Ek kaam ka rule: event bolta hai "yeh ho gaya" (OrderPlaced), aur kisi ko bhi farak pad sakta hai, toh yeh pub/sub mein fit hota hai. Command bolta hai "please yeh karo" (ek number pe SendSms), aur ise sirf ek worker ko karna chahiye, toh yeh queue mein fit hota hai.

Kafka kahan fit hota hai. Kafka in dono shapes ki line dhundhli kar deta hai. Koi message padh le toh Kafka use delete nahi karta. Balki har message ko ek append-only log mein ek set retention period tak rakhta hai (default 7 din, time ya size se configure hota hai). Har padhne wali application apna ek bookmark rakhti hai jise offset kehte hain, jo batata hai ki woh kahan tak padh chuki hai. Jo applications ek hi bookmark share karti hain, woh ek consumer group banati hain. Ek group ke andar har message ko ek hi member process karta hai, jo queue jaisa lagta hai. Alag-alag groups mein, har group ko har message milta hai, jo pub/sub jaisa lagta hai. Aur kyunki messages retain hote hain, ek bilkul naya group shuruaat se padh ke poori history replay kar sakta hai. Kafka ko Level 2 mein achhe se kholenge.

Queue: consumers badhao toh kaam bant-ta hai. Pub/sub: subscribers badhao toh message copy hota hai. Kafka: consumer group ke andar queue jaisa, groups ke beech pub/sub jaisa, aur log retain karta hai isliye replay ho sakta hai.

Level 2 How it works inside: acks, delivery guarantees, and Kafka's partitionsAndar kaise kaam karta hai: acks, delivery guarantees, aur Kafka ke partitions

The ack dance. Every broker follows roughly the same steps for one message:

  1. The broker hands the message to a consumer.
  2. The consumer does the work (creates the invoice, sends the SMS).
  3. The consumer sends an ack (in Kafka, it commits its offset, meaning it saves "I have finished everything up to position N").
  4. The broker marks the message as done (a queue deletes it; Kafka moves that group's bookmark forward).

Machines can crash between any two of these steps. Where you put the ack decides what can go wrong, and this gives us the three famous delivery guarantees:

GuaranteeHow it is doneWhat can go wrongGood for
At-most-onceFire and forget, or ack before doing the workCrash after ack but before work: the message is lost. Never duplicated.Metrics samples, "user is typing" signals
At-least-onceAck only after the work; broker redelivers if no ack arrivesCrash after work but before ack: the message is processed twice. Never lost.Almost everything: orders, payments, emails (with an idempotent consumer)
Exactly-onceAt-least-once delivery plus de-duplication on the producer side and the consumer sideCosts more coordination, latency and complexityMoney movements, counters, stream processing pipelines

Why is exactly-once so hard? Because over an unreliable network, a sender can never be sure whether a lost reply means "the message never arrived" or "it arrived but the ack got lost" (this is the Two Generals problem, covered in Topic 07). So nobody can guarantee a message is delivered exactly once. What real systems achieve is effectively-once processing: deliver at least once, and make sure a duplicate has no extra effect. Kafka's own "exactly-once semantics" works this way: an idempotent producer (each producer gets an ID and numbers its messages, so the broker can drop a retried duplicate; on by default since Kafka 3.0) plus transactions that write output messages and commit the consumer's offsets atomically. That guarantee only covers data that stays inside Kafka. The moment your consumer sends an SMS or charges a card, you need your own de-duplication.

The idempotent consumer. Since at-least-once is the normal choice, duplicates are normal, and the consumer must be idempotent: processing the same message twice must have the same effect as processing it once (Topic 05). The standard trick is to give every message a unique ID and record processed IDs in the same database transaction as the work:

Ack wala dance. Har broker ek message ke liye lagbhag yahi steps follow karta hai:

  1. Broker message ek consumer ko deta hai.
  2. Consumer kaam karta hai (invoice banata hai, SMS bhejta hai).
  3. Consumer ack bhejta hai (Kafka mein woh apna offset commit karta hai, matlab save karta hai ki "position N tak sab ho gaya").
  4. Broker message ko done mark kar deta hai (queue use delete kar deti hai; Kafka us group ka bookmark aage kar deta hai).

Machines in kisi bhi do steps ke beech crash ho sakti hain. Ack tum kahan rakhte ho, isse decide hota hai ki kya gadbad ho sakti hai, aur isi se teen famous delivery guarantees bante hain:

GuaranteeKaise hota haiKya gadbad ho sakti haiKiske liye theek
At-most-onceBhejo aur bhool jao, ya kaam se pehle ack kar doAck ke baad, kaam se pehle crash: message kho gaya. Duplicate kabhi nahi.Metrics samples, "user typing kar raha hai" signals
At-least-onceKaam ke baad hi ack; ack na aaye toh broker dobara deta haiKaam ke baad, ack se pehle crash: message do baar process. Kabhi khota nahi.Lagbhag sab kuch: orders, payments, emails (idempotent consumer ke saath)
Exactly-onceAt-least-once delivery plus producer side aur consumer side pe de-duplicationZyada coordination, latency aur complexity lagti haiPaise ka movement, counters, stream processing pipelines

Exactly-once itna mushkil kyun hai? Kyunki unreliable network pe sender kabhi pakka nahi jaan sakta ki reply nahi aaya matlab "message pahuncha hi nahi" ya "pahunch gaya par ack kho gaya" (yeh Two Generals problem hai, Topic 07 mein). Toh koi guarantee nahi de sakta ki message exactly ek baar deliver hoga. Real systems jo achieve karte hain woh hai effectively-once processing: kam se kam ek baar deliver karo, aur ensure karo ki duplicate ka koi extra effect na ho. Kafka ki apni "exactly-once semantics" bhi aise hi kaam karti hai: ek idempotent producer (har producer ko ek ID milti hai aur woh apne messages ko number karta hai, taaki broker retry wala duplicate gira sake; Kafka 3.0 se default on) plus transactions jo output messages likhna aur consumer ke offsets commit karna ek saath atomically karte hain. Yeh guarantee sirf us data ko cover karti hai jo Kafka ke andar hi rehta hai. Jaise hi tumhara consumer SMS bhejta hai ya card charge karta hai, tumhe apna khud ka de-duplication chahiye.

Idempotent consumer. Kyunki normal choice at-least-once hai, duplicates normal hain, aur consumer ko idempotent hona hi padega: same message do baar process karo toh effect utna hi ho jitna ek baar mein (Topic 05). Standard trick: har message ko ek unique ID do, aur processed IDs ko usi database transaction mein record karo jismein kaam ho raha hai:

// Invoice consumer for "OrderPlaced" events, safe under at-least-once delivery (Node.js style)
async function handleOrderPlaced(msg) {
  const { messageId, orderId, amount } = JSON.parse(msg.value);

  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    // processed_messages has a UNIQUE constraint on message_id
    const res = await tx.query(
      `INSERT INTO processed_messages (message_id) VALUES ($1)
       ON CONFLICT (message_id) DO NOTHING`,
      [messageId]
    );
    if (res.rowCount === 0) return;   // duplicate: already done, just skip

    await tx.query(
      `INSERT INTO invoices (order_id, amount) VALUES ($1, $2)`,
      [orderId, amount]
    );
  });
  // Only now ack the message / commit the Kafka offset
}

Because the "have I seen this ID?" check and the invoice insert happen in one transaction, and the unique constraint does the checking, two copies of the same message arriving at two consumers at the same millisecond still produce exactly one invoice.

Kafka inside. Now let us open Kafka, because most interview questions go here.

  • A topic (for example orders) is a named, append-only log. "Append-only" means new messages are only ever added at the end, like new lines in a diary. Each message gets a position number called its offset: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on.
  • One log on one machine would be a bottleneck, so a topic is split into partitions: several independent logs, spread across several Kafka servers (brokers). Partitions are the unit of both storage spreading and reading parallelism. Each partition is also copied to other brokers (replication) so a crashed broker does not lose data.
  • When producing, you can give each message a key, such as the orderId. Kafka's default partitioner hashes the key and takes it modulo the number of partitions, so the same key always lands in the same partition. Messages without a key are spread across partitions.
  • Consumers pull: they ask the broker "give me messages from partition 2 starting at offset 57", process them, and then commit their new offset. Kafka stores committed offsets per group in an internal topic called __consumer_offsets.

Consumer groups. A consumer group is a set of consumer processes that share one group.id and cooperate to read a topic. The golden rule: within a group, each partition is read by exactly one consumer at a time, while one consumer may own several partitions. Look at the picture below for a topic with 3 partitions:

  • 2 consumers: one owns two partitions, the other owns one.
  • 3 consumers: one partition each, the perfect fit.
  • 4 consumers: one consumer sits idle, because a partition cannot be split between two members of the same group.

So the maximum parallelism of a group equals the number of partitions. When a consumer joins, leaves or dies, Kafka runs a rebalance and reassigns partitions. Different groups are completely independent: the invoice-service group and the analytics group each read every partition with their own offsets. That is how Kafka does pub/sub.

Ordering. Inside one partition, messages are stored and read in offset order. Across partitions there is no global order. That is why the key matters: if orderId is the key, then OrderPlaced, OrderPaid and OrderCancelled for order #123 all land in the same partition and are handled in sequence by one consumer, while other orders are handled in parallel elsewhere.

Kyunki "yeh ID pehle dekha hai kya?" wala check aur invoice ka insert ek hi transaction mein ho rahe hain, aur checking unique constraint kar raha hai, toh agar same message ki do copies do consumers pe ek hi millisecond mein aa jaayein, tab bhi invoice sirf ek hi banega.

Kafka ke andar. Ab Kafka ko kholte hain, kyunki zyada interview sawaal yahin aate hain.

  • Ek topic (jaise orders) ek naam wala, append-only log hai. "Append-only" matlab naye messages sirf end mein judte hain, jaise diary mein nayi lines. Har message ko ek position number milta hai jise offset kehte hain: 0, 1, 2, 3 aur aage.
  • Ek hi machine pe ek hi log bottleneck ban jaayega, isliye topic ko partitions mein toda jaata hai: kai independent logs, jo kai Kafka servers (brokers) pe faile hote hain. Partitions hi storage ko failane ki aur parallel padhne ki unit hain. Har partition ki copy doosre brokers pe bhi hoti hai (replication), taaki ek broker crash ho toh data na khoye.
  • Message bhejte waqt tum har message ko ek key de sakte ho, jaise orderId. Kafka ka default partitioner key ka hash nikaal ke partitions ki ginti se modulo leta hai, toh same key hamesha same partition mein jaati hai. Bina key wale messages partitions mein fail jaate hain.
  • Consumers pull karte hain: broker se poochte hain "partition 2 se offset 57 se messages do", unhe process karte hain, phir apna naya offset commit karte hain. Kafka har group ke committed offsets ek internal topic __consumer_offsets mein rakhta hai.

Consumer groups. Consumer group consumer processes ka ek set hai jo ek hi group.id share karte hain aur milke ek topic padhte hain. Golden rule: ek group ke andar, har partition ko ek time pe sirf ek consumer padhta hai, jabki ek consumer kai partitions ka owner ho sakta hai. Neeche picture dekho, topic mein 3 partitions hain:

  • 2 consumers: ek ke paas do partitions, doosre ke paas ek.
  • 3 consumers: har ek ke paas ek partition, perfect fit.
  • 4 consumers: ek consumer idle baitha rehta hai, kyunki ek partition ko ek hi group ke do members mein baanta nahi ja sakta.

Toh ek group ki maximum parallelism = partitions ki ginti. Jab koi consumer judta hai, chhodta hai ya mar jaata hai, Kafka rebalance chalata hai aur partitions dobara baant-ta hai. Alag groups bilkul independent hain: invoice-service group aur analytics group dono har partition ko apne-apne offsets ke saath padhte hain. Kafka isi tarah pub/sub karta hai.

Ordering. Ek partition ke andar messages offset ke order mein store aur read hote hain. Partitions ke beech koi global order nahi hai. Isiliye key important hai: agar orderId key hai, toh order #123 ke OrderPlaced, OrderPaid aur OrderCancelled sab same partition mein jaate hain aur ek hi consumer unhe sequence mein handle karta hai, jabki baaki orders parallel mein kahin aur handle hote hain.

Level 3 Real production: when to use a queue, backpressure, retries and the dead letter queueReal production: queue kab use karein, backpressure, retries aur dead letter queue

Here is what a typical production setup looks like: one API publishes an event to a topic, several independent services consume it, and anything that keeps failing ends up in a dead letter queue.

Ek typical production setup aisa dikhta hai: ek API ek topic pe event publish karta hai, kai independent services use consume karti hain, aur jo cheez baar-baar fail hoti rehti hai woh dead letter queue mein pahunch jaati hai.

When a queue beats a direct API call. Reach for a queue when at least one of these is true:

  • The work is slow and the user does not need to wait for it: generating a PDF, processing uploaded photos or video, sending emails.
  • You need retries and guaranteed delivery. If the downstream service is down, the message waits safely in the broker instead of being lost with a failed HTTP call.
  • The two sides should scale independently. Orders arrive in spikes; invoice workers can run at a steady pace and you can add workers without touching the order service.
  • Many services react to one event, and the producer should not even know who they are. Adding a new "loyalty points" service later means adding a new consumer, not changing the order code.

Use a direct call when the caller needs the answer right now to continue: checking a password, "is this seat still free?", fetching vehicle details to render a page. A queue here only adds delay. And remember the costs of queues: the system becomes eventually consistent (the invoice appears a few seconds later), debugging spans several services, consumers must be idempotent, and you now run one more piece of infrastructure.

In real production (dealership example). Imagine a dealership uploading photos of a newly arrived vehicle. The upload API stores the files and publishes VehiclePhotosUploaded with the VIN. Image-processing workers consume it, clean up the photos, and publish VehiclePhotosReady; the listing service consumes that and updates the online listing. The upload screen never waits for image processing, and a burst of uploads just makes the queue longer for a while instead of timing everyone out.

Backpressure. Backpressure is the situation where a producer sends faster than a consumer can process, and the ways a system "pushes back". Without a queue, direct calls pile up on the slow service: its threads and connections run out, requests time out, callers retry (making it worse), and the failure spreads upstream. That spreading is called a cascading failure. With a queue in the middle, the burst is absorbed like water in a tank: the queue gets longer, consumers keep working at their safe pace, and the backlog drains when traffic drops. The size of that backlog is called consumer lag (in Kafka: the newest offset minus the group's committed offset).

But the tank is not infinite. Good teams therefore:

  • monitor consumer lag and alert when it keeps growing,
  • autoscale consumers on lag (in Kafka, only up to the partition count),
  • cap how many unacked messages each consumer holds at once (RabbitMQ calls this prefetch; Kafka consumers pull only what they can handle, so pull-based consumption gives natural backpressure),
  • and, if lag still grows, push back on the producer: reject or throttle requests (HTTP 429), or let the broker block publishers (RabbitMQ does this when it runs low on memory or disk).
Kafka deletes data when retention expires whether or not anyone read it. If a consumer group falls further behind than the retention period, those unread messages are gone. Lag that grows forever is an outage in slow motion.

Retries, poison pills and the dead letter queue. Failures come in two flavours. A transient failure fixes itself: the SMS provider timed out, the database was briefly overloaded. Retrying later, with growing waits (exponential backoff: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s...), usually works. A permanent failure never fixes itself: the JSON is malformed, a required field is missing, or your code has a bug for this exact input. A message that fails every single time is called a poison pill. With at-least-once delivery, a poison pill gets redelivered forever: it wastes consumers, fills logs, and in Kafka it blocks every message behind it in the same partition, because the consumer cannot commit past it.

The fix is a dead letter queue (DLQ): a separate queue or topic where a message goes after it has failed a maximum number of times. The main stream keeps flowing; the bad message waits in the DLQ with its error details for a human to inspect, fix and redrive (send back for processing). Each broker supports this differently:

  • RabbitMQ has dead letter exchanges built in. A message is dead-lettered when a consumer rejects it without requeue, when its TTL expires, when the queue exceeds its length limit, or (for quorum queues) when it passes the configured delivery limit.
  • AWS SQS has a redrive policy: after maxReceiveCount receives without deletion, the message moves to the DLQ.
  • Kafka has no broker-level DLQ for ordinary consumers. Your consumer (or a framework such as Spring Kafka, or Kafka Connect for connectors) publishes the failed record to a separate topic like orders.invoice.DLQ, usually after going through one or more delayed retry topics.

Queue direct API call se kab behtar hai. Queue tab use karo jab inme se kam se kam ek baat sach ho:

  • Kaam slow hai aur user ko uske liye wait karne ki zaroorat nahi: PDF banana, upload ki hui photos ya video process karna, emails bhejna.
  • Retries aur guaranteed delivery chahiye. Downstream service down hai toh message broker mein safe wait karta hai, fail hui HTTP call ke saath kho nahi jaata.
  • Dono sides ko independently scale hona chahiye. Orders spikes mein aate hain; invoice workers steady speed pe chal sakte hain, aur order service ko chhue bina workers badha sakte ho.
  • Ek event pe kai services react karti hain, aur producer ko pata bhi nahi hona chahiye ki woh kaun hain. Baad mein naya "loyalty points" service jodna matlab ek naya consumer jodna, order ka code badalna nahi.

Direct call tab use karo jab caller ko aage badhne ke liye jawab abhi chahiye: password check, "yeh seat abhi free hai?", page dikhane ke liye vehicle details laana. Yahan queue sirf delay badhayegi. Aur queues ki keemat yaad rakho: system eventually consistent ban jaata hai (invoice kuch second baad dikhta hai), debugging kai services mein phail jaati hai, consumers ko idempotent hona padta hai, aur tumhe ek aur infrastructure chalana padta hai.

Real production mein (dealership example). Socho ek dealership naye aaye vehicle ki photos upload kar rahi hai. Upload API files store karta hai aur VIN ke saath VehiclePhotosUploaded publish karta hai. Image-processing workers use consume karte hain, photos clean karte hain, aur VehiclePhotosReady publish karte hain; listing service use consume karke online listing update karti hai. Upload screen kabhi image processing ka wait nahi karti, aur agar ek saath bahut uploads aa jaayein toh bas thodi der queue lambi hoti hai, sabka timeout nahi hota.

Backpressure. Backpressure woh situation hai jab producer consumer ki processing speed se zyada tez bhej raha ho, aur system ke "wapas dhakelne" ke tareeke. Queue ke bina, direct calls slow service pe jama ho jaati hain: uske threads aur connections khatam, requests timeout, callers retry karte hain (aur bura haal), aur failure upar ki taraf phailta hai. Is phailne ko cascading failure kehte hain. Beech mein queue ho toh burst paani ki tanki ki tarah absorb ho jaata hai: queue lambi hoti hai, consumers apni safe speed pe kaam karte rehte hain, aur traffic kam hone pe backlog khaali ho jaata hai. Is backlog ke size ko consumer lag kehte hain (Kafka mein: newest offset minus group ka committed offset).

Lekin tanki infinite nahi hai. Isliye achhi teams:

  • consumer lag monitor karti hain aur lag badhta rahe toh alert lagati hain,
  • lag ke hisaab se consumers autoscale karti hain (Kafka mein sirf partition count tak),
  • limit lagati hain ki har consumer ek time pe kitne unacked messages pakde (RabbitMQ ise prefetch kehta hai; Kafka consumers utna hi pull karte hain jitna sambhaal sakein, toh pull-based consumption mein natural backpressure hota hai),
  • aur agar lag phir bhi badhe, toh producer ko wapas dhakelti hain: requests reject ya throttle karo (HTTP 429), ya broker ko publishers block karne do (RabbitMQ memory ya disk kam hone pe aisa karta hai).
Kafka retention khatam hone pe data delete kar deta hai, chahe kisi ne padha ho ya nahi. Agar koi consumer group retention period se zyada peeche reh gaya, toh woh unread messages gaye. Hamesha badhta lag slow motion mein chal raha outage hai.

Retries, poison pills aur dead letter queue. Failures do tarah ke hote hain. Transient failure apne aap theek ho jaata hai: SMS provider ka timeout, database thodi der overloaded. Baad mein badhte gaps ke saath retry karna (exponential backoff: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s...) usually kaam kar jaata hai. Permanent failure kabhi theek nahi hota: JSON hi toota hai, zaroori field missing hai, ya tumhare code mein isi input ke liye bug hai. Jo message har baar fail ho, use poison pill kehte hain. At-least-once delivery mein poison pill hamesha ke liye dobara deliver hota rehta hai: consumers waste karta hai, logs bhar deta hai, aur Kafka mein same partition mein uske peeche ke har message ko block kar deta hai, kyunki consumer uske aage commit hi nahi kar paata.

Iska ilaaj hai dead letter queue (DLQ): ek alag queue ya topic jahan message tab jaata hai jab woh maximum baar fail ho chuka ho. Main stream chalti rehti hai; kharab message apni error details ke saath DLQ mein wait karta hai, taaki koi insaan use dekhe, theek kare aur redrive kare (process ke liye wapas bheje). Har broker ise alag tarike se support karta hai:

  • RabbitMQ mein dead letter exchanges built-in hain. Message dead-letter hota hai jab consumer use bina requeue ke reject kare, jab uska TTL khatam ho, jab queue apni length limit cross kare, ya (quorum queues mein) jab woh configured delivery limit paar kar de.
  • AWS SQS mein redrive policy hai: maxReceiveCount baar receive hone ke baad bhi delete na ho, toh message DLQ mein chala jaata hai.
  • Kafka mein normal consumers ke liye broker-level DLQ nahi hai. Tumhara consumer (ya Spring Kafka jaisa framework, ya connectors ke liye Kafka Connect) fail hua record ek alag topic pe publish karta hai, jaise orders.invoice.DLQ, usually ek ya zyada delayed retry topics se guzarne ke baad.
Cap retries. Classify errors (retryable vs not). Send what is left to a DLQ with the error context. Alert on DLQ growth. A DLQ nobody watches is just silent data loss with extra steps.
Retries ki limit rakho. Errors ko classify karo (retry karne layak ya nahi). Jo bache, use error context ke saath DLQ mein bhejo. DLQ badhne pe alert lagao. Jis DLQ ko koi dekhta nahi, woh bas extra steps wala silent data loss hai.

Level 4 Senior nuances: Kafka vs RabbitMQ, where ordering breaks, and the outboxSenior nuances: Kafka vs RabbitMQ, ordering kahan tootti hai, aur outbox

Kafka vs RabbitMQ. They are both called "message queues", but their core designs are different, and that difference drives when you pick each one.

Kafka vs RabbitMQ. Dono ko "message queue" kehte hain, lekin inka core design alag hai, aur wahi difference decide karta hai ki kab kaunsa chuno.

KafkaRabbitMQ
Core modelCore modelDistributed append-only log split into partitionsPartitions mein bata hua distributed append-only logBroker with exchanges that route messages into queuesBroker jismein exchanges messages ko queues mein route karte hain
After a message is readMessage padhne ke baadKept until retention expires (time or size); can be replayedRetention khatam hone tak rehta hai (time ya size); replay ho sakta haiDeleted from the queue once acked (classic and quorum queues)Ack hote hi queue se delete (classic aur quorum queues)
Delivery styleDelivery styleConsumers pull and track their own offsetsConsumers pull karte hain aur apne offsets khud track karte hainBroker pushes to consumers, limited by prefetchBroker consumers ko push karta hai, prefetch se limited
OrderingOrderingGuaranteed within a partitionEk partition ke andar guaranteedPer queue, but competing consumers and requeues can reorder processingPer queue, lekin competing consumers aur requeue processing ka order bigaad sakte hain
RoutingRoutingSimple: topic plus key-to-partitionSimple: topic plus key se partitionFlexible: direct, topic (wildcard patterns), fanout, headers exchangesFlexible: direct, topic (wildcard patterns), fanout, headers exchanges
Scaling unitScaling unitPartitions (parallelism capped by partition count)Partitions (parallelism partition count tak hi)More consumers on a queue; more queuesQueue pe zyada consumers; zyada queues
Retries / DLQRetries / DLQBuilt by the application or framework (retry and DLQ topics)Application ya framework banata hai (retry aur DLQ topics)Built in: dead letter exchanges, per-message TTL, priority queuesBuilt-in: dead letter exchanges, per-message TTL, priority queues
Sweet spotSweet spotHigh-throughput event streams, many independent readers, replay, analytics, change data captureHigh-throughput event streams, kai independent readers, replay, analytics, change data captureTask/job queues, complex routing, per-message acknowledgement and retry controlTask/job queues, complex routing, per-message ack aur retry control

The lines are moving: RabbitMQ added Streams (a replayable, log-style structure) in version 3.9, and Kafka has been adding queue-style "share groups" (KIP-932). Kafka 4.0 also removed ZooKeeper, running only in its built-in KRaft mode. In an interview, choose by semantics (do I need replay? complex routing? per-message retry?), not by which one is "faster".

Where ordering breaks down. "Kafka keeps order" is only true within a partition, and even then you can break it yourself:

  • Events for the same entity use different keys, or no key, so they land in different partitions.
  • You increase the partition count: hash(key) % partitions changes, so new events for an old key may go to a different partition than its older events.
  • The producer retries with several requests in flight and idempotence switched off, so batch 2 can land before a retried batch 1. (The idempotent producer, default since Kafka 3.0, keeps order with up to 5 in-flight requests.)
  • The consumer processes one partition's messages in parallel threads to go faster.
  • A failed message goes to a retry topic while the next message for the same order is processed first.
  • In RabbitMQ, several competing consumers on one queue, or a requeued message, change the processing order.

Senior answer: pick the key to be the thing whose order matters (the order ID, the VIN), accept that global order across all messages needs a single partition (and so a single consumer), and make consumers tolerant anyway by carrying a version or sequence number and ignoring stale updates.

Hot partitions. A bad key choice puts too much traffic on one partition. If every event from one very large customer uses the same key, one partition and one consumer carry all of it while the others sit quiet. Choose keys with many distinct values, and only as coarse as your ordering needs.

The dual-write problem and the transactional outbox. Our order service does two things: save the order in Postgres and publish OrderPlaced to Kafka. These are two different systems, and there is no single transaction across them. If the service crashes after the DB commit but before the publish, the order exists but no one ever hears about it: no SMS, no invoice. If you publish first and the DB write fails, you announce an order that does not exist. The standard fix is the outbox pattern: in the same database transaction that inserts the order, also insert a row into an outbox table. A separate relay process (or a change-data-capture tool such as Debezium, which reads the database's change log) publishes outbox rows to the broker and marks them sent. The relay may publish a row twice if it crashes at the wrong moment, which is fine: it is at-least-once, and our consumers are idempotent.

Lines khisak rahi hain: RabbitMQ ne version 3.9 mein Streams (replay hone wala log-style structure) add kiya, aur Kafka queue-style "share groups" (KIP-932) add kar raha hai. Kafka 4.0 ne ZooKeeper bhi hata diya, ab sirf apne built-in KRaft mode mein chalta hai. Interview mein semantics se chuno (replay chahiye? complex routing? per-message retry?), is baat se nahi ki kaunsa "zyada fast" hai.

Ordering kahan tootti hai. "Kafka order rakhta hai" sirf ek partition ke andar sach hai, aur wahan bhi tum khud tod sakte ho:

  • Same entity ke events alag keys ya bina key ke bheje, toh woh alag partitions mein chale gaye.
  • Tumne partition count badha diya: hash(key) % partitions badal jaata hai, toh purani key ke naye events uske purane events se alag partition mein ja sakte hain.
  • Producer kai requests in-flight rakh ke retry karta hai aur idempotence off hai, toh batch 2 retry hue batch 1 se pehle pahunch sakta hai. (Idempotent producer, jo Kafka 3.0 se default hai, 5 in-flight requests tak order bachaye rakhta hai.)
  • Consumer jaldi karne ke liye ek partition ke messages parallel threads mein process karta hai.
  • Ek fail hua message retry topic mein jaata hai aur same order ka agla message pehle process ho jaata hai.
  • RabbitMQ mein ek queue pe kai competing consumers, ya ek requeue hua message, processing ka order badal dete hain.

Senior jawab: key usi cheez ko banao jiska order matter karta hai (order ID, VIN), maan lo ki saare messages ka global order chahiye toh ek hi partition (aur isliye ek hi consumer) chahiye, aur phir bhi consumers ko tolerant banao: ek version ya sequence number saath bhejo aur purane (stale) updates ignore karo.

Hot partitions. Galat key choice ek partition pe bahut zyada traffic daal deti hai. Agar ek bahut bade customer ke saare events same key use karein, toh ek partition aur ek consumer saara bojh uthate hain jabki baaki khaali baithe rehte hain. Aisi keys chuno jinke bahut saare alag values hon, aur utni hi moti (coarse) jitna tumhari ordering ko zaroorat hai.

Dual-write problem aur transactional outbox. Hamari order service do kaam karti hai: order Postgres mein save karna aur Kafka pe OrderPlaced publish karna. Yeh do alag systems hain, aur inke beech koi single transaction nahi hai. Agar service DB commit ke baad, publish se pehle crash ho jaaye, toh order exist karta hai lekin kisi ko pata hi nahi chalta: na SMS, na invoice. Agar pehle publish karo aur DB write fail ho jaaye, toh tumne ek aise order ka announcement kar diya jo hai hi nahi. Standard ilaaj hai outbox pattern: jis database transaction mein order insert ho raha hai, usi mein ek outbox table mein bhi row daal do. Ek alag relay process (ya Debezium jaisa change-data-capture tool, jo database ka change log padhta hai) outbox rows ko broker pe publish karta hai aur unhe sent mark karta hai. Galat moment pe crash ho toh relay ek row do baar publish kar sakta hai, jo theek hai: yeh at-least-once hai, aur hamare consumers idempotent hain.

-- Outbox pattern: the order and its event are saved atomically
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount, status) VALUES (123, 42, 349, 'PLACED');
INSERT INTO outbox (event_id, topic, msg_key, payload)
VALUES ('m-9f2', 'orders', '123', '{"type":"OrderPlaced","orderId":123,"amount":349}');
COMMIT;
-- A relay (or Debezium CDC) later reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka.
The senior checklist for any queue design: What is the delivery guarantee? Where do duplicates get absorbed (idempotent consumer)? What is the partition key, and what order do I actually need? What happens to a message that always fails (retry cap, DLQ, alert)? How do I publish reliably after a DB write (outbox)? What do I monitor (lag, DLQ depth)?
Kisi bhi queue design ke liye senior checklist: Delivery guarantee kya hai? Duplicates kahan absorb honge (idempotent consumer)? Partition key kya hai, aur mujhe asal mein kaunsa order chahiye? Jo message hamesha fail ho uska kya hoga (retry cap, DLQ, alert)? DB write ke baad reliably publish kaise karunga (outbox)? Kya monitor karunga (lag, DLQ depth)?

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Message broker
A server that stores messages from producers and hands them to consumers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS).Ek server jo producers ke messages store karta hai aur consumers ko deta hai (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS).
Producer / Consumer
The program that sends messages / the program that receives and processes them.Message bhejne wala program / message lekar process karne wala program.
Queue (point-to-point)
Each message goes to exactly one consumer and is deleted after ack.Har message sirf ek consumer ko jaata hai aur ack ke baad delete ho jaata hai.
Pub/sub, topic
Publish to a named topic; every subscriber gets its own copy.Ek naam wale topic pe publish karo; har subscriber ko apni copy milti hai.
Ack
The consumer's "done" signal; without it the broker redelivers.Consumer ka "ho gaya" signal; iske bina broker dobara deliver karta hai.
At-most / at-least / exactly-once
May lose, never duplicate / never lose, may duplicate / effect happens once, via dedup on both sides.Kho sakta hai, duplicate nahi / khoyega nahi, duplicate ho sakta hai / effect ek hi baar, dono sides pe dedup se.
Idempotent consumer
A consumer where processing the same message twice has the same effect as once, usually via a processed-ID check.Aisa consumer jismein same message do baar process karne ka effect ek baar jaisa ho, usually processed-ID check se.
Offset
A message's position number inside a Kafka partition; consumers commit offsets as bookmarks.Kafka partition ke andar message ka position number; consumers offsets ko bookmark ki tarah commit karte hain.
Partition, partition key
One of the independent logs a topic is split into; the key's hash picks the partition, so the same key keeps its order.Topic ke independent logs mein se ek; key ka hash partition chunta hai, toh same key ka order bana rehta hai.
Consumer group, rebalance
Consumers sharing a group.id; each partition has one owner in the group. A rebalance reassigns partitions when members change.Ek group.id share karne wale consumers; group mein har partition ka ek owner. Members badlein toh rebalance partitions dobara baant-ta hai.
Consumer lag
How far behind a consumer group is: latest offset minus committed offset.Consumer group kitna peeche hai: latest offset minus committed offset.
Backpressure
Producer faster than consumer, and the mechanisms that buffer or push back.Producer consumer se tez, aur woh tareeke jo buffer karte hain ya wapas dhakelte hain.
Dead letter queue (DLQ)
Where messages go after failing the maximum number of retries, for inspection and redrive.Jahan messages maximum retries fail hone ke baad jaate hain, dekhne aur redrive karne ke liye.
Poison pill
A message that fails every time it is processed, no matter how often it is retried.Aisa message jo har baar fail hota hai, chahe jitni baar retry karo.
Retention
How long Kafka keeps messages (by time or size), whether or not they were read.Kafka messages kitni der rakhta hai (time ya size se), chahe padhe gaye hon ya nahi.
Transactional outbox
Write the event into an outbox table in the same DB transaction as the data; a relay publishes it later.Event ko data ke saath same DB transaction mein outbox table mein likho; relay baad mein publish karta hai.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What is the difference between a message queue and pub/sub?Message queue aur pub/sub mein kya difference hai?
What they're really testing: whether you know the delivery semantics (one consumer gets it and it is deleted, versus every subscriber gets a copy) and that Kafka blurs the line by retaining messages.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum delivery semantics jaante ho (ek consumer ko milta hai aur delete ho jaata hai, vs har subscriber ko copy milti hai) aur kya tumhe pata hai ki Kafka messages retain karke yeh line dhundhli kar deta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A message queue is point-to-point. A producer puts a message in, exactly one of the connected consumers receives it, and once that consumer acks, the broker deletes it. Adding consumers splits the work, so it's ideal for jobs like "send this email" or "generate invoice 123". Pub/sub is broadcast: the producer publishes to a topic and every subscriber gets its own copy. That fits events: when an order is placed, the restaurant, delivery, SMS and invoice services all need to know. Kafka blurs the two. It keeps messages in a retained log and each consumer group tracks its own offset, so inside a group it behaves like a queue, across groups like pub/sub, and a new group can even replay history. The trade-off is that a retained log costs storage and offset management, while a classic queue forgets a message once it's acked.

Message queue point-to-point hota hai. Producer message daalta hai, connected consumers mein se sirf ek ko milta hai, aur woh ack kar de toh broker use delete kar deta hai. Consumers badhane se kaam bant-ta hai, isliye yeh "yeh email bhejo" ya "invoice 123 banao" jaise jobs ke liye perfect hai. Pub/sub broadcast hai: producer topic pe publish karta hai aur har subscriber ko apni copy milti hai. Yeh events ke liye fit hai: order place hua toh restaurant, delivery, SMS aur invoice sab services ko pata hona chahiye. Kafka dono ko mila deta hai. Woh messages ko ek retained log mein rakhta hai aur har consumer group apna offset track karta hai, toh group ke andar queue jaisa, groups ke beech pub/sub jaisa, aur naya group history replay bhi kar sakta hai. Trade-off: retained log mein storage aur offset management ka kharcha hai, jabki classic queue ack ke baad message bhool jaati hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

RabbitMQ builds pub/sub out of queues: a fanout (or topic) exchange copies each message into one queue per subscriber, so each subscriber service has its own queue, and within that queue its instances compete. AWS does the same with SNS fanning out to several SQS queues. Also worth separating durable from non-durable pub/sub: Redis Pub/Sub only delivers to subscribers connected at that moment, so an offline subscriber simply misses the message, while Kafka or Redis Streams keep it. A good rule of thumb is that commands ("do this") go on queues and events ("this happened") go on topics.

RabbitMQ pub/sub ko queues se hi banata hai: fanout (ya topic) exchange har message ko har subscriber ki ek alag queue mein copy kar deta hai, toh har subscriber service ki apni queue hoti hai, aur us queue ke andar uske instances compete karte hain. AWS bhi yahi karta hai, SNS kai SQS queues mein fan-out karta hai. Durable aur non-durable pub/sub ko alag samajhna bhi zaroori hai: Redis Pub/Sub sirf un subscribers ko deliver karta hai jo us waqt connected hain, toh offline subscriber message miss kar deta hai, jabki Kafka ya Redis Streams use rakh lete hain. Kaam ka rule: commands ("yeh karo") queues pe, events ("yeh ho gaya") topics pe.

Common mistake: Saying "pub/sub is just a queue with more consumers". Adding consumers to a queue splits the messages; adding subscribers to a topic duplicates them.
Galti mat karna: Yeh bolna ki "pub/sub bas zyada consumers wali queue hai". Queue mein consumers badhao toh messages bant-te hain; topic mein subscribers badhao toh messages copy hote hain.
02 Explain at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once delivery.At-most-once, at-least-once aur exactly-once delivery samjhao.
What they're really testing: that each guarantee trades loss against duplication, and that exactly-once is not magic but needs de-duplication on both the producer and consumer side.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki har guarantee "message khona" vs "duplicate hona" ka trade-off hai, aur exactly-once koi jaadu nahi, uske liye producer aur consumer dono side pe de-duplication chahiye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

It depends on where the ack happens relative to the work. At-most-once is fire-and-forget, or acking before processing: if the consumer crashes mid-way, the message is lost, but it's never duplicated. That's fine for metrics or typing indicators. At-least-once means I ack only after processing and the broker redelivers anything unacked, so nothing is lost, but a crash after the work and before the ack gives a duplicate. That's the default for orders and payments, paired with an idempotent consumer. Exactly-once means the effect happens once. Over an unreliable network you can't guarantee delivery exactly once, so in practice it's at-least-once plus dedup: the producer side, like Kafka's idempotent producer with sequence numbers, and the consumer side, like a processed-message-ID table. The trade-off is that each step up costs latency and complexity.

Yeh is baat pe depend karta hai ki ack kaam ke pehle hota hai ya baad mein. At-most-once matlab bhejo aur bhool jao, ya process karne se pehle ack: consumer beech mein crash ho toh message kho jaata hai, lekin duplicate kabhi nahi hota. Metrics ya typing indicators ke liye theek hai. At-least-once matlab main processing ke baad hi ack karta hoon aur broker har unacked message dobara deta hai, toh kuch nahi khota, lekin kaam ke baad aur ack se pehle crash hua toh duplicate aata hai. Orders aur payments ke liye yahi default hai, idempotent consumer ke saath. Exactly-once matlab effect sirf ek baar ho. Unreliable network pe exactly ek baar delivery guarantee nahi ho sakti, toh practically yeh at-least-once plus dedup hai: producer side pe, jaise Kafka ka idempotent producer sequence numbers ke saath, aur consumer side pe, jaise processed-message-ID table. Trade-off: har level upar jaane mein latency aur complexity badhti hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Kafka's exactly-once semantics combine the idempotent producer with transactions that atomically write output records and commit the input offsets; downstream consumers read with isolation.level=read_committed so they never see aborted writes. That only covers Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines. The moment the consumer sends an SMS or charges a card, I need an idempotency key with that provider. Also, Kafka's auto-commit (enable.auto.commit is true by default, every 5 seconds) commits on a timer, so depending on timing you can get loss or duplicates; for critical flows I disable it and commit manually after processing.

Kafka ki exactly-once semantics idempotent producer ko transactions ke saath jodti hai, jo output records likhna aur input offsets commit karna atomically karti hain; downstream consumers isolation.level=read_committed ke saath padhte hain taaki aborted writes na dikhein. Yeh sirf Kafka-se-Kafka pipelines ko cover karta hai. Jaise hi consumer SMS bhejta hai ya card charge karta hai, mujhe us provider ke saath idempotency key chahiye. Aur Kafka ka auto-commit (enable.auto.commit default true, har 5 second) timer pe commit karta hai, toh timing ke hisaab se loss ya duplicate dono ho sakte hain; critical flows mein main ise band karke processing ke baad manually commit karta hoon.

Common mistake: Saying "Kafka supports exactly-once, so my consumer doesn't need to be idempotent". Kafka's guarantee stops at Kafka's boundary; external side effects still need dedup.
Galti mat karna: Yeh bolna ki "Kafka exactly-once support karta hai, toh mera consumer idempotent hone ki zaroorat nahi". Kafka ki guarantee Kafka ki boundary pe khatam; bahar ke side effects ko phir bhi dedup chahiye.
03 What is a dead letter queue and when does a message end up there?Dead letter queue kya hai aur message wahan kab pahunchta hai?
What they're really testing: that you know retries must be capped, and that a DLQ protects the main queue from poison-pill messages that would otherwise be retried forever.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum jaante ho retries ki limit honi chahiye, aur DLQ main queue ko un poison-pill messages se bachata hai jo warna hamesha retry hote rehte.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A dead letter queue is a separate queue or topic where a message goes after it has failed processing the maximum number of times. The consumer retries with backoff, say five attempts, and if it still fails, instead of retrying forever, it moves the message to the DLQ with the error details and moves on. Messages usually land there because they're poison pills: malformed data, a missing field, or a bug for that input. In some brokers they also land there when a TTL expires or the queue overflows. It exists because one bad message retried forever wastes consumers and, in an ordered stream, blocks everything behind it. For example, an invoice consumer gets an order with a null amount; after five failures it goes to orders.invoice.DLQ, an alert fires, we fix the bug and redrive it. The trade-off is that DLQ messages are delayed and out of order, and someone has to own the DLQ.

Dead letter queue ek alag queue ya topic hai jahan message tab jaata hai jab woh maximum baar process hone mein fail ho chuka ho. Consumer backoff ke saath retry karta hai, maan lo paanch attempts, aur phir bhi fail ho toh hamesha retry karne ki jagah message ko error details ke saath DLQ mein daal ke aage badh jaata hai. Messages usually wahan isliye pahunchte hain kyunki woh poison pills hote hain: kharab data, missing field, ya us input ke liye bug. Kuch brokers mein TTL khatam hone pe ya queue overflow hone pe bhi wahan jaate hain. Yeh isliye hai kyunki ek kharab message hamesha retry hota rahe toh consumers waste hote hain aur ordered stream mein uske peeche sab block ho jaata hai. Example: invoice consumer ko null amount wala order milta hai; paanch failures ke baad woh orders.invoice.DLQ mein jaata hai, alert aata hai, hum bug fix karke redrive karte hain. Trade-off: DLQ messages late aur out of order hote hain, aur kisi ko DLQ ka owner banna padta hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Implementation differs. RabbitMQ has dead letter exchanges: a message is dead-lettered when it's rejected with requeue set to false, its TTL expires, the queue hits its length limit, or a quorum queue's delivery limit is exceeded. SQS uses a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount. Kafka has no broker-level DLQ for plain consumers, so the application or framework publishes to a DLQ topic, with headers recording the original topic, partition, offset, exception and attempt count. I'd also classify errors: validation errors go straight to the DLQ because retrying can't help, while timeouts get retried. And I'd build redrive tooling so replay is a button, not a script someone writes at 2 am.

Implementation alag-alag hai. RabbitMQ mein dead letter exchanges hain: message dead-letter hota hai jab use requeue false ke saath reject kiya jaaye, TTL khatam ho, queue length limit hit kare, ya quorum queue ki delivery limit cross ho. SQS maxReceiveCount ke saath redrive policy use karta hai. Kafka mein normal consumers ke liye broker-level DLQ nahi hai, toh application ya framework DLQ topic pe publish karta hai, headers mein original topic, partition, offset, exception aur attempt count likh ke. Main errors ko classify bhi karunga: validation errors seedha DLQ mein, kyunki retry se kuch nahi hoga, aur timeouts retry honge. Aur redrive tooling banaunga taaki replay ek button ho, raat 2 baje koi script likhna na pade.

Common mistake: Treating the DLQ as a bin nobody watches. Without an alert on DLQ growth, it is silent data loss.
Galti mat karna: DLQ ko aisa kooda-daan samajhna jise koi nahi dekhta. DLQ growth pe alert nahi hai toh yeh silent data loss hai.
04 What is backpressure and how do queues help handle it?Backpressure kya hai aur queues ise handle karne mein kaise madad karti hain?
What they're really testing: that you understand a consumer slower than its producer, and that a queue buffers the difference, but only up to a limit you must monitor.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum samajhte ho jab consumer producer se slow ho tab kya hota hai, aur queue us farak ko buffer karti hai, lekin sirf ek limit tak jise monitor karna padta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Backpressure is what happens when a producer generates work faster than a consumer can process it, and the mechanisms the system uses to push back. Without a queue, direct calls pile up on the slow service: threads and connections run out, requests time out, callers retry, and the failure cascades upstream. A queue acts as a shock absorber. On a festival-night spike, orders pile up in the queue, the invoice workers keep processing at their safe pace, and the backlog drains when traffic drops, while the order API stays fast. But the buffer isn't infinite, so I monitor consumer lag, autoscale consumers on it, cap in-flight messages per consumer, and if lag keeps growing I push back on the producer by throttling or returning 429. The trade-off is added latency for the queued work.

Backpressure tab hota hai jab producer consumer ki processing speed se zyada tezi se kaam bana raha ho, aur woh tareeke jinse system wapas dhakelta hai. Queue ke bina, direct calls slow service pe jama ho jaati hain: threads aur connections khatam, requests timeout, callers retry karte hain, aur failure upar tak cascade ho jaata hai. Queue shock absorber ki tarah kaam karti hai. Festival ki raat ke spike mein orders queue mein jama hote hain, invoice workers apni safe speed pe process karte rehte hain, aur traffic girne pe backlog khaali ho jaata hai, jabki order API fast bani rehti hai. Lekin buffer infinite nahi hai, toh main consumer lag monitor karta hoon, uske hisaab se consumers autoscale karta hoon, har consumer ke in-flight messages ki limit rakhta hoon, aur agar lag badhta hi rahe toh producer ko throttle karke ya 429 dekar wapas dhakelta hoon. Trade-off: queue wale kaam mein latency badh jaati hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Pull versus push matters. Kafka consumers poll, so they only fetch what they can handle (tuned with max.poll.records), which is natural backpressure. RabbitMQ pushes, so I set prefetch with basic.qos to cap unacked messages per consumer; RabbitMQ also blocks publishers when it hits memory or disk alarms. The danger in Kafka is retention: if a group falls further behind than the retention period, unread messages are deleted. Beyond scaling, options are load shedding (dropping low-priority work) and separate topics for high and low priority so a flood of analytics events can't delay payments. Tools like KEDA can autoscale Kubernetes consumers on lag, capped by partition count.

Pull vs push ka farak padta hai. Kafka consumers poll karte hain, toh utna hi fetch karte hain jitna sambhaal sakein (max.poll.records se tune hota hai), yeh natural backpressure hai. RabbitMQ push karta hai, toh main basic.qos se prefetch set karta hoon taaki har consumer ke unacked messages limited rahein; RabbitMQ memory ya disk alarm hone pe publishers ko block bhi kar deta hai. Kafka mein khatra retention ka hai: agar group retention period se zyada peeche reh gaya, toh unread messages delete ho jaate hain. Scaling ke alawa options hain load shedding (kam priority ka kaam chhod dena) aur high aur low priority ke alag topics, taaki analytics events ki baadh payments ko late na kare. KEDA jaise tools Kubernetes consumers ko lag ke hisaab se autoscale kar sakte hain, partition count tak.

Common mistake: Saying "the queue solves it because it can hold unlimited messages". Lag that grows without bound is an outage in slow motion.
Galti mat karna: Yeh bolna ki "queue solve kar degi kyunki usmein unlimited messages aa sakte hain". Bina ruke badhta lag slow motion mein outage hai.
05 How do you handle duplicate messages in a consumer?Consumer mein duplicate messages kaise handle karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you accept duplicates as normal under at-least-once delivery and make the consumer idempotent using a unique message ID, a processed check, and ack-and-skip.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum at-least-once delivery mein duplicates ko normal maante ho aur consumer ko unique message ID, processed check, aur ack-and-skip se idempotent banate ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

With at-least-once delivery, duplicates will happen: a consumer crashes after processing but before acking, a rebalance hands a partition to someone else, or a producer retries. So I make the consumer idempotent. Every message carries a unique ID, either an event ID or a business key like order ID plus event type. Before doing the work I check a processed store; if the ID is there, I ack and skip. The key detail is to record the ID and do the work in the same database transaction, with a unique constraint on the ID, so the check-and-mark is atomic. For an invoice consumer that's INSERT INTO processed_messages ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: zero rows inserted means duplicate, so skip; otherwise create the invoice, commit, then ack. The trade-off is an extra write per message and storage for the IDs.

At-least-once delivery mein duplicates aayenge hi: consumer process karke ack se pehle crash ho jaata hai, rebalance partition kisi aur ko de deta hai, ya producer retry karta hai. Toh main consumer ko idempotent banata hoon. Har message ke saath ek unique ID hoti hai, ya toh event ID ya business key jaise order ID plus event type. Kaam karne se pehle main processed store check karta hoon; ID wahan hai toh ack karke skip. Asli baat: ID record karna aur kaam karna same database transaction mein ho, ID pe unique constraint ke saath, taaki check-and-mark atomic ho. Invoice consumer ke liye yeh hai INSERT INTO processed_messages ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: zero rows insert hui matlab duplicate, skip; warna invoice banao, commit karo, phir ack. Trade-off: har message pe ek extra write aur IDs ka storage.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

If the work isn't in my database, I can use Redis SET key NX EX for fast dedup, but marking "done" before the work risks losing the message if I crash in between, so I mark "processing" with a short TTL and flip to "done" afterwards. The TTL must outlive the broker's redelivery window. Even better is making operations naturally idempotent: an upsert, or "set status to SHIPPED", instead of "increment". For out-of-order duplicates I carry a version number and ignore anything older than what's stored. For calls to a third party like an SMS or payment provider, I pass the message ID as their idempotency key (Topic 05).

Agar kaam mere database mein nahi hai, toh fast dedup ke liye Redis SET key NX EX use kar sakta hoon, lekin kaam se pehle "done" mark karna risky hai, beech mein crash hua toh message kho jaayega, isliye main short TTL ke saath "processing" mark karta hoon aur baad mein "done" karta hoon. TTL broker ki redelivery window se lamba hona chahiye. Aur bhi achha hai operations ko naturally idempotent banana: upsert, ya "status ko SHIPPED set karo", "increment" ki jagah. Out-of-order duplicates ke liye version number saath rakhta hoon aur stored se purana kuch bhi ignore karta hoon. SMS ya payment provider jaisi third party ko call karte waqt message ID ko unki idempotency key ki tarah bhejta hoon (Topic 05).

Common mistake: Doing a separate SELECT to check "already processed?" and then an INSERT. Two duplicate deliveries on two consumers can both pass the check; let a unique constraint decide.
Galti mat karna: "Pehle process hua?" check karne ke liye alag SELECT aur phir INSERT karna. Do consumers pe do duplicate deliveries dono check paar kar sakti hain; faisla unique constraint ko karne do.
06 What is a consumer group in Kafka and how does it enable scaling?Kafka mein consumer group kya hai aur yeh scaling kaise enable karta hai?
What they're really testing: that partitions are the unit of parallelism, each partition goes to exactly one consumer in a group, and so maximum parallelism equals the partition count.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki partitions hi parallelism ki unit hain, group mein har partition sirf ek consumer ko jaata hai, aur isliye maximum parallelism = partition count.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A consumer group is a set of consumers sharing a group.id that together read a topic. Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in the group, while one consumer can own several partitions. That's how it scales. With three partitions and one consumer, it reads all three. Add a second and Kafka rebalances: one gets two partitions, the other gets one. Add a third and it's one each. A fourth sits idle, because a partition can't be split between members of the same group. So maximum parallelism equals the number of partitions, and I size partitions for future peak. Different groups are independent: the invoice group and the analytics group each get every message with their own offsets. The trade-offs are that rebalances briefly pause consumption, and adding partitions later changes which partition a key maps to.

Consumer group aise consumers ka set hai jo ek group.id share karte hain aur milke ek topic padhte hain. Kafka har partition ko group ke sirf ek consumer ko assign karta hai, jabki ek consumer kai partitions ka owner ho sakta hai. Scaling aise hoti hai. Teen partitions aur ek consumer ho toh woh teeno padhta hai. Doosra jodo toh Kafka rebalance karta hai: ek ko do partitions, doosre ko ek. Teesra jodo toh sabko ek-ek. Chautha idle baithta hai, kyunki ek partition ko same group ke do members mein baanta nahi ja sakta. Toh maximum parallelism = partitions ki ginti, aur main partitions future peak ke hisaab se rakhta hoon. Alag groups independent hain: invoice group aur analytics group dono ko har message apne-apne offsets ke saath milta hai. Trade-offs: rebalance thodi der consumption rok deta hai, aur baad mein partitions badhane se key ka partition mapping badal jaata hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

A rebalance is triggered when a consumer joins or leaves, when heartbeats stop for longer than session.timeout.ms, or when a consumer takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms between polls, which is a classic cause of rebalance storms when processing is slow. The older eager protocol stops everyone; the cooperative-sticky assignor moves only the partitions that need to move, and static membership (group.instance.id) avoids a rebalance on a quick restart. Offsets are committed per group per partition in __consumer_offsets. If I need more parallelism than partitions, I can process within a partition concurrently but keyed by message key, which keeps per-key order.

Rebalance tab trigger hota hai jab consumer judta ya chhodta hai, jab session.timeout.ms se zyada der heartbeats band rahein, ya jab consumer do polls ke beech max.poll.interval.ms se zyada time le, jo slow processing mein rebalance storms ka classic kaaran hai. Purana eager protocol sabko rok deta hai; cooperative-sticky assignor sirf un partitions ko hilata hai jinhe hilna zaroori hai, aur static membership (group.instance.id) jaldi restart pe rebalance se bachata hai. Offsets har group ke har partition ke liye __consumer_offsets mein commit hote hain. Agar partitions se zyada parallelism chahiye, toh ek partition ke andar concurrently process kar sakta hoon lekin message key ke hisaab se, jisse per-key order bana rehta hai.

Common mistake: "Just add more consumers to go faster." Beyond the partition count, extra consumers in the group sit idle.
Galti mat karna: "Bas aur consumers jodo, fast ho jaayega." Partition count ke baad group ke extra consumers idle baithe rehte hain.
07 When would you use a message queue instead of a direct API call?Direct API call ki jagah message queue kab use karoge?
What they're really testing: your judgement. The good reasons are slow operations, retry logic, independent scaling and guaranteed delivery, and you should also know when a direct call is still the right tool.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: tumhari judgement. Sahi kaaran hain slow operations, retry logic, independent scaling aur guaranteed delivery, aur yeh bhi pata hona chahiye ki direct call kab abhi bhi sahi tool hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I use a direct call when the caller needs the answer right now to continue, like checking whether a payment was authorized, validating a login, or fetching vehicle details to render a page. I use a queue when the work doesn't have to finish before I respond. That's slow operations like PDF invoices, image processing or emails; work that needs retries and guaranteed delivery even if the downstream service is down; producers and consumers that should scale independently, like spiky order traffic against steady workers; and fan-out, where several services react to one event without the producer knowing about them. For example, placing an order: I save it and respond, and the restaurant notification, SMS and invoice flow through an event. The trade-off is eventual consistency, harder debugging across async hops, the need for idempotent consumers and DLQ monitoring, and one more system to run.
