A distributed lock gives mutual exclusion across processes on different machines, for example so only one of ten instances runs the nightly billing job. The common version is Redis SET lock:billing token NX PX 30000: set only if absent, with an expiry, and a random token so I only release my own lock via a Lua check-and-delete. The failure modes are the interesting part. If the holder crashes, the TTL frees the lock. But if the holder pauses longer than the TTL, say a long GC pause, the lock expires, a second worker takes it, and the first wakes up and keeps writing, so there are two holders. Redis failover can lose a lock that wasn't replicated yet, and Redlock across five nodes still depends on bounded clock drift. The senior fix is fencing tokens: every grant carries an increasing number, and storage rejects writes with an older token. So for efficiency a Redis lock is fine; for correctness, add fencing.

Distributed lock alag machines ke processes ke beech mutual exclusion deta hai, jaise dus instances mein se sirf ek nightly billing job chalaye. Common version hai Redis SET lock:billing token NX PX 30000: sirf tab set karo jab na ho, expiry ke saath, aur ek random token taaki main Lua check-and-delete se sirf apna lock release karun. Failure modes hi interesting hisse hain. Holder crash ho toh TTL lock free kar deta hai. Lekin agar holder TTL se zyada ruk jaaye, jaise lamba GC pause, toh lock expire, doosra worker le leta hai, aur pehla jaag ke likhta rehta hai, toh do holders. Redis failover woh lock kho sakta hai jo abhi replicate nahi hua tha, aur paanch nodes pe Redlock phir bhi limited clock drift pe tika hai. Senior ilaaj fencing tokens hai: har grant ke saath badhta number, aur storage purane token wale writes reject karta hai. Toh efficiency ke liye Redis lock theek hai; correctness ke liye fencing jodo.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

This is the well-known debate between Martin Kleppmann and Redis's author about Redlock. My takeaway: if a double run only wastes work, like sending a duplicate report, a Redis lock is fine. If it corrupts data, use a consensus-backed lock (ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential nodes, or an etcd lease, whose revision works as a fencing token), or push the rule into the database with a unique constraint or a conditional update such as UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND fence < ?. Lock renewal "watchdogs" extend the TTL while work continues, but they can't save you from a pause that happens right before a write.

Yeh Martin Kleppmann aur Redis ke author ke beech Redlock pe famous debate hai. Meri seekh: agar double run sirf kaam waste kare, jaise duplicate report bhejna, toh Redis lock theek hai. Agar data kharab kare, toh consensus-backed lock use karo (ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential nodes, ya etcd lease, jiska revision fencing token ki tarah kaam karta hai), ya rule database mein daal do, unique constraint ya UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND fence < ? jaise conditional update se. Lock renewal "watchdogs" kaam chalte waqt TTL badhate hain, lekin write se theek pehle hue pause se nahi bacha sakte.

Common mistake: Releasing with a plain DEL. If your lock already expired and someone else took it, you delete their lock.
Galti mat karna: Plain DEL se release karna. Agar tumhara lock expire ho chuka aur kisi aur ne le liya, toh tum uska lock delete kar doge.
06 What is the Two Generals problem and why does it matter?Two Generals problem kya hai aur yeh kyun matter karta hai?
What they're really testing: that two parties can't reliably agree over an unreliable channel, and that this is why guaranteed exactly-once delivery is impossible.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki unreliable channel pe do parties reliably agree nahi kar sakti, aur isiliye guaranteed exactly-once delivery impossible hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Two armies on opposite hills must attack at the same time to win, and their only link is a messenger through a valley where he can be captured. General A sends "attack at dawn", but can't act until he knows B received it. B replies, but can't be sure the reply arrived, so it needs an acknowledgement of the acknowledgement, forever. No finite number of messages makes both sides certain. It matters because every network call has this shape. If my call to a payment provider times out, I can't tell whether the charge happened. So you can't guarantee agreement or exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network. The engineering answer is to accept uncertainty: retry with idempotency keys so duplicates are harmless, set timeouts, query status, and run reconciliation. That's exactly why brokers offer at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers.

Aamne-saamne pahadiyon pe do armies ko jeetne ke liye ek saath attack karna hai, aur unka ek hi link hai ghaati se jaata messenger jo pakda ja sakta hai. General A bhejta hai "subah attack", lekin tab tak kuch nahi kar sakta jab tak use pata na ho ki B ko mila. B reply karta hai, lekin pakka nahi ki reply pahuncha, toh use acknowledgement ka acknowledgement chahiye, hamesha ke liye. Koi bhi finite messages dono sides ko pakka nahi kar sakte. Yeh isliye matter karta hai kyunki har network call ka yahi shape hai. Agar payment provider ko meri call timeout ho jaaye, toh main nahi bata sakta ki charge hua ya nahi. Toh unreliable network pe agreement ya exactly-once delivery guarantee nahi ho sakti. Engineering jawab hai uncertainty ko maan lena: idempotency keys ke saath retry taaki duplicates harmless hon, timeouts lagao, status poochho, aur reconciliation chalao. Isiliye brokers at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers dete hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Don't confuse it with the Byzantine Generals problem, where nodes can lie or act maliciously, which matters for blockchains and aerospace. Two Generals is about an unreliable channel with honest parties. TCP's three-way handshake doesn't solve it; it gives practical confidence, not certainty. A related result, FLP, shows deterministic consensus can't be guaranteed to terminate in a fully asynchronous system if a node may crash, which is why Raft and Paxos use timeouts. Practically, I design for the "unknown" outcome: a status endpoint to ask "did payment X succeed?", and a daily reconciliation against the provider's report.

Ise Byzantine Generals problem se confuse mat karna, jahan nodes jhooth bol sakte hain ya malicious ho sakte hain, jo blockchains aur aerospace mein matter karta hai. Two Generals imaandaar parties aur unreliable channel ke baare mein hai. TCP ka three-way handshake ise solve nahi karta; practical confidence deta hai, certainty nahi. Ek related result, FLP, dikhata hai ki fully asynchronous system mein agar koi node crash ho sakta hai toh deterministic consensus ka khatam hona guarantee nahi ho sakta, isiliye Raft aur Paxos timeouts use karte hain. Practically main "pata nahi" wale result ke liye design karta hoon: "payment X hua?" poochhne ke liye status endpoint, aur provider ki report ke saath roz ka reconciliation.

Common mistake: Saying "just add an acknowledgement". The acknowledgement can be lost too, which is the whole point.
Galti mat karna: "Bas ek acknowledgement jod do" bolna. Acknowledgement bhi kho sakta hai, poori baat yahi hai.
07 What is a heartbeat in distributed systems?Distributed systems mein heartbeat kya hota hai?
What they're really testing: that a heartbeat is a periodic "alive" message used for failure detection; after N missed seconds the node is treated as dead and traffic is rerouted.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki heartbeat failure detection ke liye ek periodic "zinda hoon" message hai; N second miss hone pe node ko dead maana jaata hai aur traffic reroute hota hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A heartbeat is a small periodic "I'm alive" message that a node sends to a monitor, a leader or its peers, say every second. If the receiver misses heartbeats for longer than a timeout, for example three in a row, it marks the node as suspected dead and acts: the load balancer stops routing to it, the cluster elects a new leader, or partitions and work get reassigned. It exists because in a distributed system silence is the only signal of failure; a crashed machine can't announce that it crashed. For example, Kafka consumers heartbeat to the group coordinator, and if they miss the session timeout, a rebalance hands their partitions to others. The trade-off is tuning the timeout. Too short, and a GC pause or network blip causes false alarms and needless failovers. Too long, and traffic keeps flowing to a dead node.

Heartbeat ek chhota periodic "main zinda hoon" message hai jo node kisi monitor, leader ya apne peers ko bhejta hai, maan lo har second. Agar receiver ko timeout se zyada der heartbeats na milein, jaise lagatar teen, toh woh node ko suspected dead mark karke action leta hai: load balancer uspe routing band karta hai, cluster naya leader chunta hai, ya partitions aur kaam dobara assign hote hain. Yeh isliye hai kyunki distributed system mein khamoshi hi failure ka ek signal hai; crash hui machine announce nahi kar sakti ki woh crash hui. Jaise Kafka consumers group coordinator ko heartbeat bhejte hain, aur session timeout miss karein toh rebalance unke partitions doosron ko de deta hai. Trade-off timeout tune karna hai. Bahut chhota, toh GC pause ya network ki chhoti gadbad false alarms aur bekaar failovers karwati hai. Bahut lamba, toh mare hue node pe traffic jaata rehta hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

A missed heartbeat means "suspected", never "proven", because dead, slow and partitioned look the same, so it must be paired with quorum or fencing before anyone takes over writes. There's push style, where nodes send heartbeats, and pull style, where a load balancer or Kubernetes probes /health (liveness and readiness). Big clusters spread heartbeat information by gossip, as Cassandra does, and use a phi accrual detector that outputs a suspicion level from arrival history instead of a fixed cutoff. A heartbeat should reflect real health: a process whose heartbeat thread is fine but whose worker is stuck is alive but useless.

Miss hua heartbeat matlab "suspected", kabhi "proven" nahi, kyunki mara hua, slow aur kata hua ek jaise dikhte hain, toh kisi ke writes sambhaalne se pehle ise quorum ya fencing ke saath jodna zaroori hai. Push style hai, jahan nodes heartbeats bhejte hain, aur pull style, jahan load balancer ya Kubernetes /health probe karta hai (liveness aur readiness). Bade clusters heartbeat ki jaankari gossip se failate hain, jaise Cassandra, aur phi accrual detector use karte hain jo fixed cutoff ki jagah aane ki history se suspicion level deta hai. Heartbeat asli health dikhaye: jis process ka heartbeat thread theek hai lekin worker atka hua hai, woh zinda hai par bekaar.

Common mistake: Treating a missed heartbeat as proof of death and promoting a replacement while the old node keeps writing. That is how split-brain starts.
Galti mat karna: Miss hue heartbeat ko maut ka saboot maan ke replacement promote kar dena jabki purana node likhta reh jaaye. Split-brain aise hi shuru hota hai.
08 What is the difference between a service mesh and a load balancer?Service mesh aur load balancer mein kya difference hai?
What they're really testing: that a load balancer distributes traffic in front of services, a mesh handles service-to-service traffic through sidecars, and the two complement each other.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki load balancer services ke aage traffic baant-ta hai, mesh sidecars ke through service-to-service traffic sambhaalta hai, aur dono ek doosre ke complement hain.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A load balancer sits in front of a group of instances and spreads incoming requests across the healthy ones, like the one in front of our API servers. It mainly handles traffic entering the system, called north-south. A service mesh handles traffic between services inside the system, called east-west. Each service instance runs next to a sidecar proxy, usually Envoy. The app just calls its local proxy, and the proxies handle per-request load balancing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, mutual TLS, and uniform metrics and traces. A control plane like Istio or Linkerd pushes configuration to every sidecar. They complement each other: an LB or ingress gateway at the edge, the mesh inside. For example, the order service calls payment and inventory with retries and mTLS without anyone writing that code in each service. The trade-off is an extra hop on every call, CPU and memory per sidecar, and a lot of operational complexity.

Load balancer instances ke group ke aage baithta hai aur aane wali requests ko healthy instances mein baant-ta hai, jaise hamare API servers ke aage wala. Yeh zyaadatar system mein aane wala traffic sambhaalta hai, jise north-south kehte hain. Service mesh system ke andar services ke beech ka traffic sambhaalta hai, jise east-west kehte hain. Har service instance ke bagal mein ek sidecar proxy chalta hai, usually Envoy. App bas apne local proxy ko call karta hai, aur proxies per-request load balancing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, mutual TLS, aur ek jaise metrics aur traces sambhaalte hain. Istio ya Linkerd jaisa control plane har sidecar ko configuration bhejta hai. Dono ek doosre ke complement hain: edge pe LB ya ingress gateway, andar mesh. Jaise order service payment aur inventory ko retries aur mTLS ke saath call karti hai bina kisi ke har service mein woh code likhe. Trade-off: har call pe extra hop, har sidecar ke liye CPU aur memory, aur bahut saari operational complexity.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Before meshes, the same features came from per-language client libraries, such as Netflix's Hystrix and Ribbon; a mesh moves them out of process so polyglot teams get uniform behaviour. Meshes also enable zero-trust networking: every service gets a certificate identity (SPIFFE), and policy says "only order-service may call payment-service". There are sidecarless options now, such as Istio's ambient mode with per-node proxies, and proxyless gRPC. One trap to watch is layered retries: three app retries times three mesh retries means nine attempts during an outage, a retry storm, so I set retry budgets in one place.

Meshes se pehle yahi features har language ki client libraries se aate the, jaise Netflix ki Hystrix aur Ribbon; mesh inhe process se bahar le jaata hai taaki kai languages wali teams ko ek jaisa behaviour mile. Meshes zero-trust networking bhi dete hain: har service ko certificate wali identity milti hai (SPIFFE), aur policy kehti hai "sirf order-service payment-service ko call kar sakti hai". Ab sidecarless options bhi hain, jaise Istio ka ambient mode per-node proxies ke saath, aur proxyless gRPC. Ek trap dhyaan dene layak hai layered retries: teen app retries guna teen mesh retries matlab outage mein nau attempts, ek retry storm, isliye main retry budgets ek hi jagah set karta hoon.

Common mistake: Saying a service mesh replaces the load balancer. You still need an entry point at the edge; the mesh governs what happens inside.
Galti mat karna: Yeh kehna ki service mesh load balancer ko replace kar deta hai. Edge pe entry point phir bhi chahiye; mesh andar ka kaam sambhaalta hai.
09 What is a quorum and why does it matter?Quorum kya hai aur yeh kyun matter karta hai?
What they're really testing: majority as N/2 + 1, how it prevents split-brain and stale reads (as in Raft), and the W + R > N rule for leaderless systems.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: majority matlab N/2 + 1, yeh split-brain aur stale reads kaise rokta hai (jaise Raft mein), aur leaderless systems ka W + R > N rule.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A quorum is the minimum number of nodes that must agree for an operation to count, usually a majority, floor(N/2) + 1. With five nodes the quorum is three, so the cluster survives two failures. It matters because any two majorities overlap in at least one node. In Raft, used by etcd, Consul and Kafka's KRaft, a leader needs a majority of votes and a write commits only once a majority has stored it. So a partitioned minority can't elect a second leader, which prevents split-brain, and any new leader already has every committed write, so no committed data is lost. Leaderless systems like Cassandra use a different form: N replicas, W write acks and R read replies. If W + R > N, say N = 3, W = 2, R = 2, every read overlaps the latest write. The trade-off is extra latency and no writes when quorum is lost.

Quorum nodes ki woh minimum ginti hai jinka agree karna zaroori hai tabhi operation count ho, usually majority, floor(N/2) + 1. Paanch nodes pe quorum teen hai, toh cluster do failures jhel leta hai. Yeh isliye matter karta hai kyunki koi bhi do majorities kam se kam ek node pe overlap karti hain. Raft mein, jo etcd, Consul aur Kafka ke KRaft mein use hota hai, leader ko majority ke votes chahiye aur write tabhi commit hota hai jab majority ne store kar liya. Toh kati hui minority doosra leader nahi chun sakti, jisse split-brain rukta hai, aur naye leader ke paas har committed write pehle se hota hai, toh committed data nahi khota. Cassandra jaise leaderless systems alag form use karte hain: N replicas, W write acks aur R read replies. Agar W + R > N, jaise N = 3, W = 2, R = 2, toh har read latest write se overlap karta hai. Trade-off: extra latency, aur quorum khone pe writes band.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Clusters use odd sizes because 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures: four nodes need three votes and still tolerate only one failure, the same as three nodes. W + R > N has caveats. Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff let stand-in nodes accept writes during failures, which temporarily breaks the overlap. Concurrent writes still conflict. And last-write-wins with clock skew can pick the wrong "newest" value, so it's not full linearizability. Tuning shifts cost: W = N, R = 1 gives fast reads and fragile writes; W = 1, R = N the opposite. In multi-datacenter Cassandra, LOCAL_QUORUM keeps the quorum inside one region to avoid cross-region latency.

Clusters odd size ke hote hain kyunki 2f + 1 nodes f failures jhelte hain: chaar nodes ko teen votes chahiye aur woh bhi sirf ek failure jhelte hain, teen nodes jitna hi. W + R > N ki shartein hain. Hinted handoff wale sloppy quorums failures ke dauraan stand-in nodes ko writes lene dete hain, jo overlap ko thodi der ke liye tod deta hai. Concurrent writes phir bhi conflict karte hain. Aur clock skew ke saath last-write-wins galat "newest" value chun sakta hai, toh yeh poori linearizability nahi hai. Tuning se keemat shift hoti hai: W = N, R = 1 se fast reads aur nazuk writes; W = 1, R = N ulta. Multi-datacenter Cassandra mein LOCAL_QUORUM quorum ko ek region ke andar rakhta hai taaki cross-region latency na lage.

Common mistake: Defining quorum as "more than half of the nodes currently up". It's a majority of the configured cluster size; otherwise each side of a partition could count itself as a majority.
Galti mat karna: Quorum ko "abhi chalu nodes ka aadhe se zyada" define karna. Yeh configured cluster size ki majority hai; warna partition ki har side khud ko majority gin sakti hai.
10 What is the difference between leader-based and leaderless replication?Leader-based aur leaderless replication mein kya difference hai?
What they're really testing: leader-based means one writer, simpler, with failover; leaderless means any node writes, higher availability, and you must resolve conflicts.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: leader-based matlab ek writer, simple, failover ke saath; leaderless matlab koi bhi node likhe, zyada availability, aur conflicts tumhe resolve karne padte hain.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

In leader-based replication, one node, the leader, accepts all writes and streams changes to followers. Reads go to the leader for freshness or to followers for scale, accepting some lag. Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB replica sets and Kafka partitions work this way. It's simple because there's one order of writes and no write conflicts, but the leader limits write throughput and its death needs a failover: detect it, promote a follower, redirect clients. With async replication, the last few writes can be lost. In leaderless replication, Dynamo-style as in Cassandra or Riak, the client or a coordinator sends each write to several replicas and it succeeds after W acks; reads ask R replicas. There's no failover step, so availability is higher and it works well across regions. The cost is conflicts: concurrent writes to one key need last-write-wins, version vectors or CRDTs, plus read repair to converge. I'd put orders on Postgres and high-volume event data on Cassandra.

Leader-based replication mein ek node, leader, saare writes leta hai aur changes followers ko stream karta hai. Reads freshness ke liye leader se ya scale ke liye followers se hote hain, thoda lag maan ke. Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB replica sets aur Kafka partitions aise kaam karte hain. Yeh simple hai kyunki writes ka ek order hai aur write conflicts nahi, lekin leader write throughput ko limit karta hai aur uski maut pe failover chahiye: detect karo, follower promote karo, clients ko redirect karo. Async replication mein aakhri kuch writes kho sakte hain. Leaderless replication mein, Dynamo-style jaise Cassandra ya Riak, client ya coordinator har write kai replicas ko bhejta hai aur W acks ke baad woh successful hai; reads R replicas se poochte hain. Koi failover step nahi, toh availability zyada hai aur regions ke beech achha chalta hai. Keemat conflicts hain: ek key pe concurrent writes ko last-write-wins, version vectors ya CRDTs chahiye, plus converge karne ke liye read repair. Main orders Postgres pe aur high-volume event data Cassandra pe rakhunga.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

There's a third option, multi-leader, with one leader per region: writes are local and fast, but cross-region conflicts need resolution. In leader-based setups, synchronous replication to at least one follower (semi-sync) prevents losing acknowledged writes on failover at the cost of write latency. Failover itself is risky: promoting a lagging follower drops writes, and a false failure detection can cause split-brain, which is why consensus-based election with terms is preferred. Replication lag creates anomalies like not seeing your own update, so I'd route read-your-writes traffic to the leader. In leaderless systems, last-write-wins with clock skew can silently discard a newer write.

Teesra option bhi hai, multi-leader, har region mein ek leader: writes local aur fast, lekin cross-region conflicts resolve karne padte hain. Leader-based setups mein kam se kam ek follower ko synchronous replication (semi-sync) failover pe acknowledged writes khone se bachata hai, write latency ki keemat pe. Failover khud risky hai: peeche chal rahe follower ko promote karo toh writes girte hain, aur galat failure detection split-brain kara sakta hai, isiliye terms wala consensus-based election pasand kiya jaata hai. Replication lag se gadbad hoti hai, jaise apna hi update na dikhna, toh main read-your-writes wala traffic leader pe bhejunga. Leaderless systems mein clock skew ke saath last-write-wins chup-chaap naya write gira sakta hai.

Common mistake: Saying leaderless means "no conflicts because there's no leader". It's the opposite: without a single writer, conflict resolution becomes your job.
Galti mat karna: Yeh kehna ki leaderless matlab "leader nahi hai toh conflicts nahi". Ulta hai: single writer ke bina conflict resolution tumhara kaam ban jaata hai.

Topic 08 · ASKED EVERYWHERETopic 08 · Har jagah poocha jaata hai

API DesignAPI Design

An API is a promise to other developers. Learn how to design that promise so it is easy to use, fast at scale, and never breaks the people who depend on it.

API doosre developers se kiya gaya ek promise hai. Seekho yeh promise kaise design karte hain taaki use karna aasaan ho, scale pe fast chale, aur jo log us pe depend karte hain unka kaam kabhi na toote.

Level 0 The story: a menu is a contractKahani: menu ek contract hai

Imagine a busy South Indian restaurant near your office. It has a printed menu. Every morning, hundreds of regulars walk in and say "one masala dosa, one filter coffee" without even looking at the menu. The kitchen can change a lot of things behind the scenes: a new cook, a new gas stove, a new supplier for rice. Customers never notice, because what they order and what they receive stays the same.

Now imagine the owner wakes up one day and decides "masala dosa" will now be called "potato crepe", and the coffee will come without sugar unless you ask. The regulars are confused, orders go wrong, and some people stop coming. The owner changed the menu, and the menu was a contract with customers.

The owner could have done something smarter: add a new "potato crepe" item and keep masala dosa. Or print a second menu, "Menu 2026", and let regulars keep using the old one for a few months. Adding is safe. Removing or renaming is painful.

Map it to software: the restaurant is your backend server. The menu is your API. The regular customers are other programs (a mobile app, a partner's website, another team's service) that call your API every day. The kitchen is your code and database. You may change the kitchen freely. You must treat the menu with great care.

Throughout this chapter we will use one running example: a car-dealership inventory and service API. A dealership website needs to list vehicles in stock (GET /v1/vehicles), show one vehicle by its VIN (Vehicle Identification Number, the unique 17-character ID of every car), and let a customer book a service appointment (POST /v1/appointments). Many apps would call this API: the dealer's website, a mobile app, a chat assistant, a partner's listing site. If we break it, all of them break at once.

API design is not about code. It is about the people who consume what you build: can they understand it, can they rely on it, and can you evolve it without breaking them?

Socho tumhare office ke paas ek busy South Indian restaurant hai. Uska ek printed menu hai. Roz subah sainkdon regular customers aate hain aur bina menu dekhe bol dete hain "ek masala dosa, ek filter coffee". Kitchen ke andar owner bahut kuch badal sakta hai: naya cook, naya gas stove, chawal ka naya supplier. Customers ko kuch pata nahi chalta, kyunki jo woh order karte hain aur jo unhe milta hai, woh same rehta hai.

Ab socho ek din owner decide karta hai ki "masala dosa" ab "potato crepe" kehlayega, aur coffee bina cheeni ke aayegi jab tak tum alag se na bolo. Regulars confuse ho jaate hain, orders galat jaate hain, kuch log aana band kar dete hain. Owner ne menu badal diya, aur menu customers ke saath ek contract tha.

Owner smart tareeka apna sakta tha: naya "potato crepe" item add kar do aur masala dosa bhi rehne do. Ya ek doosra menu print karo, "Menu 2026", aur regulars ko kuch mahine purana menu use karne do. Add karna safe hai. Hataana ya naam badalna dard deta hai.

Software se jodo: restaurant tumhara backend server hai. Menu tumhari API hai. Regular customers doosre programs hain (mobile app, partner ki website, doosri team ki service) jo roz tumhari API call karte hain. Kitchen tumhara code aur database hai. Kitchen tum freely badal sakte ho. Menu ko bahut dhyaan se sambhalna padta hai.

Is poore chapter mein hum ek hi example chalayenge: ek car-dealership inventory aur service API. Dealership ki website ko stock mein padi gaadiyan dikhani hain (GET /v1/vehicles), ek gaadi uske VIN se dikhani hai (VIN = Vehicle Identification Number, har gaadi ka unique 17-character ID), aur customer ko service appointment book karne dena hai (POST /v1/appointments). Is API ko kai apps call karengi: dealer ki website, mobile app, chat assistant, partner ki listing site. Agar humne ise tod diya, toh sab ek saath toot jaayenge.

API design code ke baare mein nahi hai. Yeh un logon ke baare mein hai jo tumhari cheez use karte hain: kya woh ise samajh paayenge, kya woh is pe bharosa kar sakte hain, aur kya tum ise bina unhe tode aage badha sakte ho?

Level 1 Vocabulary: resources, URLs, methodsVocabulary: resources, URLs, methods

Quick recap from the foundations chapter: a client (browser, app) sends an HTTP request to a server. The request has a method (GET, POST...), a URL (the address), headers (extra labels like "who am I" and "what format I send"), and sometimes a body (the data, usually JSON). The server replies with a status code (200, 404...), headers, and a body.

Resource. In a well-designed API, everything is modelled as a thing (a noun), called a resource: a vehicle, an appointment, a rooftop (one dealership location), a customer. A group of the same things is a collection: /vehicles. One item in it is addressed by its ID: /vehicles/1HGCM82633A004352.

URL rules that interviewers like to hear:

  • Use nouns, not verbs: POST /appointments, not POST /createAppointment. The method already says the verb.
  • Use plural collection names: /vehicles, /appointments.
  • Nest only to show ownership, and only one or two levels: /rooftops/42/vehicles means "vehicles belonging to rooftop 42".
  • Filtering, sorting and paging go in the query string (the part after ?): ?status=in_stock&sort=-price&limit=20.
  • Be consistent: same casing (snake_case or camelCase, pick one), same ID style, same date format (ISO 8601, e.g. 2026-10-02T09:30:00Z) everywhere.

Foundations chapter ka chhota sa recap: client (browser, app) server ko ek HTTP request bhejta hai. Request mein ek method hota hai (GET, POST...), ek URL (address), headers (extra labels jaise "main kaun hoon" aur "main kis format mein bhej raha hoon"), aur kabhi kabhi ek body (data, aam taur pe JSON). Server jawab mein status code (200, 404...), headers aur body bhejta hai.

Resource. Achhi API mein har cheez ko ek thing (noun) ki tarah model karte hain, jise resource kehte hain: vehicle, appointment, rooftop (ek dealership location), customer. Ek hi type ki cheezon ka group collection kehlata hai: /vehicles. Usme ek item ko uske ID se address karte hain: /vehicles/1HGCM82633A004352.

URL ke rules jo interviewer sunna pasand karte hain:

  • Noun use karo, verb nahi: POST /appointments, na ki POST /createAppointment. Verb toh method already bata raha hai.
  • Collection ka naam plural rakho: /vehicles, /appointments.
  • Nesting sirf ownership dikhane ke liye, aur ek-do level tak hi: /rooftops/42/vehicles matlab "rooftop 42 ki gaadiyan".
  • Filtering, sorting aur paging query string mein jaati hai (? ke baad wala hissa): ?status=in_stock&sort=-price&limit=20.
  • Consistent raho: ek hi casing (snake_case ya camelCase, ek chuno), ek hi ID style, har jagah ek hi date format (ISO 8601, jaise 2026-10-02T09:30:00Z).

The methods (verbs) and two properties you must know. Safe means "does not change anything on the server". Idempotent means "doing it once or ten times leaves the server in the same state" (Topic 05 goes deep on this).

Methods (verbs) aur do properties jo tumhe pata honi chahiye. Safe matlab "server pe kuch change nahi karta". Idempotent matlab "ek baar karo ya das baar, server ki state same rehti hai" (Topic 05 isme deep jaata hai).

MethodMethodWhat it doesKya karta haiSafeIdempotentExampleExample
GETRead a resource or listResource ya list padhnaYesHaanYesHaanGET /v1/vehicles/{vin}
POSTCreate a new item, or trigger an actionNaya item banana, ya koi action trigger karnaNoNahiNoNahiPOST /v1/appointments
PUTReplace the whole resource at this URLIs URL wala poora resource replace karnaNoNahiYesHaanPUT /v1/vehicles/{vin}
PATCHChange some fieldsKuch fields badalnaNoNahiNot guaranteed by specSpec guarantee nahi kartaPATCH /v1/vehicles/{vin} {"price": 24500}
DELETERemove the resourceResource hataanaNoNahiYesHaanDELETE /v1/appointments/{id}

Level 2 What REST actually means, and its rivalsREST ka asli matlab, aur uske competitors

REST (Representational State Transfer) is not a library or a protocol. It is an architectural style, a set of rules described by Roy Fielding in his PhD dissertation in 2000. An API is "RESTful" if it follows these constraints:

  1. Client-server. The client (UI) and the server (data and logic) are separate and evolve independently. The dealer's website team can redesign pages without touching the inventory server.
  2. Stateless. Every request carries everything the server needs to understand it (who you are, what you want). The server does not remember "what this client did last time" between requests. This is the most important one: because no request depends on memory in one particular server, any server behind a load balancer can answer any request, so you scale by just adding servers.
  3. Cacheable. Responses must say whether they can be cached and for how long (headers like Cache-Control: max-age=60, ETag). A vehicle photo list can be cached; a live appointment slot count should not be.
  4. Uniform interface. Every resource is used the same way: identified by a URL, changed by sending a representation (JSON) with standard methods, messages describe themselves (Content-Type, status codes), and ideally responses contain links to what you can do next (HATEOAS, below).
  5. Layered system. The client cannot tell whether it is talking to the real server or to a CDN, load balancer, or API gateway in the middle. You can add layers without the client changing.
  6. Code on demand (optional). The server may send code for the client to run (like JavaScript). This is the only optional one and rarely discussed.

If you remember one constraint, remember stateless. It is what lets a REST API scale horizontally. Note: stateless means the server keeps no conversation memory; your database obviously still stores data.

HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) is the part of "uniform interface" that almost nobody implements fully. The idea: like a web page with links, the response tells the client what it can do next, so the client does not hard-code URLs or business rules.

REST (Representational State Transfer) koi library ya protocol nahi hai. Yeh ek architectural style hai, rules ka ek set jo Roy Fielding ne 2000 mein apni PhD dissertation mein likha tha. Koi API "RESTful" tab kehlati hai jab woh yeh constraints follow kare:

  1. Client-server. Client (UI) aur server (data aur logic) alag hain aur alag-alag evolve hote hain. Dealer ki website team pages redesign kar sakti hai bina inventory server ko chhue.
  2. Stateless. Har request mein woh sab kuch hota hai jo server ko samajhne ke liye chahiye (tum kaun ho, tumhe kya chahiye). Server do requests ke beech yaad nahi rakhta ki "is client ne pichhli baar kya kiya tha". Yeh sabse important hai: kyunki koi request kisi ek server ki memory pe depend nahi karti, load balancer ke peeche koi bhi server koi bhi request answer kar sakta hai, toh scale karne ke liye bas aur servers add kar do.
  3. Cacheable. Response ko batana chahiye ki woh cache ho sakta hai ya nahi aur kitni der ke liye (headers jaise Cache-Control: max-age=60, ETag). Gaadi ki photos ki list cache ho sakti hai; live appointment slots ki ginti nahi honi chahiye.
  4. Uniform interface. Har resource ek hi tareeke se use hota hai: URL se pehchaana jaata hai, standard methods ke saath representation (JSON) bhej ke badla jaata hai, messages khud apne baare mein batate hain (Content-Type, status codes), aur ideally response mein aage kya kar sakte ho uske links hote hain (HATEOAS, neeche).
  5. Layered system. Client ko pata nahi chal sakta ki woh asli server se baat kar raha hai ya beech mein kisi CDN, load balancer ya API gateway se. Tum layers add kar sakte ho bina client badle.
  6. Code on demand (optional). Server client ko chalane ke liye code bhej sakta hai (jaise JavaScript). Sirf yahi optional hai aur is pe kam baat hoti hai.

Ek hi constraint yaad rakhna ho toh stateless yaad rakho. Isi ki wajah se REST API horizontally scale hoti hai. Dhyaan do: stateless matlab server koi baat-cheet ki memory nahi rakhta; database toh data store karta hi hai.

HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) "uniform interface" ka woh hissa hai jo lagbhag koi bhi poora implement nahi karta. Idea yeh hai: jaise web page mein links hote hain, waise hi response client ko batata hai ki woh aage kya kar sakta hai, taaki client URLs ya business rules hard-code na kare.

GET /v1/appointments/apt_9c1

{
  "id": "apt_9c1",
  "status": "booked",
  "service": "oil_change",
  "slot": "2026-10-02T09:30:00-05:00",
  "vehicle_vin": "1HGCM82633A004352",
  "_links": {
    "self":       { "href": "/v1/appointments/apt_9c1" },
    "reschedule": { "href": "/v1/appointments/apt_9c1", "method": "PATCH" },
    "cancel":     { "href": "/v1/appointments/apt_9c1/cancellation", "method": "POST" },
    "vehicle":    { "href": "/v1/vehicles/1HGCM82633A004352" }
  }
}
// Once status becomes "completed", the server simply stops sending "cancel".
// The client shows a Cancel button only if the link exists.

REST is not the only option. Two popular alternatives exist, and each wins in a different situation.

  • GraphQL (created at Facebook): one endpoint, usually POST /graphql. The client sends a query that names exactly the fields it wants, across related objects, in one round trip. Great for mobile apps and complex UIs where REST would cause over-fetching (getting 40 fields when you need 3) or under-fetching (needing 5 calls to build one screen).
  • gRPC (created at Google): you define functions and message shapes in a .proto file, and tools generate client and server code in many languages. Messages are sent as compact binary (Protocol Buffers) over HTTP/2, and it supports streaming in both directions. Great for internal service-to-service calls where speed and strict types matter.

REST akela option nahi hai. Do popular alternatives hain, aur har ek alag situation mein jeetta hai.

  • GraphQL (Facebook ne banaya): ek hi endpoint, aam taur pe POST /graphql. Client ek query bhejta hai jisme exactly woh fields likhe hote hain jo use chahiye, related objects ke across bhi, ek hi round trip mein. Mobile apps aur complex UIs ke liye badhiya, jahan REST mein over-fetching hota (3 fields chahiye aur 40 aa gaye) ya under-fetching (ek screen banane ke liye 5 calls).
  • gRPC (Google ne banaya): tum ek .proto file mein functions aur message shapes define karte ho, aur tools kai languages mein client aur server code generate kar dete hain. Messages compact binary (Protocol Buffers) mein HTTP/2 pe jaate hain, aur dono taraf streaming support hai. Internal service-to-service calls ke liye badhiya jahan speed aur strict types important hain.

Best forKiske liye bestPublic and partner APIs, simple CRUDPublic aur partner APIs, simple CRUDMobile and rich UIs needing flexible dataMobile aur rich UIs jinhe flexible data chahiyeInternal microservices, high throughput, streamingInternal microservices, high throughput, streaming
HTTP cachingHTTP cachingEasy (GET + URL + headers, CDNs understand it)Aasaan (GET + URL + headers, CDN samajhte hain)Hard (mostly POST to one URL)Mushkil (zyada tar ek URL pe POST)Not HTTP-cache friendlyHTTP cache friendly nahi
Browser supportBrowser supportNativeNativeNativeNativeNeeds gRPC-Web plus a proxygRPC-Web aur ek proxy chahiye

Level 3 Production contract: status codes, pagination, slow work, versioningProduction contract: status codes, pagination, slow kaam, versioning

1. Status codes are part of the contract. The client's code branches on the number, not on your English message. First digit: 2xx success, 3xx go elsewhere, 4xx the client did something wrong, 5xx the server failed. Never return 200 with {"error": ...} inside: monitoring, retries and caches all read the number and will think it worked.

1. Status codes contract ka hissa hain. Client ka code number pe decide karta hai, tumhare English message pe nahi. Pehla digit: 2xx success, 3xx kahin aur jao, 4xx client ne kuch galat kiya, 5xx server fail hua. Kabhi bhi 200 ke andar {"error": ...} mat bhejo: monitoring, retries aur caches sab number padhte hain aur samjhenge ki kaam ho gaya.

CodeNameNaamUse whenKab use kareinDealership API exampleDealership API example

204No ContentSuccess, nothing to send backSuccess, wapas bhejne ko kuch nahiDELETE /v1/appointments/{id}

403ForbiddenWe know who you are, but you are not allowedPata hai tum kaun ho, par permission nahi haiRooftop 7 user reading rooftop 42 dataRooftop 7 ka user rooftop 42 ka data padh raha

Pair the status code with one consistent error body everywhere, so clients write one error handler. A standard shape exists: Problem Details (RFC 9457, content type application/problem+json). Whatever you pick, include a machine-readable code, a human message, field-level details, and a request ID for support.

Status code ke saath har jagah ek hi consistent error body do, taaki client ek hi error handler likhe. Ek standard shape hai: Problem Details (RFC 9457, content type application/problem+json). Jo bhi chuno, usme machine-readable code, insaan ke liye message, field-level details aur support ke liye request ID zaroor ho.

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": {
    "code": "slot_in_past",
    "message": "Appointment slot must be in the future.",
    "details": [{ "field": "slot", "issue": "2026-09-01T09:30:00Z is before now" }],
    "request_id": "req_01J9ZK3T"
  }
}

2. Pagination. A rooftop may have thousands of vehicles in the database over time. You never return them all in one response; you return a page. There are two main ways.

Offset pagination: GET /v1/vehicles?limit=20&offset=40 means "skip 40, give me the next 20". Simple, and lets the UI jump to "page 57". Two problems. First, speed: the database cannot jump to row 40; it must walk through and throw away the first 40 rows. At offset=100000 it reads 100,020 rows to return 20, so deep pages get slower and slower. Second, correctness: if a new vehicle is added at the top while a user is paging, everything shifts down by one, so the user sees one vehicle twice; if one is deleted, the user silently skips one.

Cursor pagination (also called keyset pagination): the server returns an opaque token, the cursor, that encodes the sort key of the last item on this page (for example its created_at and id). The next request says "give me 20 items after this cursor". The database uses its index to jump straight there (see Topic 01) and reads only 20 rows, however deep you are. Inserts and deletes elsewhere do not shift your position. The trade-off: no "jump to page 57", no cheap total count, and the sort order must be on a unique, indexed key (add id as a tie-breaker).

2. Pagination. Ek rooftop ke database mein time ke saath hazaaron gaadiyan ho sakti hain. Tum sab ek response mein kabhi nahi bhejte; ek page bhejte ho. Iske do main tareeke hain.

Offset pagination: GET /v1/vehicles?limit=20&offset=40 matlab "40 chhod do, agle 20 do". Simple hai, aur UI seedha "page 57" pe jump kar sakta hai. Do problems hain. Pehli, speed: database seedha row 40 pe nahi kood sakta; use pehli 40 rows padh ke phenkni padti hain. offset=100000 pe woh 20 rows dene ke liye 100,020 rows padhta hai, toh gehre pages slow hote jaate hain. Doosri, correctness: agar user paging kar raha hai aur upar ek nayi gaadi add ho gayi, toh sab kuch ek position neeche khisak jaata hai, user ko ek gaadi do baar dikhti hai; agar ek delete hui, toh user chupchaap ek gaadi miss kar deta hai.

Cursor pagination (isko keyset pagination bhi kehte hain): server ek opaque token deta hai, jise cursor kehte hain, jisme is page ke last item ki sort key encoded hoti hai (jaise uska created_at aur id). Agli request kehti hai "is cursor ke baad ke 20 items do". Database apne index se seedha wahan jump karta hai (Topic 01 dekho) aur sirf 20 rows padhta hai, chahe tum kitne bhi gehre page pe ho. Kahin aur insert ya delete hone se tumhari position nahi khisakti. Trade-off: "page 57 pe jump" nahi, sasta total count nahi, aur sort order ek unique, indexed key pe hona chahiye (tie-breaker ke liye id jodo).

-- Offset: the DB walks and discards 40 rows first
SELECT id, vin, make, model, price, created_at
FROM vehicles
WHERE rooftop_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;

-- Cursor (keyset): decode cursor -> (created_at, id) of the last row seen.
-- Ask for 21 rows: if 21 come back, there is a next page.
SELECT id, vin, make, model, price, created_at
FROM vehicles
WHERE rooftop_id = 42
  AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-09-20 10:15:00', 1040)   -- row comparison (Postgres)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;

-- Response
{ "data": [ ...20 vehicles... ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJjIjoiMjAyNi0wOS0yMFQxMDoxNTowMCIsImlkIjoxMDIxfQ",
  "has_more": true }

3. Slow work: 202 Accepted and a job. Some requests take 30 seconds or more: exporting a whole rooftop's inventory to a CSV file, re-processing 500 vehicle photos, syncing with another system. If you keep the HTTP connection open that long, bad things happen: load balancers and proxies time out (often around 30 to 60 seconds by default), the user's phone switches networks, and the client retries and starts the job twice. Worker threads on your server sit blocked.

The fix: accept the request quickly, put the work on a queue (Topic 06), and return 202 Accepted with a job ID and a URL to check. The client polls GET /v1/jobs/{id} (politely, respecting a Retry-After hint), or you call the client back with a webhook (an HTTP POST from your server to a URL the client registered) when the job finishes.

3. Slow kaam: 202 Accepted aur ek job. Kuch requests 30 second ya usse zyada leti hain: poore rooftop ki inventory CSV file mein export karna, 500 gaadiyon ki photos dobara process karna, kisi doosre system ke saath sync karna. Agar tum HTTP connection itni der khula rakhoge toh gadbad hogi: load balancers aur proxies time out ho jaate hain (default aksar 30 se 60 second ke aas-paas), user ka phone network badal leta hai, aur client retry karke job do baar shuru kar deta hai. Server ke worker threads atke rehte hain.

Fix: request jaldi accept karo, kaam ek queue pe daal do (Topic 06), aur 202 Accepted ke saath job ID aur check karne ka URL wapas do. Client GET /v1/jobs/{id} poll karta hai (araam se, Retry-After hint maan ke), ya job khatam hone pe tum client ko webhook se bata dete ho (tumhare server se client ke registered URL pe ek HTTP POST).

4. Versioning. Sooner or later you need a change that would break clients. Versioning lets old clients keep the old contract while new clients get the new one. Common styles:

  • URL path: /v1/vehicles, /v2/vehicles. Most explicit, easy to see in logs, easy to route. The most common choice for public APIs.
  • Header: Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json or a custom API-Version: 2026-09-01 header. Keeps URLs clean; Stripe is a well-known example of date-based versions pinned per account. Harder to test in a browser.
  • Query parameter: ?version=2. Easy but messy; it mixes with filters and caching.

The golden rule is more important than the style: inside one version, only add, never remove, rename, or change the meaning of anything. Bump the major version only for truly breaking changes, and run old and new side by side for a published period.

Backward-compatible (safe) changes: adding a new endpoint; adding a new optional request field with a sensible default; adding a new field to a response; adding a new optional query filter.

Breaking changes: removing or renaming a field or endpoint; changing a field's type (price from number 24500 to string "24500.00"); changing units or meaning (price in cents instead of dollars); making an optional request field required; changing which status code a situation returns; tightening validation so previously valid requests now fail.

Deprecation, the polite way to retire something: announce it, mark responses with the Deprecation header and a Sunset header (the date it will stop working, RFC 8594), link a migration guide, watch the logs to see which clients still call it, contact them, and only then remove it.

4. Versioning. Kabhi na kabhi tumhe aisa change chahiye hoga jo clients ko tod dega. Versioning se purane clients purana contract use karte rehte hain aur naye clients naya. Common styles:

  • URL path: /v1/vehicles, /v2/vehicles. Sabse explicit, logs mein dikhta hai, route karna aasaan. Public APIs ke liye sabse common choice.
  • Header: Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json ya custom API-Version: 2026-09-01 header. URLs saaf rehte hain; Stripe iska famous example hai jahan date-based version har account pe pin hota hai. Browser mein test karna mushkil.
  • Query parameter: ?version=2. Aasaan par messy; filters aur caching ke saath mix ho jaata hai.

Style se zyada important golden rule hai: ek version ke andar sirf add karo, kabhi kuch remove, rename ya uska matlab change mat karo. Major version sirf sach mein breaking change ke liye badhao, aur purana aur naya ek announced time tak saath chalao.

Backward-compatible (safe) changes: naya endpoint add karna; naya optional request field add karna jiska sensible default ho; response mein naya field add karna; naya optional query filter add karna.

Breaking changes: field ya endpoint hataana ya uska naam badalna; field ka type badalna (price number 24500 se string "24500.00"); units ya matlab badalna (dollars ki jagah cents mein price); optional request field ko required banana; kisi situation ka status code badalna; validation itna tight karna ki pehle wali valid requests ab fail hon.

Deprecation, kisi cheez ko izzat se retire karne ka tareeka: announce karo, responses pe Deprecation header aur Sunset header lagao (kis date ko band hoga, RFC 8594), migration guide ka link do, logs dekho ki kaun se clients abhi bhi call kar rahe hain, unse contact karo, aur tabhi hataao.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Wed, 31 Mar 2027 23:59:59 GMT
Link: <https://docs.example.com/migrate-v1-to-v2>; rel="deprecation"

Level 4 Senior level: safe retries and rate limitsSenior level: safe retries aur rate limits

1. Idempotent POST. POST is not idempotent by spec. Picture a customer tapping "Book service appointment" on a weak mobile signal. The request reaches the server, the appointment is created, but the response is lost. The app retries. Without protection, the customer now has two appointments and the service drive has a phantom booking.

The standard fix: the client generates a unique idempotency key (a random UUID) once per user action and sends it in a header on the first try and every retry. The server stores key → (hash of request body, final response), typically in Redis or a database table with a TTL (time to live, how long it is kept). On a repeat with the same key and same body, the server returns the stored response instead of creating a second appointment. Same key but a different body means a client bug, so reject it (422 is common). If the first request is still in progress, return 409 so the client waits and retries. An alternative is letting the client choose the resource ID itself (PUT /v1/appointments/{client_uuid}, which is naturally idempotent) or a database unique constraint on a natural key.

1. Idempotent POST. Spec ke hisaab se POST idempotent nahi hai. Socho ek customer kamzor mobile signal pe "Book service appointment" dabata hai. Request server tak pahunchti hai, appointment ban jaata hai, par response kho jaata hai. App retry karti hai. Bina protection ke, customer ke ab do appointments hain aur service drive pe ek nakli booking pad gayi.

Standard fix: client har user action ke liye ek baar ek unique idempotency key (random UUID) banata hai aur pehli try aur har retry mein ise header mein bhejta hai. Server store karta hai key → (request body ka hash, final response), aam taur pe Redis ya database table mein TTL ke saath (TTL = time to live, kitni der rakhna hai). Same key aur same body ke saath dobara aaye toh server doosra appointment banane ki jagah stored response lauta deta hai. Same key par alag body matlab client mein bug hai, toh reject karo (422 common hai). Agar pehli request abhi chal hi rahi hai, toh 409 do taaki client ruk ke retry kare. Ek alternative hai ki client khud resource ID chune (PUT /v1/appointments/{client_uuid}, jo naturally idempotent hai) ya kisi natural key pe database unique constraint.

POST /v1/appointments
Idempotency-Key: 5f0c2b7e-8d1a-4a53-9b0e-2c6f1d7e9a44
Content-Type: application/json

{ "vehicle_vin": "1HGCM82633A004352", "service": "oil_change",
  "slot": "2026-10-02T09:30:00-05:00" }

// Server (pseudo-code)
const saved = await redis.get(`idem:${key}`);
if (saved) {
  if (saved.bodyHash !== hash(body)) return res(422, "key reused with different body");
  if (saved.status === "in_progress") return res(409, "still processing, retry shortly");
  return res(saved.code, saved.response);            // replay, no second booking
}
// SET ... NX = only if not exists (atomic claim); EX = expire after 24h
const claimed = await redis.set(`idem:${key}`, {status: "in_progress", bodyHash: hash(body)},
                                { NX: true, EX: 86400 });
if (!claimed) return res(409, "still processing, retry shortly");
const appt = await createAppointment(body);
await redis.set(`idem:${key}`, {status: "done", bodyHash: hash(body), code: 201, response: appt},
                { EX: 86400 });
return res(201, appt);

2. Rate limiting. One partner's buggy script can call your API thousands of times per second and slow it down for every dealer. A rate limit caps how many requests a client (identified by API key, user, or IP address) may make in a period. Common algorithms:

  • Fixed window: count requests per calendar minute. Simple, but a client can send the full limit at 12:00:59 and again at 12:01:00, a double burst at the boundary.
  • Sliding window: count over the last 60 seconds from now (either a log of timestamps or a weighted blend of the current and previous window). Smoother, a bit more work.
  • Token bucket: a bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at r tokens per second. Each request takes one token. Empty bucket means reject. It allows short bursts (up to B) but enforces the average rate r. This is the one most often drawn in interviews.

With many API servers behind a load balancer, the counter must live in a shared, atomic store, typically Redis with INCR + EXPIRE or a small Lua script (runs atomically inside Redis) for token bucket. An in-memory counter per server is wrong: with 5 servers, each client effectively gets 5 times the limit (Topic 03).

Communicate it. A rate limit the client cannot see is a bug factory. When rejecting, return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After (seconds to wait, a standard HTTP header). On every response, send the current budget: the widely used X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset headers, or the newer RateLimit / RateLimit-Policy headers being standardised by the IETF. Document the limits, and clients should back off with jitter (random extra wait) rather than retry instantly.

2. Rate limiting. Ek partner ki buggy script tumhari API ko ek second mein hazaaron baar call kar sakti hai aur har dealer ke liye sab slow kar sakti hai. Rate limit yeh cap lagata hai ki ek client (API key, user ya IP address se pehchaana gaya) ek time period mein kitni requests kar sakta hai. Common algorithms:

  • Fixed window: har calendar minute ki requests gino. Simple, par client 12:00:59 pe poora limit bhej sakta hai aur phir 12:01:00 pe dobara, boundary pe double burst.
  • Sliding window: abhi se pichhle 60 second ki requests gino (ya toh timestamps ka log, ya current aur pichhli window ka weighted mix). Smooth hai, thoda zyada kaam.
  • Token bucket: ek bucket mein zyada se zyada B tokens aate hain aur woh r tokens per second ki speed se bharta hai. Har request ek token leti hai. Bucket khaali matlab reject. Yeh chhote bursts allow karta hai (B tak) par average rate r enforce karta hai. Interviews mein yahi sabse zyada draw hota hai.

Jab load balancer ke peeche kai API servers hon, toh counter ek shared, atomic store mein hona chahiye, aam taur pe Redis mein INCR + EXPIRE ya token bucket ke liye ek chhoti Lua script (jo Redis ke andar atomically chalti hai). Har server ka alag in-memory counter galat hai: 5 servers ho toh har client ko asal mein 5 guna limit mil jaati hai (Topic 03).

Client ko batao. Jo rate limit client dekh na sake, woh bugs ki factory hai. Reject karte waqt 429 Too Many Requests ke saath Retry-After bhejo (kitne second rukna hai, ek standard HTTP header). Har response pe current budget bhejo: widely used X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset headers, ya naye RateLimit / RateLimit-Policy headers jo IETF standardise kar raha hai. Limits document karo, aur clients ko turant retry karne ki jagah jitter (random extra wait) ke saath back off karna chahiye.

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 1
X-RateLimit-Limit: 300
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1790000060
Content-Type: application/json

{ "error": { "code": "rate_limited",
             "message": "Limit of 300 requests per minute exceeded. Retry after 1 second." } }

In real production, these pieces are often handled once, at an API gateway in front of all services (authentication, rate limiting, request IDs, logging), so each team does not reinvent them. The contract is written down in an OpenAPI specification (a YAML/JSON file describing every endpoint, field and status code), from which documentation, client SDKs and contract tests are generated. Contract tests in CI catch an accidental breaking change before it ships.

Senior nuance: even "safe" additions can break careless clients. Adding a new value to an enum (say status: "reserved" next to in_stock and sold) breaks a client that has a strict switch with no default. Document that clients must ignore unknown fields and handle unknown enum values (the "tolerant reader" rule), and treat new enum values as a change worth announcing.

Real production mein yeh saare pieces aksar ek hi jagah handle hote hain, sab services ke aage ek API gateway pe (authentication, rate limiting, request IDs, logging), taaki har team inhe dobara na banaye. Contract ek OpenAPI specification mein likha jaata hai (ek YAML/JSON file jo har endpoint, field aur status code describe karti hai), jisse documentation, client SDKs aur contract tests generate hote hain. CI mein contract tests galti se hua breaking change ship hone se pehle pakad lete hain.

Senior nuance: "safe" additions bhi laaparwah clients ko tod sakti hain. Enum mein nayi value add karna (jaise in_stock aur sold ke saath status: "reserved") us client ko tod deta hai jiska strict switch hai bina default ke. Document karo ki clients unknown fields ignore karein aur unknown enum values handle karein ("tolerant reader" rule), aur nayi enum values ko announce karne layak change maano.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

API contract
The promise of URLs, fields, types and status codes that clients build against.URLs, fields, types aur status codes ka woh promise jis pe clients apna code banate hain.
Resource / collection
A thing (noun) your API exposes, e.g. one vehicle; a collection is the list, e.g. /vehicles.Woh cheez (noun) jo API expose karti hai, jaise ek vehicle; collection uski list hai, jaise /vehicles.
Stateless
Each request carries everything needed; the server keeps no per-client memory between requests.Har request mein sab kuch hota hai; server requests ke beech client ki koi memory nahi rakhta.
Idempotent
Doing it N times has the same effect as doing it once.N baar karo ya ek baar, effect same.
HATEOAS
Responses include links to the next allowed actions.Response mein aage ke allowed actions ke links hote hain.
Offset / cursor pagination
Skip N rows vs continue after the last seen sort key.N rows skip karo vs last dekhi sort key ke baad se aage badho.
202 Accepted
"Got it, working on it"; the result comes later via a job URL or webhook."Mil gaya, kaam chal raha hai"; result baad mein job URL ya webhook se aata hai.
Webhook
Your server calls the client's URL when something happens, instead of the client polling.Kuch hone pe tumhara server client ka URL call karta hai, client ko poll nahi karna padta.
Breaking change
Any change that makes an existing, correct client fail.Koi bhi change jo pehle se sahi chal rahe client ko fail kar de.
Deprecation / Sunset
Marking something as "please stop using" / the date it will be removed.Kisi cheez ko "please use karna band karo" mark karna / woh date jab woh hata di jaayegi.
Idempotency key
Client-generated unique ID that lets the server recognise a retry.Client ka banaya unique ID jisse server retry pehchaan leta hai.
Token bucket
Rate-limit algorithm: tokens refill at a fixed rate; each request spends one.Rate-limit algorithm: tokens fixed rate se bharte hain; har request ek kharch karti hai.
429 / Retry-After
"Too many requests" / how many seconds to wait before trying again."Bahut zyada requests" / dobara try karne se pehle kitne second rukna hai.
OpenAPI
A standard file format describing a REST API, used to generate docs and clients.REST API describe karne ka standard file format, jisse docs aur clients generate hote hain.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What makes an API RESTful? Explain the constraints.Kya cheez ek API ko RESTful banati hai? Constraints samjhao.
What they're really testing: whether you know REST is a set of architectural constraints (not "JSON over HTTP"), and that statelessness is the one that matters most.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tumhe pata hai ki REST architectural constraints ka set hai ("HTTP pe JSON" nahi), aur ki statelessness sabse important hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

REST is an architectural style from Roy Fielding, defined by six constraints: client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, a uniform interface, a layered system, and optional code on demand. The most important is statelessness: each request carries everything the server needs, like the auth token and the parameters, so the server keeps no session memory between calls. That is why any instance behind a load balancer can serve any request and we scale by adding servers. Uniform interface means resources are nouns addressed by URLs, like /v1/vehicles/{vin}, manipulated with standard methods and status codes. Cacheable means responses declare if and how long they can be cached. The trade-off of statelessness is that every request repeats context, such as re-sending and re-verifying the token, which is a small cost for easy scaling.

REST Roy Fielding ka diya hua ek architectural style hai, jo chhe constraints se define hota hai: client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, uniform interface, layered system, aur optional code on demand. Sabse important statelessness hai: har request mein woh sab hota hai jo server ko chahiye, jaise auth token aur parameters, toh server calls ke beech koi session memory nahi rakhta. Isi liye load balancer ke peeche koi bhi instance koi bhi request serve kar sakta hai aur hum servers add karke scale karte hain. Uniform interface matlab resources nouns hain jo URLs se address hote hain, jaise /v1/vehicles/{vin}, aur standard methods aur status codes se change hote hain. Cacheable matlab response batata hai ki woh cache ho sakta hai ya nahi aur kitni der. Statelessness ka trade-off yeh hai ki har request context repeat karti hai, jaise token dobara bhejna aur verify karna, jo easy scaling ke liye chhoti keemat hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Most "REST" APIs are really level 2 on the Richardson Maturity Model: resources plus HTTP verbs plus status codes. Level 3 adds hypermedia (HATEOAS), which Fielding considered required but which few teams implement. Stateless also does not mean the backend has no state; the database holds state, the server just does not hold conversation state in memory. If you use server-side sessions, you either need sticky sessions (a load balancer always sending a user to the same server) or a shared session store like Redis, which moves the state out of the web server and keeps the servers themselves interchangeable.

Zyada tar "REST" APIs asal mein Richardson Maturity Model ke level 2 pe hoti hain: resources plus HTTP verbs plus status codes. Level 3 mein hypermedia (HATEOAS) aata hai, jise Fielding zaroori maante the par kam teams implement karti hain. Stateless ka matlab yeh bhi nahi ki backend mein state hi nahi; state database mein hai, bas server memory mein baat-cheet ki state nahi rakhta. Agar server-side sessions use karte ho, toh ya toh sticky sessions chahiye (load balancer ek user ko hamesha same server pe bheje) ya Redis jaisa shared session store, jo state ko web server se bahar le jaata hai aur servers ko interchangeable rakhta hai.

Common mistake: saying "REST means using JSON and HTTP". JSON is not required, and HTTP with verbs in URLs like /getVehicles is not RESTful.
Galti mat karna: yeh kehna ki "REST matlab JSON aur HTTP use karna". JSON zaroori nahi hai, aur /getVehicles jaise URL mein verb wala HTTP RESTful nahi hai.
02 REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC: when would you use each?REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC: kab kaunsa use karoge?
What they're really testing: that you choose by consumer and use case (public vs mobile UI vs internal services), not by fashion.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum consumer aur use case dekh ke choose karte ho (public vs mobile UI vs internal services), fashion dekh ke nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I pick based on who consumes the API. REST is my default for public and partner APIs: it is standard, every language and tool understands it, and GET responses cache well in CDNs. GraphQL fits when one client, typically a mobile app or a rich dashboard, needs flexible data from many related objects in one round trip; for example a vehicle page that needs the vehicle, its photos, and open service appointments, where REST would need several calls or return too much. gRPC fits internal service-to-service calls: binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, generated typed clients, and streaming, so it is fast and strict. The trade-offs: REST can over- or under-fetch, GraphQL makes caching and query-cost control harder, and gRPC is hard to use from browsers and hard to read when debugging.

Main dekhta hoon ki API kaun consume karega. Public aur partner APIs ke liye REST mera default hai: standard hai, har language aur tool samajhta hai, aur GET responses CDN mein achhe se cache hote hain. GraphQL tab fit hota hai jab ek client, aam taur pe mobile app ya rich dashboard, ko kai related objects se flexible data ek round trip mein chahiye; jaise vehicle page jise vehicle, uski photos aur open service appointments chahiye, jahan REST mein kai calls lagtin ya zyada data aata. gRPC internal service-to-service calls ke liye fit hai: HTTP/2 pe binary Protocol Buffers, generated typed clients, aur streaming, toh fast aur strict hai. Trade-offs: REST over ya under-fetch kar sakta hai, GraphQL mein caching aur query-cost control mushkil hota hai, aur gRPC browser se use karna aur debug karte waqt padhna mushkil hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

GraphQL moves complexity to the server: one innocent-looking nested query can fan out into thousands of database calls (the N+1 problem inside resolvers), so you need batching (DataLoader), query depth and cost limits, and persisted queries. Authorization must be done per field, not per endpoint. gRPC needs gRPC-Web and a proxy for browsers, and load balancing is trickier because HTTP/2 keeps long-lived connections, so you balance per request, not per connection. Many companies mix them: gRPC between internal services, a REST or GraphQL layer at the edge for external clients.

GraphQL complexity server pe daal deta hai: ek seedhi-saadi dikhne wali nested query hazaaron database calls mein phail sakti hai (resolvers ke andar N+1 problem), toh batching (DataLoader), query depth aur cost limits, aur persisted queries chahiye. Authorization har field pe karni padti hai, sirf endpoint pe nahi. gRPC ko browsers ke liye gRPC-Web aur proxy chahiye, aur load balancing tricky hai kyunki HTTP/2 lambe connections rakhta hai, toh per request balance karna padta hai, per connection nahi. Kai companies mix karti hain: internal services ke beech gRPC, aur bahar ke clients ke liye edge pe REST ya GraphQL layer.

Common mistake: calling one of them "better". Each is a trade-off; say which consumer and constraint make you choose it.
Galti mat karna: kisi ek ko "better" bolna. Har ek trade-off hai; batao kaunsa consumer aur constraint tumhe use choose karwata hai.
03 How do you version an API without breaking existing clients?Existing clients ko tode bina API version kaise karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you know the versioning styles, and above all the rule that within a version you only add, never remove or rename.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tumhe versioning styles pata hain, aur sabse zyada yeh rule ki ek version ke andar sirf add karte hain, kabhi remove ya rename nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

First, I try hard not to need a new version: within a version I only make additive changes, like new optional fields or new endpoints, and never remove, rename or change a field's type. When a breaking change is truly needed, I use explicit versioning. My default is the URL path, /v1/vehicles and /v2/vehicles, because it is obvious in logs, easy to route and easy to test. Header versioning, like an API-Version date header, keeps URLs clean and is what Stripe does, but it is less visible. Then I run v1 and v2 side by side, mark v1 with Deprecation and Sunset headers, publish a migration guide, watch logs to see who still calls v1, and only retire it after the sunset date. The trade-off is that every live version is code you maintain, so versions should be rare.

Pehle toh main poori koshish karta hoon ki naya version chahiye hi na: ek version ke andar main sirf additive changes karta hoon, jaise naye optional fields ya naye endpoints, aur kabhi field remove, rename ya uska type change nahi karta. Jab sach mein breaking change chahiye, tab explicit versioning use karta hoon. Mera default URL path hai, /v1/vehicles aur /v2/vehicles, kyunki logs mein saaf dikhta hai, route aur test karna aasaan hai. Header versioning, jaise API-Version date header, URLs saaf rakhta hai aur Stripe yahi karta hai, par kam visible hai. Phir main v1 aur v2 saath chalata hoon, v1 pe Deprecation aur Sunset headers lagata hoon, migration guide publish karta hoon, logs se dekhta hoon kaun abhi bhi v1 call kar raha hai, aur sunset date ke baad hi use retire karta hoon. Trade-off yeh hai ki har live version maintain karna padta hai, toh versions kam hone chahiye.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Inside the server I avoid copying the whole codebase per version. A common pattern is one internal model plus thin translation layers per version: the v1 adapter maps the new internal shape back to the old response. Stripe-style date versions do this as a chain of small transformations applied in order. Version only the public contract, not every internal service. For mobile apps, remember old app versions stay installed for a long time, so sunset periods must be long, and you can force-upgrade only as a last resort.

Server ke andar main har version ke liye poora codebase copy nahi karta. Common pattern hai ek internal model aur har version ke liye patli translation layers: v1 adapter naye internal shape ko purane response mein map kar deta hai. Stripe jaise date versions yahi chhote transformations ki chain se karte hain jo order mein lagti hain. Sirf public contract ko version karo, har internal service ko nahi. Mobile apps ke liye yaad rakho ki purane app versions lambe time tak install rehte hain, toh sunset period lamba hona chahiye, aur force-upgrade sirf last resort hai.

Common mistake: treating versioning as a licence to break things ("we'll just ship v3"). Every version doubles support work; additive evolution is the real answer.
Galti mat karna: versioning ko cheezein todne ka licence samajhna ("bas v3 ship kar denge"). Har version support ka kaam badha deta hai; additive evolution hi asli jawab hai.
04 Cursor-based vs offset pagination: explain the difference.Cursor-based vs offset pagination: farak samjhao.
What they're really testing: that offset gets slower as N grows and shifts when data changes, while a cursor uses the last seen sort key and stays fast and stable.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki offset N badhne pe slow hota hai aur data badalne pe khisakta hai, jabki cursor last dekhi sort key use karta hai aur fast aur stable rehta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Offset pagination says "skip N, take 20", like LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000. It is simple and supports jumping to page 57, but the database still reads and discards all N skipped rows, so deep pages get slower, and if rows are inserted or deleted while someone pages, items shift and they see duplicates or miss items. Cursor pagination returns an opaque cursor encoding the last item's sort key, say created_at plus id; the next query is WHERE (created_at, id) < (cursor values) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, which uses the index to seek directly, so page 5000 costs the same as page 1 and new rows do not shift anything. For a vehicle inventory feed or infinite scroll I use cursors. The trade-off: no random page jumps and no cheap total count, so for a small admin table with page numbers, offset is fine.

Offset pagination kehta hai "N skip karo, 20 lo", jaise LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000. Simple hai aur page 57 pe jump support karta hai, par database phir bhi saari N skipped rows padh ke phenkta hai, toh gehre pages slow hote hain, aur agar koi paging kar raha hai aur beech mein rows insert ya delete hoti hain, toh items khisak jaate hain aur use duplicates dikhte hain ya items miss ho jaate hain. Cursor pagination ek opaque cursor deta hai jisme last item ki sort key encoded hoti hai, jaise created_at plus id; agli query hoti hai WHERE (created_at, id) < (cursor values) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, jo index se seedha seek karti hai, toh page 5000 ka cost page 1 jitna hai aur nayi rows kuch nahi khiskaatin. Vehicle inventory feed ya infinite scroll ke liye main cursors use karta hoon. Trade-off: random page jump nahi aur sasta total count nahi, toh page numbers wali chhoti admin table ke liye offset theek hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The sort key must be unique and indexed, which is why I add id as a tie-breaker: sorting only by price would let two cars with the same price be skipped or repeated at a page boundary. I encode the cursor (for example base64 of JSON) so clients treat it as opaque and I can change its internals later; I may sign it to prevent tampering. I fetch limit + 1 rows to know if there is a next page without a separate count. If the filters change, the cursor is invalid; the client must start over.

Sort key unique aur indexed honi chahiye, isliye main tie-breaker ke liye id jodta hoon: sirf price se sort karne pe same price wali do gaadiyan page boundary pe skip ya repeat ho sakti hain. Main cursor ko encode karta hoon (jaise JSON ka base64) taaki clients use opaque maanein aur main baad mein uske internals badal sakoon; tampering rokne ke liye sign bhi kar sakta hoon. Main limit + 1 rows fetch karta hoon taaki bina alag count query ke pata chale ki next page hai ya nahi. Agar filters badal jaayein, toh cursor invalid hai; client ko shuru se start karna hoga.

Common mistake: saying the cursor is "the page number" or sorting by a non-unique column without a tie-breaker.
Galti mat karna: cursor ko "page number" bolna, ya bina tie-breaker ke non-unique column se sort karna.
05 Which HTTP status codes would you return for common scenarios?Common scenarios mein kaunse HTTP status codes return karoge?
What they're really testing: that you know when each of 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429 and 500 applies, especially the confusing pairs 401/403 and 400/422.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tumhe pata hai 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429 aur 500 kab lagte hain, khaaskar confusing pairs 401/403 aur 400/422.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Take a service-appointment API. GET a vehicle returns 200. POST /appointments that books returns 201 with a Location header. DELETE returns 204, no body. If the JSON is malformed or a field has the wrong type, 400. If the JSON is valid but breaks a business rule, like a slot in the past, 422. No or expired token is 401, meaning "who are you?". A valid user from rooftop 7 trying to read rooftop 42's data is 403, "I know you, but no". Unknown VIN is 404. Slot already booked, or a stale version on update, is 409. Too many requests is 429 with Retry-After. An unhandled bug is 500 with a generic message and a request ID, never a stack trace. The point is that clients branch on these numbers, so they are part of the contract, and I never return 200 with an error inside.

Ek service-appointment API lo. Vehicle ka GET 200 deta hai. POST /appointments jo booking kare, 201 deta hai Location header ke saath. DELETE 204 deta hai, bina body. Agar JSON toota hai ya field ka type galat hai, toh 400. Agar JSON valid hai par business rule tootta hai, jaise past ka slot, toh 422. Token nahi hai ya expired hai toh 401, matlab "tum kaun ho?". Rooftop 7 ka valid user rooftop 42 ka data padhne ki koshish kare toh 403, "tumhe jaanta hoon, par nahi". Anjaan VIN 404 hai. Slot pehle se book, ya update pe purana version, 409 hai. Bahut zyada requests 429 hai Retry-After ke saath. Unhandled bug 500 hai generic message aur request ID ke saath, stack trace kabhi nahi. Point yeh hai ki clients in numbers pe branch karte hain, toh yeh contract ka hissa hain, aur main kabhi 200 ke andar error nahi bhejta.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Some teams return 404 instead of 403 for resources in another tenant, so they do not even reveal that the resource exists; I would do that for cross-rooftop data. 202 is for accepted-but-not-done async work, 503 plus Retry-After for planned downtime or overload, and 304 Not Modified when the client's ETag still matches. 5xx errors should be retried by clients with backoff; most 4xx should not be retried unchanged, except 429 and sometimes 409. I pair codes with one consistent error body, for example RFC 9457 Problem Details.

Kuch teams doosre tenant ke resource ke liye 403 ki jagah 404 deti hain, taaki yeh bhi pata na chale ki resource exist karta hai; cross-rooftop data ke liye main yahi karunga. 202 accepted-par-abhi-nahi-hua async kaam ke liye hai, 503 plus Retry-After planned downtime ya overload ke liye, aur 304 Not Modified jab client ka ETag abhi bhi match kare. 5xx errors ko clients backoff ke saath retry karein; zyada tar 4xx ko bina badle retry nahi karna chahiye, sivaay 429 aur kabhi kabhi 409 ke. Main codes ke saath ek consistent error body deta hoon, jaise RFC 9457 Problem Details.

Common mistake: mixing up 401 and 403. 401 is about identity (not logged in), 403 is about permission (logged in, not allowed).
