Galti mat karna: 401 aur 403 mix karna. 401 identity ke baare mein hai (logged in nahi), 403 permission ke baare mein (logged in hai, allowed nahi).
06 How would you design an endpoint for an operation that takes 30 seconds?Jo operation 30 second leta hai, uska endpoint kaise design karoge?
What they're really testing: that you do not hold an HTTP connection open; you return 202 Accepted with a job ID and let the client poll a job URL or receive a webhook.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum HTTP connection khula nahi rakhte; 202 Accepted ke saath job ID dete ho aur client job URL poll kare ya webhook paaye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I would not keep the request open for 30 seconds, because load balancers and proxies time out, mobile networks drop, and the client retries and starts the work twice, while my server threads sit blocked. Instead, say for exporting a rooftop's full inventory, POST /v1/exports validates the input, creates a job row with status queued, puts a message on a queue, and immediately returns 202 Accepted with the job ID and a Location: /v1/jobs/7f3a header. A background worker does the export and updates the job to running, then succeeded with a result URL, or failed with an error. The client polls GET /v1/jobs/7f3a, respecting Retry-After, or registers a webhook we call when it finishes. The trade-off is more moving parts: a queue, a job store, and polling traffic.

Main request 30 second tak khuli nahi rakhunga, kyunki load balancers aur proxies time out ho jaate hain, mobile network girta hai, aur client retry karke kaam do baar shuru kar deta hai, jabki mere server threads atke rehte hain. Iske bajaye, maan lo ek rooftop ki poori inventory export karni hai: POST /v1/exports input validate karta hai, status queued ke saath ek job row banata hai, queue pe message daalta hai, aur turant 202 Accepted return karta hai job ID aur Location: /v1/jobs/7f3a header ke saath. Background worker export karta hai aur job ko running, phir result URL ke saath succeeded, ya error ke saath failed karta hai. Client GET /v1/jobs/7f3a poll karta hai, Retry-After maan ke, ya ek webhook register karta hai jise hum khatam hone pe call karte hain. Trade-off: zyada moving parts, ek queue, ek job store, aur polling traffic.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Make the POST idempotent with an idempotency key, so a retry returns the same job instead of creating a second one. The worker must also be idempotent because queues deliver at least once. Webhooks need signing (an HMAC signature header) so the client can verify they came from us, plus retries with backoff, since the client's endpoint may be down. Offer cancel via DELETE /v1/jobs/{id} or a cancellation sub-resource, keep job records with a TTL, and report progress (for example percent done) so the UI can show it. For real-time UIs, server-sent events or WebSockets can replace polling.

POST ko idempotency key se idempotent banao, taaki retry pe doosra job banne ki jagah wahi job wapas mile. Worker bhi idempotent hona chahiye kyunki queues at least once deliver karti hain. Webhooks ko signing chahiye (HMAC signature header) taaki client verify kar sake ki hamari taraf se aaye, plus backoff ke saath retries, kyunki client ka endpoint down ho sakta hai. Cancel ke liye DELETE /v1/jobs/{id} ya cancellation sub-resource do, job records TTL ke saath rakho, aur progress batao (jaise kitna percent hua) taaki UI dikha sake. Real-time UIs ke liye server-sent events ya WebSockets polling ki jagah le sakte hain.

Common mistake: "just increase the timeout". It hides the problem, blocks server capacity, and still breaks on retries and network drops.
Galti mat karna: "bas timeout badha do". Isse problem chhupti hai, server capacity block hoti hai, aur retries aur network drop pe phir bhi tootti hai.
07 What is HATEOAS and is it worth implementing?HATEOAS kya hai aur kya ise implement karna worth hai?
What they're really testing: that you know responses include links to the next possible actions, and can give an honest view that it is rarely implemented because of overhead.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tumhe pata hai response mein aage ke possible actions ke links hote hain, aur tum honestly bata sako ki overhead ki wajah se yeh kam implement hota hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

HATEOAS stands for Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State. The idea is that an API response works like a web page: besides the data, it contains links to what the client can do next. For example, a booked service appointment returns _links for self, reschedule and cancel; once it is completed, the server stops sending cancel, so the client shows the Cancel button only when the link exists. The benefit is that business rules and URLs live on the server, and clients are less coupled. Honestly, it is rarely implemented fully: clients are usually hand-written against documentation anyway, the payloads get bigger, and there is little tooling. I would use it selectively, for state-driven actions and pagination links like next, rather than everywhere.

HATEOAS ka matlab hai Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State. Idea yeh hai ki API response web page ki tarah kaam kare: data ke saath usme links hon ki client aage kya kar sakta hai. Jaise, ek booked service appointment self, reschedule aur cancel ke _links return karta hai; complete hone ke baad server cancel bhejna band kar deta hai, toh client Cancel button tabhi dikhata hai jab link ho. Faayda yeh hai ki business rules aur URLs server pe rehte hain, aur clients kam coupled hote hain. Sach kahoon toh yeh kam hi poora implement hota hai: clients waise bhi documentation padh ke haath se likhe jaate hain, payloads bade ho jaate hain, aur tooling kam hai. Main ise selectively use karunga, state-driven actions aur next jaise pagination links ke liye, har jagah nahi.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

HATEOAS is level 3 of the Richardson Maturity Model and part of Fielding's uniform interface constraint, so strictly speaking most "REST" APIs are not fully RESTful. Formats exist for it, like HAL (_links), JSON:API and Siren. It helps most for long-lived APIs with many independent clients and workflow-like resources, where the server can change a URL or add a step without clients redeploying. It does not remove the need for documentation, because clients still need to know what a link relation like cancel means.

HATEOAS Richardson Maturity Model ka level 3 hai aur Fielding ke uniform interface constraint ka hissa hai, toh strictly bolein toh zyada tar "REST" APIs poori tarah RESTful nahi hain. Iske formats hain, jaise HAL (_links), JSON:API aur Siren. Yeh sabse zyada kaam aata hai lambe chalne wali APIs mein jinke kai independent clients hon aur workflow jaise resources hon, jahan server URL badal sake ya step add kar sake bina clients redeploy kiye. Isse documentation ki zaroorat khatam nahi hoti, kyunki clients ko phir bhi pata hona chahiye ki cancel jaisa link relation matlab kya hai.

Common mistake: either not knowing the term or claiming every good API must have it. Show you know it and can judge the cost.
Galti mat karna: ya toh term hi na pata hona, ya yeh kehna ki har achhi API mein yeh hona hi chahiye. Dikhao ki tum jaante ho aur cost judge kar sakte ho.
08 What makes an API change backward-compatible?Kaunsa API change backward-compatible hota hai?
What they're really testing: the rules add-never-remove, new fields optional, never change a type, and deprecate with headers and a migration guide.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: rules jaise add karo kabhi remove nahi, naye fields optional, type kabhi mat badlo, aur headers aur migration guide ke saath deprecate karo.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A change is backward-compatible if every existing, correctly written client keeps working without changing its code. Safe changes are additive: a new endpoint, a new field in a response, a new optional request field with a sensible default, a new optional filter. Breaking changes are removing or renaming a field, changing its type, for example price from a number to a string, changing units such as dollars to cents, making an optional field required, or changing status codes. For example, if we want to rename mileage to odometer_miles on vehicles, I add the new field, keep sending both, mark the old one deprecated in docs and with the Deprecation and Sunset headers, publish a migration guide, watch usage, and remove it only in the next major version. The cost is carrying some duplicate fields for a while.

Change backward-compatible tab hai jab har existing, sahi likha hua client bina code badle chalta rahe. Safe changes additive hote hain: naya endpoint, response mein naya field, sensible default ke saath naya optional request field, naya optional filter. Breaking changes hain field hataana ya rename karna, uska type badalna, jaise price number se string, units badalna jaise dollars se cents, optional field ko required banana, ya status codes badalna. Example: agar vehicles pe mileage ko odometer_miles rename karna hai, toh main naya field add karta hoon, dono bhejta rehta hoon, purane ko docs mein aur Deprecation aur Sunset headers se deprecated mark karta hoon, migration guide publish karta hoon, usage dekhta hoon, aur agle major version mein hi hataata hoon. Cost yeh hai ki kuch time duplicate fields saath le ke chalne padte hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Compatibility also depends on client discipline, so I document the tolerant reader rule: ignore unknown fields, handle unknown enum values. Even then, adding an enum value is risky for strict clients, so I announce it. Behavioural changes are breaking too: stricter validation, different default sort order, a new rate limit. I protect the contract with an OpenAPI spec and automated diff checks in CI that fail the build on a breaking change, plus consumer-driven contract tests (for example Pact) for internal consumers.

Compatibility client ke discipline pe bhi depend karti hai, toh main tolerant reader rule document karta hoon: unknown fields ignore karo, unknown enum values handle karo. Phir bhi strict clients ke liye enum value add karna risky hai, toh main use announce karta hoon. Behaviour changes bhi breaking hote hain: stricter validation, alag default sort order, naya rate limit. Main contract ko OpenAPI spec aur CI mein automated diff checks se protect karta hoon jo breaking change pe build fail kar dete hain, plus internal consumers ke liye consumer-driven contract tests (jaise Pact).

Common mistake: thinking only field removal is breaking. Type changes, new required fields and stricter validation break clients too.
Galti mat karna: sochna ki sirf field hataana breaking hai. Type change, naye required fields aur stricter validation bhi clients ko todte hain.
09 How do you make a POST endpoint for resource creation idempotent?Resource banane wale POST endpoint ko idempotent kaise banate ho?
What they're really testing: a client-generated idempotency key or unique ID, and that a duplicate returns the original result instead of creating a second resource.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: client ka banaya idempotency key ya unique ID, aur ki duplicate request doosra resource banane ki jagah original result lautaye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

POST is not idempotent by spec, so a retry after a lost response can create a duplicate, like two service appointments for one tap. I have the client generate a UUID once per user action and send it as an Idempotency-Key header on the first attempt and every retry. On the server, I atomically claim the key in Redis or a table with a unique constraint, storing a hash of the request body and status "in progress". After creating the appointment, I store the 201 response against the key with a TTL, say 24 hours. If the same key arrives again with the same body, I return the stored response, not a new booking. Same key with a different body is a client bug, so 422; if the first request is still running, 409 so the client retries shortly. The trade-off is extra storage and a lookup on every create.

Spec ke hisaab se POST idempotent nahi hai, toh response khone ke baad retry se duplicate ban sakta hai, jaise ek tap pe do service appointments. Main client se har user action ke liye ek baar UUID banwata hoon aur use pehli try aur har retry mein Idempotency-Key header mein bhejwata hoon. Server pe main Redis ya unique constraint wali table mein key ko atomically claim karta hoon, request body ka hash aur status "in progress" store karke. Appointment banne ke baad key ke against 201 response TTL ke saath store karta hoon, jaise 24 ghante. Agar same key same body ke saath dobara aaye, toh main stored response lauta deta hoon, nayi booking nahi. Same key alag body ke saath client ka bug hai, toh 422; agar pehli request abhi chal rahi hai, toh 409 taaki client thodi der mein retry kare. Trade-off: har create pe extra storage aur ek lookup.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The claim must be atomic (SET key value NX EX 86400 in Redis, or INSERT with a unique constraint) so two concurrent retries cannot both proceed. If the key store and the business database are separate, a crash between them can still leave a gap; storing the key in the same database transaction as the appointment closes it. Alternatives: let the client pick the ID and use PUT /v1/appointments/{uuid}, which is idempotent by definition, or use a natural unique key such as (vehicle VIN, slot). The TTL must be longer than the client's retry window. Topic 05 covers this in depth.

Claim atomic hona chahiye (Redis mein SET key value NX EX 86400, ya unique constraint ke saath INSERT) taaki do concurrent retries dono aage na badh sakein. Agar key store aur business database alag hain, toh dono ke beech crash hone pe gap reh sakta hai; key ko appointment ke saath same database transaction mein store karne se yeh band ho jaata hai. Alternatives: client ko ID chunne do aur PUT /v1/appointments/{uuid} use karo, jo definition se idempotent hai, ya natural unique key use karo jaise (vehicle VIN, slot). TTL client ki retry window se lamba hona chahiye. Topic 05 isko deep cover karta hai.

Common mistake: generating the idempotency key on the server, or a new key on each retry. It must come from the client and stay the same across retries of one action.
Galti mat karna: idempotency key server pe banana, ya har retry pe nayi key banana. Key client se aani chahiye aur ek action ki saari retries mein same rehni chahiye.
10 How would you implement rate limiting and communicate it to clients?Rate limiting kaise implement karoge aur clients ko kaise bataoge?
What they're really testing: an algorithm (token bucket or sliding window) in a shared store, and clear communication with 429, Retry-After and rate-limit headers.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ek algorithm (token bucket ya sliding window) shared store mein, aur 429, Retry-After aur rate-limit headers ke saath saaf communication.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I rate-limit per API key or user, and per IP for anonymous traffic. My usual algorithm is a token bucket: each key has a bucket of, say, 10 tokens refilling at 5 per second; each request takes one, and an empty bucket means reject. It allows short bursts but caps the average. Sliding window is the alternative when I want a smooth "N per rolling minute"; fixed windows are simpler but allow double bursts at the boundary. Because we run many instances, the state lives in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script or INCR plus EXPIRE, never in per-instance memory. When I reject, I return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After, and on every response I send limit, remaining and reset headers, so a partner integration can slow down before hitting the wall. The trade-off is an extra Redis call per request, which I keep cheap.

Main API key ya user ke hisaab se rate-limit karta hoon, aur anonymous traffic ke liye IP ke hisaab se. Mera usual algorithm token bucket hai: har key ka ek bucket, maan lo 10 tokens ka, jo 5 per second se bharta hai; har request ek token leti hai, aur khaali bucket matlab reject. Yeh chhote bursts allow karta hai par average ko cap karta hai. Jab smooth "rolling minute mein N" chahiye tab sliding window alternative hai; fixed window simple hai par boundary pe double burst allow karta hai. Kyunki hum kai instances chalate hain, state Redis mein rehti hai, Lua script ya INCR plus EXPIRE se atomically update hoti hai, kabhi per-instance memory mein nahi. Reject karte waqt main 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After ke saath bhejta hoon, aur har response pe limit, remaining aur reset headers bhejta hoon, taaki partner integration deewar se takrane se pehle slow ho sake. Trade-off: har request pe ek extra Redis call, jise main sasta rakhta hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Decide what happens if Redis is down: fail open (allow traffic, protect availability) or fail closed (reject, protect the backend); for most read APIs I fail open with a local fallback limit. Enforce limits at the API gateway so every service gets them for free. Use tiers (different limits per plan or per partner) and separate, stricter limits on expensive endpoints like exports or login. Headers: Retry-After is standard HTTP; X-RateLimit-* is a widely used convention; the IETF is standardising RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy. Clients should back off exponentially with jitter.

Decide karo ki Redis down ho toh kya hoga: fail open (traffic allow karo, availability bachao) ya fail closed (reject karo, backend bachao); zyada tar read APIs ke liye main local fallback limit ke saath fail open karta hoon. Limits API gateway pe enforce karo taaki har service ko free mein mil jaayein. Tiers use karo (har plan ya partner ki alag limit) aur exports ya login jaise mehenge endpoints pe alag, zyada strict limits. Headers: Retry-After standard HTTP hai; X-RateLimit-* widely used convention hai; IETF RateLimit aur RateLimit-Policy standardise kar raha hai. Clients ko jitter ke saath exponential back off karna chahiye.

Common mistake: an in-memory counter on each server (the limit multiplies by the number of instances) or returning 429 with no hint of when to retry.
Galti mat karna: har server pe in-memory counter (limit instances ki ginti se multiply ho jaati hai) ya 429 bhejna bina yeh bataye ki kab retry karein.

Topic 09 · VERY COMMONTopic 09 · Bahut common

Database DesignDatabase Design

How to shape tables so each fact lives in one place, why a schema that is fine in development falls over in production (N+1 queries, locking migrations, one database that is no longer enough), and how seniors change a live schema without downtime.

Tables ko aise design karna ki har fact ek hi jagah rahe, kyun development mein theek chalne wala schema production mein gir jaata hai (N+1 queries, lock lagane wali migrations, ek database jo ab kaafi nahi), aur seniors live schema ko bina downtime kaise badalte hain.

Level 0 The storyKahani

Imagine the service department of a small car dealership that tracks everything in one giant spreadsheet. Every time a car comes in, someone adds a row: repair order number, date, customer name, customer phone, the car's VIN, the model, and the work done, typed as "oil change, tire rotation" in a single cell.

At first it is perfect. One sheet, easy to read. Then real life happens:

  • A regular customer changes her phone number. She has twelve past visits, so her phone is typed in twelve rows. Someone updates the latest row only. Now the sheet has two different phone numbers for the same person, and nobody knows which is right. This is an update anomaly.
  • The manager asks, "how many tire rotations did we do last month?" The answer is hidden inside text cells like "oil change, tire rotation", so someone has to read them by hand.
  • A customer's only visit row is deleted because it was a duplicate, and with it the only record of that customer. This is a delete anomaly.
  • A new customer calls to book but has no visit yet. There is no row to put them in without inventing a fake visit. This is an insert anomaly.

The fix is to stop cramming different kinds of facts into one sheet. Keep one list of customers, one list of vehicles, one list of repair orders, and link them. Each fact is written once; everything else just points to it. That is the heart of database design: deciding which tables exist, what columns they hold, how they link to each other, and how the whole thing will behave when it has millions of rows, hundreds of requests per second, and has to change shape without switching the business off.

Analogy: a society's WhatsApp group where everyone keeps re-posting the maintenance schedule. After a month there are five versions and nobody knows which is current. A good society pins one notice and everyone refers to it. A good schema is the pinned notice.

Interviewers ask this topic to separate people whose schema only worked on a laptop from people whose schema survived production: the N+1 query that exploded at scale, the migration that locked a table at noon, the single database that ran out of room.

Ek chhoti car dealership ka service department socho jo sab kuch ek badi spreadsheet mein track karta hai. Har baar jab gaadi aati hai, koi ek row jod deta hai: repair order number, date, customer ka naam, customer ka phone, gaadi ka VIN, model, aur kya kaam hua, ek hi cell mein "oil change, tire rotation" likh ke.

Shuru mein sab perfect hai. Ek sheet, padhna aasaan. Phir asli zindagi aati hai:

  • Ek regular customer apna phone number badalti hai. Uske baarah purane visits hain, toh uska phone baarah rows mein likha hai. Koi sirf latest row update karta hai. Ab sheet mein ek hi insaan ke do alag phone numbers hain, aur kisi ko nahi pata kaunsa sahi hai. Isko update anomaly kehte hain.
  • Manager poochta hai, "pichhle mahine humne kitne tire rotations kiye?" Jawab "oil change, tire rotation" jaise text cells ke andar chhupa hai, toh kisi ko haath se padhna padega.
  • Ek customer ki ikloti visit row delete ho jaati hai kyunki woh duplicate thi, aur uske saath us customer ka ikloti record bhi chala jaata hai. Yeh delete anomaly hai.
  • Ek naya customer booking ke liye call karta hai par abhi tak koi visit nahi hui. Fake visit banaye bina use kahin rakhne ki jagah hi nahi hai. Yeh insert anomaly hai.

Fix yeh hai ki alag-alag type ke facts ko ek sheet mein thoosna band karo. Customers ki ek list rakho, vehicles ki ek list, repair orders ki ek list, aur inhe link karo. Har fact ek baar likha jaata hai; baaki sab bas us taraf point karte hain. Yahi database design ka dil hai: decide karna ki kaunsi tables hongi, unme kaunse columns honge, woh ek doosre se kaise judenge, aur yeh sab kaise behave karega jab millions rows hon, har second sau-sau requests aayein, aur business band kiye bina iski shape badalni pade.

Analogy: society ka WhatsApp group jahan har koi maintenance schedule baar-baar repost karta rehta hai. Ek mahine baad paanch versions hain aur kisi ko nahi pata kaunsa current hai. Achhi society ek notice pin kar deti hai aur sab usi ko refer karte hain. Achha schema woh pinned notice hai.

Interviewers yeh topic isliye poochte hain taaki un logon ko alag kar sakein jinka schema sirf laptop pe chala, un logon se jinka schema production mein bacha: woh N+1 query jo scale pe phat gayi, woh migration jisne dopahar mein table lock kar di, woh single database jisme jagah khatam ho gayi.

Level 1 Keys, relationships and normalisationKeys, relationships aur normalisation

Quick refresher: a table holds one kind of thing (customers), each row is one of them (one customer), each column is one property (phone).

  • Primary key (PK): a column (or set of columns) whose value is unique for every row and never empty, for example customers.id. It is the row's identity. The database automatically indexes it (see Topic 01).
  • Foreign key (FK): a column in one table that holds the primary key of a row in another table, for example vehicles.customer_id holding the id of the owner. It is the link between tables.
  • Relationships come in three shapes. One-to-one: a vehicle has one warranty record. One-to-many: one customer owns many vehicles; the FK goes on the "many" side (vehicles.customer_id). Many-to-many: a repair order includes many services, and a service (say "oil change") appears on many repair orders. That shape needs a third table, which we will see in Level 2.
  • JOIN: the SQL operation that stitches linked rows back together at read time, matching FK to PK.

Normalisation: storing each fact exactly once

Normalisation is a step-by-step method for removing duplication from a schema. The steps are called normal forms. You only need the first three for interviews:

  1. 1NF (First Normal Form): every cell holds one single (atomic) value, there are no repeating groups like phone1, phone2, phone3 or "oil change, tire rotation" in one cell, and every row can be identified by a key. Fix: one row per value, usually in a separate table.
  2. 2NF: be in 1NF, and every non-key column must depend on the whole primary key. This only bites when the key has several columns. In a table keyed by (ro_id, service_id), a column service_name depends only on service_id, which is half the key. It belongs in the services table.
  3. 3NF: be in 2NF, and every non-key column must depend only on the key, not on another non-key column. In a repair order table, customer_phone depends on customer_id, not on the repair order itself. That is a "transitive" dependency; move the phone to customers.

Remember the classic line: every non-key column must depend on "the key (1NF), the whole key (2NF), and nothing but the key (3NF)".

Quick yaad: table ek type ki cheez rakhti hai (customers), har row unme se ek hai (ek customer), har column ek property hai (phone).

  • Primary key (PK): ek column (ya columns ka set) jiski value har row ke liye unique hai aur kabhi khaali nahi, jaise customers.id. Yeh row ki pehchaan hai. Database is pe automatically index bana deta hai (Topic 01 dekho).
  • Foreign key (FK): ek table ka column jisme doosri table ki kisi row ki primary key hoti hai, jaise vehicles.customer_id jisme owner ki id hai. Yahi tables ke beech ka link hai.
  • Relationships teen shapes mein aate hain. One-to-one: ek vehicle ka ek warranty record. One-to-many: ek customer ki kai gaadiyan; FK "many" wali side pe jaati hai (vehicles.customer_id). Many-to-many: ek repair order mein kai services hoti hain, aur ek service (jaise "oil change") kai repair orders pe aati hai. Is shape ke liye teesri table chahiye, jo Level 2 mein dekhenge.
  • JOIN: SQL ka woh operation jo read ke time linked rows ko wapas jodta hai, FK ko PK se match karke.

Normalisation: har fact bilkul ek baar store karna

Normalisation schema se duplication hatane ka step-by-step tarika hai. Steps ko normal forms kehte hain. Interview ke liye pehle teen kaafi hain:

  1. 1NF (First Normal Form): har cell mein ek hi (atomic) value ho, koi repeating groups na hon jaise phone1, phone2, phone3 ya ek cell mein "oil change, tire rotation", aur har row ek key se pehchaani ja sake. Fix: har value ki ek row, aam taur pe alag table mein.
  2. 2NF: 1NF mein ho, aur har non-key column poori primary key pe depend kare. Yeh tabhi dikkat deta hai jab key mein kai columns hon. (ro_id, service_id) key wali table mein service_name column sirf service_id pe depend karta hai, jo key ka aadha hissa hai. Uski jagah services table hai.
  3. 3NF: 2NF mein ho, aur har non-key column sirf key pe depend kare, kisi doosre non-key column pe nahi. Repair order table mein customer_phone customer_id pe depend karta hai, repair order pe nahi. Yeh "transitive" dependency hai; phone ko customers mein le jao.

Classic line yaad rakho: har non-key column ko depend karna chahiye "the key (1NF), the whole key (2NF), and nothing but the key (3NF)" pe.

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT,
  phone TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE vehicles (
  vin         CHAR(17) PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),  -- foreign key
  model       TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE repair_orders (
  id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  vin       CHAR(17) NOT NULL REFERENCES vehicles(vin),
  opened_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Now Asha's phone changes in one place, you can count tire rotations with a simple query, deleting a repair order no longer deletes the customer, and a new customer can exist before their first visit. The price you pay is that reading a full repair order now needs JOINs across tables. That trade-off (clean writes versus more work on reads) drives most of this topic.

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT,
  phone TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE vehicles (
  vin         CHAR(17) PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),  -- foreign key
  model       TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE repair_orders (
  id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  vin       CHAR(17) NOT NULL REFERENCES vehicles(vin),
  opened_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Ab Asha ka phone ek hi jagah badalta hai, tire rotations ek simple query se gin sakte ho, repair order delete karne se customer delete nahi hota, aur naya customer apni pehli visit se pehle bhi exist kar sakta hai. Keemat yeh hai ki poora repair order padhne ke liye ab tables ke beech JOINs chahiye. Yahi trade-off (saaf writes vs reads pe zyada kaam) is topic ke zyaadatar hisse ko chalata hai.

Level 2 How tables work together: junction tables, JOINs, N+1, poolsTables saath mein kaise kaam karti hain: junction tables, JOINs, N+1, pools

Many-to-many needs a junction table

One repair order has many services, and one service appears on many repair orders. You cannot put a single FK on either side, because each side has many of the other. The answer is a junction table (also called a join, link or bridge table): each row pairs one repair order with one service, and holds a foreign key to both. If the pairing has its own data (the price charged on this RO, technician hours), those columns live on the junction row, because they describe the pair, not either side alone.

Many-to-many ke liye junction table chahiye

Ek repair order mein kai services hain, aur ek service kai repair orders pe aati hai. Kisi bhi side pe ek FK nahi daal sakte, kyunki har side ke paas doosri side ke kai hain. Jawab hai junction table (join, link ya bridge table bhi kehte hain): har row ek repair order ko ek service ke saath jodti hai, aur dono ki foreign key rakhti hai. Agar is jodi ka apna data hai (is RO pe charge hua price, technician ke hours), toh woh columns junction row pe rehte hain, kyunki woh jodi ko describe karte hain, kisi ek side ko nahi.

CREATE TABLE services (
  id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE ro_services (
  ro_id         BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES repair_orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  service_id    BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES services(id),
  price_charged NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,   -- attribute of the PAIR
  PRIMARY KEY (ro_id, service_id)          -- one row per pair; leading column = ro_id
);
CREATE INDEX ON ro_services (service_id); -- for "which ROs used service X?"

-- Which repair orders included a tire rotation?
SELECT ro.id, ro.opened_at
FROM repair_orders ro
JOIN ro_services rs ON rs.ro_id = ro.id
JOIN services s     ON s.id = rs.service_id
WHERE s.name = 'Tire rotation';

Notice the second index: the composite primary key (ro_id, service_id) serves lookups by repair order, but by the left-prefix rule from Topic 01 it cannot serve lookups by service alone, so we add (service_id). If the same pair can legitimately repeat (the same service done twice on one RO), use a surrogate id primary key instead of the composite one.

The N+1 query problem

Most backends talk to the database through an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper, a library such as Sequelize, TypeORM, Prisma, Django ORM, Hibernate) that turns rows into objects. ORMs make it easy to write code like this:

Doosra index dekho: composite primary key (ro_id, service_id) repair order se lookups serve karti hai, par Topic 01 ke left-prefix rule ke hisaab se akele service se lookup serve nahi kar sakti, isliye (service_id) jodte hain. Agar same jodi sahi mein repeat ho sakti hai (ek RO pe same service do baar), toh composite ki jagah surrogate id primary key use karo.

N+1 query problem

Zyaadatar backends database se ek ORM ke through baat karte hain (Object-Relational Mapper, jaise Sequelize, TypeORM, Prisma, Django ORM, Hibernate), jo rows ko objects mein badalta hai. ORMs aisa code likhna bahut aasaan bana dete hain:

// Show the 50 latest repair orders with the customer's name
const orders = await RepairOrder.findAll({ limit: 50 });   // 1 query
for (const ro of orders) {
  const customer = await ro.getCustomer();                  // +1 query EACH time
  rows.push({ ro: ro.id, name: customer.name });
}
// Total: 1 + 50 = 51 queries for one page load

That is the N+1 problem: one query to get N parent rows, then one more query per row to get its related data. On a laptop with 5 test rows and the database on the same machine it feels instant. In production, each query is a network round trip, so if one round trip took 2 milliseconds, 51 of them add about 100 milliseconds before any real work, and the page with 500 rows fires 501 queries. It also floods the database with tiny queries and holds a pooled connection the whole time.

Yahi N+1 problem hai: N parent rows laane ke liye ek query, phir har row ka related data laane ke liye ek aur query. Laptop pe 5 test rows ke saath aur database same machine pe ho toh yeh instant lagta hai. Production mein har query ek network round trip hai, toh agar ek round trip 2 milliseconds le, toh 51 round trips kisi asli kaam se pehle hi lagbhag 100 milliseconds jod dete hain, aur 500 rows wala page 501 queries chala deta hai. Yeh database ko chhoti-chhoti queries se bhar bhi deta hai aur poore time ek pooled connection pakde rakhta hai.

-- Fix 1: one JOIN
SELECT ro.id, ro.opened_at, c.name
FROM repair_orders ro
JOIN vehicles  v ON v.vin = ro.vin
JOIN customers c ON c.id  = v.customer_id
ORDER BY ro.opened_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

// Fix 2: ask the ORM to eager-load (Sequelize style)
const orders = await RepairOrder.findAll({
  limit: 50,
  include: [{ model: Vehicle, include: [Customer] }]   // JOIN or batched IN queries
});

How to detect N+1: turn on query logging in development and look for the same query repeated with different ids; in production, an APM or tracing tool shows dozens of identical short DB spans inside one request; pg_stat_statements shows a simple query with an enormous call count; and some teams add tests that assert "this endpoint runs at most 3 queries". GraphQL APIs hit this constantly and use a DataLoader that batches all ids requested in one tick into a single IN query.

Connection pooling (the database-design angle)

Opening a database connection is expensive: a TCP handshake, often TLS encryption setup, authentication, and on the server side memory and bookkeeping. In Postgres each connection is a whole separate operating-system process. And databases have a hard ceiling: max_connections defaults to 100 in Postgres and 151 in MySQL.

A connection pool opens a fixed number of connections once and lends them out to requests, taking them back when each query or transaction ends. Without one, every request pays the setup cost, and under load the app opens connections until the database refuses new ones ("too many connections") and the whole site fails at once. Design implication: pool size multiplies with instances. Twenty app containers with a pool of 10 each want 200 connections, more than a default Postgres allows. That is why larger setups put a pooler such as PgBouncer or RDS Proxy between the apps and the database, and why long transactions (which hold a connection) are a design smell. Topic 03 covers the concurrency side.

N+1 kaise pakdein: development mein query logging on karo aur dekho ki same query alag-alag ids ke saath repeat ho rahi hai; production mein APM ya tracing tool ek request ke andar darjanon ek jaise chhote DB spans dikhata hai; pg_stat_statements ek simple query ka bahut bada call count dikhata hai; aur kuch teams tests likhti hain jo assert karte hain ki "yeh endpoint zyaada se zyaada 3 queries chalata hai". GraphQL APIs mein yeh baar-baar hota hai aur woh DataLoader use karte hain jo ek tick mein maangi gayi saari ids ko ek IN query mein batch kar deta hai.

Connection pooling (database design ke angle se)

Database connection kholna mehnga hai: TCP handshake, aksar TLS encryption setup, authentication, aur server side pe memory aur hisaab-kitaab. Postgres mein har connection ek poora alag operating-system process hai. Aur databases ki ek hard limit hoti hai: max_connections Postgres mein default 100 aur MySQL mein 151 hai.

Connection pool ek fixed number ke connections ek baar kholta hai aur requests ko udhaar deta hai, har query ya transaction khatam hone pe wapas le leta hai. Pool na ho toh har request setup ka cost deti hai, aur load mein app connections kholti jaati hai jab tak database naye connections mana na kar de ("too many connections") aur poori site ek saath gir jaati hai. Design ka matlab: pool size instances ke saath multiply hota hai. Bees app containers, har ek ka pool 10, matlab 200 connections chahiye, jo default Postgres se zyada hai. Isliye bade setups apps aur database ke beech PgBouncer ya RDS Proxy jaisa pooler rakhte hain, aur isliye lambi transactions (jo connection pakde rakhti hain) design smell hain. Concurrency wala hissa Topic 03 mein hai.

Level 3 Production trade-offsProduction ke trade-offs

Denormalisation: breaking the rules on purpose

Denormalisation means deliberately storing a copy of data you could compute with a JOIN, to make an important read faster. Examples: keeping customer_name on each repair order so the service drive's list screen needs no join; keeping an open_ro_count on the dealer row instead of counting every time; a materialized view (a saved query result the database stores as a table and refreshes on demand) for a dashboard; or a separate read model or search index (such as Elasticsearch) built from the main tables.

When: reads vastly outnumber writes, the read is latency-critical, the JOIN or aggregation has become measurably expensive, and the business can tolerate the copy being briefly stale. The costs: every write must now update more places (slower writes, more code), and if any path forgets, the copies drift apart and you are back to the spreadsheet's update anomaly. Keep copies in sync with the same transaction, a trigger, or an event, and have a way to rebuild them from the source of truth.

Not every copy is denormalisation. The price charged on a repair order is a historical fact; it should not change when the service's list price changes next year. Storing price_charged on the junction row is correct design, not a shortcut.

SQL vs NoSQL: it is about access patterns

SQL (relational) databases such as Postgres and MySQL give you tables, a fixed schema, JOINs, strong ACID transactions (Topic 02) and the freedom to ask new questions later with ad-hoc queries. NoSQL is a family: document stores (MongoDB) keep nested JSON-like documents; key-value stores (Redis, DynamoDB) look things up by key; wide-column stores (Cassandra) are built for enormous write volume spread over many machines; graph databases (Neo4j) are built for relationship traversal.

The honest decision rule is not "NoSQL for big data". A well-indexed Postgres handles very large tables. Choose by access pattern: if your data is relational, you need joins, multi-row transactions and flexible querying, pick SQL. If your access is simple and known in advance ("get everything for this key"), you need horizontal scale across many nodes out of the box, or the shape of each record varies a lot, a NoSQL store fits. DynamoDB, for example, rewards you for designing tables around the exact queries you will run and punishes queries you did not plan. The lines blur: Postgres has JSONB for flexible fields, and MongoDB has supported multi-document transactions since version 4.0.

Foreign key constraints and when teams skip them

A foreign key constraint makes the database itself enforce referential integrity: you cannot insert a vehicle for customer 999 if customer 999 does not exist, and you cannot delete a customer who still has vehicles unless you say what should happen (ON DELETE RESTRICT refuses, CASCADE deletes children too, SET NULL clears the link). This catches bugs that app code will eventually let through.

The cost: every child insert or update checks the parent (an index lookup and a small lock on the parent row), and every parent delete checks the children (so index the FK column; Postgres does not do it for you). Teams deliberately skip FK constraints in a few cases: very high write-throughput ingestion where the check is a measurable bottleneck; sharded databases where parent and child live on different servers (a constraint cannot reach across databases); microservices where each service owns its own database; and bulk-load pipelines. When they skip, they move the check into the application and run periodic "orphan row" checks, accepting temporary inconsistency.

Soft delete vs hard delete

A hard delete is a real DELETE: the row is gone. A soft delete keeps the row and marks it, usually with a nullable deleted_at timestamp. Soft delete gives an audit trail, an "undo" button, and keeps foreign keys valid (old repair orders still point to a soft-deleted customer). The price is that every query must remember WHERE deleted_at IS NULL; one forgotten filter shows deleted data, and the reverse bug makes live data seem to "disappear" (see Topic 13). Other costs: tables keep growing, and a unique email can no longer be reused, which you solve with a partial unique index.

Denormalisation: jaan-boojh ke rules todna

Denormalisation ka matlab hai jaan-boojh ke us data ki copy store karna jo tum JOIN se nikaal sakte the, taaki ek important read fast ho jaaye. Examples: har repair order pe customer_name rakhna taaki service drive ki list screen ko join na karna pade; har baar ginne ki jagah dealer row pe open_ro_count rakhna; dashboard ke liye materialized view (ek saved query result jise database table ki tarah store karta hai aur maangne pe refresh karta hai); ya main tables se bana alag read model ya search index (jaise Elasticsearch).

Kab: reads writes se bahut zyada hon, read latency-critical ho, JOIN ya aggregation measurably mehnga ho gaya ho, aur business copy ke thodi der stale rehne ko bardaasht kar sake. Cost: ab har write ko zyada jagah update karna padta hai (slow writes, zyada code), aur agar koi bhi path bhool gaya, toh copies alag-alag ho jaati hain aur tum wapas spreadsheet wali update anomaly pe aa jaate ho. Copies ko same transaction, trigger, ya event se sync rakho, aur source of truth se unhe dobara banane ka tarika rakho.

Har copy denormalisation nahi hai. Repair order pe charge hua price ek historical fact hai; agle saal service ka list price badalne pe yeh nahi badalna chahiye. Junction row pe price_charged rakhna sahi design hai, shortcut nahi.

SQL vs NoSQL: baat access patterns ki hai

SQL (relational) databases jaise Postgres aur MySQL tumhe tables, fixed schema, JOINs, strong ACID transactions (Topic 02) aur baad mein ad-hoc queries se naye sawaal poochne ki azaadi dete hain. NoSQL ek parivaar hai: document stores (MongoDB) nested JSON jaise documents rakhte hain; key-value stores (Redis, DynamoDB) key se cheezein dhoondhte hain; wide-column stores (Cassandra) bahut saari machines pe phaile bahut bade write volume ke liye bane hain; graph databases (Neo4j) relationships mein ghoomne ke liye.

Imaandaar decision rule "big data ke liye NoSQL" nahi hai. Achhe se indexed Postgres bahut badi tables sambhaal leta hai. Access pattern se chuno: agar data relational hai, joins, multi-row transactions aur flexible querying chahiye, toh SQL. Agar access simple aur pehle se pata hai ("is key ka sab kuch do"), shuru se hi kai nodes pe horizontal scale chahiye, ya har record ki shape bahut alag-alag hai, toh NoSQL fit hota hai. Jaise DynamoDB tumhe inaam deta hai agar tables ko exactly un queries ke around design karo jo tum chalaoge, aur un queries pe sazaa deta hai jo tumne plan nahi ki. Lines dhundhli hain: Postgres mein flexible fields ke liye JSONB hai, aur MongoDB version 4.0 se multi-document transactions support karta hai.

Foreign key constraints aur teams unhe kab skip karti hain

Foreign key constraint database se khud referential integrity enforce karwata hai: customer 999 exist hi nahi karta toh uske liye vehicle insert nahi kar sakte, aur jis customer ki abhi bhi gaadiyan hain use delete nahi kar sakte jab tak batao nahi ki kya hona chahiye (ON DELETE RESTRICT mana kar deta hai, CASCADE children bhi delete kar deta hai, SET NULL link khaali kar deta hai). Yeh un bugs ko pakadta hai jo app code kabhi na kabhi jaane de hi dega.

Cost: har child insert ya update parent ko check karta hai (ek index lookup aur parent row pe chhota sa lock), aur har parent delete children ko check karta hai (isliye FK column pe index banao; Postgres tumhare liye nahi banata). Teams kuch cases mein jaan-boojh ke FK constraints skip karti hain: bahut high write-throughput ingestion jahan check measurable bottleneck hai; sharded databases jahan parent aur child alag servers pe hain (constraint databases ke paar nahi pahunch sakta); microservices jahan har service ka apna database hai; aur bulk-load pipelines. Skip karte waqt woh check ko application mein le jaate hain aur time-time pe "orphan row" checks chalate hain, thodi der ki inconsistency accept karke.

Soft delete vs hard delete

Hard delete asli DELETE hai: row gayi. Soft delete row ko rakhta hai aur mark kar deta hai, aam taur pe ek nullable deleted_at timestamp se. Soft delete audit trail deta hai, "undo" button deta hai, aur foreign keys valid rakhta hai (purane repair orders abhi bhi soft-deleted customer ki taraf point karte hain). Keemat yeh hai ki har query ko WHERE deleted_at IS NULL yaad rakhna padta hai; ek bhoola hua filter deleted data dikha deta hai, aur ulta bug live data ko "gayab" dikhata hai (Topic 13 dekho). Aur cost: tables badhti rehti hain, aur unique email dobara use nahi ho sakta, jise partial unique index se solve karte hain.

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ;   -- NULL = alive

-- "Delete"
UPDATE customers SET deleted_at = now() WHERE id = 7;

-- Every normal read must filter (ORMs call this a default scope / paranoid mode)
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE deleted_at IS NULL AND phone = '555-0199';

-- Allow a deleted user's email to be reused: uniqueness only among live rows
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_live ON customers (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

Privacy laws (for US consumers, state laws such as California's CCPA) can give people a right to have their personal data deleted, so "soft delete forever" is not always allowed; teams hard-delete or anonymise personal fields after a retention window. A view (CREATE VIEW live_customers AS ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) or row-level security can enforce the filter centrally, and an archive table can hold deleted rows away from the hot table.

Privacy laws (US consumers ke liye California ke CCPA jaise state laws) logon ko apna personal data delete karwane ka haq de sakte hain, toh "hamesha ke liye soft delete" har baar allowed nahi hai; teams ek retention window ke baad personal fields ko hard-delete ya anonymise karti hain. Ek view (CREATE VIEW live_customers AS ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) ya row-level security filter ko ek jagah se enforce kar sakti hai, aur ek archive table deleted rows ko hot table se door rakh sakti hai.

Level 4 Scale and change: sharding and zero-downtime migrationsScale aur badlaav: sharding aur zero-downtime migrations

Sharding: when one database is not enough

Eventually one database server can run out of write capacity, disk or memory. Before splitting, seniors exhaust the cheaper options: indexes and query fixes, a bigger machine (vertical scaling), read replicas (copies that serve reads), caching, and partitioning (splitting one big table into pieces inside the same server, for example by month, with Postgres declarative partitioning).

Sharding splits the data across several independent database servers, each holding a subset of rows. A shard key decides which shard owns a row, for example dealer_id: all rows for one dealer live on one shard. A routing layer (in the app, a proxy, or the database itself as in Vitess or Citus) sends each query to the right shard.

Sharding: jab ek database kaafi nahi

Aakhir mein ek database server ki write capacity, disk ya memory khatam ho sakti hai. Todne se pehle seniors saste options khatam karte hain: indexes aur query fixes, badi machine (vertical scaling), read replicas (copies jo reads serve karti hain), caching, aur partitioning (ek badi table ko usi server ke andar tukdon mein todna, jaise mahine ke hisaab se, Postgres declarative partitioning se).

Sharding data ko kai independent database servers mein baant deta hai, har ek ke paas rows ka ek hissa. Shard key decide karti hai ki kaunsa shard kis row ka maalik hai, jaise dealer_id: ek dealer ki saari rows ek shard pe. Ek routing layer (app mein, ek proxy mein, ya database khud jaise Vitess ya Citus mein) har query ko sahi shard pe bhejti hai.

The problems sharding brings, which is what the interview question is really about:

  • Cross-shard queries. Anything that does not filter by the shard key (a VIN lookup, a report across all dealers) must fan out to every shard and merge results. JOINs across shards are slow or impossible.
  • Cross-shard transactions. A single ACID transaction lives on one server. Updating rows on two shards atomically needs two-phase commit (Topic 02: slow, and blocks if the coordinator dies) or a saga (a chain of local steps with compensating undo steps).
  • Hot shards. A skewed key (one giant tenant, or a time-based key where all new writes land on the newest shard) overloads one server while others idle.
  • Resharding. Adding capacity means moving data while serving traffic. Plain hash mod N moves most rows when N changes; consistent hashing (Topic 07) or many small "logical shards" mapped onto fewer physical servers move only a fraction.
  • Everything else gets harder: globally unique ids (no single auto-increment), unique constraints across shards, foreign keys across shards, backups and schema migrations run N times.

A good shard key has high cardinality, spreads load evenly, and appears in almost every query, so most requests touch exactly one shard. In multi-tenant SaaS, the tenant id (here, dealer or rooftop) is the usual choice, with very large tenants given their own dedicated shard.

Zero-downtime migrations: expand and contract

A migration is a scripted change to the schema (add a column, rename one, split a table). Two things make it dangerous in production. First, some ALTER TABLE operations take a lock that blocks reads or writes for as long as they run, and on a big table that can be minutes. Worse, in Postgres a waiting ALTER sits in the lock queue and blocks every query that arrives behind it. Second, in a rolling deploy the old version and the new version of your app run at the same time, so at every moment the schema must work for both.

The standard technique is expand-contract (also called parallel change). Example: we want to replace a free-text phone column with a clean phone_e164 (the international "+15550199" format).

Sharding jo problems laati hai, interview ka sawaal asal mein inhi ke baare mein hai:

  • Cross-shard queries. Jo bhi query shard key se filter nahi karti (VIN lookup, saare dealers ki report) use har shard pe jaana padta hai aur results merge karne padte hain. Shards ke paar JOINs slow ya namumkin hain.
  • Cross-shard transactions. Ek ACID transaction ek server pe rehti hai. Do shards ki rows ko atomically update karne ke liye two-phase commit chahiye (Topic 02: slow, aur coordinator mar jaaye toh block ho jaata hai) ya saga (local steps ki chain, saath mein compensating undo steps).
  • Hot shards. Tircha (skewed) key (ek bahut bada tenant, ya time-based key jahan saare naye writes newest shard pe girte hain) ek server ko overload kar deti hai jabki baaki khaali baithe hain.
  • Resharding. Capacity badhane ka matlab traffic serve karte hue data move karna. Seedha hash mod N N badalne pe zyaadatar rows move karwata hai; consistent hashing (Topic 07) ya bahut saare chhote "logical shards" jo kam physical servers pe map hain, sirf ek hissa move karwate hain.
  • Baaki sab bhi mushkil ho jaata hai: globally unique ids (ek single auto-increment nahi), shards ke paar unique constraints, shards ke paar foreign keys, backups aur schema migrations N baar chalana.

Achhi shard key ki cardinality high hoti hai, load barabar baantti hai, aur lagbhag har query mein aati hai, taaki zyaadatar requests exactly ek shard ko touch karein. Multi-tenant SaaS mein tenant id (yahan dealer ya rooftop) aam choice hai, aur bahut bade tenants ko apna dedicated shard diya jaata hai.

Zero-downtime migrations: expand aur contract

Migration schema mein ek scripted badlaav hai (column jodna, rename karna, table todna). Do cheezein ise production mein khatarnaak banati hain. Pehli, kuch ALTER TABLE operations aisa lock lete hain jo jab tak chalein tab tak reads ya writes block karta hai, aur badi table pe yeh minutes ho sakte hain. Isse bhi bura, Postgres mein wait kar raha ALTER lock queue mein baitha rehta hai aur uske peeche aane wali har query ko block kar deta hai. Doosri, rolling deploy mein tumhari app ka purana aur naya version ek saath chalte hain, toh har pal schema ko dono ke liye kaam karna chahiye.

Standard technique hai expand-contract (parallel change bhi kehte hain). Example: hum free-text phone column ko ek saaf phone_e164 (international "+15550199" format) se replace karna chahte hain.

-- 1. EXPAND: nullable column, no default rewrite -> metadata-only, instant in Postgres
SET lock_timeout = '3s';            -- give up instead of queueing behind long queries
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone_e164 TEXT;

-- 2. DUAL-WRITE: application release writes both phone and phone_e164

-- 3. BACKFILL in small batches (repeat until 0 rows updated)
UPDATE customers
SET    phone_e164 = normalize_phone(phone)   -- normalize_phone: your own conversion function
WHERE  id IN (SELECT id FROM customers
              WHERE phone_e164 IS NULL AND phone IS NOT NULL
              LIMIT 5000);

-- index it without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_customers_phone_e164 ON customers (phone_e164);

-- 4. SWITCH READS: application release reads phone_e164

-- 5. CONTRACT: release that stops writing phone, then later:
ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN phone;

Other safe-migration habits: set a lock_timeout so a stuck ALTER fails fast instead of blocking the whole table; add NOT NULL on a big Postgres table by first adding CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID and then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, which does not block writes; build indexes CONCURRENTLY; in MySQL use online DDL or tools like gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change that copy the table in the background. And never rename a column in one step: a rename is just expand-contract with a new name.

In real production: the classic outage is a migration that looked instant on a dev database with 1,000 rows and, on the production table, took a lock that queued every request behind it until the API timed out. The fix is never "be more careful"; it is a migration checklist (lock timeout, batched backfills, concurrent index builds, expand-contract) enforced in code review.

Aur safe-migration aadatein: lock_timeout set karo taaki atka hua ALTER poori table ko block karne ki jagah jaldi fail ho jaaye; badi Postgres table pe NOT NULL jodne ke liye pehle CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID jodo aur phir VALIDATE CONSTRAINT karo, jo writes block nahi karta; indexes CONCURRENTLY banao; MySQL mein online DDL ya gh-ost ya pt-online-schema-change jaise tools use karo jo table ko background mein copy karte hain. Aur column ko kabhi ek step mein rename mat karo: rename bas naye naam ke saath expand-contract hi hai.

Real production mein: classic outage woh migration hai jo 1,000 rows wale dev database pe instant lagi aur production table pe aisa lock le liya jisne har request ko apne peeche queue kar diya jab tak API timeout na ho gayi. Fix kabhi "zyada dhyaan rakho" nahi hota; fix hai ek migration checklist (lock timeout, batched backfills, concurrent index builds, expand-contract) jo code review mein enforce ho.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Primary key
Column(s) uniquely identifying each row; never null.Column(s) jo har row ko uniquely pehchaante hain; kabhi null nahi.
Foreign key
A column holding another table's primary key; the link between tables. As a constraint, the DB enforces that the target exists.Column jisme doosri table ki primary key hai; tables ke beech ka link. Constraint ke roop mein DB enforce karta hai ki target exist kare.
Referential integrity
The guarantee that every foreign key points to a row that really exists (no orphans).Guarantee ki har foreign key ek sach mein existing row ki taraf point kare (koi orphan nahi).
Anomaly (update / insert / delete)
Bugs caused by duplicated data: copies disagree, you cannot add a fact without a fake one, deleting one fact loses another.Duplicate data se aane wale bugs: copies match nahi karti, ek fact bina fake fact ke jod nahi sakte, ek fact delete karne se doosra kho jaata hai.
Normalisation (1NF, 2NF, 3NF)
Removing duplication step by step: atomic values; depend on the whole key; depend on nothing but the key.Step by step duplication hatana: atomic values; poori key pe depend; key ke alawa kisi pe depend nahi.
Denormalisation
Deliberately storing redundant copies to speed up reads, paying with slower writes and sync risk.Reads fast karne ke liye jaan-boojh ke redundant copies rakhna, badle mein slow writes aur sync ka risk.
Junction table
A table with foreign keys to two tables, one row per pairing; implements many-to-many.Do tables ki foreign keys wali table, har jodi ki ek row; many-to-many implement karti hai.
ORM
Object-Relational Mapper: a library that maps rows to objects in code (Sequelize, Prisma, Hibernate).Object-Relational Mapper: library jo rows ko code ke objects mein map karti hai (Sequelize, Prisma, Hibernate).
N+1 queries
One query for N parents, then one query per parent for related data. Fixed with a JOIN or eager loading.N parents ke liye ek query, phir related data ke liye har parent ki ek query. JOIN ya eager loading se fix.
Eager loading
Telling the ORM to fetch related rows up front, in a JOIN or one batched IN query.ORM ko bolna ki related rows pehle hi le aaye, JOIN mein ya ek batched IN query mein.
Connection pool
A fixed set of open DB connections reused across requests; protects the DB's max_connections limit.Khule DB connections ka fixed set jo requests ke beech reuse hota hai; DB ki max_connections limit ko bachata hai.
Materialized view
A stored, refreshable query result, used as a denormalised read table.Store kiya hua, refresh ho sakne wala query result, denormalised read table ki tarah use hota hai.
Soft delete
Marking a row deleted (deleted_at) instead of removing it; every query must filter it out.Row ko hatane ki jagah deleted mark karna (deleted_at); har query ko use filter karna padta hai.
Partitioning vs sharding
Splitting a table into pieces on one server vs splitting data across many independent servers.Ek server pe table ko tukdon mein todna vs data ko kai independent servers mein baantna.
Shard key
The column that decides which shard owns a row (for example dealer_id).Woh column jo decide karta hai ki row kis shard ki hai (jaise dealer_id).
Hot shard
One shard receiving far more load than others because of a skewed key.Tirchi key ki wajah se ek shard pe baakiyon se kahin zyada load.
Migration
A scripted, versioned change to the schema.Schema mein scripted, versioned badlaav.
Expand-contract
Zero-downtime migration pattern: add new, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, remove old.Zero-downtime migration pattern: naya jodo, dual-write, backfill, reads switch, purana hatao.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What is normalisation? Explain 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF.Normalisation kya hai? 1NF, 2NF aur 3NF samjhao.
What they're really testing: that you can state each form precisely (1NF atomic values and no repeating groups; 2NF non-key columns depend on the whole key; 3NF they depend only on the key) and explain the anomalies it prevents.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum har form ko precisely bata sako (1NF atomic values aur koi repeating groups nahi; 2NF non-key columns poori key pe depend karein; 3NF sirf key pe depend karein) aur batao yeh kaunsi anomalies rokta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Normalisation is organising tables so each fact is stored exactly once, which prevents update, insert and delete anomalies. First normal form: every cell holds one atomic value, no repeating groups like phone1, phone2, or "oil change, tire rotation" in one cell, and every row has a key. Second normal form: every non-key column depends on the whole primary key. That matters for composite keys: in a table keyed by (ro_id, service_id), service_name depends only on service_id, so it moves to a services table. Third normal form: non-key columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns. If a repair order row stores customer_id and customer_phone, the phone depends on the customer, not the order, so it belongs in customers. The short version is "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key". The trade-off is more tables and more JOINs on reads, in exchange for writes that cannot contradict each other.

Normalisation tables ko aise organise karna hai ki har fact bilkul ek baar store ho, jisse update, insert aur delete anomalies rukti hain. First normal form: har cell mein ek atomic value, koi repeating groups nahi jaise phone1, phone2, ya ek cell mein "oil change, tire rotation", aur har row ki ek key. Second normal form: har non-key column poori primary key pe depend kare. Yeh composite keys mein matter karta hai: (ro_id, service_id) key wali table mein service_name sirf service_id pe depend karta hai, toh woh services table mein jaata hai. Third normal form: non-key columns sirf key pe depend karein, doosre non-key columns pe nahi. Agar repair order row customer_id aur customer_phone dono rakhti hai, toh phone customer pe depend karta hai, order pe nahi, isliye uski jagah customers mein hai. Chhota version: "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key". Trade-off: zyada tables aur reads pe zyada JOINs, badle mein aise writes jo ek doosre ko contradict nahi kar sakte.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Name the three anomalies with an example: update (Asha's phone changed in one of twelve rows), insert (cannot record a new customer without a fake visit), delete (removing the only visit erases the customer). A table with a single-column primary key that is in 1NF is automatically in 2NF, because there is no "part" of the key to depend on. Beyond 3NF there is BCNF (every determinant must be a candidate key) and 4NF/5NF for multi-valued dependencies, rarely needed in practice. Most production OLTP schemas aim for 3NF and then denormalise specific hot reads on purpose, with evidence.

Teeno anomalies example ke saath batao: update (Asha ka phone baarah mein se ek row mein badla), insert (fake visit ke bina naya customer record nahi kar sakte), delete (ikloti visit hatane se customer mit jaata hai). Jo table single-column primary key ke saath 1NF mein hai woh automatically 2NF mein hai, kyunki key ka koi "hissa" hai hi nahi jis pe depend kare. 3NF ke aage BCNF hai (har determinant candidate key ho) aur multi-valued dependencies ke liye 4NF/5NF, jo practically kam chahiye. Zyaadatar production OLTP schemas 3NF ka target rakhte hain aur phir specific hot reads ko jaan-boojh ke, evidence ke saath, denormalise karte hain.

Common mistake: reciting "1NF, 2NF, 3NF" with no example, or saying 2NF is about removing duplicate rows. It is about partial dependency on a composite key.
Galti mat karna: bina example ke "1NF, 2NF, 3NF" ratna, ya bolna ki 2NF duplicate rows hatane ke baare mein hai. Yeh composite key pe partial dependency ke baare mein hai.
02 When would you denormalise a database and what are the trade-offs?Database ko kab denormalise karoge aur uske trade-offs kya hain?
What they're really testing: that you denormalise only when read performance is critical and duplication is tolerable, and you can name the cost: faster reads, slower writes, inconsistency risk.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum tabhi denormalise karte ho jab read performance critical ho aur duplication bardaasht ho sake, aur cost bata sako: fast reads, slow writes, inconsistency ka risk.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I start normalised and denormalise a specific read when I have evidence it needs it: the read is latency-critical, it runs far more often than the data changes, the JOIN or aggregation is measurably expensive, and the business can tolerate a copy being briefly stale. For example, a service-drive list screen that shows open repair orders with customer names might store customer_name on the repair order, or a dashboard might read a pre-computed open_ro_count instead of counting on every load, or a materialized view refreshed every few minutes. The trade-off is clear: reads get faster and simpler, but every write has to update more places, and if any code path forgets, the copies drift apart. So I keep the sync in one place, the same transaction, a trigger or an event, and I keep a way to rebuild the copy from the source of truth.

Main normalised se shuru karta hoon aur kisi specific read ko tab denormalise karta hoon jab evidence ho ki zaroorat hai: read latency-critical hai, data badalne se kahin zyada baar chalta hai, JOIN ya aggregation measurably mehnga hai, aur business copy ke thodi der stale rehne ko bardaasht kar sakta hai. Example: service-drive ki list screen jo open repair orders customer names ke saath dikhati hai, woh repair order pe customer_name store kar sakti hai, ya dashboard har load pe ginne ki jagah pre-computed open_ro_count padh sakta hai, ya har kuch minute mein refresh hone wala materialized view. Trade-off saaf hai: reads fast aur simple ho jaate hain, par har write ko zyada jagah update karna padta hai, aur agar koi code path bhool gaya toh copies alag ho jaati hain. Isliye main sync ek hi jagah rakhta hoon, same transaction, trigger ya event, aur source of truth se copy dobara banane ka tarika rakhta hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Options range from light to heavy: a cached counter column, a copied column, a materialized view (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY in Postgres needs a unique index), a separate read model built from change events (CQRS), or a search index like Elasticsearch fed by change data capture. Try cheaper fixes first: a proper index, a covering index, or a cache. Also separate true denormalisation from historical snapshots: price_charged on a repair order is a different fact from today's list price and should be stored, not joined.

Options halke se bhaari tak: cached counter column, copied column, materialized view (Postgres mein REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY ke liye unique index chahiye), change events se bana alag read model (CQRS), ya change data capture se bhara jaane wala Elasticsearch jaisa search index. Pehle saste fixes try karo: sahi index, covering index, ya cache. Aur asli denormalisation ko historical snapshots se alag samjho: repair order pe price_charged aaj ke list price se alag fact hai aur store hona chahiye, join nahi.

Common mistake: denormalising up front "for performance" with no measured problem, or not mentioning how the copies stay consistent.
Galti mat karna: bina measured problem ke shuru mein hi "performance ke liye" denormalise kar dena, ya yeh na batana ki copies consistent kaise rahengi.
03 What is the N+1 query problem and how do you detect and fix it?N+1 query problem kya hai aur use kaise detect aur fix karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you recognise "N parents, then one query each", fix it with a JOIN or eager loading, and detect it by logging queries and spotting the same query repeated with different ids.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum "N parents, phir har ek ki ek query" pehchaan sako, JOIN ya eager loading se fix karo, aur queries log karke same query ko alag ids ke saath repeat hote dekh ke detect karo.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

N+1 is when code runs one query to fetch N rows, then loops and runs one more query per row for related data. For example, loading 50 repair orders and then calling ro.getCustomer() inside the loop fires 51 queries for one page. It usually comes from an ORM's lazy loading, so it looks harmless in code and is fast on a laptop, but in production each query is a network round trip, so latency grows with N and the database is flooded with tiny queries. To detect it, I turn on query logging and look for the same statement repeated with different ids, or look at a trace where one request contains dozens of identical DB spans, or at pg_stat_statements for a trivial query with a huge call count. To fix it, I fetch the related data in one JOIN, or ask the ORM to eager-load it, which becomes one JOIN or one batched WHERE id IN (...) query.

N+1 tab hota hai jab code N rows laane ke liye ek query chalata hai, phir loop mein har row ke related data ke liye ek aur query chalata hai. Example: 50 repair orders load karna aur phir loop ke andar ro.getCustomer() call karna ek page ke liye 51 queries chala deta hai. Yeh aam taur pe ORM ki lazy loading se aata hai, isliye code mein harmless dikhta hai aur laptop pe fast hota hai, par production mein har query ek network round trip hai, toh latency N ke saath badhti hai aur database chhoti queries se bhar jaata hai. Detect karne ke liye main query logging on karta hoon aur same statement ko alag ids ke saath repeat hote dhoondhta hoon, ya aisa trace dekhta hoon jisme ek request mein darjanon ek jaise DB spans hon, ya pg_stat_statements mein ek chhoti si query ka bahut bada call count. Fix ke liye related data ek JOIN mein laata hoon, ya ORM ko eager-load karne bolta hoon, jo ek JOIN ya ek batched WHERE id IN (...) query ban jaata hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

JOIN versus batched IN is a trade-off: a JOIN on a one-to-many relation repeats parent columns for every child row, which can bloat the result, so ORMs often use a second IN query for collections. In GraphQL, resolvers naturally cause N+1, and the standard fix is DataLoader, which collects all ids requested in one tick and issues one batched query. To stop regressions, add tests that assert the query count for key endpoints, or tools like Bullet in Rails. Also make sure the FK column used in the IN or JOIN is indexed, otherwise the "fixed" query is a slow scan.

JOIN vs batched IN ek trade-off hai: one-to-many relation pe JOIN har child row ke liye parent columns repeat karta hai, jisse result phool sakta hai, isliye ORMs collections ke liye aksar doosri IN query use karte hain. GraphQL mein resolvers naturally N+1 banate hain, aur standard fix DataLoader hai, jo ek tick mein maangi gayi saari ids ikattha karke ek batched query chalata hai. Regressions rokne ke liye key endpoints ke query count ko assert karne wale tests likho, ya Rails mein Bullet jaise tools. Aur ensure karo ki IN ya JOIN mein use hone wala FK column indexed ho, warna "fixed" query ek slow scan ban jaayegi.

Common mistake: blaming the database or adding a cache to hide N+1, instead of fixing the access pattern in the code.
Galti mat karna: N+1 ko chhupane ke liye database ko blame karna ya cache laga dena, code mein access pattern theek karne ki jagah.
04 How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL?SQL aur NoSQL mein se kaise choose karte ho?
What they're really testing: that the decision is about access patterns, not data size: SQL for relationships, joins, ACID and stable schemas; NoSQL for massive scale, flexible schemas and simple, known access patterns.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki decision access patterns ka hai, data size ka nahi: relationships, joins, ACID aur stable schema ke liye SQL; massive scale, flexible schema aur simple, pehle se pata access patterns ke liye NoSQL.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I decide by access pattern, not by how big the data is. If the data is relational, like customers, vehicles, repair orders and payments, and I need joins, multi-row transactions and the freedom to ask new questions later, I pick a relational database like Postgres; with good indexes it handles very large tables. I reach for NoSQL when the access pattern is simple and known up front, such as "fetch everything for this key", when I need horizontal scale across many nodes built in, or when records genuinely vary in shape. For example, storing session data or per-device telemetry at very high write rates fits a key-value or wide-column store well, while invoicing belongs in SQL. The trade-off is that many NoSQL stores make you design around the exact queries in advance and give up easy joins and, in some cases, strong consistency. Often the answer is both, each for the part it fits.

Main access pattern se decide karta hoon, data kitna bada hai isse nahi. Agar data relational hai, jaise customers, vehicles, repair orders aur payments, aur mujhe joins, multi-row transactions aur baad mein naye sawaal poochne ki azaadi chahiye, toh main Postgres jaisa relational database chunta hoon; achhe indexes ke saath woh bahut badi tables sambhaal leta hai. NoSQL tab leta hoon jab access pattern simple aur pehle se pata ho, jaise "is key ka sab kuch lao", jab kai nodes pe horizontal scale built-in chahiye, ya jab records ki shape sach mein alag-alag ho. Example: session data ya per-device telemetry bahut high write rate pe store karna key-value ya wide-column store mein achha fit hota hai, jabki invoicing SQL mein hi honi chahiye. Trade-off yeh hai ki kai NoSQL stores tumhe exact queries ke around pehle se design karwate hain aur aasaan joins chhod dete hain, aur kuch cases mein strong consistency bhi. Aksar jawab dono hai, har ek us hisse ke liye jahan woh fit ho.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

"NoSQL" is several families: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j). The lines have blurred: Postgres JSONB gives schema flexibility with indexing, MongoDB has supported multi-document ACID transactions since 4.0, and distributed SQL systems (CockroachDB, Spanner, Vitess, Citus) offer horizontal scale with SQL. Schema flexibility is not free: the schema still exists, it just moves into application code, and old documents in old shapes must be handled forever. Consider the team's operational experience too.

"NoSQL" kai families hain: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j). Lines dhundhli ho gayi hain: Postgres JSONB indexing ke saath schema flexibility deta hai, MongoDB 4.0 se multi-document ACID transactions support karta hai, aur distributed SQL systems (CockroachDB, Spanner, Vitess, Citus) SQL ke saath horizontal scale dete hain. Schema flexibility free nahi hai: schema phir bhi hota hai, bas application code mein chala jaata hai, aur purani shape wale purane documents ko hamesha handle karna padta hai. Team ka operational experience bhi socho.

Common mistake: "NoSQL for big data, SQL for small data", or "NoSQL because we don't want a schema".
Galti mat karna: "big data ke liye NoSQL, small data ke liye SQL", ya "NoSQL kyunki humein schema nahi chahiye".
05 What is database sharding and what problems does it introduce?Database sharding kya hai aur yeh kaunsi problems laata hai?
What they're really testing: that you know sharding splits data by a shard key across servers, and can name the costs: cross-shard queries, cross-shard transactions needing 2PC, hot shards, resharding.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tumhe pata hai sharding shard key se data ko servers mein baantti hai, aur tum costs bata sako: cross-shard queries, cross-shard transactions jinhe 2PC chahiye, hot shards, resharding.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Sharding splits one logical database across several independent servers, each holding a subset of rows, chosen by a shard key. In a multi-tenant dealer platform I would shard by dealer_id, so one dealer's customers, vehicles and repair orders live together and almost every request touches exactly one shard. It exists because one server eventually runs out of write capacity or storage. But it introduces real problems. Queries without the shard key, like a VIN lookup or a report across all dealers, must fan out to every shard and merge. A transaction spanning two shards needs two-phase commit or a saga. A skewed key creates a hot shard, for instance one huge dealer group on one server. And resharding is painful: with plain hash mod N, changing N moves most of the data. So I treat sharding as a last resort, after indexes, read replicas, caching and partitioning.

Sharding ek logical database ko kai independent servers mein baant deti hai, har ek ke paas rows ka ek hissa, jo shard key se decide hota hai. Multi-tenant dealer platform mein main dealer_id se shard karunga, taaki ek dealer ke customers, vehicles aur repair orders saath rahein aur lagbhag har request exactly ek shard ko touch kare. Yeh isliye hai kyunki ek server ki write capacity ya storage aakhir khatam ho jaati hai. Par yeh asli problems laati hai. Shard key ke bina wali queries, jaise VIN lookup ya saare dealers ki report, har shard pe jaani chahiye aur merge karni padti hain. Do shards pe phaili transaction ko two-phase commit ya saga chahiye. Tirchi key hot shard banati hai, jaise ek bahut bada dealer group ek server pe. Aur resharding dardnaak hai: seedhe hash mod N mein N badalne se zyaadatar data move hota hai. Isliye main sharding ko last resort maanta hoon, indexes, read replicas, caching aur partitioning ke baad.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Good shard keys have high cardinality, even load, and appear in nearly every query. Resharding pain is reduced with consistent hashing or by creating many logical shards (say 1,024) mapped onto a few physical servers, so growth means moving whole logical shards. Large tenants can get dedicated shards. A lookup table or directory service can map keys to shards for flexibility. You also need globally unique ids (UUIDs, Snowflake-style ids), and you lose cross-shard foreign keys and unique constraints. Tools like Vitess (MySQL) and Citus (Postgres) handle routing and resharding for you.

Achhi shard keys ki cardinality high hoti hai, load barabar hota hai, aur lagbhag har query mein aati hain.
