Resharding ka dard consistent hashing se, ya bahut saare logical shards (maano 1,024) bana ke kam kiya jaata hai jo kuch physical servers pe map hote hain, taaki growth ka matlab poore logical shards move karna ho. Bade tenants ko dedicated shards mil sakte hain. Flexibility ke liye ek lookup table ya directory service keys ko shards se map kar sakti hai. Globally unique ids bhi chahiye (UUIDs, Snowflake-style ids), aur cross-shard foreign keys aur unique constraints chale jaate hain. Vitess (MySQL) aur Citus (Postgres) jaise tools routing aur resharding tumhare liye sambhaalte hain.

Common mistake: confusing sharding with read replicas (replicas copy all data; shards split it), or proposing sharding before trying indexes and replicas.
Galti mat karna: sharding ko read replicas se confuse karna (replicas saara data copy karti hain; shards use baantte hain), ya indexes aur replicas try kiye bina sharding suggest karna.
06 How do you handle database migrations with zero downtime?Zero downtime ke saath database migrations kaise handle karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you know the expand-contract pattern: add a nullable column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, remove the old column.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tumhe expand-contract pattern pata hai: nullable column jodo, dual-write, backfill, reads switch, purana column hatao.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I use expand-contract, because during a rolling deploy old and new app versions run at the same time, so the schema must work for both at every step. Say we are replacing a messy phone column with a normalised phone_e164. Step one, expand: add phone_e164 as a nullable column, which is a metadata-only change in Postgres and does not lock the table for long. Step two, deploy code that writes both columns. Step three, backfill existing rows in small batches so no huge transaction holds locks, and verify the counts match. Step four, deploy code that reads from the new column. Step five, contract: stop writing the old column and, days later, drop it. Each step is a separate, reversible deploy. I also set a lock timeout on DDL, build indexes concurrently, and never do a rename in one step. The trade-off is more deploys and temporary duplicate data in exchange for no outage.

Main expand-contract use karta hoon, kyunki rolling deploy mein purana aur naya app version ek saath chalte hain, toh schema ko har step pe dono ke liye kaam karna chahiye. Maano hum ek ganda phone column ek normalised phone_e164 se replace kar rahe hain. Step ek, expand: phone_e164 nullable column ke roop mein jodo, jo Postgres mein metadata-only change hai aur table ko der tak lock nahi karta. Step do, aisa code deploy karo jo dono columns mein likhe. Step teen, existing rows ko chhote batches mein backfill karo taaki koi badi transaction locks na pakde, aur counts match hote hain verify karo. Step chaar, aisa code deploy karo jo naye column se padhe. Step paanch, contract: purane column mein likhna band karo aur kuch din baad use drop karo. Har step ek alag, reversible deploy hai. Main DDL pe lock timeout bhi set karta hoon, indexes concurrently banata hoon, aur rename kabhi ek step mein nahi karta. Trade-off: zyada deploys aur thodi der ka duplicate data, badle mein koi outage nahi.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Dangerous operations to know: in Postgres, adding a column with a volatile default, changing a column type, or adding NOT NULL can rewrite or scan the whole table under a strong lock; add NOT NULL via CHECK (...) NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT. A waiting ALTER in the lock queue blocks everything behind it, which is why lock_timeout plus retries matters. In MySQL, use online DDL where supported, or gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change, which build a shadow table and swap. Keep migrations backward compatible, separate from code deploys, and tested on a production-sized copy.

Khatarnaak operations jo pata hone chahiye: Postgres mein volatile default ke saath column jodna, column type badalna, ya NOT NULL jodna strong lock ke neeche poori table ko rewrite ya scan kar sakta hai; NOT NULL ko CHECK (...) NOT VALID aur phir VALIDATE CONSTRAINT se jodo. Lock queue mein wait karta ALTER apne peeche sab kuch block kar deta hai, isliye lock_timeout plus retries zaroori hai. MySQL mein jahan support ho online DDL use karo, ya gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change, jo shadow table banake swap karte hain. Migrations ko backward compatible rakho, code deploys se alag, aur production jitni badi copy pe test karo.

Common mistake: renaming or dropping a column in the same release that changes the code, which breaks the old instances still running during the rollout.
Galti mat karna: usi release mein column rename ya drop kar dena jisme code badal raha hai, jisse rollout ke dauraan abhi bhi chal rahe purane instances toot jaate hain.
07 What is connection pooling and why does it matter?Connection pooling kya hai aur kyun matter karti hai?
What they're really testing: that connections are expensive and limited, so you reuse them; without a pool you pay setup overhead per request and hit max connections under load.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki connections mehnge aur limited hain, isliye unhe reuse karte hain; pool ke bina har request pe setup overhead lagta hai aur load mein max connections hit ho jaate hain.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Opening a database connection is expensive: a TCP handshake, usually TLS, authentication, and memory on the server; in Postgres each connection is a whole OS process. Databases also cap connections, 100 by default in Postgres and 151 in MySQL. A connection pool keeps a fixed set of open connections and lends one to each request for the duration of a query or transaction, then takes it back. Without it, every request pays the setup cost, and under a traffic spike the app keeps opening connections until the database refuses with "too many connections" and every endpoint fails together. The design point is that pools multiply: 20 app instances with a pool of 10 each need 200 connections. So I size pools deliberately, keep transactions short so connections return quickly, and put a pooler like PgBouncer in front of Postgres when there are many instances or serverless functions.

Database connection kholna mehnga hai: TCP handshake, aam taur pe TLS, authentication, aur server pe memory; Postgres mein har connection ek poora OS process hai. Databases connections ki limit bhi rakhte hain, Postgres mein default 100 aur MySQL mein 151. Connection pool khule connections ka ek fixed set rakhta hai aur har request ko ek query ya transaction ke liye ek udhaar deta hai, phir wapas le leta hai. Iske bina har request setup ka cost deti hai, aur traffic spike mein app connections kholti rehti hai jab tak database "too many connections" bol ke mana na kar de aur har endpoint ek saath fail ho jaaye. Design point yeh hai ki pools multiply hote hain: 20 app instances, har ek ka pool 10, matlab 200 connections. Isliye main pools soch-samajh ke size karta hoon, transactions chhoti rakhta hoon taaki connections jaldi wapas aayein, aur jab bahut instances ya serverless functions hon toh Postgres ke aage PgBouncer jaisa pooler lagata hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Bigger pools are not faster: the database has limited CPU cores and disk, so hundreds of active connections just contend with each other. A commonly quoted starting point (from the HikariCP project) is roughly cores times two plus the number of disks, then tune with measurements. PgBouncer's transaction mode shares server connections between transactions, which breaks session-level features like session variables or some prepared statements. Watch pool wait time and "connection acquire timeout" errors; they often mean slow queries or leaked connections (a code path that never releases), not a pool that is too small.

Bade pools fast nahi hote: database ke paas limited CPU cores aur disk hain, toh sau-sau active connections bas aapas mein ladte hain. Aksar quote kiya jaane wala starting point (HikariCP project se) roughly cores guna do plus disks ki ginti hai, phir measurements se tune karo. PgBouncer ka transaction mode server connections ko transactions ke beech share karta hai, jisse session variables ya kuch prepared statements jaise session-level features toot jaate hain. Pool wait time aur "connection acquire timeout" errors dekho; inka matlab aksar slow queries ya leaked connections hota hai (aisa code path jo connection kabhi release nahi karta), chhota pool nahi.

Common mistake: fixing "too many connections" by raising max_connections or the pool size, instead of finding slow queries, long transactions or leaks.
Galti mat karna: "too many connections" ko max_connections ya pool size badha ke fix karna, slow queries, lambi transactions ya leaks dhoondhne ki jagah.
08 What is a foreign key constraint and when would you skip it?Foreign key constraint kya hai aur use kab skip karoge?
What they're really testing: that FKs enforce referential integrity at the database level, and that you know the legitimate reasons to skip them: very high write throughput, sharded databases, cases where eventual consistency is acceptable.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki FKs database level pe referential integrity enforce karti hain, aur tumhe unhe skip karne ki sahi wajah pata hain: bahut high write throughput, sharded databases, jahan eventual consistency chal jaaye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A foreign key constraint tells the database that a column must reference an existing row in another table, so it enforces referential integrity itself. You cannot create a vehicle for a customer id that does not exist, and you cannot delete a customer who still has vehicles unless you choose RESTRICT, CASCADE or SET NULL. That catches bugs no amount of app code review will fully prevent, so my default is to use them. The cost is that every child write checks the parent and takes a small lock on it, and every parent delete checks the children. I would skip them in specific cases: very high write-throughput ingestion where the check is a measured bottleneck, sharded databases where parent and child live on different servers, separate microservice databases, and bulk-load pipelines. When I skip them, the application validates, and a periodic job finds orphan rows, because I am accepting temporary inconsistency.

Foreign key constraint database ko batata hai ki ek column ko doosri table ki existing row ko reference karna hi hai, toh woh referential integrity khud enforce karta hai. Jo customer id exist nahi karti uske liye vehicle nahi bana sakte, aur jis customer ki abhi bhi gaadiyan hain use delete nahi kar sakte jab tak RESTRICT, CASCADE ya SET NULL na chuno. Yeh aise bugs pakadta hai jo kitna bhi app code review ho, poori tarah nahi rokta, isliye mera default inhe use karna hai. Cost yeh hai ki har child write parent ko check karta hai aur us pe chhota lock leta hai, aur har parent delete children ko check karta hai. Main inhe specific cases mein skip karunga: bahut high write-throughput ingestion jahan check measured bottleneck hai, sharded databases jahan parent aur child alag servers pe hain, alag microservice databases, aur bulk-load pipelines. Skip karne pe application validate karti hai, aur ek periodic job orphan rows dhoondhta hai, kyunki main thodi der ki inconsistency accept kar raha hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Postgres does not auto-index the referencing column, so a parent delete or an ON DELETE CASCADE scans the child table unless you add the index; InnoDB creates one automatically. The parent-row lock (Postgres takes FOR KEY SHARE) can cause contention when thousands of children are inserted for one hot parent. CASCADE is convenient but can delete far more than intended in one statement; RESTRICT is safer by default. For bulk loads you can create the constraint as NOT VALID and validate later. Many sharded MySQL setups using Vitess historically ran without FK constraints for exactly these reasons.

Postgres referencing column pe auto-index nahi banata, toh parent delete ya ON DELETE CASCADE child table ko scan karta hai jab tak index na jodo; InnoDB ek automatically bana deta hai. Parent-row lock (Postgres FOR KEY SHARE leta hai) tab contention kar sakta hai jab ek hot parent ke liye hazaaron children insert hon. CASCADE convenient hai par ek statement mein soch se kahin zyada delete kar sakta hai; default ke roop mein RESTRICT safe hai. Bulk loads ke liye constraint ko NOT VALID banake baad mein validate kar sakte ho. Vitess use karne wale kai sharded MySQL setups historically inhi wajahon se bina FK constraints ke chale.

Common mistake: saying "we never use foreign keys because they are slow" with no measurement, or forgetting to index the FK column.
Galti mat karna: bina measurement ke bolna "hum foreign keys kabhi use nahi karte kyunki woh slow hain", ya FK column pe index bhool jaana.
09 How do you design a many-to-many relationship?Many-to-many relationship kaise design karte ho?
What they're really testing: that you use a junction table with foreign keys to both sides (and its own key and attributes when the pairing has data), never comma-separated ids in a column.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum dono sides ki foreign keys wali junction table use karte ho (aur jodi ka data ho toh uski apni key aur attributes), kabhi column mein comma-separated ids nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I use a junction table. Take repair orders and services: one repair order includes many services, and one service appears on many repair orders, so neither side can hold a single foreign key. I create ro_services with ro_id referencing repair_orders and service_id referencing services, one row per pairing. The primary key is usually the composite (ro_id, service_id), which also prevents duplicate pairs; if the pairing can legitimately repeat, or other tables need to reference it, I give it its own id. Data that describes the pair, like price charged or technician hours, lives on the junction row. I add an index on service_id too, because the composite key only serves lookups that start with ro_id. What I never do is store "1,2,3" in a column: no foreign keys, no proper joins or indexes, and it breaks first normal form.

Main junction table use karta hoon. Repair orders aur services lo: ek repair order mein kai services hain, aur ek service kai repair orders pe aati hai, toh koi bhi side ek foreign key nahi rakh sakti. Main ro_services banata hoon jisme ro_id repair_orders ko aur service_id services ko reference karta hai, har jodi ki ek row. Primary key aam taur pe composite (ro_id, service_id) hoti hai, jo duplicate jodiyan bhi rokti hai; agar jodi sahi mein repeat ho sakti hai, ya doosri tables ko ise reference karna hai, toh main ise apni id deta hoon. Jo data jodi ko describe karta hai, jaise charge hua price ya technician hours, woh junction row pe rehta hai. Main service_id pe bhi index jodta hoon, kyunki composite key sirf ro_id se shuru hone wale lookups serve karti hai. Jo main kabhi nahi karta: column mein "1,2,3" store karna: na foreign keys, na sahi joins ya indexes, aur yeh first normal form todta hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Choose ON DELETE behaviour per side: deleting a repair order can CASCADE its junction rows, but deleting a service that appears on historical orders should be RESTRICTed (or the service soft-deleted). Once a junction table gains real attributes and lifecycle it is often a first-class entity with a real name, like "ro_lines" or "enrollments". Postgres arrays or JSONB of ids are sometimes used for small, read-only tag lists with a GIN index, but you lose referential integrity; it is a conscious trade-off, not a default. In document databases, you either embed ids on one side or keep a separate linking collection, depending on which direction you query.

Har side ke liye ON DELETE behaviour chuno: repair order delete karne pe uski junction rows CASCADE ho sakti hain, par jo service historical orders pe hai use delete karna RESTRICT hona chahiye (ya service soft-delete ho). Jab junction table ko asli attributes aur lifecycle mil jaata hai, toh woh aksar ek first-class entity ban jaati hai jiska asli naam hota hai, jaise "ro_lines" ya "enrollments". Postgres arrays ya ids ka JSONB kabhi-kabhi chhoti, read-only tag lists ke liye GIN index ke saath use hota hai, par referential integrity chali jaati hai; yeh soch-samajh ke kiya trade-off hai, default nahi. Document databases mein ya toh ek side pe ids embed karte ho ya alag linking collection rakhte ho, is pe depend karta hai ki kis direction mein query karte ho.

Common mistake: storing comma-separated ids in a text column, or forgetting the index for the second direction of lookup.
Galti mat karna: text column mein comma-separated ids store karna, ya lookup ki doosri direction ke liye index bhool jaana.
10 What is soft delete vs hard delete and when do you use each?Soft delete vs hard delete kya hai aur kab kaunsa use karte ho?
What they're really testing: that soft delete (a deleted_at column) gives audit, undo and referential integrity, but every query must filter it, and you know when a real delete is required.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki soft delete (deleted_at column) audit, undo aur referential integrity deta hai, par har query ko filter karna padta hai, aur tumhe pata hai kab asli delete zaroori hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A hard delete removes the row. A soft delete keeps it and marks it, usually with a nullable deleted_at timestamp. I use soft delete for business records people may need back or need to audit, like customers, repair orders or appointments: it gives an audit trail, an undo, and keeps foreign keys valid, since old repair orders still point to the customer. The catch is that every query must filter deleted_at IS NULL. One forgotten filter shows deleted data, or a wrong filter makes live data look like it disappeared. So I enforce it centrally with an ORM default scope, a view, or row-level security. I also fix uniqueness with a partial unique index on live rows only. I use hard delete for high-volume, low-value data like expired sessions, and when privacy rules require personal data to actually be erased, where I hard-delete or anonymise after a retention period.

Hard delete row ko hata deta hai. Soft delete use rakhta hai aur mark kar deta hai, aam taur pe ek nullable deleted_at timestamp se. Main soft delete un business records ke liye use karta hoon jo logon ko wapas chahiye ho sakte hain ya jinka audit hona hai, jaise customers, repair orders ya appointments: yeh audit trail deta hai, undo deta hai, aur foreign keys valid rakhta hai, kyunki purane repair orders abhi bhi customer ki taraf point karte hain. Pech yeh hai ki har query ko deleted_at IS NULL filter karna padta hai. Ek bhoola hua filter deleted data dikha deta hai, ya galat filter live data ko gayab jaisa dikha deta hai. Isliye main ise ORM default scope, view, ya row-level security se ek jagah se enforce karta hoon. Uniqueness ko bhi sirf live rows pe partial unique index se theek karta hoon. Hard delete main high-volume, kam-value data ke liye use karta hoon jaise expired sessions, aur jab privacy rules maangte hain ki personal data sach mein mitaya jaaye, wahan retention period ke baad hard-delete ya anonymise karta hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Soft-deleted rows still take space and index entries, so large tables benefit from partial indexes with WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, or from moving deleted rows to an archive table. Cascades need thought: soft-deleting a customer does not automatically soft-delete their appointments. An alternative for audit is a separate history or audit-log table written on every change, which keeps the main table clean. When a customer reports that data "disappeared", soft delete and filter bugs are the first things I check, along with audit logs, before assuming data loss.

Soft-deleted rows phir bhi jagah aur index entries leti hain, toh badi tables ko WHERE deleted_at IS NULL wale partial indexes se, ya deleted rows ko archive table mein bhejne se fayda hota hai. Cascades pe sochna padta hai: customer ko soft-delete karne se uske appointments automatically soft-delete nahi hote. Audit ke liye ek alternative hai alag history ya audit-log table jo har change pe likhi jaaye, jisse main table saaf rehti hai. Jab koi customer bolta hai ki data "gayab ho gaya", toh data loss maanne se pehle main sabse pehle soft delete aur filter bugs check karta hoon, audit logs ke saath.

Common mistake: adding deleted_at but relying on every developer to remember the filter in every query, or keeping personal data forever when the law requires deletion.
Galti mat karna: deleted_at jod dena par is bharose rehna ki har developer har query mein filter yaad rakhega, ya law deletion maange tab bhi personal data hamesha rakhna.

Topic 10 · VERY COMMONTopic 10 · Bahut common

Authentication & AuthorizationAuthentication & Authorization

"Who are you?" and "what are you allowed to do?" are two different problems. Learn how a secure login really works, from password storage to JWTs, OAuth, CSRF and permissions across microservices.

"Tum kaun ho?" aur "tumhe kya karne ki permission hai?" do alag problems hain. Seekho secure login asal mein kaise kaam karta hai, password store karne se leke JWT, OAuth, CSRF aur microservices mein permissions tak.

Level 0 The story: the office gate and the hotel key cardKahani: office ka gate aur hotel ka key card

Think of a big office tower in Gurgaon. At the main gate, a security guard stops you and asks for your ID card. He checks your face against the photo and your name against the list. This step answers one question only: "Who are you?" That is authentication (often shortened to authN).

Once you pass, you get an access badge. You tap it at the lift. It opens floors 3 and 5, where your team sits, but not floor 7 where the server room is, and not the director's cabin. This second step answers a different question: "What are you allowed to do?" That is authorization (authZ). The guard at the gate does not decide which floors you may enter; the badge system does. Two separate problems, two separate systems.

Now a second picture: a hotel. At check-in, the receptionist checks your passport once (authentication) and hands you a key card programmed "Room 504, valid until Friday 11 a.m." The door lock on room 504 does not phone the reception every time you arrive. It just reads the card and checks two things: "was this card programmed by our hotel?" and "has it expired?". That is exactly how a JWT (JSON Web Token) works: the server checks a signature and an expiry, with no database lookup.

But notice the weakness. If you lose that card on Wednesday, the door will still happily open for whoever finds it, until Friday 11 a.m. The lock has no way to know. Reception would have to reprogram the lock, or the hotel should issue cards that expire every few hours and let you get a fresh one at the desk. Hold on to this picture; it is the whole "how do you revoke a JWT" interview question.

Map it to software: the gate guard is your login endpoint (checks password). The badge or key card is a session cookie or a token. The lift and door readers are your API endpoints checking permissions on every request. Losing a card is a stolen token.

Our running example: a dealer group with several rooftops (individual dealership locations) uses one web portal. A service advisor (the person at the service drive who writes up repair orders) at rooftop 42 should see repair orders (ROs) for rooftop 42 only. A BDC agent (business development center, the phone and chat team) can see leads but not edit prices. A general manager sees everything at their rooftop. Getting these rules right is authorization.

Gurgaon ka ek bada office tower socho. Main gate pe security guard tumhe rokta hai aur ID card maangta hai. Woh tumhara chehra photo se milata hai aur naam list se. Yeh step sirf ek sawaal ka jawab deta hai: "Tum kaun ho?" Isi ko authentication kehte hain (chhota naam authN).

Gate paar karne ke baad tumhe ek access badge milta hai. Lift pe tap karte ho. Woh floor 3 aur 5 khol deta hai, jahan tumhari team baithti hai, par floor 7 nahi jahan server room hai, aur director ka cabin bhi nahi. Yeh doosra step ek alag sawaal ka jawab deta hai: "Tumhe kya karne ki permission hai?" Isi ko authorization (authZ) kehte hain. Gate ka guard decide nahi karta ki tum kaunse floor pe ja sakte ho; badge system karta hai. Do alag problems, do alag systems.

Ab doosri picture: ek hotel. Check-in pe receptionist ek baar tumhara passport check karta hai (authentication) aur ek key card deta hai jisme programmed hai "Room 504, Friday subah 11 baje tak valid". Room 504 ka door lock har baar reception ko phone nahi karta. Woh bas card padhta hai aur do cheezein check karta hai: "kya yeh card hamare hotel ne program kiya tha?" aur "kya yeh expire ho gaya?". Bilkul aise hi JWT (JSON Web Token) kaam karta hai: server ek signature aur expiry check karta hai, bina database lookup ke.

Par kamzori dekho. Agar Wednesday ko tumhara card kho gaya, toh door Friday 11 baje tak jisko bhi card mile uske liye khushi se khulega. Lock ke paas jaanne ka koi tareeka nahi hai. Reception ko lock reprogram karna padega, ya hotel aise cards de jo har kuch ghante mein expire hon aur desk se naya mil jaaye. Yeh picture yaad rakhna; "JWT ko revoke kaise karte ho" wala poora interview sawaal yahi hai.

Software se jodo: gate ka guard tumhara login endpoint hai (password check karta hai). Badge ya key card ek session cookie ya token hai. Lift aur door readers tumhare API endpoints hain jo har request pe permissions check karte hain. Card khona matlab token chori hona.

Hamara running example: ek dealer group ke kai rooftops hain (alag-alag dealership locations) aur sab ek web portal use karte hain. Rooftop 42 ka service advisor (service drive pe baitha woh insaan jo repair orders likhta hai) sirf rooftop 42 ke repair orders (ROs) dekhe. BDC agent (business development center, phone aur chat wali team) leads dekh sakta hai par prices edit nahi kar sakta. General manager apne rooftop ka sab kuch dekhta hai. In rules ko sahi banana hi authorization hai.

Level 1 Vocabulary: identity, credentials, cookies, tokensVocabulary: identity, credentials, cookies, tokens

  • Identity / principal: the "who" (a user, or another service).
  • Credential: the proof of identity: a password, a one-time code from an authenticator app (MFA, multi-factor authentication, means asking for two or more kinds of proof), an API key, a certificate.
  • Authentication (authN): checking the credential and deciding "this is user_812".
  • Authorization (authZ): deciding if user_812 may do this action on this resource. It happens on every request, after authentication.
  • 401 vs 403: HTTP's two codes for this (recall Topic 08). 401 Unauthorized is really "unauthenticated": no or bad credentials. 403 Forbidden means "I know who you are, and the answer is no".
  • Cookie: a small piece of data a server asks the browser to store (Set-Cookie header). The browser then automatically attaches it to every later request to that site. Remember the word "automatically"; it matters for CSRF.
  • Session: a record the server keeps ("session abc123 belongs to user_812, expires at 6 p.m."), usually in Redis or a database. The browser only holds the random session ID in a cookie.
  • Token: a string the client sends to prove who it is, usually in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header. "Bearer" means "whoever holds this is let in", like cash.
  • Claims: facts written inside a token, such as user ID, roles, expiry time.

Authentication happens once (at login). Authorization happens on every request. Mixing them up is the number one conceptual mistake in this topic.

  • Identity / principal: "kaun" (ek user, ya koi doosri service).
  • Credential: identity ka saboot: password, authenticator app ka one-time code (MFA, multi-factor authentication, matlab do ya zyada tarah ke saboot maangna), API key, certificate.
  • Authentication (authN): credential check karke decide karna "yeh user_812 hai".
  • Authorization (authZ): decide karna ki user_812 is resource pe yeh action kar sakta hai ya nahi. Yeh authentication ke baad, har request pe hota hai.
  • 401 vs 403: iske liye HTTP ke do codes (Topic 08 yaad karo). 401 Unauthorized ka asli matlab "unauthenticated" hai: credentials nahi ya galat. 403 Forbidden matlab "mujhe pata hai tum kaun ho, aur jawab hai nahi".
  • Cookie: data ka chhota tukda jo server browser se store karwata hai (Set-Cookie header). Phir browser us site ki har agli request ke saath ise automatically jod deta hai. "Automatically" word yaad rakhna; CSRF mein yahi kaam aayega.
  • Session: ek record jo server rakhta hai ("session abc123 user_812 ka hai, shaam 6 baje expire hoga"), aam taur pe Redis ya database mein. Browser ke paas cookie mein sirf random session ID hoti hai.
  • Token: ek string jo client bhejta hai yeh saabit karne ke liye ki woh kaun hai, aam taur pe Authorization: Bearer <token> header mein. "Bearer" matlab "jiske paas yeh hai woh andar aa sakta hai", cash ki tarah.
  • Claims: token ke andar likhe facts, jaise user ID, roles, expiry time.

Authentication ek baar hota hai (login pe). Authorization har request pe hota hai. Dono ko mix karna is topic ki number one conceptual galti hai.

Level 2 Storing passwords, and sessions vs tokensPasswords store karna, aur sessions vs tokens

Step one of any login: store passwords safely. Databases leak: a stolen backup, a SQL injection, an insider. Design as if the users table will one day be public.

  • Plaintext: a leak exposes every password, and people reuse passwords across sites. Never.
  • Encryption (reversible with a key): whoever steals the key gets every password. Passwords should never need to be decrypted, so do not encrypt them.
  • Hashing: a one-way function. hash("Chai@123") always gives the same output, but you cannot go backwards. At login you hash what the user typed and compare. Good idea, but the kind of hash matters.
  • Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, even plain SHA-256) were built to be fast. An attacker with GPUs can try billions of guesses per second against them. They can also use rainbow tables: huge precomputed lists of "password → hash".

Two fixes, used together:

  1. Salt: a random value, unique per user (bcrypt uses 16 random bytes), mixed into the password before hashing and stored next to the hash. Now two users with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed rainbow tables are useless because the attacker would need one per salt.
  2. Slow, adaptive hash: algorithms designed to be deliberately expensive: bcrypt (has a cost factor; cost 12 means 212 = 4096 rounds of its expensive setup), scrypt and Argon2id (also "memory-hard": they need lots of RAM, which makes GPU attacks costly). OWASP currently lists Argon2id first, with scrypt and bcrypt as acceptable. You tune the cost so one hash takes a noticeable fraction of a second on your server. A real user logs in once; an attacker needs billions of tries, so slow hurts only the attacker. As hardware gets faster, raise the cost.

Kisi bhi login ka pehla step: passwords safely store karo. Databases leak hote hain: chori hua backup, SQL injection, koi andar ka banda. Aise design karo jaise ek din users table public ho jaayegi.

  • Plaintext: leak hua toh har password khul gaya, aur log sites pe same password reuse karte hain. Kabhi nahi.
  • Encryption (key se reversible): jisne key chura li use har password mil gaya. Passwords ko kabhi decrypt karne ki zaroorat nahi honi chahiye, toh unhe encrypt mat karo.
  • Hashing: ek one-way function. hash("Chai@123") hamesha same output deta hai, par ulta wapas nahi ja sakte. Login pe user ne jo type kiya use hash karke compare karte ho. Idea achha hai, par hash ka type matter karta hai.
  • Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, plain SHA-256 bhi) fast hone ke liye bane the. GPUs wala attacker inpe har second arabon guesses try kar sakta hai. Woh rainbow tables bhi use kar sakta hai: "password → hash" ki pehle se bani hui badi lists.

Do fixes, saath mein use hote hain:

  1. Salt: ek random value, har user ki alag (bcrypt 16 random bytes use karta hai), jo hashing se pehle password mein mila di jaati hai aur hash ke saath store hoti hai. Ab same password wale do users ke hash alag honge, aur rainbow tables bekaar ho jaati hain kyunki attacker ko har salt ke liye alag table chahiye.
  2. Slow, adaptive hash: aise algorithms jo jaan-bujh ke mehenge banaye gaye hain: bcrypt (isme cost factor hota hai; cost 12 matlab uske mehenge setup ke 212 = 4096 rounds), scrypt aur Argon2id (yeh "memory-hard" bhi hain: inhe bahut RAM chahiye, jisse GPU attacks mehenge ho jaate hain). OWASP abhi Argon2id ko pehle rakhta hai, scrypt aur bcrypt ko acceptable. Cost aise tune karo ki tumhare server pe ek hash second ka ek dhyaan dene layak hissa le. Asli user ek baar login karta hai; attacker ko arabon tries chahiye, toh slow hona sirf attacker ko chubhta hai. Hardware fast ho toh cost badhao.
// Node.js with the bcrypt library
const hash = await bcrypt.hash(plainPassword, 12);   // salt is generated and embedded for you
// stored value looks like:
// $2b$12$R9h/cIPz0gi.URNNX3kh2OPST9/PgBkqquzi.Ss7KIUgO2t0jWMUW
//  |  |  |---- 22 chars salt ----||---- 31 chars hash ----|
//  |  cost = 12
//  algorithm version 2b

const ok = await bcrypt.compare(typedPassword, hash);  // re-hashes with the stored salt
if (!ok) return res(401, "Invalid email or password"); // same message for unknown email

Login endpoint hygiene: return the same error for "no such email" and "wrong password" (otherwise attackers learn which emails exist), rate-limit login attempts per account and per IP (Topic 08), and note that bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of input.

After login, how does the server remember you? HTTP is stateless (Topic 08): every request is a stranger. So after checking the password once, the server hands out something the client shows on every request. Two families:

  • Session-based (stateful): server creates a session record in Redis, sends back only a random ID in a cookie (Set-Cookie: sid=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax). On every request, the browser sends the cookie, and the server looks up the session. Logout or "ban this user" is instant: delete the record. Cost: a lookup per request, and a shared session store all servers can reach.
  • Token-based (stateless): server creates a signed token containing the claims (user ID, roles, expiry) and gives it to the client. On every request the client sends it; the server just verifies the signature and expiry with math, no lookup. Scales easily across many services. Cost: hard to revoke before expiry, because the server stores nothing.

Login endpoint ki safai: "yeh email hai hi nahi" aur "galat password" dono ke liye same error do (warna attacker seekh jaayega kaunse emails exist karte hain), login attempts ko account aur IP dono ke hisaab se rate-limit karo (Topic 08), aur yaad rakho bcrypt input ke sirf pehle 72 bytes use karta hai.

Login ke baad server tumhe yaad kaise rakhta hai? HTTP stateless hai (Topic 08): har request ek ajnabi hai. Toh ek baar password check karne ke baad server kuch aisa de deta hai jo client har request pe dikhaye. Do families hain:

  • Session-based (stateful): server Redis mein session record banata hai, cookie mein sirf ek random ID wapas bhejta hai (Set-Cookie: sid=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax). Har request pe browser cookie bhejta hai, aur server session dhoondhta hai. Logout ya "is user ko ban karo" turant hota hai: record delete karo. Cost: har request pe ek lookup, aur ek shared session store jahan sab servers pahunch sakein.
  • Token-based (stateless): server ek signed token banata hai jisme claims hote hain (user ID, roles, expiry) aur client ko de deta hai. Har request pe client use bhejta hai; server bas math se signature aur expiry verify karta hai, koi lookup nahi. Kai services mein aasaani se scale hota hai. Cost: expiry se pehle revoke karna mushkil, kyunki server kuch store hi nahi karta.

Level 3 JWT, refresh tokens, revocation, OAuth and CSRFJWT, refresh tokens, revocation, OAuth aur CSRF

JWT anatomy. A JWT is three pieces of text joined by dots: header.payload.signature. The header and payload are JSON, encoded with base64url (a way to turn bytes into URL-safe text). This is encoding, not encryption: anyone can decode and read a JWT (try pasting one into a decoder). So never put secrets or sensitive personal data in it. The signature is what makes it trustworthy: it is computed over the header and payload with a key only the auth server has. Change one character of the payload (say, "roles":["admin"]) and the signature no longer matches.

JWT ki banawat. JWT text ke teen tukde hain jo dots se jude hain: header.payload.signature. Header aur payload JSON hain, jinhe base64url se encode kiya jaata hai (bytes ko URL-safe text mein badalne ka tareeka). Yeh encoding hai, encryption nahi: koi bhi JWT ko decode karke padh sakta hai (kisi decoder mein paste karke dekho). Toh isme kabhi secrets ya sensitive personal data mat daalo. Signature hi ise bharosemand banata hai: yeh header aur payload pe ek aisi key se compute hota hai jo sirf auth server ke paas hai. Payload ka ek bhi character badlo (jaise "roles":["admin"]) aur signature match nahi karega.

Signing keys. HS256 uses one shared secret for both signing and verifying, so every service that verifies could also forge tokens. RS256 or ES256 use a key pair: the auth server signs with a private key; APIs verify with the public key, usually fetched from a JWKS URL (JSON Web Key Set). For many services, asymmetric keys are the safer choice. The kid (key ID) in the header tells the verifier which public key to use, which makes key rotation possible.

JWT end to end: (1) user logs in with password; (2) auth server verifies it and issues a short-lived access token (a JWT, for example 15 minutes) and a long-lived refresh token; (3) the client sends the access token on every API call; (4) each API verifies signature, expiry, issuer and audience, then reads the claims, with no database lookup; (5) when the access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to /auth/refresh to get a new pair.

Signing keys. HS256 signing aur verifying dono ke liye ek hi shared secret use karta hai, toh jo bhi service verify karti hai woh token forge bhi kar sakti hai. RS256 ya ES256 key pair use karte hain: auth server private key se sign karta hai; APIs public key se verify karti hain, jo aam taur pe ek JWKS URL (JSON Web Key Set) se aati hai. Kai services ho toh asymmetric keys zyada safe choice hain. Header ka kid (key ID) verifier ko batata hai kaunsi public key use karni hai, jisse key rotation possible hota hai.

JWT end to end: (1) user password se login karta hai; (2) auth server use verify karke ek short-lived access token (ek JWT, jaise 15 minute) aur ek long-lived refresh token deta hai; (3) client har API call pe access token bhejta hai; (4) har API signature, expiry, issuer aur audience verify karti hai, phir claims padhti hai, bina database lookup ke; (5) access token expire hone pe client refresh token /auth/refresh pe bhej ke naya pair leta hai.

// Verifying in an API (Node.js, jsonwebtoken library)
const claims = jwt.verify(token, publicKey, {
  algorithms: ["RS256"],                 // never accept "none" or an unexpected alg
  issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
  audience: "inventory-api",
});                                      // throws if signature, exp, iss or aud is wrong -> 401
// Authorization is a separate step:
if (claims.rooftop_id !== ro.rooftop_id) return res(403);

Access token vs refresh token.

Access token vs refresh token.

Access tokenRefresh token
LifetimeLifetimeShort (minutes)Chhota (minutes)Long (days or weeks)Lamba (din ya hafte)
Sent toKahan bheja jaata haiEvery API requestHar API request peOnly the auth server's refresh endpointSirf auth server ke refresh endpoint pe
Checked byKaun check karta haiSignature math, no lookupSignature math, koi lookup nahiAuth server, looked up in its databaseAuth server, apne database mein dekh ke
Revocable?Revoke ho sakta hai?Hard (it just expires soon)Mushkil (bas jaldi expire ho jaata hai)Easy (delete or mark it in the DB)Aasaan (DB mein delete ya mark karo)
StoredKahan storeMemory of the appApp ki memory meinHttpOnly, Secure cookie or secure device storageHttpOnly, Secure cookie ya secure device storage

This split is the hotel fix: key cards that expire quickly (small damage if stolen) plus a desk (refresh endpoint) that checks a list before issuing a new one. Refresh token rotation: every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an old one is ever used again, someone stole it, so revoke the whole family and force a login.

Revoking a JWT before it expires. Options, often combined: (a) keep access tokens short, so the damage window is small; (b) a blocklist (deny list): on logout or compromise, store the token's jti (unique token ID) in Redis with a TTL equal to its remaining lifetime, and check it on each request, which is a tiny, fast lookup of only revoked tokens; (c) a per-user token version or "valid after" timestamp: bump it on password change and reject older tokens; (d) revoke the refresh token so no new access tokens are issued.

Where should a browser keep tokens? In localStorage, any JavaScript on the page can read it, so one XSS bug (cross-site scripting, an attacker's script running on your page) steals it. In an HttpOnly cookie, JavaScript cannot read it, but the browser attaches it automatically, which brings back CSRF (below). A common, balanced setup: access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to the refresh path.

Yeh split hotel wala fix hai: jaldi expire hone wale key cards (chori hua toh kam nuksaan) plus ek desk (refresh endpoint) jo naya card dene se pehle list check karta hai. Refresh token rotation: har refresh pe ek naya refresh token milta hai aur purana invalid ho jaata hai. Agar purana kabhi dobara use hua, toh kisi ne chura liya, toh poori family revoke karo aur login force karo.

Expiry se pehle JWT revoke karna. Options, aksar saath mein: (a) access tokens chhote rakho, taaki nuksaan ki window chhoti ho; (b) ek blocklist (deny list): logout ya compromise pe token ka jti (unique token ID) Redis mein uski bachi hui lifetime jitne TTL ke saath store karo, aur har request pe check karo, yeh sirf revoked tokens ka chhota, fast lookup hai; (c) har user ka ek token version ya "valid after" timestamp: password change pe use badhao aur purane tokens reject karo; (d) refresh token revoke karo taaki naye access tokens bane hi nahi.

Browser tokens kahan rakhe? localStorage mein, page ki koi bhi JavaScript use padh sakti hai, toh ek XSS bug (cross-site scripting, attacker ki script tumhare page pe chal jaana) use chura leta hai. HttpOnly cookie mein JavaScript use padh nahi sakti, par browser use automatically jod deta hai, jisse CSRF wapas aa jaata hai (neeche). Ek common, balanced setup: access token memory mein, refresh token ek HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict cookie mein jo sirf refresh path ke liye ho.

# Revoke on logout: block this token until it would have expired anyway
SET revoked:jti:a1b2c3 1 EX 540        # 540 seconds left on a 15-minute token
# On each request (after signature check):
EXISTS revoked:jti:a1b2c3              # 1 -> reject with 401

OAuth 2.0: "Login with Google". OAuth solves delegation: letting one app act on your behalf at another service without you giving it your password. Before OAuth, apps literally asked for your email password to read your contacts. With OAuth, Google gives the app a limited, revocable token for specific scopes (permissions like "read calendar"). Four roles: the resource owner (you), the client (the app, say a dealer CRM wanting to add appointments to your Google Calendar), the authorization server (Google's login and consent screen), and the resource server (the Google Calendar API).

OAuth by itself is about authorization. For "Login with Google" (authentication), a thin layer on top called OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an ID token, a JWT that says who the user is. The recommended flow is the authorization code flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange):

  1. User clicks "Login with Google". Your app creates a random state value (against CSRF) and a random code_verifier, and redirects the browser to Google with client_id, redirect_uri, scope=openid email, state, and code_challenge (a hash of the verifier).
  2. Google shows its own login page (your app never sees the password) and a consent screen: "App X wants your email address".
  3. Google redirects the browser back to your redirect_uri with a short-lived, single-use authorization code and the same state.
  4. Your backend checks state matches, then, server to server, sends the code plus client_secret and code_verifier to Google's token endpoint.
  5. Google returns an access token (to call Google APIs within the granted scopes), an ID token (who the user is), and optionally a refresh token.
  6. Your app verifies the ID token, finds or creates the user, and starts its own session or issues its own tokens.

Why a code first, not the token directly? The code travels through the browser's URL, which can leak (history, logs, referrer). It is useless alone: it expires quickly, works once, and must be exchanged together with the client secret or the PKCE verifier, over a direct back-channel.

OAuth 2.0: "Login with Google". OAuth delegation solve karta hai: ek app ko doosri service pe tumhari taraf se kaam karne dena bina tumhara password diye. OAuth se pehle apps sach mein tumhara email password maangti thi contacts padhne ke liye. OAuth mein Google app ko specific scopes (permissions jaise "calendar padhna") ke liye ek limited, revocable token deta hai. Chaar roles: resource owner (tum), client (app, jaise ek dealer CRM jo tumhare Google Calendar mein appointments add karna chahta hai), authorization server (Google ka login aur consent screen), aur resource server (Google Calendar API).

OAuth akela authorization ke baare mein hai. "Login with Google" (authentication) ke liye upar ek patli layer hai OpenID Connect (OIDC), jo ek ID token jodta hai, ek JWT jo batata hai user kaun hai. Recommended flow hai authorization code flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange):

  1. User "Login with Google" dabata hai. Tumhari app ek random state value (CSRF ke khilaaf) aur ek random code_verifier banati hai, aur browser ko Google pe redirect karti hai client_id, redirect_uri, scope=openid email, state, aur code_challenge (verifier ka hash) ke saath.
  2. Google apna login page dikhata hai (tumhari app password kabhi nahi dekhti) aur consent screen: "App X tumhara email address chahti hai".
  3. Google browser ko tumhare redirect_uri pe wapas bhejta hai ek short-lived, single-use authorization code aur wahi state ke saath.
  4. Tumhara backend check karta hai ki state match karta hai, phir server se server, code plus client_secret aur code_verifier Google ke token endpoint pe bhejta hai.
  5. Google ek access token (granted scopes ke andar Google APIs call karne ke liye), ek ID token (user kaun hai), aur optionally ek refresh token lautata hai.
  6. Tumhari app ID token verify karti hai, user dhoondhti ya banati hai, aur apna khud ka session shuru karti hai ya apne tokens deti hai.

Seedha token kyun nahi, pehle code kyun? Code browser ke URL se guzarta hai, jo leak ho sakta hai (history, logs, referrer). Akele woh bekaar hai: jaldi expire hota hai, ek hi baar chalta hai, aur use client secret ya PKCE verifier ke saath ek direct back-channel pe exchange karna padta hai.

Step 1 redirect (line breaks added for reading):
https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?response_type=code
  &client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID
  &redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/auth/callback
  &scope=openid%20email
  &state=9f2c...                      # random, checked in step 4
  &code_challenge=E9Melhoa2Owv...     # SHA-256 of code_verifier
  &code_challenge_method=S256

Step 3 callback:
https://app.example.com/auth/callback?code=4/0AX4Xf...&state=9f2c...

Step 4 back-channel (server to server):
POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token
  grant_type=authorization_code&code=4/0AX4Xf...&redirect_uri=...
  &client_id=...&client_secret=...&code_verifier=...

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery). Remember: the browser attaches cookies automatically to every request to a site, no matter which page started the request. Suppose a sales manager is logged into the dealer portal (session cookie in the browser). In another tab they open a malicious page. That page contains a hidden form that auto-submits a POST to portal.example.com/account/email with the attacker's email. The browser sends it with the manager's session cookie. The server sees a valid session and changes the account email. The attacker then does "forgot password" and owns the account. The attacker never saw the cookie; they just borrowed the browser's habit of sending it.

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery). Yaad karo: browser kisi site ki har request ke saath cookies automatically jod deta hai, chahe request kisi bhi page ne shuru ki ho. Maan lo ek sales manager dealer portal pe logged in hai (browser mein session cookie). Doosre tab mein woh ek malicious page khol leta hai. Us page mein ek hidden form hai jo apne aap portal.example.com/account/email pe attacker ke email ke saath POST submit kar deta hai. Browser use manager ki session cookie ke saath bhejta hai. Server ko valid session dikhta hai aur woh account ka email badal deta hai. Phir attacker "forgot password" karke account le leta hai. Attacker ne cookie kabhi dekhi hi nahi; usne bas browser ki cookie bhejne ki aadat udhaar le li.

Preventing CSRF, in layers:

  • SameSite cookies: SameSite=Strict never sends the cookie on cross-site requests; Lax sends it only on top-level GET navigations (clicking a link), not on cross-site POSTs. Modern browsers such as Chrome treat cookies with no SameSite attribute as Lax by default, but set it explicitly.
  • CSRF tokens: the server puts a random secret in each real form (or a header the site's JavaScript sets) and checks it on submit. The evil page cannot read your page, so it cannot know the token. Variants: synchronizer token (stored in the session) and double-submit cookie.
  • Origin / Referer checks: browsers send an Origin header on POSTs; reject if it is not your site.
  • Never change state with GET, and ask for re-authentication on very sensitive actions (change email, add payout account).

CSRF rokna, layers mein:

  • SameSite cookies: SameSite=Strict cross-site requests pe cookie kabhi nahi bhejta; Lax sirf top-level GET navigation (link click) pe bhejta hai, cross-site POST pe nahi. Chrome jaise modern browsers bina SameSite attribute wali cookies ko default Lax maante hain, par ise explicitly set karo.
  • CSRF tokens: server har asli form mein ek random secret daalta hai (ya ek header jo site ki apni JavaScript set kare) aur submit pe check karta hai. Evil page tumhara page padh nahi sakta, toh use token pata nahi chal sakta. Variants: synchronizer token (session mein stored) aur double-submit cookie.
  • Origin / Referer checks: browsers POST pe Origin header bhejte hain; agar woh tumhari site nahi hai toh reject karo.
  • GET se kabhi state change mat karo, aur bahut sensitive actions (email change, payout account add) pe dobara authentication maango.

Level 4 Senior level: RBAC, ABAC and microservicesSenior level: RBAC, ABAC aur microservices

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): users get roles, roles get permissions. service_advisor → ro:read, ro:update; bdc_agent → lead:read, appointment:create; general_manager → everything at the rooftop. Checking is simple: "does any of this user's roles include ro:update?". Easy to understand and audit. Weakness: it cannot express conditions about the specific resource. "Service advisors may update ROs, but only at their own rooftop and only while the RO is open" leads to role explosion (advisor_rooftop_42, advisor_rooftop_43...).

ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): a policy evaluates attributes of the user (role, rooftop_id, department), the resource (rooftop_id, status, owner), the action (read, update), and the environment (time, IP, device). The rule above becomes one line. More expressive, but harder to reason about, test and audit ("who can see this RO?" requires evaluating policies). In practice most systems combine them: roles for coarse permissions plus attribute checks for ownership and tenancy.

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): users ko roles milte hain, roles ko permissions. service_advisor → ro:read, ro:update; bdc_agent → lead:read, appointment:create; general_manager → rooftop ka sab kuch. Check simple hai: "kya is user ke kisi role mein ro:update hai?". Samajhna aur audit karna aasaan. Kamzori: yeh specific resource ki conditions express nahi kar sakta. "Service advisors ROs update kar sakte hain, par sirf apne rooftop pe aur sirf jab tak RO open hai" se role explosion hota hai (advisor_rooftop_42, advisor_rooftop_43...).

ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): ek policy attributes evaluate karti hai: user ke (role, rooftop_id, department), resource ke (rooftop_id, status, owner), action ke (read, update), aur environment ke (time, IP, device). Upar wala rule ek line ban jaata hai. Zyada expressive, par samajhna, test aur audit karna mushkil ("yeh RO kaun dekh sakta hai?" jaanne ke liye policies evaluate karni padti hain). Practice mein zyada tar systems dono mix karte hain: moti permissions ke liye roles plus ownership aur tenancy ke liye attribute checks.

Authorization across microservices. Once you split into many services (inventory, appointments, leads, billing), you do not want each one re-implementing login or inventing its own rules. A common design:

  1. Authenticate once, at the edge. An API gateway (or the auth service) verifies the user's token.
  2. Propagate verified identity as a signed token, not as a plain header. Either forward the original JWT or mint a short-lived internal token. Every service verifies the signature itself with the auth server's public keys (JWKS), so a request that sneaks past the gateway with a fake X-User-Id: admin header gets nothing.
  3. Centralise the policy, enforce locally. Write rules once in a shared policy engine such as OPA (Open Policy Agent, policies in a language called Rego) or a shared authorization library, and have each service ask it "may user X do Y on resource Z?". Each service still performs the check, because only it knows the resource's attributes (this RO's rooftop).
  4. Service-to-service identity: services authenticate to each other with mTLS (both sides present certificates, often handled by a service mesh) or OAuth client-credentials tokens, and use the aud claim so a token meant for one service is not accepted by another.

In real production, the most common API security hole is not broken crypto; it is broken object-level authorization (ranked first in the OWASP API Security Top 10): the endpoint checks "is this a logged-in user?" but not "does this RO belong to this user's rooftop?". Changing /ros/1001 to /ros/1002 then leaks another dealer's data. Always check ownership or tenancy on the specific object, and prefer returning 404 for objects in another tenant.

JWT pitfalls interviewers love: accepting "alg": "none" or letting the token choose the algorithm (always pin allowed algorithms), not checking exp/aud/iss, putting personal data in the readable payload, and making tokens live for days with no revocation plan.

Microservices mein authorization. Jab tum kai services mein baant dete ho (inventory, appointments, leads, billing), toh tum nahi chahte ki har ek login dobara implement kare ya apne rules khud banaye. Ek common design:

  1. Ek baar authenticate karo, edge pe. Ek API gateway (ya auth service) user ka token verify karta hai.
  2. Verified identity ko signed token ki tarah aage bhejo, plain header ki tarah nahi. Ya toh original JWT forward karo ya ek short-lived internal token banao. Har service khud auth server ki public keys (JWKS) se signature verify karti hai, toh jo request fake X-User-Id: admin header ke saath gateway se bach ke nikal aaye, use kuch nahi milta.
  3. Policy centralise karo, enforce locally. Rules ek baar ek shared policy engine mein likho jaise OPA (Open Policy Agent, policies Rego naam ki language mein) ya ek shared authorization library, aur har service usse poochhe "kya user X resource Z pe Y kar sakta hai?". Check phir bhi har service khud karti hai, kyunki resource ke attributes (is RO ka rooftop) sirf use pata hain.
  4. Service-to-service identity: services ek doosre ko mTLS (dono taraf certificates, aksar service mesh handle karta hai) ya OAuth client-credentials tokens se authenticate karti hain, aur aud claim use karti hain taaki ek service ke liye bana token doosri service accept na kare.

Real production mein sabse common API security hole toota hua crypto nahi hai; yeh broken object-level authorization hai (OWASP API Security Top 10 mein pehle number pe): endpoint check karta hai "kya yeh logged-in user hai?" par yeh nahi ki "kya yeh RO is user ke rooftop ka hai?". Phir /ros/1001 ko /ros/1002 karne se doosre dealer ka data leak ho jaata hai. Hamesha specific object pe ownership ya tenancy check karo, aur doosre tenant ke objects ke liye 404 dena behtar hai.

JWT ki galtiyan jo interviewers ko pasand hain: "alg": "none" accept karna ya token ko algorithm chunne dena (allowed algorithms hamesha pin karo), exp/aud/iss check na karna, readable payload mein personal data daalna, aur tokens ko bina revocation plan ke kai din tak zinda rakhna.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Authentication (authN)
Proving who you are.Saabit karna ki tum kaun ho.
Authorization (authZ)
Deciding what you may do, on every request.Har request pe decide karna ki tum kya kar sakte ho.
Salt
Random per-user value mixed into a password before hashing.Har user ki random value jo hashing se pehle password mein milaayi jaati hai.
bcrypt / Argon2id / scrypt
Deliberately slow, salted password-hashing algorithms with a tunable cost.Jaan-bujh ke slow, salted password-hashing algorithms jinka cost tune ho sakta hai.
Session
Server-side record of a logged-in user, referenced by a cookie ID.Logged-in user ka server-side record, jise cookie ki ID se refer karte hain.
JWT
Signed token: header.payload.signature; readable, tamper-evident.Signed token: header.payload.signature; padh sakte ho, chhedchhad pakdi jaati hai.
Claims (sub, exp, iss, aud, jti)
Subject (user), expiry, issuer, audience (intended API), unique token ID.Subject (user), expiry, issuer, audience (kis API ke liye), unique token ID.
Access / refresh token
Short-lived token for API calls / long-lived token only for getting new access tokens.API calls ke liye short-lived token / sirf naye access tokens lene ke liye long-lived token.
Blocklist
Store of revoked token IDs (jti), checked on each request.Revoked token IDs (jti) ka store, har request pe check hota hai.
OAuth 2.0 / OIDC
Delegated access without sharing a password / identity layer on top that adds an ID token.Password share kiye bina delegated access / upar ki identity layer jo ID token jodti hai.
PKCE
Proof that the app exchanging the code is the one that started the login.Saboot ki code exchange karne wali app wahi hai jisne login shuru kiya tha.
CSRF
A malicious site makes your browser send a request with your cookies.Malicious site tumhare browser se tumhari cookies ke saath request bhejwa deti hai.
SameSite
Cookie attribute controlling whether cookies go on cross-site requests.Cookie attribute jo decide karta hai ki cross-site requests pe cookies jaayengi ya nahi.
XSS
Attacker's script running inside your page; can read localStorage.Attacker ki script tumhare page ke andar chalna; localStorage padh sakti hai.
RBAC / ABAC
Permissions by role / by rules over user, resource, action and environment attributes.Role ke hisaab se permissions / user, resource, action aur environment attributes pe rules ke hisaab se.
OPA
Open Policy Agent: a policy engine that answers allow/deny questions for many services.Open Policy Agent: ek policy engine jo kai services ke allow/deny sawaalon ka jawab deta hai.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What is the difference between authentication and authorization?Authentication aur authorization mein kya farak hai?
What they're really testing: that you see identity ("who are you?") and permission ("what may you do?") as separate problems with separate mechanisms.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum identity ("tum kaun ho?") aur permission ("tum kya kar sakte ho?") ko alag problems maante ho jinke mechanisms alag hain.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Authentication answers "who are you?": verifying a credential like a password, an MFA code or a certificate, and concluding "this is user 812". Authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?": given that identity, can they perform this action on this specific resource. Like an office: the guard at the gate checks your ID, and your badge decides which floors open. Authentication usually happens once at login and produces a session or token; authorization happens on every request. For example, in a dealer portal, a service advisor logs in successfully, but when they try to open a repair order from another rooftop, authorization says no. In HTTP terms, failing authentication is 401 and failing authorization is 403. Keeping them separate lets me change login methods, say add Google login, without touching permission rules.

Authentication "tum kaun ho?" ka jawab deta hai: password, MFA code ya certificate jaisa credential verify karke nateeja nikaalna "yeh user 812 hai". Authorization "tumhe kya karne ki permission hai?" ka jawab deta hai: us identity ke saath, kya woh is specific resource pe yeh action kar sakta hai. Office jaisa: gate ka guard tumhara ID check karta hai, aur tumhara badge decide karta hai kaunse floors khulenge. Authentication aam taur pe login pe ek baar hota hai aur session ya token deta hai; authorization har request pe hota hai. Jaise dealer portal mein ek service advisor successfully login karta hai, par jab woh doosre rooftop ka repair order kholne ki koshish karta hai, authorization mana kar deta hai. HTTP mein authentication fail hona 401 hai aur authorization fail hona 403. Dono ko alag rakhne se main login method badal sakta hoon, jaise Google login add karna, bina permission rules chhue.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Authorization has layers: function-level (may this role call this endpoint at all?) and object-level (may this user touch this particular record?). Object-level is where most real breaches happen, since it is easy to forget the ownership check. Authentication strength can itself feed authorization: sensitive actions can require a recent login or MFA ("step-up authentication"). And in OAuth, the word "authorization" means delegated access, while OIDC adds the authentication part; confusing those is common.

Authorization ki layers hoti hain: function-level (kya yeh role yeh endpoint call kar hi sakta hai?) aur object-level (kya yeh user is particular record ko chhoo sakta hai?). Zyada tar asli breaches object-level pe hote hain, kyunki ownership check bhoolna aasaan hai. Authentication ki strength khud authorization mein kaam aa sakti hai: sensitive actions ke liye recent login ya MFA maang sakte ho ("step-up authentication"). Aur OAuth mein "authorization" ka matlab delegated access hai, jabki OIDC authentication wala hissa jodta hai; inhe confuse karna common hai.

Common mistake: treating "logged in" as "allowed". Every request must still check permission on the specific resource.
Galti mat karna: "logged in" ko "allowed" samajhna. Har request pe specific resource ki permission phir bhi check honi chahiye.
02 How does JWT authentication work end to end?JWT authentication shuru se aakhir tak kaise kaam karta hai?
What they're really testing: that the server issues a signed token with claims (user ID, expiry), the client sends it each request, and the server verifies signature and expiry without a database lookup.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki server claims (user ID, expiry) ke saath signed token deta hai, client har request pe bhejta hai, aur server bina database lookup ke signature aur expiry verify karta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

The user logs in with email and password; the auth server checks the bcrypt hash and then issues a JWT. A JWT has three base64url parts, header, payload and signature. The payload holds claims like sub for the user ID, roles, exp for expiry, issuer and audience. The signature is computed over the first two parts with the auth server's private key. The client stores it and sends Authorization: Bearer <token> on every request. Each API verifies the signature with the public key, checks the algorithm, expiry, issuer and audience, and then trusts the claims, with no database or session lookup, which is why it scales across many services. Then authorization runs separately, for example checking the token's rooftop matches the RO's rooftop. The trade-off: the token is readable, so no secrets inside, and it cannot easily be revoked before it expires.

User email aur password se login karta hai; auth server bcrypt hash check karke ek JWT deta hai. JWT ke teen base64url hisse hote hain, header, payload aur signature. Payload mein claims hote hain jaise user ID ke liye sub, roles, expiry ke liye exp, issuer aur audience. Signature pehle do hisson pe auth server ki private key se compute hota hai. Client use store karta hai aur har request pe Authorization: Bearer <token> bhejta hai. Har API public key se signature verify karti hai, algorithm, expiry, issuer aur audience check karti hai, aur phir claims pe bharosa karti hai, bina database ya session lookup ke, isi liye yeh kai services mein scale hota hai. Phir authorization alag se chalta hai, jaise check karna ki token ka rooftop RO ke rooftop se match karta hai. Trade-off: token padha ja sakta hai, toh andar koi secret nahi, aur expiry se pehle aasaani se revoke nahi hota.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I prefer RS256 or ES256 over HS256 when many services verify, because with a shared HS256 secret any verifier could also mint tokens. Public keys are published at a JWKS endpoint and selected by the kid header, which allows key rotation without downtime. I pin the allowed algorithms to block the alg: none and algorithm-confusion attacks, allow a small clock skew on exp, keep access tokens short, and pair them with refresh tokens. For browsers, I avoid localStorage because of XSS.

Jab kai services verify karti hain toh main HS256 ki jagah RS256 ya ES256 prefer karta hoon, kyunki shared HS256 secret se koi bhi verifier token bana bhi sakta hai. Public keys ek JWKS endpoint pe publish hoti hain aur kid header se select hoti hain, jisse bina downtime key rotation ho sakta hai. Main allowed algorithms pin karta hoon taaki alg: none aur algorithm-confusion attacks block hon, exp pe thoda clock skew allow karta hoon, access tokens chhote rakhta hoon, aur unke saath refresh tokens deta hoon. Browsers ke liye XSS ki wajah se localStorage avoid karta hoon.

Common mistake: saying the JWT is "encrypted". It is signed and base64url-encoded; anyone can read the payload.
Galti mat karna: JWT ko "encrypted" bolna. Yeh signed aur base64url-encoded hai; payload koi bhi padh sakta hai.
03 What is the difference between an access token and a refresh token?Access token aur refresh token mein kya farak hai?
What they're really testing: access is short-lived, sent on every request and hard to revoke; refresh is long-lived, stored securely, and used only to get new access tokens.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: access short-lived hai, har request pe jaata hai aur revoke karna mushkil; refresh long-lived hai, securely store hota hai, aur sirf naye access tokens lene ke liye use hota hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

The access token is what the client sends on every API call. It is usually a JWT that APIs verify without a lookup, so it is hard to revoke; that is why I keep it short-lived, say 15 minutes, so a stolen one is only useful briefly. The refresh token is long-lived, days or weeks, but it is sent only to one place, the auth server's refresh endpoint, and the auth server checks it against its database each time, so it can be revoked. It is stored more carefully, for example in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie scoped to the refresh path, or in the phone's secure storage. Like a hotel: the key card expires quickly, but the front desk can re-issue it after checking you are still a guest. This gives the scalability of stateless tokens with a control point for revocation. The cost is a refresh round trip every few minutes.

Access token woh hai jo client har API call pe bhejta hai. Yeh aam taur pe JWT hota hai jise APIs bina lookup verify karti hain, toh revoke karna mushkil hai; isi liye main ise short-lived rakhta hoon, jaise 15 minute, taaki chori hua token thodi der hi kaam aaye. Refresh token long-lived hota hai, din ya hafte, par yeh sirf ek jagah bheja jaata hai, auth server ke refresh endpoint pe, aur auth server har baar ise apne database se check karta hai, toh ise revoke kar sakte hain. Ise zyada dhyaan se store karte hain, jaise refresh path tak limited HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie mein, ya phone ke secure storage mein. Hotel jaisa: key card jaldi expire hota hai, par front desk check karke ki tum abhi bhi guest ho, naya de deta hai. Isse stateless tokens ki scalability milti hai aur revocation ke liye ek control point bhi. Cost: har kuch minute mein ek refresh round trip.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I use refresh token rotation: each refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. If an already-used refresh token shows up again, it means two parties have it, so I revoke the whole token family and force re-login; this is reuse detection. Refresh tokens can also be bound to a device or client. On logout I delete the refresh token server side. An absolute session lifetime (for example, re-login after 30 days no matter what) limits how long a chain of refreshes can continue.

Main refresh token rotation use karta hoon: har refresh pe naya refresh token milta hai aur purana invalid hota hai. Agar pehle se use hua refresh token dobara aaye, matlab do logon ke paas hai, toh main poori token family revoke karke re-login force karta hoon; ise reuse detection kehte hain. Refresh tokens ko kisi device ya client se bhi bind kar sakte hain. Logout pe main server side refresh token delete karta hoon. Ek absolute session lifetime (jaise 30 din baad chahe kuch bhi ho, dobara login) limit karta hai ki refreshes ki chain kitni lambi chal sakti hai.

Common mistake: sending the refresh token on every API request or making the access token long-lived "for convenience". That removes the whole point of the split.
Galti mat karna: har API request pe refresh token bhejna ya "convenience ke liye" access token ko long-lived banana. Isse split ka poora matlab hi khatam ho jaata hai.
04 How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?JWT ko expire hone se pehle revoke kaise karte ho?
What they're really testing: you know JWTs are stateless so you cannot "delete" one; you use a blocklist (Redis of revoked jti) or short expiry plus refresh-token rotation.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: tumhe pata hai JWT stateless hai toh use "delete" nahi kar sakte; tum blocklist (revoked jti ka Redis) ya short expiry plus refresh-token rotation use karte ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A JWT is stateless: the server does not store it, so there is nothing to delete, and any service that checks only the signature will accept it until exp. So I design for it. First, short access-token lifetimes, a few minutes, so the natural damage window is small. Second, for immediate revocation, like logout, a stolen laptop or a fired employee, I add a blocklist: every token has a unique jti, and I store revoked ones in Redis with a TTL equal to the token's remaining lifetime, for example SET revoked:jti:a1b2c3 1 EX 540, and check it after verifying the signature. Third, I revoke the user's refresh tokens so no new access tokens are issued. The trade-off is honest: the blocklist reintroduces a lookup, but it is a tiny, fast Redis check of only revoked tokens, not a full session store.

JWT stateless hai: server use store nahi karta, toh delete karne ko kuch hai hi nahi, aur jo service sirf signature check karti hai woh exp tak use accept karegi. Toh main iske liye design karta hoon. Pehla, chhoti access-token lifetime, kuch minute, taaki natural nuksaan ki window chhoti ho. Doosra, turant revocation ke liye, jaise logout, chori hua laptop ya nikala gaya employee, main blocklist jodta hoon: har token ka unique jti hota hai, aur revoked wale main Redis mein token ki bachi lifetime jitne TTL ke saath store karta hoon, jaise SET revoked:jti:a1b2c3 1 EX 540, aur signature verify karne ke baad ise check karta hoon. Teesra, user ke refresh tokens revoke karta hoon taaki naye access tokens na banein. Trade-off seedha hai: blocklist ek lookup wapas le aata hai, par yeh sirf revoked tokens ka chhota, fast Redis check hai, poora session store nahi.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

To revoke all of a user's tokens at once (password change, account compromise), store a per-user tokens_valid_after timestamp or token version and reject any token with an older iat or version; this can be cached per user. Because the blocklist entry expires with the token, Redis never grows without bound. If revocation must be instant everywhere and checked on every call anyway, that is a sign that plain server-side sessions or opaque tokens with introspection may be the simpler design.

Ek user ke saare tokens ek saath revoke karne ke liye (password change, account compromise), har user ka ek tokens_valid_after timestamp ya token version store karo aur purane iat ya version wala har token reject karo; ise per user cache kar sakte ho. Kyunki blocklist entry token ke saath hi expire hoti hai, Redis kabhi bina limit ke nahi badhta. Agar revocation har jagah turant chahiye aur har call pe check hona hi hai, toh yeh ishaara hai ki plain server-side sessions ya introspection wale opaque tokens simpler design ho sakte hain.

Common mistake: saying "delete the token on the client" counts as revocation. An attacker holding a copy can still use it.
Galti mat karna: kehna ki "client pe token delete kar do" revocation hai. Jiske paas copy hai woh attacker ise phir bhi use kar sakta hai.
05 What is OAuth 2.0 and how does it work?OAuth 2.0 kya hai aur kaise kaam karta hai?
What they're really testing: that OAuth is about delegation, a user granting a third party limited access without sharing their password, and that you can walk through the authorization-code flow.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki OAuth delegation ke baare mein hai, user kisi third party ko bina password share kiye limited access deta hai, aur tum authorization-code flow step by step samjha sako.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

OAuth 2.0 is a delegation protocol: it lets a user give an app limited access to their data at another service without giving the app their password. Say a dealer CRM wants to add service appointments to an advisor's Google Calendar. With the authorization-code flow, the CRM redirects the advisor to Google with its client ID, the requested scope like "calendar events", a redirect URL, a random state and a PKCE challenge. The advisor logs in on Google's own page and approves. Google redirects back with a short-lived, one-time code. The CRM's backend exchanges that code, plus its client secret and PKCE verifier, for an access token and optionally a refresh token, then calls the Calendar API with it. The advisor can revoke that access anytime in Google without changing their password. The trade-off is complexity: redirects, secrets and token storage to get right.

OAuth 2.0 ek delegation protocol hai: yeh user ko kisi app ko doosri service pe uske data ka limited access dene deta hai, bina app ko password diye. Maan lo ek dealer CRM ek advisor ke Google Calendar mein service appointments add karna chahta hai. Authorization-code flow mein CRM advisor ko Google pe redirect karta hai apne client ID, maange gaye scope jaise "calendar events", redirect URL, random state aur PKCE challenge ke saath. Advisor Google ke apne page pe login karke approve karta hai. Google ek short-lived, one-time code ke saath wapas redirect karta hai. CRM ka backend woh code, apne client secret aur PKCE verifier ke saath, ek access token aur optionally refresh token se exchange karta hai, phir usse Calendar API call karta hai. Advisor kabhi bhi Google mein yeh access revoke kar sakta hai bina password badle. Trade-off complexity hai: redirects, secrets aur token storage sab sahi karne padte hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

OAuth alone does not tell you who the user is; "Login with Google" uses OpenID Connect on top, which adds a signed ID token with the user's identity. The code is exchanged on a back channel because URLs leak through history and logs. state protects the callback against CSRF, and PKCE stops a stolen code from being redeemed by someone else, which is why it is now recommended for all clients, including mobile apps and single-page apps that cannot keep a secret. Other grants: client credentials for service-to-service; the implicit and password grants are deprecated.

OAuth akela nahi batata ki user kaun hai; "Login with Google" upar OpenID Connect use karta hai, jo user ki identity wala signed ID token jodta hai. Code back channel pe exchange hota hai kyunki URLs history aur logs se leak hote hain. state callback ko CSRF se bachata hai, aur PKCE chori hue code ko kisi aur se redeem hone se rokta hai, isi liye ab yeh sab clients ke liye recommended hai, mobile apps aur single-page apps bhi jo secret nahi rakh sakte. Doosre grants: service-to-service ke liye client credentials; implicit aur password grants deprecated hain.

Common mistake: calling OAuth an authentication protocol, or describing the app receiving the user's password. The whole point is that it never does.
Galti mat karna: OAuth ko authentication protocol bolna, ya aisa batana ki app ko user ka password milta hai. Poora point hi yeh hai ki kabhi nahi milta.
06 Session-based vs token-based authentication: what are the trade-offs?Session-based vs token-based authentication: trade-offs kya hain?
What they're really testing: sessions keep state on the server and use a cookie, tokens keep nothing on the server; sessions revoke easily, tokens scale easily.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: sessions server pe state rakhte hain aur cookie use karte hain, tokens server pe kuch nahi rakhte; sessions aasaani se revoke hote hain, tokens aasaani se scale hote hain.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)
