With sessions, after login the server stores a record, session ID mapped to user and expiry, usually in Redis, and gives the browser only a random ID in an HttpOnly cookie. Every request, the server looks it up. The big win is control: logout or banning a user is instant, just delete the record. The costs are a lookup per request and a shared store all servers must reach. With tokens, the server signs a JWT containing the claims and stores nothing; any service with the public key can verify it locally, which suits many microservices and mobile clients. The cost is revocation: a token stays valid until it expires unless I add a blocklist. My rule of thumb: a single web app talking to its own backend, sessions are simple and safe; many services or third-party clients, short-lived tokens plus refresh tokens.

Sessions mein login ke baad server ek record store karta hai, session ID se user aur expiry ka mapping, aam taur pe Redis mein, aur browser ko HttpOnly cookie mein sirf ek random ID deta hai. Har request pe server use dhoondhta hai. Bada faayda control hai: logout ya user ko ban karna turant hota hai, bas record delete karo. Cost: har request pe lookup aur ek shared store jahan sab servers pahunchein. Tokens mein server claims ke saath JWT sign karta hai aur kuch store nahi karta; public key wali koi bhi service ise locally verify kar sakti hai, jo kai microservices aur mobile clients ke liye suit karta hai. Cost revocation hai: token expire hone tak valid rehta hai jab tak main blocklist na jodun. Mera rule of thumb: ek single web app jo apne hi backend se baat kare, uske liye sessions simple aur safe hain; kai services ya third-party clients ho toh short-lived tokens plus refresh tokens.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

"Cookie vs header" is a separate axis from "session vs token": you can put a JWT in a cookie, or send an opaque session ID in a header. Cookies are sent automatically, which makes CSRF defenses necessary (SameSite, CSRF tokens) but keeps tokens away from JavaScript if HttpOnly. Bearer headers avoid CSRF but the token must live somewhere JavaScript can read, which raises XSS risk. Sessions scale fine in practice with Redis; "tokens scale, sessions don't" is an oversimplification.

"Cookie vs header" ek alag axis hai "session vs token" se: tum JWT ko cookie mein rakh sakte ho, ya opaque session ID header mein bhej sakte ho. Cookies automatically jaati hain, jisse CSRF defenses zaroori ho jaate hain (SameSite, CSRF tokens) par HttpOnly ho toh tokens JavaScript se door rehte hain. Bearer headers CSRF se bachte hain par token kahin aisi jagah rehna chahiye jahan JavaScript padh sake, jisse XSS risk badhta hai. Practice mein Redis ke saath sessions bhi achhe se scale hote hain; "tokens scale karte hain, sessions nahi" ek oversimplification hai.

Common mistake: claiming JWTs are always better or "more secure". They trade revocability for statelessness.
Galti mat karna: kehna ki JWT hamesha better ya "zyada secure" hai. Woh statelessness ke badle revocability chhodte hain.
07 What is RBAC vs ABAC?RBAC vs ABAC kya hai?
What they're really testing: RBAC grants permissions through roles, ABAC through rules over attributes, and when each fits.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: RBAC roles ke through permissions deta hai, ABAC attributes pe rules ke through, aur kab kaunsa fit hota hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

RBAC, role-based access control, assigns users to roles and roles to permissions. In a dealer portal, "service advisor" gets read and update on repair orders, "BDC agent" gets read on leads and create on appointments. It is simple, and easy to audit: to know what Asha can do, look at her roles. ABAC, attribute-based access control, evaluates a policy over attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the environment, for example "an advisor may update an RO only if the RO's rooftop equals the advisor's rooftop and the RO is still open". That rule is awkward in pure RBAC; you would need a role per rooftop. ABAC is more expressive but harder to test and audit. In practice I combine them: roles for coarse "can call this kind of action", attributes for ownership and tenancy on the specific record.

RBAC, role-based access control, users ko roles mein aur roles ko permissions mein daalta hai. Dealer portal mein "service advisor" ko repair orders pe read aur update milta hai, "BDC agent" ko leads pe read aur appointments pe create. Simple hai, aur audit karna aasaan: Asha kya kar sakti hai jaanne ke liye uske roles dekho. ABAC, attribute-based access control, user, resource, action aur environment ke attributes pe ek policy evaluate karta hai, jaise "advisor RO tabhi update kar sakta hai jab RO ka rooftop advisor ke rooftop ke barabar ho aur RO abhi open ho". Pure RBAC mein yeh rule awkward hai; har rooftop ke liye ek role chahiye hoga. ABAC zyada expressive hai par test aur audit karna mushkil. Practice mein main dono mix karta hoon: moti "is type ka action kar sakte ho" ke liye roles, specific record pe ownership aur tenancy ke liye attributes.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Symptoms that RBAC is not enough: role explosion and lots of if checks hard-coded around the codebase. ABAC policies are usually externalised to a policy engine like OPA or AWS Cedar so they are versioned, tested and shared. A third model, ReBAC (relationship-based, as in Google's Zanzibar paper), decides by relationships such as "user is a member of the group that owns this document", and fits sharing-heavy apps. Whatever the model, default-deny and log every denial.

RBAC kaafi nahi hai iske lakshan: role explosion aur codebase mein jagah jagah hard-coded if checks. ABAC policies aam taur pe OPA ya AWS Cedar jaise policy engine mein bahar rakhi jaati hain taaki woh versioned, tested aur shared hon. Teesra model, ReBAC (relationship-based, jaise Google ka Zanzibar paper), relationships se decide karta hai jaise "user us group ka member hai jo is document ka owner hai", aur sharing-heavy apps ke liye fit hai. Model jo bhi ho, default-deny rakho aur har denial log karo.

Common mistake: presenting them as rivals where you must pick one. Real systems use roles plus attribute checks together.
Galti mat karna: dono ko aise rivals batana jinme se ek hi chunna hai. Asli systems roles aur attribute checks saath use karte hain.
08 How do you securely store passwords?Passwords securely kaise store karte ho?
What they're really testing: never plaintext or reversible encryption; a slow, salted hash like bcrypt, Argon2 or scrypt; never MD5 or SHA-1 alone.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: plaintext ya reversible encryption kabhi nahi; bcrypt, Argon2 ya scrypt jaisa slow, salted hash; MD5 ya SHA-1 akele kabhi nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I assume the users table will leak one day and design so a leak does not expose passwords. So never plaintext, and never reversible encryption, because whoever steals the key gets everything. I store a one-way hash, but not a fast one like MD5, SHA-1 or plain SHA-256, because attackers can try billions of guesses per second against those, and use precomputed rainbow tables. I use a slow, adaptive, salted algorithm: Argon2id, which OWASP lists first, or bcrypt or scrypt. Each user gets a unique random salt, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables are useless. The cost factor is tuned so one hash takes a noticeable fraction of a second: fine for a user logging in once, painful for an attacker trying billions. For example, bcrypt.hash(password, 12) stores the algorithm, cost and salt inside the result string. The trade-off is CPU per login, so I rate-limit login attempts too.

Main maan ke chalta hoon ki users table ek din leak hogi aur aise design karta hoon ki leak se passwords na khulein. Toh plaintext kabhi nahi, aur reversible encryption bhi kabhi nahi, kyunki jisne key churaayi use sab mil gaya. Main one-way hash store karta hoon, par MD5, SHA-1 ya plain SHA-256 jaisa fast wala nahi, kyunki attackers inpe har second arabon guesses try kar sakte hain, aur pehle se bani rainbow tables use kar sakte hain. Main slow, adaptive, salted algorithm use karta hoon: Argon2id, jise OWASP pehle rakhta hai, ya bcrypt ya scrypt. Har user ko unique random salt milta hai, toh same passwords ke hash alag bante hain aur pehle se bani tables bekaar ho jaati hain. Cost factor aise tune hota hai ki ek hash second ka dhyaan dene layak hissa le: ek baar login karne wale user ke liye theek, arabon try karne wale attacker ke liye dard. Jaise bcrypt.hash(password, 12) algorithm, cost aur salt result string ke andar hi store karta hai. Trade-off: har login pe CPU, toh main login attempts bhi rate-limit karta hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Argon2id and scrypt are memory-hard, which blunts GPU and custom-hardware attacks better than bcrypt. bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of input. An optional pepper, a secret added to all passwords and kept outside the database (for example in a secrets manager), means a DB-only leak is not enough. When I raise the cost, I rehash on the user's next successful login. Compare in constant time (the libraries do), return the same error for unknown email and wrong password, check new passwords against known-breached lists, and offer MFA.

Argon2id aur scrypt memory-hard hain, jo GPU aur custom-hardware attacks ko bcrypt se behtar rokte hain. bcrypt input ke sirf pehle 72 bytes use karta hai. Ek optional pepper, ek secret jo sab passwords mein jodte hain aur database ke bahar rakhte hain (jaise secrets manager mein), matlab sirf DB leak kaafi nahi hoga. Jab main cost badhata hoon, toh user ke agle successful login pe rehash karta hoon. Constant time mein compare karo (libraries karti hain), unknown email aur galat password pe same error do, naye passwords ko known-breached lists se check karo, aur MFA offer karo.

Common mistake: saying "SHA-256 with a salt" is enough. Salting stops rainbow tables, but a fast hash still lets attackers brute-force quickly.
Galti mat karna: kehna ki "salt ke saath SHA-256" kaafi hai. Salt rainbow tables rokta hai, par fast hash se attacker phir bhi jaldi brute-force kar leta hai.
09 What is CSRF and how do you prevent it?CSRF kya hai aur ise kaise rokte ho?
What they're really testing: that a malicious site can make the browser send a request with the logged-in user's cookies, and the defenses: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, Origin/Referer checks.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki malicious site browser se logged-in user ki cookies ke saath request bhejwa sakti hai, aur defenses: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, Origin/Referer checks.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

CSRF, cross-site request forgery, abuses the fact that browsers attach a site's cookies automatically to every request to that site, whichever page triggered it. Say a sales manager is logged into the dealer portal. They open a malicious page that auto-submits a hidden form posting to the portal's "change email" endpoint. The browser attaches the session cookie, the server sees a valid session and changes the email, and the attacker then resets the password. The attacker never saw the cookie. I defend in layers. Set session cookies with SameSite=Lax or Strict, so the browser does not send them on cross-site POSTs. Require a CSRF token, a random value embedded in real forms or sent in a header, that the attacker's page cannot read. Check the Origin or Referer header on state-changing requests. And never change state with GET.

CSRF, cross-site request forgery, is baat ka faayda uthata hai ki browsers kisi site ki cookies us site ki har request ke saath automatically jod dete hain, chahe request kisi bhi page ne trigger ki ho. Maan lo ek sales manager dealer portal pe logged in hai. Woh ek malicious page kholta hai jo apne aap ek hidden form submit karta hai jo portal ke "change email" endpoint pe POST karta hai. Browser session cookie jod deta hai, server ko valid session dikhta hai aur woh email badal deta hai, aur phir attacker password reset kar leta hai. Attacker ne cookie kabhi dekhi hi nahi. Main layers mein defend karta hoon. Session cookies SameSite=Lax ya Strict ke saath set karo, taaki browser cross-site POST pe unhe na bheje. CSRF token maango, ek random value jo asli forms mein embedded ho ya header mein jaaye, jise attacker ka page padh nahi sakta. State change karne wali requests pe Origin ya Referer header check karo. Aur GET se kabhi state change mat karo.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

APIs that authenticate with a bearer token in the Authorization header are not CSRF-prone, because browsers do not attach that header automatically; but those tokens are then readable by JavaScript and exposed to XSS, and an XSS bug defeats CSRF tokens too. SameSite=Lax still allows cookies on top-level GET navigation, which is why GET must be safe. Same-site is not same-origin: a sibling subdomain counts as same-site, so a compromised subdomain can bypass SameSite. CORS does not prevent CSRF, since a simple form POST does not need CORS permission.

Jo APIs Authorization header mein bearer token se authenticate karti hain woh CSRF-prone nahi hain, kyunki browser woh header automatically nahi jodta; par phir woh tokens JavaScript padh sakti hai aur XSS ke saamne hain, aur ek XSS bug CSRF tokens ko bhi hara deta hai. SameSite=Lax top-level GET navigation pe cookies abhi bhi bhejta hai, isi liye GET safe hona chahiye. Same-site aur same-origin ek nahi: ek sibling subdomain same-site ginta hai, toh compromised subdomain SameSite ko bypass kar sakta hai. CORS CSRF nahi rokta, kyunki simple form POST ko CORS permission ki zaroorat nahi hoti.

Common mistake: confusing CSRF with XSS, or thinking CORS protects against CSRF. CSRF borrows your cookies; XSS runs code in your page.
Galti mat karna: CSRF ko XSS samajh lena, ya sochna ki CORS CSRF se bachata hai. CSRF tumhari cookies udhaar leta hai; XSS tumhare page mein code chalata hai.
10 How do you handle authorization across microservices?Microservices mein authorization kaise handle karte ho?
What they're really testing: centralising policy (an auth service or policy library such as OPA) and passing verified claims via a signed token, rather than each service inventing rules or trusting plain headers.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: policy centralise karna (auth service ya OPA jaisi policy library) aur verified claims signed token se aage bhejna, na ki har service apne rules banaye ya plain headers pe bharosa kare.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I separate three things. Authentication happens once, at the edge: the API gateway verifies the user's token. Identity travels as a signed token, either the original JWT or a short-lived internal one, never as a plain X-User-Id header, and each service verifies the signature itself with the auth server's public keys, so nothing unverified is trusted even inside the network. Policy is centralised, written once in a policy engine like OPA or a shared authorization library, so the inventory, appointments and leads services apply the same rules. Enforcement stays local, because only the appointments service knows which rooftop an appointment belongs to; it asks the policy "may this advisor from rooftop 42 update this appointment?". Services also authenticate to each other with mTLS or client-credentials tokens, and check the aud claim. The trade-off is operational: key distribution, policy rollout and a slight latency per check.

Main teen cheezein alag karta hoon. Authentication ek baar, edge pe hota hai: API gateway user ka token verify karta hai. Identity ek signed token ki tarah travel karti hai, ya toh original JWT ya ek short-lived internal token, kabhi plain X-User-Id header ki tarah nahi, aur har service khud auth server ki public keys se signature verify karti hai, toh network ke andar bhi kuch unverified trust nahi hota. Policy centralised hoti hai, OPA jaise policy engine ya shared authorization library mein ek baar likhi, taaki inventory, appointments aur leads services same rules lagayein. Enforcement local rehta hai, kyunki sirf appointments service ko pata hai ki appointment kis rooftop ka hai; woh policy se poochhti hai "kya rooftop 42 ka yeh advisor yeh appointment update kar sakta hai?". Services ek doosre ko mTLS ya client-credentials tokens se bhi authenticate karti hain, aur aud claim check karti hain. Trade-off operational hai: key distribution, policy rollout aur har check pe thodi latency.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Doing authorization only at the gateway is not enough: it can check "may call this route" but not object-level rules, and a missing object check is the top API risk in the OWASP API Security Top 10. OPA can run as a sidecar next to each service for low latency, with policies pushed from a central repo and tested in CI. For calls on behalf of a user deep in a chain, use token exchange so each hop gets a narrowly scoped token with the right audience. Keep claims small; fetch fine-grained permissions from the policy side rather than stuffing everything into the JWT, which would go stale.

Sirf gateway pe authorization kaafi nahi: woh "yeh route call kar sakte ho" check kar sakta hai par object-level rules nahi, aur missing object check OWASP API Security Top 10 mein top API risk hai. OPA har service ke bagal mein sidecar ki tarah chal sakta hai low latency ke liye, central repo se policies push hoti hain aur CI mein test hoti hain. Chain mein gehre user ki taraf se hone wali calls ke liye token exchange use karo taaki har hop ko sahi audience ke saath narrowly scoped token mile. Claims chhote rakho; fine-grained permissions policy side se lo, sab kuch JWT mein mat thoso, warna woh stale ho jaayengi.

Common mistake: trusting an unsigned user-ID header between services because "it's inside our network". One compromised service or misrouted request then becomes full access.
Galti mat karna: services ke beech unsigned user-ID header pe bharosa karna kyunki "yeh hamare network ke andar hai". Phir ek compromised service ya galat route hui request poora access ban jaati hai.

Topic 11 · COMMONTopic 11 · Aksar poocha jaata hai

Docker & DeploymentDocker & Deployment

From "works on my machine" to "running safely in production": how code is packed into images, shipped, rolled out without downtime, checked for health and scaled.

"Mere laptop pe toh chal raha tha" se "production mein safely chal raha hai" tak: code image mein kaise pack hota hai, kaise ship hota hai, bina downtime ke kaise roll out hota hai, health kaise check hoti hai aur scale kaise karte hain.

Level 0 The story: the tiffin boxKahani: tiffin ka dabba

Imagine your mother packs your tiffin every morning. At home her rajma-chawal always tastes perfect. One day you give her recipe to the office canteen cook and ask him to make the same dish. It tastes different. His stove is hotter, his salt is another brand, he has no hing. Same recipe, different kitchen, different result.

Software has exactly this problem. A developer writes code on a laptop that has Node.js version 20, a particular set of libraries, some settings, maybe a file that happens to exist only on that laptop. It works. Then the code is copied to a production server (from the foundations chapter: a computer in a data centre that real users hit, as opposed to local, which is your own laptop). That server has Node 18, a different system library, a missing setting. It crashes. The developer says the most famous sentence in software: "But it works on my machine!"

The fix is the dabba idea. Instead of sending the recipe and hoping every kitchen has the same ingredients, you pack the finished meal and everything it needs into one sealed box: the rice, the rajma, the pickle, even the spoon. Any office, any desk: open it and it is the same meal.

Docker does this for software. You pack your code together with the exact Node version, the exact libraries and the exact files it needs into one sealed package called an image. Any computer that has Docker installed can run that image, and it behaves the same on your laptop, your colleague's laptop, the test server and production.

Two words matter from day one. The image is the recipe plus the mould: a frozen, read-only package that never changes once it is made. The container is the actual dish served from that mould: the running thing. From one mould you can make a hundred identical dishes; from one image you can start a hundred identical containers. Spill curry on one dish and the mould is untouched.

Two more problems follow. First, how does a new version of the dish reach every office without lunch service stopping? That is deployment. Second, if one box goes bad in the middle of lunch, someone must notice and replace it. That is health checks and restarts. This chapter walks from the sealed box all the way to rolling out new versions to thousands of users with zero downtime.

Recipe card = Dockerfile. Mould made from the recipe = image. Dish served from the mould = container. The central storeroom where every office picks up the mould = registry. The canteen manager who decides how many dishes to serve and replaces spoiled ones = orchestrator (Kubernetes, AWS ECS).

Socho tumhari mummy har subah tiffin pack karti hain. Ghar pe unka rajma-chawal hamesha perfect lagta hai. Ek din tum unki recipe office canteen ke cook ko de dete ho aur bolte ho same dish banao. Taste alag aata hai. Uska stove zyada garam hai, namak doosre brand ka hai, hing hai hi nahi. Recipe same, kitchen alag, result alag.

Software mein bilkul yahi problem hai. Developer apne laptop pe code likhta hai jisme Node.js version 20 hai, kuch specific libraries hain, kuch settings hain, shayad ek file bhi hai jo sirf usi laptop pe hai. Sab chal raha hai. Phir code ek production server pe copy hota hai (foundations chapter yaad karo: data centre ka woh computer jispe real users aate hain, local matlab tumhara apna laptop). Us server pe Node 18 hai, koi system library alag hai, koi setting missing hai. Crash. Aur developer software ki sabse famous line bolta hai: "Par mere machine pe toh chal raha tha!"

Solution hai dabba wala idea. Recipe bhej ke yeh umeed karne ki jagah ki har kitchen mein same ingredients honge, tum poora bana hua khaana aur uski har zaroori cheez ek sealed box mein pack kar do: chawal, rajma, achaar, chammach bhi. Koi bhi office, koi bhi desk: dabba kholo, same khaana.

Docker software ke liye yahi karta hai. Tum apna code, exact Node version, exact libraries aur exact files sab ek sealed package mein pack karte ho jise image kehte hain. Jis bhi computer pe Docker install hai, woh image chala sakta hai, aur woh tumhare laptop, colleague ke laptop, test server aur production sab jagah same behave karti hai.

Pehle din se do words yaad rakho. Image matlab recipe plus saancha (mould): ek frozen, read-only package jo ek baar banne ke baad kabhi nahi badalta. Container matlab us saanche se nikli hui asli dish: jo cheez actually chal rahi hai. Ek saanche se sau same dishes ban sakti hain; ek image se sau same containers start ho sakte hain. Ek dish pe curry gir jaaye toh saancha kharab nahi hota.

Iske baad do problems aati hain. Pehli: dish ka naya version har office tak kaise pahunche bina lunch service roke? Isko deployment kehte hain. Doosri: lunch ke beech mein koi dabba kharab ho jaaye toh kisi ko notice karke use replace karna padega. Isko health checks aur restarts kehte hain. Yeh chapter sealed dabbe se shuru karke hazaaron users tak zero downtime ke saath naya version roll out karne tak le jaayega.

Recipe card = Dockerfile. Recipe se bana saancha = image. Saanche se nikli dish = container. Central storeroom jahan se har office saancha uthata hai = registry. Canteen manager jo decide karta hai kitni dishes serve karni hain aur kharab wali replace karta hai = orchestrator (Kubernetes, AWS ECS).

Level 1 The basic words: image, container, Dockerfile, registryBasic words: image, container, Dockerfile, registry

A Dockerfile is a plain text file of instructions, read top to bottom: "start from this base", "copy these files", "run this command", "when you start, run this program". The docker build command reads it and produces an image.

An image is a static, immutable blueprint. Immutable means it cannot be changed after it is built; if you want a change, you build a new image. It contains a minimal operating-system filesystem, your runtime (Node), your libraries and your code, plus metadata such as which command to run on start.

A container is a running instance of an image. When Docker starts a container it takes the read-only image and puts a thin writable layer on top, just for that container. Anything the running program writes to disk (a temp file, an uploaded photo, a log file) goes into that writable layer. When the container is deleted, that layer is deleted with it. One image, many containers, each with its own writable layer.

A registry is a store for images, like GitHub but for images: Docker Hub, AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry. You push an image there once; every server pulls it from there. Images are named with a tag, for example inventory-api:1.4.2 or inventory-api:3f9c2ab (a git commit id).

How is a container different from a virtual machine (VM)? A VM pretends to be a whole computer and boots its own full operating system, which is heavy and slow to start. A container is just an isolated process (a running program, from the foundations chapter) on the host machine. It shares the host's operating-system kernel, but gets its own view of files, network and process list. That is why a container starts in about a second and you can run dozens on one server.

Dockerfile ek simple text file hai jisme instructions hote hain, upar se neeche padhe jaate hain: "is base se shuru karo", "yeh files copy karo", "yeh command chalao", "start hote waqt yeh program chalana". docker build command ise padhti hai aur ek image banati hai.

Image ek static, immutable blueprint hai. Immutable matlab build hone ke baad badal nahi sakti; change chahiye toh nayi image banao. Isme ek chhota sa operating-system filesystem, tumhara runtime (Node), libraries aur code hota hai, plus metadata jaise start pe kaunsi command chalani hai.

Container image ka ek running instance hai. Jab Docker container start karta hai toh read-only image ke upar ek patli si writable layer lagata hai, sirf us container ke liye. Chalta hua program disk pe jo bhi likhta hai (temp file, uploaded photo, log file) woh isi writable layer mein jaata hai. Container delete hua toh yeh layer bhi saath mein delete. Ek image, bahut saare containers, har ek ki apni writable layer.

Registry images ka godown hai, jaise code ke liye GitHub hai waise images ke liye: Docker Hub, AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry. Tum image ek baar wahan push karte ho; har server wahan se pull karta hai. Images ka naam tag se hota hai, jaise inventory-api:1.4.2 ya inventory-api:3f9c2ab (git commit id).

Container aur virtual machine (VM) mein kya fark hai? VM poora computer hone ka naatak karti hai aur apna poora operating system boot karti hai, jo bhaari aur slow hai. Container bas host machine pe ek isolated process hai (chalta hua program, foundations chapter se). Yeh host ka operating-system kernel share karta hai, par isko files, network aur process list ka apna alag view milta hai. Isliye container lagbhag ek second mein start ho jaata hai aur ek server pe darjanon chal sakte hain.

# build an image from the Dockerfile in this folder, name + tag it
docker build -t inventory-api:1.4.2 .

# start two containers from the SAME image
docker run -d --name api-a -p 3001:3000 inventory-api:1.4.2
docker run -d --name api-b -p 3002:3000 inventory-api:1.4.2

docker ps                     # list running containers
docker push registry.example.com/inventory-api:1.4.2   # upload to a registry
docker stop api-a             # sends SIGTERM, waits 10s, then SIGKILL

Image = frozen blueprint (build once). Container = running copy with its own throwaway writable layer (start many). Never "fix" a running container by hand; build a new image.

Image = frozen blueprint (ek baar build). Container = chalti hui copy jiski apni throwaway writable layer hai (bahut saare start karo). Chalte container ko haath se kabhi "fix" mat karo; nayi image build karo.

Level 2 Inside an image: layers, cache and small imagesImage ke andar: layers, cache aur chhoti images

Layers. An image is not one big blob. Each instruction in the Dockerfile that changes the filesystem (FROM, COPY, RUN, ADD) creates a layer: a snapshot of only the files that instruction added or changed. The image is these layers stacked on top of each other, like transparent sheets. Instructions like CMD, ENV and EXPOSE only add metadata.

Build cache. When you rebuild, Docker walks the Dockerfile top to bottom. For each step it asks: "is the instruction the same, and for COPY, are the copied files byte-for-byte the same as last time?" If yes, it reuses the saved layer instantly (a cache hit). The moment one step changes, that step and every step after it is rebuilt, because each layer sits on the one below.

That is why order matters: put things that rarely change first and things that change often last. Your dependencies (package.json) change rarely; your source code changes on every commit. So copy package.json first, run npm ci (the slow step that downloads libraries), and only then copy the source. Now a code change rebuilds only the last cheap layers, and the slow install is served from cache.

Layers. Image ek bada sa blob nahi hai. Dockerfile ki har woh instruction jo filesystem badalti hai (FROM, COPY, RUN, ADD) ek layer banati hai: sirf un files ka snapshot jo us instruction ne add ya change ki. Image in layers ka stack hai, ek ke upar ek, jaise transparent sheets. CMD, ENV, EXPOSE jaisi instructions sirf metadata add karti hain.

Build cache. Jab tum dobara build karte ho, Docker Dockerfile ko upar se neeche chalta hai. Har step pe poochta hai: "instruction same hai kya, aur COPY ke case mein, copy hone wali files pichli baar jaisi exact same hain kya?" Haan toh saved layer turant reuse (cache hit). Jaise hi ek step badla, woh step aur uske baad ke saare steps dobara build hote hain, kyunki har layer neeche wali ke upar baithi hai.

Isliye order matter karta hai: jo cheez kam badalti hai woh pehle, jo baar-baar badalti hai woh last mein. Dependencies (package.json) kam badalti hain; source code har commit pe badalta hai. Toh pehle package.json copy karo, npm ci chalao (slow step jo libraries download karta hai), aur uske baad source copy karo. Ab code change pe sirf last ki sasti layers rebuild hongi, aur slow install cache se aa jaayega.

Here is a Dockerfile that "works" but has almost every beginner mistake in it:

Yeh ek Dockerfile hai jo "chalti" toh hai par isme lagbhag har beginner wali galti hai:

# BAD Dockerfile - do not copy this
# (Dockerfile comments must be on their own line)
# full Debian image: big, many extra packages
FROM node:20
# copies EVERYTHING incl. node_modules, .git, .env - and busts the cache on every code change
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
# re-runs on every code change because the COPY above changed
RUN npm install
# secret baked into the image forever
ENV DB_PASSWORD=please-dont-do-this
# separate RUNs: stale apt cache, extra layers, apt lists never cleaned
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl
EXPOSE 3000
# shell form + npm: SIGTERM may never reach node; also runs as root
CMD npm start

And the multi-stage version that fixes all of it. A multi-stage build has two (or more) FROM lines in one Dockerfile. The first stage is the messy workshop: it has the compiler, TypeScript, test tools and dev dependencies, and it produces the built output. The second stage starts from a clean, small base and copies in only the finished output. Everything from the first stage that you did not copy is thrown away and never ships.

Aur yeh hai multi-stage version jo sab theek karta hai. Multi-stage build mein ek hi Dockerfile mein do (ya zyada) FROM lines hoti hain. Pehla stage gandi workshop hai: isme compiler, TypeScript, test tools aur dev dependencies hain, aur yeh final built output banata hai. Doosra stage ek saaf, chhote base se shuru hota hai aur sirf finished output copy karta hai. Pehle stage ki jo cheez copy nahi ki, woh phenk di jaati hai aur kabhi ship nahi hoti.

# GOOD multi-stage Dockerfile for a Node.js (TypeScript) API
# ---------- Stage 1: build ----------
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
# dependency manifests change rarely -> this layer and npm ci stay cached
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
# exact versions from the lockfile, incl. dev deps needed to compile
RUN npm ci
# source changes often -> only layers from here down rebuild
COPY . .
# compile to dist/, then drop devDependencies (one layer)
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

# ---------- Stage 2: runtime ----------
FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/package.json ./
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist
# do not run as root
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
# exec form: node is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

# .dockerignore - keeps junk and secrets out of the build context
node_modules
dist
.git
.env
.env.*
npm-debug.log
coverage
*.md
Dockerfile
.dockerignore

COPY vs ADD. Both put files into the image. COPY does exactly one thing: copies local files from the build context. ADD does that too, but has two hidden extras: it can download from a remote URL, and it automatically unpacks a local .tar archive. Hidden magic is surprising and less secure (a downloaded file is not checksum-verified by default and the layer is not cached predictably), so the official best practice is: use COPY; use ADD only when you specifically want auto-extraction of a local tar. For remote files, use RUN curl ... with a checksum check.

Why keep images small? Every deploy, every new server and every autoscaled container must pull the image over the network before it can start. A smaller image means faster deploys, faster scaling when traffic spikes and faster cold starts. It also means a smaller attack surface: every extra package (a shell tool, a compiler, curl) is something that can have a security vulnerability and shows up in security scans. How: pick a minimal base (-alpine, -slim, or "distroless" images that do not even have a shell), use multi-stage builds, use .dockerignore, and combine related commands into one RUN with cleanup in the same line (a file deleted in a later layer still exists in the earlier layer, so it still counts toward size).

The .dockerignore file lists what should never be sent to the Docker build. Without it, COPY . . ships your local node_modules (possibly built for macOS, wrong for Linux), your .git history and your .env file with real passwords.

COPY vs ADD. Dono files image mein daalte hain. COPY sirf ek kaam karta hai: build context se local files copy. ADD bhi yeh karta hai, par do chhupe hue extra features ke saath: remote URL se download kar sakta hai, aur local .tar archive ko automatically unpack kar deta hai. Chhupa hua jaadu surprise deta hai aur kam secure hai (download hui file ka checksum by default verify nahi hota aur cache behaviour predictable nahi), isliye official best practice hai: COPY use karo; ADD sirf tab jab tumhe local tar ka auto-extract chahiye. Remote files ke liye checksum check ke saath RUN curl ... use karo.

Images chhoti kyun rakhni hain? Har deploy, har naya server aur har autoscale hua container start hone se pehle image network se pull karta hai. Chhoti image matlab fast deploy, traffic spike pe fast scaling aur fast cold start. Aur chhota attack surface: har extra package (shell tool, compiler, curl) mein security vulnerability ho sakti hai aur woh security scan mein dikhta hai. Kaise: minimal base lo (-alpine, -slim, ya "distroless" images jisme shell bhi nahi hota), multi-stage build use karo, .dockerignore use karo, aur related commands ko ek RUN mein jodo aur usi line mein cleanup karo (baad ki layer mein delete ki gayi file pehle wali layer mein abhi bhi hai, toh size mein count hoti hai).

.dockerignore file batati hai ki kya cheez Docker build mein kabhi nahi bhejni. Iske bina COPY . . tumhara local node_modules (shayad macOS ke liye bana, Linux pe galat), .git history aur asli passwords wali .env file sab ship kar deta hai.

Level 3 Shipping it: pipelines, rollouts and secretsShip karna: pipeline, rollout aur secrets

The pipeline. In a real team nobody builds production images on a laptop. When code is merged, a CI/CD pipeline (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins) runs automatically: install, run tests, build the image, tag it with the git commit id, push it to the registry, then tell the orchestrator to run the new image. An orchestrator such as Kubernetes or AWS ECS is the software that decides which server runs which container, restarts dead ones, and swaps versions. In Kubernetes, the smallest unit it runs is a pod (one or more containers that live together); for this chapter, think "pod = one running copy of our API".

Tag images with something unique and permanent like the commit id, never just latest. latest moves every time, so two servers pulling "latest" five minutes apart may run different code, and "roll back to latest" means nothing.

Rolling deployment. Say 4 copies of the API are running v1 behind a load balancer (from the foundations chapter: the traffic cop that spreads requests across copies). A rolling deployment starts one v2 copy, waits until its health check says it is ready, adds it to the load balancer, removes one v1 copy, and repeats until all are v2. No extra environment is needed and there is no downtime. The cost: for a while v1 and v2 serve traffic at the same time, and rollback means rolling back the same slow way.

Blue-green deployment. You keep two complete environments. "Blue" runs v1 and receives all traffic. You deploy v2 to "green", test it privately, then flip the load balancer (or DNS) so all traffic goes to green in one move. If something breaks, flip back: rollback takes seconds. The cost: you pay for two full environments during the switch, and the database is usually shared, so schema changes must still work for both versions.

Canary is a cautious cousin: send 5% of traffic to v2, watch error rates and latency, then increase. It catches problems that only real traffic reveals, while hurting only a few users.

Pipeline. Real team mein koi bhi production image laptop pe build nahi karta. Jab code merge hota hai, ek CI/CD pipeline (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins) apne aap chalti hai: install, tests, image build, git commit id se tag, registry mein push, phir orchestrator ko bolna ki nayi image chalao. Orchestrator jaise Kubernetes ya AWS ECS woh software hai jo decide karta hai kaunsa container kis server pe chalega, mare hue containers restart karta hai, aur versions badalta hai. Kubernetes mein sabse chhoti chalne wali unit ko pod kehte hain (ek ya zyada containers jo saath rehte hain); is chapter ke liye socho "pod = hamari API ki ek running copy".

Images ko kisi unique aur permanent cheez se tag karo jaise commit id, sirf latest kabhi nahi. latest har baar khisakta hai, toh do servers jo paanch minute ke gap pe "latest" pull karein alag code chala sakte hain, aur "latest pe rollback karo" ka koi matlab nahi.

Rolling deployment. Maan lo API ki 4 copies v1 chala rahi hain ek load balancer ke peeche (foundations chapter se: traffic police jo requests copies mein baantta hai). Rolling deployment ek v2 copy start karta hai, uske health check ke "ready" bolne ka wait karta hai, use load balancer mein jodta hai, ek v1 copy hataata hai, aur yahi repeat karta hai jab tak sab v2 na ho jaayein. Koi extra environment nahi chahiye, koi downtime nahi. Keemat: kuch der ke liye v1 aur v2 ek saath traffic serve karte hain, aur rollback bhi utna hi dheere hota hai.

Blue-green deployment. Tum do poore environments rakhte ho. "Blue" pe v1 chal raha hai aur saara traffic wahi le raha hai. v2 ko "green" pe deploy karo, private mein test karo, phir load balancer (ya DNS) ko ek jhatke mein green pe flip kar do. Kuch toota toh wapas flip: rollback seconds mein. Keemat: switch ke time do poore environments ka kharcha, aur database aam taur pe shared hota hai, toh schema changes dono versions ke saath chalne chahiye.

Canary ek savdhaan cousin hai: 5% traffic v2 pe bhejo, error rate aur latency dekho, phir badhao. Jo problems sirf real traffic mein dikhti hain woh pakdi jaati hain, aur sirf thode users pe asar padta hai.

The full journey from a developer's git push to a safe rollout, with automatic rollback when health checks fail, looks like this:

Developer ke git push se lekar safe rollout tak ka poora safar, jisme health check fail hone pe automatic rollback hota hai, kuch aisa dikhta hai:

Because old and new versions run together during any rollout, the database schema must work for both. Never rename or drop a column in the same deploy that stops using it. Use expand-contract (Topic 09): add the new column first, ship code that uses it, remove the old one in a later deploy.

Secrets. A secret is anything that grants access: database passwords, API keys, signing keys. Never bake secrets into the image or commit them to the repo. Every layer of an image is readable by anyone who can pull it (docker history and docker inspect show ENV values), images get copied to many places, and you cannot un-leak a secret. Even deleting the file in a later layer does not help, because the earlier layer still contains it. Build arguments (ARG) are also visible in the image history. Instead, the secret is injected at runtime when the container starts: as an environment variable or a mounted file, supplied by the orchestrator from a secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager or Kubernetes Secrets. The same image then runs in staging and production with different secrets, and rotating a password does not need a rebuild.

Kyunki kisi bhi rollout ke time purana aur naya version saath chalte hain, database schema dono ke liye chalna chahiye. Jis deploy mein column use karna band kiya, usi deploy mein column rename ya drop mat karo. Expand-contract use karo (Topic 09): pehle naya column add karo, usko use karne wala code ship karo, purana column baad ke deploy mein hatao.

Secrets. Secret matlab koi bhi cheez jo access deti hai: database password, API keys, signing keys. Secrets ko kabhi image mein bake mat karo aur repo mein commit mat karo. Image ki har layer woh padh sakta hai jo use pull kar sake (docker history aur docker inspect ENV values dikha dete hain), images bahut jagah copy hoti hain, aur leak hua secret wapas nahi aata. Baad ki layer mein file delete karne se bhi kuch nahi hota, kyunki pehle wali layer mein woh abhi bhi hai. Build arguments (ARG) bhi image history mein dikhte hain. Iski jagah secret runtime pe inject hota hai jab container start hota hai: environment variable ya mounted file ki tarah, jo orchestrator ek secrets manager se laata hai jaise HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager ya Kubernetes Secrets. Phir same image staging aur production mein alag secrets ke saath chalti hai, aur password rotate karne ke liye rebuild nahi karna padta.

# Kubernetes: inject a secret as an env var at runtime (value never in the image)
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: inventory-api-secrets
        key: db-password

Level 4 Running it: health checks, restarts, graceful shutdown, scalingChalana: health checks, restarts, graceful shutdown, scaling

Health checks. A process can be "running" and still useless: stuck in an infinite loop, out of database connections, still loading. The orchestrator cannot guess; it needs your app to answer a question on a small endpoint. There are two different questions:

  • Readiness: "Can you take traffic right now?" If no, the orchestrator removes the container from the load balancer but does not kill it. Used during startup (still warming up), during shutdown, and when a critical dependency is temporarily unreachable.
  • Liveness: "Are you alive at all, or stuck?" If no (several times in a row), the orchestrator kills and restarts the container. It should check only the process itself (can the event loop answer?), never the database, otherwise a database blip would restart every copy at once.

Kubernetes also has a startup probe for slow-starting apps, so liveness does not kill them while they boot. Without health checks, the load balancer keeps sending users to a crashed or frozen container, and a rolling deploy happily replaces healthy v1 copies with broken v2 copies.

Health checks. Ek process "chal raha" ho sakta hai phir bhi bekaar: infinite loop mein atka hua, database connections khatam, ya abhi load ho raha. Orchestrator guess nahi kar sakta; use tumhari app se ek chhote endpoint pe jawab chahiye. Do alag sawaal hain:

  • Readiness: "Kya tum abhi traffic le sakte ho?" Nahi, toh orchestrator container ko load balancer se hata deta hai par use maarta nahi. Startup ke time (abhi warm up ho raha), shutdown ke time, aur jab koi zaroori dependency thodi der ke liye nahi mil rahi, tab use hota hai.
  • Liveness: "Kya tum zinda ho, ya atak gaye?" Nahi (lagatar kai baar), toh orchestrator container ko maar ke restart karta hai. Isme sirf process khud check karo (event loop jawab de pa raha hai?), database kabhi nahi, warna database ki ek chhoti si hichki pe har copy ek saath restart ho jaayegi.

Kubernetes mein slow start hone wali apps ke liye startup probe bhi hai, taaki boot ke time liveness unhe maar na de. Health checks ke bina load balancer crash ya freeze hue container ko users bhejta rehta hai, aur rolling deploy khushi-khushi healthy v1 copies ko toote hue v2 se replace kar deta hai.

# Kubernetes probe config for the API container
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 3000 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3        # 3 fails -> out of the load balancer
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz/live, port: 3000 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3        # 3 fails -> kill + restart

Restarts and statelessness. Containers are cattle, not pets: they get killed and replaced all the time (a deploy, a crash, a server being drained, autoscaling). A restarted container is a fresh one from the image: its writable layer is brand new, so anything kept in memory (sessions, an in-process cache, a job queue in an array) and any file written to local disk (uploads, temp reports) is gone. So the app must be stateless (foundations chapter: no copy remembers anything the others need). Put sessions in Redis, files in object storage like S3, data in the database, jobs in a real queue.

Graceful shutdown. Before killing a container, the orchestrator sends the signal SIGTERM ("please finish up"). It then waits a grace period (Kubernetes default 30 seconds; docker stop default 10) and sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught. A good app uses that window: fail readiness so no new traffic arrives, stop accepting new connections, finish the requests already in flight, close database pools, flush logs, then exit.

Restarts aur statelessness. Containers "cattle hain, pets nahi": inhe baar-baar maara aur replace kiya jaata hai (deploy, crash, server drain, autoscaling). Restart hua container image se bana ek fresh container hai: iski writable layer bilkul nayi hai, toh memory mein rakhi har cheez (sessions, in-process cache, array mein rakhi job queue) aur local disk pe likhi har file (uploads, temp reports) gayab. Isliye app stateless honi chahiye (foundations chapter: koi copy aisi cheez yaad na rakhe jo doosron ko chahiye). Sessions Redis mein, files S3 jaisi object storage mein, data database mein, jobs asli queue mein.

Graceful shutdown. Container maarne se pehle orchestrator SIGTERM signal bhejta hai ("please kaam samet lo"). Phir ek grace period wait karta hai (Kubernetes default 30 seconds; docker stop default 10) aur phir SIGKILL bhejta hai, jise pakda nahi ja sakta. Achhi app is window ka use karti hai: readiness fail karo taaki naya traffic na aaye, nayi connections lena band karo, jo requests chal rahi hain unhe poora karo, database pool band karo, logs flush karo, phir exit.

// server.js - health endpoints + graceful SIGTERM shutdown
const express = require('express');
const db = require('./db');          // a pg Pool
const app = express();
let shuttingDown = false;

app.get('/healthz/live', (req, res) => res.sendStatus(200));   // process only, no DB
app.get('/healthz/ready', async (req, res) => {
  if (shuttingDown) return res.sendStatus(503);                // draining: take me out
  try { await db.query('SELECT 1'); res.sendStatus(200); }
  catch { res.sendStatus(503); }
});

const server = app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on 3000'));

function shutdown(signal) {
  console.log(`${signal} received, draining`);
  shuttingDown = true;                    // 1. readiness now returns 503
  server.close(async () => {              // 2. stop new connections, wait for in-flight requests
    await db.end();                       // 3. close the DB pool, flush logs
    process.exit(0);
  });
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25_000).unref(); // 4. give up before the 30s SIGKILL
}
process.on('SIGTERM', () => shutdown('SIGTERM'));
process.on('SIGINT',  () => shutdown('SIGINT'));

Scaling. When one copy cannot keep up, there are two directions. Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger machine: more CPU and RAM. It is simple (no code changes) but there is a ceiling (the biggest machine the cloud sells), it usually needs a restart (downtime), cost rises steeply, and it is still one point of failure. Also, one Node.js process mostly uses one CPU core for your JavaScript, so a bigger box helps less than you would think unless you run several processes. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means more copies behind a load balancer. It has no practical ceiling, survives one copy dying, and can be automatic (Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds pods when CPU crosses a target). The price: the app must be stateless, and shared things like the database become the next bottleneck.

Scaling. Jab ek copy load nahi sambhaal paati, toh do raaste hain. Vertical scaling (scale up) matlab badi machine: zyada CPU aur RAM. Simple hai (code change nahi) par ek ceiling hai (cloud ki sabse badi machine), aam taur pe restart chahiye (downtime), kharcha tezi se badhta hai, aur phir bhi ek hi point of failure. Aur ek Node.js process tumhare JavaScript ke liye zyaadatar ek hi CPU core use karta hai, toh badi machine utna fayda nahi deti jitna socho, jab tak kai processes na chalao. Horizontal scaling (scale out) matlab load balancer ke peeche zyada copies. Practically koi ceiling nahi, ek copy mare toh bhi chalta rahega, aur automatic ho sakta hai (Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler CPU target cross hote hi pods badha deta hai). Keemat: app stateless honi hi chahiye, aur database jaisi shared cheezein agla bottleneck ban jaati hain.

Senior nuances that come up in real incidents. (1) PID 1 and signals: with CMD npm start (shell form) the shell or npm is PID 1 and may not forward SIGTERM to node, so every deploy hard-kills in-flight requests. Use exec form CMD ["node", "server.js"] or run with docker run --init / tini. (2) Readiness lag: load balancers take a few seconds to notice a pod is gone, so many teams add a short preStop sleep before shutdown begins. (3) Keep-alive connections can keep server.close() waiting; newer Node versions close idle ones for you, and server.closeIdleConnections() exists since Node 18.2. (4) Memory limits: if a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel kills it (OOMKilled) with no SIGTERM at all; set Node's heap (--max-old-space-size) below the container limit. (5) Docker's own HEALTHCHECK instruction is used by Docker and Swarm, but Kubernetes ignores it and uses its own probes. (6) Pin base images by version (or digest) and rebuild regularly to pick up security patches.

Senior nuances jo real incidents mein aati hain. (1) PID 1 aur signals: CMD npm start (shell form) mein shell ya npm PID 1 hota hai aur ho sakta hai SIGTERM node tak forward na kare, toh har deploy pe chalti requests hard-kill ho jaati hain. Exec form CMD ["node", "server.js"] use karo ya docker run --init / tini se chalao. (2) Readiness lag: load balancer ko pod hatne ka pata chalne mein kuch seconds lagte hain, isliye bahut teams shutdown shuru hone se pehle chhota sa preStop sleep daalti hain. (3) Keep-alive connections server.close() ko wait karwa sakti hain; naye Node versions idle wali khud band kar dete hain, aur server.closeIdleConnections() Node 18.2 se hai. (4) Memory limits: container apni memory limit cross kare toh kernel use maar deta hai (OOMKilled), koi SIGTERM nahi; Node ka heap (--max-old-space-size) container limit se neeche rakho. (5) Docker ki apni HEALTHCHECK instruction Docker aur Swarm use karte hain, par Kubernetes use ignore karta hai aur apne probes use karta hai. (6) Base images ko version (ya digest) se pin karo aur regularly rebuild karo taaki security patches mil jaayein.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Docker
Tool that packs an app with everything it needs into an image and runs it as an isolated container.Tool jo app aur uski har zaroori cheez ko image mein pack karta hai aur use isolated container ki tarah chalata hai.
Image
Read-only, immutable blueprint made of stacked layers. Built once, run many times.Read-only, immutable blueprint jo stacked layers se bana hai. Ek baar build, kai baar run.
Container
A running instance of an image, with its own thin writable layer that disappears when it is removed.Image ka running instance, apni patli writable layer ke saath jo container hatne pe gayab ho jaati hai.
Dockerfile
Text recipe of instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD) used to build an image.Instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD) ki text recipe jisse image build hoti hai.
Layer
Snapshot of files added or changed by one instruction; cached and reused if its inputs did not change.Ek instruction ne jo files add ya change ki unka snapshot; input na badle toh cache se reuse.
Build cache
Saved layers from earlier builds. A change invalidates that layer and every layer after it.Pichle builds ki saved layers. Ek change us layer aur uske baad ki sab layers ka cache tod deta hai.
Multi-stage build
Dockerfile with several FROM stages; build in one, copy only the output into a clean final stage.Kai FROM stages wali Dockerfile; ek mein build, sirf output ek saaf final stage mein copy.
.dockerignore
List of files never sent into the build (node_modules, .git, .env).Files ki list jo kabhi build mein nahi jaati (node_modules, .git, .env).
Registry
Server that stores images (Docker Hub, ECR). Push once, pull everywhere.Images store karne wala server (Docker Hub, ECR). Ek baar push, har jagah pull.
Tag / digest
Human name of an image version (1.4.2, commit id) / exact content hash that never changes.Image version ka naam (1.4.2, commit id) / exact content hash jo kabhi nahi badalta.
Orchestrator
System (Kubernetes, ECS) that places, restarts, scales and rolls out containers.System (Kubernetes, ECS) jo containers ko jagah deta hai, restart, scale aur roll out karta hai.
Pod
Kubernetes' smallest runnable unit: one or more containers scheduled together.Kubernetes ki sabse chhoti chalne wali unit: ek ya zyada containers jo saath schedule hote hain.
CI/CD
Automated pipeline: test, build image, push, deploy on every merge.Automatic pipeline: har merge pe test, image build, push, deploy.
Rolling / blue-green / canary
Replace copies gradually / switch between two full environments / send a small % of traffic to the new version first.Copies dheere-dheere badlo / do poore environments ke beech switch / pehle thoda % traffic naye version pe bhejo.
Readiness / liveness probe
"Can you take traffic?" (fail = remove from LB) / "Are you stuck?" (fail = restart)."Traffic le sakte ho?" (fail = LB se hatao) / "Atak gaye ho?" (fail = restart).
SIGTERM / SIGKILL
Polite "please stop" signal the app can handle / forced kill that cannot be caught.Politely "band ho jao" signal jise app handle kar sakti hai / zabardasti kill jise pakda nahi ja sakta.
Graceful shutdown
On SIGTERM: stop taking new work, finish in-flight work, close resources, exit.SIGTERM pe: naya kaam lena band, chalta kaam poora, resources band, exit.
Secrets manager
Service (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets) that injects passwords and keys at runtime.Service (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets) jo passwords aur keys runtime pe inject karti hai.
Vertical / horizontal scaling
Bigger machine / more copies behind a load balancer.Badi machine / load balancer ke peeche zyada copies.
Attack surface
Everything in the image an attacker could exploit; fewer packages means fewer holes.Image mein har woh cheez jiska attacker fayda utha sake; kam packages matlab kam chhed.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?Docker image aur container mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: that you know the image is a static, immutable blueprint and the container is a running instance with its own writable layer, and that one image can run as many containers.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum jaante ho ki image static, immutable blueprint hai aur container uska running instance hai apni writable layer ke saath, aur ek image se kai containers chal sakte hain.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

An image is a static, immutable blueprint: a stack of read-only layers containing a minimal OS filesystem, the runtime, my dependencies and my code, plus metadata like the start command. A container is a running instance of that image. When Docker starts it, it adds a thin writable layer on top, so the container can write files without touching the image. The relationship is one-to-many, like a class and its objects: I build inventory-api:3f9c2ab once, push it to the registry, and run ten containers from it across servers, all identical. The trade-off of that design is that the writable layer is throwaway: when a container is replaced, anything it wrote locally is gone, so real state has to live outside, in a database, Redis or S3.

Image ek static, immutable blueprint hai: read-only layers ka stack jisme minimal OS filesystem, runtime, meri dependencies aur mera code hota hai, plus start command jaisa metadata. Container us image ka running instance hai. Docker jab ise start karta hai toh upar ek patli writable layer lagata hai, taaki container image ko chhue bina files likh sake. Rishta one-to-many hai, jaise class aur uske objects: main inventory-api:3f9c2ab ek baar build karta hoon, registry mein push karta hoon, aur servers pe usse das containers chalata hoon, sab identical. Is design ka trade-off yeh hai ki writable layer throwaway hai: container replace hua toh jo usne locally likha tha sab gaya, isliye asli state bahar rehni chahiye, database, Redis ya S3 mein.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Layers are shared: ten containers from the same image on one host store the image layers once on disk, and each gets only its own copy-on-write layer; a file from a lower layer is copied up only when a container modifies it. That is why containers start in about a second and are cheap. A container is not a VM: it is an isolated process using Linux namespaces (its own view of processes, network, filesystem) and cgroups (CPU and memory limits), sharing the host kernel. You can freeze a container into a new image with docker commit, but that is an anti-pattern because it is not reproducible; the Dockerfile should be the source of truth.

Layers share hoti hain: ek host pe same image se das containers ho toh image layers disk pe ek hi baar store hoti hain, aur har container ko sirf apni copy-on-write layer milti hai; neeche ki layer ki file tabhi upar copy hoti hai jab container use modify kare. Isliye containers lagbhag ek second mein start hote hain aur saste hain. Container VM nahi hai: yeh ek isolated process hai jo Linux namespaces (processes, network, filesystem ka apna view) aur cgroups (CPU aur memory limits) use karta hai, aur host ka kernel share karta hai. docker commit se chalte container ko nayi image mein freeze kar sakte ho, par yeh anti-pattern hai kyunki reproducible nahi; source of truth Dockerfile honi chahiye.

Common mistake: saying "a container is a lightweight VM" or treating the container as a place to store data. It is a process, and its local disk is disposable.
Galti mat karna: "container ek lightweight VM hai" bolna, ya container ko data store karne ki jagah samajhna. Yeh ek process hai, aur iski local disk disposable hai.
02 What is a multi-stage build and why would you use one?Multi-stage build kya hai aur kyun use karoge?
What they're really testing: that you build with dev dependencies in one stage and copy only the artifact into a clean runtime stage, giving a smaller image with less attack surface.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum ek stage mein dev dependencies ke saath build karte ho aur sirf artifact ko saaf runtime stage mein copy karte ho, jisse image chhoti aur attack surface kam hota hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A multi-stage build is a Dockerfile with more than one FROM. The first stage is the workshop: for a TypeScript Node API it has all dependencies including dev ones like TypeScript and Jest, it runs npm ci and npm run build, and it produces a dist folder. The final stage starts from a clean slim base and uses COPY --from=build to bring in only dist, production node_modules and package.json, then runs as a non-root user. Everything else, compilers, source, test tools, caches, never ships. So the image is much smaller, pulls and starts faster, and has fewer packages that could carry vulnerabilities. The trade-off is a slightly more complex Dockerfile, and debugging tools are not in the final image, so I debug from outside or with a separate debug image.

Multi-stage build ek aisi Dockerfile hai jisme ek se zyada FROM hote hain. Pehla stage workshop hai: TypeScript Node API ke liye isme saari dependencies hoti hain, dev wali bhi jaise TypeScript aur Jest, yeh npm ci aur npm run build chalata hai, aur ek dist folder banata hai. Final stage ek saaf slim base se shuru hota hai aur COPY --from=build se sirf dist, production node_modules aur package.json laata hai, phir non-root user se chalta hai. Baaki sab, compilers, source, test tools, caches, kabhi ship nahi hota. Toh image kaafi chhoti hoti hai, jaldi pull aur start hoti hai, aur kam packages matlab kam vulnerabilities. Trade-off: Dockerfile thodi complex, aur final image mein debugging tools nahi hote, toh main bahar se ya alag debug image se debug karta hoon.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

You can have more than two stages: a deps stage that installs only production dependencies, a build stage, a test stage that CI targets with docker build --target test, and the final runtime. BuildKit builds independent stages in parallel and skips stages the target does not need. For compiled languages like Go the win is dramatic: the final stage can be scratch or distroless containing just one binary. Multi-stage also keeps build-time credentials (like a private npm token mounted with --mount=type=secret) out of the final image, because the final stage never contains them.

Do se zyada stages bhi ho sakte hain: ek deps stage jo sirf production dependencies install kare, ek build stage, ek test stage jise CI docker build --target test se chalata hai, aur final runtime. BuildKit independent stages parallel mein build karta hai aur jo stages target ko nahi chahiye unhe skip karta hai. Go jaisi compiled languages mein fayda bahut bada hai: final stage scratch ya distroless ho sakta hai jisme bas ek binary ho. Multi-stage build-time credentials (jaise --mount=type=secret se mount kiya private npm token) ko bhi final image se bahar rakhta hai, kyunki final stage mein woh kabhi hote hi nahi.

Common mistake: copying the whole /app folder from the build stage, which drags dev dependencies and source back in and defeats the purpose.
Galti mat karna: build stage se poora /app folder copy kar lena, jisse dev dependencies aur source wapas aa jaate hain aur poora fayda khatam.
03 What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?Dockerfile mein COPY aur ADD mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: that you know COPY is simple, ADD also fetches remote URLs and auto-extracts tar files, and that you prefer COPY.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki COPY simple hai, ADD remote URLs bhi fetch karta hai aur tar files auto-extract karta hai, aur tum COPY prefer karte ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Both copy files into the image, but COPY does exactly one thing: copy files from the build context into the image. ADD does that plus two implicit extras: it can fetch a remote URL, and if the source is a local tar archive it automatically extracts it. I default to COPY because it is explicit and predictable: if I write COPY app.tar.gz /tmp/ I get the tar file, while ADD would silently unpack it. For remote files, ADD url does not verify integrity by default and makes caching less predictable, so I prefer RUN curl -fsSL url -o file followed by a checksum check, all in one layer with cleanup. The only time I reach for ADD is when I genuinely want a local tarball unpacked into the image, like a root filesystem.

Dono image mein files copy karte hain, par COPY sirf ek kaam karta hai: build context se files image mein copy. ADD yeh bhi karta hai plus do chhupe extras: remote URL fetch kar sakta hai, aur source agar local tar archive hai toh use automatically extract kar deta hai. Main default COPY use karta hoon kyunki woh explicit aur predictable hai: COPY app.tar.gz /tmp/ likhoon toh mujhe tar file milti hai, jabki ADD chupchaap unpack kar deta. Remote files ke liye ADD url by default integrity verify nahi karta aur caching kam predictable ho jaati hai, isliye main RUN curl -fsSL url -o file aur uske baad checksum check, sab ek layer mein cleanup ke saath, prefer karta hoon. ADD sirf tab jab mujhe sach mein local tarball image mein unpack karna ho, jaise root filesystem.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Remote URLs are not auto-extracted by ADD, only local archives are, which surprises people. Newer Dockerfile syntax lets ADD take a --checksum=sha256:... flag for remote files and even add a git repository, which narrows the gap, but the principle "least magic" still holds. Both instructions accept --chown to set file ownership so the non-root user can read the files, and both respect .dockerignore. Both create a layer whose cache key is the content of the copied files, which is why copying only package*.json before install keeps the cache stable.

Remote URLs ko ADD auto-extract nahi karta, sirf local archives ko, aur yeh logon ko surprise karta hai. Naya Dockerfile syntax remote files ke liye ADD ko --checksum=sha256:... flag deta hai aur git repository bhi add kar sakta hai, jisse gap kam hota hai, par "kam se kam jaadu" wala principle phir bhi sahi hai. Dono instructions --chown leti hain taaki non-root user files padh sake, aur dono .dockerignore follow karti hain. Dono ek layer banati hain jiski cache key copy hui files ka content hai, isliye install se pehle sirf package*.json copy karne se cache stable rehta hai.

Common mistake: saying they are "the same" or using ADD everywhere because it "does more". More implicit behaviour means more surprises.
Galti mat karna: "dono same hain" bolna, ya ADD har jagah use karna kyunki woh "zyada karta hai". Zyada chhupa behaviour matlab zyada surprises.
04 How do you keep Docker images small and why does it matter?Docker images chhoti kaise rakhte ho aur yeh kyun zaroori hai?
What they're really testing: concrete techniques (minimal base, multi-stage, combined RUN, .dockerignore) and the reasons (faster deploys, smaller attack surface, faster cold starts).
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: concrete techniques (minimal base, multi-stage, combined RUN, .dockerignore) aur reasons (fast deploy, chhota attack surface, fast cold start).

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Four techniques. First, a minimal base image: node:20-alpine or -slim, or distroless, instead of the full Debian image. Second, a multi-stage build so compilers and dev dependencies stay in the build stage. Third, combine related commands into one RUN and clean up in the same line, like apt-get install ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*, because a file deleted in a later layer still sits in the earlier one. Fourth, a .dockerignore so node_modules, .git and .env never enter the build. Why it matters: every deploy and every autoscaled container must pull the image before starting, so smaller means faster deploys, faster scale-out during a traffic spike and faster cold starts. And every package I do not ship is one less potential vulnerability, so the attack surface shrinks. The trade-off is that minimal images lack shells and tools, which makes ad-hoc debugging harder.

Chaar techniques. Pehli, minimal base image: poori Debian image ki jagah node:20-alpine ya -slim, ya distroless. Doosri, multi-stage build taaki compilers aur dev dependencies build stage mein hi reh jaayein. Teesri, related commands ko ek RUN mein jodo aur usi line mein cleanup karo, jaise apt-get install ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*, kyunki baad ki layer mein delete hui file pehle wali layer mein abhi bhi baithi hai. Chauthi, .dockerignore taaki node_modules, .git aur .env build mein aaye hi nahi. Kyun zaroori: har deploy aur har autoscale hua container start se pehle image pull karta hai, toh chhoti image matlab fast deploy, traffic spike mein fast scale-out aur fast cold start. Aur jo package main ship nahi karta woh ek kam possible vulnerability hai, toh attack surface chhota hota hai. Trade-off: minimal images mein shell aur tools nahi hote, toh ad-hoc debugging mushkil hoti hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Alpine uses musl instead of glibc, so some native Node modules (image processing, some database drivers) can misbehave or need rebuilding; -slim is the safer small option when that bites. I measure rather than guess: docker history shows each layer's size, and tools like dive show exactly which files bloat a layer. I also run an image scanner (Trivy, Docker Scout, ECR scanning) in CI to fail builds on critical vulnerabilities. Using npm ci --omit=dev and not copying test fixtures helps too. Small is not the only goal: pinning versions and rebuilding regularly for security patches matters just as much.

Alpine glibc ki jagah musl use karta hai, toh kuch native Node modules (image processing, kuch database drivers) gadbad kar sakte hain ya rebuild maangte hain; tab -slim safer chhota option hai. Main guess nahi, measure karta hoon: docker history har layer ka size dikhata hai, aur dive jaise tools exact batate hain kaunsi files layer ko mota kar rahi hain. CI mein image scanner (Trivy, Docker Scout, ECR scanning) bhi chalata hoon taaki critical vulnerabilities pe build fail ho. npm ci --omit=dev aur test fixtures copy na karna bhi madad karta hai. Chhota hona akela goal nahi: versions pin karna aur security patches ke liye regularly rebuild karna utna hi zaroori hai.

Common mistake: adding RUN rm -rf ... as a separate later step and believing the image got smaller. The earlier layer still holds the files.
Galti mat karna: baad mein alag RUN rm -rf ... step daal ke sochna ki image chhoti ho gayi. Pehle wali layer mein files abhi bhi hain.
05 What is a Docker layer and why does the order of instructions matter?Docker layer kya hai aur instructions ka order kyun matter karta hai?
What they're really testing: that each instruction produces a cached layer, a change invalidates everything after it, so rarely-changing steps go first.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki har instruction ek cached layer banati hai, ek change uske baad sab invalidate karta hai, isliye kam badalne wale steps pehle aate hain.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Each filesystem-changing instruction, FROM, COPY, RUN, ADD, produces a layer: a read-only snapshot of what that step changed. Docker caches each layer, and on rebuild it reuses a layer if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged. But the moment one layer changes, that layer and every layer after it must be rebuilt. So I order from least to most frequently changing. In a Node service I copy package.json and the lockfile, run npm ci, and only then COPY . . the source. A normal code commit then rebuilds only the last cheap layers, and the slow dependency install comes from cache. If I copied the source first, every one-line change would re-download all dependencies. The trade-off is only discipline: the Dockerfile has to be structured around what changes, not around what reads naturally.

Har filesystem badalne wali instruction, FROM, COPY, RUN, ADD, ek layer banati hai: us step ne jo badla uska read-only snapshot. Docker har layer cache karta hai, aur rebuild pe layer reuse karta hai agar instruction aur uske inputs same hain. Par jaise hi ek layer badli, woh layer aur uske baad ki har layer rebuild hoti hai. Isliye main order rakhta hoon kam badalne wale se zyada badalne wale tak. Node service mein pehle package.json aur lockfile copy, phir npm ci, aur uske baad hi source ka COPY . .. Normal code commit pe sirf last ki sasti layers rebuild hoti hain, aur slow dependency install cache se aata hai. Agar source pehle copy karta, toh har ek-line change pe saari dependencies dobara download hoti. Trade-off bas discipline ka hai: Dockerfile ko is hisaab se likhna padta hai ki kya badalta hai, na ki jo padhne mein natural lage.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

For COPY the cache key includes a checksum of the copied files; for RUN it is only the command string, so RUN apt-get update on its own line can stay cached for months with stale package lists, which is why you combine update and install in one RUN. In CI, fresh runners have no local cache, so teams use --cache-from a registry image or BuildKit cache exports. BuildKit cache mounts (RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci) keep the npm download cache between builds without putting it in the image. Layers are also content-addressed, so servers that already have the base layers only pull the new top layers.

COPY ke liye cache key mein copy hui files ka checksum hota hai; RUN ke liye sirf command ki string, toh alag line pe RUN apt-get update mahino tak purani package list ke saath cached reh sakta hai, isliye update aur install ek hi RUN mein jodte hain. CI mein fresh runners pe local cache nahi hota, toh teams registry image se --cache-from ya BuildKit cache exports use karti hain. BuildKit cache mounts (RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci) npm ka download cache builds ke beech rakhte hain bina use image mein daale. Layers content-addressed bhi hoti hain, toh jin servers pe base layers pehle se hain woh sirf nayi upar wali layers pull karte hain.

Common mistake: COPY . . as the first step after FROM, so every code change busts the install cache.
Galti mat karna: FROM ke turant baad COPY . . likhna, jisse har code change install ka cache tod deta hai.
06 What is the difference between a blue-green deployment and a rolling deployment?Blue-green deployment aur rolling deployment mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: blue-green = two full environments with instant switch and rollback; rolling = gradual replacement, slower rollback, no duplicate environment.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: blue-green = do poore environments, turant switch aur rollback; rolling = dheere-dheere replace, slow rollback, duplicate environment nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

In blue-green I run two complete environments. Blue serves all traffic on v1; I deploy v2 to green, smoke-test it privately, then flip the load balancer so 100% goes to green at once. If errors spike, I flip back in seconds, because blue is still running. The cost is double capacity during the switch. In a rolling deployment I have, say, four pods on v1; the orchestrator starts one v2 pod, waits for its readiness probe, adds it to the load balancer, removes a v1 pod, and repeats. No duplicate environment, no downtime, and it is the Kubernetes default. The trade-offs: during the rollout v1 and v2 serve users simultaneously, so APIs and database schema must be compatible across both, and rolling back means another gradual rollout. I pick blue-green for risky releases where instant rollback matters, rolling for everyday deploys.

Blue-green mein main do poore environments chalata hoon. Blue v1 pe saara traffic serve karta hai; main v2 green pe deploy karta hoon, private mein smoke-test karta hoon, phir load balancer flip karta hoon taaki 100% traffic ek saath green pe jaaye. Errors badhe toh seconds mein wapas flip, kyunki blue abhi bhi chal raha hai. Keemat: switch ke time double capacity. Rolling deployment mein maan lo chaar pods v1 pe hain; orchestrator ek v2 pod start karta hai, uske readiness probe ka wait karta hai, use load balancer mein jodta hai, ek v1 pod hataata hai, aur repeat. Duplicate environment nahi, downtime nahi, aur yeh Kubernetes ka default hai. Trade-offs: rollout ke time v1 aur v2 ek saath users ko serve karte hain, toh APIs aur database schema dono ke saath compatible hone chahiye, aur rollback matlab ek aur dheema rollout. Risky releases jahan turant rollback zaroori hai wahan blue-green, roz ke deploys ke liye rolling.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Kubernetes rolling updates are tuned with maxSurge (how many extra pods above the desired count, default 25%) and maxUnavailable (how many can be down, default 25%). kubectl rollout undo rolls back to the previous ReplicaSet. Canary is the middle ground: route a small percentage of traffic to v2 and automatically promote or abort based on error rate and latency (Argo Rollouts, Flagger). In all three, the shared database is the hard part: blue-green does not give instant rollback of a destructive migration, so I use expand-contract migrations. Feature flags decouple deploy from release, so a bad feature can be switched off without any rollback at all.

Kubernetes rolling updates maxSurge (desired count se kitne extra pods, default 25%) aur maxUnavailable (kitne down ho sakte hain, default 25%) se tune hote hain. kubectl rollout undo pichle ReplicaSet pe rollback karta hai. Canary beech ka raasta hai: thoda percentage traffic v2 pe bhejo aur error rate aur latency ke hisaab se automatically promote ya abort karo (Argo Rollouts, Flagger). Teeno mein shared database mushkil hissa hai: blue-green destructive migration ka instant rollback nahi deta, isliye main expand-contract migrations use karta hoon. Feature flags deploy aur release ko alag karte hain, toh kharab feature bina rollback ke switch off ho sakta hai.
