Common mistake: claiming blue-green makes rollback free, while forgetting the database is shared and a breaking schema change cannot be flipped back.
Galti mat karna: bolna ki blue-green se rollback free hai, aur bhool jaana ki database shared hai aur breaking schema change wapas flip nahi hota.
07 What is a health check and why does a container orchestrator need one?Health check kya hai aur container orchestrator ko iski zaroorat kyun hai?
What they're really testing: the readiness vs liveness distinction, and that without checks the orchestrator sends traffic to crashed or stuck containers.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: readiness vs liveness ka fark, aur ki checks ke bina orchestrator crash ya atke hue containers ko traffic bhejta rehta hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A health check is an endpoint or command the orchestrator calls periodically to learn whether a container is usable, because "process is running" does not mean "process can serve". There are two kinds. Readiness asks "can you take traffic now?"; if it fails, the container is pulled out of the load balancer but left running. I use it during startup, while draining on shutdown, and when a critical dependency like the database is unreachable. Liveness asks "are you stuck?"; if it fails several times, the orchestrator kills and restarts the container. My liveness endpoint only proves the event loop responds, it never checks the database, otherwise a short DB outage would restart every pod at once. Without these, the load balancer keeps routing users to a frozen container, and a rolling deploy would replace healthy pods with broken ones because nothing tells it v2 is failing.

Health check ek endpoint ya command hai jise orchestrator baar-baar call karta hai yeh jaanne ke liye ki container kaam ka hai ya nahi, kyunki "process chal raha hai" ka matlab "process serve kar sakta hai" nahi hota. Do types hain. Readiness poochta hai "abhi traffic le sakte ho?"; fail hua toh container load balancer se nikal jaata hai par chalta rehta hai. Main ise startup ke time, shutdown pe drain karte waqt, aur jab database jaisi zaroori dependency nahi mil rahi tab use karta hoon. Liveness poochta hai "atak gaye ho?"; kai baar fail hua toh orchestrator container ko maar ke restart karta hai. Mera liveness endpoint sirf yeh prove karta hai ki event loop jawab de raha hai, database kabhi check nahi karta, warna chhote se DB outage pe har pod ek saath restart ho jaayega. Inke bina load balancer users ko freeze hue container pe bhejta rahega, aur rolling deploy healthy pods ko toote hue pods se replace kar dega kyunki koi batane wala nahi ki v2 fail ho raha hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Kubernetes adds a startup probe for slow boots; liveness and readiness do not run until it passes. Tuning matters: periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds and failureThreshold decide how fast you react versus how many false restarts you get. Checks must be cheap and fast; a heavy query on every probe becomes its own load. If readiness checks shared dependencies, a DB outage takes all pods out of rotation, which is arguably correct (return 503 quickly) but should be a conscious decision. The Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK instruction works for Docker and Swarm; Kubernetes ignores it. Load balancers like AWS ALB have their own target health checks too.

Kubernetes slow boot ke liye startup probe bhi deta hai; jab tak woh pass na ho, liveness aur readiness nahi chalte. Tuning matter karti hai: periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds aur failureThreshold decide karte hain kitni jaldi react karoge versus kitne galat restarts honge. Checks saste aur fast hone chahiye; har probe pe bhaari query khud load ban jaati hai. Agar readiness shared dependencies check kare, toh DB outage saare pods ko rotation se bahar kar deta hai, jo shayad sahi hai (jaldi 503 do) par yeh soch-samajh ke liya gaya decision hona chahiye. Dockerfile ki HEALTHCHECK instruction Docker aur Swarm ke liye hai; Kubernetes use ignore karta hai. AWS ALB jaise load balancers ke apne target health checks bhi hote hain.

Common mistake: one /health endpoint that checks the database and is used for liveness. A database blip then causes a restart storm across every pod.
Galti mat karna: ek hi /health endpoint jo database check kare aur liveness ke liye use ho. Phir database ki ek hichki pe har pod mein restart ka toofan.
08 How do you handle secrets in a containerized deployment?Containerized deployment mein secrets kaise handle karte ho?
What they're really testing: never baking secrets into images or the repo; injecting them at runtime via env vars or a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets).
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: secrets kabhi image ya repo mein nahi; runtime pe env vars ya secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets) se inject karna.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

The rule is: secrets never go into the image or the repository. Image layers are readable by anyone who can pull the image, docker history shows ENV and build args, images get copied to registries, CI caches and laptops, and deleting a file in a later layer does not remove it from the earlier one. Git history is forever too. So the image is secret-free and identical across environments, and secrets are injected at runtime. The orchestrator pulls them from a secrets manager, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or Kubernetes Secrets, and exposes them to the container as environment variables or mounted files. .env is in .dockerignore and .gitignore. The benefit is one image for staging and production, and rotating a password is a config change, not a rebuild. The trade-off is one more system to run and access-control, and env vars can leak through crash dumps or careless logging, so I never log the config object.

Rule simple hai: secrets kabhi image ya repository mein nahi jaate. Image layers woh har koi padh sakta hai jo image pull kar sake, docker history ENV aur build args dikhata hai, images registries, CI caches aur laptops tak copy hoti hain, aur baad ki layer mein file delete karne se woh pehle wali layer se nahi hatti. Git history bhi hamesha ke liye hai. Toh image secret-free aur har environment mein same hoti hai, aur secrets runtime pe inject hote hain. Orchestrator unhe secrets manager se laata hai, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager ya Kubernetes Secrets, aur container ko environment variables ya mounted files ki tarah deta hai. .env .dockerignore aur .gitignore dono mein hai. Fayda: staging aur production ke liye ek hi image, aur password rotate karna config change hai, rebuild nahi. Trade-off: ek aur system chalana aur uska access control, aur env vars crash dumps ya laparwah logging se leak ho sakte hain, isliye main config object kabhi log nahi karta.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded by default, not encrypted, so you enable encryption at rest for etcd and restrict who can read them with RBAC, or use the External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver to sync from Vault or AWS. Mounted files are slightly safer than env vars because env vars are inherited by child processes and often printed by debugging tools. For build-time secrets like a private npm token, BuildKit's RUN --mount=type=secret exposes the secret only during that step and never writes it to a layer. On AWS, IAM roles for the pod (IRSA) avoid static cloud keys entirely. Secret scanning in CI (gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning) catches accidental commits, and any leaked secret must be rotated, not just deleted.

Kubernetes Secrets by default sirf base64-encoded hote hain, encrypted nahi, toh etcd ke liye encryption at rest on karo aur RBAC se restrict karo kaun padh sakta hai, ya External Secrets Operator ya Secrets Store CSI driver se Vault ya AWS se sync karo. Mounted files env vars se thode safer hain kyunki env vars child processes ko inherit hote hain aur debugging tools aksar unhe print kar dete hain. Build-time secrets jaise private npm token ke liye BuildKit ka RUN --mount=type=secret secret ko sirf us step mein deta hai aur kabhi layer mein nahi likhta. AWS pe pod ke IAM roles (IRSA) static cloud keys ki zaroorat hi khatam kar dete hain. CI mein secret scanning (gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning) galti se hue commits pakadti hai, aur leak hua secret rotate karna padta hai, sirf delete karna kaafi nahi.

Common mistake: ENV DB_PASSWORD=... or ARG API_KEY in the Dockerfile, believing it is hidden. Both are visible in the image metadata and history.
Galti mat karna: Dockerfile mein ENV DB_PASSWORD=... ya ARG API_KEY likh ke sochna ki chhupa hua hai. Dono image metadata aur history mein dikhte hain.
09 What happens when a container restarts, and how should your application handle it?Container restart hone pe kya hota hai, aur application ko ise kaise handle karna chahiye?
What they're really testing: a fresh filesystem and lost in-memory state and local files; so the app must be stateless, persist externally and handle SIGTERM gracefully.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: fresh filesystem aur in-memory state aur local files ka khatam hona; isliye app stateless ho, data bahar persist kare aur SIGTERM gracefully handle kare.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

When a container is replaced, which happens on every deploy, crash, node drain or scale-down, the new one starts fresh from the image. Its writable layer is empty, so anything in memory, sessions, an in-process cache, a queue held in an array, and any file written to local disk, like an uploaded vehicle photo, is gone. So I design the service to be stateless: sessions in Redis, files in S3, data in the database, background jobs in a real queue. The second half is shutdown. The orchestrator sends SIGTERM, waits a grace period, 30 seconds by default in Kubernetes, then SIGKILL. On SIGTERM my Node app flips readiness to 503 so no new traffic arrives, calls server.close() to finish in-flight requests, closes the DB pool, flushes logs and exits, with a timeout safety net. The trade-off is that external state adds a network hop, but it is what makes restarts and scaling safe.

Jab container replace hota hai, jo har deploy, crash, node drain ya scale-down pe hota hai, naya container image se fresh start hota hai. Iski writable layer khaali hai, toh memory mein jo bhi tha, sessions, in-process cache, array mein rakhi queue, aur local disk pe likhi har file, jaise upload hui vehicle photo, sab gaya. Isliye main service ko stateless design karta hoon: sessions Redis mein, files S3 mein, data database mein, background jobs asli queue mein. Doosra hissa shutdown hai. Orchestrator SIGTERM bhejta hai, grace period wait karta hai, Kubernetes mein default 30 seconds, phir SIGKILL. SIGTERM pe meri Node app readiness ko 503 kar deti hai taaki naya traffic na aaye, server.close() se chalti requests poori karti hai, DB pool band karti hai, logs flush karti hai aur exit karti hai, ek timeout safety net ke saath. Trade-off: external state ek network hop add karta hai, par isi se restarts aur scaling safe hote hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Signals only reach node if node is PID 1 or the init forwards them, so use exec-form CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] or --init/tini; with npm start the SIGTERM may be swallowed and every deploy drops requests. Add a small preStop sleep so load balancers finish deregistering the pod before it stops accepting connections. Background workers should stop pulling new messages, finish or release the current one (not ack it until done), and rely on idempotency (Topic 05) because a SIGKILL mid-job means the message will be redelivered. An OOMKilled container gets no SIGTERM at all, so crash-safety still depends on external, transactional state. If something truly must be on disk, use a mounted persistent volume, not the container layer.

Signals node tak tabhi pahunchte hain jab node PID 1 ho ya init unhe forward kare, toh exec-form CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] ya --init/tini use karo; npm start ke saath SIGTERM nigla ja sakta hai aur har deploy pe requests drop hoti hain. Chhota preStop sleep daalo taaki load balancers pod ko deregister kar lein uske connections lena band karne se pehle. Background workers ko naye messages lena band karna chahiye, current wala poora karna ya release karna chahiye (khatam hone tak ack nahi), aur idempotency (Topic 05) pe bharosa rakhna chahiye kyunki job ke beech SIGKILL matlab message dobara aayega. OOMKilled container ko SIGTERM milta hi nahi, toh crash-safety phir bhi external, transactional state pe depend karti hai. Kuch sach mein disk pe chahiye toh mounted persistent volume use karo, container layer nahi.

Common mistake: storing user sessions or uploads inside the container and being surprised when users are logged out or files vanish after a deploy.
Galti mat karna: user sessions ya uploads container ke andar rakhna aur phir hairaan hona ki deploy ke baad users logout ho gaye ya files gayab.
10 What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?Horizontal aur vertical scaling mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: vertical = bigger machine with a ceiling and often downtime; horizontal = more instances behind a load balancer, which requires a stateless design.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: vertical = badi machine, ceiling aur aksar downtime; horizontal = load balancer ke peeche zyada instances, jiske liye stateless design chahiye.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Vertical scaling, scaling up, means giving the same server more CPU and RAM. It is the simplest move, no code changes, but it has a hard ceiling at the largest machine available, resizing usually means a restart, cost grows steeply, and it is still a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling, scaling out, means running more identical copies behind a load balancer. There is no practical ceiling, losing one copy is not an outage, and it can be automatic, for example Kubernetes adding pods when CPU crosses a target. The price is that the app must be stateless: if a user's session lived in one copy's memory, the next request landing on another copy would lose it, so state goes to Redis or the database. For a Node API I usually scale horizontally, because one Node process mainly uses one core anyway. Databases are the classic case where vertical scaling comes first, because scaling them out needs replicas or sharding.

Vertical scaling, scale up, matlab usi server ko zyada CPU aur RAM dena. Sabse simple step, code change nahi, par sabse badi available machine pe ek hard ceiling hai, resize karne mein aksar restart lagta hai, kharcha tezi se badhta hai, aur phir bhi single point of failure hai. Horizontal scaling, scale out, matlab load balancer ke peeche zyada identical copies chalana. Practically koi ceiling nahi, ek copy gayi toh outage nahi, aur automatic ho sakta hai, jaise CPU target cross hone pe Kubernetes pods badha deta hai. Keemat: app stateless honi chahiye: agar user ka session ek copy ki memory mein tha, toh agli request doosri copy pe gayi toh session gaya, isliye state Redis ya database mein jaati hai. Node API ke liye main aam taur pe horizontal scale karta hoon, kyunki ek Node process zyaadatar ek hi core use karta hai. Databases classic case hain jahan pehle vertical scaling hoti hai, kyunki unhe scale out karne ke liye replicas ya sharding chahiye.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Horizontal scaling moves the bottleneck: ten API pods each with a pool of 20 connections is 200 database connections, which can exceed Postgres max_connections (default 100), so you add a pooler like PgBouncer. Autoscaling needs the right signal: CPU for compute-bound services, queue depth or request rate for I/O-bound ones, and it needs small images and fast startup so new pods are useful before the spike ends. Sticky sessions let a stateful app scale out a little but break on failover and uneven load. The mature answer is "both": right-size each instance vertically, then scale the count horizontally.

Horizontal scaling bottleneck ko khiska deta hai: das API pods, har ek mein 20 connections ka pool, matlab 200 database connections, jo Postgres ke max_connections (default 100) se zyada ho sakta hai, toh PgBouncer jaisa pooler lagate hain. Autoscaling ko sahi signal chahiye: compute-bound services ke liye CPU, I/O-bound ke liye queue depth ya request rate, aur chhoti images aur fast startup chahiye taaki naye pods spike khatam hone se pehle kaam aa sakein. Sticky sessions ek stateful app ko thoda scale out karne dete hain par failover aur uneven load pe toot jaate hain. Mature jawab hai "dono": har instance ko vertically sahi size do, phir count ko horizontally badhao.

Common mistake: saying "just add more servers" without mentioning that the app must be stateless and that the database becomes the next bottleneck.
Galti mat karna: "bas aur servers add kar do" bolna, bina yeh bataye ki app stateless honi chahiye aur database agla bottleneck ban jaata hai.

Topic 12 · COMMONTopic 12 · Aksar poocha jaata hai

Error Handling & LoggingError Handling & Logging

What a mature backend does when things go wrong: which errors to handle and which to crash on, where to catch them, how to answer the client, how to retry safely, and how to write logs that let you find out why afterwards.

Jab kuch galat hota hai toh ek mature backend kya karta hai: kaunse errors handle karne hain aur kispe crash karna hai, unhe kahan pakadna hai, client ko kya jawab dena hai, safely retry kaise karna hai, aur aise logs kaise likhne hain jinse baad mein pata chale ki hua kya tha.

Level 0 The story: a busy hospitalKahani: ek busy hospital

Think of a busy city hospital. Every day hundreds of things "go wrong", but they go wrong in two completely different ways.

A patient walks in with a fever. That is a problem, but an expected one. The hospital has a process for it: check temperature, give medicine, send home with advice. Nobody panics, nobody shuts the hospital. Now imagine the ECG machine starts showing a heartbeat for a bed that has no patient. That is a different kind of problem: the equipment itself is broken. You must not keep using it and "work around" the wrong readings, because every reading from it is now untrustworthy. You take it out of service, put a sign on it, and get it repaired.

Who handles what also matters. The reception nurse fixes small things herself (a form filled in wrong: ask again). The ward doctor makes treatment decisions, because only she has the context. Anything nobody on the floor understands goes up to the senior doctor on duty, who records it in the incident register so it can be investigated.

Every visit is written in the patient's case file: time, patient ID, who saw them, what was done. A case file that just says "patient was unwell" is useless the next morning. And some things never go on the corridor whiteboard, like a patient's test results, because anyone walking past can read it.

Two more scenes. The pathology lab goes down. If every ward keeps sending samples anyway, they pile up, doctors wait, and the whole hospital slows to a crawl. The smart move: reception puts up a sign, "Lab closed, do not send samples", tells doctors immediately so they can choose a plan B, and every 30 minutes sends one test sample to see if the lab is back. And when the pharmacy phone line is busy, a nurse does not redial every second (along with fifty other nurses doing the same). She waits a minute, then two, then four, and each nurse waits a slightly different random amount so they do not all call back at the same moment.

Last scene: a vaccination camp with 2,000 forms to enter overnight. One form is unreadable. You do not stop the whole camp. You set that form aside with a note, continue, and in the morning report "1,987 entered, 13 need follow-up".

Fever = operational error (expected, handle it). Broken ECG = programmer error (a bug: stop, restart, fix). Nurse, ward doctor, senior doctor = layers that catch what they can decide on. Case file = structured log. Corridor whiteboard = never log secrets. "Lab closed" sign = circuit breaker. Calling back after 1, 2, 4 minutes plus a random bit = exponential backoff with jitter. Setting one bad form aside = per-record batch error handling.

Ek busy city hospital socho. Roz saikdon cheezein "galat" hoti hain, par do bilkul alag tarah se.

Ek patient bukhaar ke saath aata hai. Problem hai, par expected problem. Hospital ke paas iska process hai: temperature check, dawai, advice ke saath ghar. Koi panic nahi karta, koi hospital band nahi karta. Ab socho ECG machine ek khaali bed ke liye heartbeat dikhane lagi. Yeh alag tarah ki problem hai: machine khud kharab hai. Use use karte rehna aur galat readings ke saath "jugaad" karna galat hai, kyunki ab uski har reading pe bharosa nahi kiya ja sakta. Use service se bahar karo, uspe sign lagao, aur repair karwao.

Kaun kya handle karta hai yeh bhi important hai. Reception nurse chhoti cheezein khud theek karti hai (form galat bhara: dobara bharwao). Ward doctor treatment ka decision leti hai, kyunki context sirf uske paas hai. Jo cheez floor pe kisi ko samajh nahi aati woh duty pe senior doctor tak jaati hai, jo use incident register mein likhta hai taaki investigate ho sake.

Har visit patient ki case file mein likhi jaati hai: time, patient ID, kisne dekha, kya kiya. Jo case file sirf "patient ki tabiyat kharab thi" bole, woh agli subah kisi kaam ki nahi. Aur kuch cheezein corridor ke whiteboard pe kabhi nahi likhi jaati, jaise patient ke test results, kyunki guzarne wala koi bhi padh lega.

Do aur scenes. Pathology lab band ho gayi. Agar har ward phir bhi samples bhejta rahe, toh dher lag jaata hai, doctors wait karte hain, aur poora hospital dheema pad jaata hai. Samajhdaari: reception ek sign lagata hai, "Lab band hai, samples mat bhejo", doctors ko turant batata hai taaki woh plan B chun sakein, aur har 30 minute mein ek test sample bhej ke dekhta hai ki lab wapas aayi ya nahi. Aur jab pharmacy ki phone line busy ho, toh nurse har second redial nahi karti (pachaas aur nurses ke saath jo yahi kar rahi hain). Woh ek minute ruk-ti hai, phir do, phir chaar, aur har nurse thoda alag random time rukti hai taaki sab ek hi pal mein wapas call na karein.

Aakhri scene: ek vaccination camp jisme raat bhar mein 2,000 forms enter karne hain. Ek form padha nahi ja raha. Tum poora camp nahi rokte. Us form ko ek note ke saath side mein rakho, aage badho, aur subah report do "1,987 entered, 13 ko follow-up chahiye".

Bukhaar = operational error (expected, handle karo). Kharab ECG = programmer error (bug: roko, restart, fix). Nurse, ward doctor, senior doctor = layers jo utna pakadti hain jitne pe decision le sakein. Case file = structured log. Corridor whiteboard = secrets kabhi log mat karo. "Lab band" sign = circuit breaker. 1, 2, 4 minute plus thoda random ke baad call = exponential backoff with jitter. Ek kharab form side mein rakhna = per-record batch error handling.

Level 1 The basic words: throw, catch, and the two kinds of errorBasic words: throw, catch, aur do tarah ke errors

In JavaScript, when something goes wrong a function throws an error (also called an exception): an object with a message and a stack trace, which is the list of function calls that led to the failure, like a trail of footprints. Throwing immediately stops the current function and jumps up to the nearest try { } catch (err) { } block. If there is no catch anywhere, the error is uncaught.

Most backend work is asynchronous (waiting for the database, another API). An async function that fails returns a rejected Promise. With await, a rejection behaves like a throw, so the same try/catch works. A rejection that nobody awaits or catches is an unhandled rejection.

Now the key idea of this topic. Errors come in two kinds:

  • Operational errors (the fever): expected failures of a correct program in a messy world. The user sent an invalid VIN, the vehicle does not exist, a network call timed out, the database connection dropped, a downstream API returned 503, the disk is full. You handle these: return a clear 4xx message, retry, use a fallback, or report a clean 5xx.
  • Programmer errors (the broken ECG): bugs. Cannot read properties of undefined, calling a function with the wrong arguments, a forgotten await, a logic mistake. You cannot "handle" a bug at runtime, because the program is now in a state you did not design for. The safe move is to log it loudly, let the process crash, have it restarted clean, and fix the code.

Quick HTTP reminder: status codes in the 4xx range mean "the client did something wrong" (400 bad request, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 invalid data, 429 too many requests). 5xx means "the server failed" (500 bug, 502/504 a downstream service failed or timed out, 503 temporarily unavailable).

JavaScript mein jab kuch galat hota hai toh function ek error throw karta hai (ise exception bhi kehte hain): ek object jisme message aur stack trace hota hai, yaani un function calls ki list jo failure tak le gayi, jaise pairon ke nishaan. Throw karte hi current function wahin ruk jaata hai aur sabse paas wale try { } catch (err) { } block tak upar kood jaata hai. Kahin bhi catch nahi hai toh error uncaught hai.

Zyaadatar backend kaam asynchronous hai (database ka wait, doosri API ka wait). Fail hone wala async function ek rejected Promise return karta hai. await ke saath rejection throw jaisa hi behave karta hai, toh wahi try/catch kaam karta hai. Jis rejection ko koi await ya catch na kare use unhandled rejection kehte hain.

Ab is topic ka main idea. Errors do tarah ke hote hain:

  • Operational errors (bukhaar): ek sahi program ki messy duniya mein expected failures. User ne invalid VIN bheja, vehicle exist nahi karta, network call timeout hui, database connection toota, downstream API ne 503 diya, disk full. Inhe tum handle karte ho: clear 4xx message do, retry karo, fallback use karo, ya saaf 5xx report karo.
  • Programmer errors (kharab ECG): bugs. Cannot read properties of undefined, function ko galat arguments dena, bhoola hua await, logic ki galti. Runtime pe bug ko "handle" nahi kar sakte, kyunki program ab aisi state mein hai jo tumne design hi nahi ki. Safe tareeka: zor se log karo, process ko crash hone do, clean restart hone do, aur code fix karo.

HTTP ka chhota reminder: 4xx range ke status codes matlab "client ne kuch galat kiya" (400 bad request, 401 login nahi, 403 permission nahi, 404 nahi mila, 409 conflict, 422 invalid data, 429 bahut zyada requests). 5xx matlab "server fail hua" (500 bug, 502/504 downstream service fail ya timeout, 503 abhi available nahi).

// throw + catch with async/await
async function getVehicle(vin) {
  const { rows } = await db.query('SELECT * FROM vehicles WHERE vin = $1', [vin]);
  if (rows.length === 0) throw new Error(`Vehicle ${vin} not found`);   // operational: expected case
  return rows[0];
}

try {
  const v = await getVehicle('1HGCM82633A004352');
} catch (err) {
  console.error(err.message);   // "Vehicle ... not found"
  console.error(err.stack);     // where it happened: the footprints
}
Operational errorOperational errorProgrammer errorProgrammer error
WhatKyaExpected failure in the outside worldBahar ki duniya mein expected failureA bug in our codeHamare code mein bug
ExamplesExamplesInvalid input, not found, timeout, DB connection reset, 503 from a partner APIInvalid input, not found, timeout, DB connection reset, partner API se 503undefined property, wrong argument type, missing await, bad logicundefined property, galat argument type, missing await, galat logic
What to doKya karna haiHandle: 4xx message, retry, fallback, clean 5xxHandle: 4xx message, retry, fallback, saaf 5xxLog with full context, crash, restart clean, fix codePoore context ke saath log, crash, clean restart, code fix
Log levelLog levelWARN (or INFO for 4xx)WARN (4xx ke liye INFO bhi)ERROR / FATAL + alertERROR / FATAL + alert

Level 2 Where to catch: layers, bubbling and one consistent error shapeKahan pakadna hai: layers, bubbling aur ek consistent error shape

A typical backend is split into layers, like the hospital's nurse, doctor and senior:

  • Route / controller: speaks HTTP. Reads the request, validates input, calls the service, sends the response.
  • Service: the business logic. "Book a service appointment: check the vehicle exists, reserve a loaner car, save the booking."
  • Repository: speaks the database. Runs SQL and returns rows.

The golden rule: catch an error only where you have the context to do something useful with it: retry it, fall back, translate it into a meaningful error, or add information. If you cannot do any of those, do not catch it; let it bubble up (travel upward through the callers) to one top-level error handler that logs it, turns it into a proper HTTP response and triggers alerts for 5xx.

  • The repository knows that Postgres error code 23505 means "unique constraint violated", so it translates it into a ConflictError ("that slot is already booked"). Every other DB error it lets bubble.
  • The service knows that the loaner-car service is optional, so if it fails after retries, it books without a loaner (a fallback) and logs a warning. It also throws NotFoundError when the vehicle does not exist, because that is a business rule.
  • The route turns bad input into a ValidationError (422) and passes everything else on.
  • The top-level handler catches all the rest: unknown errors, bugs. It is the one place that decides the status code and response shape.

Ek typical backend layers mein bata hota hai, hospital ke nurse, doctor aur senior ki tarah:

  • Route / controller: HTTP ki bhasha bolta hai. Request padhta hai, input validate karta hai, service call karta hai, response bhejta hai.
  • Service: business logic. "Service appointment book karo: check karo vehicle exist karta hai, loaner car reserve karo, booking save karo."
  • Repository: database ki bhasha bolta hai. SQL chalata hai aur rows return karta hai.

Golden rule: error ko sirf wahan pakdo jahan uske saath kuch kaam ka karne ka context ho: retry, fallback, use meaningful error mein translate karna, ya information add karna. Inme se kuch nahi kar sakte toh mat pakdo; use bubble up hone do (callers ke through upar jaane do) ek top-level error handler tak, jo use log kare, sahi HTTP response mein badle aur 5xx pe alert bheje.

  • Repository jaanti hai ki Postgres error code 23505 matlab "unique constraint toota", toh woh use ConflictError ("yeh slot pehle se booked hai") mein translate karti hai. Baaki har DB error ko bubble hone deti hai.
  • Service jaanti hai ki loaner-car service optional hai, toh retries ke baad bhi fail ho toh bina loaner ke booking kar deti hai (fallback) aur warning log karti hai. Vehicle exist na kare toh NotFoundError throw karti hai, kyunki yeh business rule hai.
  • Route kharab input ko ValidationError (422) mein badalta hai aur baaki sab aage pass karta hai.
  • Top-level handler baaki sab pakadta hai: unknown errors, bugs. Yahi ek jagah hai jo status code aur response shape decide karti hai.

In code, operational errors get their own classes so the top-level handler can tell "expected, with a known status" apart from "unknown bug":

Code mein operational errors ki apni classes hoti hain taaki top-level handler "expected, known status wala" aur "unknown bug" mein fark kar sake:

// errors.js - one base class for every EXPECTED (operational) failure
class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, { status = 500, code = 'INTERNAL_ERROR', details, cause } = {}) {
    super(message, { cause });        // keep the original error as .cause
    this.name = new.target.name;
    this.status = status;             // HTTP status to send
    this.code = code;                 // stable, machine-readable code for clients
    this.details = details;           // e.g. which fields were invalid
  }
}
class ValidationError extends AppError {
  constructor(details) { super('Some fields are invalid.', { status: 422, code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', details }); }
}
class NotFoundError extends AppError {
  constructor(what) { super(`${what} not found.`, { status: 404, code: 'NOT_FOUND' }); }
}
class ConflictError extends AppError {
  constructor(message, cause) { super(message, { status: 409, code: 'CONFLICT', cause }); }
}

// repository: knows SQL, translates DB errors into domain errors
async function insertAppointment(a) {
  try {
    const { rows } = await db.query(
      'INSERT INTO appointments (vin, slot, loaner_id) VALUES ($1, $2, $3) RETURNING *',
      [a.vin, a.slot, a.loanerId]);
    return rows[0];
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.code === '23505') throw new ConflictError('That slot is already booked.', err); // unique_violation
    throw err;                          // anything else: not my decision, let it bubble
  }
}

// service: knows the business, decides retry / fallback
async function bookAppointment(input) {
  const vehicle = await vehicleRepo.findByVin(input.vin);
  if (!vehicle) throw new NotFoundError('Vehicle');
  let loaner = null;
  try {
    loaner = await retryWithBackoff(() => loanerApi.reserve(input.slot));  // Level 4
  } catch (err) {
    logger.warn({ err, vin: input.vin }, 'loaner service unavailable, booking without loaner');
  }
  return insertAppointment({ ...input, loanerId: loaner?.id ?? null });
}

// route: validates, calls the service, forwards errors
router.post('/v1/service-appointments', async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    const input = validateBooking(req.body);   // throws ValidationError
    res.status(201).json(await bookAppointment(input));
  } catch (err) {
    next(err);                                 // Express 4 needs this; Express 5 forwards rejections itself
  }
});

// top-level error middleware (4 arguments): the ONE place that maps errors to responses
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  const known = err instanceof AppError;
  const status = known ? err.status : 500;
  if (status >= 500) req.log.error({ err }, 'request failed');          // full stack, alertable
  else req.log.info({ code: err.code, status }, 'request rejected');    // client mistake, not our bug
  res.status(status).json({
    error: {
      code: known ? err.code : 'INTERNAL_ERROR',
      message: known ? err.message : 'Something went wrong on our side. Please try again.',
      details: known ? err.details : undefined,
      requestId: req.id,                       // lets support find the exact log line
    },
  });
});

Every error the API returns now has the same shape and the right status code. Clients can write one piece of error-handling code; they switch on the stable code, show message to humans, and quote requestId to support:

Ab API ka har error same shape aur sahi status code ke saath aata hai. Clients ek hi error-handling code likh sakte hain; stable code pe switch karte hain, message insaanon ko dikhate hain, aur support ko requestId batate hain:

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
Content-Type: application/json
X-Request-Id: req_8f3a2c71

{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
    "message": "Some fields are invalid.",
    "details": [
      { "field": "vin",  "issue": "must be exactly 17 characters" },
      { "field": "slot", "issue": "must be in the future" }
    ],
    "requestId": "req_8f3a2c71"
  }
}

Never return 200 OK with {"success": false} in the body. Monitoring counts it as success, caches may store it, retry logic and client libraries will not treat it as a failure, and every client must parse the body to learn it failed. The status code is the first, universal signal; the body adds detail.

Kabhi bhi 200 OK ke saath body mein {"success": false} mat bhejo. Monitoring ise success ginti hai, cache ise store kar sakta hai, retry logic aur client libraries ise failure nahi maanti, aur har client ko body parse karni padti hai yeh jaanne ke liye ki fail hua. Status code pehla, universal signal hai; body detail add karti hai.

Level 3 Logging: case files you can actually searchLogging: aisi case files jinhe sach mein search kar sako

A log is a record the program writes about what it did, one line per event. In production you cannot attach a debugger or watch the screen; logs (together with metrics and traces, Topic 13) are how you find out what happened at 2:14 am last night. Most teams send logs from every container to a central system (Datadog, Grafana Loki, ELK, CloudWatch) where they can be searched.

This is what a useless log looks like:

Log woh record hai jo program apne kaam ke baare mein likhta hai, har event ki ek line. Production mein tum debugger nahi laga sakte ya screen nahi dekh sakte; logs (metrics aur traces ke saath, Topic 13) hi batate hain ki kal raat 2:14 baje kya hua tha. Zyaadatar teams har container ke logs ek central system (Datadog, Grafana Loki, ELK, CloudWatch) mein bhejti hain jahan unhe search kiya ja sake.

Bekaar log aisa dikhta hai:

console.log('Error occurred');                 // which error? which request? which user? when?
console.log('failed for user ' + user);        // prints "failed for user [object Object]"

And this is a useful one. It is structured: written as JSON with named fields, so the log system can filter and count by any field ("all errors for route X in the last hour", "every line for request req_8f3a2c71"). It is shown pretty-printed here; in production it is a single line.

Aur yeh kaam ka log hai. Yeh structured hai: named fields ke saath JSON mein likha, toh log system kisi bhi field se filter aur count kar sakta hai ("pichle ek ghante mein route X ke saare errors", "request req_8f3a2c71 ki har line"). Yahan pretty-print karke dikhaya hai; production mein yeh ek hi line hota hai.

{
  "time": "2026-09-28T09:14:03.512Z",
  "level": "error",
  "service": "appointment-api",
  "env": "production",
  "version": "3f9c2ab",
  "requestId": "req_8f3a2c71",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "userId": "u_1042",
  "method": "POST",
  "route": "/v1/service-appointments",
  "status": 502,
  "durationMs": 3012,
  "msg": "loaner service call failed after 4 attempts",
  "err": {
    "type": "TimeoutError",
    "message": "timeout after 3000ms",
    "stack": "TimeoutError: timeout after 3000ms\n    at reserve (loanerApi.js:41:11) ..."
  }
}

The fields that make a log line useful: a precise timestamp (UTC, ISO format), a severity level, a short constant message (same text every time, so you can count it), the request ID or trace ID that ties together every line produced by one request, even across services, context (user ID, route, the IDs of the thing being worked on), which service and version wrote it, and for errors the error type and stack trace.

The request ID (also called correlation ID) is created once at the edge, or taken from an incoming X-Request-Id header, attached to every log line for that request, passed to downstream services, and returned to the client in the response. When a dealer's staff says "booking failed", support asks for the request ID and finds every line in seconds.

Log levels say how serious a line is, so you can filter noise and alert on what matters:

Log line ko kaam ka banane wale fields: exact timestamp (UTC, ISO format), severity level, chhota constant message (har baar same text, taaki gin sako), request ID ya trace ID jo ek request ki har line ko jodta hai, services ke paar bhi, context (user ID, route, jis cheez pe kaam ho raha uske IDs), kaunsi service aur version ne likha, aur errors ke liye error type aur stack trace.

Request ID (correlation ID bhi kehte hain) edge pe ek baar banti hai, ya aane wale X-Request-Id header se li jaati hai, us request ki har log line mein lagti hai, downstream services ko pass hoti hai, aur response mein client ko wapas milti hai. Jab dealer ka staff bole "booking fail ho gayi", support request ID maangta hai aur seconds mein har line mil jaati hai.

Log levels batate hain line kitni serious hai, taaki noise filter kar sako aur jo zaroori hai uspe alert laga sako:

LevelLevelMeaningMatlabExampleExample
DEBUGDetailed internals for developers; off in production by defaultDevelopers ke liye andar ki detail; production mein by default band"cache miss for key vehicle:1HGCM...""cache miss for key vehicle:1HGCM..."
INFONormal, meaningful business eventsNormal, meaningful business events"appointment booked", "server started on 3000""appointment booked", "server started on 3000"
WARNSomething unexpected but handled; worth watchingKuch unexpected hua par handle ho gaya; nazar rakhne layak"retrying loaner API (attempt 2)", "fell back to cached price""retrying loaner API (attempt 2)", "fell back to cached price"
ERRORAn operation failed and a human may need to actEk operation fail hua aur shayad kisi insaan ko action lena pade"request failed: 500", "payment webhook could not be saved""request failed: 500", "payment webhook could not be saved"
FATALThe process cannot continue and is exitingProcess aage nahi chal sakta aur exit ho raha hai"uncaught exception, shutting down""uncaught exception, shutting down"

If everything is logged as ERROR, nothing is: alerts fire all night for users typing wrong passwords, people learn to ignore them, and the one real outage is missed. A user's invalid input is INFO or WARN, not ERROR. Production normally runs at INFO, and the level is configurable so you can turn on DEBUG for one service temporarily.

Never leak sensitive data. Logs are copied to many systems and read by many people, and they are kept for a long time. Never log passwords, access or refresh tokens, API keys, session cookies, full card numbers or bank details, and avoid full personal data (full names with phone numbers, addresses, government IDs). Use your logger's redaction so known sensitive fields are replaced with [REDACTED] automatically, log IDs instead of personal details, and mask when you need a hint (last 4 digits). And the other direction: clients get a generic message for 500s, never the stack trace, SQL text or internal hostnames; the details stay in the logs, linked by the request ID.

Agar sab kuch ERROR mein log hota hai, toh kuch bhi ERROR nahi: galat password type karne wale users ke liye raat bhar alerts bajte hain, log unhe ignore karna seekh jaate hain, aur ek asli outage miss ho jaata hai. User ka invalid input INFO ya WARN hai, ERROR nahi. Production aam taur pe INFO pe chalta hai, aur level configurable hota hai taaki ek service ke liye thodi der DEBUG on kar sako.

Sensitive data kabhi leak mat karo. Logs bahut systems mein copy hote hain, bahut log padhte hain, aur lambe time tak rakhe jaate hain. Passwords, access ya refresh tokens, API keys, session cookies, poore card numbers ya bank details kabhi log mat karo, aur poora personal data (phone number ke saath poora naam, address, government IDs) avoid karo. Logger ka redaction use karo taaki known sensitive fields apne aap [REDACTED] ho jaayein, personal details ki jagah IDs log karo, aur hint chahiye toh mask karo (last 4 digits). Aur doosri direction: clients ko 500 ke liye generic message milta hai, stack trace, SQL text ya internal hostnames kabhi nahi; details logs mein rehti hain, request ID se judi hui.

// logger.js - structured JSON logs with redaction and a per-request child logger
const pino = require('pino');
const { randomUUID } = require('node:crypto');

const logger = pino({
  level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL || 'info',
  base: { service: 'appointment-api', env: process.env.NODE_ENV, version: process.env.GIT_SHA },
  timestamp: pino.stdTimeFunctions.isoTime,
  redact: {
    paths: ['req.headers.authorization', 'req.headers.cookie',
            '*.password', '*.token', '*.refreshToken', '*.cardNumber'],
    censor: '[REDACTED]',
  },
});

// every request gets an ID; every line logged via req.log carries it
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  req.id = req.get('x-request-id') || randomUUID();
  res.set('x-request-id', req.id);
  req.log = logger.child({ requestId: req.id, method: req.method, route: req.path });
  next();
});

Log once, where the error is handled, not at every layer it passes through. "Log and rethrow" at three layers produces three copies of the same error and makes counting impossible.

Error ko ek baar log karo, wahan jahan woh handle hota hai, har layer pe nahi jahan se woh guzarta hai. Teen layers pe "log karo aur rethrow karo" se ek hi error ki teen copies banti hain aur counting impossible ho jaati hai.

Level 4 Resilience: retries, circuit breakers, batches and crashesResilience: retries, circuit breakers, batches aur crashes

Timeouts first. Every network call needs a timeout. Without one, a slow downstream holds your request, your memory and a pool connection forever, and a slow dependency becomes your outage.

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Many failures are transient: a dropped connection, a 503 during a deploy, a 429 rate limit. Trying again often works. But retrying immediately, in a tight loop, hammers a service that is already struggling. Exponential backoff doubles the wait each time: 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms, 1,600 ms, up to a cap and a maximum number of attempts. Jitter randomises each wait. Why? If a service blips and a thousand clients all fail at the same instant, pure exponential backoff makes all thousand retry at exactly 200 ms, then exactly 600 ms: synchronised waves that knock the service over again (the thundering herd). Randomness spreads them out.

Pehle timeouts. Har network call pe timeout hona chahiye. Iske bina ek slow downstream tumhari request, memory aur pool connection ko hamesha ke liye pakad ke rakhta hai, aur ek slow dependency tumhara outage ban jaati hai.

Exponential backoff aur jitter ke saath retry. Bahut failures transient hote hain: toota connection, deploy ke time 503, 429 rate limit. Dobara try karo toh aksar chal jaata hai. Par turant, tight loop mein retry karna us service pe hathoda maarna hai jo pehle se pareshaan hai. Exponential backoff har baar wait double karta hai: 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms, 1,600 ms, ek cap aur maximum attempts tak. Jitter har wait ko random bana deta hai. Kyun? Agar service ek pal ko hichki le aur hazaar clients ek hi pal mein fail hon, toh pure exponential backoff mein saare hazaar exact 200 ms pe retry karenge, phir exact 600 ms pe: synchronised lehrein jo service ko phir gira deti hain (thundering herd). Randomness unhe faila deti hai.

// retry.js - exponential backoff with "full jitter"
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

function isRetryable(err) {
  if (['ECONNRESET', 'ETIMEDOUT', 'ECONNREFUSED', 'EAI_AGAIN'].includes(err.code)) return true;
  return [408, 429, 502, 503, 504].includes(err.status);  // NOT 400/401/403/404/409/422, NOT plain 500 by default
}

async function retryWithBackoff(fn, { retries = 4, baseMs = 200, maxMs = 5_000 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn(attempt);
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt >= retries || !isRetryable(err)) throw err;       // give up: let the caller decide
      const cap = Math.min(maxMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt);           // 200, 400, 800, 1600 ...
      const retryAfterMs = Number(err.retryAfterSeconds) * 1000;    // honour a server's Retry-After
      const delay = retryAfterMs || Math.random() * cap;            // full jitter
      logger.warn({ attempt: attempt + 1, delayMs: Math.round(delay), code: err.code, status: err.status },
                  'transient failure, retrying');
      await sleep(delay);
    }
  }
}

When NOT to retry. (1) Errors that will fail the same way again: 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422. (2) Non-idempotent operations without an idempotency key (Topic 05): if "charge the card" timed out, the charge may have succeeded; retrying blindly can charge twice. Retry only if the operation is idempotent by nature (GET, PUT, DELETE) or you send an idempotency key so the server de-duplicates. (3) When the downstream is clearly overloaded: retries add load exactly when it hurts most; that is the circuit breaker's job. (4) When the user's deadline has already passed. Also, retry at one layer only: if three layers each retry three times, one user click becomes 27 calls (retry amplification).

Circuit breaker. When a downstream service is really down, even well-behaved retries waste time: each request waits for timeouts, threads and connections pile up, and your service slows down too. That is a cascading failure: one sick service makes its callers sick. A circuit breaker, named after the electrical switch in your home, wraps the call and tracks failures:

  • Closed (normal): calls go through. Failures are counted.
  • Open: after too many failures (for example 5 in a row, or 50% of calls in 10 seconds), it trips. Calls fail fast instantly without touching the downstream, so you return a fallback or a quick 503 instead of waiting for timeouts. The sick service gets breathing room.
  • Half-open: after a cooldown (say 30 seconds), let a few trial calls through. If they succeed, go back to closed. If they fail, go back to open and wait again.

Kab retry NAHI karna. (1) Aise errors jo dobara bhi waise hi fail honge: 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422. (2) Non-idempotent operations bina idempotency key ke (Topic 05): agar "card charge karo" timeout hua, toh ho sakta hai charge ho chuka ho; aankh band karke retry karne se double charge ho sakta hai. Retry sirf tab karo jab operation nature se idempotent ho (GET, PUT, DELETE) ya tum idempotency key bhejo taaki server duplicate hata de. (3) Jab downstream saaf-saaf overloaded ho: retries tab load badhate hain jab sabse zyada dard hota hai; yeh circuit breaker ka kaam hai. (4) Jab user ki deadline pehle hi nikal chuki ho. Aur retry sirf ek layer pe karo: agar teen layers har ek teen baar retry karein, toh user ka ek click 27 calls ban jaata hai (retry amplification).

Circuit breaker. Jab downstream service sach mein down ho, toh achhe retries bhi time barbaad karte hain: har request timeout ka wait karti hai, threads aur connections ka dher lagta hai, aur tumhari service bhi dheemi ho jaati hai. Ise cascading failure kehte hain: ek beemar service apne callers ko bhi beemar kar deti hai. Circuit breaker, ghar ke electrical switch (MCB) ke naam pe, call ko wrap karta hai aur failures track karta hai:

  • Closed (normal): calls jaati hain. Failures gine jaate hain.
  • Open: bahut zyada failures ke baad (jaise lagatar 5, ya 10 seconds mein 50% calls), yeh trip ho jaata hai. Calls turant fail fast hoti hain downstream ko chhue bina, toh tum timeouts ka wait karne ki jagah fallback ya jaldi 503 dete ho. Beemar service ko saans lene ka time milta hai.
  • Half-open: cooldown (maan lo 30 seconds) ke baad kuch trial calls jaane do. Success hui toh wapas closed. Fail hui toh wapas open aur phir wait.
// a minimal circuit breaker (real ones, e.g. the "opossum" library, use rolling windows
// and limit how many trial calls are allowed in HALF_OPEN)
class CircuitBreaker {
  constructor(fn, { failureThreshold = 5, cooldownMs = 30_000 } = {}) {
    Object.assign(this, { fn, failureThreshold, cooldownMs });
    this.state = 'CLOSED'; this.failures = 0; this.openedAt = 0;
  }
  async call(...args) {
    if (this.state === 'OPEN') {
      if (Date.now() - this.openedAt < this.cooldownMs) {
        throw new AppError('Loaner service temporarily unavailable', { status: 503, code: 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE' });
      }
      this.state = 'HALF_OPEN';                       // cooldown over: allow a trial call
    }
    try {
      const result = await this.fn(...args);
      this.state = 'CLOSED'; this.failures = 0;       // healthy again
      return result;
    } catch (err) {
      this.failures++;
      if (this.state === 'HALF_OPEN' || this.failures >= this.failureThreshold) {
        this.state = 'OPEN'; this.openedAt = Date.now();
        logger.warn({ failures: this.failures }, 'circuit opened for loaner service');
      }
      throw err;
    }
  }
}
const loanerBreaker = new CircuitBreaker((slot) => loanerApi.reserve(slot));

Batch jobs. A nightly job imports a dealer's vehicle feed with thousands of rows. If you wrap the whole loop in one try/catch, row 37 with a bad VIN kills the other thousands. Instead, wrap each record: catch, log with context (job ID, row number, record ID, reason), record the failure somewhere it can be re-processed, continue, and produce a summary at the end. Make each write idempotent (upsert by VIN) so the job can be safely re-run. One more guard: if everything is failing, the problem is systemic (database down), not per-record, so abort instead of logging thousands of identical errors.

Batch jobs. Ek nightly job dealer ki vehicle feed import karta hai jisme hazaaron rows hain. Agar poore loop ko ek try/catch mein lapet diya, toh row 37 ka ek kharab VIN baaki hazaaron ko maar deta hai. Iski jagah har record ko wrap karo: catch karo, context ke saath log karo (job ID, row number, record ID, reason), failure ko aisi jagah record karo jahan se re-process ho sake, aage badho, aur end mein ek summary do. Har write ko idempotent banao (VIN se upsert) taaki job safely dobara chalaya ja sake. Ek aur guard: agar sab kuch fail ho raha hai, toh problem systemic hai (database down), per-record nahi, toh hazaaron same errors log karne ki jagah abort karo.

// batch import: one bad row must not kill the job
async function importVehicleFeed(rows, { jobId }) {
  const summary = { jobId, total: rows.length, succeeded: 0, failed: 0 };
  const failures = [];
  for (const [i, row] of rows.entries()) {
    try {
      const vehicle = parseVehicleRow(row);        // throws ValidationError on bad data
      await vehicleRepo.upsertByVin(vehicle);      // idempotent: safe to re-run the job
      summary.succeeded++;
    } catch (err) {
      summary.failed++;
      failures.push({ row: i + 1, vin: row.vin, code: err.code, reason: err.message });
      logger.warn({ jobId, row: i + 1, vin: row.vin, err }, 'vehicle row failed, continuing');
      if (summary.failed >= 50 && summary.succeeded === 0) {   // systemic, not per-record
        logger.error(summary, 'aborting import: every row is failing');
        throw new Error('Import aborted: systemic failure', { cause: err });
      }
    }
  }
  await saveFailedRows(jobId, failures);           // someone can fix and re-run just these
  logger.info(summary, 'vehicle import finished'); // e.g. { total: 2000, succeeded: 1987, failed: 13 }
  return summary;
}

Unhandled exceptions and rejections. If an error reaches the very top with nobody catching it, it is by definition something you did not expect: a programmer error. The process may now be in a corrupted state (half-updated objects, a leaked connection, a lock never released). Keeping it alive is like continuing to use the broken ECG. The mature pattern: log it immediately with full context at FATAL, stop accepting new work, give in-flight requests a very short moment, and exit with a non-zero code. A process manager (Kubernetes, PM2, systemd, ECS) sees the exit and starts a fresh, clean process. Since Node 15, an unhandled promise rejection crashes the process by default for exactly this reason. Silently swallowing it (process.on('uncaughtException', () => {})) is worse than crashing: the service keeps running broken, no one is alerted, and data can be corrupted quietly.

Unhandled exceptions aur rejections. Agar koi error bilkul top tak pahunch jaaye aur kisi ne na pakda ho, toh definition se woh kuch aisa hai jo tumne expect nahi kiya tha: programmer error. Process ab corrupted state mein ho sakta hai (aadhe update hue objects, leak hua connection, kabhi release na hua lock). Ise zinda rakhna kharab ECG ko use karte rehne jaisa hai. Mature pattern: turant poore context ke saath FATAL pe log karo, naya kaam lena band karo, chalti requests ko bahut thoda sa time do, aur non-zero code ke saath exit karo. Ek process manager (Kubernetes, PM2, systemd, ECS) exit dekhta hai aur ek fresh, clean process start karta hai. Node 15 se unhandled promise rejection by default process crash kar deta hai, isi wajah se. Chupchaap nigal jaana (process.on('uncaughtException', () => {})) crash se bhi bura hai: service tooti hui chalti rehti hai, kisi ko alert nahi jaata, aur data chupke se corrupt ho sakta hai.

// last-resort safety nets: log everything, then exit so the process manager restarts us clean
process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => {
  // funnel into the same crash path as uncaught exceptions
  throw reason instanceof Error ? reason : new Error(`Unhandled rejection: ${String(reason)}`);
});

process.on('uncaughtException', (err, origin) => {
  logger.fatal({ err, origin }, 'uncaught error, process will exit');  // make sure the logger flushes
  server.close(() => process.exit(1));        // stop new connections, let in-flight finish
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 5_000).unref();   // but never hang around in a broken state
});

Senior nuances. (1) Alert on rates and symptoms (5xx rate above 1% for 5 minutes, p99 latency), not on single error lines. (2) Logs cost money per GB ingested and stored; sample noisy INFO lines, keep all errors, and set retention by level. (3) Put the traceId from OpenTelemetry into every log line so you can jump from a log to the full distributed trace (Topic 13). (4) There is a standard error body format, RFC 9457 "Problem Details" (application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail); many teams adopt it instead of inventing their own. (5) Bulkheads (separate connection pools per dependency) stop one slow dependency from using up every connection. (6) Use Error's cause option when wrapping so the original stack is not lost.

Senior nuances. (1) Alert rates aur symptoms pe lagao (5 minute tak 5xx rate 1% se upar, p99 latency), single error lines pe nahi. (2) Logs ka kharcha har GB ingest aur store pe lagta hai; noisy INFO lines ko sample karo, saare errors rakho, aur level ke hisaab se retention set karo. (3) OpenTelemetry ka traceId har log line mein daalo taaki log se seedha poore distributed trace pe jaa sako (Topic 13). (4) Error body ka ek standard format hai, RFC 9457 "Problem Details" (application/problem+json jisme type, title, status, detail); bahut teams apna banane ki jagah ise adopt karti hain. (5) Bulkheads (har dependency ka alag connection pool) ek slow dependency ko saare connections kha jaane se rokte hain. (6) Wrap karte waqt Error ka cause option use karo taaki original stack kho na jaaye.

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Error / exception
Object describing a failure (message + stack trace) that is thrown and can be caught.Failure ko describe karne wala object (message + stack trace) jo throw hota hai aur pakda ja sakta hai.
Stack trace
The chain of function calls that led to the error, with file and line numbers.Function calls ki chain jo error tak le gayi, file aur line numbers ke saath.
Promise rejection
How an async operation reports failure; unhandled if nobody awaits or catches it.Async operation failure kaise batata hai; koi await ya catch na kare toh unhandled.
Operational error
Expected failure of correct code (bad input, timeout, 503). Handle it.Sahi code ka expected failure (kharab input, timeout, 503). Handle karo.
Programmer error
A bug. Log it, crash, restart clean, fix the code.Bug. Log karo, crash, clean restart, code fix.
Bubble up
An uncaught error travelling up through its callers to an outer handler.Na pakda gaya error apne callers ke through upar ke handler tak jaana.
Error middleware
The single top-level handler that logs errors and turns them into HTTP responses.Ek top-level handler jo errors log karta hai aur unhe HTTP responses mein badalta hai.
Fallback
A reduced but acceptable answer when a dependency fails (book without loaner, cached price).Dependency fail hone pe chhota par chalne layak jawab (bina loaner booking, cached price).
Structured logging
Logs as JSON with named fields, searchable and countable.Named fields wale JSON logs, jinhe search aur count kar sakte ho.
Request ID / trace ID
Unique ID attached to every log line of one request, across services.Unique ID jo ek request ki har log line pe lagti hai, services ke paar bhi.
Log level
Severity of a line: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL.Line ki seriousness: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL.
Redaction
Automatically replacing sensitive fields in logs with a placeholder.Logs mein sensitive fields ko apne aap placeholder se badal dena.
PII
Personally identifiable information: names, phones, addresses, IDs.Personally identifiable information: naam, phone, address, IDs.
Transient failure
A temporary failure likely to succeed if tried again later.Temporary failure jo thodi der baad try karne pe shayad chal jaaye.
Exponential backoff / jitter
Double the wait between retries / randomise it so clients do not retry in sync.Retries ke beech wait double karo / use random karo taaki clients ek saath retry na karein.
Retry amplification
Retries at many layers multiplying into a flood of calls.Kai layers pe retries multiply hokar calls ka sailaab ban jaana.
Circuit breaker
Stops calling a failing dependency after repeated failures; closed, open, half-open.Baar-baar fail hone ke baad failing dependency ko call karna rok deta hai; closed, open, half-open.
Fail fast
Return an error immediately instead of waiting for a call that will almost surely fail.Jo call lagbhag pakka fail hogi uska wait karne ki jagah turant error do.
Cascading failure
One failing service dragging down the services that call it.Ek fail hoti service ka apne callers ko bhi saath gira dena.
Process manager
Supervisor (Kubernetes, PM2, systemd) that restarts a crashed process.Supervisor (Kubernetes, PM2, systemd) jo crash hue process ko restart karta hai.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 What is the difference between an operational error and a programmer error?Operational error aur programmer error mein kya fark hai?
What they're really testing: that expected failures (timeout, invalid input) are handled gracefully, while bugs should crash and restart rather than be silently caught.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki expected failures (timeout, invalid input) gracefully handle hote hain, jabki bugs pe crash aur restart hona chahiye, chupchaap catch nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

An operational error is an expected failure of correct code running in an unreliable world: invalid input, a record that does not exist, a network timeout, a dropped database connection, a 503 from a partner API. I handle those deliberately: a clear 4xx for the client, a retry with backoff, a fallback, or a clean 503. A programmer error is a bug: reading a property of undefined, a missing await, wrong arguments. There is nothing sensible to do with a bug at runtime, because the process is in a state I never designed for. So I let it reach the top-level handler, log it with full context, and for truly uncaught ones let the process crash and be restarted by Kubernetes or PM2, then fix the code. For example, "vehicle VIN not found" is a 404; "vehicle.price is undefined" is a bug and a 500 plus an alert. The trade-off: crashing drops in-flight requests, but silently continuing risks corrupted data and hides the bug.

Operational error ek sahi code ka unreliable duniya mein expected failure hai: invalid input, record exist nahi karta, network timeout, database connection toota, partner API se 503. Inhe main soch-samajh ke handle karta hoon: client ke liye clear 4xx, backoff ke saath retry, fallback, ya saaf 503. Programmer error bug hai: undefined ki property padhna, missing await, galat arguments. Runtime pe bug ke saath karne layak kuch nahi hota, kyunki process aisi state mein hai jo maine kabhi design nahi ki. Toh main use top-level handler tak jaane deta hoon, poore context ke saath log karta hoon, aur sach mein uncaught ho toh process ko crash hone deta hoon taaki Kubernetes ya PM2 restart kare, phir code fix. Example: "vehicle VIN not found" ek 404 hai; "vehicle.price is undefined" ek bug hai, 500 plus alert. Trade-off: crash se chalti requests drop hoti hain, par chupchaap chalte rehne se data corrupt hone ka risk hai aur bug chhup jaata hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

In code I make the distinction explicit with an AppError base class carrying status and code; the central handler treats anything that is not an AppError as a bug: generic 500, ERROR log with stack, counted towards alerts. The same failure can be either kind depending on context: a JSON.parse failure on user input is operational (400), on our own config file it is a programmer or deployment error and should stop startup. Inside a request handler, a bug does not have to kill the whole process, because Express catches it and returns 500; the crash rule is for errors that escape everything, where state may be corrupted.

Code mein main yeh fark ek AppError base class se explicit karta hoon jisme status aur code hote hain; central handler jo bhi AppError nahi hai use bug maanta hai: generic 500, stack ke saath ERROR log, alerts mein count. Same failure context ke hisaab se dono mein se koi bhi ho sakta hai: user input pe JSON.parse fail hona operational hai (400), hamari apni config file pe woh programmer ya deployment error hai aur startup rok dena chahiye. Request handler ke andar bug poore process ko nahi maarta, kyunki Express use pakad ke 500 deta hai; crash wala rule un errors ke liye hai jo sab se bach nikle, jahan state corrupt ho sakti hai.

Common mistake: wrapping everything in try/catch and logging "something went wrong" so the service never crashes. That hides bugs and keeps a broken process serving users.
Galti mat karna: sab kuch try/catch mein lapet ke "something went wrong" log karna taaki service kabhi crash na ho. Isse bugs chhup jaate hain aur toota hua process users ko serve karta rehta hai.
02 Where should you catch errors in a layered backend application?Layered backend application mein errors kahan catch karne chahiye?
What they're really testing: catching only where you have the context to decide (retry, fallback, message), and letting unexpected errors bubble to a top-level handler that logs and alerts.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: sirf wahan catch karna jahan decide karne ka context ho (retry, fallback, message), aur unexpected errors ko top-level handler tak bubble hone dena jo log aur alert kare.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I catch an error only in the layer that has enough context to do something useful with it: retry, fall back, translate it into a meaningful domain error, or add context. Everywhere else I let it bubble. In a route, service, repository setup: the repository knows Postgres code 23505 means a unique violation, so it rethrows a ConflictError, "slot already booked". The service knows the loaner-car API is optional, so after retries fail it books without a loaner and logs a warning. The route validates input and throws a ValidationError. Everything else, unknown database errors and bugs, bubbles to one Express error middleware that logs once with the request ID and stack, maps to a status code and a consistent JSON body, and feeds the 5xx alert. The benefit is one place for response shape and logging; the cost is discipline, because developers are tempted to catch-and-log everywhere, which duplicates logs and can swallow errors.

Main error sirf us layer mein pakadta hoon jiske paas uske saath kuch kaam ka karne ka context ho: retry, fallback, meaningful domain error mein translate, ya context add karna. Baaki har jagah use bubble hone deta hoon. Route, service, repository setup mein: repository jaanti hai Postgres code 23505 matlab unique violation, toh woh ConflictError rethrow karti hai, "slot already booked". Service jaanti hai loaner-car API optional hai, toh retries fail hone ke baad bina loaner ke booking karti hai aur warning log karti hai. Route input validate karta hai aur ValidationError throw karta hai. Baaki sab, unknown database errors aur bugs, ek Express error middleware tak bubble hote hain jo request ID aur stack ke saath ek baar log karta hai, status code aur consistent JSON body mein map karta hai, aur 5xx alert ko feed karta hai. Fayda: response shape aur logging ki ek jagah; keemat: discipline, kyunki developers har jagah catch-and-log karna chahte hain, jisse logs duplicate hote hain aur errors nigle ja sakte hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

When I do catch to add context, I wrap rather than replace: throw new AppError('Could not reserve loaner', { cause: err }), so the original stack survives. Translating at the repository boundary also stops database details leaking upward: the service should not know SQL error codes. In Express 4, errors inside async handlers must be passed with next(err) or a wrapper, otherwise they become unhandled rejections; Express 5 forwards rejected promises automatically. Background workers and queue consumers need their own top-level handler, because the HTTP middleware never sees their errors; there the top level decides retry versus dead-letter queue.

Jab main context add karne ke liye catch karta hoon, toh replace nahi, wrap karta hoon: throw new AppError('Could not reserve loaner', { cause: err }), taaki original stack bacha rahe. Repository boundary pe translate karne se database ki details upar leak nahi hoti: service ko SQL error codes pata hone ki zaroorat nahi. Express 4 mein async handlers ke errors next(err) ya wrapper se pass karne padte hain, warna woh unhandled rejections ban jaate hain; Express 5 rejected promises apne aap forward karta hai. Background workers aur queue consumers ko apna top-level handler chahiye, kyunki HTTP middleware unke errors kabhi nahi dekhta; wahan top level decide karta hai retry ya dead-letter queue.

Common mistake: catching an error in the repository, logging it and returning null. The caller now thinks "not found" when the database was actually down.
Galti mat karna: repository mein error pakad ke log karna aur null return kar dena. Caller ab sochta hai "not found", jabki asal mein database down tha.
03 What makes a log line useful in production?Production mein ek log line ko useful kya banata hai?
What they're really testing: structured JSON, a request or trace ID, timestamp, severity and enough context to act on.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: structured JSON, request ya trace ID, timestamp, severity aur itna context ki action le sako.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A useful log line answers "what happened, to whom, where, when and why" without me having to reproduce it. First, it is structured: JSON with named fields, so I can filter and count, not grep free text. Second, it carries a request ID or trace ID, generated at the edge and attached to every line of that request, even across services, so one ID gives me the whole story. Third, a precise UTC timestamp and a severity level. Fourth, context: service name and version, route, status, duration, user ID and the IDs of the thing being processed, like the VIN or appointment ID. Fifth, for errors, the error type, message and stack. And the message itself is short and constant, "loaner service call failed", with variable data in fields, so I can count how often it happens. Compare that with console.log("error occurred"), which tells me nothing at 2 am.

Useful log line bina reproduce kiye batati hai "kya hua, kiske saath, kahan, kab aur kyun". Pehla, structured: named fields wala JSON, taaki filter aur count kar sakoon, free text grep nahi. Doosra, isme request ID ya trace ID hoti hai, jo edge pe banti hai aur us request ki har line pe lagti hai, services ke paar bhi, toh ek ID se poori kahani mil jaati hai. Teesra, exact UTC timestamp aur severity level. Chautha, context: service ka naam aur version, route, status, duration, user ID aur jis cheez pe kaam ho raha uske IDs, jaise VIN ya appointment ID. Paanchwa, errors ke liye error type, message aur stack. Aur message khud chhota aur constant, "loaner service call failed", variable data fields mein, taaki gin sakoon kitni baar hua. Iski tulna console.log("error occurred") se karo, jo raat 2 baje kuch nahi batata.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

I use a JSON logger like pino with a child logger per request, created in middleware, so every line automatically carries the request ID; AsyncLocalStorage can carry it through code that has no req. With OpenTelemetry the traceId and spanId go into each line, so the log UI links straight to the distributed trace. I log once where an error is handled, not at every layer. I watch volume and cost: sample chatty INFO lines, never sample errors, and avoid logging whole request bodies. Logs are events; for "how many per second" I use metrics, which are far cheaper to query.

Main pino jaisa JSON logger use karta hoon, har request ke liye middleware mein child logger, taaki har line mein apne aap request ID ho; AsyncLocalStorage use us code tak le jaa sakta hai jiske paas req nahi hai. OpenTelemetry ke saath traceId aur spanId har line mein jaate hain, toh log UI seedha distributed trace se link hota hai. Error ko ek baar log karta hoon jahan handle hota hai, har layer pe nahi. Volume aur cost pe nazar: chatty INFO lines sample karo, errors kabhi sample mat karo, aur poori request bodies log karne se bacho. Logs events hain; "per second kitne" ke liye metrics use karta hoon, jo query karne mein kaafi saste hain.

Common mistake: interpolating variables into the message string ("failed for VIN 1HG..."), which makes every line unique and impossible to group or count.
Galti mat karna: variables ko message string ke andar daal dena ("failed for VIN 1HG..."), jisse har line unique ho jaati hai aur group ya count karna impossible.
04 What are log levels and how do you decide which to use?Log levels kya hain aur kaunsa use karna hai kaise decide karte ho?
What they're really testing: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR used for their real meaning, and not logging everything as ERROR.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR ka sahi matlab ke saath use, aur sab kuch ERROR mein log na karna.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Log levels encode severity so we can filter noise and alert on what matters. DEBUG is developer detail, like cache hits or SQL parameters, off in production by default. INFO is normal business events: server started, appointment booked, job finished with a summary. WARN is something unexpected that we handled: a retry, a fallback to cached pricing, a slow query; worth watching as a trend. ERROR means an operation failed and a human may need to act: an unhandled 500, a webhook we could not persist. FATAL means the process is exiting. My rule is: would I want to be woken up if this happened a hundred times in five minutes? If not, it is not ERROR. A user entering an invalid VIN is INFO or WARN at most, because it is their mistake, not our failure. If everything is ERROR, alerts fire constantly, people start ignoring them, and the real outage gets missed. Production usually runs at INFO, configurable per service.

Log levels severity batate hain taaki noise filter kar sakein aur jo zaroori hai uspe alert laga sakein. DEBUG developer ki detail hai, jaise cache hits ya SQL parameters, production mein by default band. INFO normal business events: server start hua, appointment book hua, job summary ke saath khatam. WARN kuch unexpected jo humne handle kar liya: retry, cached pricing pe fallback, slow query; trend ke roop mein nazar rakhne layak. ERROR matlab operation fail hua aur shayad insaan ko action lena pade: unhandled 500, webhook jo hum save nahi kar paaye. FATAL matlab process exit ho raha hai. Mera rule: agar yeh paanch minute mein sau baar ho toh kya main neend se uthna chahunga? Nahi, toh yeh ERROR nahi. User ka invalid VIN daalna zyada se zyada INFO ya WARN hai, kyunki galti uski hai, hamara failure nahi. Sab ERROR ho toh alerts lagatar bajte hain, log ignore karne lagte hain, aur asli outage miss ho jaata hai. Production aam taur pe INFO pe chalta hai, har service ke liye configurable.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Levels drive cost and retention too: keep ERROR for months, DEBUG barely at all. I make the level changeable at runtime (an env var or config flag) so I can turn on DEBUG for one service during an incident without redeploying. Alerts should be based on rates from metrics, like 5xx above 1% for five minutes, not on individual ERROR lines, because one error is noise and a pattern is a signal. A WARN that nobody ever looks at is a smell: either it matters and should be a metric with an alert, or it does not and should be removed.

Levels cost aur retention bhi decide karte hain: ERROR mahino tak rakho, DEBUG lagbhag bilkul nahi. Main level ko runtime pe badalne layak banata hoon (env var ya config flag) taaki incident ke time ek service ke liye bina redeploy DEBUG on kar sakoon. Alerts metrics ke rates pe hone chahiye, jaise paanch minute tak 5xx 1% se upar, individual ERROR lines pe nahi, kyunki ek error noise hai aur pattern signal hai. Jis WARN ko koi kabhi nahi dekhta woh smell hai: ya toh woh important hai aur use alert wala metric hona chahiye, ya nahi hai aur use hata dena chahiye.

Common mistake: logging every 4xx, including "wrong password" and "not found", as ERROR, which floods dashboards and trains the team to ignore alerts.
Galti mat karna: har 4xx, "wrong password" aur "not found" samet, ko ERROR mein log karna, jisse dashboards bhar jaate hain aur team alerts ignore karna seekh jaati hai.
05 How do you avoid leaking sensitive data in logs and error responses?Logs aur error responses mein sensitive data leak hone se kaise bachte ho?
What they're really testing: never logging passwords, tokens or full PII; redacting; returning generic errors to clients.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: passwords, tokens ya poora PII kabhi log na karna; redact karna; clients ko generic errors dena.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Two directions: what goes into logs and what goes back to the client. Logs get shipped to third-party tools, read by many engineers and kept for months, so I treat them as semi-public. I never log passwords, access or refresh tokens, API keys, session cookies or full card numbers, and I avoid full personal data such as a customer's name plus phone number; I log IDs instead, and mask when I need a hint, like the last four digits. I enforce it with the logger's redaction config, for example pino redact on authorization and cookie headers and any password or token field, rather than relying on everyone remembering. I also never log whole request bodies or config objects. For clients, a 500 returns a generic message and a request ID, never the stack trace, SQL text or internal hostnames, because those help attackers. The details stay in the logs, linked by that ID. The trade-off is slightly harder debugging, which the request ID solves.

Do directions: logs mein kya jaata hai aur client ko kya wapas jaata hai. Logs third-party tools mein bheje jaate hain, bahut engineers padhte hain aur mahino rakhe jaate hain, toh main unhe semi-public maanta hoon. Passwords, access ya refresh tokens, API keys, session cookies ya poore card numbers kabhi log nahi karta, aur poora personal data jaise customer ka naam plus phone number avoid karta hoon; iski jagah IDs log karta hoon, aur hint chahiye toh mask, jaise last chaar digits.
