Ise logger ke redaction config se enforce karta hoon, jaise pino redact authorization aur cookie headers aur har password ya token field pe, sabke yaad rakhne pe bharosa nahi karta. Poori request bodies ya config objects bhi kabhi log nahi karta. Clients ke liye 500 pe generic message aur request ID, kabhi stack trace, SQL text ya internal hostnames nahi, kyunki yeh attackers ki madad karte hain. Details logs mein rehti hain, us ID se judi. Trade-off: debugging thodi mushkil, jo request ID solve kar deti hai.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Leaks often come from indirect places: error messages from libraries that include the SQL and its parameters, HTTP client errors that include the full request with an Authorization header, URLs with tokens in query strings (which also land in access logs and proxies), and JSON.stringify(user). So I scrub at serialisation time with custom error serializers, keep secrets out of URLs, and add a log-scanning check for patterns like JWTs or card numbers. Access to logs should be restricted and audited, retention limited, and regulations like GDPR or US state privacy laws give users rights over personal data, which is much harder if it is scattered through logs. If a secret does leak into logs, rotate it.

Leaks aksar indirect jagahon se hote hain: libraries ke error messages jisme SQL aur uske parameters hote hain, HTTP client errors jisme Authorization header ke saath poori request hoti hai, query strings mein tokens wale URLs (jo access logs aur proxies mein bhi pahunchte hain), aur JSON.stringify(user). Isliye main custom error serializers se serialisation ke time scrub karta hoon, secrets ko URLs se bahar rakhta hoon, aur JWT ya card number jaise patterns ke liye log-scanning check lagata hoon. Logs ka access restricted aur audited hona chahiye, retention limited, aur GDPR ya US state privacy laws jaise regulations users ko personal data pe rights dete hain, jo logs mein bikhra ho toh bahut mushkil ho jaata hai. Agar koi secret logs mein leak ho jaaye, toh use rotate karo.

Common mistake: returning err.message or err.stack straight to the client for 500s, exposing table names, queries and file paths.
Galti mat karna: 500 pe err.message ya err.stack seedha client ko bhej dena, jisse table names, queries aur file paths expose ho jaate hain.
06 What is a circuit breaker pattern and when would you use it?Circuit breaker pattern kya hai aur kab use karoge?
What they're really testing: stopping calls to a failing downstream after repeated failures, failing fast, preventing cascading failures, and the closed / open / half-open states.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: baar-baar fail hone ke baad failing downstream ko call karna rokna, fail fast, cascading failures rokna, aur closed / open / half-open states.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and stops calling it once it is clearly failing. It has three states. Closed is normal: calls go through and failures are counted. When failures cross a threshold, say five in a row or half the calls in ten seconds, it trips to open: every call fails fast immediately, without touching the dependency, and I return a fallback or a quick 503. After a cooldown, say 30 seconds, it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through; success closes it, failure opens it again. I use it around remote dependencies that can go down: a partner inventory API, a payment provider, a loaner-car service. Without it, every request waits for timeouts, connections and memory pile up, and my service goes down with theirs, which is a cascading failure. The trade-off is tuning: too sensitive and it trips on noise; too lax and it does not protect you. And some requests fail that might have succeeded.

Circuit breaker ek dependency ki calls ko wrap karta hai aur jab woh saaf fail ho rahi ho toh use call karna band kar deta hai. Iski teen states hain. Closed normal hai: calls jaati hain aur failures gine jaate hain. Jab failures threshold cross karein, maan lo lagatar paanch ya das seconds mein aadhi calls, toh yeh open mein trip hota hai: har call turant fail fast hoti hai, dependency ko chhue bina, aur main fallback ya jaldi 503 deta hoon. Cooldown ke baad, maan lo 30 seconds, yeh half-open hota hai aur kuch trial calls jaane deta hai; success pe closed, failure pe phir open. Main ise un remote dependencies ke around use karta hoon jo down ho sakti hain: partner inventory API, payment provider, loaner-car service. Iske bina har request timeouts ka wait karti hai, connections aur memory ka dher lagta hai, aur meri service unke saath doob jaati hai, yahi cascading failure hai. Trade-off tuning ka hai: zyada sensitive toh noise pe trip; zyada dheela toh bachata nahi. Aur kuch requests fail hoti hain jo shayad chal jaatin.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

It complements retries and timeouts: the timeout bounds one call, retry handles a blip, and the breaker handles a sustained outage, so retries should respect an open breaker rather than hammering. Real implementations use a rolling window of failure rate with a minimum request count, so three failures out of three requests at 3 am do not trip it, and they limit how many trial calls half-open allows. In Node, the opossum library does this; in a service mesh like Istio or Envoy it is called outlier detection and happens outside the code. Each instance usually has its own breaker state. I expose breaker state as a metric and alert when it opens. Pair it with bulkheads, separate pools per dependency, so one bad dependency cannot starve the others.

Yeh retries aur timeouts ka saathi hai: timeout ek call ko limit karta hai, retry ek hichki sambhalta hai, aur breaker lamba outage sambhalta hai, toh retries ko open breaker ki izzat karni chahiye, hathoda nahi maarna. Real implementations failure rate ki rolling window aur minimum request count use karti hain, taaki raat 3 baje teen mein se teen failures pe trip na ho, aur half-open mein kitni trial calls jaayein woh limit karti hain. Node mein opossum library yeh karti hai; Istio ya Envoy jaise service mesh mein ise outlier detection kehte hain aur yeh code ke bahar hota hai. Aam taur pe har instance ki apni breaker state hoti hai. Main breaker state ko metric ki tarah expose karta hoon aur open hone pe alert. Ise bulkheads ke saath jodo, har dependency ka alag pool, taaki ek kharab dependency baaki ko bhooka na maar de.

Common mistake: describing it as "just retrying"; a breaker does the opposite of retrying, it stops calling so the failing service can recover.
Galti mat karna: ise "bas retry karna" bataana; breaker retry ka ulta karta hai, woh call karna rok deta hai taaki fail hoti service theek ho sake.
07 How do you design consistent error responses in an API?API mein consistent error responses kaise design karte ho?
What they're really testing: one consistent shape (code, message, details) with the correct HTTP status, and never 200 with an error in the body.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ek consistent shape (code, message, details) sahi HTTP status ke saath, aur kabhi 200 ke saath body mein error nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Every error from every endpoint has the same JSON envelope and the correct HTTP status. The envelope has a stable machine-readable code like VALIDATION_FAILED or SLOT_TAKEN that clients can switch on, a human-readable message, optional details such as per-field problems, and a requestId for support. For example, a booking with a 16-character VIN returns 422 with details saying the vin field must be 17 characters. Status codes carry the category: 400 malformed, 401 not authenticated, 403 not allowed, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 422 invalid data, 429 rate limited, 500 our bug, 503 temporarily unavailable. I implement it with AppError classes and one error middleware, so the shape cannot drift between teams. I never return 200 with an error in the body, because monitoring, caches, retries and client libraries all trust the status code. The trade-off is agreeing on a code catalogue and treating codes as part of the API contract.

Har endpoint ka har error same JSON envelope aur sahi HTTP status ke saath aata hai. Envelope mein ek stable machine-readable code hota hai jaise VALIDATION_FAILED ya SLOT_TAKEN jis pe clients switch kar sakein, ek insaan ke padhne layak message, optional details jaise har field ki problem, aur support ke liye requestId. Example: 16-character VIN wali booking pe 422, details mein ki vin field 17 characters ki honi chahiye. Status codes category batate hain: 400 malformed, 401 authenticated nahi, 403 allowed nahi, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 422 invalid data, 429 rate limited, 500 hamara bug, 503 abhi available nahi. Main ise AppError classes aur ek error middleware se implement karta hoon, taaki teams ke beech shape badal na paaye. 200 ke saath body mein error kabhi nahi, kyunki monitoring, caches, retries aur client libraries sab status code pe bharosa karte hain. Trade-off: codes ki ek catalogue pe agree karna aur codes ko API contract ka hissa maanna.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

There is a standard: RFC 9457 Problem Details, application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail and instance, plus extension fields; adopting it saves design debates. Error codes are part of the contract, so renaming one is a breaking change (Topic 08). For 429 and 503, include Retry-After. For validation, return all field errors at once, not one per round trip. Be careful with 404 versus 403: for resources the caller should not know exist, returning 404 avoids confirming existence. Document errors in the OpenAPI spec per endpoint, and in GraphQL, where transport is usually 200, errors go in the standard errors array with an extensions.code.

Ek standard hai: RFC 9457 Problem Details, application/problem+json jisme type, title, status, detail aur instance, plus extension fields; ise adopt karne se design ki behas bachti hai. Error codes contract ka hissa hain, toh ek ka naam badalna breaking change hai (Topic 08). 429 aur 503 ke liye Retry-After bhejo. Validation mein saare field errors ek saath do, har round trip pe ek nahi. 404 vs 403 mein savdhaan: jin resources ka caller ko pata hi nahi hona chahiye, unke liye 404 dene se existence confirm nahi hoti. Har endpoint ke errors OpenAPI spec mein document karo, aur GraphQL mein, jahan transport aam taur pe 200 hota hai, errors standard errors array mein extensions.code ke saath jaate hain.

Common mistake: returning 200 OK with {"success": false}, or a different error shape per endpoint, so every client needs special-case parsing.
Galti mat karna: 200 OK ke saath {"success": false} bhejna, ya har endpoint ka alag error shape, jisse har client ko special-case parsing chahiye.
08 What is retry-with-backoff and when should you NOT use it?Retry-with-backoff kya hai aur kab ise use NAHI karna chahiye?
What they're really testing: exponential backoff plus jitter, and never retrying non-idempotent operations without an idempotency key.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: exponential backoff plus jitter, aur non-idempotent operations ko bina idempotency key ke kabhi retry na karna.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Many failures are transient: a reset connection, a 503 during a deploy, a 429. Retry-with-backoff tries again, but waits longer each time: exponential backoff doubles the wait, 200, 400, 800 milliseconds, up to a cap and a maximum number of attempts. I add jitter, a random wait between zero and that cap, because if a thousand clients failed at the same moment, pure backoff makes them all retry at the same moment again and knock the service over. I also honour Retry-After. When not to retry: errors that will fail identically, like 400, 401, 403, 404, 422; non-idempotent operations such as "charge card" or "create order" unless I send an idempotency key, because a timeout does not mean it failed and a blind retry can charge twice; when the downstream is overloaded, where a circuit breaker is better; and when the caller's deadline has passed. And I retry at one layer only, otherwise retries multiply.

Bahut failures transient hote hain: reset connection, deploy ke time 503, 429. Retry-with-backoff dobara try karta hai, par har baar zyada wait karke: exponential backoff wait double karta hai, 200, 400, 800 milliseconds, ek cap aur maximum attempts tak. Main jitter add karta hoon, zero aur us cap ke beech random wait, kyunki agar hazaar clients ek hi pal mein fail hue, toh pure backoff unhe phir ek hi pal mein retry karwata hai aur service gir jaati hai. Retry-After ko bhi follow karta hoon. Kab retry nahi: jo errors waise hi fail honge, jaise 400, 401, 403, 404, 422; non-idempotent operations jaise "card charge karo" ya "order create karo" jab tak idempotency key na bhejoon, kyunki timeout ka matlab fail nahi hota aur aankh band retry double charge kar sakta hai; jab downstream overloaded ho, wahan circuit breaker behtar hai; aur jab caller ki deadline nikal chuki ho. Aur retry sirf ek layer pe, warna retries multiply hote hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The formula I use is "full jitter": delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)), which spreads load best in practice. Retry amplification is the real danger: if the gateway, the API and the client library each retry three times, one click becomes 27 calls into a struggling service. So retries live in one place, and many teams use a retry budget, such as retries may add at most 10% extra load. Every attempt needs its own timeout, and the total must fit the user's deadline. With an idempotency key (Topic 05), even a POST becomes safe to retry because the server returns the stored result for a duplicate key. Log each retry at WARN with the attempt number, so a rising retry rate shows up before it turns into errors.

Main "full jitter" formula use karta hoon: delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)), jo practice mein load sabse achha failata hai. Asli khatra retry amplification hai: agar gateway, API aur client library har ek teen baar retry karein, toh ek click pareshaan service pe 27 calls ban jaata hai. Isliye retries ek jagah rehte hain, aur bahut teams retry budget use karti hain, jaise retries zyada se zyada 10% extra load add kar sakte hain. Har attempt ka apna timeout chahiye, aur total user ki deadline mein fit hona chahiye. Idempotency key (Topic 05) ke saath POST bhi retry ke liye safe ho jaata hai kyunki server duplicate key pe stored result lauta deta hai. Har retry ko attempt number ke saath WARN pe log karo, taaki badhta retry rate errors banne se pehle dikh jaaye.

Common mistake: a tight while loop retrying immediately on any error, including 400s and payment POSTs without an idempotency key.
Galti mat karna: ek tight while loop jo kisi bhi error pe turant retry kare, 400s aur bina idempotency key wale payment POSTs samet.
09 How do you handle errors in a batch job that processes thousands of records?Hazaaron records process karne wale batch job mein errors kaise handle karte ho?
What they're really testing: per-record catch, logging with context, continuing, and a summary at the end.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: har record pe catch, context ke saath log, aage badhna, aur end mein summary.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

The principle is that one bad record must not kill the whole job, and no failure should be silent. So the try/catch goes around each record, not around the loop. Say a nightly job imports a dealer's vehicle feed of a few thousand rows. For each row I parse and validate, then upsert by VIN. If a row fails, I catch it, log a WARN with the job ID, row number, VIN and reason, save it to a failed-rows table or file so it can be fixed and re-run on its own, and continue. At the end I log and return a summary: total, succeeded, failed, plus the failure list. Writes are idempotent, so re-running the job after a fix is safe. One guard: if the first fifty rows all fail, the problem is systemic, maybe the database is down, so I abort instead of logging thousands of identical errors. The trade-off is partial success, so the job's consumers must understand "completed with 13 failures".

Principle yeh hai ki ek kharab record poora job na maare, aur koi failure chupchaap na ho. Toh try/catch har record ke around lagta hai, loop ke around nahi. Maan lo ek nightly job dealer ki kuch hazaar rows wali vehicle feed import karta hai. Har row ko parse aur validate karta hoon, phir VIN se upsert. Row fail hui toh pakadta hoon, job ID, row number, VIN aur reason ke saath WARN log karta hoon, use failed-rows table ya file mein save karta hoon taaki alag se fix karke re-run ho sake, aur aage badhta hoon. End mein summary log aur return karta hoon: total, succeeded, failed, plus failure list. Writes idempotent hain, toh fix ke baad job dobara chalana safe hai. Ek guard: agar pehli pachaas rows sab fail hon, toh problem systemic hai, shayad database down, toh hazaaron same errors log karne ki jagah abort karta hoon. Trade-off partial success ka hai, toh job ke consumers ko "13 failures ke saath complete" samajhna padega.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Separate failure types: validation failures are permanent, so record and skip; transient ones like a timeout get a few retries with backoff first. For speed, process in chunks with limited concurrency and use Promise.allSettled so one rejection does not hide the others. For very large jobs, checkpoint progress (last processed ID) so a crash resumes instead of restarting, and consider putting each record on a queue so failed ones go to a dead-letter queue automatically (Topic 06). Decide the transaction boundary consciously: one transaction per record or per small chunk, never one giant transaction around everything, which holds locks for ages (Topic 02). Emit metrics for processed and failed counts and alert if the failure ratio crosses a threshold.

Failure types alag karo: validation failures permanent hain, toh record karo aur skip; timeout jaise transient failures ko pehle backoff ke saath kuch retries do. Speed ke liye chunks mein limited concurrency ke saath process karo aur Promise.allSettled use karo taaki ek rejection baaki ko chhupa na de. Bahut bade jobs ke liye progress checkpoint karo (last processed ID) taaki crash ke baad shuru se nahi, wahin se resume ho, aur har record ko queue pe daalne ka socho taaki failed wale apne aap dead-letter queue mein jaayein (Topic 06). Transaction boundary soch-samajh ke decide karo: har record ya chhote chunk ka ek transaction, poore kaam ke around ek giant transaction kabhi nahi, jo der tak locks pakde rehta hai (Topic 02). Processed aur failed counts ke metrics emit karo aur failure ratio threshold cross kare toh alert.

Common mistake: one try/catch around the entire loop (first bad row kills the job) or an empty catch that skips failures with no record of them.
Galti mat karna: poore loop ke around ek try/catch (pehli kharab row job maar deti hai) ya khaali catch jo failures ko bina kisi record ke skip kar de.
10 How should you handle an unhandled exception or uncaught promise rejection in Node.js?Node.js mein unhandled exception ya uncaught promise rejection ko kaise handle karna chahiye?
What they're really testing: log full context immediately, let the process crash and be restarted by a process manager; swallowing silently is worse.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: turant poore context ke saath log karo, process ko crash hone do aur process manager se restart hone do; chupchaap nigalna usse bhi bura hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

If an error reaches the very top uncaught, it is by definition something I did not anticipate, a programmer error, and the process may be in a corrupted state: a half-updated object, a leaked connection, a lock never released. So I register process.on('uncaughtException') and process.on('unhandledRejection') purely as last-resort loggers: log at FATAL with the error, stack and origin, stop accepting new connections, give in-flight requests a few seconds, then exit with a non-zero code. The process manager, Kubernetes, PM2 or systemd, starts a fresh clean process, and with several replicas behind a load balancer users barely notice. Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default for this reason. Swallowing it with an empty handler is worse than crashing: the service keeps running in an unknown state, no alert fires, and data can be quietly corrupted. Then I fix the root cause, usually a missing await or catch.

Agar koi error bilkul top tak uncaught pahunch jaaye, toh definition se woh kuch aisa hai jo maine socha nahi tha, programmer error, aur process corrupted state mein ho sakta hai: aadha update hua object, leak hua connection, kabhi release na hua lock. Toh main process.on('uncaughtException') aur process.on('unhandledRejection') sirf last-resort loggers ki tarah register karta hoon: error, stack aur origin ke saath FATAL pe log, nayi connections lena band, chalti requests ko kuch seconds, phir non-zero code ke saath exit. Process manager, Kubernetes, PM2 ya systemd, ek fresh clean process start karta hai, aur load balancer ke peeche kai replicas hon toh users ko mushkil se pata chalta hai. Node 15 se unhandled rejection isi wajah se by default process crash kar deta hai. Khaali handler se nigal jaana crash se bhi bura hai: service unknown state mein chalti rehti hai, koi alert nahi, aur data chupke se corrupt ho sakta hai. Phir main root cause fix karta hoon, aksar missing await ya catch.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

The Node docs are explicit that it is not safe to resume normal operation after uncaughtException. Make sure the fatal log actually reaches the log pipeline before exit, since async transports can lose the last line. Keep the exit grace short, because the process is untrusted. Crash-looping is itself a signal: Kubernetes shows CrashLoopBackOff and backs off restarts, and I alert on restart counts. Tools like Sentry capture the stack with context for these. The design goal is that crashing is cheap: stateless replicas, idempotent handlers and graceful shutdown mean a restart costs a few failed requests, not lost data. For worker processes, an in-flight message that was not acknowledged will be redelivered, so consumers must be idempotent.

Node docs saaf kehte hain ki uncaughtException ke baad normal operation resume karna safe nahi hai. Ensure karo ki fatal log exit se pehle sach mein log pipeline tak pahunche, kyunki async transports aakhri line kho sakte hain. Exit ka grace chhota rakho, kyunki process pe bharosa nahi. Crash-loop khud ek signal hai: Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff dikhata hai aur restarts ko back off karta hai, aur main restart counts pe alert lagata hoon. Sentry jaise tools inke liye context ke saath stack capture karte hain. Design goal yeh hai ki crash sasta ho: stateless replicas, idempotent handlers aur graceful shutdown ka matlab restart ki keemat kuch failed requests hai, lost data nahi. Worker processes ke liye, jo in-flight message acknowledge nahi hua woh dobara deliver hoga, toh consumers idempotent hone chahiye.

Common mistake: process.on('uncaughtException', err => console.log(err)) and carrying on, which keeps a broken process alive and hides the bug.
Galti mat karna: process.on('uncaughtException', err => console.log(err)) likh ke chalte rehna, jisse toota hua process zinda rehta hai aur bug chhup jaata hai.

Topic 13 · ASKED EVERYWHERETopic 13 · Har jagah poocha jaata hai

Production DebuggingProduction Debugging

How to stay calm at 2am, read metrics, logs and traces like a doctor reads a blood report, and answer every "walk me through it" scenario with a structured story: observe, hypothesise, test, fix, prevent.

Raat ke 2 baje calm kaise rehna hai, metrics, logs aur traces ko waise padhna jaise doctor blood report padhta hai, aur har "walk me through it" scenario ka jawab ek structured kahani se dena: observe, hypothesise, test, fix, prevent.

Level 0 The story: the 2am page and the good doctorKahani: raat 2 baje ka page aur ek achha doctor

It is 2:07 at night. Your phone screams with the alarm tone you picked precisely because it is impossible to sleep through. The message says: checkout-api p99 latency above 2s for 10 minutes. This week you are on-call: the engineer whose job is to respond when production (the live system that real users are using right now) gets sick. That alarm on your phone is called a page, and the thing that is going wrong is called an incident.

What do you do first? Most beginners panic and start changing things: restart the server, add more machines, clear the cache. Good engineers do what a good doctor does.

Imagine you walk into a clinic with a fever. A bad doctor hears "fever" and immediately writes strong antibiotics. A good doctor works in five steps:

  1. Symptoms: "Temperature 102. Since when? Any cough? What did you eat? Did you travel?"
  2. Possible causes: "Could be viral, could be typhoid, could be dengue."
  3. Tests: a blood test and a platelet count. Each test rules a cause in or out.
  4. Treatment: first bring the fever down with paracetamol so the patient is stable, then treat the real cause.
  5. Prevention: mosquito net, clean water, a vaccine, so it does not happen again.

Production debugging is exactly this, and the five words interviewers want to hear map one to one: observe (symptoms), hypothesise (possible causes), test (blood test), fix (treatment), prevent (vaccine).

Two details from the doctor story matter enormously:

  • The doctor treats the fever first, then the cause. In production this is called mitigation first, root cause second. If a deploy an hour ago broke checkout, you roll it back now (remember blue-green deployment from Topic 11: the old version is still standing, so switching back is instant) and you investigate the real bug calmly in the morning.
  • The doctor asks "what changed?": new food, travel, a new medicine. In production, the single most common cause of a brand-new problem is a recent change: a deploy, a config flag, a database migration, a traffic spike, or a table that quietly grew past some size.

The doctor also has instruments: a thermometer, a BP machine, a blood report, an X-ray. We have instruments too, called metrics, logs and traces, and most of this chapter teaches you to read them.

Why is this topic asked everywhere? Because every earlier chapter in this guide is a place where bugs are born. A missing index (Topic 01), a long transaction holding locks (Topic 02), a race condition (Topic 03), a cache stampede (Topic 04), a poison-pill message (Topic 06), a container killed for using too much memory (Topic 11). Debugging is the topic where all of them show up at 2am in disguise. When an interviewer says "response times doubled overnight, walk me through it", they are checking one thing: do you have a calm, structured method, or do you guess?

Remember: stabilise first, understand second, prevent third. And the first question is always: what changed?

Raat ke 2:07 baje hain. Tumhara phone us alarm tone se cheekh raha hai jo tumne jaan-boojh kar chuna tha taaki neend mein bhi sunai de. Message hai: checkout-api p99 latency above 2s for 10 minutes. Is hafte tum on-call ho: matlab woh engineer jiska kaam hai jab production (woh live system jo real users abhi is waqt use kar rahe hain) beemar ho, toh respond karna. Phone pe jo alarm aaya usko page kehte hain, aur jo gadbad ho rahi hai usko incident kehte hain.

Sabse pehle kya karoge? Zyada tar beginners ghabra kar cheezein badalne lagte hain: server restart, aur machines add, cache clear. Achhe engineers wahi karte hain jo ek achha doctor karta hai.

Socho tum bukhaar lekar clinic gaye. Ek bura doctor "bukhaar" sunte hi strong antibiotics likh deta hai. Achha doctor paanch steps mein kaam karta hai:

  1. Symptoms: "Temperature 102. Kab se hai? Khansi hai? Kya khaya tha? Kahin travel kiya?"
  2. Possible causes: "Viral ho sakta hai, typhoid ho sakta hai, dengue ho sakta hai."
  3. Tests: blood test aur platelet count. Har test kisi cause ko pakka karta hai ya hata deta hai.
  4. Treatment: pehle paracetamol se bukhaar neeche lao taaki patient stable ho, phir asli cause ka ilaaj karo.
  5. Prevention: machhardani, saaf paani, vaccine, taaki dobara na ho.

Production debugging bilkul yahi hai, aur jo paanch words interviewer sunna chahta hai woh ek-ek karke match hote hain: observe (symptoms), hypothesise (possible causes), test (blood test), fix (treatment), prevent (vaccine).

Doctor wali kahani ki do baatein bahut zaroori hain:

  • Doctor pehle bukhaar utaarta hai, phir cause dhoondhta hai. Production mein isko kehte hain mitigation first, root cause second. Agar ek ghante pehle ke deploy ne checkout tod diya, toh abhi rollback karo (Topic 11 ka blue-green deployment yaad karo: purana version abhi bhi khada hai, isliye wapas switch karna turant hota hai) aur asli bug subah aaraam se dhoondho.
  • Doctor poochta hai "kya badla?": naya khaana, travel, nayi dawai. Production mein kisi bilkul nayi problem ka sabse common cause hota hai koi recent change: ek deploy, ek config flag, ek database migration, traffic ka spike, ya koi table jo chupchaap ek size se bada ho gaya.

Doctor ke paas instruments bhi hote hain: thermometer, BP machine, blood report, X-ray. Hamare paas bhi instruments hain, jinhe metrics, logs aur traces kehte hain, aur is chapter ka zyada hissa yahi sikhata hai ki inhe padhna kaise hai.

Yeh topic har jagah kyun poocha jaata hai? Kyunki is guide ka har pichla chapter ek jagah hai jahan bugs paida hote hain. Missing index (Topic 01), locks pakad ke baitha lamba transaction (Topic 02), race condition (Topic 03), cache stampede (Topic 04), poison-pill message (Topic 06), zyada memory use karne pe kill hua container (Topic 11). Debugging woh topic hai jahan yeh sab raat 2 baje bhes badal ke aate hain. Jab interviewer kehta hai "response times raaton-raat double ho gaye, walk me through it", toh woh sirf ek cheez check kar raha hai: kya tumhare paas ek calm, structured tareeka hai, ya tum andaaza lagaate ho?

Yaad rakho: pehle stable karo, phir samjho, phir rokne ka intezaam karo. Aur pehla sawaal hamesha: kya badla?

Level 1 The vocabulary: signals and the three pillarsVocabulary: signals aur teen pillars

Before you can say "something is wrong", you need words for what is wrong. Four signals describe the health of almost any backend service (Google's SRE book calls them the "golden signals"):

  • Latency: how long one request takes, in milliseconds (ms). 1000 ms = 1 second.
  • Traffic (or throughput): how many requests per second you are getting.
  • Errors: what share of requests fail, usually counted as HTTP 5xx responses (Topic 08). "Error rate 1%" means 1 in every 100 requests fails.
  • Saturation: how full a resource is. CPU at 95%, the DB connection pool at 20 of 20 in use (Topic 03), disk at 90%, memory near the container's limit.

To measure these, teams use three kinds of data, called the three pillars of observability. Observability just means "how well can I understand what is happening inside my system from the outside".

  • Metric: a number measured over time. cpu_percent = 73 at 02:05, = 98 at 02:06. Metrics are cheap to store (just numbers), perfect for graphs and alerts. They tell you that something is wrong and how much, but not why.
  • Log: a record of one discrete event, with context. Remember Topic 12: a good log line is structured JSON with a timestamp, a level, a message and a request_id. Logs tell you what exactly happened to one request. They are rich but expensive at high volume.
  • Trace: the complete end-to-end journey of one request as it moves through many services, broken into timed pieces called spans. Traces tell you where the time went and where the error started.

In a hospital: metrics are the temperature chart on the wall (a number every hour). Logs are the nurse's notes ("02:10 patient complained of chest pain, gave medicine X"). A trace is the CCTV footage following one patient from reception to the lab to the pharmacy, with a clock showing how long they waited at each counter.

The magic is the glue between them. In Topic 12 you learned to put a request_id in every log line. In tracing, the same idea is called a trace_id. If the same ID appears in the trace and in the logs, you can walk a path: the metric says "p99 latency spiked at 02:05", you open a slow trace from 02:05, you see which service was slow, and you jump from that span to the exact log lines with that trace ID.

Two more words: an alert is a rule that watches a metric and pages a human when it crosses a line ("p99 above 2s for 10 minutes"). An SLO (service level objective) is the promise the team makes about a signal, for example "99% of checkout requests finish under 500 ms". Alerts are usually built on SLOs, so you get woken only when users actually feel pain.

"Kuch gadbad hai" bolne se pehle tumhe words chahiye ki kya gadbad hai. Chaar signals kisi bhi backend service ki health batate hain (Google ki SRE book inhe "golden signals" kehti hai):

  • Latency: ek request mein kitna time laga, milliseconds (ms) mein. 1000 ms = 1 second.
  • Traffic (ya throughput): ek second mein kitni requests aa rahi hain.
  • Errors: kitni requests fail ho rahi hain, aam taur pe HTTP 5xx responses gine jaate hain (Topic 08). "Error rate 1%" matlab har 100 mein se 1 request fail.
  • Saturation: koi resource kitna bhara hua hai. CPU 95%, DB connection pool ke 20 mein se 20 use mein (Topic 03), disk 90%, memory container ki limit ke paas.

Inhe naapne ke liye teams teen tarah ka data use karti hain, jise observability ke teen pillars kehte hain. Observability ka simple matlab hai "bahar se dekh ke main apne system ke andar kya ho raha hai, kitna achhe se samajh sakta hoon".

  • Metric: time ke saath naapa gaya ek number. 02:05 pe cpu_percent = 73, 02:06 pe = 98. Metrics store karna sasta hai (sirf numbers), graphs aur alerts ke liye perfect. Yeh batate hain ki kuch gadbad hai aur kitni, lekin kyun nahi.
  • Log: ek event ka record, context ke saath. Topic 12 yaad karo: achhi log line structured JSON hoti hai jisme timestamp, level, message aur request_id hota hai. Logs batate hain ek request ke saath exactly kya hua. Rich hote hain lekin bahut volume pe mehenge.
  • Trace: ek request ka poora end-to-end safar jab woh kai services se guzarti hai, chhote timed hisson mein toota hua jinhe spans kehte hain. Traces batate hain time kahan gaya aur error kahan se shuru hua.

Hospital mein socho: metrics deewar pe laga temperature chart hai (har ghante ek number). Logs nurse ke notes hain ("02:10 patient ne seene mein dard bataya, dawai X di"). Trace woh CCTV footage hai jo ek patient ko reception se lab se pharmacy tak follow karti hai, aur ghadi dikhati hai ki har counter pe kitna wait kiya.

Asli jaadu in teeno ko jodne wale glue mein hai. Topic 12 mein tumne seekha ki har log line mein request_id daalo. Tracing mein wahi idea trace_id kehlata hai. Agar same ID trace mein bhi ho aur logs mein bhi, toh tum ek raasta chal sakte ho: metric kehta hai "02:05 pe p99 latency upar gayi", tum 02:05 ka ek slow trace kholte ho, dekhte ho kaunsi service slow thi, aur us span se seedha un log lines pe jump karte ho jinme wahi trace ID hai.

Do aur words: alert ek rule hai jo ek metric ko dekhta hai aur line cross hone pe insaan ko page karta hai ("p99 2s se upar 10 minute tak"). SLO (service level objective) woh promise hai jo team ek signal ke baare mein karti hai, jaise "99% checkout requests 500 ms ke andar khatam hongi". Alerts aam taur pe SLOs pe bante hain, taaki tumhe tabhi jagaya jaaye jab users ko sach mein takleef ho.

Level 2 The method: observe, hypothesise, test, fix, preventTareeka: observe, hypothesise, test, fix, prevent

This is the runbook you carry in your head for every scenario question. A runbook is a written, step-by-step guide for handling a known kind of problem. The picture below shows the whole loop, including the branches when a test says "no, not this one".

Yeh woh runbook hai jo har scenario question ke liye tumhare dimaag mein honi chahiye. Runbook ek likhi hui, step-by-step guide hoti hai kisi jaani-pehchaani problem ko handle karne ke liye. Neeche wali picture poora loop dikhati hai, un branches ke saath bhi jab koi test kehta hai "nahi, yeh wala cause nahi hai".

  1. Observe: scope the problem before touching anything. Ask five questions. What is wrong: slow, failing, or wrong data? Since when: find the exact minute on the graph. Who: all users, or one region, one endpoint, one customer, one app version, one server? How bad: 1% of requests or 100%? What changed around that minute: a deploy, a config flag, a migration, a traffic spike, a cron job (a scheduled task that runs at fixed times), or an outage at a provider you depend on?
  2. Hypothesise: list two to four suspects. Rank them by how likely they are and how cheap they are to check. At 2:07 you might write: (a) the 01:50 deploy added a new query, (b) the database is saturated, (c) the payment provider is slow.
  3. Test: one cheap check per suspect, designed to prove it wrong. Look at the DB CPU graph. Open one slow trace. Diff the deploy. Change one thing at a time, so that when the graph moves you know why it moved.
  4. Fix: mitigate first, then the real fix. Mitigation stops the bleeding: roll back, switch a feature flag off, scale out, kill a runaway query, fail over to a replica. The real fix (add the index, fix the code) goes through normal review and testing, usually in daylight.
  5. Prevent: make this class of bug impossible or at least loud. Write a postmortem, add the alert that would have caught it earlier, add a test, add a guardrail (for example, a CI check that flags migrations which drop indexes).

A very useful narrowing trick at the Observe step: if every endpoint is slow, suspect a shared resource (the database, the network, CPU, the connection pool, the cache). If only one endpoint is slow, suspect that code path or its specific query. This one question halves your search space.

Do not restart everything as step one. A restart destroys evidence: the memory that was leaking, the queries that were stuck, the locks being held. Sometimes a restart is the correct mitigation, but spend 30 seconds grabbing evidence first (a list of running queries, a heap snapshot, a thread dump) so you can still find the root cause afterwards.

The "what changed?" checklist that real on-call engineers run through: deploys of our service; deploys of services we call; config and feature-flag changes; database migrations and index changes; traffic volume and shape (a new big customer, a bot, a marketing email); scheduled jobs (backups, reports, batch imports) that run at that hour; data growth (a table crossing a size where the query plan changes); expiring things (TLS certificates, cache TTLs, API keys); and the status pages of cloud and third-party providers.

  1. Observe: kuch bhi chhoone se pehle problem ka scope samjho. Paanch sawaal poochho. Kya gadbad hai: slow, fail, ya galat data? Kab se: graph pe exact minute dhoondho. Kaun affected hai: saare users, ya ek region, ek endpoint, ek customer, ek app version, ek server? Kitna bura: 1% requests ya 100%? Us minute ke aas-paas kya badla: deploy, config flag, migration, traffic spike, koi cron job (fixed time pe chalne wala scheduled task), ya kisi provider ka outage jis pe tum depend karte ho?
  2. Hypothesise: do se chaar suspects ki list banao. Unhe rank karo ki kitne likely hain aur check karna kitna sasta hai. 2:07 pe tum likh sakte ho: (a) 01:50 ke deploy ne ek nayi query add ki, (b) database saturated hai, (c) payment provider slow hai.
  3. Test: har suspect ke liye ek sasta check, jo usse galat saabit karne ke liye bana ho. DB CPU graph dekho. Ek slow trace kholo. Deploy ka diff dekho. Ek time pe ek hi cheez badlo, taaki jab graph hile toh tumhe pata ho kyun hila.
  4. Fix: pehle mitigation, phir asli fix. Mitigation khoon behna rokta hai: rollback, feature flag off, scale out, bhaagti hui query ko kill karna, replica pe fail over. Asli fix (index add karna, code theek karna) normal review aur testing se jaata hai, aam taur pe din mein.
  5. Prevent: is type ke bug ko impossible banao, ya kam se kam itna loud ki turant pata chale. Postmortem likho, woh alert add karo jo ise pehle pakad leta, test add karo, guardrail lagao (jaise ek CI check jo index drop karne wali migrations ko flag kare).

Observe step pe ek bahut kaam ki trick: agar har endpoint slow hai, toh kisi shared resource pe shak karo (database, network, CPU, connection pool, cache). Agar sirf ek endpoint slow hai, toh us code path pe shak karo ya uski specific query pe. Yeh ek sawaal tumhari search ko aadha kar deta hai.

Pehle step mein sab kuch restart mat karo. Restart saboot mita deta hai: woh memory jo leak ho rahi thi, woh queries jo atki hui thi, woh locks jo pakde hue the. Kabhi-kabhi restart sahi mitigation hota hai, lekin pehle 30 second saboot uthane mein lagao (running queries ki list, heap snapshot, thread dump) taaki baad mein bhi root cause dhoondh sako.

"Kya badla?" checklist jo real on-call engineers chalaate hain: hamari service ke deploys; jin services ko hum call karte hain unke deploys; config aur feature-flag changes; database migrations aur index changes; traffic ka volume aur shape (naya bada customer, koi bot, marketing email); us ghante chalne wale scheduled jobs (backups, reports, batch imports); data growth (koi table ek aise size ko cross kare jahan query plan badal jaata hai); expire hone wali cheezein (TLS certificates, cache TTLs, API keys); aur cloud aur third-party providers ke status pages.

Level 3 Reading the instruments: percentiles, traces, slow query logs, heap snapshotsInstruments padhna: percentiles, traces, slow query logs, heap snapshots

3a. Percentiles: why the average lies

Latency is never one number; every request takes a different time. How do you summarise thousands of them? Most beginners use the average (add all, divide by count). Production engineers use percentiles.

A percentile answers: "sort all requests from fastest to slowest; how slow is the request at position X%?" p50 (the median) is the middle one: half the requests are faster. p99 means 99% of requests were at or below this time, and 1% were slower. p999 (say "p three nines") is the 99.9th percentile: only 1 request in 1000 is slower. The slow end of the list is called the tail, so p99 and p999 are "tail latency".

Worked example (made-up teaching numbers). Ten requests took, in ms: 40, 42, 45, 45, 48, 50, 52, 55, 60, 2000. Using the simple "nearest rank" method (position = percentile x count, rounded up):

  • Average = 2437 / 10 = about 244 ms.
  • p50 = position 0.5 x 10 = 5th value = 48 ms.
  • p90 = position 9 = 60 ms.
  • p99 = position 9.9, rounded up to 10 = 2000 ms.

Look at the average: 244 ms. Nine users saw 60 ms or less; one user waited two full seconds. The average describes nobody. It hides the one terrible experience and makes the nine good ones look worse. With only 10 requests p99 and the maximum are the same; with 1000 requests, p999 is roughly the single worst one, and with a million requests a day, p99 still means around ten thousand slow requests. That is why alerts are set on p99, not the average.

3a. Percentiles: average jhooth kyun bolta hai

Latency kabhi ek number nahi hoti; har request alag time leti hai. Hazaaron requests ko ek line mein kaise summarise karein? Zyada tar beginners average use karte hain (sab jodo, count se bhaag do). Production engineers percentiles use karte hain.

Percentile ka matlab: "saari requests ko sabse fast se sabse slow tak sort karo; X% position wali request kitni slow hai?" p50 (median) beech wali hai: aadhi requests usse fast hain. p99 matlab 99% requests is time ya usse kam mein khatam hui, aur 1% usse slow thi. p999 ("p three nines" bolo) 99.9th percentile hai: 1000 mein sirf 1 request usse slow hai. List ke slow wale end ko tail kehte hain, isliye p99 aur p999 ko "tail latency" kehte hain.

Worked example (samjhane ke liye banaaye gaye numbers). Das requests ne itna time liya, ms mein: 40, 42, 45, 45, 48, 50, 52, 55, 60, 2000. Simple "nearest rank" method se (position = percentile x count, upar round karo):

  • Average = 2437 / 10 = lagbhag 244 ms.
  • p50 = position 0.5 x 10 = 5th value = 48 ms.
  • p90 = position 9 = 60 ms.
  • p99 = position 9.9, upar round karke 10 = 2000 ms.

Average dekho: 244 ms. Nau users ne 60 ms ya usse kam dekha; ek user ne poore do second wait kiya. Average kisi ko bhi describe nahi karta. Woh ek bure experience ko chhupa deta hai aur nau achhe experiences ko bura dikhata hai. Sirf 10 requests mein p99 aur maximum same hain; 1000 requests mein p999 lagbhag sabse buri ek request hoti hai, aur din ki das lakh requests mein p99 ka matlab bhi lagbhag das hazaar slow requests hai. Isiliye alerts p99 pe lagte hain, average pe nahi.

3b. Distributed tracing: the waterfall

In a system with many services (Topic 07), one click on "Pay" might go: API gateway, then auth service, then order service, which calls Redis, Postgres and a payment provider. If checkout is slow, which one is guilty? Each service's own logs only show its own piece.

Distributed tracing solves this. When the request enters at the edge, it gets a trace ID, a unique random ID. Every service that handles it records one or more spans: a named, timed piece of work ("postgres SELECT, started at 55 ms, took 365 ms") plus the ID of its parent span. When a service calls the next one, it passes the trace ID along in an HTTP header; the standard one is called traceparent (the W3C Trace Context format). The tracing backend collects all spans with the same trace ID and draws a waterfall: one bar per span, positioned on a timeline, children indented under parents.

Today most teams use OpenTelemetry, an open standard with libraries that automatically create spans for HTTP calls, database queries and Redis commands, so you get most of the waterfall without writing code for each span.

3b. Distributed tracing: waterfall

Jis system mein kai services hain (Topic 07), wahan "Pay" pe ek click aise ja sakta hai: API gateway, phir auth service, phir order service, jo Redis, Postgres aur ek payment provider ko call karti hai. Agar checkout slow hai, toh gunehgaar kaun? Har service ke apne logs sirf uska apna hissa dikhate hain.

Distributed tracing isko solve karta hai. Jab request edge pe andar aati hai, usse ek trace ID milta hai, ek unique random ID. Har service jo usse handle karti hai, ek ya zyada spans record karti hai: kaam ka ek naam wala, timed tukda ("postgres SELECT, 55 ms pe shuru, 365 ms laga") aur uske parent span ki ID. Jab ek service agli ko call karti hai, woh trace ID ko ek HTTP header mein aage bhejti hai; standard header ka naam hai traceparent (W3C Trace Context format). Tracing backend same trace ID wale saare spans ikattha karta hai aur ek waterfall banata hai: har span ki ek bar, timeline pe sahi jagah, children apne parents ke neeche indent hue.

Aajkal zyada tar teams OpenTelemetry use karti hain, ek open standard jiski libraries HTTP calls, database queries aur Redis commands ke spans apne aap bana deti hain, toh har span ke liye code likhe bina tumhe zyada tar waterfall mil jaata hai.

3c. Reading a slow query log

A trace told you "the Postgres span is slow". Now you need the database's own evidence. Databases can write every query slower than a threshold to a slow query log. In MySQL you turn it on with slow_query_log = ON and set the threshold with long_query_time = 1 (seconds). In Postgres the equivalent setting is log_min_duration_statement = 1000 (milliseconds), and the pg_stat_statements extension keeps running totals for every distinct query. Here is a sample MySQL slow-log entry (made-up values):

3c. Slow query log padhna

Trace ne bataya "Postgres wala span slow hai". Ab tumhe database ka apna saboot chahiye. Databases har us query ko jo ek threshold se slow ho, ek slow query log mein likh sakte hain. MySQL mein isko slow_query_log = ON se on karte hain aur threshold long_query_time = 1 (seconds) se set karte hain. Postgres mein iske barabar setting hai log_min_duration_statement = 1000 (milliseconds), aur pg_stat_statements extension har alag query ka running total rakhta hai. Yeh ek sample MySQL slow-log entry hai (banaaye gaye values):

# Time: 2026-09-28T02:05:41.118Z
# User@Host: app[app] @ [10.0.3.12]
# Query_time: 4.812  Lock_time: 0.000  Rows_sent: 20  Rows_examined: 2400311
SELECT * FROM appointments
 WHERE dealer_id = 42 AND status = 'booked'
 ORDER BY slot_time LIMIT 20;

How to read it, like a blood report:

  • Query_time 4.8 s: very slow for a page load.
  • Lock_time 0.000: it was not waiting for locks held by other transactions (Topic 02). It was busy doing work. If Lock_time were high, you would suspect lock contention instead.
  • Rows_examined 2.4 million vs Rows_sent 20: the database read over a hundred thousand rows for every row it returned. That ratio is the classic fingerprint of a missing or unusable index.

Next you run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on it (Topic 01). In Postgres you would see Seq Scan on appointments with a huge Rows Removed by Filter. The fix, following the left-prefix rule, is a composite index that matches both the filter and the sort. In Postgres, build it with CONCURRENTLY so it does not block writes on a live table:

Isse blood report ki tarah kaise padhein:

  • Query_time 4.8 s: ek page load ke liye bahut slow.
  • Lock_time 0.000: yeh doosre transactions ke locks ka wait nahi kar rahi thi (Topic 02). Yeh kaam karne mein busy thi. Agar Lock_time zyada hota, toh tum lock contention pe shak karte.
  • Rows_examined 2.4 million vs Rows_sent 20: database ne har ek returned row ke liye ek lakh se zyada rows padhi. Yeh ratio missing ya kaam na aane wale index ka classic nishaan hai.

Agla step: us pe EXPLAIN ANALYZE chalao (Topic 01). Postgres mein tumhe Seq Scan on appointments dikhega aur bahut bada Rows Removed by Filter. Fix, left-prefix rule ke hisaab se, ek composite index hai jo filter aur sort dono se match kare. Postgres mein isse CONCURRENTLY ke saath banao taaki live table pe writes block na hon:

-- what is running right now, longest first (Postgres)
SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS running_for, state, wait_event_type,
       left(query, 80) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY running_for DESC;

-- which queries cost the most in total (needs pg_stat_statements, PG 13+ column names)
SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time) AS total_ms, round(mean_exec_time) AS mean_ms,
       left(query, 80) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- the fix, built without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_appt_dealer_status_slot
  ON appointments (dealer_id, status, slot_time);

Sort by total time, not just by slowest. A 5 ms query that runs 10,000 times a second burns far more database CPU than one 5-second report that runs once an hour. pg_stat_statements ordered by total_exec_time finds the first kind; the slow log alone mostly finds the second.

3d. Memory leaks and heap snapshots

In Node.js, objects you create live in an area of memory called the heap. The garbage collector (GC) regularly frees objects that nothing refers to any more. A healthy service's memory graph looks like a saw: it climbs as requests create objects, then drops when GC runs, back to roughly the same floor. A memory leak is when something keeps a reference to objects you no longer need, so GC cannot free them. The floor of the saw rises, hour after hour, until the container hits its memory limit and is killed (OOM, "out of memory"), and the orchestrator restarts it (Topic 11). The tell-tale sign is a graph that climbs slowly and drops to zero at every restart.

To find what is leaking, you take heap snapshots: a full photograph of every object on the heap, what type it is, how much memory it holds, and who is holding a reference to it (its retainers). The standard technique is the three-snapshot comparison: take one after warm-up, let traffic run for a while, take a second, wait, take a third. Open them in Chrome DevTools (Memory tab) and use the Comparison view. Objects that are created and freed cancel out; the object type whose count keeps growing between every snapshot is your leak, and the retainer path tells you which variable is holding on to it.

Ways to capture a snapshot: start Node with --inspect and connect DevTools; call v8.writeHeapSnapshot() from code; or start Node with --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2 and send that signal to the running process.

Total time se sort karo, sirf sabse slow se nahi. Ek 5 ms ki query jo ek second mein 10,000 baar chalti hai, woh ghante mein ek baar chalne wali 5-second ki report se kahin zyada database CPU khaati hai. total_exec_time se sorted pg_stat_statements pehli type ko pakadta hai; akela slow log zyada tar doosri type ko.

3d. Memory leaks aur heap snapshots

Node.js mein tum jo objects banate ho woh memory ke ek hisse mein rehte hain jise heap kehte hain. Garbage collector (GC) regularly un objects ko free karta hai jinhe ab koi refer nahi karta. Ek healthy service ka memory graph aari (saw) jaisa dikhta hai: requests objects banati hain toh upar jaata hai, GC chalta hai toh neeche aata hai, lagbhag usi floor pe. Memory leak tab hota hai jab koi cheez un objects ka reference pakde rehti hai jinki ab zaroorat nahi, isliye GC unhe free nahi kar paata. Aari ka floor ghante dar ghante upar uthta hai, jab tak container apni memory limit tak na pahunch jaaye aur kill ho jaaye (OOM, "out of memory"), aur orchestrator usse restart kar de (Topic 11). Pehchaan: graph dheere-dheere upar chadhta hai aur har restart pe zero pe gir jaata hai.

Kya leak ho raha hai yeh dhoondhne ke liye tum heap snapshots lete ho: heap ke har object ki poori photo, woh kis type ka hai, kitni memory pakde hai, aur usse kaun reference kar raha hai (uske retainers). Standard technique hai three-snapshot comparison: warm-up ke baad ek lo, thodi der traffic chalne do, doosra lo, ruko, teesra lo. Inhe Chrome DevTools (Memory tab) mein kholo aur Comparison view use karo. Jo objects bante aur free hote hain woh cancel ho jaate hain; jis object type ka count har snapshot ke beech badhta hi jaata hai, wahi tumhara leak hai, aur retainer path batata hai kaunsa variable usse pakde baitha hai.

Snapshot lene ke tareeke: Node ko --inspect ke saath start karo aur DevTools connect karo; code se v8.writeHeapSnapshot() call karo; ya Node ko --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2 ke saath start karo aur chalte process ko woh signal bhejo.

The three most common leak patterns in Node.js services, with their fixes:

Node.js services mein teen sabse common leak patterns, fixes ke saath:

// 1. Cache with no eviction: a module-level Map lives forever (Topic 04)
const vehicleCache = new Map();
app.get('/vehicles/:vin', async (req, res) => {
  if (!vehicleCache.has(req.params.vin)) {
    vehicleCache.set(req.params.vin, await db.getVehicle(req.params.vin)); // grows forever
  }
  res.json(vehicleCache.get(req.params.vin));
});
// Fix: a bounded LRU cache with a max size and TTL, or Redis.

// 2. Event listener added per request, never removed
app.get('/price-stream', (req, res) => {
  const onPrice = (p) => res.write(JSON.stringify(p));
  priceBus.on('update', onPrice);                          // one more listener per request
  req.on('close', () => priceBus.off('update', onPrice));  // Fix: remove it on close
});

// 3. Timers and closures that capture big objects
const timer = setInterval(() => report(bigRequestObject), 1000);
// Fix: clearInterval(timer) when done; do not capture whole req/res objects.

A clue for pattern 2: Node prints MaxListenersExceededWarning when more than 10 listeners are attached to one event. Treat that warning as a leak alarm, not noise.

Pattern 2 ka ek clue: jab ek event pe 10 se zyada listeners lag jaate hain, Node MaxListenersExceededWarning print karta hai. Is warning ko noise mat samjho, leak ka alarm samjho.

Level 4 Senior nuances: the bugs that only live in productionSenior nuances: woh bugs jo sirf production mein rehte hain

Why do some bugs never appear on your laptop? Because production has three things your laptop does not: real concurrency (many requests at the same millisecond), real data (big, messy, old), and real infrastructure (many instances, networks, providers). Each earlier topic gives you a family of production-only bugs:

  • Race conditions (Topic 03): two requests read the same balance or the same last appointment slot, both write. On your laptop you send one request at a time, so it never happens. To catch it in production, log with precise timestamps and the request ID at both write points; when two log lines for the same record overlap in time, you have your proof. To reproduce it, run a load test at higher concurrency than production. The fix is from Topics 02 and 03: an atomic update, a row lock, an optimistic version check, or a unique constraint.
  • "1% of requests fail and nobody can reproduce it": 1% is a shape, not a random number. It is often one bad instance out of many (one server with a full disk or a stale config), one customer whose data is unusual, one app version, one region, or one input format. Group the error logs by every dimension you have until one lights up.
  • Connection pool exhaustion (Topics 03 and 09): latency goes up, but database CPU is low. Requests are not slow in the database; they are queueing inside your app, waiting for a free connection. Often caused by a long transaction or a slow external call made while holding a connection (Topic 02).
  • Cache hit rate drop (Topic 04): if Redis restarts or a key format changes in a deploy, every read falls through to the database at once. The database is fine; it simply received many times its normal load.
  • Queue lag (Topic 06): users say "my confirmation email never came". The API is healthy; the consumers are behind, or a poison-pill message is being retried forever. Check consumer lag and the dead letter queue.
  • "The data disappeared": almost always it did not. It was soft-deleted (deleted_at set, Topic 09), a filter bug is hiding it, a write that failed and rolled back was never really saved (Topic 02), or a race overwrote it (lost update). Check audit logs before saying the word "lost".
  • "Every dashboard is green but users say it is slow": your server measures from the moment a request reaches it. The user's wait also includes DNS lookup, TLS handshake, the CDN, the load balancer queue, the network, and the browser rendering JavaScript. Measure from the client (real user monitoring), and look at p99 and p999, not averages.

Tail latency amplification. If one page load calls 10 backend services in parallel and must wait for all of them, and each service is slow 1% of the time, the chance that at least one is slow is 1 - 0.9910, about 9.6%. So a "1% problem" in each service becomes roughly a "1 in 10 page loads" problem for users. This is why senior engineers care so much about p99 in fan-out systems.

Observability costs money. Metrics are cheap only if their labels have low cardinality (Topic 01's word again: number of distinct values). Putting user_id as a metric label creates one time series per user and can explode your bill. Logs at DEBUG level for every request are expensive; traces are usually sampled (you keep, say, a small fraction of normal traces but every error and every slow one).

Blameless postmortems. After every serious incident, the team writes a postmortem: a timeline, the user impact, the root cause, contributing factors, and action items with an owner and a date. "Blameless" means it asks why the system allowed a mistake, never who made it. "Engineer ran the wrong migration" is not a root cause; "our pipeline let a migration that drops an index reach production without review" is. People who fear blame hide information, and hidden information causes the next outage.

Kuch bugs tumhare laptop pe kabhi kyun nahi aate? Kyunki production ke paas teen cheezein hain jo laptop ke paas nahi: real concurrency (ek hi millisecond pe bahut saari requests), real data (bada, bikhra hua, purana), aur real infrastructure (kai instances, networks, providers). Har pichla topic tumhe production-only bugs ki ek family deta hai:

  • Race conditions (Topic 03): do requests ek hi balance ya ek hi aakhri appointment slot padhti hain, dono likhti hain. Laptop pe tum ek time pe ek request bhejte ho, isliye yeh kabhi nahi hota. Production mein pakadne ke liye, dono write points pe precise timestamps aur request ID ke saath log karo; jab same record ki do log lines time mein overlap karein, wahi tumhara saboot hai. Reproduce karne ke liye production se zyada concurrency pe load test chalao. Fix Topics 02 aur 03 se aata hai: atomic update, row lock, optimistic version check, ya unique constraint.
  • "1% requests fail hoti hain aur koi reproduce nahi kar paata": 1% ek shape hai, random number nahi. Aksar yeh kai mein se ek kharab instance hota hai (ek server jiski disk full hai ya config purani hai), ek customer jiska data alag hai, ek app version, ek region, ya ek input format. Error logs ko har dimension se group karo jab tak ek chamak na jaaye.
  • Connection pool exhaustion (Topics 03 aur 09): latency upar jaati hai, lekin database CPU kam hai. Requests database mein slow nahi hain; woh tumhari app ke andar line mein khadi hain, free connection ka wait kar rahi hain. Aksar iski wajah hoti hai lamba transaction ya connection pakde-pakde kiya gaya slow external call (Topic 02).
  • Cache hit rate drop (Topic 04): agar Redis restart ho ya kisi deploy mein key ka format badal jaaye, toh har read ek saath database pe gir jaati hai. Database theek hai; bas usse apne normal load se kai guna load mil gaya.
  • Queue lag (Topic 06): users kehte hain "mera confirmation email kabhi aaya hi nahi". API healthy hai; consumers peeche hain, ya koi poison-pill message hamesha ke liye retry ho raha hai. Consumer lag aur dead letter queue check karo.
  • "Data gayab ho gaya": lagbhag hamesha nahi hua. Woh soft-delete hua (deleted_at set, Topic 09), koi filter bug usse chhupa raha hai, koi write jo fail hoke rollback hua kabhi sach mein save hi nahi hua (Topic 02), ya kisi race ne usse overwrite kar diya (lost update). "Lost" shabd bolne se pehle audit logs check karo.
  • "Har dashboard green hai lekin users kehte hain slow hai": tumhara server us pal se naapta hai jab request usse milti hai. User ke wait mein DNS lookup, TLS handshake, CDN, load balancer ki line, network, aur browser ka JavaScript render karna bhi shaamil hai. Client side se naapo (real user monitoring), aur p99 aur p999 dekho, average nahi.

Tail latency amplification. Agar ek page load 10 backend services ko parallel mein call karta hai aur sabka wait karna padta hai, aur har service 1% time slow hoti hai, toh kam se kam ek ke slow hone ka chance hai 1 - 0.9910, lagbhag 9.6%. Matlab har service ki "1% problem" users ke liye lagbhag "10 mein se 1 page load" ki problem ban jaati hai. Isiliye fan-out systems mein senior engineers p99 ki itni parwaah karte hain.

Observability paisa khaati hai. Metrics tabhi saste hain jab unke labels ki cardinality kam ho (Topic 01 ka word phir se: kitni alag values hain). user_id ko metric label banaoge toh har user ki ek alag time series banegi aur bill phat sakta hai. Har request ke DEBUG level logs mehenge hain; traces aam taur pe sampled hote hain (normal traces ka chhota hissa rakhte ho, lekin har error aur har slow trace rakhte ho).

Blameless postmortems. Har serious incident ke baad team ek postmortem likhti hai: timeline, users pe impact, root cause, contributing factors, aur action items jinka ek owner aur ek date ho. "Blameless" ka matlab hai yeh poochhta hai system ne galti hone kyun di, kabhi nahi ki kisne ki. "Engineer ne galat migration chala di" root cause nahi hai; "hamari pipeline ne index drop karne wali migration ko bina review production tak jaane diya" root cause hai. Jo log blame se darte hain woh information chhupaate hain, aur chhupi hui information agla outage laati hai.

SymptomSymptom First suspectPehla shak First checkPehla check
Everything slower since a specific minuteEk khaas minute se sab kuch slow A change: deploy, config, migrationKoi change: deploy, config, migration Deploy and change log for that minuteUs minute ka deploy aur change log
Latency up, DB CPU normalLatency upar, DB CPU normal Connection pool exhausted, slow external APIConnection pool khatam, slow external API Pool wait time, traces of slow requestsPool wait time, slow requests ke traces
DB CPU 100%DB CPU 100% Runaway or unindexed query, cache downBhaagti ya bina index ki query, cache down pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_statements, EXPLAIN
Memory climbs, restarts every few hoursMemory chadhti hai, har kuch ghante restart Memory leakMemory leak Three heap snapshots, compareTeen heap snapshots, compare
Steady 1% errorsLagataar 1% errors One bad instance, tenant, input or versionEk kharab instance, tenant, input ya version Group error logs by every dimensionError logs ko har dimension se group karo
Green dashboards, users say slowDashboards green, users kehte slow Outside the service: DNS, CDN, network, frontendService ke bahar: DNS, CDN, network, frontend Client-side timing, p99/p999 by regionClient-side timing, region-wise p99/p999

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

On-call / page
The engineer responsible for production this week; a page is the urgent alert that wakes them.Is hafte production ka zimmedaar engineer; page woh urgent alert hai jo usse jagaata hai.
Incident
Anything in production that is hurting users right now and needs a response.Production mein koi bhi cheez jo abhi users ko nuksaan pahuncha rahi hai aur jis pe response chahiye.
Mitigation vs root cause
Mitigation stops the pain fast (rollback, flag off); root cause is the real reason, fixed properly later.Mitigation dard jaldi rokta hai (rollback, flag off); root cause asli wajah hai, jo baad mein theek se fix hoti hai.
Golden signals
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation: the four numbers that describe a service's health.Latency, traffic, errors, saturation: chaar numbers jo service ki health batate hain.
Metric
A number measured over time; cheap, great for graphs and alerts.Time ke saath naapa gaya number; sasta, graphs aur alerts ke liye badhiya.
Log
A record of one event with context (timestamp, level, request ID).Ek event ka record context ke saath (timestamp, level, request ID).
Trace / span
A trace is one request's end-to-end journey; a span is one timed step in it, with a parent.Trace ek request ka end-to-end safar hai; span usme ek timed step hai, jiska ek parent hota hai.
Trace ID / traceparent
The unique ID shared by all spans of one request; passed between services in the traceparent header.Ek request ke saare spans ki common unique ID; services ke beech traceparent header mein jaati hai.
OpenTelemetry
Open standard and libraries for producing traces, metrics and logs automatically.Traces, metrics aur logs apne aap banane ke liye open standard aur libraries.
Percentile (p50, p99, p999)
Sort all latencies; pX is the value at X% of the way. p99: 99% at or below it.Saari latencies sort karo; pX woh value hai jo X% position pe hai. p99: 99% usse kam ya barabar.
Tail latency
The slow end of the distribution (p99, p999), where the unhappy users are.Distribution ka slow end (p99, p999), jahan naaraz users hote hain.
SLO
A target the team promises, e.g. 99% of requests under 500 ms.Team ka promise kiya hua target, jaise 99% requests 500 ms se kam mein.
Slow query log
The database's record of every query slower than a threshold, with time and rows examined.Database ka record har us query ka jo threshold se slow ho, time aur rows examined ke saath.
Heap / GC
Heap is where JavaScript objects live; the garbage collector frees objects nobody references.Heap woh jagah hai jahan JavaScript objects rehte hain; garbage collector un objects ko free karta hai jinhe koi refer nahi karta.
Heap snapshot / retainer
A photo of every object in memory; a retainer is whatever holds a reference and keeps it alive.Memory ke har object ki photo; retainer woh cheez hai jo reference pakad ke usse zinda rakhti hai.
OOM
Out of memory: the process exceeded its limit and was killed.Out of memory: process ne apni limit cross ki aur kill ho gaya.
Real user monitoring (RUM)
Timing measured in the user's browser or app, including network and rendering.User ke browser ya app mein naapa gaya time, network aur rendering samet.
Audit log
An append-only record of who changed what and when; the first place to look when data "vanishes".Kisne kya kab badla ka append-only record; data "gayab" ho toh sabse pehle yahin dekho.
Postmortem (blameless)
A written review after an incident: timeline, impact, root cause, action items; blames systems, not people.Incident ke baad likha review: timeline, impact, root cause, action items; systems ko dekhta hai, logon ko blame nahi karta.

Interview questionsInterview ke sawaal

01 Your API response times doubled overnight. Walk me through how you would debug it.Tumhari API ke response times raaton-raat double ho gaye. Batao tum isse kaise debug karoge.
What they're really testing: whether you narrow down systematically (recent deployments, DB slow query log, CPU/memory/connections, external API calls, cache hit rate) instead of guessing or immediately adding servers.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum systematically narrow karte ho (recent deployments, DB slow query log, CPU/memory/connections, external API calls, cache hit rate), ya andaaza lagaate ho aur turant servers add kar dete ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

First I'd scope it before touching anything: which endpoints, which percentile, and the exact minute it started, because "overnight" usually means something changed at a specific time. So my first check is the change log around that minute: deploys, config flags, migrations and scheduled jobs. If nothing changed on our side, I'd ask whether every endpoint is slower or just one. If everything is slower, it's a shared resource, so I'd look at the database slow query log, and CPU, memory and connection-pool usage. If it's one endpoint, I'd open a slow trace for it and see which span grew: a query, an external API call, or a cache miss. I'd also check the cache hit rate, because a drop there sends every read to the database. Once I find it, I mitigate first, for example roll back, then fix the root cause and add an alert that would have caught it earlier.

Kuch bhi chhoone se pehle main scope samjhunga: kaunse endpoints, kaunsa percentile, aur exact kis minute se shuru hua, kyunki "raaton-raat" ka matlab aksar hota hai ki kisi khaas time pe kuch badla. Toh mera pehla check us minute ke aas-paas ka change log hai: deploys, config flags, migrations aur scheduled jobs. Agar hamari taraf kuch nahi badla, toh main poochhunga ki har endpoint slow hai ya sirf ek. Agar sab slow hai, toh koi shared resource hai, toh main database slow query log, aur CPU, memory aur connection-pool usage dekhunga. Agar ek endpoint hai, toh main uska ek slow trace kholunga aur dekhunga kaunsa span bada hua: query, external API call, ya cache miss. Main cache hit rate bhi check karunga, kyunki wahan drop hone se har read database pe jaati hai. Mil jaane pe pehle mitigate karunga, jaise rollback, phir root cause fix karunga aur ek alert add karunga jo ise pehle pakad leta.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Compare p50 and p99. If both doubled, the slowdown is systemic (every request pays it: a slower query plan, a slower dependency). If only p99 jumped, it's contention: lock waits, pool waits, GC pauses. A subtle "nothing changed" cause is data growth: a table crosses a size where the planner switches from an index scan to a sequential scan, or the index no longer fits in memory. Another is an overnight batch job, backup or vacuum competing for the same database. The pool signature is worth naming: latency up but database CPU flat means requests are waiting for connections, not running queries.

p50 aur p99 ko compare karo. Agar dono double hue, toh slowdown systemic hai (har request usse bhugat rahi hai: slow query plan, slow dependency). Agar sirf p99 uchhla, toh contention hai: lock waits, pool waits, GC pauses. Ek chhupa hua "kuch nahi badla" wala cause hai data growth: koi table ek aise size ko cross karta hai jahan planner index scan se sequential scan pe switch kar leta hai, ya index memory mein fit hona band ho jaata hai. Ek aur cause hai raat ka batch job, backup ya vacuum jo usi database ke liye ladta hai. Pool wala nishaan batana achha hai: latency upar lekin database CPU flat matlab requests connections ka wait kar rahi hain, queries nahi chala rahi.

Common mistake: jumping straight to "add more servers" or "add a cache". Scaling can hide a missing index for a while, costs money, and you still don't know what changed.
Galti mat karna: seedha "aur servers add karo" ya "cache laga do" pe mat koodna. Scaling thodi der ke liye missing index chhupa sakti hai, paisa khaati hai, aur tumhe ab bhi pata nahi ki kya badla.
02 Your database CPU is at 100%. What are the first five things you check?Tumhara database CPU 100% pe hai. Sabse pehle kaunsi paanch cheezein check karoge?
What they're really testing: a fixed, ordered checklist: running queries, slow query log, EXPLAIN on the top queries, missing indexes on recently added queries, recent schema changes, and only then lock contention.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ek fixed, ordered checklist: running queries, slow query log, top queries pe EXPLAIN, recently add hui queries pe missing indexes, recent schema changes, aur uske baad hi lock contention.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

One: what's running right now, using pg_stat_activity or MySQL's SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST, because often it's one runaway query or hundreds of copies of the same one. Two: the slow query log, or pg_stat_statements sorted by total time, since a fast query run thousands of times a second can cost more than one slow report. Three: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the top two or three, looking for sequential scans on big tables and rows examined far above rows returned. Four: missing indexes on queries added recently, because a new feature often ships a query nobody indexed. Five: recent schema changes or migrations, such as a dropped index or stale statistics. After that I'd check lock contention and whether traffic or cache misses changed. To mitigate, I'd cancel the runaway query, roll back the deploy, or move reads to a replica.

Ek: abhi kya chal raha hai, pg_stat_activity ya MySQL ke SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST se, kyunki aksar ek bhaagti hui query hoti hai ya ek hi query ki sainkdon copies. Do: slow query log, ya total time se sorted pg_stat_statements, kyunki ek fast query jo second mein hazaaron baar chale woh ek slow report se zyada mehengi pad sakti hai. Teen: top do-teen pe EXPLAIN ANALYZE, bade tables pe sequential scans aur returned rows se kahin zyada examined rows dhoondhte hue. Chaar: recently add hui queries pe missing indexes, kyunki naya feature aksar aisi query ship karta hai jiska kisi ne index nahi banaya. Paanch: recent schema changes ya migrations, jaise drop hua index ya purane statistics. Uske baad main lock contention check karunga aur dekhunga ki traffic ya cache misses badle ya nahi. Mitigate karne ke liye bhaagti query cancel karunga, deploy rollback karunga, ya reads ko replica pe bhejunga.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

In Postgres, pg_cancel_backend(pid) stops a query politely; pg_terminate_backend(pid) kills the connection. Stale statistics can make the planner pick a bad plan after a big data load; running ANALYZE refreshes them. Locks usually show up as waiting, not CPU, which is why they come after the first five; wait_event_type = 'Lock' in pg_stat_activity reveals them, and long transactions from Topic 02 are the usual holders. Also check if the cache hit rate fell: a Redis restart can multiply database reads with zero code change. Build the fix index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so you don't lock the table while it's already struggling.

Postgres mein pg_cancel_backend(pid) query ko politely rokta hai; pg_terminate_backend(pid) connection hi kill kar deta hai. Purane statistics ki wajah se bade data load ke baad planner bura plan chun sakta hai; ANALYZE chalane se woh refresh hote hain. Locks aam taur pe waiting ke roop mein dikhte hain, CPU ke roop mein nahi, isiliye woh pehli paanch ke baad aate hain; pg_stat_activity mein wait_event_type = 'Lock' unhe dikhata hai, aur Topic 02 ke lambe transactions aam taur pe unhe pakde hote hain. Yeh bhi check karo ki cache hit rate gira ya nahi: Redis restart bina code change ke database reads ko kai guna kar sakta hai. Fix wala index CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY se banao taaki pehle se pareshaan table ko lock na karo.

Common mistake: upgrading to a bigger database instance or restarting it first. You pay more for a missing index, a restart throws away the warm memory cache, and the same query comes straight back.
Galti mat karna: sabse pehle bada database instance lena ya restart karna. Missing index ke liye zyada paisa doge, restart garam memory cache phenk deta hai, aur wahi query turant wapas aa jaati hai.
03 How would you find a memory leak in a production Node.js service?Production Node.js service mein memory leak kaise dhoondhoge?
What they're really testing: that you know the heap snapshot technique (snapshots at intervals, compare growing object counts) and the usual culprits: event listeners never removed, closures holding references, caches without eviction.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum heap snapshot technique jaante ho (intervals pe snapshots, badhte object counts compare karna) aur aam culprits bhi: kabhi remove na hone wale event listeners, references pakde closures, bina eviction ke caches.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

First I'd confirm it's a leak and not just high usage: the memory graph should show a sawtooth whose floor keeps rising after every garbage collection, usually ending in an OOM kill and restart. Then I'd take one instance out of the load balancer and take heap snapshots at intervals: one after warm-up, another after some traffic, a third later. In Chrome DevTools' comparison view, objects that come and go cancel out; the object type whose count grows every time is the leak, and its retainer path shows which variable holds it. In my experience the usual culprits are event listeners added per request and never removed, module-level Maps used as caches with no eviction, closures or timers capturing large objects. The fix is to remove the listener on close, use a bounded LRU cache or Redis, clear timers, then add an alert on memory growth.

Pehle main confirm karunga ki yeh leak hai, sirf zyada usage nahi: memory graph mein aari dikhni chahiye jiska floor har garbage collection ke baad upar uthta rahe, aur aam taur pe OOM kill aur restart pe khatam ho. Phir main ek instance ko load balancer se bahar nikaalunga aur intervals pe heap snapshots lunga: ek warm-up ke baad, doosra thode traffic ke baad, teesra baad mein.
