Chrome DevTools ke comparison view mein aane-jaane wale objects cancel ho jaate hain; jis object type ka count har baar badhta hai wahi leak hai, aur uska retainer path dikhata hai kaunsa variable usse pakde hai. Aam culprits hote hain har request pe add hone wale aur kabhi remove na hone wale event listeners, cache ki tarah use hone wale module-level Maps jinka koi eviction nahi, bade objects pakadne wale closures ya timers. Fix hai close pe listener hatana, bounded LRU cache ya Redis use karna, timers clear karna, phir memory growth pe alert lagana.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Taking a snapshot pauses the process and can need roughly as much extra memory as the heap itself, which is why you pull the instance out of rotation first (a readiness check from Topic 11 helps). Capture methods: --inspect with DevTools, v8.writeHeapSnapshot(), or --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2. Check process.memoryUsage(): if rss grows but heapUsed stays flat, the leak is outside the JS heap, for example in Buffers or a native module, and heap snapshots won't show it. A MaxListenersExceededWarning in the logs is a strong clue for listener leaks. Restarting nightly is a mitigation, not a fix.

Snapshot lene se process ruk jaata hai aur lagbhag heap jitni extra memory chahiye ho sakti hai, isiliye pehle instance ko rotation se bahar karte ho (Topic 11 ka readiness check kaam aata hai). Capture ke tareeke: DevTools ke saath --inspect, v8.writeHeapSnapshot(), ya --heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2. process.memoryUsage() check karo: agar rss badhta hai lekin heapUsed flat hai, toh leak JS heap ke bahar hai, jaise Buffers ya kisi native module mein, aur heap snapshots usse nahi dikhayenge. Logs mein MaxListenersExceededWarning listener leak ka pakka clue hai. Har raat restart karna mitigation hai, fix nahi.

Common mistake: saying "I'd increase the memory limit" or "restart it every night" as the answer. That only makes the crash less frequent; the leak is still there.
Galti mat karna: jawab mein "memory limit badha dunga" ya "har raat restart kar dunga" bolna. Isse crash kam baar hota hai; leak wahin ka wahin hai.
04 What is distributed tracing and how does it help debug production issues?Distributed tracing kya hai aur production issues debug karne mein kaise madad karta hai?
What they're really testing: that a trace ID propagates through every service, giving you the full journey of a request: which service was slow and where an error originated.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki ek trace ID har service se hokar aage jaati hai, jisse request ka poora safar milta hai: kaunsi service slow thi aur error kahan se shuru hua.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Distributed tracing follows one request across every service it touches. At the edge, the request gets a unique trace ID. Each service records spans, which are timed steps like "Postgres query, 365 ms", each with a parent, and passes the trace ID to the next call in a header, usually the W3C traceparent header. A tracing backend stitches all spans with that ID into a waterfall. It exists because in microservices each service's logs only show its own slice. For example, a checkout takes 480 ms; the waterfall shows 365 ms in one Postgres span, so I go straight to that query instead of guessing between five services. It also shows where an error really started: the first failing span deep in the chain, not the gateway that returned 500. The trade-off is instrumentation effort, which OpenTelemetry mostly automates, and storage cost, which is why traces are sampled.

Distributed tracing ek request ko har us service mein follow karta hai jise woh chhooti hai. Edge pe request ko ek unique trace ID milti hai. Har service spans record karti hai, yaani timed steps jaise "Postgres query, 365 ms", har ek ka ek parent, aur trace ID ko agle call mein ek header mein aage bhejti hai, aam taur pe W3C traceparent header. Tracing backend us ID wale saare spans ko jod ke waterfall banata hai. Yeh isliye hai kyunki microservices mein har service ke logs sirf uska apna hissa dikhate hain. Jaise, checkout 480 ms leta hai; waterfall dikhata hai 365 ms ek Postgres span mein gaye, toh main paanch services ke beech andaaza lagaaye bina seedha us query pe jaata hoon. Yeh bhi dikhata hai ki error asal mein kahan shuru hua: chain mein gehraai mein pehla fail hua span, woh gateway nahi jisne 500 lautaaya. Trade-off hai instrumentation ki mehnat, jo OpenTelemetry zyada tar automate kar deta hai, aur storage cost, isiliye traces sample kiye jaate hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Head-based sampling decides at the start (keep, say, a small percentage), which is cheap but may drop the one slow trace you need. Tail-based sampling buffers spans and decides at the end, keeping every error and every slow trace, at the cost of more memory in the collector. Propagation must cross async hops too: put the trace context in message headers when publishing to a queue (Topic 06), or the trace breaks into orphans at the queue. Finally, write the trace ID into every log line (Topic 12) so one click takes you from a slow span to its logs.

Head-based sampling shuru mein decide karta hai (jaise chhota percentage rakho), jo sasta hai lekin shayad wahi ek slow trace gira de jo tumhe chahiye. Tail-based sampling spans ko buffer karke end mein decide karta hai, har error aur har slow trace rakhta hai, lekin collector mein zyada memory lagti hai. Propagation async hops ke paar bhi jaana chahiye: queue pe publish karte waqt trace context message headers mein daalo (Topic 06), warna queue pe trace toot ke orphans ban jaata hai. Aakhir mein, trace ID har log line mein likho (Topic 12) taaki ek click mein slow span se uske logs tak pahunch jao.

Common mistake: treating tracing as a replacement for logs and metrics, or forgetting to propagate context through queues and background jobs so traces silently break.
Galti mat karna: tracing ko logs aur metrics ka replacement samajhna, ya queues aur background jobs mein context aage bhejna bhool jaana jisse traces chupchaap toot jaate hain.
05 What is the difference between a metric, a log, and a trace?Metric, log aur trace mein kya farak hai?
What they're really testing: crisp definitions (numeric value over time; discrete event with context; end-to-end journey of one request) and knowing which one to reach for when.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: saaf definitions (time ke saath numeric value; context ke saath ek event; ek request ka end-to-end safar) aur yeh ki kab kaunsa use karna hai.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A metric is a numeric value measured over time, like p99 latency per minute or CPU percent. It's cheap and aggregated, so it's what I alert on; it tells me something is wrong and how much, not why. A log is a discrete event with context: a structured JSON line with timestamp, level, message and request ID, like "payment timeout for order 123". It tells me exactly what happened to one request, but it's expensive at volume. A trace is the end-to-end journey of one request across services, made of timed spans, and it tells me where the time went. In practice I use them in sequence: the metric alert fires, I open a slow trace from that window to find the guilty service, then I jump to that trace ID's logs to see the exact error. They're linked by the shared ID.

Metric ek numeric value hai jo time ke saath naapi jaati hai, jaise har minute ki p99 latency ya CPU percent. Sasta aur aggregated hota hai, isliye main isi pe alert lagata hoon; yeh batata hai ki kuch gadbad hai aur kitni, kyun nahi. Log context ke saath ek event hai: structured JSON line jisme timestamp, level, message aur request ID ho, jaise "order 123 ka payment timeout". Yeh batata hai ki ek request ke saath exactly kya hua, lekin volume pe mehenga hai. Trace ek request ka services ke paar end-to-end safar hai, timed spans se bana, aur yeh batata hai time kahan gaya. Practice mein main inhe sequence mein use karta hoon: metric alert bajta hai, main us time ka ek slow trace kholta hoon aur gunehgaar service dhoondhta hoon, phir us trace ID ke logs pe jump karke exact error dekhta hoon. Yeh common ID se jude hote hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Cost and cardinality decide the design. Metrics stay cheap only with low-cardinality labels like endpoint, status code and region; adding user_id or order_id as a label creates a time series per value and can explode storage. High-cardinality detail belongs in logs and traces. Logs should be sampled or kept at INFO in hot paths; traces are sampled but keep every error. A counter metric can also be derived from logs, but querying logs to draw a graph is slower and pricier than a real metric.

Cost aur cardinality design decide karte hain. Metrics tabhi saste rehte hain jab labels low-cardinality hon jaise endpoint, status code aur region; user_id ya order_id ko label banane se har value ki ek time series banti hai aur storage phat sakta hai. High-cardinality detail logs aur traces mein rehni chahiye. Hot paths mein logs sample karo ya INFO pe rakho; traces sample hote hain lekin har error rakhte hain. Logs se counter metric bhi nikaal sakte ho, lekin graph banane ke liye logs query karna asli metric se slow aur mehenga hai.

Common mistake: saying "they're all just monitoring" or describing a trace as "a log with a stack trace". A stack trace is inside one process; a distributed trace spans many services.
Galti mat karna: "yeh sab bas monitoring hai" bolna ya trace ko "stack trace wala log" batana. Stack trace ek process ke andar hota hai; distributed trace kai services ke paar hota hai.
06 Your error rate is 1% but you can't reproduce the error locally. What do you do?Tumhara error rate 1% hai lekin tum error ko locally reproduce nahi kar pa rahe. Kya karoge?
What they're really testing: that you use production evidence instead of your laptop: filter error logs by type, find a failed request ID, trace the user, input and code path, and add targeted logging if needed.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum laptop ki jagah production ka saboot use karte ho: error logs ko type se filter karna, ek failed request ID dhoondhna, user, input aur code path trace karna, aur zaroorat ho toh targeted logging add karna.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

If it doesn't reproduce locally, production has something my laptop doesn't, so I'd debug with production data. First I'd filter the error logs by error type and endpoint, because "1%" is often several different errors mixed together. Then I'd group the main one by every dimension I have: instance, region, customer, app version, input shape. A steady 1% is often one bad server out of many, one tenant with unusual data, or one client version. Next I'd pick a specific failed request ID, pull its trace and logs, and reconstruct the exact user, input and code path. Often I can then replay that input locally and it fails. If I still can't see it, I'd add targeted logging around the suspected path, with the request ID, deploy it, and wait for the next occurrence.

Agar locally reproduce nahi hota, toh production mein kuch aisa hai jo laptop pe nahi, toh main production data se debug karunga. Pehle error logs ko error type aur endpoint se filter karunga, kyunki "1%" aksar kai alag errors ka mix hota hai. Phir main wale error ko har dimension se group karunga: instance, region, customer, app version, input ki shape. Lagataar 1% aksar kai mein se ek kharab server hota hai, ek tenant jiska data ajeeb hai, ya ek client version. Agla, ek specific failed request ID uthaunga, uska trace aur logs nikaalunga, aur exact user, input aur code path reconstruct karunga. Aksar phir main woh input locally replay kar sakta hoon aur woh fail hota hai. Agar ab bhi nahi dikhta, toh suspected path ke aas-paas request ID ke saath targeted logging add karunga, deploy karunga, aur agli baar hone ka wait karunga.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Things production has that local doesn't: real data volume and edge cases (unicode names, null fields, a huge account), concurrency (a race, Topic 03), timeouts from real network latency, and other services' real behaviour, such as a rate limit (429) from a third-party API. Also check whether the errors correlate with time: every hour on the hour points to a cron job or a cache TTL expiry (Topic 04). Targeted logging should be temporary and must still avoid tokens and PII (Topic 12). If the errors cluster on one instance, take it out of rotation first; that's a quick mitigation while you investigate.

Production mein kya hai jo local mein nahi: asli data volume aur edge cases (unicode naam, null fields, bahut bada account), concurrency (race, Topic 03), asli network latency se timeouts, aur doosri services ka asli behaviour, jaise third-party API ka rate limit (429). Yeh bhi check karo ki errors time se jude hain ya nahi: har ghante theek time pe hona cron job ya cache TTL expiry (Topic 04) ki taraf ishaara karta hai. Targeted logging temporary honi chahiye aur ab bhi tokens aur PII se bachni chahiye (Topic 12). Agar errors ek instance pe ikatthe hain, toh pehle usse rotation se bahar karo; investigate karte waqt yeh jaldi ka mitigation hai.

Common mistake: ignoring it because "it's only 1%", or trying random fixes locally. At a million requests a day, 1% is ten thousand failures.
Galti mat karna: "sirf 1% hai" soch ke ignore karna, ya locally random fixes try karna. Din ki das lakh requests pe 1% matlab das hazaar failures.
07 How do you debug a race condition that only happens in production?Jo race condition sirf production mein hoti hai, usse kaise debug karoge?
What they're really testing: structured logs with timestamps and request IDs at both write points, spotting overlapping windows, then fixing with a lock or atomic operation and proving it with a higher-concurrency load test.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: dono write points pe timestamps aur request IDs wale structured logs, overlapping windows pehchaanna, phir lock ya atomic operation se fix, aur zyada concurrency wale load test se saabit karna.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Race conditions show up in production because that's where two requests really hit the same record in the same millisecond. First I'd find the affected records, say a service appointment slot booked twice, and pull every log line that touched them. If the read and the write are logged with precise timestamps and request IDs, I can line up both requests and see the overlap: request A read the slot as free, request B read it as free, then both wrote. If those logs don't exist, I add them at both the read and write points and wait. Once I've proven the overlapping window, I fix it with what Topics 02 and 03 teach: an atomic conditional update, a row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE, an optimistic version check, or a unique constraint. Then I prove the fix with a load test at higher concurrency than production.

Race conditions production mein isliye dikhti hain kyunki wahin do requests sach mein ek hi millisecond mein ek hi record pe aati hain. Pehle main affected records dhoondhunga, jaise ek service appointment slot jo do baar book hua, aur har woh log line nikaalunga jisne unhe chhua. Agar read aur write precise timestamps aur request IDs ke saath log hain, toh main dono requests ko line up karke overlap dekh sakta hoon: request A ne slot free padha, request B ne bhi free padha, phir dono ne likha. Agar aise logs nahi hain, toh main read aur write dono points pe add karke wait karunga. Overlap wala window saabit ho jaane ke baad, Topics 02 aur 03 wala fix lagaunga: atomic conditional update, SELECT FOR UPDATE se row lock, optimistic version check, ya unique constraint. Phir production se zyada concurrency pe load test karke fix saabit karunga.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Clocks on different servers drift, so compare timestamps from the database (commit times, row version columns) or order events within one service, rather than trusting milliseconds across machines (Topic 07). If multiple instances run the same job, the race may be between instances, which needs a distributed lock or, better, a database constraint. A load test tool can fire, say, 200 concurrent bookings at one slot; before the fix you see duplicates, after it exactly one success and the rest get 409 Conflict (Topic 08). Adding a random delay between read and write in a test build widens the window and makes the race easy to reproduce.

Alag servers ki ghadiyaan drift karti hain, isliye machines ke paar milliseconds pe bharosa karne ki jagah database ke timestamps (commit times, row version columns) compare karo ya ek service ke andar events ka order dekho (Topic 07). Agar kai instances ek hi job chalate hain, toh race instances ke beech ho sakti hai, jiske liye distributed lock ya, behtar, database constraint chahiye. Load test tool ek slot pe, maan lo, 200 concurrent bookings bhej sakta hai; fix se pehle duplicates dikhenge, fix ke baad exactly ek success aur baaki ko 409 Conflict (Topic 08). Test build mein read aur write ke beech random delay daalne se window chauda hota hai aur race aasaani se reproduce hoti hai.

Common mistake: adding a sleep or a retry and calling it fixed because it stopped happening for a day. Timing tweaks hide races; only atomicity or locking removes them.
Galti mat karna: sleep ya retry daal ke fixed bol dena kyunki ek din nahi hua. Timing ke jugaad race ko chhupaate hain; sirf atomicity ya locking usse hataate hain.
08 What goes into a good post-mortem?Ek achhe post-mortem mein kya hona chahiye?
What they're really testing: timeline, impact, root cause as a systemic gap (not "human error"), contributing factors, action items with owners and dates, all in a blameless tone.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: timeline, impact, root cause ek systemic kami ke roop mein ("human error" nahi), contributing factors, owners aur dates wale action items, sab blameless tone mein.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

A good post-mortem has six parts. A timeline: when it started, when we detected it, key actions, when it was mitigated and resolved, which shows detection gaps. The impact: who was affected, for how long, how many requests failed. The root cause, written as a systemic gap: not "an engineer ran a bad migration" but "our pipeline let a migration that dropped an index reach production without review". Contributing factors, like a missing alert or a confusing dashboard. Action items, each with an owner and a date, otherwise nothing changes. And what went well, so we keep it. The whole document is blameless: it asks why the system allowed the mistake, not who made it, because people who fear blame hide details, and hidden details cause the next outage.

Achhe post-mortem ke chhe hisse hote hain. Timeline: kab shuru hua, kab pata chala, main actions, kab mitigate aur resolve hua, jisse detection ki kamiyaan dikhti hain. Impact: kaun affected hua, kitni der, kitni requests fail hui. Root cause, systemic kami ki tarah likha: "ek engineer ne kharab migration chalaayi" nahi, balki "hamari pipeline ne index drop karne wali migration ko bina review production tak jaane diya". Contributing factors, jaise missing alert ya confusing dashboard. Action items, har ek ka owner aur date, warna kuch nahi badlega. Aur kya achha gaya, taaki usse banaaye rakhein. Poora document blameless hota hai: yeh poochhta hai system ne galti kyun hone di, yeh nahi ki kisne ki, kyunki blame se darne wale log details chhupaate hain, aur chhupi details agla outage laati hain.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Use the "five whys" to go past the first answer: the site was down, because the DB was at 100%, because a query lost its index, because a migration dropped it, because migrations aren't reviewed for index changes. The last "why" is where action items live. Separate time-to-detect from time-to-mitigate; a long detection time means an alerting gap. Good action items are specific and verifiable ("add a CI check for DROP INDEX, owner, date"), not "be more careful". Track them to completion and share the post-mortem widely so other teams learn.

Pehle jawab se aage jaane ke liye "five whys" use karo: site down thi, kyunki DB 100% pe tha, kyunki ek query ka index chala gaya, kyunki migration ne usse drop kiya, kyunki migrations ka index changes ke liye review nahi hota. Aakhri "kyun" pe hi action items bante hain. Time-to-detect aur time-to-mitigate alag rakho; lamba detection time matlab alerting mein kami. Achhe action items specific aur check karne layak hote hain ("DROP INDEX ke liye CI check add karo, owner, date"), "zyada dhyaan rakho" nahi. Unhe poora hone tak track karo aur post-mortem sabke saath share karo taaki doosri teams bhi seekhein.

Common mistake: writing "root cause: human error" or action items with no owner. Both guarantee the same incident happens again.
Galti mat karna: "root cause: human error" likhna ya bina owner ke action items. Dono se pakka hai ki wahi incident dobara hoga.
09 A customer reports that their data "disappeared". How do you investigate?Ek customer kehta hai ki uska data "gayab ho gaya". Tum investigate kaise karoge?
What they're really testing: that you consider soft delete, a filter bug hiding the data, a failed write that never persisted, and a race that overwrote it, and check audit logs before assuming data loss.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum soft delete, data chhupaane wala filter bug, kabhi save na hua failed write, aur overwrite karne wali race ke baare mein sochte ho, aur data loss maanne se pehle audit logs check karte ho.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

I'd start by getting specifics: which record, when they last saw it, and what they did in between. Then I'd query the database directly, bypassing the app, because "disappeared" usually means "not shown", not "gone". I check four things in order. One, soft delete: is deleted_at set, and by whom? Two, a filter bug: maybe the row exists but a recent change to a query, a tenant filter, a status filter or a stale cache hides it. Three, a failed write: maybe it was never saved, for example a transaction rolled back or a queued job went to the dead letter queue, so the user saw "saved" but nothing committed. Four, a race or lost update that overwrote it with older values. Audit logs and the request logs for that record answer most of this. Only if all four are ruled out would I treat it as real loss and restore from backups.

Main specifics se shuru karunga: kaunsa record, aakhri baar kab dekha, aur beech mein kya kiya. Phir app ko bypass karke seedha database query karunga, kyunki "gayab" ka matlab aksar "dikh nahi raha" hota hai, "chala gaya" nahi. Main chaar cheezein order mein check karta hoon. Ek, soft delete: kya deleted_at set hai, aur kisne kiya? Do, filter bug: shayad row hai lekin kisi query, tenant filter, status filter mein recent change ya purana cache usse chhupa raha hai. Teen, failed write: shayad woh kabhi save hi nahi hua, jaise transaction rollback hua ya queue ka job dead letter queue mein chala gaya, toh user ne "saved" dekha lekin kuch commit nahi hua. Chaar, race ya lost update jisne usse purani values se overwrite kar diya. Us record ke audit logs aur request logs inme se zyada tar ka jawab dete hain. Chaaron rule out hone pe hi main isse asli loss maanunga aur backups se restore karunga.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

If there's no audit table, database-level history helps: MySQL's binary log or Postgres's write-ahead log with point-in-time recovery can show or restore the state at a moment. Restore into a separate database, never over production. Check authorization too: another user with access may have deleted it legitimately, or a permission change (Topic 10) may simply hide it from this user. For prevention: an audit log of who changed what, soft delete with a restore path, and making sure the API returns an error, not "success", when a write fails (Topic 12).

Agar audit table nahi hai, toh database-level history kaam aati hai: MySQL ka binary log ya Postgres ka write-ahead log, point-in-time recovery ke saath, kisi pal ki state dikha ya restore kar sakta hai. Alag database mein restore karo, production ke upar kabhi nahi. Authorization bhi check karo: access wale kisi doosre user ne usse sahi mein delete kiya ho, ya permission change (Topic 10) ne bas is user se chhupa diya ho. Rokne ke liye: kisne kya badla ka audit log, restore path ke saath soft delete, aur yeh pakka karna ki write fail hone pe API error lautaaye, "success" nahi (Topic 12).

Common mistake: telling the customer "your data is lost" or restoring a backup over production before checking audit logs; you may overwrite everyone else's newer data.
Galti mat karna: audit logs check kiye bina customer ko "aapka data lost ho gaya" bolna ya production ke upar backup restore karna; tum baaki sabka naya data overwrite kar sakte ho.
10 Your service is healthy by every metric, but users say it's slow. What's happening?Tumhari service har metric pe healthy hai, lekin users kehte hain slow hai. Kya ho raha hai?
What they're really testing: that you know server metrics only cover part of the user's wait: check client-side timing, bottlenecks outside the service (DNS, CDN, frontend, network), and look at p99/p999, not averages.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum jaante ho server metrics user ke wait ka sirf ek hissa dekhte hain: client-side timing, service ke bahar ke bottlenecks (DNS, CDN, frontend, network) check karo, aur p99/p999 dekho, average nahi.

Say this (30–60 sec answer)Aise bolo (30–60 sec answer)

Two things usually explain this. First, my metrics might be measuring the wrong thing. If my dashboard shows average latency, it can look fine while the p99 or p999 users wait seconds, so I'd check the tail percentiles, and split them by region, customer and endpoint. Second, my server only measures from when a request reaches it. The user's wait also includes DNS lookup, the TLS handshake, the CDN, load balancer queueing, the network, and the browser downloading and running JavaScript. So I'd measure from the client side, using real user monitoring or browser timing, and compare it to server time. If the client sees 4 seconds and my server sees 200 ms, the bottleneck is outside my service: maybe a CDN cache miss, a slow DNS provider, a huge frontend bundle, or one region's network.

Aam taur pe do cheezein isko samjhaati hain. Pehli, shayad mere metrics galat cheez naap rahe hain. Agar dashboard average latency dikhata hai, toh woh theek dikh sakta hai jabki p99 ya p999 users second bhar wait karte hain, isliye main tail percentiles check karunga, aur unhe region, customer aur endpoint se todunga. Doosri, mera server sirf tab se naapta hai jab request usse milti hai. User ke wait mein DNS lookup, TLS handshake, CDN, load balancer ki line, network, aur browser ka JavaScript download aur run karna bhi shaamil hai. Toh main client side se naapunga, real user monitoring ya browser timing se, aur usse server time se compare karunga. Agar client 4 second dekhta hai aur server 200 ms, toh bottleneck meri service ke bahar hai: shayad CDN cache miss, slow DNS provider, bahut bada frontend bundle, ya ek region ka network.

If they push deeperAgar woh aur deep jaayein

Also check what the server doesn't count: time a request waits in the load balancer or in the app's own queue before your timer starts, and time waiting for a connection from the pool. Fan-out makes the tail worse: if a page waits for 10 calls and each is slow 1% of the time, about 9.6% of page loads hit at least one slow call. Look at one user's session end to end, and run synthetic checks from several regions. Finally, "slow" can be perceived: a page that shows nothing until everything loads feels slower than one that renders progressively.

Yeh bhi check karo ki server kya nahi ginta: timer shuru hone se pehle request ne load balancer ya app ki apni queue mein kitna wait kiya, aur pool se connection ka kitna wait kiya. Fan-out tail ko aur bura karta hai: agar ek page 10 calls ka wait karta hai aur har ek 1% time slow hai, toh lagbhag 9.6% page loads kam se kam ek slow call se takraate hain. Ek user ka session end to end dekho, aur kai regions se synthetic checks chalao. Aakhir mein, "slow" mehsoos bhi hota hai: jo page sab load hone tak kuch nahi dikhata woh dheere-dheere render hone wale page se zyada slow lagta hai.

Common mistake: telling the interviewer "the metrics say it's fine, so it's the user's internet". The user's experience is the real metric; your dashboard is only a proxy for it.
Galti mat karna: interviewer ko bolna "metrics keh rahe hain sab theek hai, toh user ka internet hoga". User ka experience hi asli metric hai; tumhara dashboard uska sirf ek proxy hai.

FinaleAakhri chapter

How to walk into the interviewInterview mein kaise jaana hai

You now have the pieces. This chapter turns them into answers that get you hired: how to reason out loud, what to study first, a four-week plan from zero, what to say when you don't know, and five mock drills that chain the topics together the way real interviewers do.

Ab tumhare paas saare pieces hain. Yeh chapter unhe aise jawaabon mein badalta hai jinse job milti hai: zor se reasoning kaise karein, pehle kya padhein, zero se chaar hafte ka plan, jab jawab na aata ho toh kya bolein, aur paanch mock drills jo topics ko waise jodti hain jaise asli interviewers jodte hain.

Level 0 The story: two candidates, same knowledgeKahani: do candidates, same knowledge

Two candidates sit the same interview. Both have read the same notes. The interviewer asks: "What is a database index?"

Candidate A: "An index makes queries faster."

Candidate B: "An index is a separate sorted structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database jump to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. It exists because a full scan on millions of rows is too slow for an API. The trade-off is that every insert and update now also has to update the index, and it uses storage. So I'd index the columns our slow queries actually filter and sort on, and I'd be careful on write-heavy tables."

Both answers are "correct". Only one gets the job. The PDF this guide is built on sums it up in one line: "Most candidates know the answers. Few know the reasoning."

Think of the driving licence test. One learner has memorised the entire rulebook: every sign, every fine. Another has actually driven through evening traffic, knows why you keep distance from a bus, and can tell you what they would do if a scooter cuts in. The examiner in the car cares about the second kind of knowledge. The rulebook is the floor; judgement on the road is what passes you.

Everything in the previous thirteen chapters was built so you could be Candidate B. Each lesson went from story to mechanism to trade-off for exactly this reason. This chapter shows you how to use that in the room.

Remember: the definition is the floor. Reasoning gets you hired.

Do candidates ek hi interview mein baithe hain. Dono ne same notes padhe hain. Interviewer poochta hai: "Database index kya hota hai?"

Candidate A: "Index queries ko fast bana deta hai."

Candidate B: "Index ek alag sorted structure hai, aam taur pe B-tree, jisse database poori table scan karne ki jagah seedha matching rows pe jump kar leta hai. Yeh isliye hai kyunki lakhon rows pe full scan ek API ke liye bahut slow hai. Trade-off yeh hai ki ab har insert aur update ko index bhi update karna padta hai, aur storage lagta hai. Toh main un columns pe index lagaunga jin pe hamari slow queries sach mein filter aur sort karti hain, aur write-heavy tables pe dhyaan rakhunga."

Dono jawab "sahi" hain. Job sirf ek ko milti hai. Jis PDF pe yeh guide bani hai, woh ek line mein keh deti hai: "Most candidates know the answers. Few know the reasoning." Matlab zyada tar candidates jawab jaante hain, bahut kam reasoning jaante hain.

Driving licence test socho. Ek learner ne poori rulebook ratt li hai: har sign, har fine. Doosre ne sach mein shaam ke traffic mein gaadi chalaayi hai, jaanta hai bus se doori kyun rakhte hain, aur bata sakta hai ki agar koi scooter beech mein ghuse toh kya karega. Gaadi mein baitha examiner doosri type ki knowledge dekhta hai. Rulebook floor hai; sadak pe judgement tumhe pass karwata hai.

Pichle terah chapters mein sab kuch isliye bana tha ki tum Candidate B ban sako. Har lesson kahani se mechanism se trade-off tak isi wajah se gaya. Yeh chapter dikhata hai ki room mein isko use kaise karna hai.

Yaad rakho: definition floor hai. Reasoning se job milti hai.

Level 1 The answer formula, and answering the hintJawab ka formula, aur hint ka jawab dena

Every answer in this guide follows the same four beats. Use them for any concept question, even one you have never seen:

  1. What it is: one plain sentence. "A cache is a fast copy of data kept closer to where it's needed."
  2. Why it exists: the pain it removes. "Because hitting the database for the same popular data on every request is slow and expensive."
  3. What problem it solves, with an example: something concrete. "For a vehicle details page, I'd cache the vehicle record by VIN in Redis with cache-aside."
  4. What it trades off: the price you pay. "The cost is staleness: if the price changes, users may see the old one until I invalidate the key. So I wouldn't cache things like a payment balance."

Answer the hint, not just the question. Every question in the PDF came with a hint: what the interviewer is really testing. We put that hint at the top of every answer as "What they're really testing". The question is the door; the hint is the room behind it. For "When would you NOT add an index?", the words on the surface are about indexes, but the test is whether you understand write cost. For "Idempotency key expiry", the test is the tension between unbounded storage and the client's retry window. If your answer does not touch the hint, it is incomplete, however correct it sounds.

The situation + trade-off format. Seniors almost never answer "always" or "never". They say "it depends", but they immediately say on what: "If the data can be a few seconds stale, like a view count, I'd use eventual consistency; if it's a checkout inventory count, I need strong consistency, and I'd pay for it in latency." "It depends" followed by silence is a weak answer. "It depends on X; if X then A, otherwise B, and here's what each costs" is the strongest answer there is.

Is guide ka har jawab same chaar beats follow karta hai. Inhe kisi bhi concept question ke liye use karo, chahe tumne woh kabhi dekha bhi na ho:

  1. Yeh kya hai: ek simple sentence. "Cache data ki ek fast copy hai jo zaroorat wali jagah ke paas rakhi jaati hai."
  2. Yeh kyun hai: kaunsa dard hataata hai. "Kyunki har request pe same popular data ke liye database tak jaana slow aur mehenga hai."
  3. Kaunsi problem solve karta hai, example ke saath: kuch concrete. "Vehicle details page ke liye main vehicle record ko VIN se Redis mein cache-aside ke saath cache karunga."
  4. Kya trade off karta hai: kya keemat chukaate ho. "Keemat hai staleness: agar price badle, toh key invalidate karne tak users purana price dekh sakte hain. Isliye main payment balance jaisi cheezein cache nahi karunga."

Sirf sawaal ka nahi, hint ka jawab do. PDF ke har sawaal ke saath ek hint tha: interviewer asal mein kya test kar raha hai. Humne woh hint har jawab ke upar "Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai" ki tarah rakha. Sawaal darwaza hai; hint uske peeche ka kamra hai. "Index kab NAHI lagaoge?" mein upar se baat index ki hai, lekin test yeh hai ki tum write cost samajhte ho ya nahi. "Idempotency key expiry" mein test hai unlimited storage aur client ki retry window ke beech ka tension. Agar tumhara jawab hint ko nahi chhoota, toh woh adhoora hai, chahe kitna bhi sahi lage.

Situation + trade-off format. Seniors lagbhag kabhi "hamesha" ya "kabhi nahi" nahi bolte. Woh "it depends" bolte hain, lekin turant batate hain kis pe: "Agar data kuch second purana ho sakta hai, jaise view count, toh eventual consistency; agar checkout ka inventory count hai, toh strong consistency chahiye, aur uski keemat latency mein doonga." "It depends" bolke chup ho jaana kamzor jawab hai. "It depends on X; agar X toh A, warna B, aur har ek ki keemat yeh hai" sabse strong jawab hai.

Weak answerKamzor jawab Strong answer (same topic)Strong jawab (same topic)
"I'd use Redis and add a TTL.""Main Redis use karunga aur TTL laga dunga." "Cache-aside in Redis, invalidated when the record changes, with a TTL as a safety net; I'd add jitter to TTLs so keys don't all expire together and stampede the DB.""Redis mein cache-aside, record badalne pe invalidate, TTL ek safety net ki tarah; TTLs mein jitter daalunga taaki saari keys ek saath expire hoke DB pe stampede na karein."
"Use a transaction.""Transaction use karo." "Wrap debit and credit in one transaction so it's atomic, and use an atomic UPDATE or row lock so two requests can't both read the old balance.""Debit aur credit ko ek transaction mein rakho taaki atomic ho, aur atomic UPDATE ya row lock use karo taaki do requests dono purana balance na padh lein."
"I'd check the logs.""Main logs check karunga." "First I'd check what changed at the minute it started, because recent changes are the usual cause; if nothing changed, I'd open a slow trace to find which span grew.""Pehle dekhunga jis minute shuru hua tab kya badla, kyunki recent changes aam cause hain; kuch nahi badla toh ek slow trace kholke dekhunga kaunsa span bada hua."

Do not memorise answers word for word. Interviewers ask follow-ups until they reach the edge of what you understand. A memorised paragraph survives one question; understanding survives five. Use the "Say this" answers in this guide to learn the shape of a good answer, then practise saying it in your own words.

Jawab word by word ratto mat. Interviewers follow-ups poochte rehte hain jab tak tumhari samajh ki edge tak na pahunch jaayein. Ratta hua paragraph ek sawaal jhel leta hai; samajh paanch jhel leti hai. Is guide ke "Aise bolo" answers se achhe jawab ki shape seekho, phir apne words mein bolne ki practice karo.

Level 2 What to prioritise, and telling production storiesKya pehle padhna hai, aur production stories sunaana

Not all topics are equal. The PDF marks five of them as the highest priority, the ones asked in almost every backend interview. In this guide they carry the label ASKED EVERYWHERE:

  • Topic 01 Database Indexing: the number one performance topic.
  • Topic 02 Transactions & Isolation: correctness when many things happen at once.
  • Topic 04 Caching: strategy, invalidation, failure modes.
  • Topic 08 API Design: contracts, versioning, status codes.
  • Topic 13 Production Debugging: the 2am scenario questions.

If your time is short, be excellent at these five before being good at the rest. The next tier (VERY COMMON) is Concurrency, Idempotency, Message Queues, Distributed Systems, Database Design and Auth. The COMMON tier is Docker & Deployment and Error Handling & Logging. Notice how they lean on each other: you cannot explain idempotency without transactions, or debugging without indexing, caching and logging.

Tell production stories. The strongest answer to a scenario question sounds like a story you lived: "I'd first check X because Y; if that's clear I'd look at Z." When you have a real experience, tell it in this shape:

  1. Situation: "Our appointment page started timing out on Monday mornings."
  2. What I observed: "p99 went from about half a second to several seconds, only on that endpoint."
  3. What I suspected and why: "One endpoint, so I suspected its query rather than the whole database."
  4. What I did: "EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan; I added a composite index concurrently."
  5. Result and what I changed after: "p99 came back down, and I added a p99 alert on that endpoint."

Never invent a story. Follow-up questions ("what was the table size?", "why that column order?", "what did the plan show?") expose made-up incidents within a minute, and then everything else you said is doubted. If you have not been paged at 2am yet, say so and walk through the method instead: "I haven't handled that in production yet; here is exactly how I'd approach it." That is honest and still shows the structure. Better still, create real stories now: run EXPLAIN on a real slow query in a side project, break a transaction on purpose in two terminal windows, watch a container get OOM-killed. Those are true, and you can defend every detail.

Saare topics barabar nahi hain. PDF paanch topics ko sabse zyada priority deti hai, woh jo lagbhag har backend interview mein poochhe jaate hain. Is guide mein unpe label hai ASKED EVERYWHERE:

  • Topic 01 Database Indexing: number one performance topic.
  • Topic 02 Transactions & Isolation: jab bahut kuch ek saath ho, tab correctness.
  • Topic 04 Caching: strategy, invalidation, failure modes.
  • Topic 08 API Design: contracts, versioning, status codes.
  • Topic 13 Production Debugging: raat 2 baje wale scenario questions.

Agar time kam hai, toh baaki mein achhe banne se pehle in paanch mein excellent bano. Agla tier (VERY COMMON) hai Concurrency, Idempotency, Message Queues, Distributed Systems, Database Design aur Auth. COMMON tier hai Docker & Deployment aur Error Handling & Logging. Dekho yeh ek doosre pe kaise tike hain: transactions ke bina idempotency samjha nahi sakte, ya indexing, caching aur logging ke bina debugging.

Production stories sunao. Scenario question ka sabse strong jawab aisi kahani lagta hai jo tumne jee hai: "Main pehle X check karunga kyunki Y; agar woh theek hai toh Z dekhunga." Jab tumhare paas asli experience ho, usse is shape mein sunao:

  1. Situation: "Hamara appointment page Monday subah time out hone laga."
  2. Maine kya dekha: "p99 lagbhag aadhe second se kai second ho gaya, sirf us endpoint pe."
  3. Mujhe kya shak tha aur kyun: "Ek hi endpoint tha, toh maine poore database ki jagah uski query pe shak kiya."
  4. Maine kya kiya: "EXPLAIN ANALYZE ne sequential scan dikhaya; maine concurrently ek composite index add kiya."
  5. Result aur baad mein kya badla: "p99 wapas neeche aaya, aur maine us endpoint pe p99 alert add kiya."

Kabhi kahani mat banao. Follow-up sawaal ("table kitna bada tha?", "column order yahi kyun?", "plan mein kya dikha?") ek minute mein banaayi hui kahani pakad lete hain, aur phir tumhari baaki har baat pe shak hota hai. Agar tumhe abhi tak raat 2 baje page nahi hua, toh seedha bolo aur method samjhao: "Maine production mein abhi yeh handle nahi kiya; main exactly aise approach karunga." Yeh honest hai aur structure bhi dikhata hai. Aur bhi achha, abhi se asli kahaniyaan banao: kisi side project mein asli slow query pe EXPLAIN chalao, do terminal windows mein jaan-boojh kar transaction todo, ek container ko OOM-kill hote dekho. Yeh sach hain, aur tum har detail defend kar sakte ho.

Read the picture as a follow-up chain. The client taps "Book" twice: idempotency (05). Two customers want the same slot: concurrency and transactions (03, 02). The slot query is slow: indexing (01) on a well-designed schema (09). The page is popular: caching and CDN (04). The SMS must go out even if the provider is down: queues (06), retries and circuit breakers (12). The primary dies: replication and failover (07). The new version is deployed: containers and health checks (11). Only the right people can book: auth (10). The contract with the app: API design (08). And when it all breaks at 2am, one trace ID lets you follow it end to end (13). An interviewer who starts at one box will very often walk you along the arrows to the next.

Picture ko ek follow-up chain ki tarah padho. Client "Book" do baar dabata hai: idempotency (05). Do customers same slot chahte hain: concurrency aur transactions (03, 02). Slot wali query slow hai: achhe design wale schema (09) pe indexing (01). Page popular hai: caching aur CDN (04). Provider down ho tab bhi SMS jaana chahiye: queues (06), retries aur circuit breakers (12). Primary mar jaata hai: replication aur failover (07). Naya version deploy hota hai: containers aur health checks (11). Sirf sahi log book kar sakein: auth (10). App ke saath contract: API design (08). Aur jab raat 2 baje sab toote, ek trace ID se tum usse end to end follow kar sakte ho (13). Jo interviewer ek box se shuru karta hai, woh aksar tumhe arrows ke saath agle box tak le jaata hai.

Level 3 "I don't know, but here's how I'd reason about it""Mujhe nahi pata, lekin main aise reason karunga"

You will hit a question you cannot answer. Everyone does; interviewers deliberately push until you reach your edge, because what they want to see is how you behave there. There are three bad reactions: bluffing (confidently saying something wrong), freezing (long silence), and giving up ("I don't know." Full stop). There is one good reaction, in four moves:

  1. Say it honestly and briefly: "I haven't worked with that directly."
  2. Anchor to what you do know: "But it sounds related to X, which I do understand."
  3. Reason out loud from first principles, stating your assumptions: "If it works like X, then it would have to trade off A against B..."
  4. Say how you'd verify: "To be sure, I'd check the docs for Y or test it by doing Z."

Example. Interviewer: "How do Cassandra's consistency levels work?" You have never used Cassandra. You say: "I haven't used Cassandra itself, but I know leaderless replication and quorums from distributed systems. If data is copied to N replicas, and a write waits for W of them and a read asks R of them, then when W plus R is greater than N, every read overlaps with at least one replica that saw the latest write. So I'd expect consistency levels to be a way of choosing W and R per query: lower means faster and more available, higher means more consistent. I'd confirm the exact level names in the docs." That answer, built entirely from Topic 07, is often rated higher than a memorised definition.

Two more habits that make you look senior even as a beginner:

  • Ask one or two clarifying questions before designing: How many requests per second? Mostly reads or writes? Can the data be a little stale? What happens if it's down for a minute? The answers decide whether you need a cache, a queue, or strong consistency, and asking shows you know that.
  • Think out loud and start simple. "Let me start with one server and one database, then find what breaks first." Interviewers cannot give credit for thinking they cannot hear. Starting simple and evolving is exactly what real engineers do.

Tum kisi aise sawaal pe atkoge jiska jawab nahi aata. Sab atakte hain; interviewers jaan-boojh kar tab tak push karte hain jab tak tum apni edge tak na pahuncho, kyunki woh dekhna chahte hain ki tum wahan kaisa behave karte ho. Teen bure reactions hain: bluff karna (confidence se galat bolna), freeze hona (lambi chuppi), aur haar maan lena ("Mujhe nahi pata." Bas). Ek achha reaction hai, chaar moves mein:

  1. Imaandaari se aur chhota bolo: "Maine iske saath directly kaam nahi kiya."
  2. Jo jaante ho usse jodo: "Lekin yeh X se juda lagta hai, jo main samajhta hoon."
  3. First principles se zor se reason karo, apne assumptions batate hue: "Agar yeh X ki tarah kaam karta hai, toh isse A aur B ke beech trade-off karna padega..."
  4. Batao kaise verify karoge: "Pakka karne ke liye main Y ke docs dekhunga ya Z karke test karunga."

Example. Interviewer: "Cassandra ke consistency levels kaise kaam karte hain?" Tumne Cassandra kabhi use nahi kiya. Tum kehte ho: "Maine khud Cassandra use nahi kiya, lekin distributed systems se leaderless replication aur quorums jaanta hoon. Agar data N replicas pe copy hota hai, aur write W replicas ka wait karta hai aur read R se poochhta hai, toh jab W plus R, N se bada ho, har read kam se kam ek aise replica se overlap karta hai jisne latest write dekha. Toh mujhe lagta hai consistency levels har query ke liye W aur R chunne ka tareeka hain: kam matlab fast aur zyada available, zyada matlab zyada consistent. Exact level names main docs mein confirm karunga." Yeh jawab, poora Topic 07 se bana, aksar ratti hui definition se zyada rating paata hai.

Do aur aadatein jo beginner hote hue bhi tumhe senior dikhati hain:

  • Design karne se pehle ek-do clarifying sawaal poochho: Second mein kitni requests? Zyada reads ya writes? Data thoda purana chal sakta hai? Ek minute down ho toh kya hoga? Jawab decide karte hain ki cache chahiye, queue chahiye, ya strong consistency, aur poochhna dikhata hai ki tum yeh jaante ho.
  • Zor se socho aur simple se shuru karo. "Main ek server aur ek database se shuru karta hoon, phir dekhta hoon pehle kya tootega." Jo soch interviewer sun nahi sakta, uska credit woh nahi de sakta. Simple se shuru karke evolve karna bilkul wahi hai jo asli engineers karte hain.

Level 4 A four-week plan from zeroZero se chaar hafte ka plan

This plan assumes you are starting from nothing and can give roughly two focused hours a day. Adjust the pace, not the order: each week builds on the one before, the same way the chapters do.

Yeh plan maanta hai ki tum bilkul zero se shuru kar rahe ho aur roz lagbhag do ghante focus se de sakte ho. Speed badlo, order nahi: har hafta pichle pe banta hai, bilkul jaise chapters bante hain.

WeekHafta TopicsTopics Hands-on (makes real stories)Hands-on (asli kahaniyaan banata hai)
1 · How data is stored and served1 · Data kaise store aur serve hota hai Foundations, 08 API Design, 01 Indexing, 09 Database DesignFoundations, 08 API Design, 01 Indexing, 09 Database Design Run Postgres in Docker, fill a table with a million rows using generate_series, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after adding an index. Call a public API with curl and read the status codes.Docker mein Postgres chalao, generate_series se ek table mein das lakh rows bharo, index add karne se pehle aur baad EXPLAIN ANALYZE chalao. curl se ek public API call karo aur status codes padho.
2 · Correctness when things collide2 · Jab cheezein takraayein tab correctness 02 Transactions, 03 Concurrency, 05 Idempotency02 Transactions, 03 Concurrency, 05 Idempotency Open two psql windows and create a lost update and a deadlock on purpose. In redis-cli, try INCR and SET key value NX EX 30.Do psql windows kholo aur jaan-boojh kar lost update aur deadlock banao. redis-cli mein INCR aur SET key value NX EX 30 try karo.
3 · Scale and many machines3 · Scale aur kai machines 04 Caching, 06 Message Queues, 07 Distributed Systems, 10 Auth04 Caching, 06 Message Queues, 07 Distributed Systems, 10 Auth Write a tiny cache-aside script. Run RabbitMQ or Kafka in Docker, kill a consumer mid-message and watch it get redelivered. Create a JWT yourself and decode it to see the claims.Ek chhota cache-aside script likho. Docker mein RabbitMQ ya Kafka chalao, message ke beech consumer kill karo aur use dobara deliver hote dekho. Khud ek JWT banao aur decode karke claims dekho.
4 · Running it, breaking it, rehearsing4 · Chalaana, todna, rehearse karna 11 Docker & Deployment, 12 Error Handling & Logging, 13 Production Debugging, the five drills below11 Docker & Deployment, 12 Error Handling & Logging, 13 Production Debugging, neeche ki paanch drills Build a small Node service into a multi-stage image, give it a memory limit, create a leak and take heap snapshots. Do two full mock interviews with a friend.Ek chhoti Node service ko multi-stage image mein build karo, memory limit do, leak banao aur heap snapshots lo. Ek dost ke saath do poore mock interviews karo.

The daily loop (the same every day):

  1. Read the day's lesson in Hinglish to understand it, then re-read it in English to learn the words you will actually speak.
  2. Close the page and draw one diagram from memory: the B-tree, the two transactions on a timeline, the cache-aside flow, the trace waterfall.
  3. Answer three questions aloud without looking, and record yourself on your phone. Then compare with the "Say this" answer: did you hit what the interviewer is testing?
  4. Write down one "why" you could not answer. Tomorrow starts with that.

Every weekend, redo the five ASKED EVERYWHERE topics (01, 02, 04, 08, 13), even the ones from earlier weeks. They will come up; repetition on them pays the most.

In the room, the checklist is short: ask one clarifying question; think out loud; answer in four beats (what, why, example, trade-off); touch the hint; say "it depends on X" and then say what X changes; if you don't know, anchor and reason; end with "Does that cover what you were looking for, or shall I go deeper on any part?"

Roz ka loop (har din same):

  1. Us din ka lesson pehle Hinglish mein padho samajhne ke liye, phir English mein dobara padho taaki woh words seekh jao jo interview mein sach mein bologe.
  2. Page band karo aur yaad se ek diagram banao: B-tree, timeline pe do transactions, cache-aside flow, trace waterfall.
  3. Bina dekhe teen sawaalon ke jawab zor se bolo, aur phone pe record karo. Phir "Aise bolo" answer se compare karo: kya tumne woh chhua jo interviewer test kar raha hai?
  4. Ek "kyun" likho jiska jawab nahi de paaye. Agla din usi se shuru hoga.

Har weekend paanch ASKED EVERYWHERE topics (01, 02, 04, 08, 13) dobara karo, pichle hafton wale bhi. Yeh pakka aayenge; inpe repetition sabse zyada faayda deti hai.

Room mein checklist chhoti hai: ek clarifying sawaal poochho; zor se socho; chaar beats mein jawab do (kya, kyun, example, trade-off); hint ko chhoo lo; "it depends on X" bolo aur phir batao X se kya badalta hai; nahi pata toh anchor karo aur reason karo; end mein bolo "Does that cover what you were looking for, or shall I go deeper on any part?"

Words to knowYeh words yaad rakho

Follow-up chain
A series of questions where each answer opens the next one, until the interviewer finds the edge of your understanding.Sawaalon ki ek series jahan har jawab agla sawaal kholta hai, jab tak interviewer tumhari samajh ki edge na dhoondh le.
Trade-off
What you give up to get something: speed for consistency, storage for read speed, simplicity for scale.Kuch paane ke liye kya chhodte ho: consistency ke liye speed, read speed ke liye storage, scale ke liye simplicity.
Situation + trade-off format
"It depends on X; if X then A, otherwise B, and here's what each costs.""It depends on X; agar X toh A, warna B, aur har ek ki keemat yeh hai."
The hint
What the interviewer is really testing behind the words of the question.Sawaal ke words ke peeche interviewer asal mein kya test kar raha hai.
Production story
A true experience told as situation, observation, suspicion, action, result, and what you changed after.Ek sachcha experience jo situation, observation, shak, action, result, aur baad mein kya badla, is order mein sunaaya jaaye.
First principles
Reasoning from basic facts you know are true, instead of from a memorised answer.Ratte hue jawab ki jagah un basic facts se reason karna jo tum jaante ho ki sach hain.

Mock interview drillsMock interview drills

Each drill is an opening question followed by the chain of follow-ups a real interviewer might run across topics. Answer the opener aloud, then try each follow-up before reading its short answer.

Har drill ek opening sawaal hai aur uske baad follow-ups ki chain, jo ek asli interviewer topics ke paar chala sakta hai. Opener ka jawab zor se bolo, phir har follow-up ka jawab khud try karo, uske baad uska chhota answer padho.

01 Drill: "Design a payment API for booking deposits."Drill: "Booking deposits ke liye ek payment API design karo."
What they're really testing: whether you connect idempotency (05), transactions (02), concurrency (03), retries and circuit breakers (12), queues (06), status codes (08) and auth (10) into one safe design, instead of treating payments as a plain POST.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: kya tum idempotency (05), transactions (02), concurrency (03), retries aur circuit breakers (12), queues (06), status codes (08) aur auth (10) ko ek safe design mein jodte ho, ya payments ko ek simple POST samajhte ho.

Say this (opening answer)Aise bolo (opening answer)

I'd expose POST /payments, authenticated, and require an Idempotency-Key header, because networks time out and clients retry, and a retry must never charge twice. The server first records the key with status "processing", then in one database transaction creates the payment row in a pending state. It calls the payment provider with a timeout, passing the same key if the provider supports it, then updates the row to succeeded or failed and stores the response against the key. A duplicate request with the same key gets the stored response. Receipts and notifications go onto a queue after commit, so a slow email provider can't slow down or fail the payment. I'd return 201 on success, 409 if the key is reused with a different body, 422 for invalid input and 429 when rate-limited.

Main POST /payments expose karunga, authenticated, aur Idempotency-Key header zaroori rakhunga, kyunki networks time out hote hain aur clients retry karte hain, aur retry kabhi do baar charge nahi karna chahiye. Server pehle key ko "processing" status ke saath record karta hai, phir ek database transaction mein payment row pending state mein banata hai. Woh timeout ke saath payment provider ko call karta hai, agar provider support kare toh same key bhejta hai, phir row ko succeeded ya failed pe update karta hai aur response ko key ke against store karta hai. Same key wali duplicate request ko stored response milta hai. Receipts aur notifications commit ke baad queue pe jaate hain, taaki slow email provider payment ko slow ya fail na kar sake. Success pe 201, key alag body ke saath dobara use ho toh 409, galat input pe 422 aur rate-limit pe 429.

The follow-up chainFollow-up chain

  1. "Two identical requests arrive at the same millisecond. Now what?" A unique constraint on the key (or SET key NX in Redis) lets exactly one proceed; the other waits or gets 409 "in progress" (Topics 03, 05).
  2. "The server charges the card, then crashes before responding." Because the key was written before processing, the retry finds it, checks the provider's status for that key, and returns the result instead of charging again (Topic 05).
  3. "The deposit also reduces a wallet balance. How do you keep it correct?" Same transaction, and an atomic UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - x WHERE balance >= x or a row lock, so two payments can't both read the old balance (Topics 02, 03).
  4. "The provider is timing out for everyone." Timeouts, limited retries with exponential backoff and jitter (safe only because of the key), and a circuit breaker so we fail fast instead of piling up threads (Topic 12).
  5. "How long do you keep keys?" Longer than the clients' retry window, with a TTL, so storage stays bounded (Topic 05).
  1. "Do bilkul same requests ek hi millisecond mein aayein. Ab?" Key pe unique constraint (ya Redis mein SET key NX) sirf ek ko aage jaane deta hai; doosri wait karti hai ya 409 "in progress" paati hai (Topics 03, 05).
  2. "Server card charge karta hai, phir response se pehle crash." Kyunki key processing se pehle likhi gayi thi, retry usse dhoondh leta hai, provider se us key ka status check karta hai, aur dobara charge karne ki jagah result lautaata hai (Topic 05).
  3. "Deposit ek wallet balance bhi ghataata hai. Sahi kaise rakhoge?" Same transaction, aur atomic UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - x WHERE balance >= x ya row lock, taaki do payments dono purana balance na padh lein (Topics 02, 03).
  4. "Provider sabke liye time out ho raha hai." Timeouts, exponential backoff aur jitter ke saath limited retries (key ki wajah se hi safe), aur circuit breaker taaki threads jama karne ki jagah jaldi fail karein (Topic 12).
  5. "Keys kitni der rakhoge?" Clients ki retry window se zyada, TTL ke saath, taaki storage limited rahe (Topic 05).
Common mistake: calling the provider and sending the email inside one long database transaction. It holds locks and a connection for seconds (Topic 02) and ties the payment's fate to the email provider.
Galti mat karna: ek lambe database transaction ke andar provider call karna aur email bhejna. Isse locks aur connection seconds tak pakde rehte hain (Topic 02) aur payment ki kismat email provider se jud jaati hai.
02 Drill: "Our vehicle inventory search page is slow. Fix it."Drill: "Hamara vehicle inventory search page slow hai. Theek karo."
What they're really testing: that you measure before fixing (13), then walk through indexing (01), pagination (08), N+1 queries (09), caching and CDN (04) and read replicas (07), naming the trade-off of each.
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum fix karne se pehle naapte ho (13), phir indexing (01), pagination (08), N+1 queries (09), caching aur CDN (04) aur read replicas (07) se guzarte ho, har ek ka trade-off batate hue.

Say this (opening answer)Aise bolo (opening answer)

First I'd measure, not guess: p50 and p99 for the search endpoint, and a few slow traces to see where the time goes. If most of it is in the database, I'd take the slowest query from the slow query log and run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. A typical fix is a composite index matching the filters and sort, for example rooftop, then make, then price, following the left-prefix rule. Then I'd check for an N+1 pattern, like loading photos with one query per vehicle, and replace it with a join or a single batched query. If the page uses OFFSET pagination and users scroll deep, I'd switch to cursor pagination. Only after that would I add caching for popular searches, and serve vehicle photos from a CDN. Each step I'd verify against the p99, not the average.

Pehle main naapunga, andaaza nahi lagaunga: search endpoint ka p50 aur p99, aur kuch slow traces taaki dikhe time kahan ja raha hai. Agar zyada tar database mein hai, toh slow query log se sabse slow query leke EXPLAIN ANALYZE chalaunga. Aam fix hai filters aur sort se match karta composite index, jaise rooftop, phir make, phir price, left-prefix rule ke hisaab se. Phir N+1 pattern check karunga, jaise har vehicle ke photos ke liye ek alag query, aur usse join ya ek batched query se badlunga. Agar page OFFSET pagination use karta hai aur users bahut neeche scroll karte hain, toh cursor pagination pe switch karunga. Uske baad hi popular searches ke liye caching add karunga, aur vehicle photos CDN se serve karunga. Har step ko main p99 se verify karunga, average se nahi.

The follow-up chainFollow-up chain

  1. "Why not just index every column?" Every index slows every insert and update, and inventory changes constantly; index what the real queries filter and sort on (Topic 01).
  2. "You cached search results. A car gets sold. What does the user see?" Possibly a sold car until invalidation; I'd invalidate on the "sold" event or use short TTLs for search lists, and always read live status on the details page before any action (Topic 04).
  3. "Why is OFFSET slow on page 500?" The database still reads and throws away all the skipped rows; a cursor on the last seen sort key jumps straight there via the index (Topic 08).
  4. "You moved search to a read replica. A dealer adds a car and can't find it." Replication lag; route that dealer's own reads to the primary for a short window after a write (Topic 07).
  1. "Har column pe index kyun nahi?" Har index har insert aur update ko slow karta hai, aur inventory lagataar badalti hai; sirf un columns pe index jin pe asli queries filter aur sort karti hain (Topic 01).
  2. "Tumne search results cache kiye. Ek gaadi bik gayi. User kya dekhta hai?" Shayad invalidation tak biki hui gaadi; main "sold" event pe invalidate karunga ya search lists ke liye chhote TTLs rakhunga, aur kisi bhi action se pehle details page pe live status padhunga (Topic 04).
  3. "Page 500 pe OFFSET slow kyun hai?" Database skip ki hui saari rows padhta hai aur phenkta hai; aakhri dekhi sort key pe cursor index se seedha wahan jump karta hai (Topic 08).
  4. "Search ko read replica pe le gaye. Dealer ne gaadi add ki aur usse dikh nahi rahi." Replication lag; write ke baad thodi der ke liye us dealer ke apne reads primary pe bhejo (Topic 07).
Common mistake: opening with "put Redis in front of it". Caching a slow, unindexed query hides the problem until the cache misses, and then the stampede lands on a database that still can't cope.
Galti mat karna: "iske aage Redis laga do" se shuru karna. Slow, bina index ki query ko cache karna problem ko tab tak chhupata hai jab tak cache miss na ho, aur phir stampede us database pe girti hai jo ab bhi sambhaal nahi sakta.
03 Drill: "Build service-appointment booking so two customers can never get the same slot."Drill: "Service-appointment booking aisa banao ki do customers ko kabhi same slot na mile."
What they're really testing: that you spot the race condition (03), solve it at the database with constraints or locks (02), reject in-memory locks across instances (03, 07), handle double-taps with idempotency (05), and return the right status (08).
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: ki tum race condition pehchaante ho (03), usse database pe constraints ya locks se solve karte ho (02), instances ke paar in-memory locks ko reject karte ho (03, 07), double-tap ko idempotency se handle karte ho (05), aur sahi status lautaate ho (08).

Say this (opening answer)Aise bolo (opening answer)

The danger is a race: two requests both check "is 10am free?", both see yes, and both insert. Checking in application code can't prevent that, so I'd make the database the referee. The simplest strong fix is a unique constraint on the advisor and slot time; the second insert fails, and I return 409 Conflict with a message to pick another slot. If booking involves more steps, like holding a bay and an advisor, I'd lock the slot row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a short transaction. I would not use an in-memory lock, because we run several instances behind a load balancer and each has its own memory. And since users double-tap "Book", the request carries an idempotency key so a retry returns the same booking instead of a 409.

Khatra race ka hai: do requests dono check karti hain "kya 10 baje free hai?", dono ko haan dikhta hai, aur dono insert kar deti hain. Application code mein check karna isse rok nahi sakta, isliye main database ko referee banaunga. Sabse simple strong fix hai advisor aur slot time pe unique constraint; doosra insert fail hota hai, aur main 409 Conflict ke saath doosra slot chunne ka message lautaata hoon. Agar booking mein zyada steps hain, jaise bay aur advisor dono hold karna, toh chhote transaction ke andar SELECT ... FOR UPDATE se slot row lock karunga. In-memory lock use nahi karunga, kyunki hum load balancer ke peeche kai instances chalaate hain aur har ek ki apni memory hai. Aur kyunki users "Book" double-tap karte hain, request ek idempotency key le jaati hai taaki retry ko 409 ki jagah wahi booking mile.

The follow-up chainFollow-up chain

  1. "Would SERIALIZABLE isolation solve it?" Yes, but it costs serialization failures and retries on every conflicting transaction; a constraint or a targeted row lock is cheaper and clearer (Topic 02).
  2. "Optimistic or pessimistic here?" For a popular slot on a Monday morning contention is high, so pessimistic locking or the constraint wins; optimistic versioning suits rare conflicts (Topic 02).
  3. "The reminder SMS the day before: how?" A scheduled job publishes reminder messages to a queue, the worker is idempotent by booking ID, and only one instance runs the scheduler, using a distributed lock or a leader (Topics 03, 06).
  4. "How do you prove it works?" A load test firing many concurrent bookings at one slot: exactly one 201, the rest 409 (Topics 08, 13).
  1. "Kya SERIALIZABLE isolation isse solve karega?" Haan, lekin har conflict wale transaction pe serialization failures aur retries ki keemat hai; constraint ya targeted row lock sasta aur saaf hai (Topic 02).
  2. "Yahan optimistic ya pessimistic?" Monday subah ke popular slot pe contention zyada hai, toh pessimistic locking ya constraint jeetega; optimistic versioning kam conflicts ke liye theek hai (Topic 02).
  3. "Ek din pehle ka reminder SMS: kaise?" Ek scheduled job reminder messages queue pe publish karta hai, worker booking ID se idempotent hai, aur scheduler sirf ek instance chalata hai, distributed lock ya leader se (Topics 03, 06).
  4. "Kaise saabit karoge ki kaam karta hai?" Ek slot pe kai concurrent bookings bhejne wala load test: exactly ek 201, baaki 409 (Topics 08, 13).
Common mistake: "I'll check availability first, then insert." That check-then-act gap is the race itself.
Galti mat karna: "Main pehle availability check karunga, phir insert." Yahi check-then-act ka gap khud race hai.
04 Drill: "You deploy a new version and the error rate jumps from near zero to 5%. You're on call."Drill: "Tumne naya version deploy kiya aur error rate lagbhag zero se 5% ho gaya. Tum on call ho."
What they're really testing: mitigation before diagnosis via rollback (11, 13), then using logs and traces (12, 13), understanding health checks (11), zero-downtime migrations (09), backward-compatible APIs (08) and a blameless post-mortem (13).
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: diagnosis se pehle rollback se mitigation (11, 13), phir logs aur traces ka use (12, 13), health checks ki samajh (11), zero-downtime migrations (09), backward-compatible APIs (08) aur blameless post-mortem (13).

Say this (opening answer)Aise bolo (opening answer)

The error rate jumped right after a deploy, so the deploy is my first suspect, and I'd mitigate before diagnosing: roll back. With blue-green that's an instant switch; with a rolling deploy I'd roll back to the previous image. Once the error rate is back to normal, users are safe and I can investigate calmly. Then I'd group the error logs from the bad window by error type and endpoint, pick one failed request ID and open its trace to see exactly which call failed and why. Finally I'd ask why our pipeline didn't catch it: were the health checks only checking that the process was alive, not that it could actually serve requests? That becomes an action item in the post-mortem.

Error rate deploy ke turant baad uchhla, toh deploy mera pehla suspect hai, aur main diagnosis se pehle mitigate karunga: rollback. Blue-green mein yeh turant switch hai; rolling deploy mein pichli image pe rollback karunga. Error rate normal hote hi users safe hain aur main aaraam se investigate kar sakta hoon. Phir kharab window ke error logs ko error type aur endpoint se group karunga, ek failed request ID uthaunga aur uska trace kholunga taaki dikhe exactly kaunsi call fail hui aur kyun. Aakhir mein poochhunga ki hamari pipeline ne ise kyun nahi pakda: kya health checks sirf yeh dekh rahe the ki process zinda hai, yeh nahi ki woh sach mein requests serve kar sakta hai? Yeh post-mortem mein ek action item banta hai.

The follow-up chainFollow-up chain

  1. "The logs show 'column vehicle_status does not exist'. What happened?" The migration renamed a column while old pods were still running during the rolling deploy. Fix with expand-contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, and only drop the old column in a later release (Topic 09).
  2. "Rollback fails because the migration already ran." That's why migrations must be backward-compatible with the previous code version; expand-contract makes rollback safe (Topics 09, 11).
  3. "Mobile apps on old versions also broke." We removed or renamed a response field; APIs should only add, never remove or rename, and deprecate with notice (Topic 08).
  4. "Readiness or liveness: which would have helped?" Readiness: a check that runs a real dependency query would have kept broken pods out of rotation (Topic 11).
  1. "Logs mein 'column vehicle_status does not exist' hai. Kya hua?" Rolling deploy ke dauraan purane pods chal rahe the aur migration ne column rename kar diya. Expand-contract se fix: naya column add karo, dual-write, backfill, reads switch karo, aur purana column baad ki release mein hi drop karo (Topic 09).
  2. "Rollback fail hota hai kyunki migration chal chuki hai." Isiliye migrations pichle code version ke saath backward-compatible honi chahiye; expand-contract rollback ko safe banata hai (Topics 09, 11).
  3. "Purane versions wali mobile apps bhi toot gayi." Humne response ka koi field hataaya ya rename kiya; APIs sirf add karein, kabhi remove ya rename nahi, aur notice ke saath deprecate karein (Topic 08).
  4. "Readiness ya liveness: kaunsa madad karta?" Readiness: asli dependency query chalane wala check toote hue pods ko rotation se bahar rakhta (Topic 11).
Common mistake: debugging live while 5% of users keep failing. Roll back first; the bug will still be there in the logs to study.
Galti mat karna: jab 5% users fail ho rahe hon tab live debug karna. Pehle rollback karo; bug logs mein padhne ke liye wahin rahega.
05 Drill: "Every confirmed booking must send a confirmation SMS, reliably."Drill: "Har confirmed booking pe confirmation SMS reliably jaana chahiye."
What they're really testing: async design with queues (06), at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers (05, 06), retries, backoff and circuit breakers (12), the dead letter queue (06), and the dual-write problem between the database and the queue (02).
Interviewer asal mein kya check kar raha hai: queues ke saath async design (06), at-least-once delivery aur idempotent consumers (05, 06), retries, backoff aur circuit breakers (12), dead letter queue (06), aur database aur queue ke beech dual-write problem (02).

Say this (opening answer)Aise bolo (opening answer)

I wouldn't call the SMS provider inside the booking request, because if the provider is slow or down, booking would be slow or fail for a reason the customer doesn't care about. Instead, after the booking commits, I publish a "booking confirmed" message to a queue and return 201 immediately. A worker consumes the message and calls the provider. Queues are usually at-least-once, so the same message can arrive twice; the worker records the booking ID it has sent for and skips duplicates, so the customer never gets two texts. If the provider fails, the worker retries with exponential backoff and jitter; after a maximum number of attempts the message moves to a dead letter queue, and we alert when that queue grows.

Main booking request ke andar SMS provider ko call nahi karunga, kyunki agar provider slow ya down hai, toh booking aisi wajah se slow ya fail hogi jiski customer ko parwaah nahi. Iski jagah, booking commit hone ke baad main queue pe "booking confirmed" message publish karta hoon aur turant 201 lautaata hoon. Ek worker message consume karke provider ko call karta hai. Queues aam taur pe at-least-once hoti hain, toh same message do baar aa sakta hai; worker record karta hai ki kis booking ID ke liye bhej chuka hai aur duplicates skip karta hai, taaki customer ko kabhi do texts na milein. Agar provider fail ho, worker exponential backoff aur jitter ke saath retry karta hai; maximum attempts ke baad message dead letter queue mein jaata hai, aur woh queue badhne pe hum alert karte hain.

The follow-up chainFollow-up chain

  1. "The booking committed, then the app crashed before publishing. The SMS never goes." The dual-write problem. Use a transactional outbox: write the message into an outbox table in the same transaction as the booking, and a relay publishes it afterwards (Topics 02, 06).
  2. "The provider has been down for ten minutes." A circuit breaker opens and stops hammering it; messages wait in the queue, which absorbs the backlog, and drain when it recovers (Topics 06, 12).
  3. "Kafka or RabbitMQ?" For simple task delivery with retries and routing, RabbitMQ fits; if many services need to replay the same booking events, Kafka's retained log fits better (Topic 06).
  4. "Cancellation SMS arrived before confirmation." Ordering holds only within a partition; use the booking ID as the partition key so one booking's events stay in order (Topic 06).
  1. "Booking commit hui, phir publish se pehle app crash. SMS kabhi nahi jaata." Dual-write problem. Transactional outbox use karo: booking wale same transaction mein message ek outbox table mein likho, aur ek relay baad mein usse publish karta hai (Topics 02, 06).
  2. "Provider das minute se down hai." Circuit breaker khulta hai aur usse maarna band karta hai; messages queue mein wait karte hain, jo backlog sambhaalti hai, aur provider theek hone pe khaali hoti hai (Topics 06, 12).
  3. "Kafka ya RabbitMQ?" Retries aur routing ke saath simple task delivery ke liye RabbitMQ theek hai; agar kai services ko same booking events replay karne hain, toh Kafka ka retained log behtar hai (Topic 06).
  4. "Cancellation SMS confirmation se pehle pahunch gaya." Ordering sirf ek partition ke andar hoti hai; booking ID ko partition key banao taaki ek booking ke events order mein rahein (Topic 06).
Common mistake: promising "exactly-once delivery". Say at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer, which gives an exactly-once effect.
Galti mat karna: "exactly-once delivery" ka promise karna. Bolo at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumer, jisse exactly-once effect milta hai.
